[Theorem thm.BRW of arXiv:2411.19145, 'On the intersection of critical percolation clusters and other tree-like random graphs'] Let $(\mathcal R_c^i)_{i\ge 1}$ and $(\mathcal R_\infty^i)_{i\ge 1}$, be independent copies of $\mathcal R_c$ and $\mathcal R_\infty$ respectively, on $\mathbb Z^d$, with $d\ge 5$. 
\begin{enumerate}
    \item[(i)] If $d=7$ or $d\ge 9$, then for any $k> \frac d{d-4}$, there exist positive constants $c_1,c_2$, such that for any $t>1$,  
    $$\exp(-c_1\cdot t^{1- \frac 4d})\le \mathbb P(|\mathcal R_c^1 \cap\dots\cap \mathcal  R_c^k|>t) \le \mathbb P(|\mathcal R_\infty^1 \cap\dots\cap \mathcal R_\infty^k|>t) \le  \exp(-c_2\cdot t^{1-\frac 4d}). $$
    \item[(ii)] If $d\in \{5,6,8\}$, then for any $k> \frac d{d-4}$, there exist positive constants $c_1,c_2$, such that for any $t>e$,
    $$\exp(-c_1\cdot t^{1- \frac 4d})\le \mathbb P(|\mathcal R_c^1 \cap\dots\cap \mathcal  R_c^k|>t) \le \mathbb P(|\mathcal R_\infty^1 \cap\dots\cap \mathcal R_\infty^k|>t) \le  \exp\Big(-c_2\cdot (\frac{t}{\log t})^{1-\frac 4d}\Big). $$
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem thm.BRW of arXiv:2411.19145

[Lemma generic decoupling of arXiv:2412.07936, 'Simple Norm Bounds for Polynomial Random Matrices via Decoupling'] For natural numbers $n \geq m$, let ${\bf x} = \{x_i\}^n_{i=1}$ be a sequence of $n$ independent random variables in a measurable space $(S, \mathcal S)$, and let $\{x_i^{(k)}\}^n_{i=1}$, $k = 1, \dots, m$, be $m$ independent copies of this sequence. Let $B$ be a separable Banach space, and let $h_{{\bf i}}: S^m \rightarrow B$ be a measurable function such that ${\mathbb E} (\norm{h_{{\bf i}} (x_{i_1}, \dots, x_{i_m})}) \leq \infty $ for each ${\bf i} \in {\mathcal T}^m_n$. Let $\Phi: [0, \infty) \rightarrow [0,\infty)$ be a convex nondecreasing function such that ${\mathbb E} \Phi (\norm{h_{{\bf i}} (x_{i_1}, \dots, x_{i_m})}) \leq \infty $ for all ${\bf i} \in {\mathcal T}^m_n$. Then, 
$$
{\mathbb E} \Phi \left( \norm{\sum_{{\bf i} \in {\mathcal T}^m_n} h_{{\bf i}} (x_{i_1}, \dots, x_{i_m})} \right) \leq {\mathbb E} \Phi \left( C_m\norm{\sum_{{\bf i} \in {\mathcal T}^m_n} h_{{\bf i}} (x_{i_1}^{(1)}, \dots, x_{i_m}^{(m)})} \right),
$$
where $C_m = 2^m \cdot (m^m-1) \cdot ((m-1)^{(m-1)} - 1) \cdot \ldots \cdot 3.$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Decoupling Inequality, see \cite{PG:book} Theorem 3.1.1

[Proposition pr:Fdim of arXiv:2510.09818, 'On the Fourier dimension of fractional Brownian graphs'] [LL25].
For a generic process $B$, recall that the graph and image measures $\mu_{G}$ and $\nu$ are respectively defined by~(equation mu_G of the paper) and~(equation b2 of the paper).
Suppose for every $q \in \mathbb N$, there exists $C>0$ such that
\begin{enumerate}
\item (vertical bound) $\mathbb E[|\hat{\nu}(\xi_2)|^{2q}]\le C |\xi_2|^{-\gamma_2 q}$ for all $\xi_2 \ne 0$; and
\item (horizontal bound) $\mathbb E[|\hat{\mu}_G(\xi_1,\xi_2)|^{2q}] \le C |\xi_1|^{-\gamma_1 q}$ for all $\xi_1 \ne 0$ and $\xi_2 \in \mathbb R$.
\end{enumerate}
Then $\dim_{\rm F} G(B) \ge \min\{\gamma_1,\gamma_2\}$ a.s. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem thm-extension of arXiv:2411.12623, 'Random signed measures'] Let $\mathcal{R}\subset\hat{\mathcal{S}}$ be any countable ring of bounded Borel sets generating $\mathcal{S}$. Given a collection of random variables $(\eta(U))_{U\in\mathcal{R}}$, there exists a random signed measure $\xi$ on $S$ with $\xi(U) \stackrel{a.s.}{=} \eta(U)$ for all $U\in\mathcal{R}$, iff
	\\ \textnormal{(i)}  $\eta(A\cup B)\stackrel{a.s.}{=}\eta(A)\cup\eta(B)$ for all $A,B\in \mathcal{R}$ disjoint,
	\\ \textnormal{(ii)} $\eta(A_n)\stackrel{a.s.}{\to}0$ as $A_n\downarrow\emptyset$ along $\mathcal{R}$,
	\\ \textnormal{(iii)} $\sup\big\{\sum_{k=1}^{n}|\eta(A_k)|:\, \textnormal{$n\in\mathbb{N}$, $A_k\in\mathcal{R}$ disjoint and\,$A_k\subset A$} \big\}<\infty$ a.s.~for all $A\in\mathcal{R}$.
	\\ In that case, $\xi$ is a.s.~unique. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem thm-extension of arXiv:2411.12623

[Theorem thm.fIForParablic of arXiv:2411.05534, 'Inverse problems for stochastic partial differential equations'] Let
\begin{align} 
    b^{j k}=b^{k j} \in L_{\mathbb{F}}^2\left(\Omega ; C^1\left([0, T] ; W^{2, \infty}(G)\right)\right), \quad j, k=1,2, \cdots, n,
\end{align}
$\ell \in C^{1,3}((0,T)\times G)$ and $\Psi \in C^{1,2}((0,T)\times G)$.
Let $ u $ be an $H^2(G)$-valued continuous Itô process.
Set  $\theta=e^{\ell}$ and $w=\theta u$. Then, for any $t \in[0, T]$ and a.e. $(x, \omega) \in G \times \Omega$,
\begin{align}\notag
    & 2 \theta \Big [\!-\!\sum_{j, k=1}^n \big(b^{j k} w_{x_j}\big)_{x_k}+\mathcal{A} w \Big ]\Big[d u\!-\!\sum_{j, k=1}^n\big(b^{j k} u_{x_j}\big)_{x_k} d t\Big]
    \!+\! 2 \sum_{j, k=1}^n\big(b^{j k} w_{x_j} d w\big)_{x_k}
    \\\notag
    &
     \quad+2 \sum_{j, k=1}^n\Big[\sum_{j^{\prime}, k^{\prime}=1}^n\big(2 b^{j k} b^{j^{\prime} k^{\prime}} \ell_{x_{j^{\prime}}} w_{x_j} w_{x_{k^{\prime}}}-b^{j k} b^{j^{\prime} k^{\prime}} \ell_{x_j} w_{x_{j^{\prime}}} w_{x_{k^{\prime}}}\big)
    \\
    &
     \quad \quad \quad \quad \quad  ~ +\Psi b^{j k} w_{x_j} w-b^{j k}\Big(\mathcal{A} \ell_{x_j}+\frac{\Psi_{x_j}}{2}\Big) w^2\Big]_{x_k} d t
    \\\notag
    &
     =2 \sum_{j, k=1}^n c^{j k} w_{x_j} w_{x_k} d t+\mathcal{B} w^2 d t+d\Big(\sum_{j, k=1}^n b^{j k} w_{x_j} w_{x_k}+\mathcal{A} w^2\Big)
     -\theta^2 \mathcal{A}(d u)^2,
    \\ \notag
    &
     +2\Big[-\sum_{j, k=1}^n\big(b^{j k} w_{x_j}\big)_{x_k}+\mathcal{A} w\Big]^2 d t
      -\theta^2 \sum_{j, k=1}^n b^{j k}\big(d u_{x_j}+\ell_{x_j} d u\big)\big(d u_{x_k}+\ell_{x_k} d u\big)
\end{align}
where
\begin{align}
    
    \left\{\begin{aligned}
        & \mathcal{A} \triangleq-\sum_{j, k=1}^n\big(b^{j k} \ell_{x_j} \ell_{x_k}-b_{x_k}^{j k} \ell_{x_j}-b^{j k} \ell_{x_j x_k}\big)-\Psi-\ell_t, \\
        & \mathcal{B} \triangleq 2\Big[\mathcal{A} \Psi-\sum_{j, k=1}^n\big(\mathcal{A} b^{j k} \ell_{x_j}\big)_{x_k}\Big]-\mathcal{A}_t-\sum_{j, k=1}^n\big(b^{j k} \Psi_{x_k}\big)_{x_j}, \\
        & c^{j k} \triangleq \sum_{j^{\prime}, k^{\prime}=1}^n\Big[2 b^{j k^{\prime}}\big(b^{j^{\prime} k} \ell_{x_{j^{\prime}}}\big)_{x_{k^{\prime}}}-\big(b^{j k} b^{j^{\prime} k^{\prime}} \ell_{x_{j^{\prime}}}\big)_{x_{k^{\prime}}}\Big]-\frac{b_t^{j k}}{2}+\Psi b^{j k}.
        \end{aligned}\right.
\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma EI of arXiv:2607.05418, 'On the Group Randomness of 0-1 Real Sequences from Binary Linear Codes'] Let $A,B$ be $p \times n$ real matrices with $\mathrm{rk}(B)=1$ and $p \leq n$. Let $G=AA^T$ and $G'=(A+B)(A+B)^T$ be the Gram matrices of $A$ and $A+B$ respectively. If $\lambda_1 \geq \lambda_2 \geq \cdots \geq \lambda_p$ and $\lambda_1' \geq \lambda_2' \geq \cdots \geq \lambda_p'$ are the eigenvalues of $G$ and $G'$ respectively, then for $1 \leq i \leq p$,
    $$\lambda_{i+1} \leq \lambda_i' \leq \lambda_{i-1}$$
    where by convention $\lambda_{p+1}=0$ and $\lambda_0=+\infty$.

body:
Let (X, Sigma, mu) be a finite measure space and let F be a subset of L^1(mu). Then F is relatively weakly compact in L^1(mu) if and only if F is bounded and uniformly integrable. By the Eberlein-Smulian theorem the same condition characterises relative weak SEQUENTIAL compactness, so every bounded uniformly integrable sequence has a subsequence converging weakly in L^1 to some limit in L^1.
mu finite (or sigma-finite with the tightness condition added).
Uniform integrability is the crucial half: boundedness in L^1 alone does NOT give weak compactness - the standard counterexample is an approximate identity, bounded in L^1, with no weakly convergent subsequence because its limit is a Dirac mass and not a function.

[Proposition 1 (Size biasing across the family) of arXiv:2608.13631, 'The classical discrete laws near the mode:\\ complete local expansions for the negative bi'] Let $P_\theta(k)$ denote one of the four laws in this paper, with mean $\mu(\theta)$.  Then
	\begin{equation}
		k\,P_\theta(k)=\mu(\theta)\,P_{\theta^\downarrow}(k-1),
	\end{equation}

	\[

		\Poi(\lambda) & \lambda & \lambda\\[2pt]
		\NB(r,p) & rq/p & (r+1,p)\\[2pt]
		\Hyp(N,K,n) & nK/N & (N-1,K-1,n-1).
	\end{array}
	\]
	The negative binomial is in the failures parametrisation,
	\[
		P(k;r,p)=\binom{k+r-1}{k}p^rq^k .
	\]

[Lemma 36 of arXiv:2605.31471, 'Convergence Rates of Continuous-Time Random Walks to Time-Fractional Diffusions with Unbou'] Fix $\alpha\in\R$ and $r\in\N_0$.  Let Assumptions
        \ref{asm:weighted-regular}, \ref{asm:rw}, \ref{asm:rw-bounded}, and
        \ref{asm:rw-weighted-stability} hold.  Then there are constants
        $C_{\alpha,r},q_{\alpha,r}>0$ and $h_0>0$ such that, for all
        $0<h\le h_0$,
        \[
            \|U_hg\|_{\alpha,r}
            \le
            e^{q_{\alpha,r}h}\|g\|_{\alpha,r},
            \qquad
            g\in\cC^r_{\alpha,\infty}(\cX),
        \]
        and
        \[
            \left\|
                \left(\frac{U_h-I}{h}-L\right)f
            \right\|_{\alpha,r}
            \le
            C_{\alpha,r}h\|f\|_{\alpha,r+4},
            \qquad
            f\in\cC^{r+4}_{\alpha,\infty}(\cX).
        \]

body:
[Lemma lem:raw-arrays-controlled-compensators-paper of arXiv:2606.08683, 'Exact Fourier dimensions of dyadic Mandelbrot cascades under minimal integrability'] Assume \(\mathcal G_n^{\mathrm{pre}}\) holds. For 
\(d\in\mathfrak D_{\xi,n}^{\mathrm{osc}},\)
define
\[
D^{\mathrm{pre}}_{\xi,d,n}
=
\sum_{\ell=0}^{m_{\xi,d}-1}
\sum_{I\in\mathcal D_\ell^\circ}
\sum_{\substack{J\in\mathcal D_{\ell+1}^\circ\\J\subset I}}
D_{J,n},
\]
and
\[
D^{\mathrm{post}}_{\xi,d,n,L}
=
\sum_{\ell=m_{\xi,d}}^{L-1}
\sum_{I\in\mathcal D_\ell^\circ}
\sum_{\substack{J\in\mathcal D_{\ell+1}^\circ\\J\subset I}}
D_{J,n}.
\]
Then
\[
F^{\mathrm{pre}}_{\xi,d}
=
F^{\mathrm{pre,cap}}_{\xi,d,n}
+
D^{\mathrm{pre}}_{\xi,d,n},
\]
and, for every \(L>m_{\xi,d}\),
\[
F^{\mathrm{post}}_{\xi,d,L}
=
F^{\mathrm{post,cap}}_{\xi,d,n,L}
+
D^{\mathrm{post}}_{\xi,d,n,L}.
\]
Moreover,
\[
\lvert D^{\mathrm{pre}}_{\xi,d,n}\rvert
\le
\mathfrak C^{\mathrm{pre}}_{\xi,d,n},
\qquad
\lvert D^{\mathrm{post}}_{\xi,d,n,L}\rvert
\le
\mathfrak C^{\mathrm{post}}_{\xi,d,n,L}.
\]
If the absolute post-bin compensator is finite, then the signed post-bin compensator converges as 
\(L\to\infty,\) 
and the same identity holds for the limiting post-bin arrays.

Martingale differences need not satisfy E exp(it sum X_k)=E product E[exp(it X_k)|F_{k-1}]. With independent fair signs U,W, X_1=U and X_2=(1+U)W are martingale differences, but at t=pi/2 the two sides are -i and 0. Conditional centering is not independence.

[Theorem 28 (Derivative estimates through surgery) of arXiv:2608.25971, 'Positive \texorpdfstring{$\tau$}{tau}-bi-Ricci curvature and Mean curvature flow with surg'] Fix an integer $m_0\geq2$ and choose the standard replacement so that
  Lemma~\ref{lem:standard-replacement} holds with parameter $\vartheta_n/2$
  and derivative order $m_0$.  Assume that the first surgery time is not
  earlier than $\tau_nR^2$.  Then there exists $C=C(n,\tau,\alpha,m_0)<\infty$  
  such that every surgically modified flow satisfying the hypotheses of
  Theorem~\ref{thm:surgical-cylindrical-estimates} obeys
  \begin{align}
    |\nabla A|^2
    &\leq
    C(H^4+R^{-4}),
    \\
    |\nabla^2A|^2
    &\leq
    C(H^6+R^{-6})
    
  \end{align}
  for every $t\geq\tau_nR^2$.

  More generally, for every pair of nonnegative integers $a,b$ with
  $2a+b\leq m_0$,
  \begin{equation}
    |\nabla_t^a\nabla^bA|^2
    \leq
    C_{a,b}
    \left(
    H^{4a+2b+2}+R^{-4a-2b-2}
    \right),
  \end{equation}
  where $ C_{a,b}
  =  C_{a,b}(n,\tau,\alpha,m_0,a,b)$.  
  At a surgery time the derivatives are understood one-sidedly.

AUTHOR PROOF; independent audit pending. Let G be any finite undirected forest, o,b any vertices, and A any nonempty vertex set. For independent Bernoulli edge states with arbitrary edge probabilities in [0,1], P(o connects to b)>=P(o connects to A)min_{a in A}P(a connects to b). There is also a deterministic a_star in A such that {o connects to A,a_star connects to b} is contained in {o connects to b,o connects to A} in every configuration. Consequently P(o connects to b,o connects to A)>=min_{a in A}P(o connects to A,a connects to b) holds for any edge-state law. The product inequality's coefficient 1 is sharp. Connection means an open path; overlap of terminals and relays, disconnected forests, and o=b are allowed.

Own work draft; proof (unaudited), no novelty established. For the equal-weight teacher q_a=(1/3)sum_j N(a E diag(1,3)u_j,I_d), d>=2, and canonical equal-weight identity-covariance mixture-score population DDPM risk R_a(nu) with noisy student means M=a nu, the C06 strict bad branch nu_b(a) has a dimension-uniform local slow-noise tracking property. There exist fixed positive a_cut,r,eta,c such that for any nondecreasing schedule 0<a_k<=a_{k+1}<=a_cut with a_{k+1}-a_k<=eta a_k^7, unit-step GD nu_{k+1}=nu_k-grad_nu R_{a_k}(nu_k), initialized within r a_i^2 of nu_b(a_i), stays within r a_k^2 of nu_b(a_k). If noise is held at a_f<=a_cut eventually, it converges to the strict non-global minimum nu_b(a_f). The capped schedule a_{k+1}=min(a_f,a_k+eta a_k^7) takes at most 1+(a_f-a_i)/(eta a_i^7) changing-noise steps. This is a local high-noise continuation application, not a general tracking novelty, full annealed random-start failure theorem, empirical guarantee or resolution of well-separated K=3 learning. The distinction between noisy-mean and underlying-location GD is explicit: unit noisy-mean GD corresponds to underlying-location step size a^(-2), while this statement uses unit underlying-location steps.
d>=2 and the specified equal-weight anisotropic spherical teacher
canonical mixture-score population DDPM risk; persistent underlying locations nu with noisy means a nu
unit-step GD on nu, not unit-step GD on noisy means M
initial distance <=r a_i^2 and monotone increments <=eta a_k^7 inside a fixed sufficiently small range

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:a0c99588640e91190f9fda873e3c781fe1d44cec3a6431156037dab7192f5142","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/a0/a0c99588640e91190f9fda873e3c781fe1d44cec3a6431156037dab7192f5142.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:de1724eba3c38a828716f6d349e408c59c49bdd88bc1e6627745242f9ea4a390","bundle_entry_key":"t309-c20","bundle_id":"population.t309-anisotropic-slow-noise-tracking-draft","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"Gaussian mixture learning and diffusion objectives","draft":"w721/bundle_013.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.learning:gaussian-mixture-ddpm-anisotropic-slow-noise-bad-branch-tracking","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"Own work draft; T309-w721-C20 v1; proof (unaudited); Target 2 route 12 auxiliary continuation lemma.

# Slow noise changes can track the anisotropic bad branch at sufficiently high noise

This is a local continuation application of C06's bad minimum, not a new general tracking theorem. It fixes the parameterization before changing noise. It does not cover a jump to moderate or low noise, a complete annealing schedule, or general well-separated K=3 learning. No novelty finding is asserted; all analytic inputs remain unaudited.

## Statement

Use the teacher q_a=(1/3)sum_j N(a E diag(1,3)u_j,I_d), d>=2, E^T E=I_2. Parameterize the student's three noisy means as M=a nu, where nu is a d-by-3 matrix of underlying unit-scale locations. Write R_a(nu) for the canonical mixture-score population single-time DDPM excess risk. In particular changing a while holding nu fixed changes the noisy means.

C06 supplies a smooth bad critical branch nu_b(a)=-E diag(1,3)U+O(a^2), up to a fixed label permutation. There are dimension-independent positive a_cut,r,eta,c,C such that the following holds. For any nondecreasing schedule

    0<a_k<=a_{k+1}<=a_cut,
    a_{k+1}-a_k<=eta a_k^7,                     (1)

apply unit-step GD to the underlying locations at the current noise:

    nu_{k+1}=nu_k-grad_nu R_{a_k}(nu_k).         (2)

If ||nu_0-nu_b(a_i)||<=r (a_i)^2, where a_i is the schedule's first value, then

    ||nu_k-nu_b(a_k)||<=r a_k^2                  (3)

at every step. If the schedule eventually holds at a_f<=a_cut, the iterates converge to the strict bad minimum nu_b(a_f). The cutoff a_cut denotes a small fixed high-noise amplitude, not the original unsmoothed noise endpoint.

One explicit admissible schedule is a_{k+1}=min(a_f,a_k+eta a_k^7), followed by holding at a_f. For fixed a_f, its changing-noise phase has at most 1+(a_f-a_i)/(eta a_i^7) steps from initial a_i>0. Thus inverse-polynomial initial amplitudes permit a polynomial-length slow continuation phase. This is conditional on the local initialization in (3), not a complete random-initialization runtime statement.

## 1. Uniform spectral and derivative estimates

Near C06's branch, its bounded-location expansion in orthogonal centroid/shape coordinates is

    R_a=a^2||b||^2
       +a^4[||ZZ^T-D||^2/4-b^T ZZ^T b]+a^6 H_a(b,Z),
    D=E diag(1,9)E^T.

The coordinates (b,Z) are a fixed linear transformation of nu with singular values bounded above and below independently of d. All fixed finite orders of derivatives of H_a are bounded on this fixed neighborhood by C06's finite-span Gaussian argument. The leading order-a^2 term is quadratic, so

    ||D_nu^3 R_a||<=C a^4.                     (4)

The upper Hessian bound is ||D_nu^2 R_a||<=C a^2 there.

At the bad critical point, C06's eliminated-centroid block has order a^2 positive curvature. After eliminating it, the covariance and perpendicular blocks have order a^4 positive curvature, and the angular Schur complement has order a^6 positive curvature, with leading coefficient inherited from H''(pi/3)=603/4. The covariance-angular mixed block is O(a^6); its inverse-normal Schur correction is O(a^8). The centroid mixed block is O(a^6), whose Schur correction is O(a^10). The eliminating triangular coordinate maps and the critical-point chart Jacobian have uniformly bounded norms and inverses. Consequently there exist c_0,C_0>0 such that

    c_0 a^6 I <= D_nu^2 R_a(nu_b(a)) <= C_0 a^2 I. (5)

Here the lower bound includes every free-centroid and perpendicular direction, not just the angular restriction. C06 supplies those normal positivities; no invariant covariance section is assumed.

Choose a sufficiently small fixed r. By (4), Hessian displacement on the Euclidean ball B_a={||nu-nu_b(a)||<=r a^2} is at most C r a^6. Choosing C r<=c_0/2 gives

    c a^6 I <= D_nu^2 R_a(nu) <= C' a^2 I     (6)

throughout B_a. Shrink a_cut so C' a_cut^2<=1. This justifies a shrinking Euclidean convexity ball; an arbitrary fixed-radius ball would not follow from the different curvature scales.

C06's smooth implicit reductions extend to a=0 after division by the specified powers of a. Parity and uniqueness make the branch even in a, and its second derivative is bounded near zero. Therefore

    ||nu_b'(a)||<=C_b a.                       (7)

In particular the O(a^2) branch displacement is not used alone to infer a derivative bound; smoothness, parity and the differentiated implicit equations supply it. All constants above can be chosen independently of d by the same bounded finite-span directional estimates as C06.

## 2. A contraction at fixed noise

Let T_a(nu)=nu-grad R_a(nu). The straight segment from nu_b(a) to any point of B_a stays inside B_a. The fundamental theorem of calculus writes

    T_a(nu)-nu_b(a)=(I-H_avg)(nu-nu_b(a)),

where H_avg is the segment-average Hessian. By (6), it is symmetric with eigenvalues in [c a^6,1]. Hence

    ||T_a(nu)-nu_b(a)||<=(1-c a^6)||nu-nu_b(a)||. (8)

This uses the fixed Euclidean metric in the underlying locations. It is not a flow approximation or a bound obtained by multiplying conditional event probabilities.

## 3. The moving branch

Let h=a_{k+1}-a_k>=0. Shrink eta or a_cut so eta a_cut^6<=1, hence a_{k+1}<=2a_k. By (7),

    ||nu_b(a_{k+1})-nu_b(a_k)||<=2 C_b a_k h.

With e_k=||nu_k-nu_b(a_k)||, (8) yields

    e_{k+1}<=(1-c a_k^6)e_k+2 C_b a_k h.       (9)

Choose eta<=c r/(4 C_b), interpreting the condition as unnecessary if C_b=0. On the boundary e_k<=r a_k^2, equations (1),(9) give

    e_{k+1}<=r a_k^2-c r a_k^8+2 C_b eta a_k^8
             <=r a_k^2-(c r/2)a_k^8
             <=r a_{k+1}^2.

Induction proves (3); it also keeps every update segment in the relevant convexity ball. Once a_k=a_f forever, (8) gives geometric convergence to nu_b(a_f). For the explicit capped schedule, every nonfinal increment is at least eta a_i^7, proving the displayed bound on the number of changing-noise steps.

## 4. Parameter conversion and scope

At fixed a, M=a nu implies grad_nu R_a=a grad_M F_a. Thus physical noisy-mean unit GD is equivalent to

    nu_+=nu-a^(-2)grad_nu R_a,

whereas (2) is equivalent to physical noisy-mean GD with step size a^2 before changing a. Across noise levels this statement uses one persistent nu; it does not hold M fixed and silently relabel it. For original mixture means R E A u_j with fixed R, write original student locations Theta=R nu and use OU factor exp(-t)=a/R. Unit GD on nu is GD on Theta with step size R^2; any different learning rate must be converted explicitly.

C19's fixed-noise physical-GD trajectory converges on its bad event and therefore eventually enters the local ball needed here. However no polynomial bound for that preliminary waiting time is supplied by C19, and the change of learning rate must be specified before composing those algorithms. Accordingly this lemma does not claim a polynomial-time random-start failure theorem for a full schedule.

The substantive conclusion is limited: sufficiently slow noise reduction does not force escape while a stays inside this small-amplitude range. What happens when a approaches order one remains unpaid. The next step is an explicit stability or bifurcation certificate for the bad branch outside the local a->0 regime, or a scheduled escape proof that uses that change.

## Checks

Exact checks cover the learning-rate chain rule, the a^8 contraction/branch-drift balance, and the rational constants in the induction. They do not certify the analytic Schur bounds, third-derivative domination, branch regularity or independent validity of C06. Rung: proof (unaudited). Let $\Omega_k\subseteq J^{(k)}$ be uniform of size $r(k)$, and let $\delta_k\downarrow0$ satisfy
\[
\delta_k \frac{n_k}{k}\to\infty,

If $|B_1^{(k)}|\ge\delta_k n_k$, then with probability $1-o(1)$, the graph $G^{(k)}[\Omega_k]$ contains distinct degree-one right vertices $j,j'$ with the same unique left neighbor.

[Lemma Regularity of the area functional of arXiv:2602.08591, 'The Yang--Mills measure on compact surfaces as a \\ universal scaling limit of lattice gau'] For $\theta_0\in [0,2\pi)$, let us denote by $\square(c,\theta_0)$ the eventually broken flow rectangle 
\[ \{ x\in \mathcal{S}: \theta(x)\in [0,\theta_0], f(x)\leqslant c    \} .\]
Then for all interval $I_i$, the map
\begin{align*}
\theta\in I_i\mapsto \int_{\square(r,\theta)  } \sigma    
\end{align*}
belongs to $W^{1,p}(I_i)$ for all $p\in \mathbb{N}$ and is $C^\infty$ in the interior of $I_i$. 
\EN{Is $r$ here fixed or what ? I feel we need a similar result in $(r,\theta)$ to be able to bound the integral
\[\int_{[\min(f),\max(f)]^2\times I^2} \frac{ \left(\int_{\square(r_1,r_2,\theta_1,\theta_2)} \sigma(r,\theta)\mathrm{d} rd\theta \right) ^p }{ \vert r_1-r_2 \vert^{1+2\alpha p}\vert \theta_1-\theta_2 \vert^{1+2\alpha p}  }  \mathrm{d} r_1\mathrm{d} r_2\mathrm{d}\theta_1\mathrm{d}\theta_2\]
in the next section.}\\
\EN{I think what we need is the following. 
Let
\[F:(r,\theta)\in [\min(f),\max(f)]\times I_i\mapsto F(r,\theta)=\int_{\square(r,\theta)  } \sigma \in  \mathbb{R}  \],
then $F$ is in $\mathcal{W}^{\alpha;p}_r\mathcal{W}^{\alpha;p}_\theta([\min(f),\max(f)]\times I_i,\mathfrak{g})$}
Moreover, the map
\begin{align*}
(r,\theta)\in [\min(f),\max(f)]\times I_i \longmapsto  \partial_\theta \left(\int_{\square(r,\theta)  } \sigma \right),   
\end{align*}
is partially $C^\infty$ of the $r$ variable on 
\[[\min(f),\max(f)]\times I_i \setminus \{(f,\theta)(\mathrm{Crit}(f)_1)\}\] and given 
\[r\in [\min(f),\max(f)]\setminus \mathrm{Critical}\,\ \mathrm{values}(f),\]
it is $C^\infty$ in $\theta\in \mathrm{int}(I_i)$ with at worst $\log$ blow--up at the endpoints of $I_i$.

Under ALL C016 raw-input Gaussian-kernel GP task-law, bounded attention-plus-residual-MLP class and comparator hypotheses (iid fresh-GP tasks, exogenous joint input design and length, independent N(0,s) observation noises, d>=1,n>=0,ell,s,epsilon>0, raw cube inputs, original unclipped target posterior, context labels clipped only in predictor encoding), fix class P,W_max,Lambda,U,0<v0<=v1,V and all approximation constants before sampling. Let alpha in (0,1), eta>0 and xi>=0. Put C=0.5log(v1/v0)+U^2/v0, K=4(C+V/v0), Q=1/(2v0)+(U+sqrt(V))/v0+(U^2+V)/v0^2, gamma=eta/[4Q(1+2/alpha)], q=max(1,ceil(2W_max Lambda/gamma)), u=log(4/alpha)+Plog(q+1), m0=max(1,ceil(2048K^2u/eta^2),ceil(16Ku/eta)). For every integer m>=m0, any measurable xi-approximate global empirical minimizer has fresh original-task expected forward KL <=epsilon+eta+xi, with probability >=1-alpha. Markov on the nonnegative sample-average output-loss sensitivity gives population/empirical cover transfer <=gamma Q(1+2/alpha)=eta/4, with failure probability <=alpha/2. The fixed-cover Chernoff bound, which separately requires iid tasks and a finite exponential loss moment, costs the other alpha/2; the explicit sample requirement makes beta_m<=eta/4. Thus uniform risk deviation <=eta/2, and ERM excess <=eta+xi. This is a standard composition with an explicit m-independent cover tolerance, not a novelty or efficient-training claim. Saved C007 and C013-C016 dependencies remain unaudited. The 54 exact rational budget checks are finite algebra checks, not a universal or probabilistic certificate. Kind: bound. Target: none. Status: proof (unaudited). No novelty claim.

The sample requirement can be stated without m inside the covering tolerance. The change is to bound average loss sensitivity rather than the largest observed query. All approximation and task-law assumptions of C016 remain in force.

## 1. Statement
Fix C016's approximation parameters, bounded class, P, W_max, Lambda, U, v0,v1 and V before sampling. In particular v0=s>0, V=s+1 and 0<v0<=v1. Let alpha in (0,1) and let eta>0 be the desired ESTIMATION excess-risk allowance, distinct from the approximation allowance epsilon. Put

    C=0.5 log(v1/v0)+U^2/v0,
    K=4(C+V/v0),
    Q=1/(2v0)+(U+sqrt(V))/v0+(U^2+V)/v0^2,
    gamma=eta/[4 Q(1+2/alpha)],
    q=max(1,ceil(2 W_max Lambda/gamma)),
    u=log(4/alpha)+P log(q+1),
    m0=max(1,ceil(2048 K^2 u/eta^2),ceil(16 K u/eta)).     (1)

For every integer m>=m0, with probability at least 1-alpha over iid training tasks, every measurable xi-approximate global empirical minimizer satisfies

    E_fresh W KL(P_W || h_theta_hat(c_B(W)))
                     <= epsilon+eta+xi.                 (2)

The target posterior and task law are the ORIGINAL, unclipped ones of C016. The predictor input alone clips context labels at C016's fixed B. The class is exactly C016's counted raw-input normalized ReLU attention plus residual MLP class, with its explicit parameter radius and fixed output clips. No new optimization algorithm or independent audit is asserted. Dependencies C007 and C013-C016 remain unaudited.

Unlike C016's maximum-query formulation, every quantity in (1) is fixed before selecting m. There is no claim of an optimal sample requirement or efficient architecture size.

## 2. Hypotheses and named inequalities
The C016/C007 loss-envelope argument supplies, for every fixed predictor, a nonnegative normalized Gaussian log loss with a finite exponential moment and

    log E exp(z(loss-E loss)) <= 8 K^2 z^2/(1-2K|z|),
                  |z|<1/(2K).

IID tasks and this mgf, not just finite variance, are the hypotheses for the Chernoff bound. The bound is exponential: for a fixed predictor the probability that its empirical risk differs from its risk by more than

    beta_m=4sqrt(2) K sqrt(u/m)+2K u/m

is at most 2exp(-u). The fixed C014 cover has J_cover=(q+1)^P members and output radius gamma. Union over that cover therefore costs at most 2J_cover exp(-u)=alpha/2.

The other event uses Markov's inequality. Its hypothesis is a nonnegative integrable random variable. Its conclusion is an upper bound P(Z>b)<=E Z/b, which is a reciprocal, not exponential, threshold bound. Independence is NOT needed for this event.

## 3. Average sensitivity event
On the fixed output rectangle the loss is Lipschitz in the two output coordinates, in their maximum norm, with random constant

    L(Y)=1/(2v0)+(|Y|+U)/v0+(|Y|+U)^2/(2v0^2).

As established in C007 and used in C016, the Gaussian query marginal has E|Y|<=sqrt(V), EY^2<=V. The ordinary scalar inequality (|Y|+U)^2<=2Y^2+2U^2 gives E L(Y)<=Q. These are marginal statements: no independence of Y from the context or predictor is assumed.

Let Lbar_m=(1/m)sum_i L(Y_i). It is nonnegative and E Lbar_m<=Q. Markov's inequality gives

    P(Lbar_m>2Q/alpha)<=alpha/2.                        (3)

On the intersection of this event's complement and the fixed-cover concentration event, choose a covering predictor g for any theta. This choice can depend on theta but the finite cover itself was fixed before sampling. The population loss difference is <=gamma E L(Y)<=gamma Q, and the empirical loss difference is <=gamma Lbar_m<=2gamma Q/alpha. Hence uniformly in theta,

    |R(theta)-Rhat(theta)|
       <= beta_m+gamma Q(1+2/alpha)
       = beta_m+eta/4.                                 (4)

The two events jointly have probability at least 1-alpha by a union bound; independence between them is not asserted. No maximum-query cutoff or union over query extremes is needed in this transfer.

## 4. Explicit sample budget and excess risk
All constants in (1) are positive: v0,V,eta>0, Q>=1/(2v0)>0, K>0, W_max>=1, Lambda>0, alpha in (0,1) and u>0. Thus every division and square root below is valid. For m>=m0,

    m eta^2 >= 2048 K^2 u,
    m eta >= 16 K u.

Since all terms are nonnegative, the first inequality implies

    (4sqrt(2)K sqrt(u/m))^2
       =32 K^2 u/m <= eta^2/64,

and therefore 4sqrt(2)K sqrt(u/m)<=eta/8. The second gives 2K u/m<=eta/8. No sign reversals occur: all reciprocals divide strictly positive quantities. Thus beta_m<=eta/4 and (4) is at most eta/2.

An xi-approximate empirical minimizer then satisfies

    R(theta_hat)
       <= Rhat(theta_hat)+eta/2
       <= inf_theta Rhat(theta)+xi+eta/2
       <= inf_theta R(theta)+xi+eta.

Subtract the same expected conditional Gaussian entropy as in C016 and use its comparator KL<=epsilon. This proves (2). Fresh-task expectations are conditional on the trained predictor; the event is uniform over the whole parameter class.

## 5. Checks and limitations
The rerunnable scripts/check_C017_budget.py checks 54 exact rational parameter combinations, including small/large eta and small confidence, the ceiling sample requirement, the squared square-root allocation, the linear allocation and the transfer allocation. The log is logs/C017_budget.json. These are finite algebraic checks, not a certificate for all parameters or for probability statements. The universal inequalities are the analytic argument in Sections 2-4.

Boundary checks: m0>=1; eta is strictly positive and may be arbitrarily large or small; alpha cannot be zero or one under the stated confidence convention; n=0 is already allowed by C016 and leaves all statistical constants finite since s>0. Query dependence within a task is permitted and unused; dropping it changes nothing. Independence BETWEEN tasks is used in the loss-mgf product. Without it, repeated copies of one nonconstant random loss need not concentrate as m grows. The finite exponential moment is used for the Chernoff rate; an arbitrary finite-variance heavy-tailed loss cannot be substituted there. The finite first moment of L alone is sufficient for (3). Positive variance floor and bounded mean outputs are used by the derivative envelope. Fixed cover and data-independent class are used by the finite union bound. These checks concern the precise statement, not a claim that every assumption is necessary for every possible theorem.

A Lean budget statement is written in proofs/C017_budget.lean. It certifies nothing yet: it is UNVERIFIED, and no compiler or dependency audit is asserted. Mathlib checking was previously measured above this worker's 1 GB allowance; no repeat heavy check is launched. Its intended mathematical content is only the final scalar allocation, not the Gaussian mgf, Markov argument, covering theorem, or task-law composition. The analytic rung is proof (unaudited), not Lean-checked or independently checked proof.

Let (X, Sigma, mu) be a measure space, f measurable, and d_f(t) = mu({|f| > t}). (a) Chebyshev / Markov: for 0 < p < infinity and t > 0, d_f(t) <= t^{-p} int_X |f|^p dmu. (b) Layer cake: for 0 < p < infinity, int_X |f|^p dmu = p int_0^infinity t^{p-1} d_f(t) dt, both sides possibly infinite. More generally, if phi: [0, infinity) -> [0, infinity) is nondecreasing, absolutely continuous on compacts with phi(0) = 0, then int_X phi(|f|) dmu = int_0^infinity phi'(t) d_f(t) dt. (c) Consequently ||f||_{L^{p,infinity}} <= ||f||_{L^p}, and an L^p bound can always be recovered from a bound on the distribution function.
(X, Sigma, mu) is a measure space
f is Sigma-measurable
0 < p < infinity
for the general form: phi nondecreasing, absolutely continuous on compact subsets of [0, infinity), phi(0) = 0

			\[ I_{j,k}\subset\mathbb N, \qquad 1\le j\le d,\quad 1\le k\le L,
			\]
			and an absolute constant $c_d$ (only depending on $d$)  with the following properties. \\	
			First, every \(i\in I_{j,k}\) satisfies
			\begin{equation}
				i\asymp_{\beta,d} n.
			\end{equation}
			Second, for each \(k\),
			\begin{equation}
				|\left\{(i_1,\ldots,i_d)\in I_{1,k}\times\cdots\times I_{d,k}:
				i_1+\cdots+i_d=s\right\}|
				\asymp_d H^{d-1}.
			\end{equation}
			Third, suppose that for every \(1\le k\le L\) one chooses a tuple
			$(i_{1,k},\ldots,i_{d,k}) \in I_{1,k}\times\cdots\times I_{d,k}$
			such that
			\begin{equation}
			i_{1,k}+\cdots+i_{d,k}=s.
			\end{equation}
			Then, whenever $(k_1,\ldots,k_{d-1})\succ(k_d,\ldots,k_d)$,
			one has
			\begin{equation}
			i_{1,k_1}+\cdots+i_{d,k_d}\ge s+c_d H.
			\end{equation}

body: For a subset A of a topological space X: the interior int(A) is the union of all open sets contained in A (the largest open set inside A); the closure cl(A) is the intersection of all closed sets containing A - which is closed, being an arbitrary intersection of closed sets, contains A, and lies inside every closed superset of A, hence is the smallest closed set containing A; the boundary is cl(A) minus int(A), equivalently cl(A) intersect cl(X\A). Then A is open iff A = int(A) and closed iff A = cl(A). Point characterization: x is in cl(A) iff every open neighborhood of x meets A (if not, X\cl(A) is an open neighborhood of x missing A; conversely a neighborhood U of x missing A makes X\U a closed superset of A avoiding x). The closure operator satisfies the Kuratowski axioms - cl(empty)=empty, A subset of cl(A), cl(cl(A))=cl(A), cl(A union B)=cl(A) union cl(B) - and these four axioms on a set determine a unique topology whose closed sets are exactly the closure-fixed subsets.
title: Closure, Interior, and Boundary

body: [Definition def:MRF of arXiv:2412.07710, 'An H-theorem for a conditional McKean-Vlasov process related to interacting diffusions on '] Let $G = (V, E)$ be a finite graph. Let $(Y_v)_{v \in V}$ be a random element of $(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^d)^V$ with distribution $P \in \mathcal{P}((\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^d)^V)$. Then  $Y = (Y_v)_{v \in V}$, or equivalently its distribution $P$, is said to be a \emph{first-order Markov random field} (abbreviated as 1-MRF) on $(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^d)^V$ if $Y_A$ is conditionally independent of $Y_{(\bar{A})^c}$ given $Y_{\partial A}$, for every finite set $A \subset V$. Similarly,  $Y = (Y_v)_{v \in V},$ or equivalently its distribution $P$, is said to be a \emph{second-order Markov random field} (abbreviated as 2-MRF) on $(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^d)^V$ if $Y_A$ is conditionally independent of $Y_{(A \cup \partial^2 A)^c}$ given $Y_{\partial^2 A}$.
title: Markov random field

Then, there exists $C>0$ such that the following bound holds:
\[
\vert\esp [W_{n}^{-\alpha}\ind_{E_{n}} ] - 1 \vert \leq C\Big(\frac{1}{n} + A(a_n)\Big)

body: In set theory, the constructible universe (or Gödel's constructible universe), denoted by $L,$ is a particular class of sets that can be described entirely in terms of simpler sets. $L$ is the union of the constructible hierarchy $L_{\alpha }$. It was introduced by Kurt Gödel in 1938, who proved that the constructible universe is an inner model of ZF set theory, and also that the axiom of choice and the generalized continuum hypothesis are true in the constructible universe. This shows that both propositions are consistent with the basic axioms of set theory, if ZF itself is consistent. Since many other theorems only hold in systems in which one or both of the propositions is true, their consistency is an important result.

body: Let $M$ predictors produce, on $n$ calibration cases with vector-valued targets $y_i \in \mathbb{R}^D$, the per-case error vectors $e_{im} \in \mathbb{R}^D$ (member $m$'s prediction minus $y_i$). For one output coordinate $d$ write $e_i^{(d)} \in \mathbb{R}^M$ for the vector of the $M$ members' errors on that coordinate. The ordinary error covariance is $\Sigma_E^{(d)} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i (e_i^{(d)} - \bar e^{(d)})(e_i^{(d)} - \bar e^{(d)})^T$. The error covariance in the per-sample relative metric is the same average with each case weighted by the inverse squared norm of its target, $$\Sigma_E^{\mathrm{rel},(d)} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i \frac{(e_i^{(d)} - \bar e^{(d)}_{w})(e_i^{(d)} - \bar e^{(d)}_{w})^T}{\|y_i\|^2}, \qquad \bar e^{(d)}_w = \frac{\sum_i e_i^{(d)}/\|y_i\|^2}{\sum_i 1/\|y_i\|^2}.$$ It is the covariance whose minimum-variance portfolio $w = \Sigma^{-1}\mathbf{1}/(\mathbf{1}^T\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf{1})$ minimises the calibration value of the objective $\frac{1}{n}\sum_i \|\hat y_i - y_i\|^2/\|y_i\|^2$ restricted to that coordinate, i.e. the squared version of the mean per-sample relative $L^2$ error that emulator benchmarks report, rather than the unweighted squared error that ordinary least squares minimises. Its spectrum is typically far more heavy-tailed than the ordinary one, because the cases with the smallest $\|y_i\|$ carry weights orders of magnitude larger than the rest.

[Thm 18 of arXiv:2605.05986, '\bf Convergence rate of the occupation measure of { classes of ergodic processes toward th'] Let $(Y_t)_{t\ge0}$ denote the stationary one-dimensional fractional Ornstein-Uhlenbeck  process solution to:
$$ dY_t=-\lambda Y_t dt+\sigma dB_t^H,$$
where $\lambda$ and $\sigma$ are positive numbers. Then, for any $H\in(0,1)$, $\AUNgamma$ holds for any $q>0$, with $\pi_t=\nu$ (where $\nu$ denotes the-first marginal of-the invariant distribution of $(Y_t)_{t\ge0}$), $\beta=1/2$ and  
$$\gamma=\begin{cases} \frac{1}{2}&\textnormal{if $H<1/2$,}\\
1-H &\textnormal{if $H>1/2$}.
\end{cases}
$$
Thus,  
$$\big\| {\cal W}_p(\nu_t,\nu) \big\|_p\lesssim t^{-\frac{1}{p}(\frac 12\wedge\left(1-H\right))}.$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Own work draft, proof (unaudited), classical counting application with novelty unverified. Fix unit probe q, theta in (0,pi/2], ell=d-1>=2 and N independent isotropic Gaussian covariates. A teacher is w=cos(theta)q+sin(theta)u with u uniform on the unit sphere in q-perp, and labels are noiseless signs. Any learner outputting a unit linear-classifier normal from the full labeled pool, q, theta and independent randomness has prior-average expected Gaussian test error at least sin(theta)*(2*(e*max(1,N/ell))^ell)^(-1/(ell-1))/(2*pi). An affine arrangement has at most sum_{j=0}^ell binomial(N,j)<=(e*max(1,N/ell))^ell label patterns, and each output captures latitude prior mass at most (delta/sin(theta))^(ell-1) for angular tolerance delta<=sin(theta)/2. The union bound proves the claim. For a rotation-equivariant learner the expected bound holds for each fixed teacher-probe pair. Hence if N/(d-1)->beta>0, liminf expected error is at least sin(theta)/(2*pi*e*max(1,beta)). Threshold max-margin is rotation equivariant, so an exponential ORIGINAL-pool envelope is impossible at fixed nonzero theta. The bound does not rule out an exponential retained-data regime or determine its crossover. No independent audit or novelty claim.

Let g: {-1, 1}^n -> {-1, 1}. Then Var(g) = I(g) if and only if g is constant or g = +-x_i for some i. Equivalently, for f: {0, 1}^n -> {0, 1} with flip influence I_flip(f) = sum_i P(f(X) != f(X with bit i flipped)) under the uniform measure, I_flip(f) = 4 Var(f) if and only if f is constant or f is the indicator of a half-cube {x_i = 0} or {x_i = 1}. A direct recursive certificate: with D(f) = I_flip(f) - 4 Var(f), restricting coordinate i to 0 and 1 gives D(f) = (D(f_0) + D(f_1))/2 + Var(f_1 - f_0) with every term nonnegative, so D(f) = 0 iff D(f_0) = D(f_1) = 0 and f_1 - f_0 is constant.

body: The characteristic polynomial of an n x n matrix A is p(lambda) = det(A - lambda I), a degree-n polynomial whose roots are the eigenvalues of A. Its coefficients are basis-independent (similar matrices share it): the coefficient of lambda^{n-1} is -trace(A) and the constant term is det(A), so the sum of eigenvalues is the trace and their product is the determinant.
title: Characteristic Polynomial

body:
[Theorem 32 (one-shot) of arXiv:2606.22611, 'Upper and Lower Bounds on Expected Soft Maxima\\of Gaussian Processes'] Let $X = (X_t)_{t\in T}$ be a centered subgaussian process
with a finite index set $T$. Let $\tau$ be a random element of $T$ jointly distributed with $X$, such that $P_\tau=\nu$.
Then 
\begin{align*}
\Ex{X_\tau} \lesssim \Delta + \int_0^\Delta 
\Big(\sM_{\nu}^*(\epsilon) \wedge \sqrt{I(X ; \tau) }\Big) \dif \epsilon,
\end{align*}
where, as before, $\Delta$ denotes the diameter of $(T,d)$. If $X$ is a Gaussian process, 
then there exists a probability measure $\mu\in \eP(T)$, such that 
\begin{align*}
\eF_\beta(X;\mu_\beta^*) + \Delta
&\gtrsim \sup_{t\in T}\int_0^\Delta 
 \Big(\sM_{\delta_t}(\mu,\epsilon)\wedge \beta \epsilon\Big) \dif \epsilon
\end{align*}
In particular,
\begin{align*}
\Ex X_{\uptau_\beta^*}+ \Delta \gtrsim 
\sup_{\nu\in\eP(T)}\int_0^\Delta 
\Big(\sM_\nu^*(\epsilon)\wedge
\sqrt{I(X ; \uptau_\beta^*) }\Big) \dif \epsilon.
\end{align*}
title: one-shot

[Lemma stablifting of arXiv:2605.28430, 'Limit theory for Lipschitz-localized statistics in random geometric models'] Let \(\mathcal{P}\) be a simple, stationary point process on \(\mathbb{R}^{d}\) with bounded
(reduced) Palm intensity function, as in~(equation bdedreduced of the paper).
Let \(\Psi=\Psi(\cdot)\) be a stabilizing interaction graph on finite windows with
respect to~\(\mathcal{P}\), in the sense of Definition~(d:stabilizing-graph of the paper).
Assume that the Gibbs specification~(equation eqn:gibbs of the paper) satisfies averaged weak
spatial mixing on~\(\Psi\) with respect to~\(\mathcal{P}\), as in
Definition~(d:ssm-pp of the paper).
Then for all $p \in \mathbb{N}$ there are fast decreasing functions  $\varphi_p$ and constants such that 

\begin{align} 
\sup_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \sup_{x_1,\ldots,x_p \in W_n} d_{\textnormal{BL}, \bk x1p}(V_{\bk x1p}(\Psi(\mathcal{P}_n)), V_{\bk x1p}(\Psi(\mathcal{P}_n \cap B_r(\bk x1p))))  \leq 2\varphi_p(r), \ r > 0
\end{align}
and for all $l \in \{1,\ldots,p-1\}$ and $x_1,\ldots,x_p\in\mathbb{R}^d$ such that  $0< r < d(\bk{x}{1}{l},\bk{x}{l+1}{p})$, we have 

\begin{align}

& 
d_{\textnormal{BL},\bk{x}{1}{p}}
\left(V_{\bk x1p}(\Psi(\mathcal{P}_n \cap B_r(\bk x1p))),
\left(V_{\bk x1l}(\Psi(\mathcal{P}_n \cap B_r(\bk x1l))), V_{\bk x{l+1}p}(\Psi(\mathcal{P}_n \cap B_r(\bk x{l +1}p)))
\right)\right)
\;\le\; 2\varphi_p(r),
\end{align}

where $V_{\bk x1l}(\Psi(\mathcal{P}_n \cap B_r(\bk x1l))), V_{\bk x{l+1}p}(\Psi(\mathcal{P}_n \cap B_r(\bk x{l+1}p)))$ are conditionally independent (given $\mathcal{P}_n$) spin vectors with laws $\pi_{\bk x1l}$ and $\pi_{\bk x{l+1}p}$ induced respectively by graphs $\Psi(\mathcal{P}_n \cap B_r(\bk x1l))$ and $\Psi(\mathcal{P}_n \cap B_r(\bk x{l+1}p))$.

The above   bound also holds under the stronger total variation distance.
title: Fast  \BL~cluster-localization of spins  on stabilizing graphs

body:
[Definition 5 of arXiv:2609.02105, 'Contact fundamental forms and \\ adjoint varieties'] Let $\fh = \fh_1 + \fh_2$ be a graded Heisenberg algebra.  Let $U(\fh) = \oplus_{k \geq 0} U_k(\fh)$ be its  universal enveloping algebra with the grading induced by the grading of $\fh$ and let $U(\fh)^* = \oplus_{k \geq 0} U_k(\fh)^*$ be its graded dual.
We can identify $U(\fh)^*$ with the space of polynomial functions on the Heisenberg group $\sH$ of $\fh$ by regarding $U(\fh)$ as the space of left-invariant differential operators on $\sH$ (see Remark \ref{r.jet}). Let $\iota:\fh_2\hookrightarrow U_2(\fh)$ be the natural inclusion and let $\rho_2:=\iota^*:U_2(\fh)^*\to\fh_2^*$ be the restriction map.  
 A finite-dimensional graded subspace $$S = \oplus_{k \geq 0} S^k \subset U(\fh)^*, S^k \subset U_k(\fh)^*,$$ is called a {\em contact symbol system} on $\fh$,
if $S^0 = \C, S^1 = \fh_1^*$, $\rho_2(S^2)=\fh_2^*$, and $S$ is preserved under the operation of right-invariant vector fields on $\sH$.  The {\em rank} of a contact symbol system $S$ is ${\rm rk}(S):=\max\{k\mid S^k\ne0\}.$
title: Definition 5 of arXiv:2609.02105

[Definition def:delgd of arXiv:2606.02472, 'Correlated uniform attachment trees'] For $K\in \N$, $\delta\in (0,1)$, and $c_1\geq 1$,  we say a tree $T$ on vertices $\{0,\ldots, n\}$  is $(K,\delta, c_1)$-good if
    \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
      \item $\sum_{ \delta K/2-1< k \leq n} \mathbbm{1}_{\left\{ F_{T}(k) \geq 0.4 n \right\} } = 0$,
        \item $\sum_{k=0}^{n} \mathbbm{1}_{\left\{F_{T}(k) \geq n/(c_1 K) \right\} } \leq \ceil{(c_1+\delta)K} - \delta K/2$, and
        \item $\sum_{k=0}^{K-1} \mathbbm{1}_{\left\{ F_{T}(k) \geq n/(c_1 K) \right\} } \geq  ( c_1 (1-e^{-1/c_1})- \delta/2)K$.
        \end{enumerate}
title: Definition def:delgd of arXiv:2606.02472

[Lemma lem:velocity-conjugacy of arXiv:2607.00149, '\bf Uniform-in-time Propagation-of-Chaos for\\ Stein Variational Gradient Descent'] Let $\rho_H=H_\#\widetilde\rho$.  Then, writing $\widetilde v_{\widetilde \rho}$ for the SVGD velocity at $\widetilde \rho$ for potential $\widetilde V$ and kernel $\widetilde K$, and $ v_{\rho_H}^H$ for the velocity at $\rho_H$ for potential $V_H$ and kernel $K_H$, we have
\begin{equation}
        v_{\rho_H}^H(H(y))=J(y)\widetilde v_{\widetilde\rho}(y).
\end{equation}
Consequently, if $Y_t$ solves the base characteristic equation
\[
        \dot Y_t=\widetilde v_{\widetilde\rho_t}(Y_t),
\]
then $X_t:=H(Y_t)$ solves the transformed characteristic equation
\[
        \dot X_t=v_{\rho_t^H}^H(X_t),
        \qquad \rho_t^H=H_\#\widetilde\rho_t.
\]

Let Ω ⊂ R^n be open and F: Ω × R × R^n → R continuous. (i) If u ∈ C^1(Ω) satisfies F(x,u(x),Du(x)) = 0 for every x ∈ Ω, then u is a viscosity solution. (ii) Conversely, if u ∈ C(Ω) is a viscosity solution and u is differentiable at a point x0 ∈ Ω, then F(x0,u(x0),Du(x0)) = 0; if u is only a viscosity subsolution then F(x0,u(x0),Du(x0)) ≤ 0, and if only a supersolution then ≥ 0. (iii) Consequently a locally Lipschitz viscosity solution satisfies the equation pointwise at almost every point of Ω. The converse of (iii) is false: an almost-everywhere solution need not be a viscosity solution.

F continuous
in (i): u ∈ C^1(Ω) and the equation holds at every point
in (ii): u continuous and differentiable at the single point x0
in (iii): u locally Lipschitz (to invoke Rademacher)

[Lem 36 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] The following functions are $C_6$-Lipschitz, with $C_6 = 2/\iota$:
    \begin{enumerate}[(a)]
        \item  $z \mapsto m^{-1}(1/z)$, on $(0,+\infty)$.
        \item  $\gamma \mapsto g(\gamma^2)$, on $[0,+\infty)$.
        \item  $\gamma \mapsto \beta_\star(\gamma^2)$, on $[0,+\infty)$.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{proof}
    A routine calculation and application of Lemma~\ref{l:fp-m-fns-conversion} implies
    \[
        \frac{d}{dz} m^{-1}(1/z) = \frac{1/z^2}{m_2(m^{-1}(1/z))}
        \le \frac{1/z^2}{\iota / z^2} = \frac{1}{\iota}\,.
    \]
    This proves part~\eqref{i:fp-m-inv-lipschitz}.
    Since $m$ is strictly decreasing, and $\beta_\star \ge \beta_{
    \min}$, we also have, for $\gamma > 0$,
    \[
        \frac{d}{d\gamma} g(\gamma^2) 
        = 2\gamma m(\beta_\star(\gamma^2))
        \le 2\gamma m(\beta_{\min}(\gamma^2))
        = 2\gamma m(s_2(1/\gamma^2))
        \le \frac{2}{\iota^{1/2}}\,,
    \]
where the final inequality is by Lemma~\ref{l:fp-m-fns-conversion}.
This shows that $\gamma \mapsto g(\gamma^2)$ is $2/\iota^{1/2}$-Lipschitz on $(0,+\infty)$, and the estimate extends to $[0,+\infty)$ since $g$ was defined to be continuous on $[0,\infty)$ (see the comments below \eqref{e:freeprob.g.of.gamma}). 
    This proves part~\eqref{i:fp-g-sq-lipschitz}. For part~\eqref{i:fp-betast-sq-lipschitz}, it suffices to prove that the function
    \[
        \gamma \mapsto \beta_{\min}(\gamma^2)
        = s_2\bigg(\frac1{\gamma^2}\bigg)
    \]
    is $O(1)$-Lipschitz on $[0,+\infty)$. Similarly as above, a routine calculation and application of Lemma~\ref{l:fp-m-fns-conversion} shows that at any $\gamma > 0$, 
    \[
        \frac{d}{d\gamma} 
        s_2\bigg(\frac1{\gamma^2}\bigg)
        = \frac{1/\gamma^3}
            {m_3(s_2(1/\gamma^2))}
        \le \frac{1/\gamma^3}{\iota / \gamma^3}
        = \frac{1}{\iota}\,.
    \]
This shows that $\gamma \mapsto \beta_{\min}(\gamma^2)$ is $1/\iota$-Lipschitz on $(0,+\infty)$, and the estimate extends to $[0,+\infty)$ since the function $\beta_{\min}$ was defined to be continuous on $[0,\infty)$ (again we refer to the comments below \eqref{e:freeprob.g.of.gamma}). 
This proves part~\eqref{i:fp-betast-sq-lipschitz}.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
Let Omega in R^n be open, L = -div(A grad u) + b.grad u + c u uniformly elliptic with A measurable and b, c in L^infinity(Omega), and f in L^2_loc(Omega). Put B[u,phi] = integral_Omega ( sum_{i,j} a^{ij} D_j u D_i phi + (b.grad u) phi + c u phi ) dx. A function u in H^1_loc(Omega) = W^{1,2}_loc(Omega) is a weak solution of Lu = f in Omega if B[u,phi] = integral_Omega f phi dx for every phi in C_c^infinity(Omega); a weak subsolution (Lu <= f) if B[u,phi] <= integral f phi for every phi in C_c^infinity(Omega) with phi >= 0; a weak supersolution (Lu >= f) if B[u,phi] >= integral f phi for every such phi >= 0. By density the test class extends to phi in H^1(Omega) with compact support in Omega (phi >= 0 for the one-sided notions), and, when u in H^1(Omega) and f in L^2(Omega), to all phi in H^1_0(Omega) (nonnegative ones for the one-sided notions). A right-hand side in H^{-1}(Omega), e.g. f = f_0 + sum_i D_i f_i with f_0, f_i in L^2, is paired as <f,phi> = integral (f_0 phi - sum_i f_i D_i phi). If a^{ij} in C^1 and u in C^2, u is a weak solution iff it is a classical solution (integrate by parts). The energy class u in H^1_loc is part of the definition; distributional solutions with less integrable gradients need not enjoy any of the regularity theory.
Omega open in R^n
A measurable and uniformly elliptic; b, c in L^infinity(Omega)
u in H^1_loc(Omega)
f in L^2_loc(Omega), or more generally in H^{-1}
title: Weak Solution, Subsolution and Supersolution of a Divergence-Form Elliptic Equation

\begin{equation*}
\sqrt X\,
\mathbb E_{X,Y}

=
G\left(\frac{P^k}{X}\right)+o_k(1),

locally uniformly in $P^k/X$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem kpartW2 of arXiv:2607.00149, '\bf Uniform-in-time Propagation-of-Chaos for\\ Stein Variational Gradient Descent'] Let Assumption~(ass:Wass of the paper) hold and suppose the joint
initial law of the particles is exchangeable. For fixed \(k\ge1\), define
the random \(k\)-fold empirical occupation measure
\[
        \widehat\mu_T^{N,k}
        :=
        \frac1T\int_0^T (\mu_t^N)^{\odot k}\,dt,
        \qquad
        \overline{\mu^{\otimes k}}_T
        :=
        \frac1T\int_0^T \mu_t^{\otimes k}\,dt,
\]
where
\[
(\mu_t^N)^{\odot k}
:=
\frac{1}{(N)_k}
\sum_{\substack{1\le i_1,\ldots,i_k\le N\\
i_1,\ldots,i_k\ {\rm distinct}}}
\delta_{\bigl(x_{i_1}^N(t),\ldots,x_{i_k}^N(t)\bigr)},
\qquad
(N)_k:=N(N-1)\cdots(N-k+1).
\]
Let \(W_2^{(k)}\) be the Wasserstein distance on \((\mathbb R^d)^k\)
associated with the quadratic product cost
\(
        d_k(x,y)^2:=\sum_{\ell=1}^k \|x_\ell-y_\ell\|^2 .
\)
Then, with $\mathfrak r=\mathfrak r(d,\nu)$ as in~(equation eq:rdef of the paper), there is \(C_k<\infty\)
such that, for all sufficiently large \(N\),
\[
\sup_{T>0}
\mathbb P\left(
W_2^{(k)}
\left(
\widehat\mu_T^{N,k},
\overline{\mu^{\otimes k}}_T
\right)
>
(\log N)^{-r/4}
\right)
\le
C_k(\log N)^{-\min\{r/4,\beta_{\rm init}\}} .
\]

\[
\beta_d:=1+(d-1)^2.

Let $G=(I,J,M)$ be $C_4$-free and suppose every right vertex has degree at most $d$. Fix $j_\star\in J$, set $I_\star=N_G(j_\star)$, and assume that for every $i\in I_\star$ there is a \hyperref[def:c4-witness-block]{\textcolor{PineGreen}{\emph{reservoir}}}{}

\mathcal R_i\subseteq N_G(i)\setminus\{j_\star\}

For fixed finite t in sparse critical Z4 parking, full-space SRW Green weighted sums over Euclidean radius R have variance (16p/pi^2)log R+O_{t,p}(1) for the signed field S_t=A_t-H_t, equal to the initial iid coefficient. For exploration mean K_t=A_t-q V_t, q=p/(1-p), the coefficient is (8/pi^2)[2p-(1-q)h_t]. The exact finite-R variance difference equals (1-q)h_t sum G_R^2. Initial scenery at R=sqrt(T) has variance (8p/pi^2)log T+O_p(1). Assumptions: Z4; fixed finite t; 0<p<1/2 sparse critical iid law; Euclidean spatial cutoff, full-space discrete-time nearest-neighbor G; C19 signed susceptibility; C23 exploration posterior; R->infinity with t fixed for evolved fields. Limitation: No uniform t-dependent error or simultaneous t,R asymptotic for evolved fields; no nearest-distance conclusion. Novelty: KNOWN stationary convolution/covariance methods; UNCHECKED exact parking coefficients. Status: independently checked proof. The model is discrete-time uniform nearest-neighbor synchronous parking on Z^d with stationary capacity-one holes; A_t(x) is the active-particle count and H_t(x) the unfilled-hole indicator. In the sparse law eta(x) is initially +1 and -1 each with probability p, and zero otherwise, independently across sites. Here h_t=E H_t(0), V_t(x) is the indicator of no initial active particle and no arrival through t, and W_R(X)=sum_{|y|_2<=R}G(y)X(y), with G=sum_{n>=0}p_n.

Status: proof (unaudited). Novelty: KNOWN stationary convolution/total
covariance methods; UNCHECKED these exact parking/exploration coefficients.

Fix a finite time t in the sparse critical parking process on Z^4,
0<p<1/2. Put S_t=A_t-H_t, q=p/(1-p), V_t as in C23,
K_t=A_t-q V_t=E[S_t|E_t], and h_t=E H_t(0). Let G be the full-space
discrete-time uniform nearest-neighbor SRW Green kernel, and

    W_R(X)=sum_{|y|_2<=R}G(y) X(y).

The three fields X=eta,S_t,K_t have mean zero. As R tends to infinity,

    Var W_R(eta)=(16p/pi^2)log R+O_p(1),
    Var W_R(S_t)=(16p/pi^2)log R+O_{t,p}(1),
    Var W_R(K_t)=(8/pi^2)[2p-(1-q)h_t]log R+O_{t,p}(1).

Moreover at every finite R,

    Var W_R(S_t)=Var W_R(K_t)+(1-q)h_t sum_{|y|<=R}G(y)^2.

This is a fixed-t, growing-R assertion. Its t-dependent error is not
controlled for a simultaneous choice such as R=sqrt(t). For the initial
iid eta only, the first error is t-independent, so R=sqrt(T) directly
gives initial variance (8p/pi^2)log T+O_p(1). The raw individual fields
do not have finite full-space Green-potential variance in d4.

## 1. Susceptibilities and posterior covariance

Finite propagation makes the covariances of S_t and K_t finitely
supported; all relevant counts have finite second moments at fixed t.
C19 gives sum_z Cov(S_t(0),S_t(z))=2p. C23 gives conditional mean K_t
and conditional covariance

    Cov(S_t(0),S_t(z)|E_t)=q(1-q)V_t(0)1{z=0}.

On averaging, q E V_t(0)=h_t, so total covariance yields

    Cov(S_t(0),S_t(z))=Cov(K_t(0),K_t(z))+(1-q)h_t 1{z=0}.

Thus K_t susceptibility is 2p-(1-q)h_t. The initial eta susceptibility
is Var eta(0)=2p. Weighting the same covariance identity immediately
proves the exact finite-R variance decomposition.

## 2. The full-space Green-square coefficient

Lawler--Limic Theorem 4.3.1, including its SRW bipartite convention, gives

    G(y)=(2/pi^2)|y|_2^(-2)+O(|y|_2^(-4)).

Squaring and summing, the error is summable, while
sum_{1<=|y|<=R}|y|^(-4)=2pi^2 log R+O(1), by unit-cube comparison
with the radial integral. Consequently for G_R=G 1_{B_R^Euclidean},

    ||G_R||_2^2=(8/pi^2)log R+O(1).

For each fixed displacement z,

    sum_y G_R(y)G_R(y+z)=||G_R||_2^2
                                  -(1/2)||G_R-shift_z G_R||_2^2
                         =(8/pi^2)log R+O_z(1).

To justify the uniform-in-R shift bound, on the common cutoff region at
large |y| the Green asymptotic gives a difference at most
C_z |y|^(-3)+C|y|^(-4), whose square is summable in dimension four.
The cutoff mismatch is in a shell of width O_z(1), with O_z(R^3) sites
and squared kernel O(R^(-4)), so it contributes O_z(1/R). The finitely
many sites near the origin cause only a finite additional constant.

## 3. Finite-range covariance summation

For a mean-zero stationary field X with finitely supported covariance
c_X(z), expansion of the finite weighted sum gives

    Var W_R(X)=sum_z c_X(z) sum_y G_R(y)G_R(y+z)
      =(8/pi^2)[sum_z c_X(z)]log R+O_X(1).

There are only finitely many displacements here, so Step 2's individual
error bounds can be summed. Substitute the three susceptibilities from
Step 1 to obtain all displayed coefficients.

## Scope and source

This identifies a real logarithmic variance in conserved source charges,
not just a Gaussian comparison. It does not show a parking pair bound
fails at mean spacing, because the evolved-field errors have no uniform
t estimate. It also does not prevent the charge difference eta-S_t from
having a well-defined potential; its cross-covariances must be retained.

posterior, Lawler--Limic Theorem 4.3.1 for the normalized Green asymptotic,

body: In graph theory, the handshaking lemma is the statement that, in every finite undirected graph, the number of vertices that touch an odd number of edges is even. For example, if there is a party of people who shake hands, the number of people who shake an odd number of other people's hands is even. The handshaking lemma is a consequence of the degree sum formula, also sometimes called the handshaking lemma, according to which the sum of the degrees equals twice the number of edges in the graph. Both results were proven by Leonhard Euler in his famous paper on the Seven Bridges of Königsberg that began the study of graph theory.
title: Handshaking lemma

[Thm 16 (\cite{MR51275}; see also \cite{MR317760}) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $A$ and $C$ be real matrices of dimensions $m\times n$ and $q\times n$ respectively. Let $b$ and $d$ denote vectors in $\R^m$ and $\R^q$ respectively. Define
	\begin{align*}
	S_{A,C}(b,d)
	&\equiv \Big\{x\in\R^n: Ax\le b, Cx=d\Big\}\,,\\
	F(A,C)
	&\equiv\Big\{(b,d) \in\R^{m+q}:
	S_{A,C}(b,d) \ne\emptyset\Big\}\,.\end{align*}
Let $(b,d)\in F(A,C)$, so that 
$S_{A,C}(b,d)$ is nonempty. If $\hat{x}$ is any point in $\R^n$, then there is a point $\bar{x}\in S_{A,C}(b,d)$ with
	\[
	\|\bar{x}-\hat{x}\|_2
	\le \sigma(A,C)\left\|
	\begin{pmatrix}
	(A\hat{x}-b)_+\\ C\hat{x}-d
	\end{pmatrix}\right\|\,,
	\]
where $\sigma(A,C)$ is a finite number depending only on $A,C$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: \cite{MR51275}; see also \cite{MR317760}

[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] Any Hilbert space $H$ has an orthonormal basis $\{e_i\}_{i\in I}$, which is by definition a set of vectors whose span is dense in $H$, and which satisfy
$$<e_i,e_j>=\delta_{ij}$$
with $\delta$ being a Kronecker symbol. The cardinality $|I|$ of the index set, which can be finite, countable, or uncountable, depends only on $H$, and is called dimension of $H$. We have
$$H\simeq l^2(I)$$
in the obvious way, mapping $\sum\lambda_ie_i\to(\lambda_i)$. The Hilbert spaces with $\dim H=|I|$ being countable, such as $l^2(\mathbb N)$, are all isomorphic, and are called separable.

THE HYPOTHESIS THAT GETS DROPPED IN QUOTATION: the symmetric two-point (Bernoulli a/b) law is load-bearing. The survey records why: 'This specific distribution was needed to take advantage of Talagrand's influence inequality on the hypercube.' Any statement of the form 'BKS proved sublinear variance for FPP' without the two-point qualifier is a misquotation of the 2003 paper; the general-distribution version is Damron-Hanson-Sosoe, a decade later.
CONSTANT DEPENDENCE: C depends only on a, b and d - not on v and not on the direction.
VERSION TRAP: the arXiv comment on v5 reads 'Replaced theorem 2 (which was incorrect) by a new theorem'. Cite v5 or the journal version; a citation resolved to an earlier version can carry a withdrawn Theorem 2.
SOURCE: arXiv:math/0203262v5; Ann. Probab. 31 (2003), 1970-1978. (The arXiv journal-ref field prints '31:197-1978', a typo for 1970-1978; the survey bibliography gives 1970-1978.) Hypothesis set read in the authors' own abstract, and corroborated in Auffinger-Damron-Hanson, '50 years of first passage percolation', arXiv:1511.03262v2 (AMS University Lecture Series 68, 2017), tex line 1170, and in the abstract of arXiv:2604.01214 ('...used hypercontractivity to obtain an improvement of a factor of log n when passage times take two values with equal probability').
VERIFICATION STATUS: theorem-checked-against-source. The v5 abstract states the hypotheses, the conclusion and the constant dependence in full; the proof was not read.
title: Benjamini-Kalai-Schramm (2003): for first-passage percolation on Z^d with d > 1 whose edge weights are i.i.d. and TWO-VALUED - omega_e equal to a or to b with probability 1/2 each, for fixed 0 < a < b < infinity - the distance from the origin to a vertex v with |v| > 2 satisfies Var dist_omega(0,v) <= C |v| / log |v|, where C = C(a,b,d). The theorem as published is NOT a general-distribution result: the symmetric two-point law is a hypothesis, not an illustration.

body: Lemma (campaign status: proved): Number the batches in deletion order, let h_s be the witness form at batch s, and choose a pivot p_s from the witness matching pair in B_s. Then h_s(p_s) != 0 and h_s(p_t) = 0 for t > s (tag 33), because every pair in a later batch was still present when h_s was chosen so h_s cannot meet either of its endpoints. Hence T = (h_s(p_t))_{1<=s,t<=m} (34) is triangular with nonzero diagonal, and B' = {h_1,...,h_m} union {x_j : j not in {p_1,...,p_m}} (35) is an admissible coordinate basis. Notes: S6: 'This simultaneous exchange lemma is completely correct.' What it does NOT say is that another row is close, modulo a low-rank space, to a member of B'; triangularity concerns only the m-by-m pivot minor of the selected witnesses.

  suppose that for all $\gamma \in \mathcal P$,
  \begin{align}
    
    \sum_{\gamma' \nsim \gamma}  |w_{\gamma'} |e^{\alpha_1(\gamma') + a_2(\gamma')}  &\le \alpha_1 (\gamma) \,.
  \end{align}
  Then the cluster expansion for the polymer model defined by
    any finite subset of polymers converges absolutely. Moreover, for
  all $\gamma \in \mathcal P$ we have
  \begin{equation}
    
    \sum_{\substack{X \in \mathcal X :\\ \exists \gamma' \in X, \gamma' \nsim
        \gamma }}   |w(X) | \prod_{\gamma' \in X} e^{\alpha_2(\gamma')} \le
    \alpha_1(\gamma) \,. 
  \end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: Record of outside readings, 14 October 2026, of Y. Shmalo, The storage capacity of the Ising perceptron: verification of the outstanding numerical conditions (arXiv:2607.11010; repository yspennstate/ising-perceptron-capacity, tag v1.0). The first reader (a Claude model, fresh clone) found it correct with fixable gaps. F1: the third clause of Ding and Sun's Condition 1.2, that S_*'(lambda) has a positive limit as lambda -> 1, is asserted in Ding-Sun (journal p. 704) but not proved there, and the paper credits it to their endpoint calculation. F2: A = inf_s B is used as a C^2 function at 0 without the implicit-function step. F4: phi_v(0) = phi_v'(0) = 0 in Lemma 4.4 is asserted without computation. F5: two reductions in the Huang sweep are argued in prose only. The reader's own floating-point recomputation gives alpha_* = 0.833078599740, inside the stated interval, and every Ding-Sun sign matches. A follow-up proof closes F1, F2 and F4: S_*'(lambda) = -K_0/(2 c_lambda) + O(1 + log(1/(1-lambda))) with c_lambda = sqrt((1-lambda)/(1+lambda)) and K_0 < 0, so S_*'(lambda) -> +infinity as lambda -> 1, uniformly along the fixed-point curve in a box containing Ding-Sun's; A''(0) = -alpha E[E(xi)^2 (1 - E'(xi))] < 0 by the implicit function theorem; and phi_v(0) = phi_v'(0) = 0 is computed in every ray direction. That fix has had one review and is not yet in the posted repository; F5 remains open. The second reader (a Codex model), still auditing the Huang code and certificates on 14 October, found M. Stojnic, Binary perceptrons capacity via fully lifted random duality theory (arXiv:2312.00073, November 2023), which obtains the same value 0.8330786 at zero threshold from the fully lifted random duality theory at its second (stationarized) lifting level, in agreement with the replica-symmetry-breaking prediction; the reader judged that derivation to rest on assumptions not verified there. The repository's paper does not cite it. Not refereed.
title: Outside readings of the Ising perceptron capacity proof (arXiv:2607.11010), 14 October 2026: correct with fixable gaps, three of them since closed; earlier derivation by Stojnic

[Theorem thm:localization-modulus of arXiv:2609.03264, 'Certified Spherical MUSIC for 3D Localization under Adversarial Subspace Perturbations'] Under (equation eq:oracle-base-feasibility of the paper), every nonempty
\(\mathfrak X\subset
\mathfrak X_{s,\kappa}(\gamma,\overline\mu)\) satisfies
\begin{equation}

    \mathfrak R_{\mathfrak X}(\eta)
    \leq
    \frac{2}{\sqrt3c_\eta}\frac{\eta}{\kappa},
    \qquad 0\leq\eta<\eta_\star,
\end{equation}
where  $$  c_\eta
    :=\frac23-\overline C_2-\left(\frac{2}{\sqrt5}+\frac23\right)\eta.$$

Suppose, in addition, that there exist
\(X_0=\{{\bm x}_1,\ldots,{\bm x}_s\}\in\mathfrak X\), a unit vector
\({\bm v}\in\mathbb R^3\), and \(t_0>0\) such that
\begin{equation}

    X_t:=\{{\bm x}_1+t{\bm v},{\bm x}_2,\ldots,{\bm x}_s\}\in\mathfrak X,
    \qquad 0\leq t\leq t_0,
    \qquad t_0\leq\frac{\delta_{X_0}}4.
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}

    \frac{\sqrt{3(1-\bar\mu)}}2\frac{\eta}{\kappa}
    \leq
    \mathfrak R_{\mathfrak X}(\eta)
    \leq
    \frac{2}{\sqrt3c_\eta}\frac{\eta}{\kappa}
\end{equation}
whenever
\begin{equation}

    0<\eta<\eta_\star,
    \qquad
    \eta\leq\frac{\kappa t_0}{\sqrt{3(1-\overline\mu)}}.
\end{equation}
Consequently, on every uniform class containing such an interior
one-point displacement path,
\[
    \mathfrak R_{\mathfrak X}(\eta)
    \asymp_{\bar\mu, s}\frac{\eta}{\kappa}
    \qquad(\eta\downarrow0).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Localization modulus

\[

\;\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\;
V[\pi]
\]
induced by mapping $T \otimes v \mapsto T(v)$ for $T \in \mathrm{Hom}_G(E_\pi, V)$ and $v \in V$.

\]

\[
\bigoplus_{[\pi]\in \widehat{G}} \mathrm{Hom}_G(E_\pi, V)\otimes E_\pi
\;\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\;
V
=
\bigoplus_{[\pi]\in \widehat{G}} V[\pi].
\]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Definition def:two-stream of arXiv:2602.21315, 'The Instability of all Backoff Protocols\thanks{For the purpose of Open Access, the author'] Fix $\lambda \in (0,1)$,
a \emph{send sequence}  
$\overline{p}$ with $p_0=1$, and a non-negative integer~$\tau$.
A \emph{two-stream process} 
with birth rate~$\lambda$, send sequence~$\overline{p}$ and start time~$\tau$ 
is a pair $Z=(Z^A,Z^B)$ of generalised backoff processes with 
send sequence~$\overline{p}$, start time~$\tau$, 
birth distribution
 $\mathcal{D} =  \mathsf{Po}(\lambda/2)$
and some initial populations $\overline{\mathbf{arr}}^{Z^A}(\tau)$ and $\overline{\mathbf{arr}}^{Z^B}(\tau)$. 
We refer to $Z^A$ and $Z^B$ as the \emph{streams} of~$Z$. 
The streams
evolve independently  
except 
that $\mathbf{e}_j^{Z^A}(t)$ and $\mathbf{e}_j^{Z^B}(t)$ are defined as follows for $t> \tau$. 
\begin{itemize}
    \item  
If there are distinct $C$ and $D$ in $\{A,B\}$ such that
$s^{Z^C}(t) = 0$ and $s^{Z^{D}}(t)>0$ then for all $j$, $\mathbf{e}_j^{Z^C}(t)=\emptyset$. In this case, a bin~$J^D$ is chosen with probability proportional to $s^{Z^{D}}_{J^D}(t)/s^{Z^{D}}(t)$ and $\mathbf{e}_{J^D}^{Z^D}(t)$
contains a single uniformly-chosen ball from 
$\mathbf{s}^{Z^D}_{J^D}$.
Also, 
for all $j\neq J^D$, $\mathbf{e}_j^{Z^D}(t)=\emptyset$. 
\item Otherwise, for   all $j$, $\mathbf{e}_j^{Z^A}(t)= \mathbf{e}_j^{Z^B}(t)=\emptyset$.
\end{itemize}
There are no end-of-step arrivals after step~$\tau$. That is, for all $D\in \{A,B\}$, all $t> \tau$, and all positive integers~$j$, $\mathbf{arr}_j^{Z^D} = \emptyset$.

[Theorem 2 of arXiv:2605.02771, 'Universality in Deep Neural Networks:\\ An approach via the Lindeberg exchange principle'] Let \(L,n_0,n_{L+1},r\in\N\) be fixed, and assume that \(\sigma\) is  polynomially bounded
    to order \(r\) in the sense of \cite[Definition \(2.1\)]{MR4898096}. Under \textbf{Assumptions \ref{assum:weights}} and \textbf{\ref{assum:biases}}, the process
    \[
        x\mapsto z^{(L+1)}(x)
    \]
    converges weakly in \(C^{r-1}(\R^{n_0},\R^{n_{L+1}})\) to a Gaussian process
    \[
        x\mapsto \Zcal^{(L+1)}(x),
    \]
    whose \(n_{L+1}\) components are i.i.d.\ and whose covariance structure is defined recursively by
    \[
        K^{(\ell+1)}(x,y)=
        \begin{cases}
            c_b+C_W \E[\sigma(\Zcal^{(\ell)}(x))\sigma(\Zcal^{(\ell)}(y))], & \ell\geq 1,\\[0.3em]
            c_b+\dfrac{C_W}{n_0}x\cdot y, & \ell=0.
        \end{cases}
    \]
    The same convergence is true when the DNN \(z^{(L+1)}\) has zero biases and weights satisfying \textbf{Assumption \ref{assum:weights}}. The limiting Gaussian process is defined recursively as above, with \(c_b=0\). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 2 of arXiv:2605.02771

body:
[Lem 17 of arXiv:2605.15501, 'Well-posedness of the obstacle problem for generalized Dean--Kawasaki equation\thanks{ The'] (Existence of solutions to the approximated penalized equation)
Let Assumption \ref{assu:assu for existence} and Assumption \ref{assu:assum for F} hold.
For $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $\alpha,\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, there exists a solution $u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}$ of \eqref{eq:appro penalized eq}, defined on the original probability space $\Omega$, in the sense of Definition \ref{def:Weak solution approximating penalized}.
Furthermore, let $\chi_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}(x,\xi,t):=\mathbf{1}_{\{0<\xi<u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}(x,t)\}}$ be the kinetic function of $u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}$.
Then, $u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}$ satisfies that, almost surely for every $\phi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{d}\times(0,\infty)\times[0,T))$,
\begin{align}
& -\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\chi_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}(x,\xi,s)\partial_s\phi(x,\xi,s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}\xi\mathrm{d}s\\
 & =\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\bar{\chi}(u_{\mathrm{init}},\xi)\phi(x,\xi,0)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}\xi-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\Phi^{\prime}(u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon})\nabla_x u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}\cdot(\nabla_x\phi)(x,u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon},s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\nonumber \\
  & \quad-\alpha\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\nabla_{x}u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}\cdot(\nabla_{x}\phi)(x,u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon},s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\nonumber\\
 & \quad-\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\big(F_{1}(x)[\sigma_n^{\prime}(u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon})]^{2}\nabla_x u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}+\sigma_n(u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon})\sigma_n^{\prime}(u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon})F_{2}(x)\big)\cdot(\nabla_x\phi)(x,u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon},s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\nonumber\\
 & \quad-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\partial_{\xi}\phi(x,\xi,s)\mathrm{d}m_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}(x,\xi,s)-\int_0^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\phi(x,u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon},s)\nabla_x\cdot g(u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon})\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\nonumber \\
 & \quad+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\Big(\sigma_n(u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon})\sigma_n^{\prime}(u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon})\nabla_x u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}\cdot F_{2}(x)+\sigma_n^{2}(u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon})F_{3}(x)\Big)(\partial_{\xi}\phi)(x,u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon},s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\nonumber \\
 & \quad-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\phi(x,u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon},s)\frac{1}{\varepsilon}(u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}-\psi)^+\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\phi(x,u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon},s)\nabla_x\cdot(\sigma_n(u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon})f_{k})\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}B_{s}^{k},\nonumber
\end{align}
where the kinetic measure $m_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}$ is
\begin{align}\notag
m_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}&:=\delta_{0}(\xi-u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon})\Big(\Phi^{\prime}(\xi)|\nabla u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}|^{2}+\alpha|\nabla u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}|^{2}\Big).
\end{align}
It follows from  (\ref{eq:priori}) that the $\{m_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}\}_{(\alpha,n)\in(0,1)\times\mathbb{N}}$ are finite kinetic measures.

[Lemma CVtV of arXiv:2504.00512, 'Localization-delocalization transition for a random block matrix model at the edge'] Under the assumptions of Theorem (MixEV of the paper), there exists a constant $\mathfrak c>0$ depending on ${\varepsilon}_A$ and $\delta_A$ such that the following holds for ${\mathfrak t}= N^{-1/3+\mathfrak c}$.  
For any fixed $n\in \mathbb{N}$, there exists a constant $c_n=c_n(\mathfrak c,\delta_A,{\varepsilon}_A)$ such that

\begin{align}
&\left|	\mathbb{E} O\pa{ \left({DN}\right)^{2/3}\pa{E^+-\lambda_1^{{\mathfrak t}}},\ldots, \left({DN}\right)^{2/3}\pa{E^+-\lambda_n^{{\mathfrak t}}}}\right.\nonumber\\
&\left.-\mathbb{E} O\pa{ \left({DN}\right)^{2/3}\left({E^+-\lambda_1}\right),\ldots, \left({DN}\right)^{2/3}\left({E^+-\lambda_n}\right)}   \right|\le N^{-c_n}.
\end{align}
The corresponding result also holds at the left edge $E^-$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma CVtV of arXiv:2504.00512

[Lem reach-join of arXiv:2605.14910, 'Sharp Phase Transition for the Formation of Infinite Tubes'] For each $w>0$, the following statements hold$:$
  \begin{itemize}
    \item $($From reachability to join$)$.
    If $\Delta\rightsquigarrow_w\Delta'$, then
    \[
    S_\Delta\approx_wS_{\Delta'}.
    \]
    \item $($From join to reachability$)$.
    Let $S,S'$ be discrete $(k-1)$-spheres.
    If $S\approx_wS'$, then there exist $\Delta,\Delta'\in V_{2w+4}$ with $S_\Delta=S$ and $S_{\Delta'}=S'$ such that
    \[
    \Delta\rightsquigarrow_{2w+4}\Delta'.
    \]
  \end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lem reach-join of arXiv:2605.14910

[Theorem 38 of arXiv:2607.04138, 'Hives from deformed GUE minor processes'] \lab{thm:main}
Let \(w,w'>0\) and \(u,u'\geq 0\), and assume
\[
\frac{u}{w^2}=\frac{u'}{(w')^2}.
\]
Set
\[
a^2=w^2+u^2,\qquad b^2=(w')^2+(u')^2,
\qquad \delta=u+u'.
\]
Suppose 
\(c_{**}\) is the positive solution of
\[
\delta^2
=
\frac{
2c_{**}^4(c_{**}^2-a^2-b^2)
}{
(c_{**}^2-a^2+b^2)(c_{**}^2+a^2-b^2)
}.
\]

Let \(h_n\) be the hive obtained from the two deformed GUE minor processes by
applying the octahedron recurrence, and write
\[
q_n:=\operatorname{Density}(h_n).
\]
Then
\[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(
q_n\,
\middle\|\,
\operatorname{Density}\bigl(\mathcal H_n(a\sqrt n,b\sqrt n,c_{**}\sqrt n)\bigr)
\right)
=
O(n\log n).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 38 of arXiv:2607.04138

[Proposition adj2 of arXiv:2609.03988, 'A $p$-summability approach to the weak maximizing property'] Let $X$ and $Y$ be Banach spaces and let $1\leq p<\infty$. \\
{\rm (1)} If the pair $(X^*,Y^*)$ has the $\mathrm{SMP}_p$, then it has the $\mathrm{SMP}_p$ for adjoint operators. \\
{\rm (2)} If the pair $(X^*,Y^*)$ has the $\mathrm{SMP}_p$ for adjoint operators, then it has the $\mathrm{SMP}_q$ for adjoint operators for every $q>p$.\\
{\rm (3)} If the pair $(X^*,Y^*)$ has the $\mathrm{SMP}_p$ for adjoint operators, then it has the weak$^*$-to-weak$^*$ maximizing property.
title: Proposition adj2 of arXiv:2609.03988

body:
[Lemma 21 (Pseudo-dimension after affine parameter tying) of arXiv:2608.31157, 'Sharp Approximation Rates for Neural Networks with Affine Latent Parameterizations'] Let $\Phi$ be a fully connected $d$-input ReLU architecture with at least
one hidden unit, let $P_\Phi$ be its number of scalar weight and bias entries,
and let
$\calA\in\aff(M,P_\Phi)$.  If $U_\Phi$ is the total number of hidden
ReLU units, then
\begin{equation}
 \VCdim(\calF_{\Phi,\calA})
 \le\Pdim(\calF_{\Phi,\calA})
 \le8r_{\calA}(U_\Phi+1)
 \le8r_{\calA}P_\Phi.
\end{equation}
In particular, if $P_\Phi\le P$, then
\begin{equation}
 \Pdim(\calF_{\Phi,\calA})
 \le8P\min\{M,P\}.
\end{equation}

body: [Definition 3.3 (Hypergraph) of arXiv:2505.15746, 'Higher-order Structure Boosts Link Prediction on Temporal Graphs'] A hypergraph can be represented by a tuple (V, H). V = {n1, n2, ...} is the set of nodes. And the set of hyperedges is H = {Ei |Ei ⊆V; 1 ≤ i ≤m}, where Ei is hyperedge and m is the number of hyperedges. Furthermore, in homogeneous graphs, the construction of hyperedges usually relies on the enumeration of maximal cliques (Wang & Kleinberg, 2024).
title: Definition 3.3 (Hypergraph) of arXiv:2505.15746: Higher-order Structure Boosts Link Prediction on Temporal Graphs

[Definition Thurston norm of arXiv:2608.30973, 'Pseudo-Anosov flow and dynamics on guts'] Let \(M\) be a compact oriented 3-manifold and \(Y\) be a subsurface of \(\partial M\).
For any \(z\in H_{2}(M,Y)\), we define the \emph{Thurston norm} of \(z\) to be
\[ x(z)=\min \{\chi_{-}(S): (S,\partial S)\subset (M,Y), [S]=z\in H_{2}(M,K)\}. \]
title: Thurston norm
