Let k_s(theta)=p(y|x,theta), m_lambda(s)=E_q_lambda k_s>0 for nu-almost every s, and define the one-sample update qtilde_lambda,s(dtheta)=k_s(theta)q_lambda(dtheta)/m_lambda(s), then qbar_lambda=E_s~nu qtilde_lambda,s. The new likelihood factor is untempered, and each updated posterior is normalized before averaging. Assume the covariance differentiation identity applies to each k_s, B(q_lambda)=E_nu[-log m_lambda] is finite, differentiation through nu is justified by a nu-integrable local envelope for |d log m_lambda/dlambda|, and E_nu E_qtilde_lambda,s |L|<infinity. Then Bprime(lambda)=J(qbar_lambda)-J(q_lambda)=n[Ghat(qbar_lambda,D)-Ghat(q_lambda,D)]. At lambda=1, Bprime(1)=0 iff the two empirical Gibbs losses agree; this is a stationarity criterion, not a minimization theorem. Under the covariance regularity also for f=-L, local CPE Bprime(1)<0 implies that, for every sufficiently small h>0, q_(1+h) has strictly smaller Bayes loss and empirical Gibbs loss than q_1, so q_1 underfits in the authors simultaneous-loss sense. If the finite minimum a=min_theta[-L(theta)] exists, local CPE also forces J(q_1)>a, or Ghat(q_1,D)>a/n.

[Lemma lem:chain_of_pockets of arXiv:2411.13133, 'Connectivity of the adjacency graph of\\ complementary components of the $\SLE$ Fan'] For any $p,\delta \in (0,1)$ there exists $a > 0, \epsilon_0 \in (0,1)$ (depending only on $\kappa, \delta$ and $p$) such that for every $\epsilon \in (0, \epsilon_0)$ the following events hold with probability at least $1 - p$. 
    \begin{enumerate}[(i)]
        \item There exist $x_1,\dots,x_n \in a \mathbf{Z}^2 \cap A_0^a$ and $y_1,\dots,y_m \in a \mathbf{Z}^2 \cap A_2^a$ such that $A_0 \subseteq \cup_{j=1}^n F_j \subseteq A_0^a$ where $F_j$ is the pocket with opening point $x_j$ for every $1 \leq j \leq n$, and $A_2 \subseteq \cup_{i=1}^m L_i \subseteq A_2^a$,  where $L_i$ is the pocket with opening point $y_i$ for every $1 \leq i \leq m$, and where all such pockets exist. 
        \item For each $z \in (a\mathbf{Z}^2 \cap A_0^a) \cup (a\mathbf{Z}^2 \cap A_2^a)$, the flow lines $\eta_z^0$ and $\eta_z^{-\epsilon}$ are $\delta$-close until $\eta_z^0$ exits $A_4^a$, and the flow lines $\eta_z^{-\pi}$ and $\eta_z^{-\pi-\epsilon}$ are $\delta$-close until $\eta_z^{-\pi}$ exits $A_4^a$.
    \end{enumerate}
title: Lemma lem:chain_of_pockets of arXiv:2411.13133

[Defn def: DP of arXiv:2604.10446, 'Least singular values of shifted sparse random combinatorial matrices'] Let $n, m\geq 1$ and 
    let $M$ be an $m \times n$ matrix with non-negative entries. 
    Given $S\subset [m], T \subset [n]$, define the edge count as  
    \[
    e_{M}(S,T):=\sum_{i \in S}\sum_{j \in T} M_{ij}.
    \]
    Furthermore, we say that the matrix $M$ has the discrepancy property $DP(\delta,\kappa_1, \kappa_2)$ with parameters 
    $\delta \in (0,1)$, $\kappa_1>0$, $\kappa_2 \geq 0$ 
    if for all nonempty $S \subset [m]$ and $T \subset [n]$  either 
    \begin{itemize}
        \item[(1)] $\frac{e_{M}(S,T)}{\delta|S||T|} \leq \kappa_1$, or 
        \item[(2)] $e_{M}(S,T) \log \frac{e_{M}(S,T)}{\delta|S||T|} \leq \kappa_2 (|S| \vee |T|) \log \frac{en}{|S| \vee |T|}$.
    \end{itemize}
title: Defn def: DP of arXiv:2604.10446

body:
[Thm 2 of arXiv:2605.07050, 'Universality of the fluctuations of the free energy in generalized Sherrington--Kirkpatric'] Suppose that Assumption \ref{assump:decay} holds for $W$. Suppose that $\sqrt{N} x_k$  $(1 \leq k \leq N)$ are i.i.d., symmetric, and strictly sub-Gaussian random variables with variance $1$, independent of $W$. Define the likelihood ratios by
\beq
	 \caL(\SNR) := \E_\caX \left[ \prod_{i<j} \frac{p(\sqrt{N} W_{ij} - \sqrt{\SNR N} x_i x_j /\| \bsx \|^2)}{p(\sqrt{N} W_{ij})} \prod_k \frac{p_d(\sqrt{N} W_{kk} - \sqrt{\SNR N} x_k^2  /\| \bsx \|^2)}{p_d(\sqrt{N} W_{kk})} \right]
\eeq
and
\beq
	\ol \caL (\SNR) := \E_\caX \left[ \prod_{i<j} \frac{p(\sqrt{N} W_{ij} - \sqrt{\SNR N} x_i x_j)}{p(\sqrt{N} W_{ij})} \prod_k \frac{p_d(\sqrt{N} W_{kk} - \sqrt{\SNR N} x_k^2)}{p_d(\sqrt{N} W_{kk})} \right].
\eeq
Define
\[
	F_p:= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{(p'(x))^2}{p(x)} \dd x, \quad F_d:= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{(p_d'(x))^2}{p_d(x)} \dd x, \quad G_p:= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{(p''(x))^2}{p(x)} \dd x.
\]
Then, for any $\SNR \in (0, 1/F_p)$,
\[
	\log \caL(\SNR) \Rightarrow \caN(-\rho_L, 2\rho_L), \quad \log \ol \caL(\SNR) \Rightarrow \caN(-\rho_L, 2\rho_L),
\]
as $N \to \infty$, i.e., $\log \caL(\SNR)$ and $\log \ol\caL(\SNR)$ converge in distribution to the Gaussian with mean $-\rho_L$ and the variance $2\rho_L$ as $N \to \infty$, where
\[
	\rho_L:= -\frac{1}{4} \left( \log (1-\SNR F_p) + \SNR(F_p- 2F_d) + \frac{\SNR^2}{4} (2F_p^2 - G_p) \right).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Thm 2 of arXiv:2605.07050

body: [Theorem 12 of arXiv:2512.19517, 'Spiking and Resetting'] Let $\mu$ be a non-atomic measure on $[0,t]\times[\delta,1]$, finite on bounded sets. Suppose that the simple point process $\mathcal{N}$ is such that for any set $\Delta$ which is a finite union of rectangles (32) $P(\mathcal{N}(\Delta)=0)=\exp\{-\mu(\Delta)\}.$ Then $\mathcal{N}$ is a Poisson process with intensity measure $\mu$.

[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2608.21701, 'Superdiffusivity of random walks on the three-dimensional randomly oriented Manhattan latt'] When $d=3$, for each $\eps>0$ there exists a constant $C_{\eps}\in (1,\infty)$ such that for each $\lambda\in (0,e^{-2})$,

[Prop link-with-compositions of arXiv:2411.03065, 'Growing conditioned BGW trees with\\ log-concave offspring distributions'] Let ${\mathbf{w}}=(w_0,w_1,\dots)$ be a non-negative sequence which has no internal zeros and such that $w_0w_1>0$.
	Set ${\mathbf{b}}=(\PFtrees{{\mathbf{w}}}{n})_{n\geq 1}$.
	Then $({\mathbf{w}},{\mathbf{b}})$ is a non-degenerate weight pair.
	For $n\geq 1$ we have $\PFtrees{\mathbf{w}} n=\PFComp{{\mathbf{w}},{\mathbf{b}}}{n-1}$, and for $T\in\trees_n$ if we write $c(T)=\underline{n}_1 \cdots  \underline{n}_i$ and $\varphi(T)=(T^{[1]},\dots,T^{[i]})$, then
	\begin{align}
	\SimpGen{{\mathbf{w}}}{n}(T)=\PComp{{\mathbf{w}},{\mathbf{b}}}{n-1}\bigl(c(T)\bigr)\cdot\left(\SimpGen{{\mathbf{w}}}{n_1}\bigl(T^{[1]}\bigr)\cdots \SimpGen{{\mathbf{w}}}{n_i}\bigl(T^{[i]}\bigr)\right).
	\end{align}

[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] Given a Hilbert space $H$, consider the linear operators $T:H\to H$, and for each such operator define its norm by the following formula:
$$||T||=\sup_{||x||=1}||Tx||$$
The operators which are bounded, $||T||<\infty$, form then a complex algebra $B(H)$, which is complete with respect to $||.||$. When $H$ comes with a basis $\{e_i\}_{i\in I}$, we have
$$B(H)\subset M_I(\mathbb C)$$
with the correspondence $T\to M$ coming via the usual linear algebra formulae, namely:
$$T(x)=Mx\quad,\quad M_{ij}=<Te_j,e_i>$$
In infinite dimensions, the inclusion $B(H)\subset M_I(\mathbb C)$ is not an equality.

body: Publication record. P. Thévenin (Electron. J. Probab. 25, 2020, Section 6.2) proved a central limit theorem for the numbers of vertices of fixed outdegree in a subcritical Galton-Watson tree conditioned to have n vertices when the offspring law has a power-law tail, and conjectured that it extends to every subcritical law without exponential moment and every critical law with infinite variance. Y. Shmalo, Non-Gaussian fluctuations of degree counts in conditioned Galton-Watson trees (2026) gives two offspring laws for which the extension fails, an explicit subcritical law with finite third moment and no exponential moment and a critical law with infinite variance: along a sequence of sizes the centred and normalised number of vertices of outdegree one has a non-Gaussian limit, a mixture of two Gaussian laws. The second version (13 October 2026) adds, for Problems 21.2-21.4 of S. Janson, Simply generated trees, conditioned Galton-Watson trees, random allocations and condensation (Probab. Surveys 9, 2012), a joint central limit theorem for the box counts of balls-in-boxes models below the critical density, and at the critical density under a second moment condition when the number of balls exceeds its critical value by at most O(sqrt(n)), and the two-Gaussian mixture for every fringe count with 0 < pi_A < 1, the leaves included. Paper: https://github.com/yspennstate/non-gaussian-degree-counts (commit 16f5fcef7b00); ResearchGate record 414333267. Not refereed; an outside audit is owed.
title: Thevenin's conjecture (EJP 2020, Section 6.2) refuted, Janson Problems 21.2-21.4 answered in part: non-Gaussian fluctuations of degree counts in conditioned Galton-Watson trees (Shmalo 2026, repository yspennstate/non-gaussian-degree-counts)

[Theorem thm:gaussian:series of arXiv:2605.28106, 'Gaussian Processes with Sample Paths in Reproducing Kernel Banach Spaces'] Let \( \gamma \) be a centered Radon Gaussian measure on \( (X,\mathcal{B}(X)) \) with covariance operator \( R \) and \( (h_k) \) an orthonormal basis for \( H(R) \).
    Then the series
    \begin{equation} 
        \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \xi_k h_k
    \end{equation}
    converges almost surely in \( X \).
    The distribution of its sum is \( \gamma \).
title: Theorem thm:gaussian:series of arXiv:2605.28106

For simply connected semisimple algebraic groups G (such as SL_n or Sp_{2n}), H^1(k, G) = 0 and H^1(k_v, G) = 0 for all places by the Kneser-Harder-Chernousov theorem. Consequently, BG satisfies both the Hasse principle and strong approximation trivially because every torsor is trivial.

[Prop equiv-model-structure of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] The ${\mathcal{F}}$-equivariant weak equivalences and fibrations participate in a model structure on the category $\textbf{\textup{$\bm G$-Top}}$ of topological spaces with an action of $G$. This model structure is proper, topological, and cofibrantly generated with generating cofibrations
    \[
        \{G/H\times\partial D^n\hookrightarrow G/H\times D^n : H\in{\mathcal{F}},n\ge0\}
    \]
    and generating acyclic cofibrations
    \[
        \{G/H\times D^n\hookrightarrow G/H\times D^n\times[0,1] : H\in{\mathcal{F}},n\ge0\}.
    \]
    \begin{proof}
        [schwede2018global]*{Proposition B.7} constructs this model structure and proves that it is topological, proper, and cofibrantly generated. The description of the generating (acyclic) cofibrations is pointed out in the proof of \emph{loc.\ cit.}
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Prop equiv-model-structure of arXiv:2608.28504

[Lem 174 (eighth moment bounds for $X^{\Ising}$, $X^{\trunc,\Ising}$, and $X^{\frozen,\Ising}$) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] The bound of Lemma~\ref{l:subgaus.X.II}
also holds with $X^{\Ising}$ in place of $X^{\RomII}$: for $N$ large enough, we have
	\[
	\E\bigg[\bigg(
	\sum_{\ell=a}^{b-1} 
	\Delta X^{\Ising}(q_d,
	{i(q_{d+1})})
	\bigg)^8\bigg]
	\le L^{O(1)} (q_b-q_a)^4
	\]
for all $0\le a\le b\le \dmax$. The same bound holds with 
$X^{\trunc,\Ising}$ or $X^{\Isplus}$ in place of $X^\Ising$. 

\begin{proof}
Recall from \eqref{e:Delta.X.Ising} that
	\[
	\Delta X^{\Ising}(q_d,i(q_{d+1}))
	= \sqrt{\delta_d}
	({\boldsymbol e}_i,\by(q_{d+1}))
	\]
where ${\boldsymbol e}_i$ is the $i$-th standard basis vector in $\R^N$.
The claim then follows essentially by the argument of Lemma~\ref{l:subgaus.X.II}, replacing $\bar{\bg}(q_d)/N^{1/2}$ with
${\boldsymbol e}_i$. (Moreover, since clearly $\|{\boldsymbol e}_i\|=1$, we can skip the step of restricting to the event that
$\|\bar{\bg}(q_d)\|$ is not atypically large.) It is straightforward to verify that the same argument applies with $X^{\trunc,\Ising}$ or $X^{\Isplus}$ in place of $X^\Ising$.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: eighth moment bounds for $X^{\Ising}$, $X^{\trunc,\Ising}$, and $X^{\frozen,\Ising}$

Let N be a positive integer, R a commutative ring, f: D(N) -> R and F(n) = sum_{d | n} f(d) for n | N. Then f(n) = sum_{d | n} mu(n/d) F(d) for every n | N, where mu is the arithmetic Moebius function: mu(1) = 1, mu(m) = 0 if p^2 divides m for some prime p, and mu(m) = (-1)^omega(m) for squarefree m, omega(m) the number of distinct prime divisors. Equivalently, with P(n) the set of prime divisors of n, f(n) = sum over S subset of P(n) of (-1)^{|S|} F(n / prod_{p in S} p) (empty product 1).
N is a positive integer
R is a commutative ring
F(n) = sum_{d | n} f(d) for n | N

[Proposition symmetrized gap upper bound proposition of arXiv:2606.01683, 'Singular-value gap of nonreversible Markov processes'] Consider a jump process on a measurable space $S$ with generator (equation jump process generator of the paper)
and an invariant probability measure $\mu$.
Assume the jump rates are bounded:
\[
        q(x,S)\le q_{\max}<\infty
        \qquad \text{for \(\mu\)-a.e. }x .
\]
Let \(\gamma\) be the singular-value gap of \(L\) on \(L_0^2(\mu)\), and
let \(\gamma_s\) be the spectral gap of the symmetrized generator $L_s$,
which is a bounded self-adjoint operator.
Then
\[
        \gamma\le \sqrt{2q_{\max}\gamma_s}.
\]

On the uniform cube {-1, 1}^n let f be real, f^(S) = E[f chi_S] its Walsh coefficients and W_k = sum over |S| = k of f^(S)^2. For rho in [-1, 1], T_rho is the noise operator: T_rho f(x) = E[f(Y)] where the Y_i are independent with P(Y_i = x_i) = (1 + rho)/2, so T_rho chi_S = rho^|S| chi_S. For convex Phi on an interval containing the values of f, Phi(T_rho f(x)) <= T_rho(Phi o f)(x) for every x, and hence E[Phi(T_rho f(X))] <= E[Phi(f(X))] for uniform X. In particular ||T_rho f||_p <= ||f||_p for 1 <= p <= infinity. If -1 < rho < 1 and f is not constant, then min f < T_rho f(x) < max f at every x; for all rho in [-1, 1], min f <= T_rho f(x) <= max f.

[Corollary 29 of arXiv:2605.08844, 'Signature Kernel and Schwinger-Dyson Kernel Equations as Two-Parameter Rough Differential '] For every $1 \le i \le m \le 2^N - 1$, let $\mathrm{Poly}_{\emptyset}$ denote the number of operations required to compute
\[
\sum_{|\omega| = 1}^{\kappa} \sum_{m=i+1}^{j+1} K^{(\omega)}(i,m) \, \mathbf{X}^{(\omega)}_{m-1, m}.
\]

Then, for $d > 1$, there exists $\alpha^* \in [0,1/2]$ that maximizes the expression on the left, such that
\[
c\left(d^{1 - \alpha^*} \frac{2^{H(\alpha^*)}}{\sqrt{\kappa + \zeta}}\right)^{\kappa + \zeta}
\;\leq\; \mathrm{Poly}_{\emptyset} \;\leq\; C(d+1)^{\kappa+\zeta},
\]
where $H(\alpha) = -\alpha \log_2 \alpha - (1-\alpha) \log_2 (1-\alpha)$ is the binary entropy function and some constants $C,c \geq 0$ independent from $\kappa, \zeta$ and $d$.

In the special case $d=1$, we have
\[
\frac{2^{\kappa + \zeta}}{\kappa + \zeta + 1}  \leq \mathrm{Poly}_{\emptyset} \leq C\left(2^{\kappa + \zeta}\right).
\]

[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] Given an ellipse, parametrized as usual as
$$\left(\frac{x}{a}\right)^2+\left(\frac{y}{b}\right)^2=1$$
with $a,b>0$, its area is $A=\pi ab$. As for the length, this is given by the formula
$$L=4\int_0^{\pi/2}\sqrt{a^2\sin^2t+b^2\cos^2t}\,dt$$
and with this integral being generically not computable.

body:
Attributed primary-source theorem, not independently audited here. Let pi_t be the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck evolution of a law pi_0 on R^d with E_pi_0||X||^2<=M_2^2<infinity. Let e be in (0,1], and suppose supplied score estimates s_t have E_pi_t||s_t-grad log pi_t||^2<=e^2 at all relevant times up to T. Require global spatial Lipschitz control of the relative estimated score tilde_s_t(x)=s_t(x)+x: ||tilde_s_t(x)-tilde_s_t(y)||<=beta_tilde_0||x-y||/(1-exp(-2t)) for positive times. With T asymptotic to max{1,log((d+M_2^2)/e^2)}, the analysed denoising diffusion randomized midpoint method with its decaying schedule has output hat_pi and an intermediate pi_approx satisfying KL(pi_approx||hat_pi)<=O_tilde((1+log^2((1 vee beta_tilde_0)(d+M_2^2)))e^2) and W2^2(pi_approx,pi_0)<=O(e^2), using N=Theta_tilde(beta_tilde_0 sqrt(d+M_2^2)/e) steps. The theoretical variant samples each midpoint time tau_k on [0,rho_k h_k] with density proportional to exp(tau_k-h_k), with source-prescribed rho_k<1 sufficiently near 1. The bounds retain the source universal constants and logarithmic factors. The guarantee is hybrid KL/Wasserstein and assumes smooth supplied relative-score estimators; it is not a generic L2-oracle TV bound to unsmoothed data.

[Proposition 19 of arXiv:2609.02416, '2609.02416'] The following three estimates will be used in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:mainwholeline}.

\textup{(i)} Assume $\lambda<\Lp(\R)$. Suppose that there exist $W\in C^1(\R)$, $W\ge1$, $W(x)\to+\infty$ as $|x|\to\infty$, a compact interval $K$, and $\delta>0$ such that
\[
\cA_\R W+\lambda W\le-\delta W\;\hbox{in }\R\setminus K.
\]
Then $\cA_\R+\lambda$ satisfies the bounded maximum principle.

\textup{(ii)} Let $\lambda<\Lp(\R)$ and assume $\limsup_{|x|\to\infty}(a(x)+\lambda)<0$.
Then $\cA_\R+\lambda$ satisfies the bounded maximum principle. In particular, if $\Lp(\R)>0$ and $\limsup_{|x|\to\infty}a(x)<0$, then $\cA_\R$ satisfies the bounded maximum principle.

\textup{(iii)} For every $\mu\in\R$,
\[
\Lp(\cA_\R+\mu)\ge \mathfrak G(\mu).
\]
In particular, $\Lp(\cA_\R+\mu)\ge H_d(q_0)-\sup_\R(a+\mu)$.

[Proposition of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] A variable $f:X\to\mathbb R$ follows the exponential law of parameter $\lambda>0$ precisely when the following happens, for any measurable function $\phi:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$:
$$E(\phi(f))=\lambda\int_0^\infty\phi(x)e^{-\lambda x}dx$$
Equivalently, we must have $f:X\to[0,\infty)$, up to a set of null measure, and given a measurable set $Y\subset[0,\infty)$, the following must happen:
$$P(f\in Y)=\lambda\int_Ye^{-\lambda x}dx$$
Also, in this latter statement, we can restrict the attention to the intervals $Y\subset[0,\infty)$.

[Thm 51 (Sawashita) of arXiv:2608.26698, 'Mapping class groups of simply connected closed spin 5-manifolds with no 2- and 3-torsion '] Given a space $X$, let $\mathcal{I}^h(X)$ be the group of homotopy classes of homotopy equivalences of $X$ that act trivially on $H_*(X)$.

[Proposition 33 of arXiv:2609.02416, '2609.02416'] For later perturbation arguments we also record the adjoint critical limit and the resulting first-variation limit.

\textup{(i)} Let $\phi_\sigma^*>0$ be the positive adjoint eigenfunction of $\cA_{\sigma,2,L}$. Normalize it by $\|\phi_\sigma^*\|_{L^2(-L,L)}=1$. Then
\[
\phi_\sigma^*\longrightarrow\phi_0^*\quad \hbox{strongly in }L^2(-L,L),
\]
where $\phi_0^*>0$ is the normalized Dirichlet principal eigenfunction of
\[
d_Jv''-(qv)'+av+\lambda_0v=0\quad \hbox{in }(-L,L),\qquad v(-L)=v(L)=0.
\]
The zero-extension energies satisfy
\[
E_\sigma(\phi_\sigma^*)\longrightarrow d_J\int_{-L}^{L}|(\phi_0^*)'|^2\,dx,
\]
and $\phi_\sigma^*(L)\to0$.

\textup{(ii)} Let $h\in C([-L,L])$ and, for $|\tau|$ small, replace $a$ by $a+\tau h$. Denote the corresponding principal eigenvalue by $\lambda_\sigma(\tau)$. Then
\[
\partial_\tau\lambda_\sigma(0)=-\frac{\int_{-L}^{L}h(x)\phi_\sigma(x)\phi_\sigma^*(x)\,dx}{\int_{-L}^{L}\phi_\sigma(x)\phi_\sigma^*(x)\,dx}.
\]
After normalizing the direct and adjoint eigenfunctions in $L^2$,
\[
\partial_\tau\lambda_\sigma(0)\longrightarrow-\frac{\int_{-L}^{L}h(x)\phi_0(x)\phi_0^*(x)\,dx}{\int_{-L}^{L}\phi_0(x)\phi_0^*(x)\,dx}.
\]
The right-hand side is the first variation of the local Dirichlet principal eigenvalue.

body: Let f(n) be a space-constructible function, computable in O(f(n)) space in a way that marks off exactly f(n) cells on inputs of length n, with f(n) >= log n. If g(n) = o(f(n)), then there is a language decidable by a deterministic Turing machine using O(f(n)) space that is not decidable by any deterministic Turing machine using O(g(n)) space; equivalently DSPACE(g(n)) is strictly contained in DSPACE(f(n)) whenever the bounds are sufficiently far apart. Thus more memory strictly increases computational power for space-bounded computation. A corresponding nondeterministic space hierarchy theorem also holds.
title: Space hierarchy theorem

[Proposition L:compact-family-split-localization of arXiv:2607.17113, 'Two-time spatial decorrelation for the flat KPZ fixed point'] Fix $0<s<t$ and put $\rho=s/t$ and $m_{s,t}(z,x)=(1-\rho)z+\rho x$.  Fix an
  endpoint $x_0\in\mathbb{R}$, and let $Y^-_{z,x_0}\le Y^+_{z,x_0}$ be the leftmost and
  rightmost maximizers of
  \[
    y\mapsto \mathcal{L}(z,0;y,s)+\mathcal{L}(y,s;x_0,t).
  \]
  For all $R,U\ge1$,
  \begin{align}
    &\mathbb{P}\Bigg(
      \begin{aligned}
      &\{\exists |z-x_0|\le R:
        Y^+_{z,x_0}-m_{s,t}(z,x_0)>U\}\\
      &{}\cup\{\exists |z-x_0|\le R:
        Y^-_{z,x_0}-m_{s,t}(z,x_0)<-U\}
      \end{aligned}
    \Bigg)\notag\\
    &\qquad \le
    C\Big(1+\frac{R}{U}\Big)^2\exp\{-cU^3/t^2\},
    
  \end{align}
  where $C,c$ depend only on $s,t$.

$G=(G_{ab})_{1\le a,b\le d}$ be positive semidefinite, and let $q\ge1$.

\begin{align}
 q!\ip{u_{N,a}}{u_{N,b}}&=G_{ab},
 \\
 \norm{u_{N,a}\otimes_ru_{N,b}}&=O(N^{-1/2})
 \qquad(1\le r<q).
 
\end{align}
Consequently $(I_q(u_{N,a}))_{a\le d}\weak N_d(0,G)$.

[Definition Graphical visualization of certain generalized diagrams of arXiv:2506.06559, 'Bi-infinite incipient cluster in high dimensions'] The diagram of a diagrammatic graph ${\bf G}$ is simply represented by its multigraph component $G$ where the vertices in $S$ are labelled according to $\ell$.

If $\mathcal{G}$ is a generalized diagrammatic graph, then
\begin{itemize}
\item if $G'$ is a fully-labeled diagrammatic graph, the graphical representation of $\mathcal{G}\uplus G'$ is that of $\mathcal{G}$ where we take the union of the two graphs but identify vertices with the same label,
\item if $u\in \mathbb{Z}^d$, for the graphical representation of $\mathcal{G} \circledast u$, we add a label, say $A$, to each edge in the graphical representation of $\mathcal{G}$ and we add a point $u$ connected to an \lq\lq edge\rq\rq~whose other endpoint will be labelled \lq\lq$A?$\rq\rq. That last edge is called a connecting edge and can be labelled in future iterations.
\end{itemize} 

Since a generalized diagrammatic graph is obtained as an iteration of the two previous iterations, we can give a graphical visualization of generalized diagrammatic graphs. We refer to this graphical visualization as a generalized diagram.
title: Graphical visualization of certain generalized diagrams

[Corollary 21 of arXiv:2606.15432, 'A Concavity Theorem for the Parisi PDE'] Fix \(h_1,h_2\in \Hoelder{\alpha/2}([0,1])\).

\begin{multline*}
D^2\Psi^\gamma[h_1,h_2](s,x)
=
-

\iint_{[s,\sigma]^2}
h_1(\rho_1)h_2(\rho_2)
\dd{\rho_1}\dd{\rho_2}

+

\dd\rho_1\dd\rho_2

\dd{\rho}
\biggr)
\dd{\sigma}.
\end{multline*}

body:
[Lemma lem:P_j of arXiv:2607.01946, 'Second-order fluctuations for a phase transition in random partitions'] Let $(P_j^\downarrow)_{j\in{\mathbb N}}$ follow the Poisson--Dirichlet distribution with parameter $(\alpha,\theta)$, and $S_\alpha$ be as in (equation eq:S_alpha 2 of the paper). Set
\begin{equation}
\Gamma_j:=\frac{S_{\alpha}}{\Gamma(1-\alpha)}\pp{P_j^\downarrow}^{-\alpha}, j\in{\mathbb N}.
\end{equation}
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item When $\theta=0$, the sequence $(\Gamma_j)_{j\in{\mathbb N}}$ has the law of consecutive arrival times of a standard Poisson process.
\item More generally for all $\theta>-\alpha$, 
the law of $(P_j^{\alpha,\theta,\downarrow})_{j\in{\mathbb N}}$ is absolutely continuous with respect to the law of $(P_j^{\alpha,0,\downarrow})_{j\in{\mathbb N}}$. 
More precisely, for every continuous and bounded function $f:\Delta_\infty\to{\mathbb R}$, we have 
\[
{\mathbb E} f\pp{(P_j^{\alpha,\theta,\downarrow})_{j\in{\mathbb N}}} = {\mathbb E} \pp{\frac{\Gamma(\theta+1)}{\Gamma(\theta/\alpha+1)}S_\alpha^{\theta/\alpha}f\pp{(P_j^{\alpha,0,\downarrow})_{j\in{\mathbb N}}}},
\]
where $S_\alpha$ on the right-hand side is defined via (equation eq:S_alpha 2 of the paper) using $P_j^\downarrow\equiv P_j^{\alpha,0,\downarrow}$. 

\end{enumerate}
In particular,  by (equation eq:S_alpha 2 of the paper) and (equation eq:Gamma_j of the paper), for all $\alpha\in(0,1)$ and $\theta>-\alpha$, as $j\to\infty$
\[
P_j^\downarrow =  \pp{\frac{S_{\alpha}}{\Gamma(1-\alpha)}}^{1/\alpha} \Gamma_j^{-1/\alpha}    \sim \pp{\frac{S_{\alpha}}{\Gamma(1-\alpha)}}^{1/\alpha} j^{-1/\alpha}, \mbox{ almost surely.}
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma lem:P_j of arXiv:2607.01946

body:
# Co-scaled noise phases: double descent versus preference for late stopping

T267 / Target 2 / C011 / proof draft (unaudited); novelty unestablished.
This is an asymptotic phase comparison in C010's restricted model, not
an exact finite-scale two-critical-noise-level theorem.

## 1. Model and statement

Keep the four-point design, unit-norm centered-ReLU teacher, paired
nonzero initialization and both-layer GD of BOUNDED_RELU_PAIRED.md.
Write alpha=alpha_e and replace label noise +/-2alpha by
+/-2alpha sqrt(rho), for any fixed rho>0. Thus the noise standard deviation
is c_e sqrt(rho), which tends to zero. Each Walsh noise variance is
rho alpha^2. Average clean risk over the sixteen noise patterns as before.
All width limits are over even widths m=2N, before e decreases to zero.

Let b_h be the full-kernel rates of C009, q_h=exp(-b_h), and define

K_e=ceil(e^(-3/2)), T_e=ceil(e^(-5/2)),
E(rho)=rho+2+rho/(1+rho),
L(rho)=2rho+2rho/(1+rho).

For small e, K_e<T_e. The following minima of the ACTUAL nonlinear risk
converge in probability in the iterated width-then-scale sense:

min_(0<=k<=K_e) Q_(m,e)(k)/alpha^2 -> min{3,E(rho)},
min_(K_e<=k<=T_e) Q_(m,e)(k)/alpha^2 -> L(rho),
min_(0<=k<=T_e) Q_(m,e)(k)/alpha^2 -> min{3,L(rho)}.

Here convergence means for every epsilon>0, lim_(e->0) limsup_(N->infinity)
P(absolute discrepancy>epsilon)=0. These statements do not control actual
nonlinear risk after T_e or exchange the two limits.

Moreover there are strict descent-rise-descent witnesses at every fixed
rho>0. With k0=ceil(e^(-1/2)),
k1=floor(log(1+1/rho)/b1), k2=K_e,
k3=floor(log(1+1/rho)/b2), their risks divided by alpha^2 converge to

rho+3, E(rho), 2rho+2, L(rho).

Their three limiting strict margins are
1/(1+rho), rho^2/(1+rho), 2/(1+rho).
For all fixed rho<1, the best risk in the late phase is strictly lower
than the best in the early phase with probability tending to one.
For all fixed rho>1, the early phase is strictly better. At rho=1 the
leading phase minima tie at 3; no finite-e ordering is asserted.

Thus rho=1 is the limiting late-versus-early preference boundary in this
model, whereas strict double descent survives on both sides. No lower
critical-noise rate or exact finite-e second threshold is established.

## 2. Exact frozen risk and nonlinear transfer

The frozen zero-output curve is

F_e(k)=Q_e^0(k)/alpha^2
      =rho(1-q0^k)^2
       +sum_(h=1,2,12)[q_h^(2k)+rho(1-q_h^k)^2].

This follows from Walsh Parseval, identical teacher coefficients alpha
and Walsh noise variances rho alpha^2. The paired initialization gives
zero output exactly. Let p_r(q)=q^2+rho(1-q)^2. Completing the square,

p_r(q)=(1+rho)(q-rho/(1+rho))^2+rho/(1+rho).

For each fixed e and rho the labels are bounded; indeed max|y_i| is at
most (3+2sqrt(rho))alpha, which tends to zero. For all sufficiently small
e the residual bound R_0=2 used in C010 is therefore valid. Its pairwise
finite-horizon transfer applies uniformly through T_e (a finite integer
for this fixed e), and over all noise patterns. It follows that

max_(k<=T_e)|Q_(m,e)(k)/alpha^2-F_e(k)| ->0 in probability as N->infinity.

For this step alpha^2 is a FIXED positive number; no uniform-in-e width
bound is inferred. Consequently it suffices to prove the deterministic
frozen limits for the two ranges and the four witnesses.

## 3. Early-phase minimum

At k=0, F_e=3 exactly. At
k1=floor(log(1+1/rho)/b1), the constant mode has learned, q1^k1 tends to
rho/(1+rho), and q2^k1,q12^k1 tend to one. Hence F_e(k1)->E(rho).
These give the upper bound min{3,E(rho)} for the limiting early minimum.

For the lower bound, take any sequence e->0 and early-phase integers
k_e<=K_e. Choose a subsequence such that k_e is bounded or tends to
infinity, and such that b1 k_e converges in [0,infinity].
If k_e is bounded, all nonconstant q_h^k_e tend to one, so liminf F_e>=3.
If k_e tends to infinity, q0^k_e tends to zero. Uniformly for k<=K_e,
b2 k and b12 k tend to zero, since b2 K_e=O(e^(1/2)). Thus the slow-mode
contribution tends to two, while the fast-mode contribution is at least
rho/(1+rho) by the exact completed square. The limit inferior is at least
E(rho), whether the fast scaled time is finite or infinite. This proves
the matching early lower bound. The subsequence argument applies to
minimizers, which exist because the integer range is finite.

## 4. Late-phase minimum

Uniformly for k>=K_e, q0^k and q1^k tend to zero, since b1 K_e tends to
infinity. Their combined risk tends to 2rho, uniformly in this range.
Each of the two slow contributions is bounded below by rho/(1+rho),
so the late minimum has limit inferior at least L(rho).
For k3=floor(log(1+1/rho)/b2), both slow q's tend to rho/(1+rho), because
b12/b2->1. Also K_e<k3<T_e for all small e, since b2 K_e->0 and
b2 T_e->infinity. Thus F_e(k3)->L(rho), proving the matching upper bound.
Combining Sections 3-4 gives the full finite-horizon minimum as
min{3,E(rho),L(rho)}. The simplification in Section 6 proves the stated
min{3,L(rho)} form.

## 5. Strict double-descent witnesses

At k0 all nonconstant modes remain at one and the constant noise mode
has saturated, so F_e(k0)->rho+3. At k1 the limit is E(rho).
At K_e fast q1 tends to zero and the slow q's to one, giving 2rho+2.
At k3 the limit is L(rho). Subtraction gives exactly the three positive
margins in Section 1. This applies to every fixed rho>0, including rho>1.
The strict finite-e margins transfer to nonlinear GD by Section 2.

For rho=0 the frozen curve is sum_(h=1,2,12)q_h^(2k), strictly decreasing.
This zero-noise frozen statement does not imply monotonic actual nonlinear
risk for all times, nor locate a finite-e onset as rho_e tends to zero.
Pointwise positive-rho results must not be promoted to such a uniform
noise-window theorem.

## 6. Which phase wins?

Exact subtraction yields

E(rho)-L(rho)=(2-rho^2)/(1+rho),
L(rho)-3=(rho-1)(2rho+3)/(1+rho).

If 0<rho<1, then L<3 and L<E, so late training beats the entire early
phase, not just its fast-mode stationary point. If rho>1, then L>3,
so the early phase containing k=0 beats the late phase. Also E>3 for
rho>1, since E-3=(rho^2+rho-1)/(1+rho)>0. Consequently the overall
minimum is min{3,L}. At rho=1 the leading early and late values both
are 3, so a finer expansion is needed to decide finite-scale ordering.

Comparing ONLY E and L would instead produce sqrt(2). That would be the
wrong early-stopping boundary because it omits the allowed initialization
time k=0. This is why the early-phase minimization includes every time
from zero rather than only the first fast-signal minimum. The tiny initial
transient may shift the finite-e preference threshold; it does not change
these strict comparisons for rho bounded away from one.

## Scope and source distinction

Stephenson--Lee, arXiv:2108.12006, Section4, EDD-NES/EDD-ES phases and
P3/P4, distinguish onset of double descent from the higher noise level
where early stopping is preferable. This source does not supply this
model's threshold. Our computation is self-contained and restricted to
the paired four-point model. The lower onset at finite scale, its rate,
a full two-threshold window, iid Gaussian inputs, fixed-positive-noise
unit-teacher dynamics, high probability over label noise, and actual
nonlinear convergence after T_e remain open. Mathematical and novelty
review are pending; no independent audit or full Target2 solution.
All paired four-point model definitions and restrictions of C010
Noise-to-signal Walsh variance ratio rho>0 fixed as e decreases; actual noise standard deviation tends to zero
Width tends to infinity before feature scale decreases; nonlinear comparison is only through finite T_e for each fixed e
Clean risk averages over all sixteen training-label-noise sign patterns
title: Epoch-wise double descent versus early stopping: co-scaled noise phases for paired ReLU GD (w713 T267, unaudited restricted case)

[Defn 52 of arXiv:2609.02561, 'NON-NEF LOCI IN MIXED CHARACTERISTIC'] Let $(R,\Delta)$ be a BCM-regular pair.
\begin{enumerate}
\item 
The BCM-regular threshold $\bcmt(R,\Delta;r)$ of $(R,\Delta)$ with respect to $0\neq r\in\m$ is defined as
\begin{align*}
\bcmt(R,\Delta;r)
&:=\sup\{t\in\Q_{\geq0} \mid \text{$(R,\Delta+t\cdot\divi(r))$ is BCM-regular} \} \\
&=\inf\{t\in\Q_{\geq0} \mid \text{$(R,\Delta+t\cdot\divi(r))$ is not BCM-regular} \}.
\end{align*}
\item
The local BCM-alpha invariant $\alpha_{\BCM}(R,\Delta)$ of $(R,\Delta)$ is defined as
\[ \alpha_{\BCM}(R,\Delta) := \inf_{0\neq r\in\m} \bcmt(R,\Delta;r)\cdot\nord_{\m}(r), \]
where $\nord_{\m}(r)$ denotes the normalized order of $r$.
\end{enumerate}
When $R$ is of characteristic $p>0$,
the BCM-regular threshold coincides with the $F$-pure threshold, and
the local BCM-alpha invariant $\alpha_{\BCM}(R,\Delta)$ coincides with the local $F$-alpha invariant $\alpha_{F}(R,\Delta)$ recently introduced by Takagi and Yamaguchi \cite[Definition~3.3]{TY}.
title: Definition 52 of arXiv:2609.02561

[Definition of arXiv:2411.05534, 'Inverse problems for stochastic partial differential equations'] Let  $ (\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P}) $  be a probability space. 
    \begin{enumerate}[(i)]
        \item Let $ A, B \in \mathcal{F} $. We say that  $ A, B $ are independent w.r.t $ \mathbb{P} $ if $ \mathbb{P} (A \cap  B) = \mathbb{P} (A) \mathbb{P}(B) $.
        \item Let $ \mathcal{J}_{1} $ and $ \mathcal{J}_{2} $ be two subfamilies of $ \mathcal{F} $. We say that $ \mathcal{J}_{1} $ and $ \mathcal{J}_{2} $ are independent if for all $ (A,B) \in \mathcal{J}_{1} \times \mathcal{J}_{2} $, it holds that $ \mathbb{P}(A \cap B) = \mathbb{P}(A) \mathbb{P}(B) $.
        \item Let $f, g:(\Omega, \mathcal{F}) \rightarrow(\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{B}(\mathcal{X}))$ be two random variables. We say that $f$ and $g$  are independent if $\sigma(f)$ and $\sigma(g) $ are independent.
        \item Let $f: (\Omega, \mathcal{F}) \rightarrow(\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{B}(\mathcal{X}))$ be a random variable and $ \mathcal{J} \subset \mathcal{F} $. We say that $f$ and $ \mathcal{J} $  are independent if $\sigma(f)$ and $ \mathcal{J} $ are independent.
    \end{enumerate}

[Proposition 4 (Reduction to the convergence of \(Z^n\)) of arXiv:2608.16256, 'Error Distribution of the Local Linearization Method for Stochastic Differential Equations'] \label[proposition]{prop:ll_reduction_to_forcing}
Assume that
\begin{equation}
    Z^n
    \Rightarrow^{\mathrm{st}}
    Z
    \qquad
    \text{in }C([0,1],\mathbb R^d) .
\end{equation}
Then
\[
    \hat U^n
    \Rightarrow^{\mathrm{st}}
    U
    \qquad
    \text{in }C([0,1],\mathbb R^d),
\]
where \(U\) is the unique continuous solution of
\begin{equation}
    U_t^i
    =
    Z_t^i
    +
    \int_0^t
    f^i_j(X_s)U_s^j\,ds,
    \qquad
    U_0=0.
\end{equation}
Equivalently,
\begin{equation}
    dU_t^i
    =
    f^i_j(X_t)U_t^j\,dt
    +
    \frac{1}{4\sqrt3}
    f^i_{jk}(X_t)
    \sigma^j_\alpha\sigma^k_\beta
    \bigl(
        dW_t^{\alpha\beta}
        +
        dW_t^{\beta\alpha}
    \bigr),
    \qquad
    U_0=0.
\end{equation}

\]

body:
Let Omega be a bounded CONVEX domain in R^n with Lipschitz boundary and let u belong to H^2(Omega) intersected with H_0^1(Omega). Then the integral over Omega of |D^2 u|^2 (the squared Frobenius norm of the Hessian) is at most the integral over Omega of (Laplacian u)^2. The constant is 1, with no dependence on the domain; equality holds when the boundary term that convexity discards vanishes. The inequality gives H^2 a priori bounds for the Dirichlet problem on convex domains with NO smoothness of the boundary beyond Lipschitz, which is exactly why it is the tool of choice on polygons and other corner domains where elliptic regularity theory for smooth boundaries does not apply.
CONVEXITY is what makes the boundary term have a sign - on a non-convex domain the inequality with constant 1 can fail.
Membership in H^2 intersected with H_0^1 is assumed, so the inequality is an a priori estimate, not by itself a regularity theorem;
combined with an approximation argument it yields H^2 regularity of the weak solution on convex domains.

Own work draft; PROOF (UNAUDITED); NO NOVELTY CLAIM. Let K=[0,1]^2, c1=(0,0), c2=(1,0), c3=(0,1), phi_i(x)=max(0,1/2-||x-c_i||_1), and f(x)=sum_i phi_i(x)v_i for unit planar v_i at pairwise angle 120 degrees. Let h:K -> R^m and D:R^m -> R^2 be finite piecewise linear maps with D composed with h=f. Either h has a two-dimensional affine image cell or X=h(K) is an embedded finite graph. In the graph case Z=h(f^{-1}(0))=X intersect D^{-1}(0) is a connected subgraph after finite subdivision, and X minus Z has exactly three connected components. With b the number of edge incidences leaving Z and beta_1(Z)=|E(Z)|-|V(Z)|+1, b>=3. The hidden graph satisfies sum_{v in Z}(deg_X(v)-2)=b-2+2 beta_1(Z)>=1. Therefore some vertex in Z has degree at least three and its incident positive tangent rays span dimension at least two. No constancy of h on final fibres is assumed. Every prefix after the first image-dimension drop in an exact finite PL network has this graph property. Branch vertices may move, and their incident edges may map locally to zero rather than to three positive target legs. The charge identity supplies no weight-cost inequality and does not determine R_infinity.
Exactly the specified square tripod
Finite PL prefix and exact finite PL recovering suffix
Graph conclusion applies when no two-dimensional affine image cell exists
Finite graph subdivision includes all suffix zeros on edges; b counts incidences, not distinct complementary components
Own-work draft; proof unaudited; no novelty or parameter-cost conclusion claimed

T276 Target 2. Proof unaudited. Structural reduction, not a determination
of R_infinity. No novelty claim; the graph degree identity is elementary.

Use the fixed square tripod f:K=[0,1]^2 -> Y. Its corner tents are
phi_i=max(0,1/2-||x-c_i||_1), with c1=(0,0),c2=(1,0),c3=(0,1),
and f=sum_i phi_i v_i for three unit 120-degree planar rays v_i.
Let h:K -> R^m be finite PL, and let D be a finite PL suffix satisfying
D composed with h=f on K. A network prefix and its suffix meet these
conditions, including biases and a final linear output.

THE DICHOTOMY. Either h has a two-dimensional affine image cell, or
X=h(K) is an embedded finite graph. In the latter case Z=h(f^{-1}(0))
is a connected subgraph, X minus Z has exactly three connected components,
and at least one vertex of Z has degree at least three in X. In particular
a common hidden graph branch point exists without assuming fibre constancy.
Its incident edges need not be mapped to three positive target legs locally.

STEP 1: the source pieces. The zero fibre is exactly the convex polygon

 F0=K intersect {x+y>=1/2, x-y<=1/2, y-x<=1/2}.

Indeed, positive tent supports are disjoint, so f can vanish only where
all three tents vanish. The other three pieces U_i={phi_i>0} in K are
nonempty convex relative-open corner triangles. They are exactly the
inverse images of the three positive legs of Y. Thus F0 and every U_i
are connected and K is their disjoint union.

STEP 2: the hidden pieces. Put Z=h(F0), X_i=h(U_i). Exact recovery
implies Z=X intersect D^{-1}(0) and
X_i=X intersect D^{-1}({t v_i:0<t<=1/2}). These four sets are disjoint,
cover X, and are connected as continuous images of connected sets.
Each X_i is relatively open in X minus Z (indeed in X), because a
positive leg is relatively open in Y. Hence X_1,X_2,X_3 are precisely
the three connected components of X minus Z. No assumption that h is
constant on a fibre of f was used.

STEP 3: graph structure. A finite PL map on a two-dimensional polytope
has an image which is a finite union of polytopes of dimension at most 2.
If no image cell is two-dimensional, X is a finite union of segments
and points, and it is connected. Nonconstancy of f excludes a singleton.
Subdivide segment intersections and the breakpoints of D on the segments
to obtain an embedded finite graph Gamma. Since D is affine on each
subdivided edge, its zero set there is an endpoint, the entire edge,
or empty; after also subdividing any interior zero, Z is a subgraph.
It is nonempty, compact, and connected by Step 2.

STEP 4: a branch charge on the distributed zero fibre. Let V_Z,E_Z
be the numbers of vertices and edges of Z. Let b count incidences
at vertices of Z of edges of Gamma which are not edges of Z. An edge
with both endpoints in Z, if present outside Z, is counted twice.
Every one of the three components of X minus Z has an attaching edge,
by connectedness of the finite graph Gamma. Thus b>=3. Degree counting
at vertices of Z gives the exact identity

 sum_{v in V(Z)} (deg_Gamma(v)-2)
       =2 E_Z+b-2 V_Z
       =b-2+2 beta_1(Z) >=1,                                 (1)

where beta_1(Z)=E_Z-V_Z+1>=0 because Z is connected.
Therefore some vertex in Z has degree at least three in Gamma.
In an embedded PL graph, distinct edges incident at a vertex have
distinct initial positive tangent rays: overlapping initial segments
would be one edge after subdivision. Three distinct positive rays
cannot lie in one linear line, so their joint linear span has dimension
at least two. This is a local geometric consequence, not a Jacobian-
rank-two assertion for h (whose image is still one-dimensional).

COROLLARY FOR A WHOLE NETWORK. Let h_j be the successive prefix maps.
The maximum dimension of an affine image cell cannot increase after
composition with a finite PL layer: subdivide the image cells into
the next layer's finitely many affine regions, each of which is mapped
affinely and cannot increase dimension. Since h_0 is the square and
the final image is the tripod, there is a first dimension drop from
2 to 1. Every subsequent prefix has a graph image and obeys (1).
Thus its zero fibre may stay distributed, but each graph stage has
an intrinsic branch vertex on that zero fibre.

WHAT THIS RESOLVES. A previous common-center reduction demanded that
all hidden features collapse each final fibre. That hypothesis is
unnecessary merely to find branching in a one-dimensional hidden image.
The branch point is not necessarily the image of one fixed source point
or a point with three positive target directions. It can change from
layer to layer, and the zero subgraph can contain many edges or cycles.

WHAT REMAINS. The charge in (1) is combinatorial. No inequality here
relates its propagation to squared Frobenius weights or bias cost.
The existing acute-pair telescope still needs its angle hypotheses;
degree three does not supply one common acute pair through all layers.
Also the first dimension drop can be arbitrarily late. This reduction
does not imply R_infinity=2 or any new normalized cost bound.

Use the network and assumptions below. In particular, (epsilon_n,B)-orthonormal means | ||x_alpha||^2-1 |<=epsilon_n, |x_alpha^T*x_beta|<=epsilon_n for alpha!=beta, ||X||_op<=B, and sum_alpha (||x_alpha||^2-1)^2<=B^2, with constant B and epsilon_n*n^(1/4)->0. Put b=E sigma'(Z), Z~N(0,1). For a probability law nu on [0,infinity), let MP_gamma(nu) be its Marcenko-Pastur sample-covariance map with dimension/sample ratio gamma: if a deterministic PSD n-by-n matrix Phi has empirical law nu and G is d-by-n with independent N(0,1/d) entries, n/d->gamma, it is the limiting law of Phi^(1/2)*G^T*G*Phi^(1/2). Equivalently its Stieltjes transform m(z)=integral(lambda-z)^(-1)dMP_gamma(nu)(lambda) solves m(z)=integral[x*(1-gamma-gamma*z*m(z))-z]^(-1)dnu(x), with the Stieltjes branch. Recursively set nu_l=Law(1-b^2+b^2*lambda), lambda~mu_(l-1), and mu_l=MP_gamma_l(nu_l). Then for every fixed l=1,...,L, the empirical eigenvalue distribution of X_l^T*X_l converges weakly almost surely to mu_l. In particular K_CK=X_L^T*X_L has limit mu_L and ||K_CK||_op<=C almost surely for all sufficiently large n. If b=0, mu_l is the ordinary Marcenko-Pastur law with ratio gamma_l. These are bulk limits; convergence of individual extreme eigenvalues to support edges is not asserted.
Fixed integer depth L>=1; n,d_0,...,d_L tend to infinity; n/d_l->gamma_l in (0,infinity) for l=1,...,L.
All weights W_l in R^(d_l by d_(l-1)) and w in R^d_L have independent N(0,1) entries, independent of the input matrices.
sigma:R->R is twice differentiable with globally bounded first and second derivatives. For Z~N(0,1), E sigma(Z)=0 and E sigma(Z)^2=1.
X_0 is (epsilon_n,B)-orthonormal as in the companion definition for constant B, epsilon_n*n^(1/4)->0; the ESD of X_0^T X_0 converges to a deterministic probability measure mu_0.
X_l=d_l^(-1/2)*sigma(W_l*X_(l-1)) entrywise, l=1,...,L. The input is fixed, or the stated input conditions hold almost surely independently of the Gaussian weights.

[Definition defn:Dd of arXiv:2604.10020, 'The directed landscape in half-space'] For each $d\in \mathbb{N}$, let $\Lambda_d$ be the following directed graph. Its vertices consist of all $(x, a)\in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0} \times \mathbb{Z}_{2d}$ with $x+a\in 2\mathbb{Z}$, where $\mathbb{Z}_{2d}=\mathbb{Z}/2d\mathbb{Z}=\{0,\ldots, 2d-1\}$.
For each vertex $(x,a)$, there is a directed edge from it to $(x+1, a+1)$, and a directed edge from it to $(x-1, a+1)$, if $x\ge 1$. (Here our space is periodic, so $a, a + 1$ are understood modulo $2d$).
We let $D_d:\Lambda_d^2\to \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$ be the resulting directed metric on $\Lambda_d$, i.e., $D_d((x,a), (y,b))$ is the length of the shortest directed path from $(x,a)$ to $(y,b)$.
title: Definition defn:Dd of arXiv:2604.10020

body: [Abstract of arXiv:2609.03669, 'Volterra Integral Reduction \\ for Boundary Diffusion Problems'] This paper addresses a class of integral representations of the form \begin{equation} f(t,x)=g(t,x)+\int_0^t k(t,s)\, p(t-s,x,y)\, \partial_x f(s,y^+)\,ds, \qquad 0 \le t \le T, \end{equation} where $f$ is unknown, $p$ is the transition density of a diffusion process, and $g, k$ are prescribed functions. For an arbitrary diffusion process with sufficiently regular coefficients, we prove that this problem is equivalent to a Volterra integral equation of the second kind. This reduction provides a unified framework for both theoretical analysis and numerical approximation. An example of the implementation in the context of financial mathematics is presented.
title: Abstract of arXiv:2609.03669: Volterra Integral Reduction \\ for Boundary Diffusion Problems

Let m,n be positive integers, x_1,...,x_m and y_1,...,y_m be points in R^n, and let d be a finite-valued metric on R^n. Repeated points are allowed. For 1<=p<infinity set mu=m^(-1) sum_i delta_(x_i) and nu=m^(-1) sum_i delta_(y_i). Then W_p(mu,nu)^p = min_(pi in S_m) m^(-1) sum_i d(x_i,y_(pi(i)))^p. Equivalently the p-Wasserstein distance is the p-th root of this minimum. Thus an optimal Kantorovich cost for two equal-cardinality, equal-weight empirical measures can be attained by a permutation matching. No independence of the two point clouds, or within either cloud, is needed for this deterministic identity. It gives no bound on how small the matching cost is, and does not by itself give a convergence rate for dependent neurons.
finite point clouds of the same positive cardinality
each atom has weight 1/m; repeated locations permitted
finite-valued ground metric; 1<=p<infinity

[Theorem 9 (Well-posedness of RDEs) of arXiv:2512.04646, '\textbf{Canonical Rough Path over Tempered Fractional Brownian Motion: Existence, Construc'] Let $H > 1/4$, $\lambda > 0$,
$f \in C^3_b(\mathbb{R}^d,\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^m,\mathbb{R}^d))$,
and $y_0 \in \mathbb{R}^d$. The rough differential equation
\begin{equation}

dY_t = f(Y_t)\,d\mathbf{B}_{H,\lambda}(t), \qquad Y_0 = y_0,
\end{equation}
admits a unique solution
$Y \in \mathscr{C}^p([0,T],\mathbb{R}^d)$ for any $p > 1/H$.
The solution map $(y_0,f,\mathbf{B}_{H,\lambda})\mapsto Y$ is
locally Lipschitz continuous.

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Deterministic strong convergence from LPS generators structural calculation Result: Weak freeness plus the usual adjacency norm is insufficient in general. Start with any strongly convergent r-unitary model and append a one-dimensional block in which every generator equals z=exp(i*theta), with cos(theta)=sqrt(2r-1)/r. This block does not change limiting traces and its adjacency eigenvalue is exactly2*sqrt(2r-1). Yet the phase-twisted adjacency polynomial has value2r on that block, above its free norm2*sqrt(2r-1). Check: Normalized trace weight of the added block tends to0. Multiplying each free Haar generator by a fixed phase preserves the free law and norm. Thus both asserted facts hold while a different linear polynomial has a persistent outlier. Obstruction: This is an obstruction to inferring strong convergence from one spectral-gap theorem; the constructed scalar blocks are not the actual LPS representation, so the source conjecture is not refuted.

[Defn 11 of arXiv:2605.15501, 'Well-posedness of the obstacle problem for generalized Dean--Kawasaki equation\thanks{ The'] For fixed $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, a stochastic kinetic
solution of \eqref{eq:penalized eq} is a nonnegative, almost surely continuous $L^{1}(\mathbb{T}^{d})$-valued $\mathcal{F}_{t}$-predictable function $u_\varepsilon\in L^{1}(\Omega\times[0,T];L^{1}(\mathbb{T}^{d}))$ satisfying following properties.
\begin{itemize}
\item[(i)] Preservation of mass: almost surely for every $\phi\in C_c^{\infty}([0,T))$,
\begin{align}
    -\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d} u_\varepsilon\partial_s\phi(s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s+\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\phi(s)\varepsilon^{-1}(u_\varepsilon-\psi)^{+}\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s=\int_{\mathbb{T}^d} u_{\mathrm{init}}\phi(0)\mathrm{d}x
\end{align}
\item[(ii)] $\sigma(u_\varepsilon)\in L^{2}(\Omega;L^{2}(Q_T))$,\quad $g(u_\varepsilon)\in L^{1}(\Omega;L^{1}(Q_T;\mathbb{R}^d))$.
\item[(iii)] For every $K\in\mathbb{N}$,
\[
[(u_\varepsilon\land K)\lor(1/K)]\in L^{2}(\Omega\times[0,T];H^{1}(\mathbb{T}^{d}))).
\]
Furthermore, there exists a kinetic measure $m_\varepsilon$ satisfying the following properties.
\item[(iv)] Almost surely as a nonnegative measure, $m_\varepsilon$ satisfies
\[
\delta_{0}(\xi-u_\varepsilon)\Phi^{\prime}(\xi)|\nabla u_\varepsilon|^{2}\leq m_\varepsilon\quad\text{on}\quad\mathbb{T}^{d}\times(0,\infty)\times[0,T].
\]
\item[(v)] (Vanishing)
\[
\lim_{N\to\infty}\mathbb{E}\big[m_\varepsilon(\mathbb{T}^{d}\times[N,N+1]\times[0,T))\big]=0.
\]
\item[(vi)] Preservation of energy: for every $\phi\in C_c^{\infty}([0,T))$,
\begin{align}
&-\mathbb{E}\int_0^T\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}u_\varepsilon^2(x,s)\partial_s\phi(s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s+\frac{2}{\varepsilon}\mathbb{E}\int_0^T\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\phi(s)\psi(x,s)(u_\varepsilon-\psi)^+\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\\
&+\frac{2}{\varepsilon}\mathbb{E}\int_0^T\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\phi(s)|(u_\varepsilon-\psi)^+|^2\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s+2\mathbb{E}\int_0^T\phi(s)\mathrm{d}m_\varepsilon(\mathbb{T}^d,[0,\infty),s)\nonumber\\
&=\mathbb{E}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}u^2_{\mathrm{init}}(x)\phi(0)\mathrm{d}x-\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\phi(s)\sigma^2(u_{\varepsilon})(\nabla_{x}\cdot F_{2}-2F_3)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s.\nonumber
\end{align}
\item[(vii)] For every $\phi\in C_{c}^{1}(\mathbb{T}^{d}\times(0,\infty)\times[0,T))$, the kinetic function $\chi_\varepsilon$ of $u_\varepsilon$ almost surely satisfies
\begin{align}
& -\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\chi_\varepsilon(x,\xi,s)\partial_s\phi(x,\xi,s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}\xi\mathrm{d}s\\
 & =\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\bar{\chi}(u_{\mathrm{init}},\xi)\phi(x,\xi,0)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}\xi-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\Phi^{\prime}(u_\varepsilon)\nabla_x u_\varepsilon\cdot(\nabla_x\phi)(x,u_\varepsilon,s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\nonumber \\
 & \quad-\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\big(F_{1}(x)[\sigma^{\prime}(u_\varepsilon)]^{2}\nabla_x u_\varepsilon+\sigma(u_\varepsilon)\sigma^{\prime}(u_\varepsilon)F_{2}(x)\big)\cdot(\nabla_x\phi)(x,u_\varepsilon,s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\nonumber\\
 & \quad-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\partial_{\xi}\phi(x,\xi,s)\mathrm{d}m_\varepsilon(x,\xi,s)-\int_0^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\phi(x,u_\varepsilon,s)\nabla_x\cdot g(u_\varepsilon)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\nonumber \\
 & \quad+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\Big(\sigma(u_\varepsilon)\sigma^{\prime}(u_\varepsilon)\nabla_x u_\varepsilon\cdot F_{2}(x)+\sigma^{2}(u_\varepsilon)F_{3}(x)\Big)(\partial_{\xi}\phi)(x,u_\varepsilon,s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\nonumber \\
 
 & \quad-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\phi(x,u_\varepsilon,s)\frac{1}{\varepsilon}(u_\varepsilon-\psi)^+\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\phi(x,u_\varepsilon,s)\nabla_x\cdot(\sigma(u_\varepsilon)f_{k})\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}B_{s}^{k}.\nonumber
\end{align}
\end{itemize}

[Proposition 6 of arXiv:2608.13631, 'The classical discrete laws near the mode:\\ complete local expansions for the negative bi'] Fix $t$ and $n\ge1$, and let $r\to\infty$, $q\to0$ with $rq=\lambda$ held fixed.  Then the
	$n$-th term of \eqref{eq:nb-main} converges to the $n$-th term of the Poisson expansion
	\eqref{eq:poi-local}:
	\[
		\frac{A_n(t;p)}{r^{n}}\;\longrightarrow\;
		-\frac{(-1)^{n+1}B_{n+1}(t+1)}{n(n+1)}\,\frac1{\lambda^{n}} ,
	\]
	and $\sigma^{2}=rq/p^{2}\to\lambda$: the negative binomial expansion degenerates
	coefficientwise to the Poisson one.

[Proposition 7 of arXiv:2606.00945, 'Ising model and percolation: from hexagonal lattice to 3-12 lattice'] Fix $N\ge 1$ and $2N$-polygon $(\Omega;y_1,\ldots,y_{2N})$. 
Suppose $(\Omega_{\312}^\delta;y_1^\delta,\ldots, y_{2N}^\delta)$ is a family of discrete polygons such that $(\Omega_{\312}^\delta;y_1^\delta,\ldots,y_{2N}^\delta)$ converges to $(\Omega;y_1,\ldots,y_{2N})$ in the close-Carathéodory sense as $\delta\to 0$. 
Let $\LA^\delta_{\312}$ be the link pattern for percolation with $p=1/2$ in $(\Omega_{\312}^{\delta, *}; y_1^\delta,\ldots, y_{2N}^\delta)$ with alternating boundary conditions. Then the scaling limits for probabilities for the link pattern are conformally invariant:
\begin{align}
\lim_{\delta\to 0}\PP_{\Perco}\left[\LA_{\312}^{\delta}=\alpha\right]=\LZ_{\alpha}^{(6)}(\Omega; y_1, \ldots, y_{2N}), \qquad\text{for all }\alpha\in\LP_N, 
\end{align}
where $\{\LZ_{\alpha}^{(6)}: \alpha\in\LP_N\}$ are the pure partition functions for multiple $\SLE_6$ given in Definition~\ref{def::pure_partition}. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: For a real n by n matrix B_n with mutually independent uniform {-1,1} entries, the exact-one target asks for one c in (0,1) such that P(s_min(B_n)<=epsilon/sqrt(n))<=epsilon+c^n for every n>=1 and epsilon>=0. Current openness is UNKNOWN. Sah-Sahasrabudhe-Sawhney, arXiv:2405.20308v2 Theorem 1.1, prove a coefficient 1+O((log n)^(-1/16)), which does not by itself prove exact one. The original source is Spielman-Teng ICM 2002 Conjecture 2, p.605. These results do not extend an exact-one assertion to arbitrary entry laws or deterministic shifts.
title: CONJECTURE: exact-one Spielman-Teng target and scope

body:
Let X be a random vector in a real separable Hilbert space with E||X||^2<infinity and covariance H=E[X tensor X]. Assume exact interpolation: Y=<X,theta_star> almost surely for a fixed theta_star in the Hilbert space. Assume R>0 and the operator fourth-moment bound E[||X||^2*(X tensor X)]<=R*H in positive-semidefinite order. Start theta_0=0 and use fresh IID examples with the single-example SGD update theta_(t+1)=theta_t-gamma*(<X_(t+1),theta_t>-Y_(t+1))*X_(t+1), where gamma>0 is constant during the run. Put D=||theta_star||^2 and f_t=E Rcal(theta_t), where Rcal(theta)=E(<X,theta>-Y)^2/2 =||H^(1/2)*(theta-theta_star)||^2/2; the outer expectation is over SGD samples. For each integer horizon T>=2, choose gamma=1/[4*R*ln(T)]. Then E Rcal(theta_T)<=3*R*||theta_star||^2*ln(T)/T. This concerns the final iterate with a horizon-dependent step size held constant for that run. It does not assert the same rate for one fixed step size simultaneously at all horizons, for additive label noise, or for arbitrary interpolating nonquadratic losses. No strong convexity is assumed.
Fresh IID noiseless samples, theta_star in the real Hilbert space, theta_0=0.
H=E[X tensor X] with E||X||^2<infinity; E[||X||^2*(X tensor X)]<=R*H for R>0.
Integer T>=2; known horizon; gamma=1/[4*R*ln(T)] is constant within the run.

[Definition 16 (Factor of i.i.d.) of arXiv:2603.28734, 'Free energy analyticity of the disordered XY model and Debye screening in the 2D Coulomb g'] Consider a locally finite transitive graph $G=(V,E)$
    (with respect to some group $\Theta\subset\operatorname{Aut}(G)$).
    Let $S$ denote a measurable space,
    and let $\mu$ denote the distribution of a $\Theta$-stationary random field on $S^V$.
    Let $(T,\lambda)$ denote a probability space, and consider $\P:=\lambda^V$.
    A \emph{factor of i.i.d.}\ (FIID) is a map $\phi:T^V\to S^V$
    with the following properties:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $\phi$ is measurable with respect to the product $\sigma$-algebras on $T^V$ and $S^V$,
        \item $\phi$ is equivariant with respect to $\Theta$,
        \item If $X\sim\P$, then $\phi(X)\sim\mu$.
    \end{itemize}
title: Factor of i.i.d.

body: [Theorem rep theorem of arXiv:2609.04023, 'Characterizing Contractions and Weighted Blowdowns'] Suppose $\mathcal{X}$ and $\mathcal{Z}$ are smooth separated Deligne--Mumford stacks, and there is a representable contraction morphism $f : \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{Z}$ whose exceptional $\mathcal{E}$ is a smooth Cartier divisor. Moreover, suppose there is a smooth closed Deligne--Mumford substack $\mathcal{Y} \subseteq \mathcal{Z}$, such that $f^{-1}(\mathcal{Y}) \simeq \mathcal{E}$ set-theoretically, and $f : \mathcal{X} \setminus \mathcal{E} \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathcal{Z} \setminus \mathcal{Y}$. Then $f$ is an ordinary blowup with reduced center $\mathcal{Y}$, in particular $f|_{\mathcal{E}} : \mathcal{E} \to \mathcal{Y}$ is a projective bundle, and $\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X}}(\mathcal{E})|_{\mathcal{E}} \simeq \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{E}}(-1) \otimes f^*\mathcal{L}$ for some line bundle $\mathcal{L}$ on $\mathcal{Y}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem rep theorem of arXiv:2609.04023

[Theo 25 of arXiv:2602.14618, 'Finitary coding and Gaussian concentration\\ for random fields'] Let $d\ge1$ and let $Y=(Y_i)_{i\in\Zd}$ be a random field taking values in a finite set $B$.
If $Y$ satisfies exponential strong spatial mixing, then $Y$ satisfies Gaussian concentration.
If $d=2$ and $Y$ satisfies exponential weak spatial mixing for squares and has no hard constraints, that is, if the topological support of its law is $B^{\Zd}$, then $Y$ also satisfies Gaussian concentration. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theo 25 of arXiv:2602.14618

[Theorem 7 (\cite{VanDenBerg}) of arXiv:2507.06186, '2507.06186'] Suppose that $D$ is simply connected and that $\partial D$ is Minkowski nondegenerate with
Minkowski dimension $\msf d_M(\partial D)\in[1,2)$. That is,
\[0<\liminf_{r\to0}\frac{\msf{A}(\partial D_r)}{r^{2-\msf d_M(\partial D)}}\leq
\limsup_{r\to0}\frac{\msf{A}(\partial D_r)}{r^{2-\msf d_M(\partial D)}}<\infty,\]
where we define
\[\partial D_r=\left\{x\in\mbb R^2:\inf_{y\in\partial D}|x-y|<r\right\}.\]
There exists constants $c\in(1,\infty)$ and $\th>0$ such that
\begin{align}

c^{-1}t^{1-\msf d_M(\partial D)/2}\leq\msf{A}(D)-\msf M_0(t)\leq ct^{1-\msf d_M(\partial D)/2},\qquad t\in(0,\th).
\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: \cite{VanDenBerg}

[Proposition 48 of arXiv:2608.05931, 'Effective Lagrangian regularity and the uniqueness threshold for random H\"older velocity '] Suppose $u : \T^d \to \R^d$, $\alpha \in (0,1)$, and $Z := \{u =0\} \subseteq \T^d$ are such that
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $\nabla \cdot u=0,$
        \item $u \in C^\alpha(\T^d)$,
        \item $\liminf_{r \to 0} r^{-(1-\alpha)} |\{ x \in \T^d : d_{\T^d}(x,Z) \leq r\}| =0$,
        \item and for all $\tau>0, y \in \T^d$, if $X^1, X^2$ are solutions to~\eqref{eq:abstract ode} on $[0,\tau]$ such that for all $t \in [0,\tau]$, $X^1_t, X^2_t \not \in Z$, then $X^1|_{[0,\tau]} = X^2|_{[0,\tau]}$.
    \end{enumerate}
    Then for almost every $y \in \T^d$,~\eqref{eq:abstract ode} admits a unique solution on $[0,\infty)$.

body:
[Definition def:gamma of arXiv:2509.04333, 'The limiting law of the Discrete Gaussian level lines'] Let $\phi$ be a
		$\mathbb Z$-valued height function on the vertices of a connected domain $V\subset \mathbb Z^2$. Associate to each bond $e\in (\mathbb Z^2)^*$, dual to some edge $(x,y)\in\mathbb Z^2$, the gradient $(
abla \phi)_e := \phi_x - \phi_y$, where $x$ is taken to be the 	extsc{north} vertex if $(x,y)$ is vertical and the 	extsc{west} vertex if $(x,y)$ is horizontal. We say the bond $e$ is a \emph{disagreement bond} of $\phi$ if $(
abla\phi)_e
eq 0$ (including when $\phi_x$ or $\phi_y$ are specified by the boundary conditions). A \emph{disagreement polymer}~$\gamma$ is a (maximal) connected component of the disagreement bonds of $\phi$, and we let $\ensuremath{\mathcal P}_\phi$ denote the disagreement polymers in $\phi$. For such a polymer, let $D_i$ be the connected components of $V \setminus \gamma$, noting that by the maximality of $\gamma$, within each $D_i$, all the vertices that are $*$-adjacent to $V\setminus D_i$ must have the same height $h_i$ in~$\phi$. Call the triple $(\gamma, \{D_i\}, \{h_i\})$ a \emph{labeled disagreement polymer}. For brevity,  we denote labeled disagreement polymers by $\gamma$ (omitting the $\{h_i\}$ from the notation).
title: Disagreement polymer

[Proposition 11 of arXiv:2607.23640, '{\sl Non-equilibrium fluctuations of a two-species exclusion process with slow boundary }'] Let \(\bm f=(f_1,f_2)^\top\in\mathscr S^\dagger \). The sequence of martingales $ \left\{
	\bm M_t^n(\bm f):0\le t\le T \right\}_{n\in \mathbb{N} }$ converges in 
	the topology of  $ \mathcal D([0,T], \mathbb{R})$, as $ n  \to \infty $, towards a mean-zero Gaussian process \(W_t(\bm f)\) with quadratic variation given by
	\[
	\Phi_{11}+\Phi_{12}+\Phi_{21}+\Phi_{22},
	\]
	where, for \(k=1,2\),
	\[
	\begin{aligned}
		\Phi_{kk}
		&=
		\int_0^t
		\Bigg\{
		\int_0^1
		2\rho_k(s,u)
		\left(
		1-\rho_k(s,u)
		\right)
		\left(
		\partial_u f_k(u)
		\right)^2
		\,\mathrm du                                     
		+
		\int_0^1
		\left(
		\gamma_1\rho_1(s,u)
		+
		\gamma_2\rho_2(s,u)
		\right)
		f_k(u)^2
		\,\mathrm du                                      \\
		&\quad
		+
		\left(
		\alpha_k\rho_0(s,0)
		+
		\alpha_0\rho_k(s,0)
		\right)
		f_k(0)^2                                  
		+
		\left(
		\beta_k\rho_0(s,1)
		+
		\beta_0\rho_k(s,1)
		\right)
		f_k(1)^2
		\Bigg\}
		\,\mathrm ds,
	\end{aligned}
	\]
	and, for \(k\neq l\),
	\[
	\begin{aligned}
		\Phi_{kl}
		&=
		-
		\int_0^t
		\Bigg\{
		\int_0^1
		2\rho_1(s,u)\rho_2(s,u)
		\partial_u f_1(u)
		\partial_u f_2(u)
		\,\mathrm du                                      \\
		&\quad
		+
		\int_0^1
		\left(
		\gamma_1\rho_1(s,u)
		+
		\gamma_2\rho_2(s,u)
		\right)
		f_1(u)f_2(u)
		\,du
		\Bigg\}
		\,\mathrm ds .
	\end{aligned}

Let u: {-1, 1}^n -> R under the uniform measure, with Fourier coefficients u^(S) = E[u chi_S], derivatives D_i u(x) = (u(x with x_i = 1) - u(x with x_i = -1))/2 and total influence I(u) = sum_i E[(D_i u)^2]. Then I(u) - Var(u) = sum over |S| >= 2 of (|S| - 1) u^(S)^2. Hence Var(u) <= I(u) (the Poincare inequality of the cube), with equality iff u is affine, u^(S) = 0 for |S| >= 2. With Pi u = u^(empty) + sum_i u^({i}) x_i the affine part, ||u - Pi u||_2^2 = sum over |S| >= 2 of u^(S)^2 <= I(u) - Var(u), with equality iff u^(S) = 0 for every |S| >= 3.

[Lemma funclimit-bev of arXiv:2412.03325, 'Functional limit theorem for branching processes \\ in nearly degenerate varying environme'] Assume that conditions (C1)--(C3) and either (C4) or (C4') hold.
Then for the BPVEI $(Y_n)$ defined in (equation eq:Y of the paper),
\[
\lim_{n \to \infty} g_{A(nu),A(nt)}(s) =
\frac{f_Y(s)}{f_Y(h_{u/t}(s))},
\]
and for any $y \in \mathbb{N}$
\[
\lim_{n \to \infty} \mathbf{E} [ s^{Y_{A(nt)}} | Y_{A(nu)} = y ]
= \frac{f_Y(s)}{f_Y(h_{u/t}(s))} \left( h_{u/t}(s) \right)^y.
\]
Furthermore, the transition generating functions
\begin{equation*} 
G_y(s, t) = \frac{f_Y(s)}{f_Y(h_{e^{-t}}(s))} \left( h_{e^{-t}}(s) \right)^y
\end{equation*}
define a homogeneous standard honest transition function of a Markov branching 
process with immigration.

body: In arithmetic combinatorics, Szemerédi's theorem is a result concerning arithmetic progressions in subsets of the integers. In 1936, Erdős and Turán conjectured that every set of integers A with positive natural density contains a k-term arithmetic progression for every k. Endre Szemerédi proved the conjecture in 1975.

[Lemma lem:mmean of arXiv:2608.30254, 'Exact Recovery Thresholds for Weighted Data Selection\\ in Vector-Valued Linear Regression'] Let $z_i\in\mathbb{R}^m$ carry weights $p_i>0$ with $\sum_ip_iz_i=0$, and let
$E=\sum_ip_i\lVert z_i\rVert^2$. Then some convex combination $\delta$ of at most

attained by the uniformly weighted regular simplex.

[Defini 15 of arXiv:2608.27934, 'An example of biquandle and an invariant of long virtual knots defined through it'] (Sieblings)\\
For a long virtual knot $K$, take its long virtual knot diagram $D$. 
Let $-D$ denote the long virtual knot diagram obtained by reversing the orientation of $D$. 
Let $D^{\#}$ denote the long virtual knot diagram obtained by replacing each classical crossing of $D$ by a crossing of the opposite sign. 
Let $D^{*}$ denote the long virtual knot diagram obtained by applying a planar reflection of $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ to $D$. 
Set $-K$, $K^{\#}$ and $K^{*}$  to be long virtual knots represented by $-D$, $D^{\#}$ and $D^{*}$, respectively, and call them {\it the reverse of} $K$, {\it the vertical mirror} of $K$ and {\it the horizontal mirror} of $K$, respectively.
title: Definition 15 of arXiv:2608.27934

[Lem 3 of arXiv:2609.00598, 'Supercritical mean--field limit for magnetized Hamiltonian dynamics'] Let $u,v,w:\mathbb{T}^{d}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{d}$ be given smooth vector fields. 
Then the following formulas hold{\rm:} 
\begin{itemize}  \item[{\rm(i)}]
$\mathrm{div}_{x}(u\otimes v)=\mathrm{div}_{x}(v)u+(D_xu)^{\top}v$.
 \item[{\rm(ii)}]
$u(v\cdot w)=(u\otimes v)w.$ 
 \item[{\rm(iii)}] If $f:\mathbb{T}^{d}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ and 
$\mathbf{a}:\mathbb{T}^{d}\rightarrow M_{d}(\mathbb{R})$ are smooth, 
then 
\begin{align*}
\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\mathbf{a}(x)\nabla_{x}f(x)\ \dd x
=-\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\mathrm{div}_{x}(\mathbf{a})f(x)\ \dd x.     
\end{align*}
 \item[{\rm(iv)}] If $\mathbf{a}:\mathbb{T}^{d}\rightarrow M_{d}(\mathbb{R})$ is smooth, 
 then 
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{div}_{x}(\mathbf{a}u)
=\mathrm{div}_{x}(\mathbf{a}^\top)\cdot u+\mathbf{a}^\top:D_{x}u.
\end{align*}

 \item[{\rm(v)}] If $v:\mathbb{T}^{2}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{2}$ 
 is a smooth divergence-free vector field, {\it i.e.}, $\mathrm{div}_{x}v=0$,
 then 
\begin{align*}
-\nabla^{\perp}_{x}(v\cdot \nabla_{x} \mathrm{div}_{x}(v^{\perp}))
=\Delta_{x} \mathrm{div}_{x}(v\otimes v)-\nabla_{x} \mathrm{div}_{x}\mathrm{div}_{x}(v\otimes v).    
\end{align*}
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

DRAFT; author proof, independent mathematical review pending. For n>=81 put t=floor(sqrt(n)), a=t, b=2t+1, k=t+1, and m=floor(n/2). Let D_n be the interior of the union of the rectangles [0,a/n]x[0,1], [b/n,1]x[0,1], and [a/n,b/n]x[(m-1/2)/n,(m+1/2)/n]. Each D_n is a simply connected Jordan polygon with fixed corner marks A=(0,1), B=(0,0), C=(1,0), D=(1,1). Its closure Hausdorff distance from the closed unit square is <=k/(2n), its boundary Hausdorff distance is <=b/n, its area loss is k(n-1)/n^2, and its unmarked Caratheodory kernel at (1/2,1/2) is the open unit square. Yet in the induced nearest-neighbor graph on mesh-1/n vertices in its closure, independent bonds p=1/2 give P(AB connects CD)<=2^-k, tending to zero: only the row y=m/n joins the chambers. Canonical square crossings are uniformly positive by classical RSW. The missing marked-prime-end convergence is essential; this example refutes an overstrong approximation bridge, not the properly marked C0017 target.

Independent square-lattice bonds p=1/2
Source AB is x=0; sink CD is x=1
No external wiring
Geometric convergence is unmarked; marked prime ends need not converge

[Lemma 42 (One-step Wasserstein inequality) of arXiv:2605.24937, '2605.24937'] Let $L>0$ be the $W_2$-Lipschitz constant from Proposition~\ref{prop:W2-Lip-app}, let $\Gamma(x,y,\lambda)$ be the coupling increment from Proposition~\ref{prop:coupling-increment-app}, and let $E_{\mathrm{weak}},E_{\mathrm{strong}}:\R^d\to[0,\infty)$ denote the weak and strong one-step local errors of \eqref{eq:kTULA} (Propositions~\ref{prop:weak-error-app}--\ref{prop:strong-error-app}). Then, for all $x,y\in\R^d$,
\[

\]

Let X be a Banach space, Y a normed space, and {T_i : i in I} a family (of any cardinality) of bounded linear operators from X to Y. If the family is pointwise bounded, meaning sup over i of ||T_i(x)|| is finite for every x in X, then it is uniformly bounded: sup over i of the operator norms ||T_i|| is finite. Consequently, if a sequence of bounded operators on a Banach space converges pointwise, the limit operator is bounded. Completeness of the domain is essential.

[Lemma 8 of arXiv:2604.09248, '\bfseries Limit laws for longest edges in empty region graphs'] Suppose that the assumptions of Theorem \ref{thm:PoisConvAbstract} are satisfied and that $\log(t)+\tau+b>0$. Then, for the point process $\xi_t|_{W \times [b,\infty)\times\LL^d}$, the quantities $E_2$, $E_3$, and $E_4$ in Theorem \ref{thm:BSY} {with $S_{(x,y)}:=S(x,y)\cup\{x,y\}$ for $x,y\in\mathbb{R}^d$} are bounded by
    \[
    E_2 \le C_2 \frac{1+ b+ \log(t) + \tau}{e^{2b}t}, \quad E_3 \le \frac{C_3}{e^b(b+\log(t)+\tau)^{\max\{d-2, 1/2\}}},\quad
    E_4 \le \frac{C_{4,1}}{e^b(b+\log(t)+\tau)^{d-1}}+\frac{C_{4,2}}{e^{2b}t}.
    \]
    Here, $C_2$, $C_3$, $C_{4,1}$, and $C_{4,2}$ are constants in $(0,\infty)$ depending only on $d$ and $W$ as well as the constants $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ in Theorem \ref{thm:PoisConvAbstract}. Possible choices are
    \[
    C_2 := \frac{2^{d+1} \kappa_d \alpha^d}{\gamma}\vol(W),\quad C_3 := \begin{cases}
        \frac{4 d \kappa_d^2 M_{d-1}\gamma^{d-2}}{\beta^d(d-2)}\vol(W), & d \ge 3,\\
        {\frac{16\sqrt{2} \pi^{5/2}}{\beta^2\sqrt{\gamma}}\vol(W),} & d = 2,
    \end{cases}\quad
    C_{4,1} := \frac{2^{d+4} d \kappa_d M_{d-1}\gamma^{d-1}}{\beta^d} \vol(W), 
    \]
and $C_{4,2}:=16\vol(W)$, where $M_{d-1} := (2(d-1)/e)^{d-1}$.

[Proposition 13 of arXiv:2604.25336, 'Central limit theorem for slow-fast system under mixed fractional Brownian motion'] Under assumptions \textbf{H1}-\textbf{H3}. Define \(\hat g(x,y):=g(x,y)-\bar g(x)\) and 
\begin{equation}
\Psi(x,y) =\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathcal{P}_t^x \hat g(x, Y_t^x) \dd t.
\end{equation} 
The \(\Psi(x,y)\) is the solution to the Poisson equation \eqref{Poisson_eq} where \(h\) is replaced by \(\hat g\).
Moreover, \(\Psi(x,y)\in C^2\). For all \((x,y)\in \mathbb{R}^n\times \mathbb{R}^m\), \(D_x\Psi(x,y)\) and \(D^2_{xx}\Psi(x,y)\) are linear growth. Specially,
\(D_y\Psi(x,y), D^2_{xy}\Psi(x,y), D^2_{yy}\Psi(x,y)\) are globally bounded. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition Continuous function spaces of arXiv:2609.01984, 'Instantaneous shrinking of supports for stochastic PDEs\footnote{JY was supported by a KIA'] For $A\subset\mathbb{R}$, let $C(A)$ denote the space of real-valued continuous
functions on $A$. We define
\[
    C_{\rm tem}(A)
    :=
    \left\{
        u\in C(A):
        \sup_{x\in A}|u(x)|e^{-a|x|}<\infty
        \text{ for every }a>0
    \right\}.
\]
For $\delta\in(0,1)$, define
\[
C^\delta(A)
:=
\left\{
u\in C(A):
\|u\|_{C^\delta(A)}
:=
\sup_{x\in A}|u(x)|
+
\sup_{\substack{x,y\in A\\x\ne y}}
\frac{|u(x)-u(y)|}{|x-y|^\delta}
<\infty
\right\}.
\] 
For any subsets $A$ and $B$ of Banach spaces, we denote by $C(A;B)$  the space of continuous functions from $A$ to $B$. We omit $A$ (or $B$) if $A$ (or $B$) is $\mathbb{R}$. We define $C_{c}^{\infty}$ as the space of infinitely differentiable function with compact support.

 r_{h,k}(M_{h,k}-2)=2.

body:
[Lemma lem:universal-root of arXiv:2608.29403, 'Kac's Walk on Rotation Matrices Mixes in $\boldsymbol{\Theta(n^2)}$ Steps:\\ A Proof Disco'] Let $X,Z\in\operatorname{End}(W)$ be arbitrary, let $a_1,\ldots,a_N$ be the Kac
orthonormal basis of $W=\mathfrak{so}(n)$, and put $A_i=\operatorname{ad}_{a_i}$.
Define
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \mathcal R_i(X,Z)&=\{X,[A_i,Z]\}a_i,&
 U_i(X,Z)&=\{X,Z\}a_i,\\
 E_i(X,Z)&=\{[A_i,X],Z\}a_i,&
 \bar E(X,Z)&=\frac1N\sum_iE_i(X,Z).
\end{aligned}
\tag{3.2.10a}
\]
Put $\Psi(T)=\sum_jA_jTa_j$.  Then, with no projection onto curvature
summands,
\[
 \mathcal R_i=A_iU_i-(E_i-\bar E)-\bar E,
 \qquad
 \bar E=\frac1N\sum_jA_jV_j+H(X,Z),\qquad V_j=XZa_j,
\tag{3.2.10b}
\]
where
\[
 H(X,Z)=\frac1N\{-X\Psi(Z)+Z\Psi(X)\}.
\tag{3.2.10b$'$}
\]
Moreover, writing $\|\cdot\|_2$ for Hilbert--Schmidt norm,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \frac1N\sum_i\|U_i\|^2
 &\le\frac4N\|X\|_2^2\|Z\|_\mathrm{op}^2,\\
 \frac1N\sum_j\|V_j\|^2
 &\le\frac1N\|X\|_2^2\|Z\|_\mathrm{op}^2,\\
 \frac1N\sum_i\|E_i-\bar E\|^2
 &\le\frac{16(n-2)}N\|X\|_2^2\|Z\|_\mathrm{op}^2.
\end{aligned}
\tag{3.2.10c}
\]
The residue satisfies
\[
 \|H(X,Z)\|
 \le\frac{\sqrt{n-2}}N
 \bigl(\|X\|_\mathrm{op}\|Z\|_2+\|Z\|_\mathrm{op}\|X\|_2\bigr).
\tag{3.2.10e}
\]

[Theorem thm:main of arXiv:2609.01464, 'Removability of non-isolated singularities for Einstein metrics and RCD spaces'] For every integer $n\geqslant 1$ and every $\kappa>0$, there are $
 \varepsilon=\varepsilon(n,\kappa)>0$ and $
 C=C(n,\kappa)>0$
with the following property. Let $(X,\ensuremath{\mathrm d},\mathcal H^n,x)$ be a pointed
$\operatorname{RCD}(-\eta,n)$ space, where $0\leqslant\eta\leqslant1$, and let
\[
 u=(u^1,\ldots,u^n):B_2(x)\to \mathbb R^n
\]
have harmonic components. Denote by $I$ the $n\times n$ identity matrix and put
\begin{equation}
 G_u:=\left(\langle\nabla u^i,\nabla u^j\rangle\right)_{i,j=1}^n,
 \qquad
 D:=\fint_{B_1(x)}|G_u-I|\,\mathrm{d}\mathcal H^n.
\end{equation}
If $D+\eta\leqslant \varepsilon$, then
\begin{equation}
 \fint_{B_r(x)}|G_u-I|\,\mathrm{d}\mathcal H^n
 \leqslant Cr^{-\kappa}(D+\eta)
 \qquad\forall 0<r<\frac14.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma lem:interior-dirichlet-gmc-comparison of arXiv:2608.02459, 'Response Calculus for Spectral Simplicity\\ and Joint Eigenvalue Densities'] Let $M_{h_D}^{\rm can}$ and $M_{h_U}^{\rm can}$ be the canonical GMC measures
obtained from the construction of Lemma~(lem:canonical-borel-gmc of the paper) on $D$
and $U$, respectively.  Under the coupling above, for every fixed $V\Subset U$,
almost surely,
\begin{equation}
 M_{h_D}^{\rm can}|_V
 =w_{D,U}\,M_{h_U}^{\rm can}|_V,
 \qquad
 w_{D,U}(z)
 :=\exp\!\left(
   \gamma\chi_{D,U}(z)
   -\frac{\gamma^2}{2}\mathbb E[\chi_{D,U}(z)^2]
  \right),
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
 w_{D,U},\ w_{D,U}^{-1}\in C_b(V).
\end{equation}
In particular, the two measures in
(equation eq:interior-dirichlet-gmc-comparison of the paper) have the same null sets on $V$.

[Corollary 18 of arXiv:2608.17509, '2608.17509'] Let \(a>1\). For every \(x>0\), there exists a unique
\(\theta_a(x)\in\mathbb R\) such that
\[
        \Lambda_a'(\theta_a(x))=x,
        \qquad
        J_a(x)=\theta_a(x)x-\Lambda_a(\theta_a(x)).
\]
Moreover, \(J_a\) is differentiable and strictly convex on \((0,\infty)\), with
\(J_a'(x)=\theta_a(x)\) and
\(J_a''(x)=1/\Lambda_a''(\theta_a(x))\). Finally, \(J_a\ge0\) on
\([0,\infty)\), and it vanishes uniquely at
\(\lambda_a=\frac{1}{4\pi}(1-\frac{1}{a})\).

[Proposition 17 of arXiv:2609.03191, 'On lifting representations and actions on curves of the metacyclic groups $C_{p^s}\rtimes '] Suppose that $\chi$ is injective. Let $V$ be a $k[G]$-module with $\ell_V$ constant. Let $a\in C_m$ and $W:=U(a,1)$. We assume that $V$ is constant-indecomposable and we consider a direct sum decomposition into indecomposable $k[G]$-modules $V=\oplus_{i=1}^{\imath_V} U(a_i,b_i)$. Let 
$$J:=\{a_i+\epsilon|i\in\llbracket1,\imath_V\rrbracket\}.$$
Then the following properties hold.

\medskip
{\bf (1)} We have an identity
$$\dim_k\bigl(\Hom_{k[G]}(V,W)\bigr)=\begin{cases}1\quad\textup{if}\quad a\in J\\0\quad\textup{if}\quad a\notin J.\end{cases}$$

{\bf (2)} Let $(c,b)\in\mathbb J_{m,p^s}$. Then 
$$\dim_k\bigl(\Ext^1_{k[G]}(U(c,b),W)\bigr)=\begin{cases}1\quad\textup{if}\quad  a=c+\epsilon\;\textup{and}\;b<p^s\\0\quad\textup{if}\quad a\neq c+\epsilon\;\textup{or}\;b=p^s.\end{cases}$$

{\bf (3)} Suppose that $\jmath_V=0$. Then 
$$\dim_k\bigl(\Hom_{k[G]}(V,W)\bigr)=\dim_k\bigl(\Ext^1_{k[G]}(V,W)\bigr).$$
title: Proposition 17 of arXiv:2609.03191

  every $k \in \mathbb{N}$, $i = 0, \ldots, \nu$ and $(a_1, \ldots, a_k) \in

  \begin{equation}
    \varphi^{(i)} (a_1 \ldots a_k) = \sum_{\pi = \{V_1, \ldots, V_p \} \in

Theorem \ref{theorem 1.20.1} are satisfied
and $p_{b}<\infty$,
let    $T\in(0,\infty]$, 
 and

Assume that for some constants $\rho,\rho_{1},\xi>0$, $\rho_{1}\in[0,\rho/2)$, and 
any $r\in [\rho_{1},\rho)$ we have $|B_{r}\cap G^{c}|\geq \xi
|B_{r}|$. Let $u\in W^{1,2}_{(q,p)}(Q)\cap C(\bar Q)$, and let $\omega(r)$, $r\geq0$, be a concave function such that
$$
|u(t,x)-u(s,y)|\leq \gamma+\omega(\gamma+|x-y|+\sqrt{ |t-s| }),
$$ 
whenever  $(t,x), (s,y)\in   \partial' Q$, where the constant $\gamma\geq 0$. Then there exist  $\beta >0$
and $N$, depending only on $ d,\delta $, 
    $\xi$,  $p$, with 
 $N$ also depending on $\rho$, $\rho_{b}$ and
 the diameter of $G$, 
such that  for $x\in G$, satisfying $|x|\geq \rho_{1}$,

|u(t,x)-u(t,0)|
\leq \gamma+N|x|^{\beta}\sup_{C\in\bC_{1}}\|I_{Q}\cL u\|_{L_{(q,p)}(C)}+
\omega\big(\gamma+N_{0} |x|^{\beta_{0}}\big),
\end{equation}
where $\beta_{0} >0$
and $N_{0}$, depend  only on $ d,\delta $,
    $\xi$,  $p$,  $p_{b}$ with 
 $N_{0}$ also depending on $\rho$, $\rho_{b}$ and
 the diameter of $G$, (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

$$\exp(\pi G_D(z_1,z_2)) = \frac{\theta_3(q^{1/2})}{\theta_2(q^{1/2})}$$

from $(D, z_1, z_2)$ to the disk with two marked points $(\mathbb{D}, -r,r)$.
