ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Conservation, explicit coupling reduction, exact law comparison or spectral calculation Result: A useful sufficient condition is a common local coding from instruction stacks. Suppose the output on a finite window W can be determined by stacks within a random radius R, with the same coding rule for both source geometries after their fronts pass, and P(R>r)<=C*r^(-beta). Coupling the stacks then bounds total variation of the two W-laws by 2*C*r^(-beta) whenever both available bulk neighborhoods have radius r. With r proportional to inverse mesh, this gives a quantitative microscopic universality rate. Check: On the intersection of the two successful coding events the outputs are identical; the union bound supplies the factor two. The argument remains valid without independence of the coding radii. Obstruction: A common finite-radius coding rule is unproved at criticality and may itself be too strong. This is an explicit coupling reduction, not an assertion that ARW has a finite influence radius.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-p0375-independence-of-arw-bulk-microstructure-from-the-initial-source-shape
No independent review
title: Attempt on Independence of ARW bulk microstructure from the initial source shape

[Corollary 14 (Use of deterministic upper bounds) of arXiv:2607.13210, 'Punctured Wilson--Evolving Sets and Root Identities for Massive Kirchhoff Forests'] Let $H_q(x,U)\geq h_q(x,U)$ for every $x$ and $U$. Every upper bound obtained from
non-negative sums and products of $h_q$ remains valid after replacing $h_q$ by $H_q$.
Identities involving $h_q$ give the corresponding upper inequalities. For example,
\begin{equation*}
  \forall x,y \in V\,,\qquad \Pp(x\leftrightarrow_q y)
  \leq\sum_{z\in V}H_q(x,z)H_q(y,z),
\end{equation*}
and
\begin{equation*}
    \forall x \in V\,,\qquad  \Ee[\pi(R_x^{\mathrm{raw}})]
  \leq\sum_{z\in V}\pi(z)H_q(x,z).
\end{equation*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Use of deterministic upper bounds

[Prop diff-dimensions of arXiv:2606.01627, 'The geometry of the giant component of random geometric graphs'] Let $M_1$ and $M_2$ be connected compact Riemannian manifolds of dimension $d_1 > d_2 \geq 2$ and volume $1$.  Let $\Delta_c(d_j)$ denote the critical average degree for having a giant component. 
    There is $\alpha = \alpha(M_1,M_2)$ so that for each $\Delta_0 > \max\{\Delta_c(d_1),\Delta_c(d_2)\}$ there is $c = c(M_1,M_2,\Delta_0)$ so for all $\Delta \in [\Delta_0, \alpha n]$, given the adjacency matrices of the random geometric graphs  $G_{M_1}(n;r_1)$ and $G_{M_2}(n;r_2)$ of expected average degree $\Delta$, there is a $O(n^2 \Delta)$ algorithm which can correctly identify which graph came from $M_1$ and $M_2$ with probability at least $1- \exp(-c \log^2 n)\,.$

[Lemma 8 of arXiv:2609.02019, '2609.02019'] Let Assumption~\ref{Hypo-Q} hold, and let $\delta_{\mathcal Q}$ be defined
		by \eqref{delta-Qi}. For $n\ge1$, set
		\[
		\mathcal Q_n\triangleq J_n\mathcal QJ_n.
		\]
		Then the following properties hold.
		\begin{enumerate}[label={\bf (\arabic*)},leftmargin=0.79cm]
			\setlength\itemsep{0.2em}
			\item For each $n\ge1$,
			$\mathcal Q_n\in\mathrm{OP}\mathcal S^{-\infty}$.
			If the description selected in Assumption~\ref{Hypo-Q} is
			$\mathcal Q\in\mathbb A^\alpha$, then
			$\{\mathcal Q_n\}_{n\ge1}$ is bounded in $\mathbb A^\alpha$.
			If the selected description is
			$\mathcal Q\in\mathbb B^\beta$, then
			$\{\mathcal Q_n\}_{n\ge1}$ is bounded in $\mathbb B^\beta$.
			
			\item For every $r\ge0$,
			\[
			\lim_{n\to\infty}
			\|\mathcal Q_nf-\mathcal Qf\|_{H^r}=0,
			\quad f\in H^{r+\delta_{\mathcal Q}},
			\]
			and
			\[
			\lim_{n\to\infty}
			\|\mathcal Q_n^2f-\mathcal Q^2f\|_{H^r}=0,
			\quad f\in H^{r+2\delta_{\mathcal Q}}.
			\]
			
			\item Let $r,\theta\ge0$ and
			$r>\theta+\delta_{\mathcal Q}$. Then
			\[
			\|\mathcal Q_n-\mathcal Q_m\|_{
				\mathscr L(H^r;H^\theta)}
			\lesssim
			(n\wedge m)^{-(r-\theta-\delta_{\mathcal Q})}.
			\]
			Moreover, for all $f,g\in H^r$,
			\begin{align*}
				\left|
				\left\langle
				\mathcal Q_nf-\mathcal Q_mg,
				f-g
				\right\rangle_{H^\theta}
				\right| \lesssim
				(n\wedge m)^{-2(r-\theta-\delta_{\mathcal Q})}
				\bigl(\|f\|_{H^r}+\|g\|_{H^r}\bigr)^2
				+
				\|f-g\|_{H^\theta}^2.
			\end{align*}
			The implicit constants are independent of $n,m$.
			
			\item Let $r,\theta\ge0$ and
			$r>\theta+2\delta_{\mathcal Q}$. Then
			\[
			\|\mathcal Q_n^2-\mathcal Q_m^2\|_{
				\mathscr L(H^r;H^\theta)}
			\lesssim
			(n\wedge m)^{-(r-\theta-2\delta_{\mathcal Q})}.
			\]
			Moreover, for all $f,g\in H^r$,
			\begin{align*}
				\left|
				\left\langle
				\mathcal Q_n^2f-\mathcal Q_m^2g,
				f-g
				\right\rangle_{H^\theta}
				+
				\|\mathcal Q_nf-\mathcal Q_mg\|_{H^\theta}^2
				\right| \lesssim
				(n\wedge m)^{-(r-\theta-\delta_{\mathcal Q})}
				\bigl(\|f\|_{H^r}+\|g\|_{H^r}\bigr)^2
				+
				\|f-g\|_{H^\theta}^2.
			\end{align*}
			The implicit constants are independent of $n,m$.
			
			\item For every $r\ge0$ and $f\in H^r$,
			\begin{equation}
				\sup_{n\ge1}
				\left|
				\langle\mathcal Q_nf,f\rangle_{H^r}
				\right|
				\lesssim
				\|f\|_{H^r}^2,
				\quad
				\sup_{n\ge1}
				\left|
				\langle\mathcal Q_n^2f,f\rangle_{H^r}
				+
				\|\mathcal Q_nf\|_{H^r}^2
				\right|
				\lesssim
				\|f\|_{H^r}^2.
				
			\end{equation}
			
			\item For every $r\ge0$ and $f\in H^r$,
			\begin{equation}
				\sup_{n\ge1}
				\left|
				\langle J_n\mathcal Qf,J_n f\rangle_{H^r}
				\right|
				\lesssim
				\|f\|_{H^r}^2,
				\quad
				\sup_{n\ge1}
				\left|
				\langle J_n\mathcal Q^2f,J_n f\rangle_{H^r}
				+
				\|J_n\mathcal Qf\|_{H^r}^2
				\right|
				\lesssim
				\|f\|_{H^r}^2.
				
			\end{equation}
		\end{enumerate}

Own-work draft: independently checked proof of this exact claim version; reviewer PASS recorded. For the fixed-n common-Hessian RR model f_i=x^2/2+kappa_T*y^2/2+b_i*x+c_i*y with n>=2, fixed deterministic x0!=0,y0, fixed zero-sum linear terms with mean squares s1>=0,s2>0, and fresh independent uniform epoch permutations, take T=nK and exactly kappa_T=4*T/log(T). Define D_n=n/(n-1) for even n and (n+1)/n for odd n. The globally minimized expected final-epoch error is asymptotic to s2*D_n*log(T)^2/(16*T*log(log(T))). Every sequence of global minimizing constant steps obeys kappa_T*eta_T=2-(4+o(1))*log(log(T))/log(T). This does not cover all sequences satisfying only kappa_T*log(T)/T->4 or the general RR conjecture.
mu=1; n and initialization fixed, x0!=0; fixed zero-sum linear terms, s1>=0,s2>0; independent fresh uniform epoch permutations shared across coordinates; exact kappa=4T/log(T), T=nK.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:4d0dd9163c5404d1fe99c89990ea2a179ab857eff446b8793059554d2ce64afd","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/4d/4d0dd9163c5404d1fe99c89990ea2a179ab857eff446b8793059554d2ce64afd.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:55abb58d3893dd65e266367c9d71a1a8b37c9321e1077a89f6666981c945dcea","bundle_entry_key":"transition-kappa-common-hessian","bundle_id":"population.t362-transition-kappa-005","claim_kind":"theorem","conditions":[],"domain":"optimization; random reshuffling; transition condition number; optimal constant step","draft":"w732/bundle_005.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:optimization.randomreshuffling:common-hessian-random-reshuffling-exact-transition-condition-number-optimizer","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Target 1: the exact transition path kappa=4T/log(T)

Status: proof draft (unaudited). This is an exact transition path, not a theorem for every sequence with kappa*log(T)/T->4. No priority claim.

## Statement

Use the normalized common-Hessian model of C001 with fixed n>=2, fixed deterministic x0!=0,y0, fixed zero-sum linear terms of mean squares s1>=0,s2>0, and fresh independent uniform epoch permutations shared across coordinates. For T=nK->infinity set exactly kappa=4T/log T. Put ell=log T, m=log ell and

    D_n = n/(n-1) if n is even,
          (n+1)/n if n is odd.

Then the globally minimized final-epoch expected function error P_T obeys

    min_{eta>=0} P_T(eta) ~ s2*D_n*ell^2/(16*T*m).         (1)

Every sequence of global minimizers has

    kappa*eta_T = 2 - (4+o(1))*m/ell.                    (2)

The exact transition path is essential to the proof; subleading changes in kappa can change the competing transient scale.

## Endpoint residue

In the settled recursion put q=kappa*eta, a=1-q,

    W_n(q)=sum_{0<=i<j<n}(a^i-a^j)^2,
    J_n(q)=q^2*W_n(q)/[2(n-1)(1-a^(2n))],  0<q<2.

The stiff variance is exactly (s2/kappa)*J_n(q)*(1-a^(2T)). At q=2, the n powers (-1)^i have floor(n/2) of one parity and ceil(n/2) of the other. Thus

    W_n(2)=4*floor(n/2)*ceil(n/2)
          = n^2 (n even), or n^2-1 (n odd).

For delta=2-q->0 positively, 1-a^(2n)=1-(1-delta)^(2n)~2n*delta. Hence

    delta*J_n(2-delta) -> W_n(2)/[n(n-1)] = D_n.         (3)

Here n is fixed; n-1>0 and the stationary denominator is positive on (0,2). The finite-horizon variance, including q=2 and q>2, is always

    R_T = [s2*q^2*W_n(q)/(2(n-1)*kappa)]
                *sum_{r=0}^{K-1}(1-q)^(2nr).             (4)

## Upper bound

1. Choose z_c=2m-3log m, delta_c=2z_c/ell and q_c=2-delta_c. For all sufficiently large T, z_c>0, delta_c->0 and delta_c*T->infinity. Thus 0<q_c<2. From (3)-(4),

    R_T(eta_c) ~ s2*D_n/(kappa*delta_c)
              = s2*D_n*ell^2/(8*T*z_c)
              ~ s2*D_n*ell^2/(16*T*m).                 (5)

We used (1-delta_c)^(2T)<=exp(-2delta_c*T)->0.

2. Let A=x0^2/2>0. Since eta_c=q_c/kappa and T/kappa^2->0, the flat deterministic contribution is

    A*(1-eta_c)^(2T)
       = (A/T)*exp(z_c+O(T/kappa^2))
       ~ A*ell^2/(T*m^3),                               (6)

which is o(ell^2/(T*m)). The identity -2q_c*T/kappa=-ell+z_c uses the exact definition kappa=4T/ell, not merely its leading ratio.

The stiff deterministic term is at most (kappa*y0^2/2)*exp(-2delta_c*T), negligible compared with the scale in (5). Indeed delta_c*T is of order T*m/ell, which dominates log T, whereas the logarithms of kappa and the reciprocal target scale are O(log T). The flat variance is O(eta_c^3)=O(ell^3/T^3), also negligible. Thus the minimum is at most (1+o(1)) times (5), and tends to zero.

## Localization of every unrestricted global optimizer

3. A global minimizer exists because the exact error is a continuous coercive polynomial: the last epoch and pair (0,1) in (4) give P_T>=s2*q^4/[2(n-1)*kappa]. Write q_T=kappa*eta_T for any sequence of global minimizers. Eventually q_T<2. In fact if q_T>=2, then W_n(q_T)>=q_T^2 and every term of the geometric sum in (4) is >=1, so

    P_T(eta_T) >= 8*s2*K/[(n-1)*kappa]
                 = [2*s2/(n(n-1))]*ell ->infinity,

contradicting the vanishing upper bound. This excludes all unstable steps, not only those close to the endpoint.

4. For 0<=q_T<2, eta_T->0 and T*eta_T^2=O(ell^2/T)->0. Uniformly in this interval the flat transient equals

    A*exp(-q_T*ell/2+o(1)).

If q_T<=2-epsilon along a subsequence for any fixed epsilon>0, that transient is at least A*T^(-1+epsilon/2)*exp(o(1)), exceeding the candidate bound of order ell^2/(T*m). Therefore q_T->2 from below. Set delta_T=2-q_T->0.

5. Necessarily delta_T*T->infinity. Otherwise take a subsequence on which delta_T*T<=M. For large T on that subsequence delta_T<=1/2 and log(1-delta_T)>=-2delta_T. Every summand in (4) is then at least

    (1-delta_T)^(2n(K-1)) >= exp(-4delta_T*T)>=exp(-4M).

Since q_T->2 and W_n(q_T)>=q_T^2, (4) gives P_T>=const*K/kappa, diverging like ell. This contradicts the upper bound. The constant can depend on M but is strictly positive. Hence (3) applies and the finite-horizon variance multiplier tends to one.

## Optimization on the transition scale

6. Define z_T=delta_T*ell/2>0. By the endpoint residue and step 5,

    R_T(eta_T) = (1+o(1))*s2*D_n*ell^2/(8*T*z_T).        (7)

The flat transient is (A/T)*exp(z_T+o(1)), by the same uniform expansion used in step 4. Comparing this transient with the upper bound gives

    z_T <= 2m-log m+O(1),                               (8)

so limsup z_T/m<=2. Comparing (7) with that upper bound gives liminf z_T/m>=2. Consequently z_T/m->2, which is (2). Substitution into (7), combined with the upper bound, proves (1). All other objective contributions are nonnegative, so no cancellation or exchange of expectation and minimization is required.

## Hypotheses and unpaid step

x0!=0 is used in (8); if initialization is exactly the optimum, eta=0 gives zero error and (1) would fail. s2>0 is used in every noise localization and in (7); with no stiff noise the endpoint pole is absent. Fixed n is used in (3) and the stationary estimates. n>=2 makes n-1 positive. Independent epoch permutations enter the inherited recursion; coordinate-noise independence is not needed because the objective is diagonal. Exact kappa=4T/log T is used in (6) and (8).

This proves a named-target-1 transition path in draft form. General sequences satisfying only kappa*log(T)/T->4 remain unpaid, as do general finite-sum Hessians and the full T362 obstruction. Independent audit should focus on the uniform all-minimizer localization in steps 3-5 and the two comparisons in step 6. Exact finite algebra checks are checks of (3)-(4), not certificates of the asymptotic theorem. [Definition def:surface of arXiv:2608.24830, 'Motion helps the contact process: survival below\\ the percolation threshold on Poisson Br'] A \emph{two-sided Lipschitz surface} $F$ is a set of base-height cells $(b,h)\in\mathbb{Z}^{d+1}$ such
that for every $b\in\mathbb{Z}^d$ there are exactly two, possibly equal, integers $F_+(b)\ge0$ and
$F_-(b)\le0$ with $(b,F_+(b)),(b,F_-(b))\in F$, and such that $F_+$ and $F_-$ are Lipschitz
functions. We say that $F$ \emph{exists} if $F_+(b)<\infty$ and $F_-(b)>-\infty$ for every $b$.
For $D\in\mathbb{N}$ we say that $F$ \emph{surrounds} a cell $(b',h')$ at distance $D$ if every path
$(b',h')=(b_0,h_0),(b_1,h_1),\dots,(b_n,h_n)$ with $\|(b_k,h_k)-(b_{k-1},h_{k-1})\|_1=1$ for all
$k$ and $\|(b_n,h_n)-(b_0,h_0)\|_1>D$ intersects $F$. We say that a space-time cell belongs to
$F$ if its base-height index does.
title: Two-sided Lipschitz surface

[Definition Def:urd of arXiv:2411.13030, 'Classification of the limit shape for 1+1-dimensional FPP'] Let  $p$ be a semi-directed path from the origin to a point $(n,m)$. The number of \emph{right-turns} of $p$ is defined as 
\[
R(p):=\left| k \in \{0,...,n\} : \, f_p(k)=f_p(k+1)\right|.
\] 
similarily, we define the number of \emph{up-turns} by
\[
U(p):=\left| k \in \{0,...,n\} : \, f_p(k)<f_p(k+1)\right|,
\] 
and the number of \emph{down-turns} by
\[
D(p):=\left| k \in \{0,...,n\} : \, f_p(k)>f_p(k+1)\right|.
\]
title: Definition Def:urd of arXiv:2411.13030

[Cor 19 of arXiv:2602.14618, 'Finitary coding and Gaussian concentration\\ for random fields'] Fix \(n\in\mathbb N\), and let \(r^{(n)}_\varphi\) denote the truncated coding radius. Define
\[
b_m := \mathbb E\!\big[
|B_\infty(0,r^{(n)}_0)\cap B_\infty(m,r^{(n)}_{m})|
\big],
\qquad m\in\mathbb Z^d.
\]
For each \(L\ge 1\), let \(\Lambda_L := [-L,L]^d\cap\mathbb Z^d\), and let \(f^{(L)}\) be a local observable such that
\[
\delta_k f^{(L)} = 1 \quad \text{for all } k\in \Lambda_L,
\qquad
\delta_k f^{(L)} = 0 \quad \text{for } k\notin \Lambda_L.
\]
Then \(\|\delta f^{(L)}\|_2^2 = |\Lambda_L|\), and
\[
\liminf_{L\to\infty}
\frac{\mathbb E\sum_{i\in\mathbb Z^d}\big(c_i^{(n)}(X)\big)^2}
{\|\delta f^{(L)}\|_2^2}
=
\|b\|_1.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Cor 19 of arXiv:2602.14618

[Propn weakRepPropn of arXiv:2605.04860, 'Branching Brownian motion with rank-based selection and reaction-diffusion equations'] Let $(\mu_t^N)_{t\geq 0}$ be the measure-valued Markov process corresponding to the $(\psi,r,N)$-BBM process. Let $f(x,t)\in \mathcal{BC}^{2,1}(\mathbb{R}\times [0,\infty),\mathbb{R})$. Then $\mu^N$, and $f$ satisfy the following equation:
    \begin{align}\langle \mu_t^N,f(\cdot,t)\rangle = \langle \mu_0^N, f(\cdot,0)\rangle &+ \int_0^t \langle \mu_s^N, \frac12 f_{xx}(\cdot,s) + f_t(\cdot,s) + r(s)f(\cdot,s)\rangle \\
    \nonumber&-\left\langle \mu_s^N, Nf(\cdot,s)r(s)\int_{(H\star \mu^N_s)(\cdot)-1/N}^{(H\star \mu^N_s)(\cdot)}\psi(u)du\right\rangle ds + M_t^{N,W} + M_t^{N,P},\end{align}
    where $M^{N,W}_t$ is a continuous local martingale with $\mathbb{E}[[M^{N,W}]_t]\xrightarrow[N\to\infty]{}0$ for fixed $t$, and $M^{N,P}_t$ is a local martingale with $\mathbb{E}[[M^{N,P}]_t]\xrightarrow[N\to\infty]{}0$ for fixed $t$.

[Theo 4 of arXiv:2609.02261, 'Quantization and process'] i) For all $F\in D_h( \R^{2n})$,  we have, 
  
    
      $$ F(X) =  ( \pi h)^{-n} \int _{\R^{2n}}e^{ - \frac {1 }  {h}   |X-T|^2 }
      H_hF(T) dT, $$
      
         for every $X\in \R^{2n}$ where
      
      $$  H_hF(T) =  ( 4 \pi h)^{-n}   \int _{\R^{2n}} 
       F^{\rm ext} \Big(  T+\frac{Z}{2} , T-\frac{Z}{2}\Big ) 
      e^{ - \frac {1 }  {4h}   |Z|^2 } dZ,$$
      for any $T\in \R^{2n}$.
      
      
    ii) The operator $H_h$ maps $D_h (\R^{2n})$ into 
    $ L^{\infty} (\R^{2n}) $. It is  commuting with translations and its symbol equals to  $u\rightarrow e^{ \frac { h|u|^2}   {4} }$. 
   
    iii)  Let  $F\in D_h( \R^{2n})$. There exists a function $\widetilde F$ on $\C^{2n} \simeq \R^{4n} $ which is holomorphic in the following sense,     
    \be (\partial _1 + i \partial _2 ) \widetilde F = 0,\
    (\partial _3  + i \partial _4 ) \widetilde F = 0
  \ee 
    
   with a restriction to $\R^{2n}$ 
     equals to $F$, that is to say,  $\widetilde F (x , 0, \xi , 0) = F(x , \xi)$. Moreover, for $X,Y\in\R^{2n}$,
      
      \be   | \widetilde F (X+iY) |  \leq 
    ( 4 \pi h)^{-n}   \Vert \psi_F \Vert _{L^1 (\R^{2n})} 
  \  e^{  \frac {1}  {h}   |Y|^2 }, \ee 
  
that is to say, for any $(x_1 , x_2 , x_3 , x_4)\in\R^{4n}$,
  
  $$  | \widetilde F (x_1 , x_2 , x_3 , x_4) | \leq
  ( 4 \pi h)^{-n}   \Vert \psi_F \Vert _{L^1 (\R^{2n})} 
  \  e^{  \frac {1}  {h}  ( |x_2|^2 + |x_4|^2) }.$$ 
      
    iv) Fix $F\in D_h( \R^{2n})$. We have,  with  $X = (x , \xi)\in \R^{2n}$ and $Y = (y , \eta)\in \R^{2n}$, 
   
   \be   F^{\rm ext}(X , Y)=  \widetilde F \left ( 
 \frac {x+y} {2} ,   \frac {\xi - \eta } {2} , 
 \frac {\xi + \eta} {2} ,   \frac {y-x} {2}\right ) .\ee 
 
 If $\widetilde F$ is satisfying  (\ref{Cauchy-Riem}) then $F^{\rm ext}$ 
 is verifying (\ref{CR-et-anti}). 
 
 v)  If a function  $F$ on $\R^{2n}$  has a holomorphic extension 
  $\widetilde F$ in the sense of  (\ref{Cauchy-Riem}) on  $\C^{2n}$ which satisfies,
 
  \be  | \widetilde F (X+iY) |  \leq 
     | \psi_F (Y) | 
  \  e^{  \frac {1}  {h}   |Y|^2 }, \ee 
  
  where $\psi_F \in L^1 (\R^{2n}) \cap L^{\infty} (\R^{2n}) $, 
  then the function  $F\in D_h (\R^{2n})$. 
  
  vi) The  convolution by a bounded measure is an operator in $D_h (\R^{2n})$ having a norm smaller or equal than $1$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Prop P:half-space-horizon-marginals of arXiv:2604.10020, 'The directed landscape in half-space'] As $n\to\infty$, the process $R^{(n)}$ has a distributional limit $R^{\mathsf{DL}}=\{R^{\mathsf{DL}}_i\}_{i=1}^k$, under the uniform-on-compact topology. 
    We can describe the process $R^{\mathsf{DL}}$ explicitly as follows.
	
Let $\mathcal{B} = (\mathcal{B}_1, \mathcal{B}_2, \ldots, \mathcal{B}_{2k})$ be $2k$ independent Brownian motions on $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ of diffusivity $2$, drift $\lambda_i$ for $\mathcal{B}_i, i\in\llbracket1, k \rrbracket$ and $-\lambda_i$ for $\mathcal{B}_{2k+1-i}$. Next, let $\{X(-i, j) : i\in\llbracket1, k \rrbracket, j \in \llbracketi +1, 2k +1 - i \rrbracket\}$ be an array of exponential random variables, independent of each other and $\mathcal B$, satisfying 
\[
X(-i, j) \sim \begin{cases}
\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda_i/2 - \lambda_j/2), \qquad &j \in \llbracketi + 1, k \rrbracket, \\
\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda_i/2 + \lambda_{2k + 1 -j}/2), \qquad &j\in\llbracketk + 1, 2k - i \rrbracket, \\
\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda_i/2 - \rho), \qquad &j=2k + 1- i.
\end{cases}
\]
We turn this array into a 
sequence of cadlag functions $X = (X_1, \dots, X_{2k})$ on $(-\infty, 0]$ by the rule that $X_j(0) = 0$ for all $j$, and the measure $dX$ has atoms of size $X(-i, j)$ at each coordinate $(-i, j)$ where $X(-i, j)$ is defined (and is supported on these points). Equivalently, the path $X_j$ has a jump of size $X(-i, j)$ at location $-i$.

Let $X \mathcal{B}$ be the concatenation of $X$ and $\mathcal{B}$. (See Figure (fig:hfsh of the paper) for an illustration.) Then:
$$
R^{\mathsf{DL}}_i(x) = \begin{cases}
X\mathcal{B}(-i, i; x, 2k) - X\mathcal{B}(-i, i; 0, 2k), \qquad &x \ge 0, \\
X\mathcal{B}^{\Delta_{2k+1}}(-i, i; |x|, 2k) - X\mathcal{B}(-i, i; 0, 2k), \qquad &x \le 0.
\end{cases}
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Prop P:half-space-horizon-marginals of arXiv:2604.10020

Definition~(def.A2 of the paper). Consider the functionally constructed mark $V(x) :=\xi(\tilde{x}, \tilde{\mathcal{P}})$, with 
  $\xi:
\mathbb{R}^d \times\mathbb{K}\times\mathcal{N}_{\mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{K}} \longrightarrow \mathbb{K}'$ and set $\dbtilde\mathcal{P} :=  \sum_{x \in \mathcal{P}}
\delta_{(x, V(x))}$, a marked point process on $\mathbb{R}^d\times \mathbb{K}'$. Fix $p,q \in \mathbb{N}$.
\begin{enumerate}[wide,label=(\roman*),labelindent=0pt]
\item  If $\xi$ satisfies 
   fast \textnormal{BL}-localization  
   (equation Lp-stab-infinite of the paper) on $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}$ for $p,q$ and $p+q$, 
   then  $\dbtilde\mathcal{P}$ 
satisfies the fast \textnormal{BL}-mixing correlation condition for $p$ and $q$, that is to say (equation e.mppmixing of the paper) holds  for $f \in \textnormal{BL}((\mathbb{K}')^{p})$, $g \in \textnormal{BL}((\mathbb{K}')^{q}),$ and some fast decreasing function $\omega_{p+q}$. 
\item   Part~(i.BL-iterated-marks of the paper)
 above remains valid if
$\xi$ satisfies fast \textnormal{BL}~cluster-localization---that is,
conditions~(equation Lp-stab-infinite-weak1 of the paper) and~(equation Lp-stab-infinite-weak2 of the paper)---on
$\tilde{\mathcal{P}}$ for  $p,q$, and $p+q$.

 \item  If 
  $\xi$ is fast stabilizing on $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}$ as in (equation stab-infinite of the paper) (via stopping sets) for $p,q$ and $p+q$, 
then  $\dbtilde\mathcal{P}$ has fast $\mathbb{B} $-mixing correlations for $p$ and $q$, i.e., (equation e.mppmixing of the paper) holds for $f \in \mathbb{B} ((\mathbb{K}')^{p})$, $g \in \mathbb{B} ((\mathbb{K}')^{q}),$ and some fast decreasing function $\omega_{p+q}$.
\end{enumerate}
In  all cases~(i.BL-iterated-marks of the paper), (i.BLc-iterated-marks of the paper), and~(i.iterated-marks of the paper), the  fast decreasing function $\omega_{p+q}$ associated to $\dbtilde \mathcal{P}$ depends on the functions $\varphi_{p+q}$ and $\phi $ as well as on  the constants $(C_k)_{k = 1}^{\infty}$ and $\kappa_{p+q}$ related to $\xi$ and $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}$, respectively. In particular, there exist constants $C<\infty$, $c>0$ which  depend on $p,q$,  such that for all $s > 0$
  
\begin{equation} \omega_{p+q}(s) \leq C \exp(-cs^b) + C\varphi_{p + q}\big( cs^{b(1-a)/2( p + q + d)} \big),
\end{equation}
where $a,b$ are as in~(equation eqn:sum of the paper) and (equation phibd of the paper), respectively. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Fast mixing properties of point processes with functionally constructed iterated marks

Let X_1, ..., X_n be INDEPENDENT random variables taking values in arbitrary measurable spaces - they need NOT be identically distributed and need not be real-valued - and let Z = f(X_1, ..., X_n) with E[Z^2] < infinity. Let X_i' be an independent copy of X_i, independent of everything else, and put Z^{(i)} = f(X_1, ..., X_{i-1}, X_i', X_{i+1}, ..., X_n). Then Var(Z) <= (1/2) sum_{i=1}^n E[ (Z - Z^{(i)})^2 ] = sum_{i=1}^n E[ ((Z - Z^{(i)})_+)^2 ]. Equivalently, and often more convenient, Var(Z) <= sum_{i=1}^n E[ (Z - Z_i)^2 ] for ANY random variables Z_i that are measurable functions of the n-1 variables other than X_i; taking Z_i = inf over the i-th coordinate of f gives the version used for suprema and for first-passage times. Equality holds if and only if f is a sum of functions of the individual coordinates. Independence is the only structural hypothesis and it is essential; the inequality is FALSE for dependent coordinates. Applied with a bounded-difference function it recovers the variance half of McDiarmid's inequality; applied to first-passage percolation with the geodesic length as the influence bound it produces the linear variance upper bound. [Efron and Stein (1981), Steele (1986); see Boucheron, Lugosi and Massart, Concentration Inequalities, Theorem 3.1]
X_1, ..., X_n independent (arbitrary measurable state spaces, not necessarily identically distributed)
E[Z^2] < infinity
X_i' an independent copy of X_i

[Theorem 4 (Characterization of limits of global empirical measures) of arXiv:2510.22533, 'Marginal dynamics of probabilistic cellular automata on trees'] Let any of the following three cases hold for $\{G_n\}_{n \in \N}$:
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
    \item Let $\kappa \ge 2$ be an integer. For each $n \ge \kappa+1$ with $n\kappa$ even, there exists at least one $\kappa$-regular graph on $n$ vertices, and we let $G_n$ be chosen uniformly at random.
    \item Let $\lambda > 0$, and let $G_n$ be the \Erdos graph $G(n,\lambda/n)$, on the vertex set $\{1,\ldots,n\}$.
    \item Let $G_n$ be drawn from the configuration model with vertex set $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ and with degree distribution converging weakly to $\rho_{\myroot}$.
    Assume $\rho_{\myroot}$ has finite first and second moments, that is, $\sum_{k=0}^\infty k^2 \rho_{\myroot}(k) < \infty$.
\end{enumerate}
Suppose the initial states $\{X^{G_n}_v(0) : v \in G_n, n \in \N\}$ are i.i.d.\ with law $\mu_0$.
Let $\Xbar$ and $G$ be given as follows, for each case above:
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
    \item Let $\Xbar$ be as in Construction \ref{constr:regulartree_local}, with $(\Xbar_v(0))_{v=0}^{\kappa}$ i.i.d.\ with law $\mu_0$.
    \item Let $\Xbar$ be as in Construction \ref{constr:UGWlocal}, with $\rho_{\myroot}=\mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda)$ and with $(\Xbar_v(0))_{v\in\V_1}$ i.i.d.\ with law $\mu_0$.
    \item Let $\Xbar$ be as in Construction \ref{constr:UGWlocal}, with $(\Xbar_v(0))_{v\in\V_1}$ i.i.d.\ with law $\mu_0$.
\end{enumerate}
Then the $\PolishX^\infty$-valued random trajectory 
$X^{G_n}_{\myroot_n}$ converges in law  to $\Xbar_{\myroot}$ (or $\Xbar_0$ in case (i)). Moreover, 
the $\P(\PolishX^\infty)$-valued random measure  
$\mu^{G_n}$ converges in law  to $\Lmc(\Xbar_{\myroot})$ (or  $\Lmc(\Xbar_0)$ in case (i)).

[Lemma lem:churn of arXiv:2608.23638, 'Replicable Conformal Prediction'] For any two runs of a shared-grid threshold rule with outputs $\tau,\tau'\in u+\beta\mathbb{Z}$ and any input $x$,

Consequently $\mathbb{E}_X\big[|\mathcal{C}_\tau(X)\triangle\mathcal{C}_{\tau'}(X)|\,\big|\,\tau\neq\tau'\big]\ge\min_{C}m_\beta(C)$, the minimum over grid cells $C$ meeting the localization window of Theorem~(thm:upper of the paper)(ii) of $m_\beta(C):=\mathbb{E}_X\#\{y:s(X,y)\in C\}$. Let (T, d) be a metric space and alpha > 0. An admissible sequence of partitions of T is an increasing sequence of partitions (A_n)_{n >= 0} such that |A_0| = 1 and |A_n| <= 2^{2^n} for all n >= 1. Let A_n(t) denote the set in A_n containing t. The Talagrand gamma_alpha functional is defined by gamma_alpha(T, d) = inf_{(A_n)} sup_{t in T} sum_{n=0}^infinity 2^{n / alpha} * diam(A_n(t), d).
(T, d) is a metric space

body:
[Prop max_action of arXiv:2604.23751, 'Large deviation principles for pattern-avoiding permutations, and limit shapes for constra'] For any $\beta\in \mathbb R$, the action $A_{\beta}$ has a unique minimizer $(\pi_1^{(\beta)}, \pi_2^{(\beta)})$ in $\mathcal{D}$. For $\beta \leq 0$, we have $\pi_1^{(\beta)}=\pi_2^{(\beta)}=\frac{1}{2}\Leb_{[0,1]}$. 
    For $\beta>0$, the densities of $\pi_1^{(\beta)}$ and $\pi_2^{(\beta)}$ on $[0,1]$ are given by
	\begin{equation}
	    \rho_1^{(\beta)}(x) := \frac{1}{1+\exp\left(\beta(\frac12-x) \right)}, 
        \quad \rho_2^{(\beta)}(x) := \frac{1}{1+\exp\left(\beta(x-\frac12) \right)}.
	\end{equation}
	In particular, both $\pi_1^{(\beta)}$ and $\pi_2^{(\beta)}$ have total mass $\frac{1}{2}$.

[Corollary 20 of arXiv:2609.03191, 'On lifting representations and actions on curves of the metacyclic groups $C_{p^s}\rtimes '] Let $l_0:=0$. For a strictly increasing sequence $l_1<\cdots<l_s$ of positive integers, the following statements are equivalent.

\medskip
{\bf (1)} There exists a cyclic $C_{p^s}$-extension of $k((t))$ whose lower jumps are $l_1<\cdots<l_s$.

\smallskip
{\bf (2)} The following conditions hold.

\medskip\noindent
{\bf (2.a)} We have $p\nmid l_1$.

\smallskip\noindent
{\bf (2.b)} For each $j\in\llbracket1,s-1\rrbracket$ we have $p^j\mid l_{j+1}-l_j$ and
$$l_{j+1}-l_j\ge (p-1)\sum_{i=0}^{j-1} p^{j-i}(l_{i+1}-l_i).$$

\noindent
{\bf (2.c)} For each $j\in\llbracket1,s-1\rrbracket$ such that $l_{j+1}-l_j> (p-1)\sum_{i=0}^{j-1} p^{j-i}(l_{i+1}-l_i)$, the positive integer $l_1+\sum_{i=1}^{j}\frac{l_{i+1}-l_i}{p^i}$ is not divisible by $p$.

[Theorem thm:inv_mp_ex of arXiv:2412.04589, 'Inverting the Markovian projection for pure jump processes'] Let Assumption~(asm:2 of the paper) hold. Suppose that $\Omega$ supports a sequence of i.i.d.\ $\operatorname{Exp}(1)$ random variables $(E_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}^*}$ and a sequence of i.i.d.\ $\nu$-distributed random variables $(J_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}^*}$ such that $\mathcal{F}_\infty$, $(E_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}^*}$ and $(J_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}^*}$ are independent. Then, there exist an enlarged filtration $\mathbb{G}$ (satisfying the usual conditions) and a $\mathbb{G}$-adapted pure jump process $X$ starting from $0$ whose jump measure has $\mathbb{G}$-compensator
	\begin{equation}
		\frac{\eta_t}{\mathbb{E}[\eta_t \,|\, X_{t-}]} \lambda(t, X_{t-}) \nu(d\xi) dt.
	\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Lemma uniform-lipschitz of arXiv:2608.12056, 'Deviation inequalities for U-processes of growing order, with applications to half-space d'] Let $X_1, X_2 \ldots$ be i.i.d. copies of a random variable $X \in \mathbb R^d$ with $\mathbb E X = 0$ and $\mathrm{cov} (X) = I_d$. Moreover, assume that $X$ has elliptically symmetric distribution with characteristic generator $\psi : \mathbb R_+ \mapsto \mathbb R$. Given $u \in \mathcal{S}^{d-1}$, let $Z_n(u) = \dotp{\frac{\sum_{j=1}^n X_j}{\sqrt{n}}}{u}$. Assume that there exists $\alpha > 0$ and $M > 0$ such that $\psi(t^2) = o\left(\frac{1}{t^\alpha}\right)$ whenever $t > M$. Then for $n_0 \in \mathbb N$ large enough and all $n \geq n_0$, the density of $Z_n(u)$ exists and is Lipschitz continuous with a uniform Lipschitz constant for all $n$ sufficiently large.

[Lemma lem.one-slice-renewal of arXiv:2605.26082, 'Quantitative Einstein relation for reversible diffusions in a random environment'] Fix $k\ge1$ and $n\ge2k$. Let $H_{\rm past}$ be a bounded random variable measurable with respect to
		\[
			\sigma(X^\lambda_s:0\le s\le n\Delta-\Delta)\vee\sigma(Y_0,\ldots,Y_{n-2}),
		\]
			let $G$ be a Borel subset of $\mathbb{R}^d$, and let $F\colon\mathbb{R}^d\times\Omega\to\mathbb{R}$ be bounded measurable with $F(y,\cdot)$ $\mathcal H_{\mathsf L(y\cdot e_1-4R)}$-measurable for each $y$. Define
				\begin{equation}
					H=\mathbf 1_{\{\tau_k=n\Delta\}} H_{\rm past} \mathbf 1_{\{X^\lambda(n\Delta)\in G\}} F(X^\lambda(n\Delta),\omega),\qquad n\ge 2k\, ,
				\end{equation}
			and let $\Phi$ be a bounded function of the shifted future data that has the following form: for bounded measurable $f$ of the shifted path and marks and bounded measurable $g$ of the shifted environment restricted to $\mathsf R_+$,
			\[
				\Phi(\gamma,\beta,\omega_+)=f(\gamma,\beta)g(\omega_+)\, .
			\]
			Then
			\[
				\widehat{\mathbb E}_0^\lambda[\Phi(\mathcal Y_k)H]
				=\widehat{\mathbb E}_0^\lambda[\Phi(\mathcal Y_0)\mid D=\infty]\,
			\widehat{\mathbb E}_0^\lambda[H]\, .
		\]

[Corollary cor:label-configuration-reversal of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] For fixed $h\geq2$ and $k\geq3$, as $q\to\infty$ a uniformly random
$A\in\binom{[q]}k$ satisfies
\[
 \mathbb P(A\text{ is not }B_h)
 =\frac{k!K_{h,k}}q+O_{h,k}(q^{-2}),
 \qquad K_{h,k}\asymp_k h^{k-2}.
\]
For each $2\leq r\leq h$,
\[
 \mathbb P(|hA|=M_{h,k}-M_{h-r,k})
 =\frac{k!\kappa_{k,r}}q+O_{h,k}(q^{-2}).
\]
Moreover,
\begin{equation}
 \begin{aligned}
  \mathbb P\bigl(r_{h,k}(|hA|)\leq1\bigr)
   &=1-O_{h,k}(q^{-2}),\\
  \mathbb P\bigl(r_h(A)=1\mid A\text{ is not }B_h\bigr)
   &=1-O_{h,k}(q^{-1}).
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
By contrast, if $k\geq4$ is fixed and $N_{h,k}$ is uniform in the finite set
$\mathcal R(h,k)$, then, as $h\to\infty$,
\begin{equation}
 \mathbb P\bigl(r_{h,k}(N_{h,k})\leq1\bigr)
 =\frac{h}{|\mathcal R(h,k)|}
 =h^{-(k-2)+o_k(1)}\longrightarrow0.
\end{equation}
Thus principal labels are asymptotically negligible among attainable
cardinalities, although their realizations account for asymptotically almost
every fixed-order configuration in a growing interval.
Here $h$ is fixed before $q\to\infty$;
no joint $(h,q)$ assertion is made.

[Pro Pro_basic_properties of arXiv:2606.22183, 'Expected loss of quasi-arithmetic means of exchangeable random variables'] Let $I\subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be a nondegenerate interval.
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
 \item If $L_i:I\to\mathbb{R}$ is strongly $\alpha_i$-convex for $i=1,2$, where $\alpha_1,\alpha_2:(I-I)\to\mathbb{R}_+$ are even error functions
       and $c_1,c_2\in\mathbb{R}_+$, then $c_1L_1+c_2L_2$ is strongly $(c_1\alpha_1+c_2\alpha_2)$-convex.
 \item If $\alpha_1,\alpha_2:(I-I)\to\mathbb{R}_+$ are even error functions with $\alpha_1\leqslant\alpha_2$ and $L:I\to\mathbb{R}$ is strongly $\alpha_2$-convex, then $L$ is strongly $\alpha_1$-convex as well.
 \item If, for each $n\in\mathbb{N}$, $L_n:I\to\mathbb{R}$ is strongly $\alpha_n$-convex, where $\alpha_n:(I-I)\to\mathbb{R}_+$ is an even error function,
 and the sequences $(L_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ and $ (\alpha_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ pointwise converge to $L:I\to\mathbb{R}$ and to $\alpha:(I-I)\to\mathbb{R}_+$ as $n\to\infty$, respectively, then $L$ is strongly $\alpha$-convex.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Measured 2026-09-05 on the EMIT and OCO-2 stacking pools (70 cells, the pool protocol, full calibration, paired). Given that the long-only gain is the estimation variance the constraint removes at the rows the stack is scored on, the amount of constraint was chosen with the evaluation inputs: a blend w(t) between the simplex and least-squares stacks with t minimising the cross-validated calibration error plus the excess bootstrap variance of the blend at the evaluation rows over the calibration rows, and a per-row version t_i = 1/(1 + kappa v_i/median v) that leans to the simplex where least squares is uncertain. P24 (a) HELD: on EMIT the per-cell blend reads +0.08 vs the simplex and beats least squares on 39 of 40 cells; (b) HELD: on OCO-2 t* is at or above 0.5 on 30 of 30 cells and the blend reads +0.66 vs least squares; (c) REFUTED: the per-row blend vs the per-cell blend is +0.70 on Y2 and -0.14 on EMIT overall; falsifier (blend worse than the simplex by more than 1 on EMIT, or than least squares by more than 0.3 on OCO-2) not triggered. Fresh-split replication (P25, split C, SPLIT_SEED 11, the criterion uses no evaluation targets): P25 (a) HELD: on split C the EMIT blend reads +0.63 vs the simplex and beats least squares on 35 of 40 cells; (b) HELD: on OCO-2 the blend reads +0.84 vs the simplex (wins 30 of 30) and +0.65 vs least squares; (c) HELD: t* averages 0.34 on EMIT and 0.67 on OCO-2; falsifier (blend worse than the simplex by more than 1 on EMIT, or than least squares by more than 0.3 on OCO-2) not triggered. Bootstrap-size stability (P28, B = 16 against B = 8 on split B): P28 (a) HELD: t*(16) equals t*(8) on 86 pct of the 70 cells and is within 0.2 on 100 pct; (b) HELD: the blend's mean gain against the simplex moves from +0.08 to +0.06 on EMIT and from +0.83 to +0.83 on OCO-2, and the both-endpoints win count on OCO-2 is 30 of 30 at B = 16; falsifier (agreement below 50 pct or a gain moving by more than 0.5) not triggered. Break test: a fixed midpoint t = 0.5 matches the criterion on OCO-2 (+0.96 / +1.01 against +0.83 / +0.84 on the two splits) but loses 1.6 and 4.4 pct on EMIT where the criterion stays at +0.08 and +0.63 - the criterion's value is knowing, without labels, when not to leave the simplex; the EMIT shortfall against the hindsight-best t is the bias-shift term of the risk identity. Scarce calibration (P30, 240 of the calibration rows per cell, split B): P30 (a) HELD: at n = 240 the simplex beats least squares by +14.10 on EMIT (full calibration +8.83); (b) REFUTED: t* averages 0.22 on EMIT and the blend reads -2.61 vs the simplex; (c) HELD: on OCO-2 the blend beats both endpoints on 30 of 30 cells and the simplex reads +2.27 vs least squares (full calibration -0.18); falsifier (blend worse than the simplex by more than 1 on EMIT) TRIGGERED. The observable part of the bias shift (P31): adding t^2 (D_ev - D_cal), the shift in the two bases' mean squared disagreement between the evaluation and calibration rows, to the criterion - P31 (a) REFUTED: the R'-blend reads -0.71 vs the simplex on EMIT split B (R-blend +0.08) and +0.71 on split C (R-blend +0.63); (b) HELD: on OCO-2 the R'-blend is -0.11 vs the R-blend on split B and -0.12 on split C; (c) REFUTED: mean t** 0.39 against t* 0.33 on EMIT, share of the hindsight optimum 0.07 -> -0.62; falsifier (R'-blend worse than the R-blend by more than 0.3 on any corpus or split) TRIGGERED.

\]

[Df 10 ({\cite{constructions}*{Theorem 3.3}}) of arXiv:2609.03836, 'Koszul Orlik--Solomon Algebras from Non-supersolvable Arrangements'] The following are equivalent for a flat $F$ in a matroid $M$:
    \begin{enumerate}[(i)]
    \item For any flat $G$ in $L$, we have
    \(
        \rk_M F + \rk_M G = \rk_M (F \vee G) + \rk_M (F \cap G).
    \)
    \item For any flat $G$ of $M$ with $\rk_M F + \rk_M G > \rk M$, we have $\rk_M (F \cap G) > 0$.
    \end{enumerate}
    We say $F$ is \textbf{{modular}} in $M$ if it satisfies these equivalent conditions.
title: {\cite{constructions}*{Theorem 3.3}}

[Theorem 19 of arXiv:2609.01098, 'Gaussian upper bounds for averaged heat semigroups on graphs'] Let $x,y\in X$, $p\in[1,\infty]$, $r_2\geq r_1\geq0$, $t>0$, and $\delta\in(0,1)$. Assume that for $z\in\{x,y\}$ and all $\omega\in\ell^\infty(X)$ there are $\phi_z(h)=\phi_z(p,r_1,r_2,\delta,t,h)>0$, monotone increasing in $h$, such that 
\[
\left(\fint_{t/2-\delta r_1^2}^{t/2+\delta r_1^2}\|{B_z(r_1)}P_\tau^\omega\|_{2,2p}^{2p}\drm \tau\right)^\frac{1}{p}
\leq \phi_z(h(\omega))^2\fint_{t/2-\delta  r_2^2}^{t/2+\delta r_2^2}\| P_\tau^\omega\|_{2,2}^2\drm \tau.
\] 
Then, for $t\geq 2r_1^2$,  we have
\[
\left(
\fint_{t-2\delta r_1^2}^{t+2\delta r_1^2} \|{B_x(r_1)}P_{\tau}{B_y(r_1)}\|_{(2p)',2p}^p\drm \tau
\right)^\frac{1}{p}
\leq 
\phi_x(\sigma)\phi_y(\sigma)\euler^{\sigma(\delta r_2^2-t/2)-\Lambda(t-2\delta r_1^2)-tS^{-2}\zeta(\rho(B_x(r_1),B_y(r_1))S/t)},
\]
where 
\[
\sigma=\sigma(\rho(B_x(r_1),B_y(r_1))S/t),\qquad \sigma(x)=\sqrt{1+x^2}-1.
\]
title: Theorem 19 of arXiv:2609.01098

Let H: R^n → R be convex and superlinear, i.e. H(p)/|p| → +∞ as |p| → ∞. Its Legendre (Fenchel) transform is L(q) := sup_{p ∈ R^n} ( p·q - H(p) ), q ∈ R^n, and L is called the Lagrangian associated with H. Then: (i) the supremum is attained for every q, and L is finite, convex and superlinear; (ii) L* = H, i.e. H(p) = sup_q ( p·q - L(q) ) (duality of H and L); (iii) Fenchel-Young: p·q ≤ H(p) + L(q) for all p,q, with equality iff q ∈ ∂H(p) iff p ∈ ∂L(q); (iv) if in addition H ∈ C^2 with D^2H(p) ≥ θ I for all p and some θ > 0, then DH: R^n → R^n is a bijection, L ∈ C^1, DL = (DH)^{-1}, DL is Lipschitz with constant 1/θ, and consequently L(q+w) + L(q-w) - 2L(q) ≤ |w|^2/θ for all q,w.
H: R^n → R is finite everywhere and convex (hence continuous)
H is superlinear: H(p)/|p| → ∞ as |p| → ∞
for part (iv): H ∈ C^2 and D^2H ≥ θI with θ > 0 (which already implies superlinearity)

[Lemma 8 (Laplace transform of the ordinary uniform collector) of arXiv:2605.14511, 'Clumsy and Careless:\\ Stationary-Entry Flux in Non-monotone Coupon Collectors'] Let $C_n$ be the ordinary uniform coupon collector time measured in standard-coupon draws.  Then, for $0\le x<1$,
\[
        \phi_n(x)=\prod_{j=1}^n\frac{(j/n)x}{1-(1-j/n)x}.
\]
Consequently, with $q_n=1-\rho_n$,
\[
        s_n=\phi_n(q_n)
        =\prod_{j=1}^n\frac{j}{j+n\rho_n/q_n}
        =\frac{\Gamma(n+1)\Gamma(1+n\rho_n/q_n)}
        {\Gamma(n+1+n\rho_n/q_n)}.
\]

[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] The chi laws in small dimensions are as follows:
\begin{enumerate}
\item At $n=1$ the chi law and its moments are as follows:
$$\chi_{1t}=\sqrt{\frac{2}{t\pi}}\,e^{-x^2/2t}dx\quad,\quad 
M_k=\sqrt{\frac{(2t)^k}{\pi}}\,\Gamma\left(\frac{k+1}{2}\right)$$

\item At $n=2$ the chi law and its moments are as follows:
$$\chi_{2t}=\frac{1}{t}\,xe^{-x^2/2t}dx\quad,\quad 
M_k=\sqrt{(2t)^k}\,\Gamma\left(\frac{k}{2}+1\right)$$

\item At $n=3$ the chi law and its moments are as follows:
$$\chi_{3t}=\sqrt{\frac{2}{t^3\pi}}\,x^2e^{-x^2/2t}dx\quad,\quad 
M_k=2\sqrt{\frac{(2t)^k}{\pi}}\,\Gamma\left(\frac{k+3}{2}\right)$$
\end{enumerate}
The law $\chi_{2t}$ is called Rayleigh law, and the law $\chi_{3t}$ is called Maxwell-Boltzmann law.

(i) If $\|S_nf\|_{L^2}\not\to \infty$ then $\mathsf{H}=\bbR$.
\vskip0.2cm

(ii) If $(f_j)$ is irreducible then $\mathsf{H}=\{0\}$.
\vskip0.2cm

(iii) If $(f_j)$ is reducible and $\|S_nf\|_{L^2}\to \infty$    then 
$
\mathsf{H}=t_0\bbZ
$
for some $t_0>0$.

body: [Theorem thm:twolist of arXiv:2608.23638, 'Replicable Conformal Prediction'] Fix public constants $\Delta>0$, $0<f_{\min}\le f_{\max}<\infty$; let $\mathfrak F$ be the nonempty class of continuous score distributions satisfying Assumption~(ass:margin of the paper) with these constants, $\kappa=f_{\max}/f_{\min}$, $\beta=\varepsilon/(2f_{\max})\le\Delta/2$, and $0<\varepsilon<\min(\alpha,1-\alpha)$. \emph{(a)} For $F\in\mathfrak F$ and $n\ge\lceil32\kappa^{2}\log(2/\delta)/\varepsilon^{2}\rceil$, deterministic-grid \textsc{ReCal}{} ($u=0$) satisfies, with probability $\ge1-\delta$ over the calibration sample, the \emph{joint} event that $\tau$ lies in a sample-independent two-element list $\mathcal{L}_{n,\delta}(F)=\{g,g+\beta\}\subset\beta\mathbb Z$, depending only on $F$ and the public parameters and hence unknown to the analysts, \emph{and} $F(\tau)\in[1-\alpha-\tfrac{\varepsilon}{4\kappa},\,1-\alpha+\tfrac\varepsilon2+\tfrac{\varepsilon}{4\kappa}]\subseteq[1-\alpha\pm\varepsilon]$; any $m$ analysts all land in the common list with probability $\ge1-m\delta$, marginal validity is preserved, and no $\rho^{-2}$ factor appears. \emph{(b)} For $\delta<\tfrac12$, list size two is optimal within $\mathfrak F$: no procedure (any sample size, any seed law) has both a deterministic singleton output $v_F$ and the two-sided band, each with probability $\ge1-\delta$, for every $F\in\mathfrak F$; this is already impossible on $\{\mathrm{Unif}[t,t+f_{\min}^{-1}]\}\subseteq\mathfrak F$, whose membership needs only $f_{\min}\Delta\le\min(\alpha,1-\alpha)$, forced by $\mathfrak F\neq\varnothing$ (Lemma~(lem:translate of the paper)). The optimality claim is about numerical thresholds; it transfers to classifier maps whenever $t\mapsto\mathcal{C}_t$ is injective on the admissible range (Appendix~(app:twolist of the paper)). (Proof: Appendix~(app:twolist of the paper).) (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 7 of arXiv:2608.08242, 'Bang--bang representation of $3\times 3$ embeddable stochastic matrices'] Let $L=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3)$ and
$R=\operatorname{diag}(\rho_1,\rho_2,\rho_3)$ be positive, and put
$\lambda=\det L$ and $\rho=\det R$. Let $A\in \mathcal M_+$ and put $B=LAR$. Then
\[
T_{ij}(B)=\frac{\lambda\rho}{\lambda_i\rho_j}T_{ij}(A),
\qquad
G(B)=\lambda\rho G(A),
\]
\[
V_{ii}(B)=\lambda\rho V_{ii}(A),
\qquad
V_{ij}(B)=\lambda\rho\lambda_j\rho_iV_{ij}(A)
\quad(i\neq j),
\]
\[
C_{ij}(B)=\frac{\rho_j}{\rho_i}C_{ij}(A),
\]
and
\[
q_{ij}^{B}(c)
=\lambda\rho\lambda_i\rho_j\,
 q_{ij}^A\!\left(\frac{\rho_i}{\rho_j}c\right).
\]
Moreover,
$T_{ij}(A^t)=T_{ji}(A)$ and
$V_{ij}(A^t)=V_{ji}(A)$.

[Definition def:optimalweightoperator of arXiv:2608.23765, '\texorpdfstring{Tight Majorizations and Convergence Rates\\ of Nuclear Norm Minimization I'] Let $\varepsilon > 0$ and $\mathbf{X} \in \R^{d_1 \times d_2}$ be a matrix with the full singular value decomposition 
$\mathbf{X}= \mathbf{U}_{\mathbf{X}} \diag (\boldsymbol{\sigma}) \mathbf{V}_{\mathbf{X}}^\top$, 
where $\mathbf{U}_{\mathbf{X}}  \in \R^{d_1 \times d_1}$ and $\mathbf{V}_{\mathbf{X}} \in \R^{d_2 \times d_2}$ are orthogonal
and $\diag (\boldsymbol{\sigma}) \in \R^{d_1 \times d_2}$ is the rectangular diagonal matrix with the extended vector of singular values $\boldsymbol{\sigma} \in \R^{D}$ of $\mathbf{X}$ on the diagonal.
Then the  \emph{weight operator}  $\W{\mathbf{X}}{\varepsilon}: \R^{d_1 \times d_2} \to \R^{d_1 \times d_2}$ 
is defined by
\begin{equation} 
	\W{\mathbf{X}}{\varepsilon}(\mathbf{Z}) = \mathbf{U}_{\mathbf{X}} \left[\mathbf{H}_{\boldsymbol{\sigma},\varepsilon} \circ (\mathbf{U}_{\mathbf{X}}^{\top} \mathbf{Z} \mathbf{V}_{\mathbf{X}})\right] \mathbf{V}_{\mathbf{X}}^{\top}
\end{equation}
for each $\mathbf{Z} \in \R^{d_1 \times d_2}$.
Here $\mathbf{H}_{\boldsymbol{\sigma},\varepsilon}$ is the 
weight operator core matrix of (def:weightcore of the paper).

[Theorem pre:gamblersRuin of arXiv:2605.19835, 'Reemergence of the Epidemic Threshold in SIRS Infections on Connected Stars'] {feller1957introduction}}]
    In the gambler's ruin game, a player starts with some amount of money $P_0 \in \mathOrText{\mathds{N}}_{\geq 1}$ and then repeatedly throws a coin that shows head with probability $p \in (0,1)$, independent of all other outcomes. If it shows heads, the player's money increases by~$1$, otherwise, it decreases by~$1$. The game ends at time~$T$ when the player either reaches the lower bound $\ell \in \mathOrText{\mathds{N}}_{< P_0}$ or the upper bound $u \in \mathOrText{\mathds{N}}_{> P_0}$ of money.
    Let $(P_t)_{t \in \mathOrText{\mathds{N}}}$ be the amount of money that a player has in a gambler's ruin game that has a probability of $p \in (0,1)\setminus\{1/2\}$ for them to win in each step. Let $q=1-p$.  Then
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $\Pr{P_T = \ell} = \frac{1-(p/q)^{u-P_0}}{1-(p/q)^{u-\ell}}$ and
        \item $\Pr{P_T = u} = \frac{1-(q/p)^{P_0-l}}{1-(q/p)^{u-\ell}}$.\qedhere
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 1 ($L_p$ Brunn-Minkowski inequality) of arXiv:2609.00743, '$L_p$ Brunn-Minkowski inequality for the eigenvalue of generalized Monge-Ampère equation'] Suppose $k\ge 0$. Let $\Omega_0$ and $\Omega_1$ be bounded, smooth and strictly convex domains containing the origin as an interior point, and $\Omega_\alpha:=(1-\alpha)\Omega_0+_p \alpha\Omega_1$ be the $L_p$-Minkowski addition of $\Omega_0$ and $\Omega_1$, where $p:=k+1\ge 1$ and $\alpha\in[0,1]$. Then
\begin{equation}
    \lambda(\Omega_\alpha)^{-\frac{p}{2n}}\ge (1-\alpha)\lambda(\Omega_0)^{-\frac{p}{2n}}+\alpha\lambda(\Omega_1)^{-\frac{p}{2n}}.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma lem:Ttransform-2coord of arXiv:2601.04079, 'TV homogenization inequalities'] Fix $a,b\in[0,1]$ and $\lambda\in[0,1]$, and define
\[
a' := \lambda a + (1-\lambda)b,
\qquad
b' := \lambda b + (1-\lambda)a.
\]
Let
\[
\eta := 
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle \frac{\lambda(1-\lambda)(a-b)^2}{2(1-ab)}, & ab<1,\\
[1ex]
0, & ab=1,
\end{cases}
\]
and consider the row--stochastic $4\times4$ matrix (indexed by $00,01,10,11$)
\begin{equation}

M_{\lambda}(a,b):=
\left(\begin{array}{cccc}
1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
\eta & \lambda-\eta & (1-\lambda)-\eta & \eta \\
\eta & (1-\lambda)-\eta & \lambda-\eta & \eta \\
0 & 0 & 0 & 1 
\end{array}\right).
\end{equation}
Then all entries of $M_{\lambda}(a,b)$ are nonnegative, and for both $s\in\{+,-\}$,
\[
\Bigl(\Ber\!\left(\tfrac12+s\,\tfrac a2\right)\otimes \Ber\!\left(\tfrac12+s\,\tfrac b2\right)\Bigr)\,M_{\lambda}(a,b)
=
\Ber\!\left(\tfrac12+s\,\tfrac {a'}2\right)\otimes \Ber\!\left(\tfrac12+s\,\tfrac {b'}2\right).
\]

[Corollary Dynamic formulation of $W_p$ of arXiv:2603.14163, '\LARGE \bf Tail Bounds for Queues with Abandonment: Constant, Moderate, Large Deviations, '] Let $\mathcal{L}(X), \mathcal{L}(Z') \in \mathcal{P}_p(\mathbb{R})$ and suppose there exists a weakly continuous curve $\mu_t:(0,\infty)\to\mathcal{P}_p(\mathbb{R})$ and a Borel vector field $v_t$ such that
    $\partial_t \mu_t + \partial_x(\mu_t v_t)=0$,
    $\sup_{t\in(0,\infty)} \|x\|_{L^p(\mu_t)}<\infty$. Moreover, suppose
    $\mu_t \Rightarrow \mathcal{L}(X)$ as $t\downarrow 0$, and
    $\mu_t \Rightarrow \mathcal{L}(Z')$ as $t\uparrow \infty$.
    Then
    \[
    W_p(\mathcal{L}(X),\mathcal{L}(Z'))
    \le
    \inf\left\{
    \int_{0}^{\infty}
    \left(\int_{\mathbb{R}} |v_t(x)|^p\,d\mu_t(x)\right)^{1/p}\!dt
    :\ \partial_t \mu_t + \partial_x(\mu_t v_t)=0,\ 
    \mu_t \overset{t\downarrow 0}{\Rightarrow} \mathcal{L}(X),\ 
    \mu_t \overset{t\uparrow \infty}{\Rightarrow} \mathcal{L}(Z')
    \right\},
    \]
    where $\Rightarrow$ denotes weak convergence. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Dynamic formulation of $W_p$

[Lemma 1 of arXiv:2609.03750, '\bf Pullback Measure Attractors, Zero-Noise Limits, and Moderate Deviations for 2D Stochas'] For every $v, \widetilde{v}, \widehat{v}\in V$, the trilinear form $b$ is continuous on $V\times V\times V$, and there exists a constant $C>0$ such that
 \begin{align}
&|b(v,\widetilde{v}, \widehat{v})|\leq C\left(|v|^{\frac{1}{2}}\|v\|^{\frac{1}{2}}\|\widetilde{v}\||\widehat{v}|^{\frac{1}{2}}\|\widehat{v}\|^{\frac{1}{2}}+|\partial_xv||\partial_z \widetilde{v}||\widehat{v}|^{\frac{1}{2}}\|\widehat{v}\|^{\frac{1}{2}}\right),\\
&\left| \langle B(\widetilde{v}, \widetilde{v}) - B(\widehat{v}, \widehat{v}), \widetilde{v} - \widehat{v} \rangle \right|
\leq C \|\widetilde{v}\| |\widetilde{v} - \widehat{v}| \|\widetilde{v} - \widehat{v}\|
+ C |\partial_z \widetilde{v}|  |\widetilde{v} - \widehat{v}|^{1/2} \|\widetilde{v} - \widehat{v}\|^{3/2}.
\end{align}
 Moreover, for all $v,\widetilde v,\widehat v\in V$,
 \[
 b(v,\widetilde v,\widetilde v)=0,
 \qquad b(v,\widetilde v,\widehat v)=-b(v,\widehat v,\widetilde v).
 \]
 If, in addition, $v\in D(A)$, then
\begin{align}
	\langle v\partial_xv+\mathcal W(v)\partial_zv,\partial_{zz}v\rangle=0.
\end{align}
The last identity is used at the Galerkin level before passage to the limit.
If \( v, \widetilde{v} \in V \) and \( \partial_z \widetilde{v} \in V \), then
\begin{equation}
	\|B(v, \widetilde{v})\|_{V'} \leq C\bigl( (|v| + |\partial_z v|)|\partial_{x} \widetilde{v}| + |v| \cdot \|\partial_z \widetilde{v}\| + |v| \cdot |\partial_z \widetilde{v}|^{1/2}\|\partial_z \widetilde{v}\|^{1/2} \bigr).
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 1 of arXiv:2609.03750

body:
[Theorem thm:vonLuxburg of arXiv:2606.14895, 'Effective Resistances and Commute Times in Sparse Random Geometric Graphs'] Let $G_n = (V_n, E_n)$ be an RGG with radius of connection $r_n$ from $n$ uniformly distributed points on $\mathbb{T}^2$ with vertex degrees $D_u$ and graph volume $\mathrm{Vol}(G_n) = \sum_{u\in V_n} D_u$. Suppose that the fixed pair of vertices $u$ and $v$ at positions $X_u$ and $X_v$ are separated by Euclidean distance $d(X_u,X_v) > 8r_n$. Assuming that $n r_n^2 / \ln n \to \infty$ as $n\to\infty$, there exists a constant $c$ such that the commute distance satisfies, with probability converging to $1$, 
\[
nr_n^2\left\vert\frac{1}{\mathrm{Vol}(G_n)}C_{uv} -
\left(\frac{1}{D_u}+\frac{1}{D_v}\right)\right| \leq c/nr_n^3\,.
\]
Therefore, further requiring that $r_n\to 0$ and $nr_n^3\to\infty$ yields
\[
C_{uv} \;\to\; \mathrm{Vol}(G_n)\left(\frac{1}{D_u} + \frac{1}{D_v}\right)\qquad almost\;surely\,.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 3 of von Luxburg et al.\ \cite{vonLuxburg2014} as applied to uniformly distributed points on $\mathbb{T}^2$

Let H: R^n → R be convex and superlinear, L = H*, g: R^n → R Lipschitz, and let u(x,t) = min_y ( tL((x-y)/t) + g(y) ) be the Hopf-Lax function. (i) If g is semiconcave with constant C, i.e. g(x+z) - 2g(x) + g(x-z) ≤ C|z|^2 for all x,z ∈ R^n, then u(x+z,t) - 2u(x,t) + u(x-z,t) ≤ C|z|^2 for all x,z ∈ R^n and all t > 0. (ii) If instead H ∈ C^2 with D^2H(p) ≥ θ I for all p and some θ > 0 (uniform convexity), and g is merely Lipschitz, then u(x+z,t) - 2u(x,t) + u(x-z,t) ≤ |z|^2 / (θ t) for all x,z and all t > 0. In dimension one, (ii) is equivalent to the one-sided (Oleinik) derivative bound u_x(x+h,t) - u_x(x,t) ≤ h/(θ t) for h > 0 in the distributional sense. This one-sided bound is what distinguishes the Hopf-Lax solution from other Lipschitz almost-everywhere solutions.
H convex and superlinear; L = H*
g Lipschitz (plus, in (i), semiconcave with constant C)
in (ii): H ∈ C^2 with D^2H ≥ θI, θ > 0
t > 0 (the bound in (ii) degenerates as t ↓ 0)

body: For differentiable problems, the KKT conditions at a point are: primal feasibility, dual feasibility (lambda >= 0), complementary slackness (lambda_i g_i(x) = 0 for each i), and stationarity (the gradient of the Lagrangian in x vanishes). Under a constraint qualification they are necessary for optimality; for convex problems they are also sufficient, and with Slater's condition they characterize the optima.
title: Karush-Kuhn-Tucker Conditions

Let X be a nonnegative random variable (or f a nonnegative measurable function on a measure space, integrated against the measure) and a > 0. Then P(X >= a) <= E[X] / a. More generally, if phi: [0, infinity) -> [0, infinity) is nondecreasing and phi(a) > 0, then for any real random variable X, P(X >= a) <= E[phi(X^+)] / phi(a), and for any X and a > 0, P(|X| >= a) <= E|X|^p / a^p for every p > 0 (Markov applied to |X|^p). The bound is attained: for X taking the value a with probability m/a and 0 otherwise (0 < m <= a), E X = m and P(X >= a) = m/a.

Let d,m>=1 and x in R^d be deterministic with ||x||_2=sqrt(d). Let w_i be iid N(0,I_d/d), a_i iid N(0,1/m), and suppose all hidden and output weights are independent. Put f(x)=sum_(i=1..m) a_i sigma(w_i^T x). Assume sigma:R->R is continuous and nonconstant, differentiable almost everywhere, has an almost-everywhere continuous derivative, and |sigma_prime(t)|<=C_sigma(1+|t|^(k-1)) almost everywhere for a fixed integer k>=1 and constant C_sigma>0. There is a C>0 depending only on sigma such that, for every delta in (0,1), with probability at least1-delta, ||grad f(x)||_2 <= C(1+log(1/delta)/sqrt(d))(1+1/sqrt(m delta)). Consequently for any deterministic s>0 and x_s=x-sign(f(x))*s*grad f(x), on the same event ||x_s-x||_2/||x||_2 <= (Cs/sqrt(d))(1+log(1/delta)/sqrt(d))(1+1/sqrt(m delta)). This is the size estimate; no sign-reversal success rate is asserted here.

Independent hidden Gaussian vectors of variance1/d and Gaussian output weights of variance1/m
Finite m,d; no relative-width restriction
Continuous nonconstant activation with a.e. differentiability and a.e. continuous derivative
Fixed polynomial growth bound on the derivative
delta in (0,1), deterministic positive step s

body: In calculus, Taylor's theorem gives an approximation of a -times differentiable function around a given point by a polynomial of degree , called the -th-order Taylor polynomial. For a smooth function, the Taylor polynomial is the truncation at the order of the Taylor series of the function. The first-order Taylor polynomial is the linear approximation of the function, and the second-order Taylor polynomial is often referred to as the quadratic approximation. There are several versions of Taylor's theorem, some giving explicit estimates of the approximation error of the function by its Taylor polynomial.
title: Taylor's theorem

body:
[Proposition 19 of arXiv:2609.03191, 'On lifting representations and actions on curves of the metacyclic groups $C_{p^s}\rtimes '] We consider a cyclic $C_{p^s}$-extension of $k((t))$, its lower jumps $l_1<\cdots <l_s$, and its upper jumps $u_1<\cdots<u_s$. Then the following properties hold. 

\medskip
{\bf (1)} The lower and upper jumps determine uniquely each other by the recursive identities $l_1:=u_1$ and $l_i:=l_{i-1}+p^{i-1}(u_i-u_{i-1})$ for each $i\in\llbracket2,s\rrbracket$. 

\smallskip
{\bf (2)} For each $j\in\llbracket1,s\rrbracket $ we have $l_j=u_1+\sum_{i=1}^{j-1} p^i(u_{i+1}-u_i)$.

\smallskip
{\bf (3)} For each $j\in\llbracket1,s\rrbracket$ we have identities 
$$\sum_{i=1}^j \frac{l_i}{p^i}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^j p^{i-1}u_i}{p^j}$$
and
$$p^{j-1}u_j:=l_j+(p-1)\sum_{i=1}^{j-1}l_ip^{j-i-1}.$$

{\bf (4)} For $b\in\llbracket0,p^s-1\rrbracket$, write
\[
b=\delta_{1,b}+\delta_{2,b}p+\cdots+\delta_{s,b}p^{s-1}
\]
with $\delta_{i,b}\in\llbracket0,p-1\rrbracket$ for each $i\in\llbracket1,s\rrbracket$ and define
\[
N_{s,b}:=\sum_{i=1}^s p^{s-i}\bigl[p-1+(p-1-\delta_{i,b})l_i\bigr].
\] Then for each $b\in \llbracket1,p^s-1\rrbracket$, if $j\in\llbracket0,s-1\rrbracket$ is the largest such that $p^j\mid b$, then we have identities 
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
N_{s,b-1}-N_{s,b}&=p^{s-j-1}\Big[l_{j+1}-(p-1)\sum_{i=1}^j p^{j+1-i}l_i\Big]\\
&=p^{s-j-1}[l_1+\sum_{i=1}^j p^i(u_{i+1}-pu_i)].
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
In particular, $N_{s,b-1}-N_{s,b}\ge p^{s-j-1}l_1\ge l_1>0$ and therefore we have $\frac{l_{j+1}}{p^{j+1}}-(p-1)\sum_{i=1}^j\frac{l_i}{p^i}\ge\frac{l_1}{p^{j+1}}>0$.

[Definition 4 of arXiv:2608.25725, 'Gr\"obner Bases for Alexander Fitting Ideals of Links'] Let \(L\) be an oriented \(\ell\)-component link without a chosen ordering.
Choose a temporary labeling, with corresponding positive meridians
\(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_\ell\). For each \(\sigma\in S_\ell\), let
\(\phi_\sigma\colon\pi_1(X_L)\twoheadrightarrow\Z^\ell\) be defined by
\(\phi_\sigma(\mu_i)=e_{\sigma(i)}\). 
The \(k\)th Alexander--Gr\"obner invariant of the unordered link
is the \(S_\ell\)-indexed family
\[
\Bigl(
\AG_k(\pi_1(X_L),\phi_\sigma)
\Bigr)_{\sigma\in S_\ell},
\]
considered up to the reindexing induced by a change of the
temporary labeling. Since a
permutation of the variables need not preserve the fixed lexicographic
order, each member is reduced separately with respect to the order in
Remark~\ref{rem:term-order}.

[Lemma 39 of arXiv:2511.10535, 'Eigenvalues of Brownian Motions on $\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$'] There is a universal constant $c>0$ such that the following holds. 
    Let $G$ be an $N\times N$ matrix with standard real Gaussian entries, and assume the $N(N+1)/2$ pairs $\{(G_{ij},G_{ji}): 1\le i\le j\le N\}$ are jointly independent. 
    Then for any $N\times N$ complex matrix $A$, deterministic or random and independent of $G$, and any $k\ge c^{-1}\log N$,
    \[
    \sigma_{N-\ell} ( G + A) \ge c\ell/N\qquad \forall \ell\, \ge k
    \]
    with probability at least $1-e^{-ck}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Theorem thm:persistence pairing of arXiv:2608.29719, 'Persistence Pairing Graphs: Tracking Changes of Selected Homology Bases'] For the cellwise filtration
\[
K^0 \subseteq K^1 \subseteq \cdots \subseteq K^N,
\]
every persistence pair $(i,j)$ determines the interval
\[
[i,j),
\]
and every unpaired positive index $i$ determines the interval
\[
[i,\infty).
\]
For every positive index $i$, the interval cycle $\rho_i$ defined in~(equation eq:interval-cycle of the paper) represents the corresponding homology class throughout exactly this lifetime.

For the original filtration determined by $f$, a persistence pair $(i,j)$ determines the interval
\[
[f(\sigma_i),f(\sigma_j)),
\]
whereas an unpaired positive cell $\sigma_i$ determines
\[
[f(\sigma_i),\infty).
\]
If $f(\sigma_i)=f(\sigma_j)$, then the interval $[i,j)$ is created entirely by the auxiliary tie-breaking refinement and has zero length on the original filtration value scale. Such an interval is omitted from the usual
barcode.

[Lemma MCL of arXiv:2410.23899, 'Tightness for interlacing geometric random walk bridges'] Assume the same notation as in Definition (DefAvoidingLawBer of the paper). Fix $k \in \mathbb{N}$, $T_0, T_1 \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $T_0 < T_1$, two functions $g^t, g^b: \llbracket T_0, T_1 \rrbracket  \rightarrow [-\infty, \infty)$ as well as $\vec{x}\,^b, \vec{y}\,^b, \vec{x}\,^t, \vec{y}\,^t \in \mathfrak{W}_k$. We assume that 
$$g^t(r) \geq g^b(r) \mbox{ for } r \in \llbracket T_0, T_1 \rrbracket \mbox{, } x_i^t \geq x^b_i \mbox{, and } y_i^t \geq y_i^b \mbox{ for } i = 1, \dots, k,$$
and also that $\Omega_{\mathsf{Inter}}(T_0, T_1, \vec{x}\,^b, \vec{y}\,^b, \infty,g^b)$ and $\Omega_{\mathsf{Inter}}(T_0, T_1, \vec{x}\,^t, \vec{y}\,^t, \infty,g^t)$ are both non-empty. Then, there exists a probability space $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})$, which supports two $\llbracket 1, k \rrbracket$-indexed geometric line ensembles $\mathfrak{Q}^t$ and $\mathfrak{Q}^b$ on $\llbracket T_0, T_1 \rrbracket$ such that the law of $\mathfrak{Q}^{t}$ {\big (}resp. $\mathfrak{Q}^b${\big )} under $\mathbb{P}$ is given by $\mathbb{P}_{\mathsf{Inter},\operatorname{Geom}}^{T_0, T_1, \vec{x}\,^t, \vec{y}\,^t, \infty, g^t}$ {\big (}resp. $\mathbb{P}_{\mathsf{Inter},\operatorname{Geom}}^{T_0, T_1, \vec{x}\,^b, \vec{y}\,^b, \infty, g^b}${\big )} and such that $\mathbb{P}$-almost surely $Q_i^t(r) \geq Q^b_i(r)$ for all $i \in \llbracket 1, k \rrbracket$ and $r \in \llbracket T_0, T_1 \rrbracket$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
For the minimal spanning forest of a homogeneous Poisson process in R^d, connectivity (a single tree) is proved only for d = 2 (Alexander) and is open for every d >= 3. The Lyons-Peres-Schramm theory (Minimal spanning forests, Ann. Probab. 2006, on transitive graphs; the Poisson case is its continuum analogue) does not settle it: uniqueness of the infinite cluster makes the free and wired minimal spanning forests coincide, and the absence of percolation at criticality makes every tree of the wired forest one-ended, but neither gives a single tree. The same argument would make the minimal spanning forest of Z^d connected for d >= 11, where theta(p_c) = 0 is known from the lace expansion and uniqueness holds by Burton-Keane, and that question is open (Lyons-Peres, Probability on Trees and Networks, Question 11.35). The Newman-Stein heuristic predicts infinitely many trees when d > 8.

Assumes: homogeneous Poisson process in R^d, Euclidean edge lengths

Let $\cD$ be such that $m$ is large enough, $d(n) \le \sqrt{m}(\log{m})^6$, and $D^*\ge\eps m$. [Proposition prop:tight1 of arXiv:2412.02160, 'A functional central limit theorem for weighted occupancy processes of the Karlin model'] Assume $|a_{i+j}-a_i| \le Cj^\beta$ with $\beta\in[0,\alpha/2)$. 
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item For all 
$p\in[1,\alpha/{2\beta})$,
 we have, for some constant $C$, 
\begin{equation}
{\mathbb E}\abs{\what W_n(t)-\what W_n(s)}^{2p} \le C \pp{\sigma_n^2|t-s|^{\alpha} + \sigma_n^{2p}|t-s|^{\alpha p}}, \mbox{ for all } 0\le s<t\le 1, n\in{\mathbb N}.
\end{equation}
\item For some constant $C>0$, almost surely, 
\begin{equation}
\abs{\what W_n(t)-\what W_n(s)}\le C (N(nt)-N(ns) + n(t-s)), \mbox{ for all } 0\le s\le t\le 1.
\end{equation} 
\end{enumerate}
As a consequence, if in addition 
\[
\beta\in\bigg[0,\frac{\alpha^2}2\bigg) \quad\mbox{ and }\quad p\in\pp{\frac1\alpha,\frac{\alpha}{2\beta}}, 
\]
the process $\sigma_n^{-1}\what W_n$ is tight in $D([0,1])$.

body:
[Lemma lemm_BH of arXiv:2503.24372, 'A criterion on the free energy for log-Sobolev inequalities in mean-field particle systems'] Let $N \geq 1$ and $\mu$ be a probability measure on $\R^N$ satisfying a log-Sobolev inequality with constant $\gamma_{\rm LS}>0$. 
Take $F:\R^N\to\R$ to be smooth and compactly supported and a Lipschitz function $H:\R^N\to\R$.
Then:

\begin{equation} 

\cov_{\mu}(F^2,H)^2
\leq 
\frac{4}{\gamma_{\rm LS}^2}  \sup_{x\in\R^N}|\nabla H (x)|^2 \, 
\E_{\mu}[F^2] \; \E_{\mu}\big[|\nabla F|^2\big],
\end{equation}

with the notation $|\nabla H (x)| = \big( \sum_{i =1}^N (\partial_{x_i}  H (x))^2 \big)^{1/2}$.
The same bound holds for a vector valued function $H(x)\in\R^d$.

Let $H_i:\R\to\R$ be Lipschitz ($1\leq i\leq N$) and let $F:\R^N\to\R$ be smooth and compactly supported. Then:

\begin{equation}

\sum_{i=1}^N\cov_{\mu}(F^2,H_i(x_i))^2
  \leq 
  \frac{4}{\gamma_{\rm LS}^2} \max_{1\leq i\leq N}\|H'_i\|^2_\infty \;  \E_{\mu}[F^2] \;  \E_{\mu}\big[|\nabla F
  |^2\big] 
  .
\end{equation}

[Definition of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] A Hilbert space is a complex vector space $H$, with a scalar product on it $<x,y>$, taken linear at left and antilinear at right,
$$<\lambda x,y>=\lambda<x,y>\quad,\quad <x,\lambda y>=\bar{\lambda}<x,y>$$
which is complete with respect to corresponding norm
$$||x||=\sqrt{<x,x>}$$
in the sense that any sequence $\{x_n\}$ which is a Cauchy sequence, having the property $||x_n-x_m||\to0$ with $n,m\to\infty$, has a limit, $x_n\to x$.

[Defn of arXiv:2605.06429, '\large \bf $\mathsf{GL}_N(\mathbb{C})$ BROWNIAN MOTION AND STOCHASTIC PDE ON ENTIRE FUNCTI'] Let $[a,b]\subset\mathbb{R}_+$, $k\in\mathbb{N}$, and $\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\mathbf{W}_{k}$.
Denote by
$\mathbf{P}^{a,b;\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}}$ the law of $k$ independent $\mathsf{A}$-bridges
started at $\mathbf{x}$ at time $a$ and ending at $\mathbf{y}$ at time $b$ and write

TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For simple random walk on the incipient infinite cluster of critical percolation, or more generally on critical random media with anomalous volume growth, Kesten's argument establishes subdiffusive behavior, that the walk's typical displacement after n steps scales as n^{1/(2+theta)} for some theta>0 rather than the diffusive n^{1/2}, by combining a volume-growth estimate showing balls of radius r typically contain of order r^{d_f} points, with d_f the fractal (volume) dimension of the cluster, and an effective-resistance estimate showing R_eff(0, B(0,r)^c) grows faster than linearly, of order r^{1+theta}, reflecting the long dangling ends and low-conductance bottlenecks characteristic of the critical cluster. Combining volume growth and resistance growth via the Nash/heat-kernel machinery, or a direct expected-exit-time computation, gives the subdiffusive exponent. The argument does not give the exact value of the subdiffusivity exponent in most dimensions, only bounds, with the precise exponent known rigorously only in specific settings such as sufficiently high dimension or tree-like/hierarchical models, and it is specific to critical (not subcritical or supercritical) percolation geometry, where the fractal, tree-like structure with many bottlenecks is essential to the argument. Typical failure: Assuming the subdiffusivity exponent established for one setting, such as high-dimensional or tree-based incipient infinite clusters where exact computation is possible, transfers to two-dimensional critical percolation, where the exact random-walk dimension remains a major open problem; volume-growth and resistance-growth exponents are model- and dimension-specific quantities that must be independently estimated rather than imported across models with superficially similar critical geometry. Canonical reference: Kesten, 1986, Annales de l'Institut Henri Poincare, Probabilites et Statistiques; Barlow, Jarai, Kumagai and Slade, 2008, Communications in Mathematical Physics.
the walk is on the incipient infinite cluster or a similarly statistically self-similar critical random graph
a known or boundable volume-growth exponent d_f for balls in the cluster
a known or boundable effective-resistance-growth exponent reflecting the bottleneck/dangling-end structure
typically also requires the cluster's law to have appropriate scale-invariance, or at least comparable behavior across scales
title: Technique: Kesten's Subdiffusivity Argument

[Theorem 12 (Sharp Stieltjes moment determinacy of the factor) of arXiv:2606.18458, 'Stable size-biasing and the positive scale-mixture order of generalized Gaussian laws'] Let $0<p\le q$, and let $V_{p,q}$ be the unique positive factor in Theorem~\ref{thm:main}. Then $V_{p,q}$ is Stieltjes moment-determinate if and only if
\[
\frac1p-\frac1q\le2 .
\]
Equivalently, it is Stieltjes moment-indeterminate if and only if $1/p-1/q>2$. In particular, $V_{p,p}=1$ and the boundary case $1/p-1/q=2$ are determinate.

body: [Theorem 5.3 of arXiv:2509.26030, 'Muon Outperforms Adam in Tail-End Associative Memory Learning'] If Assumptions 5.1 and 5.2 hold, with fixed $\alpha,\beta$ such that $\alpha\neq\beta$, and $K$ goes to infinity, we obtain the following results for one-step gd, Muon, and Adam. • For gd, for any $\widetilde{E}$ and $E$ satistifying Assumption 5.1, we have $\displaystyle\varrho_{\text{GD}}^{\epsilon}=O(\epsilon^{-r(\alpha,\beta)}K^{r(\alpha,\beta)-1}),\text{ where }r(\alpha,\beta)=\min\bigg\{\frac{\alpha(1-\beta)}{\beta(1-\alpha)},\frac{\beta(1-\alpha)}{\alpha(1-\beta)}\bigg\}<1.$ • For Muon, for any $\widetilde{E}$ and $E$ satistifying Assumption 5.1, we have $\displaystyle\varrho_{\text{Muon}}^{\epsilon}\geq 1-\epsilon\bigg(1+O\bigg(\frac{\log K}{K}\bigg)\bigg),\text{ and }G_{\text{Muon}}(W_{0})=-\widetilde{E}E^{\top}+O\bigg(\frac{1}{K}\widetilde{E}J_{K,K}E^{\top}\bigg),$ where $J_{K,K}\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times K}$ is the matrix with all elements equal to $1$. The big- $O$ notation for matrices means that for $A=O(B)$, each entry satisfies $A_{ij}=O(B_{ij})$ for all $i,j$. • For Adam, there exist $\widetilde{E}$ and $E$ satisfying Assumption 5.1 such that $\varrho_{\text{SignGD}}^{\epsilon}\geq 1-\epsilon.$ There also exist $\widetilde{E}^{\prime}$ and $E^{\prime}$ satisfying Assumption 5.1 such that $\displaystyle\varrho_{\text{SignGD}}^{\epsilon}=O(\epsilon^{-0.7}K^{-0.3}),\text{ and }\frac{\sigma_{\min}\big(G_{\text{SignGD}}(W_{0})\big)}{\sigma_{\max}\big(G_{\text{SignGD}}(W_{0})\big)}\leq 25\%,$ where $\sigma_{\max}$ and $\sigma_{\min}$ are the largest and smallest singular values, respectively.

[De 1 of arXiv:2607.28078, '2607.28078'] (1) Fix a filtered probability space carrying an $\mathbb{R}^m$-valued Brownian motion $B$ and an $\mathcal{F}_0$-measurable random variable $X_0$. An adapted continuous $\mathbb{R}^d$-valued process $X$ is called a \emph{strong solution} of (\ref{2.1}) if
\[
\mathbb{E} \int_{0}^{t}\bigg\{\big\|b(s,X(s),\mathcal{L}_{X(s)})\big\|_{\mathbb{R}^d}+\big\|\sigma(s,X(s),\mathcal{L}_{X(s)})\big\|^2_{\mathbb{R}^{d\times m}}\bigg\}ds<\infty,\,\, t\geq0,
\]
and if, $\mathbb{P}$-almost surely,
\[
X(t)=X_0+\int_{0}^{t}b(s,X(s),\mathcal{L}_{X(s)})ds+\int_{0}^{t}\sigma(s,X(s),\mathcal{L}_{X(s)})dB(s),\,\, t\geq0,
\]
where $\mathcal L_{X(t)}\in\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)$ for every $t\geq0$. \emph{Pathwise uniqueness} holds if any two such strong solutions defined with respect to the same $B$ and the same $X_0$ coincide almost surely.
		
(2) A pair $(\tilde{X}(t),\tilde{B}(t))_{t\geq0}$ is called a \emph{weak solution} of $(\ref{2.1})$ if it solves the equation on some stochastic basis $(\tilde{\Omega},\tilde{\mathcal{F}},\{\tilde{\mathcal{F}}_t\}_{t\geq0},\tilde{\mathbb{P}})$ and $\tilde B$ is an $\mathbb R^m$-valued Brownian motion on that basis.

[Lemma 154 of arXiv:2601.16377, '2601.16377'] Under Assumptions~\ref{Assumptions_Theta}, \ref{Assumptions_basic}, \ref{Assumptions_offcrit} and \ref{Assumptions_analyticity}, there exist $\eps>0$, $(2K - 1)$ real deterministic constants $\mathfrak{t}^{\textnormal{b}}_{1},\ldots,\mathfrak{t}^{\textnormal{b}}_K,\mathfrak{t}_{2}^{\textnormal{a}},\ldots,\mathfrak{t}_K^{\textnormal{a}}$ in the above rules, a $\N$-independent constant $C > 0$ depending only on the constants in the assumptions, and an event $\mathcal{A}$ of probability at least $1 - Ce^{-\frac{\N}{C}(\log \N)^2}$, having the following properties in combination with the above rules.
 \begin{itemize}
 \item[(P1)] The segments $[\hat a^\circ_k,\hat b^\circ_k]$ indexed by $k\in[K]$ are disjoint and at distance at least $\eps$ from each other.
 \item[(P2)] $\forall k \in [K] \qquad [\alpha_k-\eps,\beta_k+\eps]\subseteq [\hat a^\circ_k,\hat b^\circ_k]\subseteq [\hat a_{h^k},\hat b_{h^k}]$.
 \item[(P3)] $\forall k \in [K] \qquad \big|N^\circ_k-\N \mu([\hat a^\circ_k,\hat b^\circ_k])\big|< C \N^{\frac{1}{2}} \log \N$.
 \item[(P4)] $\forall k \in [K] \quad N^\circ_k = \# \big\{i \in [N] \quad \big| \quad \ell_i \in [\N \hat{a}_k^{\circ},\N \hat{b}_k^{\circ}]\big\}$.
 \item[(P5)] The complement of $\,\bigcup_{k = 1}^{K} (\hat a^\circ_k,\hat b^\circ_k)$ in $\bigcup_{h = 1}^{H} [\hat a_h,\hat b_h]$ splits into finitely many segments, such that on each segment there are either no particles or no holes in the configuration $\boldsymbol{\ell}$, corresponding to whether the equilibrium measure $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ is void or saturated on these segments.
 \item[(P6)] The random $3K$-tuple $(\hat{\boldsymbol{a}}^\circ, \hat{\boldsymbol{b}}^\circ, \boldsymbol{N}^\circ)$ is a deterministic affine function of the random $K$-tuple $\boldsymbol{Q}^\circ$. Furthermore, for any $k \in[K]$, the difference $N^{\circ}_k-\N \mu([\hat a^{\circ\,\prime}_k, \hat b^{\circ\,\prime}_k])$ is a deterministic affine function of $(Q_1^\circ,\ldots,Q_k^\circ)$ and the linear coefficient of $Q_k^\circ$ takes values in $\big\{1,-\frac{1}{\theta_{1,1}},\ldots,-\frac{1}{\theta_{H,H}}\big\}$.
\end{itemize}

[Thm 17 of arXiv:2608.27934, 'An example of biquandle and an invariant of long virtual knots defined through it'] Let $D$ be a long virtual knot diagram. 
Take arbitrary $a\in X$. 
Then there exists  unique $(X; \underline{\triangleright}, \overline{\triangleright})-$coloring $\mathcal{C}_{a}$ of $D$ such that the element assigned to the initial semiarc of $D$ is $a$. 
Moreover, there exists an element $F_{D}(s,u,t)\in X$, which is independent of $a$, such that the element assigned to the terminal semiarc of $D$ by $\mathcal{C}_{a}$ is $F_{D}(s,u,t)\cdot a$.

body:
[Lemma lem:reduced-same-shell-increment of arXiv:2607.29330, 'Large deviations for the maximum of\\ the generalized TAP free energy'] Fix a regular \(f\in(f_{\mathrm{eq}},f_1)\), write
		\(\theta=\theta_f\) and \(\zeta=\zeta_f\), and let \(q\) be the first
		positive contact point of \(\zeta\). Let \(X\) be the
		Auffinger--Chen process associated with \(\zeta\). For
		\(\varepsilon>0\), fix \(\mathbf{m}\in(-1,1)^N\), and define \(b_i\) by
		\[
		m_i=\partial_x\Phi_\zeta(q,b_i).
		\]
		Write \(\mathbf{b}=(b_i)_{i\le N}\).
		Assume that
		\[
		|q_\mathbf{m}-q|\le\varepsilon,
		\qquad
		W_2\left(
		\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\delta_{b_i},
		\mathrm{Law}(X_q)
		\right)\le\varepsilon.
		\]
		For \(f'\in[f-\varepsilon,f+\varepsilon]\), condition on
		\[
		F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})=Nf',
		\qquad
		\nabla F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})=0.
		\]
		Assume also that
		\[
		\left|
		f'
		+\frac1N\left(
		F_{\mathrm{TAP}}(\mathbf{m})-F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})
		\right)
		-f
		\right|
		\le\varepsilon.
		\]
		Denote the corresponding conditional expectation by
		\(\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{m},f'}\).
		There is a centered Gaussian field \(G_\mathbf{m}\), independent of the
		conditioned value and gradient, such that, for every fixed
		\(r\in(-q,q)\),
		\begin{equation}
			\begin{aligned}
				F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m}')-F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})
				&=G_\mathbf{m}(\mathbf{m}')
				+\sum_{i=1}^N\left[
				\frac{\xi'(r)}{\xi'(q)}m'_i b_i
				+\Phi_\zeta^*(q,m'_i)-\Phi_\zeta(q,b_i)
				\right]\\
				&\quad+N\theta\bigl[\xi(r)-r\xi'(r)-\xi(q)+q\xi'(q)\bigr]
				+N o_\varepsilon(1)+N o_\delta(1)+o_N(N),
			\end{aligned}
		\end{equation}
		uniformly when \(\lvert q_{\mathbf{m}'}-q\rvert\le\delta\) and
		\(\lvert R(\mathbf{m},\mathbf{m}')-r\rvert\le\delta\). Here
		\(o_N(N)/N\to0\) for fixed \(\varepsilon,\delta\), while
		\(o_\varepsilon(1)\to0\) and \(o_\delta(1)\to0\) as their respective
		parameters tend to zero. All errors are uniform over the displayed
		\(\varepsilon\)-window conditions. For two points
		\(\mathbf{m}'^1,\mathbf{m}'^2\) in this slice,
		\[
		\frac1N\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{m},f'}\left[
		G_\mathbf{m}(\mathbf{m}'^1)G_\mathbf{m}(\mathbf{m}'^2)
		\right]
		=
		\xi(R_{12})-

body: Noether's theorem states that every continuous symmetry of the action of a physical system with conservative forces has a corresponding conservation law. This is the first of two theorems published by the mathematician Emmy Noether in 1918. The action of a physical system is the integral over time of a Lagrangian function, from which the system's behavior can be determined by the principle of least action. This theorem applies to continuous and smooth symmetries of physical space. Noether's formulation is quite general and has been applied across classical mechanics, high energy physics, and recently statistical mechanics.
title: Noether's theorem

body: The heat equation is the parabolic partial differential equation u_t = k Laplacian(u) for a function u(x, t), with k > 0 the diffusivity. On R^n with initial data u(x, 0) = f(x), the solution is the convolution of f with the heat kernel (4 pi k t)^(-n/2) exp(-|x|^2 / (4 k t)); solutions smooth out instantly and obey the maximum principle.
title: Heat Equation

body:
[Lemma 5 (Slope-jump representation) of arXiv:2608.31157, 'Sharp Approximation Rates for Neural Networks with Affine Latent Parameterizations'] Let $\varphi:\R\to\R$ be continuous and piecewise linear with breakpoints
$\kappa_1<\cdots<\kappa_J$.  Suppose its slope is $m_0$ to the left of
$\kappa_1$, is $m_j$ between $\kappa_j$ and $\kappa_{j+1}$ for
$j=1,\ldots,J-1$, and is $m_J$ to the right of $\kappa_J$.  Then
\begin{equation}
 \varphi(x)
 =\varphi(\kappa_1)+m_0(x-\kappa_1)
 +\sum_{j=1}^{J}(m_j-m_{j-1})\varrho(x-\kappa_j).
\end{equation}
Consequently, $\varphi$ is realized by an architecture in
$\Arch(5,2J+2)$.  If $\varphi(\kappa_1)$ and all its slopes are affine
functions of a latent vector, the realization can be chosen so that every
parameter slot is affine in that vector.

\[
(W_L(\sigma)f)(x')
=

\int_{\mathbb R}\sigma(\xi)e^{i\xi(x'-x)}f(x)
