Let U subset R^d be an open submanifold (open connected domain) of Euclidean space. An autonomous stochastic differential equation on U is an Itô differential equation dX_t = mu(X_t) dt + sigma(X_t) dW_t, where W_t is a standard m-dimensional Brownian motion, mu: U -> R^d is a measurable drift vector field, and sigma: U -> R^(d x m) is a measurable dispersion matrix field, such that any solution trajectory X_t remains almost surely in U for all t in [0, tau_e), where tau_e is the explosion time.
U is an open subset of R^d
W_t is an m-dimensional standard Brownian motion
title: Autonomous Stochastic Differential Equation on an Open Submanifold

[Cor uniformlycontinuous of arXiv:2609.03129, 'A Closed-Form Formula for Consistent Lipschitz Regression on Metric Spaces with Sparse Neu'] Let $(X,\rho)$ be a compact metric space, $\omega$ be a concave, continuous, and strictly increasing modulus of continuity, and let $f:(X,\rho)\to (\mathbb{R},|\cdot|)$ be $\omega$-uniformly continuous.  

Then, for every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists some $M\in \mathbb{N}_+$, and some $\theta \in [\mathbb{R}\times X\times \times \{1\}]^M$ such that $\hat{f}_{\theta}(\cdot|G^0)$ in~(equation eq:formula__realizable___snowflaked of the paper) satisfies
\[
    \sup_{x\in X}
    \,
    \big|
        \hat{f}_{\theta}(x|G^0)
        -
        f(x)
    \big|
    <\varepsilon
.
\]
Moreover, $\hat{f}_{\theta}(\cdot|G^0):(X,\rho)\to (\mathbb{R},|\cdot|)$ is $\omega$-uniformly continuous. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Universal Approximation

Let n>=2 and let f_i:R^d->R be convex C1 functions with globally L_i-Lipschitz gradients, L_i>0. Let psi be proper closed convex, f=(1/n)sum_i f_i, and suppose F=f+psi has a finite minimum attained at x*. Put v_i=grad f_i(x*), vbar=(1/n)sum_i v_i, Lbar=(1/n)sum_i L_i, sigma_any^2=(1/n)sum_i ||v_i||^2 and sigma_rand^2=sigma_any^2+n||vbar||^2. For a permutation sigma of [n] define R(sigma)=(1/n)sum_(i=2)^n L_(sigma_i)||sum_(j=1)^(i-1) v_(sigma_j)||^2. Every permutation satisfies R(sigma)<=n^2 Lbar sigma_any^2. If sigma is uniform among all n! permutations, E R(sigma)<=(2/3)n Lbar sigma_rand^2. The second assertion is a single-permutation expectation, with all vectors and weights fixed. Source: Liu--Zhou Lemma E.1, here stated in the convex setting of the last-iterate theorem; its algebraic proof uses only the displayed vectors and positive weights.
n>=2, all norms Euclidean
Convex C1 components with globally L_i-Lipschitz gradients and L_i>0
Proper closed convex psi; F=f+psi attains its finite minimum at x*
For the expected bound, sigma is uniform and the displayed vectors and weights are fixed

Own-work draft, proof (unaudited), T280-w716-C7 v1, kind special, Target 3 curriculum case. C5 v1 is independently checked (urn:mb-agent:7a4f9e38007c2a28 PASS), classified SPECIAL. Fix k>=2 and 0<q<1. For each sufficiently large d, x is uniform on the unit sphere, Z=sqrt(d)*x.u for a prepared unit axis u, and p_{k,d}(Z) is the unit-L2 degree-k zonal harmonic. Start an exponential population mean-field network with m=k+1 equally weighted atoms, a_i=b_i=0 and w_i=sqrt(d)*i*h*u for i=0,...,k; h is selected by C5 at residual fraction q1=q/64. Train on target Z until residual energy first reaches q1, at time tau1<=T1. Change only the target to Z+p_{k,d}(Z), retaining every parameter and the original Euclidean mean-field clock. Within a further time T2 depending only on k,q, both full and degree-k residual energies are at most q times their respective energies at the switch. The retained nonzero output/bias state obeys b_i=a_i^2/2. For second-target reference coefficients |c_i|<=C2=2C, the nonnegative coefficient potential starts at V<=H1^2+6C2, and its derivative remains -2<r,f-g_t>. Uniform scalar-feature drift is O(1/d). The explicit constants and first-exit proof are in the canonical file. This removes output reset in an actual two-stage trained state, but prepared aligned nodes and an explicit target switch remain assumptions. It is not a single fixed joint-objective theorem, random-start alignment theorem, novelty claim, independent audit, or full T280 solution.

[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] Any system of linearly independent vectors $\{f_1,\ldots,f_n\}$ can be turned into an orthogonal system $\{e_1,\ldots,e_n\}$ by using the Gram-Schmidt procedure,
$$e_1=f_1$$
$$e_2=f_2+\alpha_1f_1$$
$$e_3=f_3+\beta_1f_1+\beta_2f_2$$
$$e_4=f_4+\gamma_1f_1+\gamma_2f_2+\gamma_3f_3$$
$$\vdots$$
with the needed scalars $\alpha_i,\beta_i,\gamma_i,\ldots$ being uniquely determined.
title: Unnumbered theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'

[Lemma 7 (Local normalization and decoupled normal form) of arXiv:2606.16662, '2606.16662'] Fix a cutoff and a dyadic block \((N,Q,M)\).  Consider either one value of the
centered kernel, one increment between two Volterra pairs, or one member of
the finite cutoff family used in the tail argument.  In an increment
estimate, collect jointly all first-Wiener kernels at the two endpoints and
in the finite telescope connecting them.  There exists an integer \(d_0\),
depending only on the finite color family and on the number of telescope
terms, with the following properties.

For every \(\underline m\in\Z^d_+\), there is a standard real Gaussian vector
\[
        G_{\underline m}
        =(G_{\underline m,\mu})_{1\le\mu\le d_0},
\]
and these vectors are independent for distinct representatives.  With
\[
        a=(\underline\ell,\mu),\qquad
        b=(\underline r,\lambda),\qquad c=q,\qquad e=n,
\]
the centered kernel has a finite expansion
\begin{equation}
        B_{\Lambda,N,Q,M}^{i;j,k}(e,c;t,s)
        =\sum_{\nu}\sum_{a,b}
        H_{\nu;a,b,c,e}(t,s)
        \wick{G_{\underline\ell,\mu}G_{\underline r,\lambda}} .
\end{equation}
The pattern index \(\nu\) contains the two Fourier signs, together with the
finite sine--cosine, color and cutoff choices.  For fixed \(\nu\), there are
signs \(\epsilon_{\nu,1},\epsilon_{\nu,2}\in\{+1,-1\}\) such that the
coefficient tensor is supported by
\begin{equation}
        n=q+\epsilon_{\nu,1}\underline\ell
              +\epsilon_{\nu,2}\underline r,
        \qquad |\underline\ell|\sim|\underline r|\sim N,
        \qquad |q|\sim Q,
        \qquad |n|\sim M,
        \qquad Q\le c_{\rm ap}N,
\end{equation}
up to the fixed Littlewood--Paley overlap, and
\begin{equation}
        |H_{\nu;a,b,c,e}(t,s)|
        \lesssim N^{-\Gamma_{i;j,k}}.
\end{equation}
For an increment tensor, the right-hand side carries the additional
increment factor from Assumption~\ref{ass:coeff}.  The number of patterns
and the auxiliary dimension \(d_0\) are uniform in the dyadic scales,
cutoff and time points.

For every finite-dimensional Banach space \(X\), every finite coefficient
family \((C_{a,b})\subset X\), and every \(p\ge2\), write
\(G_a=G_{\underline\ell,\mu}\) for \(a=(\underline\ell,\mu)\),
and similarly for \(G_b\).  Then
\begin{equation}
        \left\|\sum_{a,b}C_{a,b}\wick{G_aG_b}
        \right\|_{L^p(\Omega;X)}
        \le C_{\rm dec}
        \left\|\sum_{a,b}C_{a,b}G_a\widetilde G_b
        \right\|_{L^p(\Omega\times\widetilde\Omega;X)},
\end{equation}
where \((\widetilde G_b)\) is an independent copy.  The constant
\(C_{\rm dec}\) depends only on the chaos order.

metadata_json:
{"artifact_digest":"sha256:eb418b274856442f80372f89e3d5d864447c143629364e9df6f4efae0ba366b6","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/eb/eb418b274856442f80372f89e3d5d864447c143629364e9df6f4efae0ba366b6.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:e46b93d5bf149b2fff836bcc7c52bd70b1d1130f4c72842e2b881bd3fbe0cbc1","bundle_entry_key":"t309-c02","bundle_id":"population.t309-equilateral-ddpm-symmetry-breaking-drafts","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"probability, score matching, Gaussian mixture learning","draft":"w721/bundle_001.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.learning:equilateral-gaussian-ddpm-invariant-family","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# T309: a population GD symmetry-breaking step for equilateral triples

T309-w721-C02 v1 (invariance) and C03 v2 (population convergence).
Status: proof (unaudited). No novelty claim. The general empirical Target 2 remains open.

The next unpaid step is to reach this invariant family from a generic random triple in an unknown plane, or to replace exact population equivariance with an empirical argument. The initialization here is random in angle, has known radius and plane, and is exactly equilateral. These are substantive extra assumptions. It can be outside every componentwise warm-start basin.

## The population statement

Let the target be an equal-weight mixture N(a u_j,I_d), j=0,1,2, where u_j are the unit equilateral vectors in a known plane, centered at zero. Its orientation in that plane need not be known. Assume 0<a<=a_0 for a sufficiently small absolute constant. Parameterize the student by three unrestricted mean vectors m_j in R^d, using exactly Eq. (9) of Shah--Chen--Klivans. Train on the population DDPM objective at this fixed noise level, with all three means updated by ordinary Euclidean GD with the same step h.

Initialize m_j=a R_Theta u_j, where Theta is uniform on the circle, independently of the target orientation. There are absolute h_0,c,C>0 such that for 0<h<=h_0/a^2 the following hold:

1. Every iterate has m_j=a r_n R_{theta_n}u_j, with 1/2<r_n<2.
2. Except at the three exact unstable initial angles (a probability-zero event), the iterates converge to the true mean triple up to permutation.
3. If the initial angle is at distance at least delta from every unstable angle, then for 0<delta,eta<=1/10, after at most

       C/(h a^4) [1+log(1/delta)+log(1/eta)]

   iterations, the matched mean error is at most C a eta. Consequently the probability statement can be made 1-p by taking delta=pi p/3, or a smaller delta<=1/10. The dependence on d is absent at population level. This does not yet establish polynomial sample complexity or arbitrary random initialization.

The same statement applies to the high-noise training stage of a well-separated original mixture with center radius R: choose t so that R exp(-t)=a. Rescaling the recovered means multiplies the error by R/a. Learning to an arbitrary original mean error therefore requires eta of the corresponding order. This observation does not remove the known-plane and known-radius initialization assumptions.

## 1. The invariant family under unrestricted mean updates

Let Q be rotation by 2pi/3 in the target plane and identity on its orthogonal complement. The target law and population DDPM loss are invariant under Q. The objective is also invariant under permutations of the three student labels. Combining the rotation with the inverse cyclic label permutation gives an orthogonal linear action on the whole parameter space which fixes every configuration satisfying m_{j+1}=Q m_j (indices modulo 3).

For a differentiable function L invariant under an orthogonal map A, differentiating L(Ax)=L(x) gives grad L(Ax)=A grad L(x). If Ax=x, then A grad L(x)=grad L(x). Both a GD step and the gradient flow therefore preserve its fixed-point subspace.

There is another exact symmetry: reflection S which is identity on the target plane and minus identity on its orthogonal complement. At a planar configuration, every parameter is fixed by S, so the gradient is planar. Intersecting the two fixed-point subspaces leaves precisely

    m_j=Q^j z,    z in the target plane.

For z nonzero write z=a r R_theta u_0. This is the full radius-angle equilateral family. Its invariance is exact, holds for every a, and concerns the unrestricted population objective. In particular its proof does not assume that two spaces of the same dimension coincide: it explicitly solves the fixed-point equations. For d=2 the perpendicular reflection is unnecessary.

The radius-one angular circle alone is generally not invariant. Section 2 below gives F_r(1,theta)=(3a^6/4)(1-cos(3theta))+O(a^8), which is nonzero away from the aligned angles for sufficiently small a.

## 2. Uniform expansion with a variable radius

Let F_a(r,theta) denote the population excess score loss between this student and the target. Uniformly for r in [1/4,3], and with every fixed finite number of r,theta derivatives needed below,

    F_a(r,theta)=a^4 A4(r)+a^6 A6(r,theta)+O(a^8),                    (1)
    A4(r)=(r^2-1)^2/2,
    A6(r,theta)=(r^6+1-2r^3 cos(3theta))/8
                 -(r^2-1)(r^4-1)/2+(r^2-1)^2/4.                   (2)

The proof uses the same dominated Taylor argument as angular_landscape.md. In that argument the logit has magnitude at most 3|a| ||y|| instead of |a| ||y||. This still has Gaussian-integrable domination. It supplies any fixed derivative order, not merely a pointwise remainder.

For completeness, the score expansions through order four are

    b_student = a^2 r^2 y/2 + a^3 r^3 T_theta[y,y]/2
                  -a^4 r^4 y||y||^2/16 + O(a^5),
    b_target  = a^2 y/2 + a^3 T_0[y,y]/2
                  -a^4 y||y||^2/16 + O(a^5).

The teacher density relative to phi_2 is 1+a^2(||y||^2/4-1/2)+O(a^3). Squaring the score difference and integrating gives (1)--(2): the order-six contributions are the squared order-three term, the cross term between orders two and four, and the order-two teacher-density correction multiplying the squared order-two term. Their expectations respectively are

    (r^6+1-2r^3 cos(3theta))/8,
    -(r^2-1)(r^4-1)/2,
    (r^2-1)^2/4.

Odd powers again vanish by the exact a -> -a, y -> -y symmetry. The script scripts/check_angular.py verifies these Gaussian polynomial identities with exact symbolic arithmetic. It is not used to prove the domination.

Periodicity and reflection give, by the zero-preserving remainder argument in angular_landscape.md, uniformly on 1/2<=r<=2,

    F_theta(r,theta)=a^6 k_a(r,theta) sin(3theta),
    c <= k_a(r,theta) <= C.                                       (3)

Here the leading coefficient is 3r^3/4, bounded above and below on this annulus. Bounds on the remainder after two theta derivatives force its first derivative to vanish linearly at each n pi/3. This justifies the uniform division by the sine, including near its zeros.

Near r=1, the expansion and the exact identity F_r(1,0)=0 give

    F_r(r,0)=a^4 g_a(r)(r-1),       c<=g_a(r)<=C,                   (4)
    |F_r(r,theta)-F_r(r,0)|<=C a^6 theta^2                        (5)

for |r-1|<=1/10 and |theta|<=pi/3, interpreting theta relative to the nearest minimum. To check (4), F_rr(r,0)=2a^4(3r^2-1)+O(a^6) is positive throughout this radial neighborhood; apply the mean value theorem. For (5), the a^4 term is independent of theta, the mixed derivative F_{r theta theta} is O(a^6), and F_{r theta}(r,0)=0 by exact evenness; integrate twice in theta. All constants are absolute.

## 3. The exact discrete update

At an equilateral configuration, the symmetry from Section 1 implies that every gradient is the same linear combination of its own radial and tangential unit vectors v_j=R_theta u_j and Jv_j. Differentiating with respect to r and theta fixes the coefficients:

    grad_{m_j} L = F_r v_j/(3a) + F_theta Jv_j/(3ar).

Set

    A = r-h F_r/(3a^2),     B=-h F_theta/(3a^2 r).

Then ordinary GD on the three means gives the exact update

    r_next=sqrt(A^2+B^2),    theta_next=theta+atan2(B,A).             (6)

The Euclidean gradient is not the coordinate gradient of F in (r,theta). Formula (6) accounts for the induced metric and for the discrete tangential step's second-order radial effect.

## 4. Radial confinement and descent

On r in [1/4,3], the gradient in the z-coordinate of the invariant linear subspace is O(a^3), and its Hessian is O(a^2), by (1) and the chain rule away from z=0. The three-mean Euclidean metric on this subspace is 3 times the metric of z, which only changes absolute constants. Choose h_0 sufficiently small to satisfy the descent bound h<=1/(L a^2) and to make the largest possible one-step radial displacement from r in [0.9,1.1] less than 0.1. Both choices use uniform bounds on the larger annulus.

Initially r=1 and F_a=O(a^6). Suppose an iterate lies in [0.9,1.1] and has F_a<=C_0 a^6, where C_0 is an absolute bound for all initial angles. The step segment stays in [1/2,2] by the displacement bound, so the descent lemma applies along that segment. It gives F_next<=F_current. Equation (1) then implies

    (r_next^2-1)^2 <= C a^2,

because A6 and the remainder are uniformly bounded on the annulus. Thus |r_next-1|<=C' a. Decrease a_0 until C' a_0<0.1. This proves the induction and confinement. It also proves monotone descent. No assumption about a sublevel barrier preventing a discrete jump is needed; the step-segment bound was established first.

## 5. Angular convergence and rate

Confinement implies A is bounded above and below by positive absolute constants after further decreasing h_0 if needed. By (3) and (6), the angular displacement has the opposite sign to sin(3theta), and its absolute value lies between

    c h a^4 |sin(3theta)|    and    C h a^4 |sin(3theta)|.           (7)

Indeed |B/A|<=C h a^4<=C h_0 a^2, so arctan(|B/A|) is between |B/A|/2 and |B/A|. Make a_0 small enough that 3C h a^4<1/2. Since |sin(3theta)| is at most three times the distance to either neighboring zero of the sine, no step can cross a minimum or maximum. Every open angular basin is invariant.

The same geometric-growth and geometric-decay argument as in angular_landscape.md, now using h a^4 rather than h a^6, proves that the angle reaches distance eta from its basin's minimum in at most

    C/(h a^4) [1+log(1/delta)+log(1/eta)]

steps. It remains there and continues toward zero. An exact maximum is stationary in angle; it is excluded. There are exactly three such initial angles modulo 2pi, and their delta-neighborhood has probability 3delta/pi under a uniform angle.

## 6. Radius follows the angular convergence

Write e=r-1, and let theta be measured relative to the basin's minimum. From (4)--(5),

    F_r=a^4 g_a(r)e+f,       |f|<=C a^6 theta^2.

The relation sqrt(A^2+B^2)-A=B^2/(sqrt(A^2+B^2)+A) and A>=c>0 bound the radial correction by C h^2 a^8 theta^2. Since h a^2<=h_0, it is bounded by C h a^4 theta^2 (after adjusting an absolute constant). Shrinking h_0 so the radial linear factor is nonnegative, (6) gives

    |e_next| <= (1-c h a^2)|e| + C h a^4 theta^2.                  (8)

After the angular stage makes |theta|<=eta, iteration of (8) yields

    |e_{n+k}| <= (1-c h a^2)^k |e_n| + C' a^2 eta^2.

An additional C/(h a^2)[1+log(1/eta)] steps therefore makes |e|<=C'' eta. This is bounded by the iteration order asserted in the theorem since a<=a_0<1. The matched mean error is at most a(|e|+r |theta|)<=C a eta. Letting eta tend to zero proves convergence, and using the rate at a fixed eta proves the finite-time claim.

## Checks and scope

The proof uses equal weights, exact equilateral geometry, known centering and plane, and a population objective. Removing any of them breaks the fixed-point argument or the single-angle landscape reduction. At a=0 every student center in this initialization is zero and there is no angular signal, so the strict requirement a>0 is necessary. At an exact antipodal angle the gradient cannot choose a component labeling; this is why a measure-zero exception and a distance-from-saddles parameter appear. The dimension-independent reduction does not apply to an arbitrary initial triple with perpendicular components.

For an empirical objective, an individual sample set usually lacks the target's rotational invariance. Orbit augmentation by the known 120-degree rotation could preserve the invariant family, but the needed uniform gradient estimates and the resulting finite-sample convergence theorem are not supplied here. For an unknown plane, estimating and entering the plane is also unpaid. These are limitations of the result, not details covered by the population theorem.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:dd2cd7dabd7ec9f2c960407731e32a2f94dbb925d22de6cdbb0cfb15c3f46028","revision_digest":"sha256:bce43c5597434f532ae5a290273d478e05b4b5e47ec764d2b87ccb6a05e0650b","source_id":"own-work:T309-w721-C02-v1","source_revision":"C02 version 1; saved 2026-10-20","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Proposition prop:parametric-corrected-potential of arXiv:2608.25182, 'Minimax Alternating Regret \\for the Experts Problem and Online Convex Optimization'] Fix a round $t$, a score vector $R_{t-1}\in\mathbb{R}^d$, a signed-loss vector
$y_{t-1}\in[-1,1]^d$, and $z\in\mathbb{R}^d$ such that
$y_{t-1}+s_tz\in[-1,1]^d$. For $\theta\in[0,1]$, let
$R(\theta)\triangleq R_{t-1}-\theta z$ and
$y(\theta)\triangleq y_{t-1}+\theta s_tz$. For $\alpha>0$, define
$U_\alpha(R,y)\triangleq F(R)-\alpha\eta\operatorname{Var}_{q[\eta R]}(y)$ and
$G_\alpha(\theta)\triangleq U_\alpha(R(\theta),y(\theta))$.

Let $\mathbb{E}_\theta[\cdot]$ denote expectation under $q[\eta R(\theta)]$, and
write $\widetilde z(\theta)\triangleq z-\mathbb{E}_\theta[z]$ and
$\widetilde y(\theta)\triangleq y(\theta)-\mathbb{E}_\theta[y(\theta)]$. Then
\begin{align}
G_\alpha'(\theta)
=-\mathbb{E}_\theta[z]
-2\alpha\eta s_t\mathbb{E}_\theta[\widetilde z(\theta)\widetilde y(\theta)]
+\alpha\eta^2\mathbb{E}_\theta[\widetilde z(\theta)\widetilde y(\theta)^2],

\end{align}
and
\begin{align}
G_\alpha''(\theta)
&=
(1-2\alpha)\eta\mathbb{E}_\theta[\widetilde z(\theta)^2]
+4\alpha s_t\eta^2\mathbb{E}_\theta[\widetilde z(\theta)^2\widetilde y(\theta)]
\notag\\
&\qquad-\alpha\eta^3\mathbb{E}_\theta[\widetilde z(\theta)^2\widetilde y(\theta)^2]
+\alpha\eta^3\mathbb{E}_\theta[\widetilde z(\theta)^2]
  \mathbb{E}_\theta[\widetilde y(\theta)^2]
\notag\\
&\qquad+2\alpha\eta^3\mathbb{E}_\theta[\widetilde z(\theta)\widetilde y(\theta)]^2.
\end{align}
In particular, we have
\begin{align}
G_\alpha''(\theta)
\le
\left[(1-2\alpha)\eta+8\alpha\eta^2+3\alpha\eta^3\right]
\operatorname{Var}_{q[\eta R(\theta)]}(z).
\end{align}

Let n,m,rho be positive integers with m<=n, q=rho*n, and fix any map psi:[q]->[n] with exactly rho preimages of every label. Sample b uniformly from {0,1}^n and let Y=PerturbDifference(n,m,b) using the uniform-injection algorithm. Conditional on Y and psi, sample Z_j independently and uniformly from psi^{-1}(Y_j), for j=1,...,m. Then Z is exactly uniform on [q]^m, for each fixed balanced psi. In particular the conclusion also holds conditional on an independently sampled balanced psi. The conclusion requires fresh independent fiber choices at different positions; it does not follow from uniform one-coordinate marginals alone.
Fixed balanced map psi with integer fiber size rho=q/n.
Uniform binary input; independent randomness as in PerturbDifference.
Fresh conditionally independent uniform fiber sample at every coordinate.

[Lemma lem:canonical-borel-gmc of arXiv:2608.02459, 'Response Calculus for Spectral Simplicity\\ and Joint Eigenvalue Densities'] There exist a deterministic sequence $\varepsilon_j\downarrow0$ and a set
\[
 \Omega_{\rm GMC}\in\mathcal B(X),
 \qquad \mathbb P(\Omega_{\rm GMC})=1,
\]
together with a measurable map
\begin{equation}
 M^{\rm can}:(X,\mathcal B(X))
 \longrightarrow
 (\mathcal M_{\mathrm{fin}}^+(D),\mathcal B(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{fin}}^+(D)))
\end{equation}
such that
\begin{equation}
 M_{x,\varepsilon_j}\Longrightarrow M^{\rm can}(x),
 \qquad x\in\Omega_{\rm GMC}.
\end{equation}
Here $\Longrightarrow$ denotes narrow convergence of finite measures.
Moreover, $M^{\rm can}(h)$ agrees almost surely with the subcritical GMC
measure.

[Lemma lem:h-conc-sends of arXiv:2602.21315, 'The Instability of all Backoff Protocols\thanks{For the purpose of Open Access, the author'] Fix a send sequence $\overline{p}$ with $p_0=1$. Let $j\ge 1$ be an integer, and suppose $j$ is sufficiently large. Fix an integer $\tau \ge 0$, a real number $\nu\ge 0$, and $\overline{a} \in (\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0})^j$. Let $E^+$ be a constant-escape process on $[j]$ with send sequence~$\overline{p}$, start time $\tau$, end-of-step arrival rate $\nu$, and $\overline{\mathrm{arr}}_{[j]}^{E^+}(\tau) = \overline{a}$. Fix integers $t > \tau$ and $k \in [j]$, and let
\[
\mu = p_k\sum_{t'=0}^{t-\tau-1}h_k^{\nu,\overline{a}}(t').
\]
Suppose $\mu \ge j(\log j)^2$. Then with probability at least $1-j^{-3j}$,
\[
\Big|\bigcup_{t'=\tau+1}^t \mathbf{s}_k^{E^+}(t')\Big| \ge \Big(1 - \frac{j}{\mu^{1/2}}\Big)\mu.
\]

An odd prime p is expressible as a sum of two integer squares, p = a^2 + b^2, if and only if p ≡ 1 (mod 4). More generally a positive integer is a sum of two squares iff every prime ≡ 3 (mod 4) in its factorization occurs to an even power.

[Coro convergenceepsilonn of arXiv:2601.20502, 'Optimal matching under size priority'] Let $(G_n,w_n)$ be a sequence of weighted finite graphs.
    Under assumptions and notations of Theorem~(th:reciproquegamarnik of the paper) and Theorem~(thm:convergenceZ of the paper), define $M_{\max}^{(\varepsilon)}(G_n)$ to be the matching on $G_n$ maximising the sum of $1+w_n$ on its edges, then
    \[  (G_n,o_n, M_{\max}^{(\varepsilon)}(G_n)  \]
    converges locally weakly as $n \to +\infty, \varepsilon \to 0$ to
    \[ \left( \mathbb{T},o,\mathbb{M}_{\mathrm{opt}}(G_n) \right) . \] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition 33 of arXiv:2608.03497, 'Connective Constants on Nested Fractal Graphs'] Let \(N=4k+\ell\notin\{3,5,6,9\}\), where
\(\ell\in\{1,2,3\}\).  There is a unique value
\(\beta_{*,N}>0\) such that
\[
  \begin{array}{ll}
  \beta>\beta_{*,N}:&(X_m,Y_m)\longrightarrow(0,0),\\[1mm]
  \beta<\beta_{*,N}:&(X_m,Y_m)\longrightarrow(+\infty,+\infty).
  \end{array}
\]
At \(\beta=\beta_{*,N}\),
\[
  (X_m,Y_m)\longrightarrow(X_{*,N},Y_{*,N}),
\]
where \(Y_{*,N}\in(0,1)\) is the unique solution of
\[
  Y_{*,N}^{\,N}+2Y_{*,N}^{\,2k+2}=1
\]
and
\[
  X_{*,N}
  =
  \bigl(Y_{*,N}^{\,k}+Y_{*,N}^{\,3k+\ell-2}\bigr)^{-1}.
\]
Consequently,
\(\beta_{*,N}
=\beta_{\mathrm c,N}^{\mathrm{cr}}
=\beta_{\mathrm c,N}\).

[Definition of arXiv:2412.07936, 'Simple Norm Bounds for Polynomial Random Matrices via Decoupling'] [Schatten norm] 
For ${\bf A} \in {\mathbb R}^{d_1 \times d_2}$ and $t \geq 1$, the Schatten $2t$-norm is defined as
$$
\ensuremath{\left\lVert {\bf A} \right\rVert}_{2t} := (\tr ({{\bf A}}^{\mathsf{T}}{\bf A})^t)^{1/2t}.
$$

[Lem 47 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Suppose $J_+ \neq \emptyset$.
    Then, the supremum in \eqref{e:fp.F.rviii} is attained at a point of the form
    \[
        \btheta_+ = \hbA_+(\gamma) \hbg_+\,,
    \]
where we define
    \begin{align}
        
        \gamma
        &\equiv 
        \gamma(\btheta_+)
        \equiv \frac{\|\btheta_+\|^2}{M\alpha} + \gamma_-\,,\\
        
        \hbA_+(\gamma)
        &\equiv \bigg((\hbD_+)^{-1} -
        \frac{m(\beta_\star(\gamma))}{\alpha} \bI_{B_+} \bigg)^{-1}\,.
    \end{align}
    Furthermore, this value of $\gamma$ satisfies
    \beq
        
        m(\beta_\star(\gamma)) \le \frac{\alpha}{\hv_1}\,.
    \eeq

\begin{proof}
Recall that Lemma~\ref{l:fp-g2}\eqref{i:fp-g-growth} shows that $g(\gamma) = \Theta(\gamma^{1/2})$ as $\gamma \to \infty$. It follows that $F^{\rviii,+}(\btheta_+) \to -\infty$ as $\|\btheta_+\| \to +\infty$, so the supremum of $F^{\rviii,+}(\btheta_+)$ is attained at a local maximizer $\btheta_+$.
    We will show that this local maximizer must in fact be a stationary point.
    By Lemma~\ref{l:fp-g2}\eqref{i:fp-g-diff}, $g$ is differentiable on $(0,+\infty)$. Therefore, the only possible non-stationary local maximum $\btheta_+$ must satisfy $\gamma = 0$, which implies $\gamma_-=0$ and $\btheta_+=\bzero$. However, in this case let us consider a small $\bv \in \bbR^{B_+}$ with $(\bv,\hbg_+) = 0$. For such $\bv$, we have
    \[
        F^{\rviii,+}(\bv) - F^{\rviii,+}(\bzero) 
        = g\bigg(\frac{\|\bv\|^2}{M\alpha}\bigg) - g(0)
        - \frac{((\hbD_+)^{-1} \bv,\bv)}{M}\,.
    \]
Lemma~\ref{l:fp-g2}\eqref{i:fp-g-diff} characterizes the behavior of $g(\gamma)$ as $\gamma\downarrow0$, and implies that the above is positive for sufficiently small $\|\bv\|$.
    Thus $\btheta_+=\bzero$ is not a local maximizer, and the only possible local maximizers are stationary points $\btheta_+$.
Therefore, consider any stationary local maximizer $\btheta_+ \in \bbR^{B_+}$ of $F^{\rviii,+}(\btheta_+)$.
    Stationarity implies
    \[
        \btheta_+ = \bigg((\hbD_+)^{-1} -
        \frac{g'(\gamma)}{\alpha} \bI_{B_+} \bigg)^{-1} \hbg_+
    \stackrel{\eqref{e:fp-viii-hbA}}{=}
    \hbA_+(\gamma) \hbg_+\,.
    \]
    In the last equality, we used Lemma~\ref{l:fp-g2}\eqref{i:fp-g-diff} with the above observation that $\gamma>0$. This proves \eqref{e:fp-gamma-btheta-plus}.
    Similarly, for any $\bv$ orthogonal to $\btheta_+$
    (or, if $\btheta_+=\bzero$, for any $\bv$), we have 
    \[
        \frac{d^2}{dt^2}
        F^{\rviii,+}(\btheta_+ + t\bv)
        \bigg|_{t=0}
        = -\frac{2}{M} \bv^\st \bigg(
        (\hbD_+)^{-1} -
        \frac{m(\beta_\star(\gamma))}{\alpha} \bI_{B_+}
        \bigg) \bv\le0\,,
    \]
where the last inequality is because 
$\btheta_+$ is a maximizer. Since $(\hbD_+)^{-1}$ has smallest eigenvalue $1/\hv_1$ with multiplicity at least $\iota N$ (because $(\lambda,\mu) \in \Lambda$), this implies the bound \eqref{e:fp-m-betast-gamma-bd}.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lem 47 of arXiv:2608.29416

[Prop of arXiv:2507.09421, 'Stability of randomly switching stochastic reaction networks with asymptotically linear tr'] Suppose the CRN from Example (ex: many environments of the paper) is started in a state with $n$ total molecules of $X$ and $X'$ combined. If $n\alpha>2\beta$ and $\kappa$ is sufficiently large, then the CRN is evanescent. If $n\alpha<2\beta$ and $\kappa$ is sufficiently large, it is exponentially ergodic.
\begin{proof}
    The existence of the reaction with source complex $X+Y$ means that Theorems (thm:fast-switching-ergodicity of the paper) and (thm:fast-switching-transience of the paper) cannot be applied to this CRN if we view it as $3$-species network in a single environment. However, notice that the sum of the number of $X$ and $X'$ molecules is a conserved quantity. If the process is started in a state with $n$ total molecules of $X$ and $X'$ for $n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$, then we can change perspectives and view this stochastic process as CRN with one species in $n+1$ environments, where the network has $i-1$ molecules of $X$ when in environment $i\in[n+1]=\{1,\cdots,n+1\}$. With this perspective, the environment transitions with rate matrix $\kappa Q$ for
    \begin{align*}
        Q&=
        \begin{pmatrix}
            -n & n & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & 0\\
            1 & -n & n-1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & 0\\
            0 & 2 & -n & n-2 & \cdots & 0 & 0\\
            0 & 0 & 3 &  -n  & \ddots & 0 & 0\\
            \vdots &\vdots &\vdots &\ddots &\ddots & \ddots &\vdots\\
            0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & \ddots & -n & 1\\
            0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & n & -n\\
        \end{pmatrix},
    \end{align*}
    and for $i\in[n+1]$ we have the change of $Y$ in environment $i$ is described by the $1\times 1$ matrix
    \begin{align*}
        M_i&=((i-1)\alpha-\beta).
    \end{align*}
    Let $w_i=2^{-n}\binom{n}{i-1}$ and consider the vector $w=(w_1,\cdots,w_{n+1})$. Since $X\leftrightarrows X'$ is complex balanced, it follows from [Anderson_Craciun_Kurtz_2010] that $w$ is the stationary distribution for $Q$; alternatively, one can check directly that
    \begin{align*}
        (wQ)_i&=w_{i-1}(n+2-i)-w_in+w_{i+1}i\\
        &=2^{-n}\left[(n+2-i)\binom n{i-2}+i\binom ni - n \binom n{i-1}\right]\\
        &=2^{-n}n\left[\binom{n-1}{i-2}+\binom{n-1}{i-1} - \binom n{i-1}\right]\\
        &=0.
    \end{align*}
    In any case, the mixed matrix $M$ is the $1\times 1$ matrix whose lone element is
    \begin{align*}
        \sum_{i=1}^{n+1} 2^{-n}\binom{n}{i-1} ((i-1)\alpha-\beta)
        &=\left(\sum_{i=0}^{n} 2^{-n}\binom{n}{i}i\right)\alpha-\beta\\
        &=\frac n2 \alpha - \beta.
    \end{align*}
    It follows from Theorem (thm:fast-switching-transience of the paper) that if $n\alpha>2\beta$ then the network is evanescent for sufficiently large $\kappa$, and it follows from Theorem (thm:fast-switching-ergodicity of the paper) that if $n\alpha<2\beta$ then it is exponentially ergodic for sufficiently large $\kappa$.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Store P patterns xi^1, ..., xi^P in {-1, +1}^N, with all N P entries independent and uniform on {-1, +1}, in a Hopfield network by the Hebbian rule W_{ij} = (1/N) sum over mu of xi_i^mu xi_j^mu for i not equal to j, W_{ii} = 0. Present the stored pattern xi^nu; the local field at neuron i is h_i = sum_j W_{ij} xi_j^nu = ((N-1)/N) xi_i^nu + C_i, where the crosstalk C_i = (1/N) sum over mu not equal to nu, sum over j not equal to i, of xi_i^mu xi_j^mu xi_j^nu has mean 0 and variance (P-1)(N-1)/N^2, which tends to alpha = P/N as N -> infinity with P/N -> alpha. The (P-1)(N-1) summands are pairwise uncorrelated products of independent signs, so by the central limit theorem C_i is approximately N(0, alpha) for large N and P, and the probability that the update flips neuron i away from the pattern - the event xi_i^nu h_i < 0, that is xi_i^nu C_i < -(N-1)/N - is approximately Phi(-1/sqrt(alpha)) = (1/2) erfc( 1/sqrt(2 alpha) ). This is the signal-to-noise ratio 1 : sqrt(alpha): at alpha = 0.138 the single-neuron error probability is about 0.0036 and at alpha = 0.185 about 0.01. The heuristic capacity read from this lemma, alpha of order 0.1-0.2, is only the ONE-STEP stability of a single neuron; the replica computation of Amit, Gutfreund and Sompolinsky gives the true retrieval threshold alpha_c = 0.138 (retrieval with a small fraction of errors), while error-free recall of every stored pattern as a fixed point (all N P neuron-pattern pairs stable at once) holds with probability tending to one only for P <= N / (4 ln N) (1 + o(1)), and recall of a fixed stored pattern (its N neurons stable) for P <= N / (2 ln N) (1 + o(1)) (McEliece, Posner, Rodemich and Venkatesh 1987): the Gaussian tail exp(-N/(2P)) has to beat a union bound over N P, respectively N, events.
patterns with independent uniform +-1 entries
Hebbian weights with zero diagonal, a single synchronous (or single-neuron) update from a stored pattern
the Gaussian approximation is asymptotic in N and P with P/N -> alpha; the capacity numbers quoted are for that regime

CAMPAIGN RESULT [independently checked proof; E0095-C8ABS v4; no novelty claim]. Start from the cycle C8 with vertices0,...,7. Among all new-edge perfect matchings, and also among all105 pairings if existing edges are added as parallel unit edges, exactly the four cyclic rotations of M=((0, 2), (1, 3), (4, 6), (5, 7)) minimize the augmented cubic non-lazy worst-start total-variation mixing time t_mix(1/4), at four steps. Every other pairing takes at least five steps or is periodic. These four also uniquely maximize the absolute SRW gap at 1-sqrt(5)/3. The ordinary gap optimum is2/3, attained by seven different matchings; the two optimizing sets are disjoint. The four absolute optimizers also minimize non-lazy TV mixing for every sufficiently small epsilon, while eventual half-lazy optimizers lie in that disjoint seven-matching ordinary-optimal set; no tie among those seven is asserted. The four-step optimum has ordinary gap below the original cycle ordinary gap1-sqrt(2)/2. This is a finite special case of Diaconis Question4, not a general optimization or novelty claim.

integers \(p,h,q\) satisfy
\begin{equation}
 q=p+Dh,\qquad (p,h)=1,\qquad 2p\ge Dh,\qquad p\ne Mh.
\end{equation}
If the two families \(\B^q_{p,*}\) and \(\B^q_{Mh,*}\) admit disjoint
translations,
then
\[
 (p,h,q)=(2M,1,4M-1).
\]

[Lemma lem:pairing of arXiv:2602.08591, 'The Yang--Mills measure on compact surfaces as a \\ universal scaling limit of lattice gau'] Let $M$ be some $C^\infty$ manifold.
Let $T\in \mathcal{D}^\prime(M)$ be a top degree current whose coefficients are in the 
H\"older--Besov space $\mathcal{C}^{\alpha}$ for $\alpha>-1$. Then for every 
domain $\Omega\subset M$ which has smooth boundary, 
the pairing
$$ \int_\Omega T=\int_M T 1_\Omega  $$
is well--defined. It is bilinear continuous when we endow the indicator function $1_\Omega$ with the topology of $\mathcal{B}^{-\alpha}_{1,1}$.

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Small-density straight paths and lack of an order argument Result: At q=0 a ray moves indefinitely along its Manhattan street. The event that its first N potential collisions contain no mirror has probability (1-q)^N. This only controls a finite initial flight and gives no positive lower bound as N increases at fixed q. Check: The finite-run probability agrees with independence and has the correct q=0 endpoint. Adding a mirror changes routing rather than merely deleting traversable states, so an edgewise percolation monotonicity proof has not been supplied. Obstruction: The known localization interval near and above one-half cannot be extended to every q>0 using this finite-run bound or an unproved monotonicity assumption.

[Lemma lem:qtaylor of arXiv:2607.28817, 'Limiting spectral distribution for the adjacency matrix of the Watts--Strogatz random grap'] There exists a constant $C > 0$ so that 
    \begin{align*}
        &\left| \mathbb{E}[s_{Q_n'((\tilde{X}_n)_{ab})}(z)] - \mathbb{E}[s_{Q_n'((\tilde{Y}_n)_{ab})}(z)] \right| \\
        &\qquad\leq C \frac{(A_n)_{ab}}{\varepsilon n K_n}   \left( \mathbb{E}[( X_n)^2_{ab}\chi_{ \{|(X_n)_{ab}| > \varepsilon \sqrt{K_n} \} }] + \mathbb{E}[( Y_n)^2_{ab}\chi_{ \{|(Y_n)_{ab}| > \varepsilon \sqrt{K_n} \} }] \right) \\
        &\qquad\qquad + C \frac{(A_n)_{ab}}{ n K_n} \varepsilon \left( \mathbb{E}[|(X_n)_{ab}|^2] + \mathbb{E}[|(Y_n)_{ab}|^2] \right),
    \end{align*}
    if $a < b$,
    and 
    \[ \left| \mathbb{E}[s_{Q_n'((\tilde{X}_n)_{aa})}(z)] - \mathbb{E}[s_{Q_n'((\tilde{Y}_n)_{aa})}(z)] \right| \leq \frac{C \varepsilon}{n}(A_n)_{aa} \]
    if $a = b$.
    The constant $C$ is independent $a,b$, and $\varepsilon$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let X_1, ..., X_n be drawn without replacement from a finite real population a_1, ..., a_N (N >= 2, 1 <= n <= N), S = X_1 + ... + X_n, and for each k let Y_k be a uniform draw from the population, independent of the sample, with S^(k) = S - X_k + Y_k. Then (1/2) sum_k E[(S - S^(k))^2] = n sigma^2 with sigma^2 = (1/N) sum_i (a_i - a_bar)^2, and Var(S) = ((N-n)/(N-1)) (1/2) sum_k E[(S - S^(k))^2]. For a nonconstant population the factor (N-n)/(N-1) is the only one that makes this an equality. At the full census n = N, S = a_1 + ... + a_N is deterministic, so Var(S) = 0, while the energy is N sigma^2 > 0. The identity is additive and about this marginal replacement: S^(k) need not have the law of a sum drawn without replacement, and it is not a dependent-coordinate Efron-Stein theorem.

[Lemma 9 of arXiv:2607.23640, '{\sl Non-equilibrium fluctuations of a two-species exclusion process with slow boundary }'] There exist constants \( C,M>0 \) and \( N_0 \in \mathbb{N} \), such that, for every
	density \(f\) with respect to \(\nu_{\bm r}^n\),
	\[
	\left\langle L_n^\pm \sqrt f,\sqrt f\right\rangle_{\nu_{\bm r}^n}
	=
	-\frac12 D_{\nu_{\bm r}^n}^\pm(\sqrt f), \quad \forall  n \ge N_0,
	\]
	 \[
	 \left\langle L_n^s \sqrt f,\sqrt f\right\rangle_{\nu_{\bm r}^n}
	 \le
	 -MD_{\nu_{\bm r}^n}^s(\sqrt f)+\frac{C}{n}, \quad \forall n \ge 1,
	 \]
	 and
	 \[
	 \left\langle L_n^c \sqrt f,\sqrt f\right\rangle_{\nu_{\bm r}^n}
	 \le
	 Cn, \quad \forall n \ge 1.
	 \]
	 Here 
	 \begin{align*}
	 	 D_{\nu_{\bm r}^n}^-(\sqrt{f}) 
	 	 &= \frac{1}{n} \int \sum_{k=1}^{2} \left[ \alpha_k \eta_0^1 \left(  \sqrt{f}(\eta - \delta_0^1 + \delta_{k}^1 ) - \sqrt{f}(\eta) \right) ^2 \right. \\
	 	 &\quad \left. 
	 	 + \alpha_0 \eta_k^1 \left(  \sqrt{f}(\eta - \delta_{k}^1 + \delta_0^1 ) - \sqrt{f}(\eta) \right) ^2 \right] \,\mathrm d \nu_{\bm r}^n,
	 \end{align*}
	 \begin{align*}
	 	D_{\nu_{\bm r}^n}^+(\sqrt{f}) 
	 	&= \frac{1}{n} \int \sum_{k=1}^{2} \left[ \beta_k \eta_0^{n-1} \left(  \sqrt{f}(\eta - \delta_0^{n-1} + \delta_{k}^{n-1} ) - \sqrt{f}(\eta) \right) ^2 \right. \\
	 	&\quad \left. + \beta_0 \eta_k^{n-1} \left(  \sqrt{f}(\eta - \delta_{k}^{n-1} + \delta_0^{n-1} ) - \sqrt{f}(\eta) \right) ^2 \right] \,\mathrm d \nu_{\bm r}^n,
	 \end{align*}
	 and
	 \begin{align*}
	 	D_{\nu_{\bm r}^n}^s(\sqrt{f}) 
	 	= \int \sum_{x=1}^{n-2} \sum_{k,l=0}^{2} \eta_k^x \eta_l^{x+1}  
	 	\left(  \sqrt{f}(\eta -\delta_{k}^{x} + \delta_{l}^{x} + \delta_{k}^{x+1} - \delta_{l}^{x+1}) - \sqrt{f}(\eta) \right)^2 \,\mathrm d \nu_{\bm r}^n.
	 \end{align*}

[Lemma lem:Salins of arXiv:2504.11107, 'An Invariance Principle for some\\% Reaction-Diffusion Equations with a Multiplicative Ran'] Suppose that $X=\{X(t\,, x)\}_{t>0,x\in\mathbb{T}}$ is a 
	predictable random field and formally define the stochastic convolution $I_X$ via
	(equation IX of the paper).
	If\\ $\mathrm{E}(\|X\|_{L^k([0,T_*]\times\mathbb{T})}^k)<\infty$ for some $T_*>0$
	and $k\in(6\,,\infty)$, then $I_X$ is a well-defined Walsh integral, and 
	has a continuous version that satisfies the following for all $T\in[0\,,T_*]$
	and all stopping times $\tau$:
	\begin{equation*}\textstyle
		\mathrm{E} \left( \| I_X \|_{C([0,T\wedge\tau]\times\mathbb{T})}^k\right)
		\lesssim T^{(k-6)/4} \mathrm{E}\left( \int_0^T{\rm d} s\int_\mathbb{T}{\rm d} y\
		|X(s\wedge\tau\,,y)|^k\right),
	\end{equation*}
	where the implied constant depends only on $(T_*,k)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma lem:Salins of arXiv:2504.11107

For a nonconstant uniform Boolean f, let S have probabilities fhat(s)^2, v=Var(f)=Pr[S!=0]>0, and Q be the law of S conditioned on S!=0. Then H(f)=h2(v)+v H(Q) and I(f)=v E_Q|S|, where h2 is binary entropy. No finite absolute C makes H(Q)<=C I(f) hold for all such f. For f_r=1-2*1_(x_1=...=x_r=0), r>=2, Q is uniform on 2^r-1 nonzero vectors, H(Q)=log2(2^r-1), and I(f_r)=r*2^(1-r); their ratio is at least ((r-1)/r)*2^(r-1) and diverges. The counterexample refutes the unweighted conditioned bridge, not the FEI conjecture. Constants have v=0 and Q is undefined.

[Proposition prop:boundarycase of arXiv:2602.08591, 'The Yang--Mills measure on compact surfaces as a \\ universal scaling limit of lattice gau'] The sequences $A_N^{\mathrm{bulk}}$ and $A_N^{\mathrm{sing}}$ are independent. Moreover, the following convergence statements hold.
\begin{itemize}
    \item The noise component $A_N^{\mathrm{noise}}$ converges in law, in anisotropic Hölder spaces of regularity $(-\frac{1}{2}^-, \frac 1 2^-)$, to a de Rham primitive of a $\mathfrak g$--valued white noise on $\mathcal{S}$.
    \item The flat component $A_N^{\mathrm{flat}}$is a constant random $1$--current of the form $
        \sum_{a=1}^{2g} U_a\left(\log g_a\right),
    $
    where $(U_a)_{0\leqslant a\leqslant 2g}$ are de Rham currents of degree $1$ supported on smooth curves in $\mathcal{S}$, 
    and $(g_a)_{1\leqslant a\leqslant 2g}$ are independent Haar--distributed random variables on $G$.
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 20 (Operator-norm bound at fixed-point solutions) of arXiv:2606.27774, 'Variational Formulas for the Spectrum of\\ Block Wishart Matrices'] Fix $\bZ\in\bbH_+^k$ and let $\bS\in\bbH_+^k$ be a solution of $\bK_{\alpha,\nu}(\bS) = \bZ$. 
With $\bB := \Im(\bS)$, we have the bound
\begin{equation}

\Gamma_\bS(\bB) \le \alpha- \alpha^2\lambda_{\min}\big(\bB^{-1/2}\bS\,\Im(\bZ)\, \bS^*\bB^{-1/2}\big)\, .
\end{equation}
In particular, 
$$\frac{1}{\alpha}\Gamma_\bS(\bB) < 1$$.

[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] The normal law $g_t$, shifted to the right by $a\in\mathbb R$, has density
$$g_t^a=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi t}}\,e^{-(x-a)^2/2t}\,dx$$
and the basic properties of this shifted law $g_t^a$ are as follows:
\begin{enumerate}
\item The mean is $E=a$, the variance is $V=t$.

\item The moments satisfy $M_k=aM_{k-1}+(k-1)tM_{k-2}$.

\item The central moments are $M_k'=\delta_{2|k}t^{k/2}k!!$.

\item The normalized central moments are $M_k''=\delta_{2|k}k!!$.

\item The skewness is $\gamma=0$, the kurtosis is $\kappa=3$.

\item The Fourier transform is $F(x)=\exp(iax-tx^2/2)$.

\item We have the convolution formula $g_s^a*g_t^b=g_{s+t}^{a+b}$.
\end{enumerate}

For a centered probability mu on R^n with exponential moments in a neighborhood of zero and f in L2(mu), define F_f(z)=integral f(x)exp(<z,x>) dmu(x)/integral exp(<z,x>) dmu(x) near zero. The degree-d Taylor tensor is T_d f=(1/d!)D^d F_f(0). Its Hilbert--Schmidt norm sums the squares of all n^d ordered-index entries. For a multi-index alpha of total degree d, if c_alpha is the coefficient of z^alpha in F_f, those entries equal (alpha!/d!)c_alpha, and their multiplicity is d!/alpha!. Thus ||T_df||^2=sum_{|alpha|=d}(alpha!/d!)|c_alpha|^2.

body:
[Lemma of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] Any $G$-global level weak equivalence is in particular a $G$-global weak equivalence.
    \begin{proof}
        Let $H$ be any compact Lie group. By [broecker-tom-dieck]*{Theorem~4.1}, there exists a faithful $H$-representation $V$, which we may assume without loss of generality to be a subrepresentation of the chosen complete $H$-universe $\mathcal U_H$. Then the subposet of $s(\mathcal U_H)$ of all subrepresentations containing $V$ is cofinal, whence so is the (larger) subposet of all faithful subrepresentations. To complete the proof it then suffices to observe that if $f\colon X\to Y$ is any $G$-global level weak equivalence and $W$ a \emph{faithful} $H$-representation classified by some $\rho\colon H\to {\textup{O}}(W)$, then $(\varphi^*f)(W)$ is an $H$-equivariant weak equivalence as $(\varphi^*f)(W)^K=f(W)^{\varphi\rho^{-1}|_{\rho(K)}}$ for any $K\subset H$.
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Unnumbered lemma of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'

[Definition 19 of arXiv:2608.31171, '\bf Finite-energy spacetimes with torus symmetry. \\ \Large Cauchy stability of Einstein--'] Consider a Navier--Stokes potential~$\chi$ on a domain $\mathscr F\subset\mathscr E$ of a bundle as defined in \autoref{def-pot-hyperbolic}.  It is said to be \textbf{torus-adapted} if $\mathscr E \subset \mathscr E_\pi$ is a sub-bundle of the rank-$2$ bundle~\eqref{rank-2-bundle} and the potential depends covariantly on the vector~$\beta$ and on $\zeta\in\mathscr E$, namely can be written as a function $\chi=\chi(s_\perp,s_\parallel,\xi_\perp,\xi_\parallel)$ of four scalar variables, where
\be
s_\perp = - \beta_\alpha \pi^{\perp\,\alpha\beta} \beta_\beta , \qquad
s_\parallel = \beta_\alpha \pi^{\parallel\,\alpha\beta} \beta_\beta , \qquad
s_\perp \geq s_\parallel \geq 0 .
\ee
By extension, a Navier--Stokes triple $(\mathscr F, \chi, \mathscr B)$ is said to be torus-adapted if~$\chi$ is torus-adapted.

body: Let g be a norm on R^2 even in the first coordinate (every lattice-symmetric FPP limit-shape norm qualifies). Fix a transversal offset h and span length r, and for a dogleg from (0,0) through v = (h, j) to (0, r) consider F(j) := g((h, j)) + g((h, r-j)) (the second leg g((0,r) - v) = g((-h, r-j)) equals g((h, r-j)) by evenness). F is convex in j (a sum of compositions of g with affine maps) and satisfies F(r - j) = F(j), so it is symmetric about j = r/2 and therefore minimized there: F(j) >= F(r/2) for EVERY real j, including j < 0 and j > r. Consequence: any lower bound on the dogleg excess assumed only for the MIDPOINT-displaced point (the enclosing-ball statement as classically printed) extends free of charge to every longitudinal position at the same transversal offset - for axis-aligned spans, the 'displaced point arbitrary at its distance' reading is a theorem, not an added assumption. For tilted spans the reflection symmetry fails and the extension is genuinely false (measured deficits up to 4.5 percent at small tilts), so this reduction is exactly the boundary of what symmetry buys. Verified: zero violations over 80,000 fresh trials on four norms (weighted p-norms and a polygonal norm), worst ratio 1 + 2e-12; independently verified by its originating referee at zero violations over 5 norms x 3 scales x 5 offsets x 1401 positions.

body:
[Lem Mes lemma 10 of arXiv:2505.11700, 'Distribution of the cokernels of determinantal row-sparse matrices'] Assume that $\gcd(|G|,k_n)=1$. Let $\underline{n} = (n_a)_{a \in G} \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}^{G}$ such that $\sum_{a \in G} n_a = n$. Let $\nu = \nu_{\underline{n}}$ and $\mu = \mu_{\underline{n}}$.
Then there is a positive real number $C_n = O_G(k_n^4)$ (which does not depend on the choice of $\underline{n}$) and a subgroup $H$ of $G$ such that the following two conditions hold. 
\begin{enumerate}
\item 
$\left | \nu_H(a) - \nu(a) \right | \le C_n\sqrt{D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\nu || \mu)}$ for every $a \in G$.
\item 
$\nu(G \backslash H) \le C_n D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\nu || \mu)$.    
\end{enumerate}
title: Lem Mes lemma 10 of arXiv:2505.11700

[Proposition 5 of arXiv:2604.17973, 'Schauder estimates and classical solutions of the Dirichlet problem for stochastic parabol'] Let $\alpha\in(0,1)$ and $\gamma\ge 2$. Suppose that $u$ is a quasi-classical solution of \eqref{eq:model-half-space}--\eqref{eq:model-half-space-bc} such that
\[
f\in C_x^{\alpha}(\bar Q_T^+;L_\omega^\gamma),
\qquad
f|_{\Sigma_T}\in C_{x,t}^{\alpha,\alpha/2}(\Sigma_T;L_\omega^\gamma),
\qquad
f(0,\cdot)|_{\partial\R_+^n}=0,
\]
and
\[
g\in C_x^{1+\alpha}(\bar Q_T^+;L_\omega^\gamma(\elltwo)),
\qquad
g|_{\Sigma_T} = 0.
\]
Then
\begin{align}
|D_x^2u|_{(\alpha,\alpha/2);Q_T^+}^{L_\omega^\gamma}
\le C\Bigl(
|u|_{0;Q_T^+}^{L_\omega^\gamma}
+|f|_{\alpha;Q_T^+}^{L_\omega^\gamma}
+|f|_{(\alpha,\alpha/2);\Sigma_T}^{L_\omega^\gamma}
+|g|_{1+\alpha;Q_T^+}^{L_\omega^\gamma(\elltwo)}
\Bigr),
\end{align}
where $C$ depends only on $n$, $\alpha$, $\gamma$, $\kappa$, and $K$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition 5 of arXiv:2604.17973

[Theorem 23 of arXiv:2606.26496, 'Homeomorphism of the Revuz correspondence under Dynkin class assumptions'] Let ${\sf A}^n,{\sf A}\in\mathbf{A}_c^+$. Denote by $\mu_n$, $\mu$ their Revuz measures in ${\sf S}_0$ for each $n$. Assume that $\mu\in {\sf S}^1_{G\!D}$ and $\{\mu_n\}$ is 1-order uniformly  Green-tight measure of Dynkin. If the resolvent kernel $R_1(x,y)$ is continuous on $E\times E$. Then $R_1 \mu,R_1\mu_n \in C_b(E)$ and the following conditions are equivalent:
		\begin{itemize}
			\item[{\rm (i)}] $\mu_n$ converges to $\mu$ vaguely on $E$.
			\item[{\rm (ii)}] $U_1 \mu_n$ converges to $U_1 \mu$ strongly in $\mathcal{E}_1$-norm.
			\item[{\rm (iii)}] $\displaystyle \lim_{n\to \infty}\mathbb{E}_x\left[ \sup_{0\leq t\leq T} \left|  {\sf A}^n_t - {\sf A}_t \right|  \right] =0  \text{ for any }T>0\text{ and q.e. }\  x\in E.$
			\item[{\rm (iv)}] $R_1 \mu_n$ converges to $R_1 \mu$ locally uniformly on $E$.
		\end{itemize}

body:
[Lemma lem:admissible-classes of arXiv:2609.00777, 'Universal murmuration and Hecke augmentation'] Suppose that $P\nmid rd$.  There is a set
$\mathcal R_{r,d}(Q)\subset\mathbb Z/d^2\mathbb Z$ such that
\[
\mathcal A_{r,d}(Q)
=
\left\{
N\in\mathbb Z_{>0}:
\mu^2(N)=1,\ P\nmid N,\
N\bmod d^2\in\mathcal R_{r,d}(Q)
\right\}.
\]
Every class in $\mathcal R_{r,d}(Q)$ is coprime to $d$, and
\[
\#\mathcal R_{r,d}(Q)
=
\begin{cases}
1,&(r,d)=1,\quad 2\nmid rd,\\
1,&(r,d)=1,\quad 2\mid r,\\
1,&(r,d)=2,\quad 2\Vert d,\\
2,&(r,d)=2,\quad 4\mid d,\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
If $d$ is even, every integer represented by an admissible class is odd.
Writing
\[
s=\frac{N(r^2N-4Q)}{d^2},
\]
the parity information is
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{case}&\text{parity of }s\\ \hline
2\Vert d,\ 2\Vert r&\text{even}\\
2\Vert d,\ 4\mid r&\text{odd}\\
4\mid d&\text{one even class and one odd class}.
\end{array}
\]
In particular, the number and parity type of these classes are independent of $k$.

body:
[Lemma lem:complex-freedman-paper of arXiv:2606.08683, 'Exact Fourier dimensions of dyadic Mandelbrot cascades under minimal integrability'] Let \(
(S_j,\mathcal H_j)_{j=0}^{N}\) be a complex-valued martingale with \(S_0=0\) and differences
\(\Delta_j=S_j-S_{j-1}\), \(1\le j\le N.\)
Let \(R,V\in(0,\infty)\). Assume that \(\lvert\Delta_j\rvert\le R\)
almost surely for every \(j\), and
\[
\sum_{j=1}^{N}
\mathbb{E}\left(\lvert\Delta_j\rvert^2\mid\mathcal H_{j-1}\right)
\le V
\]
almost surely.  Then, for every \(t>0\), 
\[\mathbb{P}\left(
\max_{0\le j\le N}\lvert S_j\rvert>t
\right)
\le
4\exp\left(
-\frac{t^2}{8(V+Rt)}
\right).\]

[Thm 9 ($\Gamma$-Convergence) of arXiv:2608.30445, 'Derivation of a linearly elastic elliptic membrane shell theory in the framework of magnet'] The family
			$(\overline{\mathcal G}_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ is
			equi-coercive and sequentially $\Gamma$-converges to
			$\overline{\mathcal G}_0$ with respect to the weak topology of
			$\boldsymbol{\mathcal X}$. More precisely, the following assertions
			hold.
			\begin{enumerate}
				\item If
				\[
				\sup_{\varepsilon>0}
				\overline{\mathcal G}_\varepsilon
				(\boldsymbol v(\varepsilon),\boldsymbol m(\varepsilon))
				<+\infty,
				\]
				then there exists a subsequence, not relabeled, and
				$(\boldsymbol\eta,\boldsymbol m)
				\in\boldsymbol{\mathcal A}_M(\omega)$ such that
				\begin{align}
					
					v_\alpha(\varepsilon)&\rightharpoonup\eta_\alpha
					&&\text{weakly in }H^1(\Omega),\nonumber\\
					v_3(\varepsilon)&\rightharpoonup\eta_3
					&&\text{weakly in }L^2(\Omega),\\
					m_i(\varepsilon)&\rightharpoonup m_i
					&&\text{weakly in }H^1(\Omega),\nonumber\\
					m_i(\varepsilon)&\to m_i
					&&\text{strongly in }L^2(\Omega).\nonumber
				\end{align}
				All the limits in \eqref{sec5-eqn3} are independent of
				$x_3$.
				
				\item For every sequence
				$(\boldsymbol v(\varepsilon),\boldsymbol m(\varepsilon))$
				converging weakly in $\boldsymbol{\mathcal X}$ to
				$(\boldsymbol v,\boldsymbol m)$,
				\begin{equation}
					
					\overline{\mathcal G}_0(\boldsymbol v,\boldsymbol m)
					\leq
					\liminf_{\varepsilon\to0}
					\overline{\mathcal G}_\varepsilon
					(\boldsymbol v(\varepsilon),\boldsymbol m(\varepsilon)).
				\end{equation}
				
				\item For every
				$(\boldsymbol v,\boldsymbol m)\in\boldsymbol{\mathcal X}$, there exists
				a sequence
				$(\boldsymbol v(\varepsilon),\boldsymbol m(\varepsilon))$
				converging strongly in $\boldsymbol{\mathcal X}$ to
				$(\boldsymbol v,\boldsymbol m)$ such that
				\begin{equation}
					
					\overline{\mathcal G}_0(\boldsymbol v,\boldsymbol m)
					\geq
					\limsup_{\varepsilon\to0}
					\overline{\mathcal G}_\varepsilon
					(\boldsymbol v(\varepsilon),\boldsymbol m(\varepsilon)).
				\end{equation}
			\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Thm 48 (\cite{Falk01}*{Theorem 3.7}) of arXiv:2609.03836, 'Koszul Orlik--Solomon Algebras from Non-supersolvable Arrangements'] \label[Thm]{prop:tensorreducedos}
    Let $M$ and $N$ be matroids and let us identify the symbol $f$ with an element in each.
    Then we have the graded $\QQ$-algebra isomorphism
    \[
        \rOS(P_{f}(M, N)) \cong \rOS(M)\otimes_{\QQ} \rOS(N).
    \]
    \begin{proof}
        Let $E_0 = E(M) - \{f\}$ and $E_1 = E(N) - \{f\}$.
        We will prove the isomorphism 
        $$\OS(\mathbf{d}_f P_{f}(M, N)) \cong \OS(\mathbf{d}_f M)\otimes_{\QQ} \OS(\mathbf{d}_f N).$$
        Both sides are canonically quotients of the free exterior algebra 
        $A = \bigwedge(E_0 \sqcup E_1)$.
        We will show that the kernel ideals are equal.
        As discussed in \Cref{subsec:OS_algebras},
        $\OS(\mathbf{d}_f P_{f}(M, N))$ is the quotient of $A$ by 
        (i) the monomials 
        $e_D$ for subets $D \subseteq E_0 \sqcup E_1$ containing $f$ in their span
        and (ii) the elements $\partial e_C$ for all circuits of $P_f(M, N)\del f$.
        Since a subset of $E_0$ (or $E_1$) spanning $f$ still spans it in $P_f(M, N)$ and since every circuit of $M \del f$ (or $N \del f$) is a circuit of $P_f(M, N) \del f$, every relation in the defining ideal of 
        $\rOS(M)\otimes_{\QQ} \rOS(N)$ lies in the defining ideal of
        $\OS(\mathbf{d}_f P_{f}(M, N))$. The converse follows from the following two observations:
        \begin{itemize}
            \item If $D \subseteq E_0 \sqcup E_1$ contains $f$ in its span in $P_f(M, N)$, then so does at least one of $D \cap E_0$ or $D \cap E_1$.
            \item If $C \subseteq E_0 \sqcup E_1$ is a circuit of $P_f(M, N)$ then either $C \subseteq E_0$, or 
            $C \subseteq E_1$, or else both 
            $C \cap E_0$ and $C \cap E_1$ contain $f$ in their span.
        \end{itemize}
        The first observation shows that every element of type (i) in the defining ideal of $\OS(\mathbf{d}_f P_{f}(M, N))$ is a multiple of an element of type (i) in the defining ideal of 
        $\rOS(M)\otimes_{\QQ} \rOS(N)$. 
        The second observation shows that every element of type (ii) in the defining ideal of $\OS(\mathbf{d}_f P_{f}(M, N))$ is either equal, up to sign, to a type (ii) element for $\rOS(M)\otimes_{\QQ} \rOS(N)$ or else every term in its expansion into monomials is a multiple of an element of type (i) in the defining ideal of $\rOS(M)\otimes_{\QQ} \rOS(N)$.
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

    Let $\{ \mu_t \}$ be a family of probability measures that satisfy the LDP with a good rate function $\mathcal{I}(\cdot)$ on a Hausdorff topological space $\mathcal{X}$, and for $\epsilon > 0$ let $f_{\epsilon}: \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{Y}$ be continuous functions, with $(\mathcal{Y}, d)$ a metric space. Assume there exists a measurable map $f : \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{Y}$ such that for every $\lambda < \infty$,
    \[  
    \limsup_{\epsilon \to 0} \sup_{\{x : \mathcal{I}(x) \le \lambda \}} d(f_{\epsilon} (x), f(x)) = 0.
    \]
    Then any family of probability measures $\mu_t'$ for which $\mu_t \circ f_{\epsilon}^{-1}$ are exponentially good approximations satisfies the LDP in $\mathcal{Y}$ with the good rate function $\mathcal{I}'(y) = \inf \{ \mathcal{I}(x) : y = f(x) \}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition p:properties dual of arXiv:2411.04773, 'Meeting of squared Bessel flow lines and application to the skew Brownian motion'] Let $\mathcal S$ be a general $\rm BESQ^\delta$ flow and $\mathcal S^*$ be its dual. The following statements hold almost surely.
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item For any $r<x$, $b\ge 0$ and $a\ge \mathcal S^*_{-x,-r}(b)$,  $\mathcal S_{r,x}(a)>b$ and 
\begin{equation}
    \mathcal S_{r,y}(a)\ge \mathcal S^*_{-x,-y}(b),\qquad  y\in [r,x].
\end{equation}
Moreover  $\mathcal S_{r,y}(a)> \mathcal S^*_{-x,-y}(b)$ if $y\in (r,x)$ and $\mathcal S_{r,y}(a)>0$.
\item  For any $r<x$, $b\ge 0$ such that $a:=\mathcal S^*_{-x,-r}(b)>0$ and $0\le a'< a$, 
\[
\mathcal S_{r,y}(a')\le \mathcal S^*_{-x,-y}(b),\qquad  y\in [r,x].
\]
 Moreover $\mathcal S_{r,y}(a')< \mathcal S^*_{-x,-y}(b)$ if  $y\in (r,x)$ and $\mathcal S^*_{-x,-y}(b)>0$.
\end{enumerate}

[Proposition 6 of arXiv:2606.26619, 'Ergodicity of stochastic reaction-diffusion equations on unbounded domains driven by space'] Assume that (S1)--(S3) and (H5) hold, and that
\[
\theta> \frac{G_{\sigma}^2}{8}.
\]
Then the unique solution $u$ to equation (\ref{3.1}) satisfies
\begin{align}
  \sup_{t\geq 0}\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}} \mathbb{E}|u(t,x)|^2 <\infty.
\end{align}

\begin{align*}

[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2608.27433, 'Scalar curvature on K\"ahler blow-ups and systolic inequalities'] Let \((X^n,\omega)\) be a compact K\"ahler manifold with positive scalar curvature and let \(r=r(X)\) be its rational dimension. Then
\begin{equation}
        \min_XS(\omega)\,\sys_2(\omega)
        \le
        2\pi r(r+1).
\end{equation}
Moreover, equality holds if and only if the universal cover
\[
        (\widetilde X,\widetilde\omega)
        \cong
        (\PP^r,\sigma\omega_{\mathrm{FS}})
        \times(Y^{n-r},\omega_{\mathrm{RF}}),
        \qquad \sigma=\sys_2(\omega),
\]
where \(\omega_{\mathrm{RF}}\) is Ricci-flat and the \(2\)-systole is realized by a rational curve. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 1 of arXiv:2608.27433

[Lemma lem:green-hilbert-schmidt of arXiv:2608.02459, 'Response Calculus for Spectral Simplicity\\ and Joint Eigenvalue Densities'] The inclusion $\Omega_{\rm Fr}\subseteq\Omega_{\rm HS}$ holds.  For every
$x\in\Omega_{\rm HS}$, the operator $G_x$ is positive, self-adjoint,
and Hilbert--Schmidt, with
\begin{equation}
 \|G_x\|_{\rm HS}^2
 =\iint_{D^2}G_D(z,w)^2\,M_x(dz)M_x(dw)<\infty.
\end{equation}
For all $\theta,\eta\in L^2(M_x)$,
\begin{align}
 \iint_{D^2}|G_D(z,w)\theta(z)\eta(w)|\,M_x(dz)M_x(dw)
 &\le \|G_x\|_{\mathrm{HS}}\|\theta\|_2\|\eta\|_2,              \\
 I_D(\theta M_x,\eta M_x)
 &=\langle\theta,G_x\eta\rangle_{L^2(M_x)},                       \\
 |I_D(\theta M_x,\eta M_x)|
 &\le \|G_x\|_{\mathrm{HS}}\|\theta\|_2\|\eta\|_2.            
\end{align}
Consequently, $\theta M_x\in\mathcal M_{\rm fe}(D)$ for every $\theta\in L^2(M_x)$, and
\begin{equation}
 \theta\ne0
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \langle\theta,G_x\theta\rangle_{L^2(M_x)}
 =I_D(\theta M_x)>0.
\end{equation}
In particular, $\kerG_x=\{0\}$.

body:
Let X, Y and Z be random variables with finitely many values, with Z = f(Y) almost surely. Then H(X | Y) <= H(X | Z), with equality if and only if X and Y are conditionally independent given Z. The hypothesis that Z is a function of Y cannot be dropped: if Y is constant, X is a fair bit and Z = X, then H(X | Y) = ln 2 while H(X | Z) = 0. Entropies use natural logarithms with 0 ln 0 = 0, and a conditional entropy averages only over conditioning values of positive probability; dividing every term by ln 2 gives the same statement in bits.

body: In statistics, the Gauss–Markov theorem states that the ordinary least squares (OLS) estimator has the lowest sampling variance within the class of linear unbiased estimators, if the errors in the linear regression model are uncorrelated, have equal variances and expectation value of zero. The errors do not need to be normal, nor do they need to be independent and identically distributed. The requirement that the estimator be unbiased cannot be dropped, since biased estimators exist with lower variance. See, for example, the James–Stein estimator, ridge regression, or simply any degenerate estimator.

Let 1 < p < infinity and let f: (0, infinity) -> [0, infinity] be measurable. Define the averaging (Hardy) operator (Hf)(x) = (1/x) int_0^x f(t) dt. Then ||Hf||_{L^p(0,infinity)} <= (p/(p-1)) ||f||_{L^p(0,infinity)}. The constant p/(p-1) = p' is best possible, and for f in L^p there is equality only when f = 0 a.e. Discrete form: for a_n >= 0 and 1 < p < infinity, sum_{n>=1} ((a_1 + ... + a_n)/n)^p <= (p/(p-1))^p sum_{n>=1} a_n^p, again with the sharp constant. The inequality is FALSE for p = 1: no finite constant works there (see the proof sketch for the counterexample). At p = infinity the operator is bounded on L^infinity with norm exactly 1, consistent with p/(p-1) -> 1.
1 < p < infinity strictly for the stated inequality; at p = 1 it fails with no finite constant, and at p = infinity the sharp bound is ||Hf||_infinity <= ||f||_infinity
f measurable and nonnegative on (0, infinity) (the general complex case follows by applying the result to |f|)
Lebesgue measure on (0, infinity)

body:
[Proposition 3 of arXiv:2608.07879, 'Sharp Wasserstein Convergence Rates for Empirical Path Laws of It\^o Processes'] Let $\rho>p\geq1$. Under Assumption~\ref{assum:regularity}, let $\mu$ and
$\mu_N$ be as in Theorem~\ref{thm:endpoint-path-law}. Suppose in addition
that, for some $C_T>0$, $\mu$
satisfies the quadratic transport inequality
\begin{equation}
    \Wc_2^2(\nu,\mu)
    \le
    2C_T\,\mathrm H(\nu\mid\mu)
\end{equation}
for every probability measure $\nu$ on $\Cc^d$, where $\mathrm H$ denotes
relative entropy. Then there exists
$C=C\bigl(d,T,p,\rho,\E\Lambda_X^\rho\bigr)>0$ such that, for every $t>0$
and $N\ge2$,
\begin{equation}
    \P\left(
        \Wc_p(\mu_N,\mu)
        >C(\log N)^{-1/2}+t
    \right)
    \le
    \exp\left(
        -\frac{N^{2/\max\{p,2\}}t^2}{2C_T}
    \right).
    
\end{equation}
In particular, the exponent in \eqref{eq:transport-concentration} is
$-Nt^2/(2C_T)$ when $1\le p\le2$.
title: Proposition 3 of arXiv:2608.07879

	f(X^\sigma(q_d,a))
	\]
are $(L^{O(1)}/(\delta N^{1/2}))$-Lipschitz on $U_\MAX$. Likewise the empirical averages
	\[\frac1N
	\sum_{i\in[N]}
	f(X^\Ising(q_d,i) )
	\]
are $(L^{O(1)}/(\delta N^{1/2}))$-Lipschitz on $U_\MAX$.

Let $\sigma\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII\}$.
Recall from Lemma~\ref{l:X.lip}
that the $\R^M$-valued functions $h^{\sigma,d}$ are $L^{O(1)}$-Lipschitz on the set $U_\MAX$. It follows that
the $\R^M$-valued functions 
	\[
	H^{\sigma,d}(\bXi)

	= \sum_{\ell=0}^{d-1}
	h^{\sigma,\ell}(\bXi)
	\]
are $(L^{O(1)}/\delta)$-Lipschitz on the set $U_\MAX$. Let $F:\R^M\to\R^M$ denote the map obtained by applying $f$ coordinatewise, and note that $F$ is $L^{O(1)}$-Lipschitz. Therefore,
	\[
	\frac1M
	\sum_{a\in[M]}
	f(X^\sigma(q_d,a))
	=
	\frac1M
	(\ind_M, F(H(\bXi))
	\]
is $(L^{O(1)}/(\delta M^{1/2}))$-Lipschitz on the set $U_\MAX$. A similar argument applies for $X^\Ising$ (in this case in fact the restriction to $U_\MAX$ is not necessary, since as we mentioned in the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:X.lip}, the functions $h^{\Ising,d}$ are Lipschitz on the full space).
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition 18 (Optimality of the $\ell^1$ convolution bound) of arXiv:2602.14618, 'Finitary coding and Gaussian concentration\\ for random fields'] Let $b=(b_m)_{m\in\mathbb Z^d}$ be a nonnegative function in $\ell^1(\mathbb Z^d)$, that is,
$b_m\ge 0$ for all $m\in\mathbb Z^d$ and $\sum_{m\in\mathbb Z^d} b_m < \infty$.
For any $\delta=(\delta_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}\in \ell^2(\mathbb Z^d)$ with finite support, define
\[
Q(\delta) := \sum_{k,\ell\in\mathbb Z^d} \delta_k\,\delta_\ell\, b_{\ell-k}.
\]
Then
\[
\sup_{\delta\in \ell^2(\mathbb Z^d),\, \delta\neq 0}
\frac{Q(\delta)}{\|\delta\|_2^2}
= \|b\|_1.
\]
Moreover, if $\delta^{(L)}=\1_{\Lambda_L}$ with
$\Lambda_L := [-L,L]^d\cap\mathbb Z^d$, then
\[
\frac{Q(\delta^{(L)})}{\|\delta^{(L)}\|_2^2}
\longrightarrow
\|b\|_1
\qquad\text{as } L\to\infty.
\]

[Theo 17 of arXiv:2602.14618, 'Finitary coding and Gaussian concentration\\ for random fields'] Let $d\ge 1$. 
Let $X=(X_i)_{i\in\mathbb Z^d}$ be an i.i.d.\ $A$-valued random field, where $A$ is a standard Borel space, 
and let $Y=\varphi(X)$ for some finitary coding $\varphi:A^{\mathbb Z^d}\to B^{\mathbb Z^d}$. 
If the coding satisfies the short-range factorization property with constant $\alpha\in(0,1]$, then for every local function
$f:B^{\mathbb Z^d}\to\R$ with the bounded-difference property,
\[
\log \E\big[\exp\{\lambda(f(Y)-\E f(Y))\}\big]
\;\le\;
3\,\alpha^{-d}\,\lambda^2\,
\big(\E\big[(2r_\varphi(X)+1)^{d}\big]\big)^2\,
\|\delta f\|_2^2,
\qquad \forall\, \lambda>0.
\]

[Ppn 243 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Assume that $L\ge1$ and that condition \eqref{e:deriv.p.bound} holds. Let $\vX\equiv \vX^N$ be the process defined by \eqref{e:X.decomp} and \eqref{e:Delta.X.Ising}. Let $X(q_d)$ denote the random variable $X(q_d,a(q_d))$ where $a(q_d)$ is sampled uniformly at random from $[M]$. Similarly denote $\vX(q_d)\equiv \vX(q_d,(a(q_d),i(q_d)))$, where $i(q_d)$ is sampled uniformly at random from $[N]$. Assume that for some fixed measure $\mu$ on $\R$ with finite second moment, we have
	\beq
	\bbW_2(\mathscr{L}(X(1)),\mu)
	\le \epsilon\,,\eeq
where the bound holds uniformly over $N$. Then each of the preprocessing steps defined in \S\ref{ss:preprocessing} incurs a negligible $\bbW_2$ error on the endpoint distribution: the processes $\vX, \vX^\trstar, \vX^\frstar,\vX^\trunc, \vX^\frozen$ can be coupled so that
	\[
	\E\bigg[ 
	\|\vX(1)-\vX^\trstar(1)\|^2
	+\|\vX^\trstar(1)-\vX^\frstar(1)\|^2
	+\|\vX^\trstar(1)-\vX^\trunc(1)\|^2
	+\|\vX^\frstar(1)-\vX^\frozen(1)\|^2
	\bigg]
	\le O(\epsilon) + o_{\trK}(1)\,,
	\]
uniformly in $N$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let (X, \mathcal{A}, \mu) be a measure space, and let f_n, f be non-negative integrable functions such that f_n(x) \to f(x) \mu-almost everywhere as n \to \infty and \int_X f_n d\mu \to \int_X f d\mu < \infty. Then \lim_{n \to \infty} \int_X |f_n - f| d\mu = 0. In particular, if f_n and f are probability densities with respect to a common dominating measure \mu and f_n \to f \mu-almost everywhere, then the laws converge in total variation, since d_{TV}(P_n, P) = \frac{1}{2} \int_X |f_n - f| d\mu.

[Theorem intro:1-d continuum T>0:1RSB of arXiv:2605.05631, 'Wandering Exponents and the Free Energy of the High-Dimensional Elastic Polymer'] Let us assume that $(B''(x))^{-1/3}$ is strictly convex or linear, and that the model is not RS. Then the model is 1RSB. Moreover, if we write the Parisi measure as $\zeta_c=m\delta_{q_0}+(1-m)\delta_{q_*}$, then $(q_0,q_*,q_c,m)$ is the unique solution to the following equations: $0<q_0<q_*<q_c$,
		\[\beta(q_c-q_*+m(q_*-q_0))=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu t}},\]
		\[F(q_0)=F(q_*)=\int_{q_0}^{q_*}F(u)du=0.\]
		where here $F$ is the function
		\[F(x)=-2B'(2(q_c-x))-2q_0\sqrt{\mu^3 t}-\frac{1}{\beta m t}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu t}}+\beta m(q_0-x)\right)^{-2}+\frac{\mu}{\beta m },\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem thm: R X (T,X_T) of arXiv:2411.17109, 'On the maximal correlation of some stochastic processes'] Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n$ be non-degenerate independent random variables taking values in a general measurable space $(F,\mathcal{F})$. Fix a special point $\partial$ outside of $F$. Let $T$ be a random subset of $[n]=\{1,2,\ldots,n\}$. Suppose that $T$ is independent of $(X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n)$. For $i=1,2,\ldots,n$, define
\[Y_i=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}
X_i, & \text{if }i\in T,\\
\partial, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{array}\right.\]
Then for $n\geq 1$, we have
\[R((X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n),(Y_1,Y_2,\ldots,Y_n))=
\sqrt{\max\{P(i\in T):i\in[n]\}}.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: In probability theory, Girsanov's theorem or the Cameron-Martin-Girsanov theorem explains how stochastic processes change under changes in measure. The theorem is especially important in the theory of financial mathematics as it explains how to convert from the physical measure, which describes the probability that an underlying instrument will take a particular value or values, to the risk-neutral measure which is a very useful tool for evaluating the value of derivatives on the underlying instrument.
title: Girsanov theorem

\tau(C)=O(\kappa(C)).

and $\kappa=\kappa(W)$ is its total cost.

[Lemma l:properties_extrapolated_spaces of arXiv:2607.15140, 'On the absence of blow-up in the 3D Navier-Stokes equations with transport noise'] Let $A$ be a positive, invertible, and self-adjoint operator on a Hilbert space $X$. Let $(\mathscr{X}^A_\sigma)_{\sigma\in{\mathbb R}}$ be the scale of Hilbert spaces defined in (equation eq:extrapolated_space1 of the paper)-(equation eq:extrapolated_space2 of the paper). 
Then the following assertions hold:
\begin{itemize}
\item {\rm (Extrapolated operator)}
For each $\sigma <0$ (resp.\ $\sigma>0$), the operator $A$ uniquely extends (resp.\ restricts) to a positive, invertible, and self-adjoint operator $A_\sigma$ on $\mathscr{X}^A_{\sigma}$ with domain $\mathsf{D}(A_\sigma)=\mathscr{X}_{1+\sigma}^A$. 

\item {\rm (Interpolation)}
For $\sigma_0,\sigma_1\in {\mathbb R}$ and $\theta\in (0,1)$, 
$$
\mathscr{X}_{\sigma}^A = [\mathscr{X}_{\sigma_0}^A ,\mathscr{X}_{\sigma_1}^A]_{\theta} \quad \text{ where }\quad \sigma=(1-\theta)\sigma_0+\theta\sigma_1.
$$
\item {\rm (Duality)} For each $\sigma \geq 0$, it holds that $
 \mathscr{X}_{-\sigma}^{A}
 =(\mathscr{X}_{\sigma}^{A})^*
$ and
$$
\langle x^*,x\rangle_{-\sigma,\sigma}^{A}
= ((A^{-\sigma})_{-\sigma} x^*,A^{\sigma}x)_{X} \ \text{ for all }\ x^*\in \mathscr{X}^A_{-\sigma}, \ x\in \mathscr{X}^A_{\sigma}.
$$
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 13 of arXiv:2512.08595, 'Small time asymptotics of spectral heat content of isotropic processes'] Let $\phi:\R^d\to\R$ be a $C^{1,\kappa}$ function with $0<\kappa<1$ and assume that 
		\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
			\item $\Omega=\phi^{-1}(0,\infty)$ is pre-compact,
			\item $|\nabla \phi|$ is bounded away from $0$ in a neighborhood of $\partial\Omega$.
		\end{enumerate}
		Then for any translation invariant isotropic process $X=(X_t)_{t\ge 0}$ satisfying Assumption~\ref{assump1} we have
		\begin{align*}
			\Per(\Omega)\le \liminf_{t\downarrow 0}\frac{\Vol(\Omega)-Q^X_\Omega(t)}{\mu(t)}\le \limsup_{t\downarrow 0}\frac{\Vol(\Omega)-Q^X_\Omega(t)}{\mu(t)}\le \frac{\sup_{\partial\Omega}|\nabla\phi|}{\inf_{\partial\Omega}|\nabla \phi|}\Per(\Omega).
		\end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 13 of arXiv:2512.08595

[Proposition prop:density-robust of arXiv:2608.13452, 'Wasserstein stability of the zero cell of a Poisson hyperplane tessellation under directio'] Let $\hat{f}^{(1)}_{\gamma, n}$ and $\hat{f}^{(2)}_{\gamma, n}$ be the estimators of a density $f$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$ for $d \geq 2$ as in (equation e:tree_estimate of the paper) obtained from two stationary Poisson hyperplane tessellations or STIT tessellations $\mathcal{P}_1(\gamma)$ and $\mathcal{P}_2(\gamma)$ with intensity/lifetime parameter $\gamma$ and directional distributions $\phi_1$ and $\phi_2$, respectively. Assume the tessellations are independent of the data samples $\mathcal{D}_n$.
    Then, there exist random probability densities \(\hat{g}_{\gamma,n}^{(1)}\) and \(\hat{g}_{\gamma,n}^{(2)}\), defined on a common probability space, such that, for every fixed \(x \in \mathbb{R}^d\),
    \[ 
    \hat{g}_{\gamma,n}^{(i)}(x) 
    \overset{(d)}{=} 
    \hat{f}_{\gamma,n}^{(i)}(x), \qquad i=1,2, 
    \]
     and such that, for all $\phi_2$ satisfying assumption (equation e:closetophi1-bnd of the paper), we have
    \begin{align*}
        2 \mathbb{E}[d_{\operatorname{TV}}(\hat{g}^{(1)}_{\gamma, n},\hat{g}^{(2)}_{\gamma, n})]
        =
    \mathbb{E} \left[\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \left|\hat{g}^{(1)}_{\gamma, n}(x) - \hat{g}^{(2)}_{\gamma, n}(x)\right| \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} x\right]
    &\leq C(\phi_1, d) W_{\mathrm{geo}}(\phi_1,\phi_2)^{1/d}, 
\end{align*}
for some constant $C(\phi_1,d)$ depending only on $\phi_1$ and $d$, where the expectation is taken with respect to the random tessellations and $\mathcal{D}_n$.

body: FIRES WHEN you reduce an exact symbolic computation modulo a polynomial that ANNIHILATES your root but is not its MINIMAL polynomial. WHAT HAPPENED: the first exact check of det(z I - U_q - V_q) reduced over Z[m] modulo m^q + 1, which m = e^{i pi / q} certainly satisfies, and reported nonzero coefficients for odd q - which reads exactly like a refutation of the nilpotency claim. Those coefficients are integer multiples of Phi_{2q}(m) and therefore zero: for q = 3 the leftover was exactly plus or minus (m^2 - m + 1) = Phi_6(m). CONDITION OF FAILURE: m^q + 1 is reducible whenever q is odd, since Phi_{2q} is then a proper factor, so the quotient ring is not a field and a nonzero representative need not be a nonzero element. FIX: reduce modulo the MINIMAL polynomial, here Phi_{2q}, which makes the vanishing visible rather than leaving it to be noticed. GENERAL FORM: a 'nonzero' residue in a quotient by a reducible modulus is not evidence of anything.

[Lemma l: 1wr thm step1 of arXiv:2507.04505, 'Heights of butterfly trees'] Let $\pi = (\pi_{\rho(1)} | \cdots | \pi_{\rho(m)}) \in S_n \wr S_m$, where $\rho \in S_m$ and $\pi'_j = \pi_{\rho(j)} - \min(\pi_{\rho(j)}) + 1 \in S_n$ for each $j$. For node $v$ in $\mathcal T(\pi_{\rho(j)}) \subset \mathcal T(\pi)$, let $x = v - \min(\pi_{\rho(j)}) + 1$, and $\V y = (y_1,y_2,\ldots,{\rho(j)})$ the subsequence of $\rho$ that denotes the node sequence in the shortest path in $\mathcal T(\rho)$ connecting the root $\rho(1) = y_1$ to node ${\rho(j)}$. Let $\ell_n^{(j)} = \ell(\pi_j)$ and $r_n^{(j)} = r(\pi_j)$ denote the top-left and top-right edge lengths of $\mathcal T(\pi_j)$, and define
    $$
    G({s,t},u,v) = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll}
    u, & {s > t},\\ v, & {s < t}.
    \end{array}\right.
    $$ Then
    \begin{equation*}
        \operatorname{depth}_{\pi}(v) = \operatorname{depth}_{\pi'_j}(x) +\sum_{k=1}^{\operatorname{depth}_{\rho}(\rho(j))} G(y_k,y_{k+1}, \ell_n^{({y_k})}+1,r_n^{({y_k})}+1).
    \end{equation*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

A balanced neural network on a compact domain E subset R^d consists of n excitatory and n inhibitory neurons with spatial positions x_n^j in E. Their states z_{e, t}^j and z_{i, t}^j satisfy dz_{e, t}^j = [f_e(z_{e, t}^j) + n^{-1/2} sum_{k=1}^n (K_{ee}(x_n^j, x_n^k) G_{ee}(z_{e, t}^k) - K_{ei}(x_n^j, x_n^k) G_{ei}(z_{i, t}^k))] dt + sigma_e(x_n^j, z_{e, t}^j) dW_{e, t}^j, and dz_{i, t}^j = [f_i(z_{i, t}^j) + n^{-1/2} sum_{k=1}^n (K_{ie}(x_n^j, x_n^k) G_{ie}(z_{e, t}^k) - K_{ii}(x_n^j, x_n^k) G_{ii}(z_{i, t}^k))] dt + sigma_i(x_n^j, z_{i, t}^j) dW_{i, t}^j.
Positions x_n^j in compact domain E
Kernels K_{alpha beta} continuous
Interaction scaled by n^{-1/2}

[Lemma lem:varianceupperbounds of arXiv:2411.08848, 'Stationary random measures: Covariance asymptotics, variance bounds and central limit theo'] Let ${\mathcal X}$ be a stationary random measure on $\mathbb{R}^d$. Assuming $\|{\bf K}\| < \infty$, 
\[
{\rm Var}\!\left({\mathcal X}(f)\right) \le (\lambda_D + \|\widehat{{\bf K}}\|_{\infty})\|f\|_2^2 \;\; \mbox{ for any }f\in L^1\cap L^2.
\]
If $\lambda_D + I(0)=0$ and $I(\gamma)=0$ for $|\gamma|<2k$ for some $k\ge 1$, then assuming that $\widehat{{\bf K}}\in C^{2k}$ and that all its partial derivatives up to order $2k$ are uniformly bounded, with  $\|D^{2k}\widehat{{\bf K}}\|_{\infty}:=\sup\limits_{|\gamma|= 2k}\|\partial^{\gamma}\widehat{{\bf K}}\|_{\infty}$, we have
\[
{\rm Var}\!\left({\mathcal X}(f)\right) \le \frac{d^k}{(2k-1)!}\|D^{2k}\widehat{{\bf K}}\|_{\infty}\, |f|_{H^{k}}^2 \;\; \mbox{ for any }f\in L^1\cap H^k.
\]
title: Lemma lem:varianceupperbounds of arXiv:2411.08848

body: In mathematics, the Rellich–Kondrachov theorem is a compact embedding theorem concerning Sobolev spaces. It is named after the Austrian-German mathematician Franz Rellich and the Russian mathematician Vladimir Iosifovich Kondrashov. Rellich proved the L2 theorem and Kondrashov the Lp theorem.
title: Rellich–Kondrachov theorem
