Let Z be standard normal, g(z)=phi(z)+z Phi(z), a=1/sqrt(pi), and v=1/3+(sqrt(3)-2)/(2*pi). Then E[g(Z)]=a and Var(g(Z))=v. W=(a-g(Z))/sqrt(v) has support (-infinity,a/sqrt(v)] and no atom at its finite endpoint. For w<a/sqrt(v), with z=g^{-1}(a-sqrt(v)w), its CDF is 1-Phi(z) and its density is sqrt(v)*phi(z)/Phi(z). This non-Gaussian law is the standardized-degree limit only conditional on the earlier degree/moment convergence being established in a stated regime.
All hypotheses and scope restrictions in the statement apply.

Let Z be standard normal, phi its density, Phi its distribution function, and g(z)=phi(z)+z*Phi(z). Put a=1/sqrt(pi), v=1/3+(sqrt(3)-2)/(2*pi), and W=(a-g(Z))/sqrt(v). Then E[W]=0, Var(W)=1, W has support (-infinity,a/sqrt(v)], has no atom at the finite endpoint, and is not Gaussian. For w<a/sqrt(v), define z=g^{-1}(a-sqrt(v)*w). Then

    P(W<=w)=1-Phi(z),
    density_W(w)=sqrt(v)*phi(z)/Phi(z).

Proof: differentiation gives g'=Phi>0 and g''=phi. Also g(z)=E[(z-Y)_+] for an independent standard normal Y, so g is positive; it tends to zero as z tends to minus infinity and diverges at plus infinity. Thus it is a continuous increasing bijection onto (0,infinity). The distribution and density follow by reversing its monotone change of variables. No finite Z maps to the upper endpoint, so that endpoint has no mass.

For the constants, normal integration by parts gives E[phi(Z)]=1/(2*sqrt(pi)) and E[Z*Phi(Z)]=E[phi(Z)], hence E[g(Z)]=a. Write A=E[phi(Z)^2]=1/(2*pi*sqrt(3)) and B=E[Z*phi(Z)*Phi(Z)]=A/2, by integrating the derivative of phi^2. Since Phi(Z) is uniform, E[Phi(Z)^2]=1/3. Applying E[Z^2*h(Z)]=E[h(Z)]+E[h''(Z)] to h=Phi^2 gives E[Z^2*Phi(Z)^2]=1/3+2A-2B=1/3+A. Therefore E[g(Z)^2]=A+2B+(1/3+A)=1/3+sqrt(3)/(2*pi). Subtracting a^2 gives v. All integrations have Gaussian tails, so the boundary terms vanish. A nondegenerate Gaussian has no finite upper endpoint; W does.

Conditional application: if the earlier packet proves (k-D)/sqrt(k) converges to g(Z) with convergence of the first two moments in a specified k,n regime, subtracting its mean and dividing by its standard deviation gives (D-E[D])/sqrt(Var(D)) converging to W. This consequence does not extend the packet to other k regimes. The saved attempt's error O(k^2/n+k^5/n^2) tends to zero, for example, when k tends to infinity and k=o(n^(2/5)); that observation alone is not a proof of the whole graph limit.

Check: deterministic quadrature of the first two moments, normalization, and inverse-transform round trips. [Proposition prop_omega_rk1 of arXiv:2609.00978, 'Towards Categorical K\"ahler Geometry'] Suppose that $E$ is a complex of ``rank 1'' representations of $Q$, i.e.\ $\dim E_i^n\leq 1$ for all $i\in Q_0,n\in\bZ$.
Then the component of $\Omega$ on $E_i^n$ (complex scalar) is given by
\begin{align*}
\Omega_i^n= \,&(-1)^n  e^{-\beta_i^n-\beta_i^{n+1}}\Bigg(z_i \\
&+\sum_{a\colon i\to j}\left(\alpha_a^n +(\alpha_a^n-\alpha_a^{n-1})(\beta_i^n-\beta_j^n)\varphi_2(\beta_i^n-\beta_j^n+\beta_i^{n+1}-\beta_j^{n-1})\right) \\
&+\sum_{a\colon k\to i}\left(-\alpha_a^n+(\alpha_a^{n+1}-\alpha_a^{n})(\beta_i^{n+1}-\beta_k^{n+1})\varphi_2(\beta_i^{n+1}-\beta_k^{n+1}+\beta_i^{n}-\beta_k^{n+2})\right)\Bigg)    
\end{align*}
where
\[
\alpha_a^n\coloneqq\rho^n(a)\rho^n(a)^\dagger,\qquad \beta_i^n\coloneqq d^n_i(d^n_i)^\dagger,\qquad \varphi_2(s)\coloneqq\frac{e^s-s-1}{s^2}.
\]
Here, $d_i^n\colon E_i^{n-1}\to E_i^n$ and $\rho^n(a)\colon E_i^n\to E_j^n$ for $a\colon i\to j$ and $\alpha_a^n$, $\beta_i^n$ are considered as non-negative real scalars.

in the category of topological groups as follows. The objects of $D$ are $\Diff^+_{\pi_0 \partial}(M_j)$ and $\Diff^+(T_i)$ for every $j$ and $i$. Let $\pi_0 D$ be the diagram in the category of groups obtained from $D$ by applying $\pi_0$ to every object and morphism.

Own-work draft; status: independently checked proof. For a fixed pair of internally compatible nearest-neighbor path halves under independent iid fair two-color scenery, let V^- and V^+ be their observed spatial sites, and K=|V^- intersect V^+|. Let A mean that the two records prescribe the same color at every shared site. The joint record likelihood equals L^- L^+ 2^K 1_A, where each half likelihood is 2^(-|V^sign|) and is zero for internal incompatibility. Because the two increment halves are independent before color conditioning, their joint two-sided posterior is the product of the separate half-posteriors reweighted by 2^K 1_A and normalized by its positive expectation. Spatial zero is included in K if both halves revisit it; the origin color is not fixed in this identity. Bounding this overlap reweighting uniformly is an unproved input for transferring one-sided escape estimates.

[Corollary 16 (Absorption of multiplicative noise) of arXiv:2609.02728, 'Momentum in large-batch training: Polyak enlarges the critical batch size, Nesterov improv'] For $\sigma > 0$, under the stability condition $\eta \lesssim \min\{1,B(1-\rho)\}$, the multiplicative gradient noise is strictly bounded by the additive label noise up to a constant factor:
\[
    \frac{\eta^2}{B}\sum_{\tau=0}^{k-1}\mathcal{K}_{\polyak}(\tau)\EE[\cE(\btheta_{k-1-\tau})] \le \frac{M}{\sigma^2} \left( \frac{\eta^2\sigma^2}{B}\sum_{\tau=0}^{k-1}\mathcal{K}_{\polyak}(\tau) \right).
\]
Consequently, the multiplicative noise can be absorbed, and the expected excess risk is asymptotically equivalent to the sum of the deterministic bias and the label noise:
\[
    \EE[\cE(\btheta_k)] \eqsim \cS_{\polyak}(k) + \frac{\eta^2\sigma^2}{B}\sum_{\tau=0}^{k-1}\mathcal{K}_{\polyak}(\tau).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Dfn 56 of arXiv:2507.08909, 'Annealed almost periodic entropy'] A completely positive map $\phi\in \B(\A,\rmM_k)_+$ is \textbf{asymptotically associated} to $(\pi_n)_{n\ge 1}$ (or to $(\t{\pi_n})_{n\ge 1}$) if, for every neighbourhood $U$ of $\phi$ in $\B(\A,\rmM_k)_+$, there are $k$-tuples $V_n$ in $H_{\pi_n}$ such that $\Phi^{\pi_n}_{V_n} \in U$ for infinitely many $n$.
title: Definition 56 of arXiv:2507.08909

[Theorem 30 (\citet{liuSimpleSharpGeneralization2025}) of arXiv:2606.22611, 'Upper and Lower Bounds on Expected Soft Maxima\\of Gaussian Processes'] Let $X = (X_t)_{t\in T}$ be a centered subgaussian process
indexed by a finite set $T$. Let $\tau$ be a random element of
 $T$ jointly distributed with $X$, such that $P_\tau=\nu$.
Then 
\begin{align*}
  \Ex X_\tau \lesssim \int_0^\Delta 
  \sqrt{R_{\nu}(\epsilon^2)\wedge I(X;\tau)} \dif \epsilon.
\end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Lemma 33 of arXiv:2609.02808, 'Minimizers of Laplace eigenvalues under a lower curvature bound'] For each fixed $\theta\in(0,\pi)$, the map
$\mu\mapsto\bar\gamma(\theta;\mu)$ is strictly increasing. Moreover, for
every $j\ge1$,
\begin{equation}
\bar\gamma(\theta;j(j+1))
+
\bar\gamma(\pi-\theta;j(j+1))
=
j\pi.
\end{equation}
In particular, if $\mu<j(j+1)$, then
\[
\bar\gamma(\theta;\mu)
+
\bar\gamma(\pi-\theta;\mu)
<j\pi.
\]

with $\binom{-m}{s}$ being a generalized binomial coefficient.

body:
Let (X, B, mu, T) be a measure-preserving system on a STANDARD Borel (Lebesgue) probability space, and let I be the sub-sigma-algebra of T-invariant sets.

ERGODIC DECOMPOSITION. There is a measurable family x -> mu_x of T-invariant Borel probability measures on X such that (i) mu_x is a version of the conditional measure of mu given I, so mu(A) = integral of mu_x(A) d mu(x) for every A in B and integral of f d mu = integral over x of (integral of f d mu_x) d mu(x) for f in L^1(mu); (ii) mu_x is ERGODIC for mu-a.e. x; (iii) the family is essentially unique. Writing P for the law of the random measure x -> mu_x, one gets mu = integral of nu dP(nu) supported on the ergodic T-invariant measures -- the Choquet representation of mu in the simplex of invariant measures.

AFFINITY OF ENTROPY. Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy is affine in the measure, with values in [0, +infinity]:
  for every finite measurable partition Q,   h_mu(T, Q) = integral of h_{mu_x}(T, Q) d mu(x);
  and                                        h_mu(T)    = integral of h_{mu_x}(T) d mu(x).
In particular, for T-invariant mu and nu and t in [0,1],  h_{t mu + (1-t) nu}(T) = t h_mu(T) + (1-t) h_nu(T).

SHARP EDGES. (1) AFFINE IS NOT CONTINUOUS: nu -> h_nu(T) is affine on the simplex of invariant measures but is in general NOT weak-* continuous; for expansive homeomorphisms it is upper semicontinuous, and in general it can fail even that. Do not use affinity to pass to weak-* limits. (2) The decomposition genuinely needs a standard/Lebesgue space; on a pathological measure space conditional measures need not exist and the statement can fail. (3) The convex combination must be of INVARIANT measures -- entropy is undefined for a non-invariant measure, so there is no affinity statement along an arbitrary path in the space of measures. (4) The identity holds in [0, +infinity]; if h_mu(T) = +infinity the integral is +infinity, and no finiteness is assumed anywhere. (5) The affinity is a property of measure-theoretic entropy, not of topological entropy: the variational principle gives h_top(T) = sup over invariant nu of h_nu(T), which is a supremum over the simplex, so it is attained (if at all) at ergodic measures precisely BECAUSE h is affine -- but h_top itself is not an average.
(X, B, mu, T) is measure-preserving on a standard Borel (Lebesgue) probability space
mu is T-invariant; entropies are Kolmogorov-Sinai entropies with values in [0, +infinity]
the ergodic decomposition is taken over the sigma-algebra of T-invariant sets
convex combinations are of T-INVARIANT measures only
no finiteness of entropy and no continuity of the entropy map is assumed or asserted

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:517281da6fc4fded44e85d52dcf610db117316849f2f169c606a5b7dd0cefac8","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/51/517281da6fc4fded44e85d52dcf610db117316849f2f169c606a5b7dd0cefac8.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:6dfc6007a8df781d09125f492dcccf14d7708dde09a4ec3265fdaa6178c78c83","bundle_entry_key":"ergodic_decomposition_entropy_affine","bundle_id":"population.pivot2-dynamics-b","claim_kind":"theorem","conditions":[],"domain":"ergodic theory, entropy","draft":"claude-pivot2-dynamics-b/bundle_pivot2-dynamics-b.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:dynamics.ergodic:ergodic-decomposition-and-affinity-of-entropy","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"Existence and uniqueness of the ergodic decomposition is the disintegration of mu over the factor map onto the invariant sigma-algebra I, available on a standard space (Rokhlin); ergodicity of almost every fibre measure follows since the conditional measures are, almost surely, invariant and their own invariant sigma-algebra is trivial -- concretely, by the Birkhoff ergodic theorem the limits of ergodic averages of a countable dense family of continuous functions are I-measurable, and they identify mu_x-a.e. with the corresponding mu_x-integrals.

Affinity, finite convex combinations first. Let phi(s) = -s log s (concave on [0,1]). For any finite partition Q and t in [0,1]:
  lower bound: H_{t mu + (1-t) nu}(Q) >= t H_mu(Q) + (1-t) H_nu(Q) by concavity of phi applied atom by atom;
  upper bound: H_{t mu + (1-t) nu}(Q) <= t H_mu(Q) + (1-t) H_nu(Q) + log 2, obtained by adjoining a Bernoulli(t) label L that records which of the two measures a point is drawn from and using H(X) <= H(X, L) = H(L) + H(X | L), with H(L) <= log 2.
Apply both bounds to Q_n = the join of T^{-i} Q for 0 <= i < n, divide by n and let n go to infinity: the additive log 2 disappears and h_{t mu + (1-t) nu}(T, Q) = t h_mu(T, Q) + (1 - t) h_nu(T, Q).

The integral version (Jacobs' theorem) is the same estimate with the two-point mixture replaced by the integral decomposition: the concavity bound integrates directly, and the label term is replaced by the entropy of a finite measurable partition of the index space, whose contribution is again O(1) and is killed after dividing by n; measurability of x -> h_{mu_x}(T, Q) holds because each H_{mu_x}(Q_n) is a measurable function of x.

From partitions to the entropy itself: on a standard space choose an increasing sequence of finite partitions Q_1 < Q_2 < ... generating B modulo mu. Since a mu-null set is mu_x-null for a.e. x and the algebra generated is countable, the same sequence generates modulo mu_x for mu-a.e. x. By the Kolmogorov-Sinai theorem h_mu(T) = lim_k h_mu(T, Q_k) and h_{mu_x}(T) = lim_k h_{mu_x}(T, Q_k) for a.e. x, both limits increasing. Apply the partition-wise identity for each k and pass to the limit by monotone convergence. (This last step is where a bare supremum over all partitions would not suffice: a supremum of affine functions is only convex, so the generating sequence is doing real work.)","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:d37b643574863d0d87862b211345cdbd8fa1472dd80b325dff599f991ba15499","revision_digest":"sha256:c423ff08a284a7ccfc7dc1d8f089019abb153806f7c00355fd50d003464125fc","source_id":"wikipedia:Measure-theoretic_entropy","source_revision":"as-read-2026-09-12","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

$$
 where ${\mathcal L}(X^{0,N},X^{1,N},\cdots,X^{k,N})$ denotes the distribution of  $(X^{0,N},X^{1,N},\cdots,X^{k,N})$ in the particle system (equation particleCN of the paper) and ${\mathcal L}(X^0,X^1,\cdots,X^k)$ the distribution of the $X^0$ component of the weak solution to (equation eq.barXsigma=0BISCN of the paper) given by Theorem (thm.existenceCN of the paper) together with $k$ conditionally independent copies $(X^1,\cdots,X^k)$ distributed according to the conditional law of the $X$ component given $X^0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2603.26217, 'On associative neural networks for sparse patterns with huge capacities'] Consider Amari's model with fixed interaction order $n$, defined by
	\eqref{multdyn} and \eqref{multhebb}, and choose
	\[
	h=\gamma \log^{n-1} N
	\]
	for some $0<\gamma<1$. Then there exists $\alpha_0=\alpha_0(n,\gamma)>0$ such that
	for every $\alpha<\alpha_0$, the choice
	\[
	M=\alpha \frac{N^n}{(\log N)^n}
	\]
	satisfies
	\[
	\mathbb P\bigl(T(\xi^\mu)=\xi^\mu\bigr)\longrightarrow1
	\qquad\text{as }N\to\infty
	\]
	for every fixed stored pattern $\xi^\mu$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 1 of arXiv:2603.26217

[Proposition 10 (Persistence through reset) of arXiv:2608.16701, 'Order-Sensitive Fast-Synapse Limits in Sparse Excitatory--Inhibitory Threshold--Reset Netw'] Fix $\rho>0$ and $T_P>\rho$.  There are uniformly bounded-degree,
Dale-compatible networks with the same initial data in both orderings such
that, for every $t_*>T_P$ and every $\varepsilon_N\downarrow0$,
\begin{equation}
 F_N^{\varepsilon_N,\E}(\rho/2)
 -F_N^{\varepsilon_N,\I}(\rho/2)\longrightarrow\frac14,
 \qquad
 F_N^{\varepsilon_N,\E}(t_*)
 -F_N^{\varepsilon_N,\I}(t_*)\longrightarrow\frac12.
 
\end{equation}
For all sufficiently large $N$ along the stated sequence, every nonisolated
target has fired twice by $t_*$ under E-first and has not fired under
I-first.

Measured 2026-09-05 on the EMIT and OCO-2 stacking pools (70 cells, the pool protocol, full calibration, paired). After the optimism reading was refuted (P20), the gain was located row by row: the per-evaluation-row relative-score gain of the long-only stack over least squares against the bootstrap variance of the least-squares stack at that row. P22 (a) REFUTED at the pre-registered 0.2: the within-cell median Spearman between a row's gain and the least-squares variance load at that row is 0.13 over the 40 EMIT cells (positive in 36 of 40; 0.37 on Y2, 0.01 on Y1); (b) HELD on Y2, REFUTED as an every-group claim: the top-decile-load rows carry 47 pct of Y2's gain (a uniform spread gives 10) but only 11 pct on Y1 (20 on Y3, 32 on Y4); (c) HELD: across the 40 EMIT cells the gain rank-correlates 0.54 with the variance-load share of least squares' error, and 0.65 with the share the constraint removes (least squares minus nn1) - the between-cell statistic that optimism (P20) failed to be; (d) REFUTED as written: the OCO-2 top-decile share reaches 0.40 on sco2, but as the share of a gain of -0.55 pct it is the ratio of two near-zero numbers and does not test the clause; falsifier (within-cell correlation at or below zero) not triggered. Reading: where the gain is large (Y2, +18) it sits where least squares is uncertain - row-level rank correlation 0.37, 47 pct of the gain on the tenth of rows with the largest variance; where it is modest (+5 to +6) it is spread over the rows; between cells the variance-load share of least squares' error predicts the gain (0.54) and the variance the constraint removes predicts it better (0.65). The calibration and evaluation rows share the same target-norm distribution, so this is not a split shift; the gain leans toward the small-norm evaluation rows the reported metric weights most. Cell level: the variance the constraint removes (least squares' bootstrap variance share minus the long-only stack's) predicts the gain within every output group (Spearman 0.79, 0.87, 0.54, 0.43 on Y1-Y4; 0.69 across 40 cells with the group effect removed), while the L1 norm of the least-squares weights does not survive the group adjustment (0.02): the constraint pays what it saves in estimation variance at the rows it is scored on. Fresh-split replication (split C, SPLIT_SEED 11): P23 (a) REFUTED at the per-group 0.5, HELD in the aggregate: on split C the within-group Spearman between the gain and the variance removed is +0.59, +0.49, +0.64, +0.22 on Y1..Y4 and +0.74 across the 40 cells with the group effect removed (split B: +0.69); (b) REFUTED: the split-B variance-removed share predicts the split-C gain only on Y1 and Y2 (+0.72, +0.47; Y3 +0.09, Y4 -0.24; demeaned +0.17), and the split-B gain itself predicts the split-C gain only weakly (Y1 +0.82, Y4 +0.47, Y2 +0.15, Y3 -0.14); (c) HELD: the long-only stack beats least squares on 35 of 40 split-C cells (mean +9.59 against +8.83 on split B); falsifier (any group at or below 0.2, or the demeaned correlation at or below 0.3) not triggered. Fresh-split check of the calibration-side correlates (P32, the P20 driver on split C): P32 (a) HELD: on split C the between-cell Spearman of the gain with the least-squares L1 is +0.55 and with n_eff -0.44; (b) REFUTED: group-demeaned, L1 +0.29 and members kept +0.21; (c) HELD: the nn0 RMSE gain with the smallest relative eigenvalue +0.29 and with the condition number -0.31; falsifier (L1 above +0.3 after the group adjustment) not triggered. The gain off the tail (P36, the top tenth of evaluation rows by |gain| removed): P36 (a) HELD for the sign, REFUTED for the size: the trimmed gain is positive on 36 and 36 of 40 EMIT cells (splits B, C) but reads +7.67 and +8.30 against untrimmed +8.83 and +9.59 - the body keeps 87 pct of the gain, not less than half; (b) HELD: on OCO-2 the trimmed gain is +0.25 against -0.18 untrimmed; (c) REFUTED: the smallest trimmed gain is on Y4, not Y1; falsifier (negative trimmed gain on EMIT) not triggered. Removing the two-sided tail leaves 87 pct of the EMIT gain: the constraint pays broadly across the rows, and the non-transfer between splits comes from the tails' noise, not from where the gain sits. P46: the mechanism on the third family (P46): P46 (a) REFUTED: within-family Spearman(gain, variance removed) = burgers +0.55, darcy +0.80, pkanrtm -0.12 (families with at least ten cells; threshold 0.3); (b) HELD: family-demeaned across 55 cells +0.65 (threshold 0.4); (c) HELD: the family with the most negative gain is pkanrtm, the family with the smallest variance removed is pkanrtm; falsifier (demeaned correlation at or below 0.1) not triggered.

[Definition of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] The orthogonal polynomials with respect to $d\mu(x)=f(x)dx$ are polynomials $P_k\in\mathbb R[x]$ of degree $k\in\mathbb N$, which are orthogonal inside $H=L^2(\mathbb R,\mu)$:
$$\int_\mathbb RP_k(x)P_l(x)f(x)dx=0\quad,\quad\forall k\neq l$$
Equivalently, these orthogonal polynomials $\{P_k\}_{k\in\mathbb N}$, which are each unique modulo scalars, appear from the Weierstrass basis $\{x^k\}_{k\in\mathbb N}$, by doing Gram-Schmidt.

body: Let f : M -> N be a C^k map between smooth manifolds of dimensions m and n respectively, with k >= max(1, m - n + 1). Call x in M a critical point if the differential df_x : T_xM -> T_(f(x))N fails to be surjective, and call f(x) a critical value for such x. Then the set of critical values of f has Lebesgue measure zero in N, measured in any smooth chart, so almost every point of N is a regular value, even though the critical set in M can itself be large, even all of M in degenerate examples.
title: Sard's theorem

body:
[Theorem 39 of arXiv:2608.17374, '\textbf{On the Pseudo-Mixing of Kac's Walk}'] There is a universal constant $C<\infty$ with the following property. Let $Q$ be an $\So{n}$-valued random matrix whose law is $(d_{\mathrm{ph}},L)$-pseudo-Haar in the sense of \eqref{EqJLPseudoHaarDef}. Let $\mathcal X\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ have $N\geq2$ points, and let $0<\varepsilon,\delta<1$. Set
\be 
r=\left\lceil C\log\frac{N}{\delta}\right\rceil.
\ee
Assume
\be 
4r\leq d_{\mathrm{ph}},\qquad
\ell\geq C\varepsilon^{-2}r,
\qquad
L\log n\geq \log\frac{2\binom{N}{2}}{\delta}+2r\log\frac{n}{\varepsilon\ell}.
\ee
Then, with probability at least $1-\delta$ over $Q$,
\be 
(1-\varepsilon)\|x_i-x_j\|_2^2
\leq
\|A_Q(x_i-x_j)\|_2^2
\leq
(1+\varepsilon)\|x_i-x_j\|_2^2
\ee
for every pair $1\leq i<j\leq N$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 39 of arXiv:2608.17374

body:
[Theorem 1 (\cite{efron1981jackknife}, \cite{steele1986efron}) of arXiv:2605.05388, 'The Efron-Stein inequality for identically distributed pairs'] Let \(X_1,\ldots, X_n,Y_1,\ldots,Y_n\) be \(2n\) independent random variables with \(X_i\stackrel{d}{=} Y_i\) for all \(i\). Let \(f\) be a measurable function, and let \(Z_i=f(X_1\ldots X_{i},Y_{i+1},\ldots Y_n)\) for \(i=0,\dots,n\). Then
$$
E(Z_n-Z_0)^2\le \sum_{i=1}^n E(Z_i-Z_{i-1})^2.
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
Let H be a complex Hilbert space and T a compact operator on H. List its nonzero eigenvalues lambda_1, lambda_2, ... with |lambda_1| >= |lambda_2| >= ... , repeated according to algebraic multiplicity and padded with zeros if there are finitely many, and let s_1(T) >= s_2(T) >= ... be the singular values. Then for every n, the product of |lambda_1| ... |lambda_n| is at most the product of s_1(T) ... s_n(T). Consequently, for every p > 0 and every n, sum_{k <= n} |lambda_k|^p <= sum_{k <= n} s_k(T)^p; in particular, if T is Hilbert-Schmidt then sum_k |lambda_k|^2 <= ||T||_2^2 (Schur's inequality), and if T is trace class then sum_k |lambda_k| <= ||T||_1. The inequalities are equalities for normal T.
H is a complex Hilbert space
T is a compact operator on H
eigenvalues are listed with algebraic multiplicity in nonincreasing order of modulus
p > 0

Using the Riesz-Schauder theory, the generalized eigenspaces for lambda_1, ..., lambda_n span a T-invariant subspace, and inside the last generalized eigenspace one can choose a T-invariant subspace of the right dimension (a Jordan flag), so there is an n-dimensional T-invariant subspace M with the eigenvalues of the matrix T|_M equal to lambda_1, ..., lambda_n. Then the absolute value of det(T|_M) is the product of |lambda_1| ... |lambda_n|. On the other hand, for an n-dimensional subspace the absolute value of the determinant of the compression P_M T|_M equals the product of the n singular values of that compression, and the singular values of a compression are dominated by those of T (s_k(P_M T|_M) <= s_k(T) by the min-max / approximation-number characterisation). Since M is T-invariant, P_M T|_M = T|_M, giving the multiplicative inequality. The additive form follows from multiplicative majorization: if a nonincreasing nonnegative sequence (a_k) satisfies the partial-product inequalities against (b_k), then sum f(a_k) <= sum f(b_k) for every function f with f(e^t) convex and nondecreasing in t, and f(t) = t^p is such a function for p > 0 (Weyl's lemma).","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:2225456d23e042d16fa41a4883a1acf0ad8f28160beb6e99ce53d176a31bf47b","revision_digest":"sha256:c446db4b2e55b169d304622d0d2097308ab3105e60f4e040b228bd1ee13f692e","source_id":"wikipedia:Singular value","source_revision":"as-known-2026-09-12","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Prop 11 of arXiv:2608.05185, '\large\bf ON THE HEAT FLOW CONJECTURE FOR RANDOM MATRICES'] Let \(N\geq1\), let \(c_0,c_1\in\C\), let
\(v>\max(\left|c_0\right|,\left|c_1\right|)\), and let \(a\in\C\).
For every polynomial \(p\in \mathbb{C}[z]\), put
\[
 q=\exp\!\left(-\frac{c_1-c_0}{2N}\partial_z^2\right)p.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
 \int_{\C}\left|q(z)\right|^2\dd\gamma_{N;v,c_1,a}(z)
 =
 \int_{\C}\left|p(z)\right|^2\dd\gamma_{N;v,c_0,a}(z).
\end{equation}
title: Prop 11 of arXiv:2608.05185

[Theo thm:frostman-intro of arXiv:2512.06984, 'Infinite Dimensional Multifractal Analysis of the Wiener measure'] Let $ (X,d) $ be a $\sigma$-compact metric space and $ A \subset X$ a Borel subset. Then for every Hausdorff function $h$  such that $\mathcal{H}^h(A) > 0 $, there exist a compact set $K\subset A$,
a  probability Borel measure $\mu$ supported by $K$, and a constant $C\in(0,\infty)$
such that 
\begin{equation*} 
\mu\bigl(B(x,r)\bigr)\ \le\ C\,h( 6 r) , \qquad\forall\,x\in X,\ \forall\,r>0.
\end{equation*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

SOURCE-SCOPE GUARD for P0003. Grimmett Question 2.2 samples a uniform n-step walk from one fixed origin with a free endpoint. The critical chordal conjecture samples walks of variable length between two boundary points with fugacity x_c per visited vertex. The two statements have different length and endpoint conditions. The finite path-deletion, martingale and local-observable identities in this packet do not transfer convergence between them; such a transfer requires an additional theorem.
Compare Grimmett Question 2.2 with arXiv:1206.2092 Conjecture 1.5 and Section 3.3
title: Fixed-length and critical chordal SAW are different ensembles

[Lemma lem:janson-geo of arXiv:2602.21315, 'The Instability of all Backoff Protocols\thanks{For the purpose of Open Access, the author'] [Janson]
Let $X_1,\dots,X_z$ be independent geometric variables where $X_i$ has parameter $p_i$, and let $X = X_1 + \dots + X_z$. Let $\mu = \sum_{i=1}^z 1/p_i$ and let $p_* = \min_i p_i$. Then for all $C \ge 1$,
\[
\mathbb{P}(X \ge C\mu) \le e^{-p_*\mu(C-1-\log C)}.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Proposition prop:generatorXt of arXiv:2411.14876, 'Limit theorems for stochastic exponentials of matrix-valued L\'evy processes \\'] Let $L=(L_t)_{t\geq 0}$ be a Lévy process in $\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ with characteristics $(\Sigma_L,\gamma_L,  \nu_L)$ fulfilling (equation eq-nonsingular of the paper), and let $X=(X_t)_{t\geq 0}$ be its stochastic exponential. Then $X$ is a rich Feller process in $\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ and  its extended generator is given by
		\begin{align*}\mathcal{A}_{X} f(x) &= \sum_{i,j=1}^d \ell(x)^{(i,j)} \frac{\partial}{\partial x^{(i,j)}} f(x) + \frac12 \sum_{i,j, k,l=1}^{d} Q(x)^{(i,j,k,l)} \frac{\partial}{\partial x^{(i,j)}}\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{(k,l)}} f(x) \\
			&\quad  + \int_{y\in \mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\setminus \{0\}} \Big( f(x+y) - f(x) -  \sum_{i,j=1}^d y^{(i,j)} \frac{\partial}{\partial x^{(i,j)}} f(x)\mathds{1}_{\{\|y \|\leq 1\}}  \Big) N(x, dy), \end{align*}
		for all $f\in C_c^2(\mathbb{R}^{d\times d})\subseteq D(\mathcal{A}_{X})$, the latter denoting the domain of $\mathcal{A}_X$. For any $x\in \mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$, the triplet $(\ell(x), Q(x), N(x,dy))$ is given by
		\begin{align*}
			\ell(x)&=  x \gamma_L +  \int_{y\in \mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\setminus\{0\}}  x y  \left(  \mathds{1}_{\{ \| x y  \| \leq 1\}}- \mathds{1}_{\{ \|y \| \leq 1\}} \right) \nu_L(dy),  \\
			Q(x)^{(i,j,k,l)} &= \sum_{n,m=1}^{d} 	x^{(i,m)} \sigma_{(m,j),(n,l)} x^{(k,n)} , \, i,j,k,l=1,\ldots, d,\quad \text{and} \\
			N(x,dy)&= \nu_L(T_x^{-1}(dy)),
		\end{align*}
		being the image measure of $\nu_L$ under the transform $T_x$ defined by
		$$T_x(y): \mathbb{R}^{d\times d} \to \mathbb{R}^{d\times d} , y\mapsto x y, \quad x\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}.$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition prop:generatorXt of arXiv:2411.14876

[Theorem homo multilinear recursion of arXiv:2412.07936, 'Simple Norm Bounds for Polynomial Random Matrices via Decoupling'] [Homogeneous Multilinear Recursion]

Let ${\bf x} = \{x_i\}_{i = 1}^n$ be a sequences of i.i.d random variables with ${\mathbb E} x_i= 0$,  ${\mathbb E} x_i^2= 1$ and $|x_i| \leq L$ for all $1\leq i \leq n$. Let $\{{\bf A}_{{\bf i}}\}_{{\bf i} \in {\mathcal T}^d_n}$ be a multi-indexed sequence of deterministic matrices of the same dimension. Define a permutation symmetric, homogeneous multilinear polynomial random matrix of degree $d$ as
$$
{\bf F}({\bf x}) =  \sum_{{\bf i} \in {\mathcal T}^d_n} \left( {\bf A}_{{\bf i}} \cdot \prod_{j \in \{i_1,\dots, i_d \}} x_j\right).
$$
Let $a,b,c\in {\mathbb Z}_{\geq 0}$ and $d = a+b+c$. Then for $2 \leq t \leq \infty,$
$$
{\mathbb E} \norm{{\bf F}({\bf x}) - {\mathbb E} {\bf F}({\bf x})}_{4t}^{4t} ~\leq~ \sum_{\substack{a,b,c: \\ a+b+c=d}} (48dt)^{4dt} \cdot L^{4ct} \norm{{\bf F}_{a,b,c}}_{4t}^{4t}.
$$

body: In mathematics, the connective constant is a numerical quantity associated with self-avoiding walks on a lattice. It is studied in connection with the notion of universality in two-dimensional statistical physics models. While the connective constant depends on the choice of lattice so itself is not universal, it is nonetheless an important quantity that appears in conjectures for universal laws. Furthermore, the mathematical techniques used to understand the connective constant, for example in the recent rigorous proof by Duminil-Copin and Smirnov that the connective constant of the hexagonal lattice has the precise value , may provide clues to a possible approach for attacking other important open problems in the study of self-avoiding walks, notably the conjecture that self-avoiding walks converge in the scaling limit to the Schramm–Loewner evolution.
title: Connective constant

## C037: inverse occupation is a positive angle-moment problem

For every finite T, there are epsilon>0 and constants C_T,n0 such that the
following holds. Start the Gaussian/ReLU angle chain at any deterministic
theta0 in (0,epsilon], with width n>=n0. Kill it when it leaves that angle
interval or becomes degenerate, and set its killed angle to zero. One may
also kill it when u=1/(n theta) exceeds any fixed K. For p=1,2 and 0<=k<=Tn,

    E[theta_k^p; alive at k] <= C_T/(k+1)^p.                 (1)

This holds both for the normalized-Gram self-loop regularization and for
the exact chain. In particular, with U_k=1/(n theta_k) only on alive states,

    E[U_k^(-p); alive at k] <= C_T n^p/(k+1)^p.             (2)

Here inverse powers at the cemetery are excluded by the alive indicator.
The statement is a small-angle stopped-chain estimate; it does not assign
the initial time of entrance from an arbitrary fixed theta0.

Proof. Write the normalized output multiplier as theta'/theta=1/T_theta
on the C032 good box. For p=1,2 the coordinate test Phi_p=T_theta^(-p)
has uniformly bounded first and second derivatives on that box for all
small theta. Its deterministic value is (F(theta)/theta)^p, where F is
the deterministic ReLU angle map. A second-order sample-average Taylor
bound, uniform normalized row second moments, and exponential deletion
outside the box imply

    E[(theta'/theta)^p]
       <= (F(theta)/theta)^p+C_p/n
       =1-p a theta+O_p(theta^2)+C_p/n,  a=1/(3pi).

To justify the first inequality explicitly, the linear centered-average
term has mean zero before good-box truncation and an exponentially small
deleted mean; the quadratic Taylor remainder is bounded by the coordinate
Hessian bound times E|Zbar-mu_theta|^2=O(1/n). Off the good box the
regularized multiplier is one. No reciprocal-angle moment is used.

Choose epsilon small so the O(theta^2) term is at most p a theta/2. Killing
only decreases positive angle moments. Thus, for p=1,2 and constants c_p>0,

    E[theta_(k+1)^p | theta_k=theta]
       <= theta^p(1+C_p/n)-c_p theta^(p+1).

Let m_k=E theta_k^p, with theta_k=0 after killing. Jensen gives

    m_(k+1) <= rho m_k-c_p m_k^(1+1/p), rho=1+C_p/n.

Put v_k=rho^(-k)m_k. Since rho>=1,

    v_(k+1) <= v_k-(c_p/rho)v_k^(1+1/p).

Decrease the constant if necessary so z=(c_p/rho)v_k^(1/p)<=1/2; this is
possible because v_k<=m_k<=epsilon^p. If v_(k+1)>0, the elementary inequality
(1-z)^(-1/p)>=1+z/p implies

    v_(k+1)^(-1/p) >= v_k^(-1/p)+c_p/(p rho).

If a term becomes zero, the killed nonnegative chain has zero subsequent
moments and the desired bound is immediate. Otherwise summing yields
v_k<=C/(k+1)^p. As rho^k<=exp(C_p T), (1) follows for the regularized chain.

For the exact chain, use the same independent Gaussian rows until a
good-box failure. Its conditional probability is at most C exp(-cn),
uniformly in every alive small angle. A union bound through k<=Tn gives
disagreement probability at most C k exp(-cn). Both killed angles lie in
[0,epsilon], so their pth moments differ by at most
C epsilon^p k exp(-cn). For k<=Tn this is bounded by C_T/(k+1)^p,
uniformly in n>=n0. This proves (1) for the exact chain, and (2) is the
identity U_k^(-p)=n^p theta_k^p on alive states.

## C038: summing the C036 local remainder after a layer cutoff

Use the regularized stopped chain of C037, with the additional upper
cutoff U<=K. Let N<=Tn, 0<=m<N, and let f_(n,k) be deterministic bounded
C^5 tests whose supremum and derivative bounds through order five are
uniform in n,k. Define the *unstopped-kernel* local remainder, evaluated
only at alive prestop states, by

    R_(n,k)(u)=n(P_n f_(n,k)-f_(n,k))(u)
                               -A f_(n,k)(u)-B f_(n,k)(u)/n.

Choose the angle cutoff epsilon at most C036's theta_star. Then

    (1/n) sum_(k=m)^(N-1) E[|R_(n,k)(U_k)|; alive at k]
      <= C_(K,T)[n^(-3/2)+log(n+1)/n^2
                             +1/(n(m+1))+n exp(-cn)].         (3)

The same estimate holds using the exact kernel and its stopped chain.
This is an accumulated estimate for the indicated local remainders. It
does not discard boundary terms or prove a stopped-semigroup comparison.

Proof. C036 applies to every alive state, since 0<U_k<=K and
theta_k=1/(nU_k)<=epsilon. Its (u+sqrt(u))/n^(3/2) term sums after the
outer factor1/n to at most C_(K,T)n^(-3/2). The constant/n^2 term sums to
C_T/n^2. By (2), the other two algebraic terms contribute at most

    C/n^3 sum_(k=m)^(N-1) n/(k+1) <= C_T log(n+1)/n^2,
    C/n^3 sum_(k=m)^(N-1) n^2/(k+1)^2 <= C_T/[n(m+1)].

The exponential term sums to C_T n exp(-cn). This proves (3), separately
for each chain using the C037 moment bounds and C036's exact-kernel bound.

For any m=m_n tending to infinity, the right side is o(1/n). This pays
for the pointwise Taylor-remainder accumulation after a growing cutoff.
The main singular correction B-A^2/2 still needs an asymptotic occupation
calculation matched to the early network chain. An upper bound for its
occupation is not that asymptotic calculation. Neither (1) nor (3) proves
that the network coefficient is D_t/(2pi).","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:ef5cf8d24593c8c15d39382f642a60f6bd9f0b66fde78d07f243e32a0c98ecb5","revision_digest":"sha256:c494d6599867161f2613d0eaecee62ddab723d99f1a52cc291e65c8a01331fdf","source_id":"own-work:T244-w691-C038:v1","source_revision":"2026-10-20-v1","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Lem 15 of arXiv:2605.07050, 'Universality of the fluctuations of the free energy in generalized Sherrington--Kirkpatric'] Suppose that Assumption \ref{assump:second_moment} holds with a constant $\SNR_c$. Then, there exists a sequence of events $\Omega_N'$ in $\caX$ with $\p(\Omega_N'^c) = o(1)$ such that for any $\SNR < \SNR_c$,
\beq 
	\E_{\bsx, \bsx' \sim \caX} \left[ \indi(\Omega_N' (\bsx)) \indi(\Omega_N' (\bsx')) \exp \left( \frac{N \SNR \langle \bsx, \bsx' \rangle^2}{2} \right) \right] = (1-\SNR)^{-1/2} + o(1)
\eeq
and
\beq 
	\E_{\bsx, \bsx' \sim \caX} \left[ \indi(\Omega_N' (\bsx)) \indi(\Omega_N' (\bsx')) \exp \left( \frac{N \SNR \langle \bsx, \bsx' \rangle^2}{2 \| \bsx \|^2 \| \bsx' \|^2} \right) \right] = (1-\SNR)^{-1/2} + o(1).
\eeq (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Lem 179 (annealed second moment bounds for 
$\bar{D}^{\RomII}$ and 
$\bar{D}^{\frozen,\RomII}$) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $\bar{D}^{\RomII}$ and $\bar{D}^{\frozen,\RomII}$ 
be defined by \eqref{e:barD} and \eqref{e:barD.plus} (see also \eqref{e:drift.error.II}). We have 
the second moment bound 
	\[\frac{\E[\Delta\bar{D}^{\RomII}(q_d)^2]}
		{p(q_d)}
	\le \frac{L^{O(1)}\BUCKETS \delta}{N}\,,
	\]
for all $0\le d\le \dmax-1$. The same bound holds with $\bar{D}^{\frozen,\RomII}$ in place of $\bar{D}^{\RomII}$.
\begin{proof}
Recalling the notation from
\eqref{e:normalized.vectors.g} and \eqref{e:normalized.vectors.y},
we can rewrite \eqref{e:drift.error.II} as
	\[
	\frac{\Delta\bar{D}^{\RomII}(q_d)}
		{[\delta_d p(q_d)]^{1/2}}
	= 
	\frac1{|B|^{1/2}}
	\bigg(\frac{1}{N^{1/2}}\sum_{a\in B}
	\frac{\bar{\bg}^a(q_d)}{|B|^{1/2}},\by(q_{d+1})\bigg)
	\equiv
	\frac1{|B|^{1/2}}
	\bigg( \frac{\bar{\bg}^B(q_d)}{N^{1/2}},\by(q_{d+1}) \bigg)\,.
	\]
Note that $\bar{\bg}^B(q_d)$ is measurable with respect to $\cG(q_d)$. 
It follows by applying Lemma~\ref{l:y.subgaus} that 
	\[
	\frac{\E[\Delta\bar{D}^{\RomII}(q_d)^2]}{\delta_d p(q_d)}
	=\frac{1}{M}\E\bigg[\sum_{B\in\mathcal{B}(q_d)} 
	\bigg( \frac{\bar{\bg}^B(q_d)}{N^{1/2}},\by(q_{d+1}) \bigg)^2
		\bigg]
	\le \frac{L^{O(1)}}{M}
	\E\sum_{B\in\mathcal{B}(q_d)} 
	\frac{\|\bar{\bg}^B(q_d)\|^2}{N}\,.
	\]
We then note that if $\ind_B\in\R^M$ is the indicator of the coordinates in $B$, then
	\[
	\|\bar{\bg}^B(q_d)\|
	=\bigg\| \bar{\bG}(q_d) \frac{\ind_B}{|B|^{1/2}}\bigg\|
	\le \|\bar{\bG}(q_d)\|\,,
	\]
from which it follows that
	\[\frac{\E[\Delta\bar{D}^{\RomII}(q_d)^2]}{\delta_d p(q_d)}
	\le
	\frac{L^{O(1)}\BUCKETS 
		\E[\|\bar{\bG}(q_d)\|^2]}{MN}
	\le \frac{L^{O(1)}\BUCKETS}{N}\,,
	\]
where the last bound follows from Lemma~\ref{l:wishart}.
This proves the claim for $\bar{D}^{\RomII}$, and the claim for
$\bar{D}^{\frozen,\RomII}$ follows by using \eqref{e:barD.vs.plus}.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Theorem 16 (From scalar wavelets to vector-valued wavelets) of arXiv:2608.30589, 'Vector-Valued Wavelet Bases as Hilbert $\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})$-Module Bases: A Construc'] Let $(\phi,\psi)$ be an orthonormal wavelet basis of $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ associated with an MRA.
Fix $m\ge 2$ and set $D=2^m$. Define $\Phi,\Psi$ by \eqref{eq:Phi-def}--\eqref{eq:Psi-def}.
For $k\in\mathbb Z$ and $j\ge 0$ set
\[
\widetilde\Phi_k=\Phi(\cdot-k),
\qquad
\widetilde\Psi_{j,k}=D^{j/2}\Psi(D^j\cdot-k).
\]

Then the family
\[
\{\widetilde\Phi_k\}_{k\in\mathbb Z}\ \cup\ \{\widetilde\Psi_{j,k}\}_{j\ge 0,\ k\in\mathbb Z}
\]

\begin{itemize}
\item[(a)] is an orthogonal wavelet basis of the Hilbert space $L^2(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R}^m)$ (for the usual scalar $L^2$ inner product); moreover $\|\widetilde\Phi_k\|_{L^2}^2=\|\widetilde\Psi_{j,k}\|_{L^2}^2=m$,
\item[(b)] is an $\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})$--orthonormal system in the Hilbert $\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})$--module
$\big(L^2(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R}^m),\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})}\big)$, i.e.
\[
\big\langle \widetilde U_\alpha,\widetilde U_\beta\big\rangle_{\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})}
=\delta_{\alpha,\beta}\,I_m
\quad(\alpha,\beta\in\{(0,k)\}\cup\{(j,k):j\ge 0\}),
\]
and it is a Parseval $\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})$--module frame with the canonical reconstruction
\[
f=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\big\langle f,\widetilde\Phi_k\big\rangle_{\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})}\,\widetilde\Phi_k
+\sum_{j\ge 0}\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\big\langle f,\widetilde\Psi_{j,k}\big\rangle_{\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})}\,\widetilde\Psi_{j,k},
\qquad f\in L^2(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R}^m),
\]
with convergence in the module norm.
Moreover, each component inherits compact support, regularity and vanishing moments from $\phi$ and $\psi$.
\end{itemize}

[Proposition 6 of arXiv:2604.07207, 'Mixing times of step-reinforced random walks'] (i). Under Assumption \ref{mainassum}, if $\mu$ is a class function, then for any $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$ and $n\geq 1$,
       \begin{equation}
      
 t^{(\alpha)}_{\mathrm{mix}}(\varepsilon) \leq  \frac{8}{1-\alpha} \max\left\{t^{(0)}_{\mathrm{mix}}\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\right),\ 12\log \left(\frac{10}{\varepsilon}\right)  \right\}+1.
    \end{equation}
 (ii). Assume that for each $n\geq 1$, $\mu_n$ is a probability measure on a finite group $G_n$ such that $P_{\mu_n}$ is irreducible and aperiodic and $\mu_n$ is a class function. If for any $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$, we have $t^{(0, G_n,\mu_n)}_{\mathrm{mix}}\left(\varepsilon/2\right) \to \infty$ as $n\to \infty$, then for any $\alpha \in [0,1)$,
 $$
\limsup_{n\to \infty}\frac{t^{(\alpha,G_n,\mu_n)}_{\mathrm{mix}}(\varepsilon)}{t^{(0, G_n,\mu_n)}_{\mathrm{mix}}(\varepsilon/2)} \leq\frac{1+\alpha}{1-\alpha}.
 $$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Definition of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] We call a map in ${\mathfrak d\kern-.25pt}{\mathfrak S\kern-.5pt\mathfrak p}_\text{$G$-lvl}$ a \emph{$G$-global weak equivalence} if it is sent to an equivalence under the Bousfield localization $L$. A map in $\cat{$\bm G$-$\textbf{\textup{L}}$-Sp}$ will be called a $G$-global weak equivalence if and only if its image in ${\mathfrak d\kern-.25pt}{\mathfrak S\kern-.5pt\mathfrak p}_\textup{$G$-lvl}$ is so.\footnote{A concrete description of the $G$-global weak equivalences will be given in Proposition~(prop:he-preserve-but-he-also-reflec of the paper).} We denote the localization of $\cat{$\bm G$-$\textbf{\textup{L}}$-Sp}$ at the $G$-global weak equivalences (which is equivalent to ${\mathfrak d\kern-.25pt}{\mathfrak S\kern-.5pt\mathfrak p}_G^\Omega$ in a preferred way) by ${\mathfrak d\kern-.25pt}{\mathfrak S\kern-.5pt\mathfrak p}_\text{$G$-gl}$.

[Definition 13 of arXiv:2605.30560, 'Projected McKean--Vlasov Dynamics for Entropic Weak Optimal Transport'] A weak solution of \eqreftag{eq:cond-Fokker-planck-a} is a measurable map
\[
    \tilde \P:\R_+\times\Xc\longrightarrow \Pc(\R^d),
    \qquad
    (t,x)\longmapsto \tilde\P_{t,x},
\]
together with a Borel vector field
$
    \hat A:\R_+\times\R^d\longrightarrow\R^d,
$
such that the following conditions hold.

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), ref=(\roman*)]
    \item 
    For \(\mu\)-a.e. \(x\in\Xc\), the map
    \(t\mapsto \tilde \P_{t,x}\) is weak continuous.

    \item 
    There exists \(p>1\) such that, for every \(T>0\),
    \[
    \int_0^T
    \int_\Xc
    \int_{\R^d}
    \left|
    \hat A(t,y)
    -
    a\bigl(t,x,y,\tilde\P_{t,x}\bigr)
    -
    \nabla_y V(y)
    \right|^p
    \tilde\P_{t,x}(dy)\,\mu(dx)\,dt
    <\infty.
    \]

    \item 
    For every \(h\in C_c^\infty(\R^d; \R)\) and every \(t\ge0\), one has,
    for \(\mu\)-a.e. \(x\in\Xc\),
    \[
    \E^{\tilde\P_{t,x}}[h]
    =
    \E^{\tilde\P_{0,x}}[h]
    +
    \int_0^t
    \E^{\tilde\P_{s,x}}\!\left[
    \nabla h(Y)\cdot
    \left(
    \hat A(s,Y)
    -
    a\bigl(s,x,Y,\tilde\P_{s,x}\bigr)
    -
    \nabla_y V(Y)
    \right)
    +
    \Delta h(Y)
    \right]ds .
    \]

    \item 
    If
    $
    \P_t(dx,dy)
    :=
    \mu(dx)\,\tilde\P_{t,x}(dy),
$
    then, for a.e. \(t\ge0\),
    \[
    \hat A(t,y)
    =
    \E^{\P_t}\!\left[
        a\bigl(t,X,y,(\P_t)_X\bigr)
        \mid Y=y
    \right],
    \qquad
    \P_t\text{-a.s.}
    \]
\end{enumerate}

body:
[Proposition 26 of arXiv:2609.02416, '2609.02416'] We collect the adjoint and interval-size differentiability statements in one proposition.

\textup{(i)} The formal adjoint is
\[
\cA_L^*v=d\int_{-L}^{L}J(x-y)v(y)\,dy-(qv)'(x)+b(x)v(x).
\]
It possesses a positive principal eigenfunction $\phi_L^*$ satisfying
\[
\cA_L^*\phi_L^*+\lambda_p(L)\phi_L^*=0\ \hbox{in }(-L,L),\quad \phi_L^*(-L)=0,
\]
and this eigenfunction is unique up to multiplication. For all $u,v\in C^1([-L,L])$ satisfying $u(L)=0$ and $v(-L)=0$,
\[
\int_{-L}^{L}v\cA_Lu\,dx=\int_{-L}^{L}u\cA_L^*v\,dx.
\]
Moreover,
\[
\phi_L'(L)<0,\quad \phi_L^*(L)>0,\quad \phi_L(-L)>0.
\]

\textup{(ii)} Let $\Omega_{\alpha,\beta}=(\alpha,\beta)$ and let $\lambda(\alpha,\beta)=\Lp(\cA_{\Omega_{\alpha,\beta}})$. Assume the coefficients are $C^2$ and normalize the direct and adjoint eigenfunctions by
\[
\int_\alpha^\beta\phi_{\alpha,\beta}(x)\phi_{\alpha,\beta}^*(x)\,dx=1.
\]
Then $\lambda$ is $C^1$ in $(\alpha,\beta)$ and
\[
\partial_\beta\lambda(\alpha,\beta)=q(\beta)\phi_{\alpha,\beta}'(\beta)\phi_{\alpha,\beta}^*(\beta)<0,
\]
while
\[
\partial_\alpha\lambda(\alpha,\beta)=d\phi_{\alpha,\beta}(\alpha)\int_\alpha^\beta J(x-\alpha)\phi_{\alpha,\beta}^*(x)\,dx>0.
\]
Thus moving the outflow endpoint to the right and moving the inflow endpoint to the left both strictly decrease the principal eigenvalue, but the two shape derivatives have different structures.

\textup{(iii)} The maps $L\mapsto\lambda_p(L)$ and, after pull-back to $(-1,1)$ and the above normalization, $L\mapsto\phi_L$, $L\mapsto\phi_L^*$ are continuous. On every compact interval $[L_0,L_1]\Subset(0,\infty)$ the convergence is uniform in $C^1$ for the eigenfunctions.

\textup{(iv)} The map $L\mapsto\lambda_p(L)$ is of class $C^1$ on $(0,\infty)$. With the normalization above,
\[
\partial_L\lambda_p(L)=q(L)\phi_L'(L)\phi_L^*(L)-d\phi_L(-L)\int_{-L}^{L}J(x+L)\phi_L^*(x)\,dx.
\]
In particular, $\partial_L\lambda_p(L)<0\quad L>0$.
Thus $L\mapsto\lambda_p(L)$ is strictly decreasing.

body: Let V and W be vector spaces over a field F with V finite-dimensional, and let T : V -> W be a linear map. Then dim(V) = dim(ker T) + dim(im T), i.e. dim(V) = nullity(T) + rank(T), where the kernel ker T = {v in V : T(v) = 0} is a subspace of V and the image im T = T(V) is a subspace of W. Equivalently, for any m by n matrix A over F regarded as a linear map F^n -> F^m, rank(A) + nullity(A) = n, the number of columns of A.
title: Rank-nullity theorem

[Proposition prop:variance-monotone of arXiv:2605.17082, 'Spectral Purification in Reversible Markov Chains: Hidden Parameters, Observable Equivalen'] Fix $\lambda_2$, $c_2$, $c_3$, and the contribution $\mathcal{A}_{\ge4} := \sum_{i\ge4}c_i^2(1+\lambda_i)/(1-\lambda_i)$ of the remaining modes, and write $\lambda_3=\rho_\star\lambda_2$ for $\rho_\star\in(0,1]$. Then
\[
\mathcal{A}(\rho_\star) = c_2^2\,\frac{1+\lambda_2}{1-\lambda_2} + c_3^2\,\frac{1+\rho_\star\lambda_2}{1-\rho_\star\lambda_2} + \mathcal{A}_{\ge4}
\]
is strictly increasing in $\rho_\star$ on $(0,1]$, with
\[
\frac{\partial\mathcal{A}}{\partial\rho_\star} = c_3^2\,\frac{2\lambda_2}{(1-\rho_\star\lambda_2)^2} > 0.
\]

Own-work draft; independently checked proof; D0007-C003 v1; audits w667:PASS, w668:PASS. In Yin-Zhu arXiv:1706.05499v4 Example 2.4 (p.7), let f=sum_{j>=1}alpha_j*C_j*x^(2j)/sqrt(1-x^2) on (-1,1), alpha_j>0 and sum alpha_j=1. This law is n-CM for every even n>=2 and every odd n>=96*pi/alpha_1. A symmetric 3-CM reserve generated by a random sign and permutation of (A,A,-2A), A uniform on [1/4,1/3], has density 4 on the two small bands and 1 on the two doubled bands. It is dominated with weight p=alpha_1/(32*pi), since C_1=2/pi. The source assertion that this mixture fails every odd order is therefore false. This does not settle general D0007.

Status: proof (unaudited). Refutes a specific published-preprint counterexample claim, not D0007 itself.

Primary source: Chuancun Yin and Dan Zhu, Joint mixability of elliptical distributions and related families, arXiv:1706.05499v4, Example 2.4, PDF p.7. Its proposed law on (-1,1) is

    f(x)=sum_{j>=1} alpha_j f_j(x),
    f_j(x)=C_j x^(2j)/sqrt(1-x^2),
    alpha_j>0, sum_j alpha_j=1.

It asserts: "This distribution is not (2n + 1)-completely mixable for any n >= 1."

We show instead that f is N-CM for every even N>=2 and every odd N>=96*pi/alpha_1.

1. The j=1 normalization is C_1=2/pi, since x=sin(theta) gives integral_{-1}^1 x^2/sqrt(1-x^2) dx=integral_{-pi/2}^{pi/2} sin^2(theta) dtheta=pi/2. Therefore f(x)>=alpha_1*(2/pi)*x^2/sqrt(1-x^2) almost everywhere.

2. Let A be uniform on [1/4,1/3], let S be an independent equiprobable sign, and uniformly permute the three coordinates of (SA,SA,-2SA). Each coordinate has the same symmetric law H, and the sum is zero. Thus H is symmetric and 3-CM. Its density h is 4 on each of [1/4,1/3] and [-1/3,-1/4], 1 on each of [1/2,2/3] and [-2/3,-1/2], and zero elsewhere. Indeed each small band receives weight 1/3 and length 1/12; each large band receives weight 1/6 and length 1/6. Its total mass is 2*4*(1/12)+2*1*(1/6)=1.

3. Everywhere on these four bands, x^2>=1/16 and 1/sqrt(1-x^2)>=1, giving f(x)>=alpha_1/(8*pi). Since h(x)<=4, choose p=alpha_1/(32*pi), which lies strictly between zero and one. Then p*h(x)<=alpha_1/(8*pi)<=f(x) on the bands, and domination elsewhere is automatic. The residual density g=(f-ph)/(1-p) is nonnegative, integrates to one and is symmetric. Thus F=pH+(1-p)G satisfies D0007-C002 with m=3.

4. Apply the reserve lemma: odd N with Np>=3 are CM, namely N>=96*pi/alpha_1. Even orders follow from symmetry. Consequently the specific mixture in Example 2.4 cannot be a law failing all odd orders, for any positive sequence alpha_j specified there.

This does not show each f_j is 3-CM, and does not claim every symmetric density is 3-CM. It only shows their specified mixture is CM for all sufficiently large orders, with an explicit finite threshold. The claim about no odd order in the source therefore has a concrete contradiction. [Theorem ex-hypothesis of arXiv:2608.29986, 'Khovanov-Rozansky homology over $\F[U,V]$'] [gorsky2024tautological,chandler2024structures,sano2026ification]
    
    There exists an $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ triple $(E, F, H)$ acting on reduced Khovanov-Rozansky homology $\widehat{H}(K)$. In terms of grading $\mathrm{gr}_{\mathit{DGR}} = (\mathrm{gr}_a, \mathrm{gr}_q, \mathrm{gr}_t)$ the maps have degrees $\mathrm{gr}_{\mathit{DGR}}(E) = (0, -4, -2)$, $\mathrm{gr}_{\mathit{DGR}}(F) = (0, 4, 2)$ and $\mathrm{gr}_{\mathit{DGR}}(H) = (0, 0, 0)$. Moreover, the endomorphisms $E$, $F$, and $H : \widehat{H}(K) \to \widehat{H}(K)$ commute with the same chain homotopy equivalences that establish the invariance of Khovanov-Rozansky homology $\widehat{H}(K)$ under Reidemeister moves from [rasmussen2016some]. Finally, there is a way to define the map $F$ on $\widehat{H}(K_1)\otimes\widehat{H}(K_2)$ such that for all $n, k \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}} $, the $k$-fold iterated commutator $\ad_F^k(d_n)$, and thus $d_{i|j} = \frac{1}{j!}\ad_F^k(d_n)$ commute with the chain homotopy equivalences that establish the connect sum formula in Khovanov-Rozansky homology [rasmussen2016some]. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 10 (Orbit collapse) of arXiv:2608.15805, 'Spectral duality structures and the Fisher--Rao geometry of reset distributions'] Under \textup{(S3)--(S4)}, for each orbit $O=\{z,\sigma(z)\}$ the
matrix
\[
M_O=\begin{pmatrix}1-C^\ast & -C^\ast\kappa(z)\\[2pt]
-C^\ast\kappa(\sigma(z)) & 1-C^\ast\end{pmatrix}
\]
has rank exactly one, with
\[
\operatorname{im}M_O=\mathbb R\,\mathbf d_O,\qquad
\mathbf d_O:=\bigl(\sqrt{\kappa(z)},\,-\sqrt{\kappa(\sigma(z))}\bigr),
\qquad
\ker M_O=\mathbb R\bigl(\sqrt{\kappa(z)},\,\sqrt{\kappa(\sigma(z))}\bigr).
\]
Consequently, for every $\nu$ the pair
$\big([\mathbf n_\nu]_z,[\mathbf n_\nu]_{\sigma(z)}\big)$ is a scalar
multiple of the single fixed vector $\mathbf d_O$: the restriction of
every normal direction to a given orbit collapses onto one line.

Let X_1, X_2, ... be i.i.d. real random variables with cumulant generating function Lambda(lambda) = log E[ exp(lambda X_1) ] and Legendre transform Lambda^*(x) = sup_{lambda in R} ( lambda x - Lambda(lambda) ). Assume Lambda(lambda) < infinity for every lambda in a neighbourhood of 0. Then the empirical means S_n/n satisfy the LARGE DEVIATION PRINCIPLE with speed n and good convex rate function Lambda^*: for every closed set C, limsup_n (1/n) log P( S_n/n in C ) <= - inf_{x in C} Lambda^*(x), and for every open set G, liminf_n (1/n) log P( S_n/n in G ) >= - inf_{x in G} Lambda^*(x). In particular, for x > E[X_1], (1/n) log P( S_n/n >= x ) -> - Lambda^*(x), so the Chernoff upper bound is exact at the level of the exponential rate although it can be off by polynomial factors: the sharper Bahadur-Rao asymptotic supplies a factor of order n^{-1/2}. The exponential moment hypothesis is what makes Lambda^* a GOOD rate function, meaning its sublevel sets are compact; on the real line the large deviation principle itself continues to hold without it, but the rate function may fail to be good and the statement must then be handled with care. Heavy-tailed laws with no exponential moments have Lambda^* identically 0 above the mean, and their large deviations are governed by a single big jump rather than by a rate function of this shape. [Cramer (1938); see Dembo and Zeitouni, Large Deviations Techniques and Applications, 2nd ed., Theorem 2.2.3]

[Lemma lem:saddle of arXiv:2411.13875, 'Large deviations at the origin of random walk in random environment'] Fix $\kappa > 0$ and let $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_j \in \mathcal P_\mathbb V^{(\kappa)}$ be all distinct. Define the mapping  $\Lambda : \Delta_j \times \mathbb R^d \to \mathbb{R}$ by the formula
\[
\Lambda(t,\theta) := \Lambda_{\langle t , \sigma\rangle}(\theta)=\log \Big(  \sum_{i=1}^j t_i \sum_{e \in \mathbb V} \mathrm e^{\langle \theta,e\rangle} \sigma_i(e)\Big),
\] where $\langle t , \sigma \rangle:=\sum_{i=1}^j t_i \sigma_i \in \mathcal P_{\mathbb V}$ for $t \in \Delta_j$. Then, $\Lambda$ has at least one saddle point, by which we refer to the (global) property that there exists some $(t^*,\theta^*) \in \Delta_j \times \mathbb R^d$ such that $\Lambda(t,\theta^*) \leq \Lambda(t^*,\theta^*) \leq \Lambda(t^*,\theta)$ for all $t \in \Delta_j$, $\theta \in \mathbb R^d$. Observe that such $(t^*,\theta^*)$ necessarily
satisfies
\[
\Lambda(t^*,\theta^*) = \max_{t \in \Delta_j} \inf_{\theta \in \mathbb R^d} \Lambda(t,\theta) = \inf_{\theta \in \mathbb R^d} \max_{t \in \Delta_j} \Lambda(t,\theta).
\]

Novelty: UNCHECKED. Elementary free-walk/product-void argument; no earlier separate statement found in the limited I0005 searches. This strengthens v1/v2. It never supplies a fixed-law counterexample.

Fix d≥1 and let R_t be the range through round t of one free nearest-neighbor simple random walk on Z^d. For each observation time t start a new particle–hole process with iid P(η=1)=P(η=−1)=p_t, P(η=0)=1−2p_t. Assume

p_t→0 and p_t E_0|R_t|→0.

Then, with synchronous rounds, stationary capacity-one holes, and graph distance,

P_{p_t}(origin strictly nearer an unfilled hole than an active particle at time t)→1/2.

In particular p_t(t+1)→0 suffices in every dimension, because |R_t|≤t+1. This condition is weaker than v2's sufficient condition in d>2. For d=1 one can also use E|R_t|≤C√(t+1), by the maximal-walk moment argument in v2. Each initial law is bounded and mean zero; convergence is not uniform over laws even when d≤3, but no fixed p satisfies these asymptotic assumptions.

## 1. Couple to full free walks

Assign an independent infinite walk to every site, independently of all initial signs. If a site is initially +1, its particle follows this path until it settles; continue the path freely after settlement for comparison. Independent tie-breaking marks select uniformly which arriving particles settle. Let C_t^{free}(B) count initial particles whose completed free endpoints at time t lie in B. The actual active particles are precisely the nonsettled labeled particles in this free configuration at time t.

An initial hole z filled by time t must have been visited by the free path of an initial +1 particle y≠z. Independence of different initial sites and the union bound give

E[number of filled initial holes in B]
≤p_t² sum_{z∈B}sum_y P_y(T_z≤t)
=p_t² |B| E_0|R_t|.

For y=z, the opposite initial signs are impossible; including the nonnegative term in the upper bound is harmless. Translation invariance gives sum_y P_y(T_z≤t)=sum_y P_0(T_{z−y}≤t)=E_0|R_t|.

Every settled particle's free path through t visited an initial hole. The expected number of settled labeled particles with completed free endpoint in B is therefore at most

p_t² sum_y E_y[1_{Z_t∈B}|R_t|]
=p_t² |B| E_0|R_t|.

The last equality follows by fixing a path from zero and summing its translations: exactly |B| translated paths end in B, and translation leaves the range size unchanged. All sums are nonnegative; Tonelli applies. A visit to the particle's own initial site cannot hit a hole and may again be included in the upper bound. The completed prefix includes the path up to actual settlement, so the containment of events is valid even though future free instructions are unused by the actual process.

Put s_t=p_t^{−1/d}. For any fixed M≥0 and B=B_floor(Ms_t), the two discrepancy expectations are at most C_{d,M}p_t E_0|R_t|+o(p_t E_0|R_t|), hence tend to zero. By Markov, within B the surviving holes coincide with initial −1 sites and the actual active-particle counts coincide with the free-endpoint counts, with probability tending to one. Multiplicities at a site are harmless for the nearest-site event.

## 2. Joint initial-hole/free-particle void probabilities

For fixed r,s≥0, let B_H=B_floor(rs_t), B_C=B_floor(ss_t), a_y=1_{y∈B_H}, and b_y=P_y(Z_t∈B_C). At site y, the two mutually exclusive forbidden choices are an initial hole in B_H (probability p_t a_y) and an initial particle whose free endpoint lies in B_C (probability p_t b_y). The signs and free walks are independent across sites. Therefore the exact probability of no initial hole in B_H and no free endpoint in B_C is

product_{y∈Z^d}(1−p_t a_y−p_t b_y).

At fixed t this is a finite product: a_y has finite support and b_y=0 outside B_C+B_t by finite propagation. Moreover sum_y a_y=|B_H| and sum_y b_y=|B_C|, the latter by translation invariance of the transition probabilities. For p_t≤1/4, the logarithm differs from −p_t(|B_H|+|B_C|) by absolute value at most

C p_t² sum_y(a_y+b_y)²≤2C p_t²(|B_H|+|B_C|),

because 0≤a_y,b_y≤1, a_y²=a_y, and b_y²≤b_y. This estimate is uniform in time; no negligible-displacement assumption is needed.

The lattice ℓ1-ball count is |B_R|=v_dR^d+O_d(R^{d−1}+1), v_d=2^d/d!. It follows by counting cubes in the dilated cross-polytope and bounding the boundary layer. Thus p_t|B_H|→v_d r^d and p_t|B_C|→v_d s^d, while the preceding logarithmic error tends to zero. The joint void probability tends to

exp(−v_d(r^d+s^d)).

This is the survival function of two independent identically distributed continuous nearest-distance variables with marginal tail exp(−v_d u^d).

## 3. Transfer to actual surviving holes and active particles

For each fixed pair r,s, Step 1 shows that the actual joint void probability differs from Step 2 by a quantity tending to zero. Therefore the scaled actual nearest-hole and nearest-active distances converge jointly to the same independent continuous pair. The continuous limiting marginals ensure tightness, and the joint survival function determines the joint law. The set {first distance = second distance} has zero limiting probability. Portmanteau applied to the strict comparison now gives the desired limit 1/2.

## Quantifier limitation

The density p_t is reselected for every observation time. With fixed p>0, the expected range tends to infinity and p E|R_t| does not tend to zero, so this proof cannot refute the fixed-law d4 statement. TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). Kalikow's zero-one law (1981; Zerner-Merkl 2001 for the sharp form): for random walk in an i.i.d. elliptic random environment on Z^d and a direction l, let A_l = {X_n . l -> +infinity}. Then P_0(A_l union A_{-l}) is 0 or 1. It does NOT say that P_0(A_l) itself is 0 or 1: the directional zero-one law P_0(A_l) in {0,1} is a theorem in d = 1 (Solomon) and d = 2 (Zerner-Merkl, using planarity: two walks in the same environment must intersect), and is an OPEN PROBLEM for d >= 3 (Drewitz-Ramirez Open Question 3.2; Kalikow's law is often misquoted as the directional one). Kalikow's proof: the event A_l union A_{-l} is invariant under a coupling of walks started at different points that follow the same environment after they meet in a slab, and its probability is a function of the environment's tail sigma-field, hence 0 or 1 by Kolmogorov. Consequences: under transience in some direction the regeneration structure of Sznitman-Zerner applies to the union event; Zerner's law of large numbers then gives X_n/n -> v or -c v. Typical failure: Treating Kalikow's zero-one law as if it determines transience, mistaking the statement that the probability is 0 or 1 for a claim that it equals 1; the theorem only rules out intermediate probabilities and leaves open, often genuinely unresolved, which side of the dichotomy holds for a specific environment law, which is precisely the content of the still largely open general ballisticity conjecture for random walk in random environment in dimension d>=2. Canonical reference: Kalikow, 1981, Annals of Probability; Zeitouni, 2004, Ecole d'Ete de Probabilites de Saint-Flour, Springer Lecture Notes in Mathematics.
i.i.d. (or stationary ergodic with care) elliptic environment on Z^d
The statement concerns the UNION of the two directional events
Directional 0-1 law is open for d >= 3

[Definition of arXiv:2605.15066, 'The critical activation density in graph bootstrap percolation'] For each $e$ in $A^*$, put ${\mathcal R}_e^*=\emptyset$
and recall that $W_e^*=e$.  
For edges $e$ activated at time $t\geqslant1$, 
we put 
\[
{\mathcal R}_e^*=\{e\}\cup\bigcup_{f\in E(H_e^*\setminus e)}{\mathcal R}_f^*. 
\]
We call the edges in ${\mathcal R}_e^*$ the {\it red edges}
of $W_e^*$. 
The edges in $W_e^*$ itself are its {\it black edges}. 
Note that if the black edges of $W_e^*$ are
initially active then the $H$-dynamics will 
activate each red edge of $W_e^*$, towards
eventually activating $e$ itself. We let ${\mathcal R}^*={\mathcal R}^*_{e^*}$
denote the set of red edges of $W^*$.

[Theorem 10 of arXiv:2608.26974, 'Why not to use the Gaussian kernel'] Consider a Gevrey kernel with $\eta \in (0, 1)$. 
  Let $\sigma \geq 0$ and $X_n = \{x_1, \ldots, x_n \} \subset \R^d$.
  If $\delta(x, X_n) = \min_{x_i \in X_n} \lVert x - x_i \rVert_2$ is sufficiently small, then
  \begin{equation*}
    \V_\sigma(x \mid \mathcal{D}_n) \geq C \exp(- c \,\delta(x, X_n)^{-\kappa}) ,
  \end{equation*} 
  where $C, c, \kappa > 0$ are constants that do not depend on $\sigma$, $x$, or $X_n$.

Let $U\subset\mathbb R^n$ be bounded and open, $T>0$, $a^{ij}=a^{ji}$, $a^{ij},b^i,c\in L^\infty(U_T)$, uniformly parabolic with constant $\theta>0$, $f\in L^2(0,T;L^2(U))$, $g\in L^2(U)$. Then there exists exactly one weak solution $u\in L^2(0,T;H^1_0(U))$ with $u'\in L^2(0,T;H^{-1}(U))$ of $u_t+Lu=f$ in $U_T$, $u=0$ on $\partial U\times[0,T]$, $u(0)=g$. It satisfies $u\in C([0,T];L^2(U))$ and the energy estimate. No boundary regularity and no compatibility condition are needed for this basic existence statement. Improved regularity: if moreover $g\in H^1_0(U)$ and the coefficients are time independent and smooth enough, then $u\in L^\infty(0,T;H^1_0(U))$ with $u'\in L^2(0,T;L^2(U))$; if in addition $\partial U$ is of class $C^2$ (or $U$ is convex), then also $u\in L^2(0,T;H^2(U))$. The $H^2$ conclusion is elliptic regularity applied at a.e. time and genuinely needs that boundary hypothesis -- on a domain with a reentrant corner the solution need not lie in $H^2(U)$ -- whereas the $L^\infty_tH^1_0$ and $u'\in L^2_tL^2$ bounds do not.
U bounded open, T > 0
a^{ij} = a^{ji}, a^{ij}, b^i, c in L^infty(U_T)
uniform parabolicity with theta > 0
f in L^2(0,T;L^2(U)), g in L^2(U)
improved-regularity clause only: g in H^1_0(U) and coefficients time independent and smooth; the H^2(U) conclusion needs in addition partial U of class C^2, or U convex

Seek $u_m(t)=\\sum_{k=1}^m d^k_m(t)w_k$ solving the $m\\times m$ linear ODE system $(u_m',w_k)+B[u_m,w_k;t]=(f,w_k)$, $k\\le m$, with $u_m(0)$ the $L^2$-projection of $g$; the system has absolutely continuous solutions by Caratheodory's ODE theory since the coefficients are bounded and measurable in $t$. The energy estimate, proved exactly as for weak solutions (test with $u_m$, use Garding and Gronwall), bounds $u_m$ uniformly in $L^\\infty(0,T;L^2)\\cap L^2(0,T;H^1_0)$ and $u_m'$ in $L^2(0,T;H^{-1})$. Extract a weakly convergent subsequence; the problem being linear, weak convergence already suffices to pass to the limit in the weak formulation against test functions of the form $\\varphi(t)w_k$ (the uniform bound on $u_m'$ plus the Aubin-Lions compactness lemma also gives strong $L^2(U_T)$ convergence), and the initial value $u(0)=g$ is identified by integrating by parts in time. Uniqueness is the energy estimate with zero data. The improved regularity comes from testing with $u_m'$, which for time-independent $B$ gives $\\frac{d}{dt}B[u_m,u_m]+2\\|u_m'\\|_{L^2}^2\\le C$ and hence the $L^\\infty_tH^1_0$ and $L^2_tL^2$ bounds; the $H^2$ bound then follows by reading $-\\partial_i(a^{ij}u_{x_j})=f-u'-b^iu_{x_i}-cu\\in L^2(U)$ for a.e. $t$ and applying elliptic $H^2$ regularity, which is exactly where $\\partial U\\in C^2$ (or convexity) is used.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:8c63a8268bf675ad950611db31579958d081924d598eb93e13ca0714c7d98924","revision_digest":"sha256:c4f743a99742ee35989f4d6c9486d23d390a524de933f246a1208336a3e9f957","source_id":"wikipedia:Galerkin method","source_revision":"as-known-2026-09-12","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Prop prop_diagonal_expansion of arXiv:2606.23648, '\textsc{Optimal Stopping for a Diffusion with Unobserved Bernoulli Drift}'] If \((x,y)\in\mathcal C\) and \(h\ge0\), then
    \(
        (x+h,y-h)\in\mathcal C.
    \)
    Consequently, if \(\mathcal I\neq\varnothing\), then \(\mathcal I\) is a right interval $(x_{birth},\infty)$ or $[x_{birth},\infty)$. Moreover, for every \(x\in\mathcal I\) and every \(h\ge0\),
    \begin{equation}
        a(x+h)\le a(x)-h,
        \qquad
        b(x+h)\ge b(x)-h.
    \end{equation}
    In particular, the distance-from-the-diagonal function $d(\cdot)$ of (equation def_d_lower_boundary of the paper) is non-increasing on \(\mathcal I\). Hence, if \(a(\bar x)=-\bar x\) for some \(\bar x\in\mathcal I\), then we have
    \(
        a(x)=-x
    \)
    for all
    \(
        x\in\mathcal I,\, x\ge\bar x.
    \)

[Proposition prop:star of arXiv:2606.27073, 'Retention Profiles and KL Contraction Bounds in Finite Markov Chains'] For the lazy random walk on the star graph with $n\ge3$ vertices, labelled
so that vertex~$0$ is adjacent to vertices $1,\ldots,n-1$ and there are no
other non-loop edges, the stationary distribution satisfies
$\pi(0)=1/2$ and $\pi(i)=1/(2(n-1))$ for $i\ge 1$.
In addition, $L(P)=1/2$.

body: [Lemma app:lem_conti of arXiv:2606.12143, 'Continuous stochastic flows driven by white noise and their duals'] Suppose that Assumption~(assu:H of the paper) and conditions~(item:1a of the paper), (item:1b of the paper), (item:2c of the paper), and~(item:2d of the paper) hold. Then the map $(x,t)\mapsto \bar\sigma(x,t)$ is continuous. Moreover, if conditions~(item:1c of the paper) and~(item:1d of the paper) hold, then $(x,t)\mapsto -b(x,t)+\tfrac12\partial_x\bar\sigma(x,t)$ is also continuous on ${\mathbb R}^2$.
title: Lemma app:lem_conti of arXiv:2606.12143

[Proposition prop:dynkin-lamperti of arXiv:2411.10113, 'Long-range one-dimensional\\ internal diffusion-limited aggregation'] Suppose that~(equation ass:irreducible of the paper) holds, 
and that~(equation ass:stable-alpha of the paper) holds with $\alpha \in (0,2)$. Then,
for every $x \in {\mathbb Z}$ and every $u \geq 0$,
\[ \lim_{y \to \infty} \bP_x \left( \frac{S_{\rho_y} -y}{y} > u \right) = \int_u^\infty f_\alpha (v) {\mathrm d} v , \]
where
\[ f_\alpha (v) := \frac{ \sin (\pi \alpha/2)}{\pi} \frac{1}{v^{\alpha/2} (1+v)}, ~\text{ for } v > 0.\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Theorem Lyapunov of arXiv:2411.16651, 'On a problem of optimal mixing'] Let $\mu_1,\dots,\mu_n$ be atomless Borel probability measures on a Souslin space $X$. Then, for every Borel probability measure $\nu$ on $X$ there exists a Borel transformation $T: X\to X$ such that $\mu_i\circ T^{-1}=\nu$ for all $1\leq i\leq n$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Thm 21 of arXiv:2607.06242, 'Exponential mixing and Freidlin--Wentzell large deviation principle for Markov cocycles'] Assume
  \[
     \|F\|^2\in L^1(\Sigma,m),\qquad
     \|Q\|_{\mathcal L_2(\Rb^{ \mathbf{d}},H^1)}^2\in L^1(\Sigma,m),\qquad
     Q_\infty:=\operatorname*{sup}_{\sigma\in\Sigma}
     \|Q(\sigma)\|_{\mathcal L(\Rb^{ \mathbf{d}},H)}<\infty .
  \]
  Suppose that there exist an integer
  $N_0\geq 1$ and a measurable family of linear maps
  $R_0(\sigma):P_{N_0}H\to \Rb^{ \mathbf{d}}$ such that
  \[
      Q(\sigma)R_0(\sigma)P_{N_0}=P_{N_0},\qquad
      \|R_0\|_{\mathcal L(P_{N_0}H,\Rb^{ \mathbf{d}})}^2\in L^1(\Sigma,m),
  \]
  and $N_0$ is chosen large enough to satisfy the determining mode gap
  \begin{align}
    \nu\lambda_{N_0+1}>
    C_*\int_\Sigma \left(\|F(\sigma)\|^2+\|Q(\sigma)\|_{\mathcal L_2(\Rb^{ \mathbf{d}},H)}^2\right)\,m(d\sigma),
  \end{align}
  where $C_*>0$ 
  is an embedding constant 
  depending  only on $\nu$, $\lambda_1$, and the domain $D$.

  Then the Navier--Stokes system \eqref{e.072601} has a unique stationary measure $\mu_{\s}^{\varepsilon}$ that attracts transition probabilities exponentially under the Wasserstein metric $\mathbb{W}_{\|\cdot\|\wedge 1}$. Moreover, for $m$-a.e. $\s\in \Sigma$, the family $\{\mu_{\s}^{\varepsilon}\}_{\varepsilon\in(0,1]}$ obeys an upper bound Freidlin--Wentzell LDP with a good rate function, which also gives a lower bound, and hence the full Freidlin--Wentzell LDP, in the case when the random attractor of the limiting system consists of a single random point. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Thm 21 of arXiv:2607.06242

	$C^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^2)$ if
	\(Q \in C^1(\mathbb{R}^2)\)
	and its gradient $\nabla Q$ is locally Lipschitz on $\mathbb{R}^2$.

[Lem 5 of arXiv:2605.07369, '2605.07369'] \cite[Theorem 3.13]{M-C} Let $\{Y_k, \FF_k\}_{k\ge 1}$ be a martingale difference sequence with $a_k\le Y_k\le b_k$ for each $k$, for suitable constants $a_k, b_k$. Then for any $t\ge 0$,
$$
\pp\left(\left|\sum_{k=1}^n Y_k\right|\ge t\right)\le 2\exp\left(-\frac{2t^2}{\sum_{k=1}^n\left(b_k-a_k\right)^2}\right).
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lem 5 of arXiv:2605.07369

body: [Definition 1.1 of arXiv:2512.19063, 'Sharp Decoupling Inequalities for the Variances and Second Moments of Sums of Dependent Ra'] Let {di}, {ei} be two sequences of random variables adapted to an increasing sequence of σ-algebras {Fi}. Then {di} is said to be tangent to {ei} with respect to {Fi} if for all i, L(di|Fi−1) = L(ei|Fi−1), i.e., the conditional distributions of di given Fi−1 and ei given Fi−1 are the same.

[Definition def:3.1 of arXiv:2608.27474, 'Nonlocality of Cover-Time Changes Under Edge Addition'] For a marked configuration
\((G;s,u,v)\), its radius-\(r\) local datum is the isomorphism class of
the induced subgraph on

\[
B_r(G;\{s,u,v\})
=\{x:\operatorname{dist}_G(x,\{s,u,v\})\le r\},
\]

with \(s,u,v\) preserved as three individual marks and every visible
vertex labelled by its degree in the full ambient graph. Unless
explicitly stated, this datum contains neither the graph order nor any
other global scalar.

body:
[Theorem ps to ps of arXiv:2411.04238, 'Holomorphic jump-diffusions'] Let $X=(X_t)_{t\in [0,T]}$ be an $S$-valued jump-diffusion with characteristics $(b,a,K)$ and extended generator $\mathcal A$.  Assume that $b_j,a_{ij}\in\mathcal O(S)$, $K$ is a kernel with holomorphic jump size, and let $F$ be the corresponding non-negative measure on the measurable space $E$. 
Fix $G=(G_1,\ldots,G_d)$ for $G_j$ such that for some $\varepsilon>0$
\begin{equation}
    G_j>\sup_{z\in P^d_{R(S)+\varepsilon}(0)}\sup_{ y\in \textup{supp}(F)}|z_j|+|\underline{\bm{j}}( y)^j|_z.
\end{equation}
For each $h\in H(P_G^d(0))$, $z\in P^d_{R(S)+\varepsilon}(0)$, and $y\in E$ set 
$$
Jh(z,y):=\lambda(z)\big(h(z+j_\varepsilon(z,y))-h(z)-\nabla h(z)^\top j_\varepsilon(z,y)\big)
$$
and
\begin{equation}
    \mathcal D(J):=\{h\in H(P_G^d(0))\colon Jh(z,\cdot)\in L^1(E,F)\text{ for each }z\in P^d_{R(S)+\varepsilon}(0)\}.
\end{equation}
Set 
\begin{align*}
     \mathcal{V}&\subseteq\{h\in \mathcal D(J)\colon
     \text{the map $P^d_{R(S)+\varepsilon}\ni z\to Jh(z,\cdot)\in L^1(E,F)$ is continuous}\},
\\  \mathcal{V}^*&:=\{\mathbf{u}\in \mathcal{S}^* \colon h_\mathbf{u}=h|_{{P}^d_{R(S)}(0)},  \ h\in \mathcal{V}\}.
 \end{align*}
Then $X$ is an $S$-valued $\mathcal V$-holomorphic process and for all $\mathbf{u}\in\mathcal{V}^*$, $$\mathcal{A}h_\mathbf{u}=h_{L(\mathbf{u})}|_S,$$ where $L:\mathcal{V}^*\rightarrow \mathcal{S}^*$  is given by
\begin{align}
    L(\mathbf{u}) =\sum_{|\beta|=1}\mathbf{u}^{(\beta)}\ast \underline{\mathbf{b}}^{\beta} &+\sum_{|\beta|=2}\frac{1}{\beta!}\mathbf{u}^{(\beta)}\ast \underline{\underline{\mathbf{a}}}^{\beta}\\
    &+\bm{\lambda}\ast \int_{E}\mathbf{u}\circ^s \underline{\bm{j}} ( y)-\mathbf{u}-\sum_{|\beta|=1}\mathbf{u}^{(\beta)}\ast \underline{\bm{j}}( y)^{\ast\beta} \ F(d y).\nonumber 
\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem ps to ps of arXiv:2411.04238

[Definition 3 of arXiv:2605.21424, 'A dice game, a multinomial walk, and the inverted Dirichlet distribution'] Consider paths of the random walk \(R\) defined above. 
\begin{enumerate} 
\item The winning probability of player \(\ell\), 
i.e., the probability that \(R_{n,\ell}\) reaches \(n_\ell\) before any \(R_{n,k}\) reaches \(n_k\), \(k\ne \ell\),
is 
\[
\pi_\ell:=\P\Big(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty \big\{R_{n,\ell}=n_\ell,R_{n-1,\ell}=n_\ell-1,R_{n,k}<n_k,  1\leq k\leq m,k\ne \ell\big\}\Big).
\]
\item The probability of player \(\ell\) being last (for short: losing probability of player \(\ell\)), 
i.e., the probability that \(R_{n,\ell}\) reaches \(n_\ell\) after each \(R_{n,k}\) reaches \(n_k\), \(k\ne \ell\),
is 
\[
\tau_\ell:=\P\Big(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty \big\{R_{n,\ell}=n_\ell,R_{n-1,\ell}=n_\ell-1,R_{n-1,k}\ge n_k,  1\leq k\leq m,k\ne \ell\big\}\Big).
\]
\end{enumerate}

[Theorem 201 of arXiv:2601.16377, '2601.16377'] If $\boldsymbol{\Theta}$ is a diagonal matrix with positive diagonal elements, then the solution operator is
\begin{equation}

\Upsilon_h[\boldsymbol{E}\,;\,\boldsymbol{\kappa}](z) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{(z - \alpha_h)(z - \beta_h)}}\left(\kappa_h + \oint_{\gamma_h} \frac{\dd\zeta}{2\ii\pi}\,\frac{E_h(\zeta)}{\theta_{h,h}(\zeta - z)} \right),
\end{equation}
where $\gamma_h\subset \amsmathbb{M}_h$ encloses $\amsmathbb{A}_h^{\mathfrak{m}}$, but not $z$.

If $\theta_{g,h} = \theta > 0$ is independent of $g,h \in [H]$, then the solution operator is uniquely determined by the identity
\[
\sum_{h = 1}^{H} \Op_h[\boldsymbol{E}\,;\,\boldsymbol{\kappa}](z) = \frac{1}{\sigma(z)}\Pi^{-1}\left[\boldsymbol{\kappa} - \bigg(\oint_{\gamma_g^+} \frac{\dd \zeta}{2\ii\pi}\,\mathcal{K}[\boldsymbol{E}](\zeta)\bigg)_{g = 1}^{H}\right](z) + \mathcal{K}[\boldsymbol{E}](z),
\]
where
\[
\mathcal{K}[\boldsymbol{E}](z) = \sum_{h = 1}^{H} \frac{1}{\sigma(z)} \oint_{\gamma_h^-} \frac{\dd\zeta}{2\ii\pi}\,\frac{\sigma(\zeta)}{\zeta - z}\,\frac{E_h(\zeta)}{\theta \sqrt{(\zeta - \alpha_h)(\zeta - \beta_h)}}
\]
and $\Pi^{-1}$ term is a polynomial in $z$ of degree at most $H-1$, defined through the hyperelliptic period map $\Pi$, whose more detailed definition is in \eqref{periodmap}. Contours $\gamma_h^-\subset\amsmathbb{M}_h$ enclose $\amsmathbb{A}_h^{\mathfrak{m}}$, but not $z$. Contours $\gamma_h^+\subset \amsmathbb{M}_h$ enclose the respective $\gamma_h^-$, as Figure~\ref{Fig:Kdomain}. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 201 of arXiv:2601.16377

body: (1) One omitted value is not enough. The family {exp(nz) : n ≥ 1} on the unit disk omits the value 0 everywhere, but it is not normal, not even in the extended sense: on the left half of the disk exp(nz) → 0 while on the right half |exp(nz)| → ∞, and a locally uniform limit on the connected set D would have to be holomorphic throughout or identically ∞. Montel's fundamental normality test needs two distinct omitted values, and that is sharp. (2) When two values are omitted, the conclusion is normality in the extended sense: the constant functions f_n = n omit 0 and 1 and converge to ∞, so a proof that assumes the limit is a finite holomorphic function must first exclude the ∞ branch (typically by a bound at one point or by the maximum principle). (3) Pointwise bounds are not local bounds. Montel's first theorem needs a bound uniform on each compact set; pointwise boundedness of the family is genuinely weaker (Runge's theorem produces sequences of polynomials converging pointwise on C to a discontinuous function, so such a sequence is pointwise bounded and not normal). (4) Normality is not convergence: it only yields subsequences, and the limit may leave the class one is working in — the injective maps z/n converge to a constant, and the limit of a normal family of functions in some prescribed family need not satisfy the same constraint unless Hurwitz-type arguments are added.
title: Pitfall: normality needs two omitted values (or local boundedness), and the limit may be ∞

[Definition eq:bounded-Lipschitz-cut-fibered-probability-measures of arXiv:2606.21556, 'Mean field limit of non-exchangeable interacting diffusions on co-evolutionary networks'] Given any two fibered probability measures \(\mu,\bar{\mu} \in \mathcal{P}_{\nu}(\mathcal{X}\times [0,1])\), we define
	the bounded-Lipschitz cut distance as 
	\begin{equation} 
		d_{\text{BL},\square}(\mu,\bar{\mu}):= \sup_{S\subset [0,1]} d_{\text{BL}} \left( \int_{S} \mu^{\xi} d\xi, \int_{S} \bar{\mu}^{\xi} d\xi \right), 
	\end{equation}
	where the supremum is taken over all measurable sets \(S\subset [0,1]\), and 
	\(\int_{S}\mu^{\xi}d\xi \in \mathcal{M}_+(\mathcal{X})\) denotes the finite positive measure defined
	by 
	\[
