[Proposition 19 (Uniform overlap after $N$ steps) of arXiv:2608.03353, '\bfseries A Direct Route to Markov Chain Convergence\\[2mm] \Large via Asymptotic Equivale'] Let $M \in [1,\infty)$ and $N \in \N$ be numbers, let $\YY, \YY' \in \XXA$ be sets and
let $s : \XX \times \XX \to [0,\infty)$ be a $\XXA\otimes\XXA$-measurable map. Put
$\delta := 1/(4M)$ and assume:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),nosep,topsep=3pt]
  \item $\pi(\XX \setminus \YY) \le \delta$ and $\pi(\XX\setminus\YY') \le \delta/4$;
  \item $T^{N}(A \mid x) \ge \displaystyle\int_{A} s(y \mid x)\,\pi(\dd y)$ for every $x \in \YY$ and every $A \in \XXA$;
  \item $\pi(\{x \in \YY : s(y\mid x) = 0\}) \le \delta/4$ for every $y \in \YY'$.
\end{enumerate}
Then there is a number $\gamma \in (0,1]$, depending only on $M, N, \YY, \YY', s$ and
$\pi$, such that
\[
  \tv{T^{N}\circ\mu - T^{N}\circ\nu} \;\le\; 1 - \gamma
  \qquad\text{for all } \mu,\nu \in \Prob \text{ with } \mu \le M\pi \text{ and } \nu \le M\pi .
\]

[Theo 31 of arXiv:2609.02261, 'Quantization and process'] Let  $(X_t)$ be a L\'evy process on $\R^{2n}$ with a definite positive diffusion matrix. The processus $(X_t)$ is considered as function $X(t , \omega)$ where $\omega $ belongs to a probability space $(\Omega,\mu_\Omega)$. For all  $t>0$, set   the Weyl translation operator $V(t , \omega)$
associated with $ X(t , \omega)$. 
Let  $A_0 =  {\rm Op}_h^{\rm Wick}(F)$ be the operator associated with a function  $F\in D_h( \R^{2n})$ as in Section \ref{Wick calculus}. For every  $t>0$, set
   
 $$ A(t , \omega) =  V(t , \omega)^{\star}  A_0  V(t , \omega).$$
 
Then, we have the identity,

$$  {\rm Op}_t^{\nu_t}(F) = \int _{\Omega}  A(t , \omega) d \mu_\Omega(\omega). $$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Thm quantitative-pinching of arXiv:2608.30847, 'An Almgren-type formula for planar $p$-harmonic functions'] Let $u$ be a nonconstant planar $p$-harmonic function in $B_{r_0}(x_0)$.
Assume that $H(s)>0$ and that $\Theta\in L^1(a,b)$ for some
$0<a<b<r_0$. Then
$$
\mathcal N_a(b)-\mathcal N_a(a)= p
\int_a^b \Gamma_a(s) \frac{s}{H(s)} \int_{\partial B_s(x_0)} A \left( \partial_\nu u-\frac{N_\ast(s)}{s}v
\right)^2 \,dS\,ds .
$$
In particular,
$$
\mathcal N_a(b)-\mathcal N_a(a)\ge 0.
$$

Assume moreover that
$$
  \mathcal N_a(b)-\mathcal N_a(a)\le \epsilon
$$
and
$$
   \omega(a,b):=\int_a^b |\Theta(s)|\,ds\le \eta .
$$
Then
$$
  \mathcal R(a,b) \le  \frac{e^\eta}{p}\,\epsilon .
$$
If, in addition, $N_\ast(a)\le \Lambda$, and if we set
$ \lambda=N_\ast(a),$
then
$$
 \sup_{a\le s\le b}|N_\ast(s)-\lambda|  \le    e^\eta\epsilon+\Lambda(e^\eta-1),
$$
and
$$
\mathcal R_\lambda(a,b)
\le \frac{2e^\eta}{p}\,\epsilon
+ 2\log\frac ba
\left[ e^\eta\epsilon+\Lambda(e^\eta-1)
\right]^2 .
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Thm quantitative-pinching of arXiv:2608.30847

[Definition 68 of arXiv:2608.26084, 'Localic Esakia Duality\\via Conic Frames'] A conic frame~$(L,\dc)$ satisfies the \emph{Priestley separation axiom} if for all compact~$a,b\in K(L)$:
	\[
	a\wedge \dc b = \bot
	\quad\implies\quad
	\exists c\in \Kdc(L): a\sqleq c\text{ and } b\sqleq \neg c.
	\]

[Proposition eq:general-mixture of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[proposition]{prop:general-moment-correction}
Fix \(q\ge1\).  Let \(Q\) be any symmetric probability law with finite
moments through order \(2q\).  For all sufficiently small
\(\varepsilon>0\), there exists a symmetric compactly supported
\(C^\infty\) density \(\nu_\varepsilon\) such that
\begin{equation}
 \mu_\varepsilon=\varepsilon Q+(1-\varepsilon)\nu_\varepsilon
\end{equation}
matches the standard Gaussian moments through order \(2q\).  If \(\nu_\varepsilon\) is supported in \([-R,R]\), then
\[
 \mu_\varepsilon(A)=\varepsilon Q(A)
 \quad\text{for every Borel }A\subset\mathbb R\setminus[-R,R].
\]
In particular, \(\mu_\varepsilon\) and \(Q\) have identical logarithmic tail asymptotics.
If \(Q\) has a strictly positive \(C^\infty\) density, then so does
\(\mu_\varepsilon\).

[Prop role-of-shifted-a of arXiv:2411.03065, 'Growing conditioned BGW trees with\\ log-concave offspring distributions'] Let $({\mathbf{a}},{\mathbf{b}})$ be a non-degenerate weight pair, with $r({\mathbf{a}})\geq2$ so that $({\mathbf{a}}^+,{\mathbf{b}})$ is also non-degenerate.
	Let $C_n$ be a $\PComp{{\mathbf{a}},{\mathbf{b}}}n$-distributed random composition  for some fixed $n\geq 1$.
	If we let $X_n=\mathrm{proj}_1(C_n)$ and $C'_n=\mathrm{proj}_{>1}(C_n)$, then $X_n$ has distribution given by
	\begin{align}
	\Prob{X_n=m}=\frac{b_m\cdot\PFComp{{\mathbf{a}}^+,{\mathbf{b}}}{n-m}}{\PFComp{{\mathbf{a}},{\mathbf{b}}}{n}},
	\qquad
	m=1,\dots,n,
	\end{align}
	and conditionally on $X_n$, the composition $C'_n$ has distribution $\PComp{{\mathbf{a}}^+,{\mathbf{b}}}{n-X_n}$.
title: Prop role-of-shifted-a of arXiv:2411.03065

body: [Definition def:twosided-lerw of arXiv:2411.13505, 'Capacity of loop-erased random walk'] Let $d\geq5$. Let $S_1,S_2$ be independent simple random walks on $\mathbb{Z}^d$ started from~0, conditioned such that $\LE(S_1)[1,\infty)\cap S_2[1,\infty)=\varnothing$. The two-sided loop-erased random walk $\hat\eta$ is defined as the union of $\LE(S_1)$ and $\LE(S_2)$, i.e., for $n\geq0$, $\hat\eta(n)=\LE(S_1)(n)$ and $\hat\eta(-n)=\LE(S_2)(n)$.
title: Definition def:twosided-lerw of arXiv:2411.13505

TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For the Ising model, or more generally ferromagnetic spin systems with finite-range interactions (with merely summable long-range couplings G(x,y) >= tanh(beta J_xy) by Griffiths' inequality, so exponential decay can fail), let G(x,y) = <sigma_x sigma_y> be the two-point function. The Simon-Lieb inequality bounds G(x,y) across any finite set Lambda separating x from y (x in Lambda, y outside Lambda) by G(x,y) <= sum_{u in Lambda, v not in Lambda} G_Lambda(x,u) beta J_{uv} G(v,y), with G_Lambda the two-point function of the model restricted to Lambda (free boundary condition) and beta the inverse temperature (forms with tanh(beta J_{uv}) in place of beta J_{uv} are also used), a one-step recursive bound relating the two-point function across a separating surface to the two-point function up to the boundary of Lambda times the coupling crossing it. Iterating the inequality over a sequence of nested separating sets, such as concentric boxes, yields exponential decay of G(x,y) once the associated generating function drops below its self-consistency threshold, giving a classical route, predating and complementary to the Duminil-Copin-Tassion approach, to sharpness of the phase transition and analyticity of the free energy in the high-temperature regime. It does not determine the exact critical temperature directly, only characterizing it implicitly through the inequality's self-consistency condition, and it applies specifically to ferromagnetic spin systems with a workable notion of finite separating surfaces; it does not transfer automatically to percolation, which uses combinatorially different, though philosophically related, inequalities. Typical failure: Iterating the Simon-Lieb inequality across many nested separating surfaces while implicitly assuming a geometric decay rate that has not actually been verified to be summable; turning the one-step recursive bound into exponential decay requires checking that the relevant generating function, summing G times J over the boundary, lies strictly below its self-consistency threshold, and this check is exactly where the difficulty of locating beta_c resides, so skipping it silently assumes the conclusion. Canonical reference: Simon, 1980, Communications in Mathematical Physics; Lieb, 1980, Communications in Mathematical Physics.
ferromagnetic pairwise interactions; the exponential-decay conclusion needs finite-range (or exponentially decaying) couplings, since G(x,y) >= tanh(beta J_xy) by Griffiths' inequality
finite volume, or an infinite-volume Gibbs state for which the relevant correlation inequalities (e.g. Griffiths inequalities) hold
existence of a family of finite sets separating the two points of interest
the model's symmetry, such as spin-flip Z_2 symmetry, used in the classical derivation of the inequality

body: [Proposition 41 (Conditional LAN at the true depth) of arXiv:2604.10792, 'Variable-Length Markov Chains on Finite Quivers: Boundary-Window Identifiability, Exact De'] Assume exact depth $r$ at $\theta_0$. Suppose, after shrinking to a neighborhood of $\theta_0$ if necessary, that the depth-$r$ chain has fixed finite support, is irreducible, the positive transition coordinates depend smoothly on $\theta$, and the initial law is either stationary or contributes only an $o_{P_{\theta_0}}(1)$ term to the local log-likelihood ratio. If a standard finite-state Markov-chain LAN theorem is invoked under these hypotheses for the chosen parameterization, then the experiment generated by $Z^{(r)}$ is LAN at $\theta_0$ on every fixed tangent block $T\subset T_{\theta_0}\Theta$. This proposition records only bare LAN, not the factorized form required by \cref{ass:lan}.

TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). To bound the distance, in Kolmogorov, Wasserstein, or total variation metric, between the law of a random variable W and a target distribution, classically the standard normal but also Poisson, exponential, and other targets, Stein's method characterizes the target law via a characterizing (Stein) equation: for the normal, E[f'(Z) - Zf(Z)] = 0 for all sufficiently smooth f if and only if Z is standard normal. Given a test function h, one solves the associated Stein equation f'(x) - xf(x) = h(x) - E[h(Z)] for f, and then bounds E[f'(W) - Wf(W)] directly using structural information about W, typically supplied by an auxiliary coupling such as an exchangeable pair, a size-biased coupling, or a dependency-graph/local-dependence construction, without going through characteristic functions or moment matching. This yields explicit, often near-optimal-rate, quantitative bounds on distributional distance for sums of dependent or weakly dependent random variables and for counts in combinatorial structures, settings where classical central limit theorem machinery is difficult to apply directly because of dependence. It does not automatically give a good bound for an arbitrary random variable, since constructing the right coupling matched to the problem's dependence structure is the substantive and typically hardest step, and the quality of the final bound is entirely determined by the quality of that coupling. Typical failure: Treating Stein's method as an automatic black box that produces a good rate on its own, when in fact the rate is entirely determined by the quality of the coupling constructed for the specific problem, such as an exchangeable pair with a large error term or a dependency graph with high maximum degree; a poorly constructed coupling yields a valid but far-from-optimal, or even useless, bound, and this construction step, rather than the abstract Stein equation itself, is where nearly all the technical difficulty and risk of error lies. Canonical reference: Stein, 1972, Proceedings of the Sixth Berkeley Symposium on Mathematical Statistics and Probability; Chen, Goldstein and Shao, Normal Approximation by Stein's Method, 2011, Springer.

sufficient smoothness or explicit derivative bounds on the solution f of the Stein equation for the specific target distribution
control of the resulting expectation bound in terms of the coupling's own closeness or error parameters

body: [Theorem 1.4 of arXiv:2512.17823, 'van den Berg-Kesten--type correlation inequalities for disjoint polymers in the KPZ univer'] There exist $C,c>0$ such that the following holds. Let $y\in\mathbb R$, $K,R\geq 0$, and $\mathsf{A}\subseteq\mathcal{C}([0,K],\mathbb R)$ be an increasing Borel measurable set. For any $t>0$, $M>0$, and a.e. $f\in\mathcal{C}([y-R,y],\mathbb R)$, (1.8) $\begin{split}&\mathbb P\Bigl(\hat{\mathfrak{h}}_{t,2}|_{[y,y+K]}-Ct^{-1/3}\log M\in\mathsf{A}\ \Big|\ \hat{\mathfrak{h}}_{t,1}|_{[y-R,y]}=f\Bigr)\\ &\leq\mathbb P\left(\hat{\mathfrak{h}}_{t,1}|_{[y,y+K]}\in\mathsf{A}\right)+\frac{3(K+1)t^{2/3}\exp(-cM^{2})}{\mathbb P(\hat{\mathfrak{h}}_{t,1}|_{[y-R,y]}\geq f)}.\end{split}$ The same also holds when the conditioning is replaced by $\hat{\mathfrak{h}}_{t,1}|_{[y-R,y]}\geq f$, in which case we may relax the continuity assumption and allow any $f:[y-R,y]\to\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\}$ which is upper semicontinuous. All of the previous also hold under both conditionings when $+K$ is replaced by $-K$ and $-R$ by $+R$ simultaneously.

Lojasiewicz gradient inequality. Let U be an open subset of R^n, f: U -> R real analytic, and p in U. There are an open neighbourhood W of p in U and constants theta in (0,1) and c > 0 such that |f(x) - f(p)|^theta <= c |grad f(x)| for every x in W. Consequence (finite length and convergence of bounded gradient trajectories). Let x: [0, infinity) -> U solve x'(t) = -grad f(x(t)) and suppose the trajectory {x(t): t >= 0} has compact closure in U. Then x has finite length, int_0^infinity |x'(t)| dt < infinity, and x(t) converges as t -> infinity to a single critical point a of f. Near a, the tail length obeys int_t^infinity |x'(s)| ds <= (c/(1-theta)) (f(x(t)) - f(a))^(1-theta), with c and theta the constants of the inequality at a. The same holds for gradient ascent x' = +grad f(x) with f replaced by -f. Critical points need not be isolated; smoothness alone is not enough (there are smooth functions with bounded gradient trajectories that spiral forever without converging).
f real analytic on an open set U in R^n
x solves the gradient flow x' = -grad f(x) on [0, infinity)
the trajectory has compact closure in U (precompact; bounded is enough when U = R^n)

body: A Hopfield network is a form of recurrent neural network, or a spin glass system, that can serve as a content-addressable memory. The Hopfield network, named for John Hopfield, consists of a single layer of neurons, where each neuron is connected to every other neuron except itself. These connections are bidirectional and symmetric, meaning the weight of the connection from neuron i to neuron j is the same as the weight from neuron j to neuron i. Patterns are associatively recalled by fixing certain inputs, and dynamically evolve the network to minimize an energy function, towards local energy minimum states that correspond to stored patterns. Patterns are associatively learned by a Hebbian learning algorithm.
title: Hopfield network

[Thm main of arXiv:2509.03065, 'Mathematical research with GPT-5: a Malliavin-Stein experiment'] For integers $p\neq q$, with $p$ odd, $q$ even, let
\begin{equation}
X = I_p(f), \qquad Y = I_q(g), \qquad Z = X+Y,
\end{equation}
satisfying $E[Z^2]=1$. Write $\kappa_4(Z)=\mathbb E[Z^4]-3$.
Then, we have
\begin{equation}
d_{\mathrm{TV}}(Z,N(0,1)) \;\le\; \sqrt{6\,\kappa_4(Z)},
\end{equation}
with $d_{\mathrm{TV}}$ the total variation distance.
In particular, if $Z_n = I_p(f_n) + I_q(g_n)$ with $E[Z_n^2]=1$ and $\kappa_4(Z_n)\to 0$, then
\[
d_{\mathrm{TV}}(Z_n,N(0,1)) \;\longrightarrow\;0.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Write Y_q=tanh(sqrt(q)Z)^2/q for q>0 and Z standard Gaussian, and
S_(n,q)=n^(-1)sum_(i=1)^n Y_q(Z_i), with iid rows.

## C044: uniform inverse sample moments and deleted tails

For every fixed Q<infinity and positive integer p, there is a finite
C_(Q,p) such that

    sup_(0<q<=Q, n>=4p) E[S_(n,q)^(-p)] <= C_(Q,p).            (1)

For any fixed sufficiently small eta>0, with m(q)=E Y_q and
G_(n,q)={|S_(n,q)-m(q)|<=eta},

    P(G_(n,q)^c)<=C_Q exp(-c_Q n),
    E[S_(n,q)^(-p);G_(n,q)^c]<=C_(Q,p)exp(-c_Q n/2), n>=8p.   (2)

Constants can be made explicit from the Gaussian expectations in the
proof. The sample mean is strictly positive almost surely. These are
exact-chain inverse moment estimates, in contrast with the ReLU atom and
near-collinearity obstruction.

Proof. tanh(x)/x decreases for x>0: tanh(x)-x sech(x)^2 has derivative
2x sech(x)^2 tanh(x)>0 and value0 at zero. Therefore Y_q>=Y_Q for q<=Q,
and Y_q<=Z^2. Let H=Y_Q>0 and phi(s)=E exp(-sH). For small y>0,

    P(H<=y)=P(|Z|<=arctanh(sqrt(Qy))/sqrt(Q))<=C sqrt(y),

using arctanh(w)<=2w for w<=1/2 and the bounded Gaussian density.
Increasing C_Q extends P(H<=y)<=C_Q sqrt(y) to every y>0.
Integration by parts gives phi(s)<=C'_Q s^(-1/2). Also for0<=s<=1,

    phi(s)<=1-c_Q s<=exp(-c_Q s), c_Q=E[H exp(-H)]>0,

and rho_Q=phi(1)<1. The Gamma identity and independence yield

    E[(n^(-1)sum_i H_i)^(-p)]
       =n^p/Gamma(p) integral_0^infinity s^(p-1)phi(s)^n ds.    (3)

Choose s0>=max(1,(2C'_Q)^2). On [0,1], (3) is bounded by c_Q^(-p).
On [1,s0], use rho_Q^n, giving at most
n^p s0^p rho_Q^n/(p Gamma(p)), uniformly bounded in n. On [s0,infinity),
for n>=4p,

    integral_(s0)^infinity s^(p-1)(C'_Q/sqrt(s))^n ds
      <= s0^p 2^(-n)/(n/2-p).

After multiplication by n^p/Gamma(p), this is uniformly bounded too.
This proves (1), since S_(n,q)>=n^(-1)sum H_i under the common-row coupling.

Uniform exponential integrability follows from0<=Y_q<=Z^2; m(q)>=E H>0.
Centered exponential-moment bounds and Chernoff give the first part of(2),
uniformly in q. Choose eta< E H/2 so G also stays uniformly away from zero.
Cauchy-Schwarz, (1) at order2p and the first bound in(2) prove its second
bound. All integrations use nonnegative integrands, so Tonelli applies.

Consider the exact scalar critical chain K_next=q S_(n,q) and
v=1/(nq), V_next=1/(n K_next). There are epsilon>0,C,c,n0 such that for

In particular the singular next correction is negative. On any fixed

    E[(V_next/v)^j]<=1+C_(Q,j)(q+1/n), j=1,2,
    E[(V_next-v)^2]<=C_Q(v^2/n+1/n^2),                        (5)
    |E(V_next-v)-(2v+2)/n|
                         <=C_Q[q/n+1/n^2+v/n^(3/2)].         (6)

Proof of(4). Global Taylor inequalities for tanh, using boundedness on
|x|<=1 and polynomial domination on |x|>=1, imply

    m(q)=1-2q+(17/3)q^2+O(q^3),
    Var(Y_q)=2-16q+O(q^2),
    kappa_3(Y_q)=8+O(q).

For example tanh(x)^2=x^2-(2/3)x^4+(17/45)x^6+O(x^8), with a global
remainder bound C|x|^8. Similarly E Y_q^2=3-20q+O(q^2). Every fixed
positive row moment is bounded; its first variation is O(q) since
|Y_q-Z^2|<=Cq Z^4.

sample-average moment is O(n^(-5/2)); it follows, for instance, from the
sixth moment bound for centered iid sample sums and Holder. The exact
sample-mean third moment is kappa_3(Y_q)/n^2, and its fourth moment is
3 Var(Y_q)^2/n^2+O(n^-3). Deleted inverse tails are exponentially small
by C044. Therefore uniformly on0<q<=epsilon,

    E S^(-1)=m^(-1)+Var(Y_q)/(n m^3)
              +[-kappa_3(Y_q)/m^4+3 Var(Y_q)^2/m^5]/n^2
              +O(n^(-5/2))+O(exp(-cn))

E S^(-1)=1+2q+2/n+O(q^2+q/n+n^(-3/2)) for small q, which gives(6).

body:
[Proposition 45 of arXiv:2609.00567, 'Hodge--Tate splitting and Akizuki--Nakano vanishing in positive characteristic'] Let $f_1,\ldots,f_r\in S_X$ be a homogeneous regular sequence, and set
\[
A \defeq S_X/(f_1,\ldots,f_r).
\]
Let
\[
\widehat Z
 \defeq 
V(f_1,\ldots,f_r)\cap U_X
\subset
\operatorname{Spec}(A)
\]
and $Z\defeq\widehat Z/G_X\subseteq X$.

Then \(Z\) is HT-split.
In particular, if \(Z\) is smooth, then there is an isomorphism
\[
F_{*}\Omega^\bullet_{Z/k}
\simeq
\bigoplus_{i=0}^{\dim Z}
\Omega^i_{Z/k}[-i]
\]
in \(\mcalD_{\qcoh}(Z)\).
Consequently, the Hodge-to-de Rham spectral sequence of \(Z\)
degenerates at \(E_1\), and \(Z\) satisfies the
Akizuki--Nakano-type vanishing theorem.

[Definition 17 of arXiv:2605.02002, 'Glauber dynamics for random field Ising models on bounded degree graphs and MLSI'] (Event-field denoising) Let $\mu$ be a distribution on $\{0,1\}^V$ and consider a collection of events $\mathcal{A}$. Denote by $\pi$ the joint distribution on $\{0,1\}^{V\cup\mathcal{A}}$ and let $(Y_t')_{t\in[0,1]}$ be the vertex-field denoising process for the marginal $\pi_{\mathcal{A}}$ with $\pi_{\mathcal{A}}=\operatorname{Law}(Y_1')$.
    Then event-field denoising process for $\mu$ through $\mathcal{A}$, which we denote by $(Y_t)_{t\in[0,1]}$ is defined via
\begin{enumerate}
    \item Sample $Y_1\sim\pi_V(\cdot\mid Y_1')$,
    \item For $t\in[0,1)$, we set $Y_t=Y_t'$. 
\end{enumerate} In other words, the process follows the vertex field denoising process applied to the event indicators, and finally at $t=1$ projects onto the vertices in $V$ via the conditional law $\pi_V(\cdot\mid Y_1')$.

Suppose that the interaction is given by
\[
W(x,y) = - J x y
\]
for $J \in (0, J_\textnormal{c})$, where
\[
J_\textnormal{c} \coloneqq
\frac{\int_{\mathds R} e^{-V(x)} \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} x}
{\int_{\mathds R} x^2e^{-V(x)} \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} x}.
\]
Then Theorem~(thm:sharp of the paper) applies with
$m_*$ being the centered measure
$\propto e^{-V(x)} \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} x$ and
\begin{align*}
\rho &= \biggl(1 - \frac{J}{J_\textnormal{c}}\biggr)^{\!2}\rho_0,\\
\gamma &= \frac{64(1+\delta_N)^2J^2}{\lambda_N},\\
M &= 4J^2 \biggl( \frac{\delta_N}{\lambda_NN} + \frac{d}{\rho_0}\biggr),
\end{align*}
where $\rho_0$, $\lambda_N$, $\delta_N$ are given by
\begin{align*}
\rho_0 &=
\begin{cases}
\sigma, & \sigma \geqslant 1, \\
\exp \bigl( - 7(1-\sigma)^2\!/36\theta \bigr),
& \sigma < 1,
\end{cases} \\
\lambda_N &= \biggl( 1 - \frac{J}{J_\textnormal{c}}\biggr)\frac{\rho_0}{2}
- \frac{3\bigl(1/\sqrt{\min(J_\textnormal{c}/J-1,1)}+3\bigr)J}{N}, \\
\delta_N &=
3\bigl(1/\sqrt{\min(J_\textnormal{c}/J-1,1)}+3\bigr)\frac{dJ}{\rho_0},
\end{align*}
whenever $N$ is large enough such that $\lambda_N > 0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma lem:remove0s of arXiv:2509.16541, 'Two-stage Bootstrap Percolation'] Consider two dynamics with the same initial configurations of $1$s and $2$s on ${\mathbb Z}^2$. 
    The first dynamics is the standard one on the full ${\mathbb Z}^2$, and denote by $A_f\subset {\mathbb Z}^2$ the set of vertices that are eventually occupied by $2$s in these dynamics. 
    For the second dynamics, we remove from ${\mathbb Z}^2$ all the vertices that are initially $0$s, then run the standard dynamics on the induced subset of ${\mathbb Z}^2$ and obtain the set $A_r$ of vertices that are eventually in state $2$. 
    Then $A_r\subset A_f$.

[Lemma 4 of arXiv:2604.17732, 'Exact Simulation from Tempered Stable Distributions with Infinite Variation ($\alpha\ge1$)'] 1. Let $p>2$, $a,b>0$, and 
$
m= \left(\frac{a}{bp}\right)^{1/(p-1)}.
$
If
$$
L(x) = ax- b x^{p}, \ \ x\ge0,
$$
then for $x\ge m$
$$
L(x) \le  L(m) - \frac{|L''(m)|}{2}(x-m)^2 
$$
where
$$
|L''(m)| =  bp(p-1)m^{p-2}.
$$
2. For any $t\ge0$ and $a,b>0$
\begin{eqnarray}
t^{a} e^{-bt}\le (a/b)^{a} e^{-a}.
\end{eqnarray}

body:
Let (T(t)) be a C_0-semigroup on a Banach space X satisfying the growth bound ||T(t)|| <= M exp(omega t). Then there is an EQUIVALENT norm on X, namely |||x||| = sup over t >= 0 of exp(-omega t) ||T(t) x||, in which the semigroup satisfies |||T(t) x||| <= exp(omega t) |||x||| - that is, the constant M is normalised away and the semigroup becomes a quasi-contraction. The new norm satisfies ||x|| <= |||x||| <= M ||x||, so it is equivalent and the generator, its domain and its spectrum are unchanged; only the operator NORMS and the numerical range move. This is the standard reduction that lets one prove results for contraction semigroups and transfer them to general ones.
The uniform growth bound with constants M and omega, which every C_0-semigroup has by the uniform boundedness principle.
The renorming changes the geometry of the space - the new norm need not be, for instance, a Hilbert norm even if the original was, so any argument relying on inner-product structure must be checked rather than assumed to survive.

[Proposition 7 (Convergence rate for L\'evy area) of arXiv:2512.04646, '\textbf{Canonical Rough Path over Tempered Fractional Brownian Motion: Existence, Construc'] Let $\mathbb{B}^{(N)}_{H,\lambda}$ be the piecewise linear
approximation of $\mathbb{B}_{H,\lambda}$ on a uniform partition of
$[0,T]$ with $N$ sub-intervals. For $H > 1/4$,
\begin{equation}

\mathbb{E}\bigl[|\mathbb{B}^{(N)}_{H,\lambda}(0,T)
  - \mathbb{B}_{H,\lambda}(0,T)|^2\bigr]^{1/2}
\le C(H,\lambda,T)\cdot N^{-2H},
\end{equation}
where
$C(H,\lambda,T) = \widetilde{C}(H)\cdot\max\{1,\lambda^{-2H}\}\cdot
T^{2H}$ with $\widetilde{C}(H)$ depending only on $H$. The rate
$N^{-2H}$ is optimal: no first-order piecewise linear scheme can
achieve a better rate.
title: Convergence rate for L\'evy area

[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2608.26490, 'Bayesian methods and Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms for curve reconstruction and poin'] For a fixed $n=1,\dots,N$, let $r_n$ be a random position generated according to the sampling scheme in \cref{eq:un,eq:sn,eq:pi,eq:L}. Then \cref{eq:rn} follows.
\begin{proof}
Given a geometry $G$, the position $r_n$ specifies and is specified by a global coordinate $v_n$ that equals the arc-length from $h^1$ along the curve $\mathcal{G}$ encoded by $G$. Consequently, it suffices to show that $v_n$ is uniformly distributed over $[0,L^G]$ where $L^G=\sum_{k=1}^K L_k^G$ is the total arc-length of $\mathcal{G}$.

Conditional on $s_n$ and $u_n$, such global coordinate $r_n$ is obtained deterministically by
\begin{align*}
v_n|s_n,u_n
&\sim\delta_{C^G_{s_n-1}+u_nL_{s_n}^G},
\end{align*}
where the cumulative segment lengths are defined by
\begin{align*}
C^G_0&=0,
\\
C^G_k&=\sum_{k'=1}^K L^G_{k'},
&
k&=1,\dots,K.
\end{align*}
According to the law of total probability, we obtain the marginal
\begin{align*}
p(v_n)
&=
\sum_{s_n=1}^K\int_0^1du_n\,
p(v_n|s_n,u_n)p(s_n,u_n),
\end{align*}
and, because of independence in \cref{eq:sn,eq:un}, we obtain
\begin{align*}
p(v_n)
&=
\sum_{s_n=1}^K\int_0^1du_n\,
p(v_n|s_n,u_n)p(s_n)p(u_n)
\\
&=
\sum_{s_n=1}^K\int_0^1du_n\,
\delta_{C^G_{s_n-1}+u_nL_{s_n}^G}(v_n)\pi_{s_n}^G
\\
&=
\sum_{s_n=1}^K\int_0^1du_n\,
\frac{1}{L_{s_n}^G}\delta_{u_n}\left(\frac{v_n-C^G_{s_n-1}}{L_{s_n}^G}\right)\frac{L_{s_n}^G}{L^G}
\\
&=\frac{1}{L^G}
\sum_{s_n=1}^K\int_0^1du_n\,
\delta_{u_n}\left(\frac{v_n-C^G_{s_n-1}}{L_{s_n}^G}\right)
\\
&=\frac{1}{L^G}
\end{align*}
indicating that, indeed, $v_n$ is uniformly distributed over $[0,L^G]$ which completes our proof. Here, the last equality holds because, from the $K$ different summands $\int_0^1du_n\,
\delta_{u_n}\left(\frac{v_n-C^G_{s_n-1}}{L_{s_n}^G}\right)$, only one integrates over the singularity.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition of arXiv:2609.00978, 'Towards Categorical K\"ahler Geometry'] Let $T\colon (V,\|\cdot\|)\to (W,\|\cdot\|)$ be a linear map between vector spaces with diagonalizable norms.
    \begin{enumerate}[(1)]
        \item Define an increasing $\bR$-filtration, $\cF^-(T)$, on $\operatorname{gr}V$ whose restriction to $(\operatorname{gr}V)_\alpha$ is 
        \[
        \left(\cF^-(T)_{\leq\beta}\right)_\alpha\coloneqq\left\{v\in (\operatorname{gr}V)_\alpha\mid\exists\text{ lift }\tilde{v}\in V:\|T\tilde{v}\|\leq e^{\alpha+\beta}\right\}.
        \]
        (Note the inequality can be written, for $v\neq 0$, as $\log(\|T\tilde v\|/\|\tilde v\|)\leq \beta$.)
        
        \item Define a decreasing $\bR$-filtration, $\cF^+(T)$, on $\operatorname{gr}W$ whose restriction to $(\operatorname{gr}W)_\alpha$ is 
        \[
     \left(\cF^+(T)_{\geq\beta}\right)_\alpha\coloneqq\left\{w\in (\operatorname{gr}W)_\alpha\mid\exists v\in V:Tv \text{ lifts }w,\|v\|\leq e^{\alpha-\beta}\right\}.
        \]
        (Note the inequality can be written, for $w\neq 0$, as $\log(\|Tv\|/\|v\|)\geq \beta$.)
        
        \item The \textbf{singular values}\footnote{They should really be called \textit{logarithms of singular values}, in analogy with the Archimedean case.} of $T$ are the numbers $\sigma_1\geq\ldots\geq \sigma_r$, $r=\operatorname{rk}T$, where the filtration $\cF^-(T)$ (equivalently: $\cF^+(T)$) jumps, where the multiplicity of the jump $\sigma_i$ in the descending list is  $\dim_\mathbf k\cF^-(T)_{\leq\sigma_i}/\cF^-(T)_{<\sigma_i}$.
    \end{enumerate}
title: Unnumbered definition of arXiv:2609.00978, 'Towards Categorical K\"ahler Geometry'

# A constant random-initialization bad-basin probability at fixed high noise

This composes the unaudited C17 entry and C18 unrestricted local trapping lemmas. It is a fixed-noise population result for a particular anisotropic three-component teacher. It neither refutes annealed learning nor settles the well-separated K=3 target. No novelty finding is asserted.

## Statement

Let d>=2, E^T E=I_2, A=diag(1,3), and use the teacher (1/3)sum_j N(a E A u_j,I_d), where u_j are unit equilateral vertices. Optimize the canonical equal-weight identity-covariance mixture score by physical Euclidean unit-step GD on the single-time population DDPM excess risk, with all entries of the d-by-3 initial mean matrix iid N(0,3a^2/(2d)). There is a fixed positive constant c_* such that taking a^2=c_* d^(-420) gives probability greater than 79/600 that the unrestricted trajectory converges to a strict non-global local minimum. Entry into its trapping neighborhood takes O(d^420 log d) steps. The convergence assertion is asymptotic; no finite-time identification rate is claimed here.

The statement depends on C06, C17 and C18 as analytic proof drafts, not independently checked theorems. In particular the original well-separated means need not resemble the small noisy means displayed here, and the statement is not a result about changing noise levels, empirical gradients, bit complexity or every random initialization.

## 1. Fix angular margins before the noise level

Set beta=acos(-61/128) and p=1-beta/pi. Since -61/128>-1/2 and acos is strictly decreasing on (-1,1), beta<2pi/3, hence p>1/3. Also beta>pi/2, so p<1/2. Set

    g=p-1/3>0, delta=pi*g/18.

C18's three bad sectors in each determinant branch have endpoints

    l_j=beta/3+2pi*j/3,
    r_j=(2pi-beta)/3+2pi*j/3, j=0,1,2.

Each width is 2pi*p/3. The chosen delta is less than one fourth of this width, so it is allowed in C18. Erode each sector by 3delta at each endpoint. Their total uniform angular measure, divided by 2pi, is

    3[(2pi*p/3)-6delta]/(2pi)
       =p-9delta/pi=(p+1/3)/2>1/3.              (1)

The intervals are disjoint modulo 2pi. Thus this measure calculation neither double-counts labels nor treats the three sectors as independent events.

## 2. Match all entry hypotheses simultaneously

Choose K in C18 large enough for C17's bound ||b_N||<=C_0 a^4. With this K and the fixed delta above, C18 supplies a fixed normal radius rho_T and smallness threshold a_T. The constants are independent of d.

Near the compact orbit {E A O:O in O(2)}, the polar chart is uniformly Lipschitz in Frobenius norm, independent of d: its planar part is a two-by-two positive-definite polar map, and its perpendicular part is a projection followed by a two-by-two rotation. Therefore factor distance at most rho implies

    ||c-c_*||+||Y||<=C_chart rho.               (2)

C17 also gives actual-to-surrogate polar angle distance at most C_phase rho at time N, with the same determinant branch. Choose a fixed entry tolerance 0<rho<=1/100 so that C_chart rho<rho_T/4 and C_phase rho<delta. Shrink rho further if necessary to stay within the uniform chart. Since cbar_a(theta)-c_*=O(a^2) uniformly in theta, sufficiently small a makes

    ||(c_N-cbar_a(theta_N),Y_N)||<rho_T.         (3)

The O(a^2) section displacement is explicitly included here; covariance-orbit distance alone is not the normal hypothesis in C18.

For this fixed rho, choose the absolute constant c in C17's prescription a^2=c rho exp(-84(S+1)), S=10log(8000 sqrt(d)/rho), small enough to enforce a<a_T, (3) and all its own assumptions for every d>=2. This prescription is exactly a^2=c_* d^(-420) with a fixed positive c_*. Consequently the constants and tolerances are chosen before d, and the polynomial exponent does not hide dimension dependence.

## 3. Conditional uniform phase, not independence

Let G be C17's joint good event: its right-invariant shape event together with ||b_0||<=10. It satisfies P(G)>=79/200. Conditional on G and either determinant branch, the C16 surrogate phase at the deterministic terminal time N gamma is uniform. The terminal time depends on d and fixed constants only, not on the random trajectory. Both determinant branches have positive conditional mass by the reflection symmetry of the Gaussian initialization and G.

Let A_good be the event that this surrogate phase lies in one of the three eroded sectors in Section 1. Formula (1) gives

    P(A_good | G, branch)=(p+1/3)/2>1/3.

Summing over the two branches gives exactly the same conditional probability given G. There is no factor one half: in the negative branch C18 uses a fixed reflection J that permutes the equilateral vertices, so R_theta J U=R_theta U Pi, and the same angular sectors apply by label symmetry. Nor is A_good asserted independent of G; its conditional probability is supplied by right-rotation invariance.

On G intersect A_good, the actual phase differs from the surrogate by less than delta. Its distance from each bad-sector endpoint is therefore greater than 2delta. Equations (3) and the centroid bound meet the remaining C18 hypotheses. C18 then gives convergence to that sector's strict bad minimum. Thus

    P(converges to a strict non-global minimum)
       >=P(G) P(A_good|G)
       >=(79/200)*(p+1/3)/2
       >79/600>1/8.                            (4)

This multiplication is the conditional-probability identity with an established conditional measure, not a product of unproved independent bounds. Component-label sectors and determinant branches have both been accounted for.

## Scope, checks and the unpaid target

Exact rational checks certify -61/128>-1/2 and 79/600>1/8; elementary algebra certifies the erosion formula (1). They do not validate C17's phase coupling or C18's analytic normal contraction. All those inputs and the present composition remain proof (unaudited), with no independent reviewer PASS.

The result explains a fixed-noise obstruction to the intermediate-noise route for this teacher. The noisy teacher here is not itself well separated when a is small. General Target 2 concerns efficient learning of well-separated components and may use a schedule; nothing here excludes that. The next unpaid step toward that target is to determine whether lowering the noise after this bad basin destabilizes it before one can claim either a scheduled failure or a successful escape route. Fix a sufficiently small $\lambda \in (0,1/3)$.

Let $E^+$ be a constant-escape process on $[j]$ with send sequence~$\overline{p}$, start time $\tau$, end-of-step arrival rate $\nu_j^\mathrm{lo}$, and $\overline{\mathrm{arr}}_{[j]}^{E^+}(\tau) = \overline{a}$. 
Let $d \ge 0$ be real, and suppose $\overline{a}$ satisfies (Con(item:Con1 of the paper)) for $d$.

body: [Theorem 3 of arXiv:2605.25323, 'Slow Convergence of Ising and Spin Glass Models with Well-Separated Frustrated Vertices'] Let $\Lambda\subset{\mathbb{Z}}^{2}$ be an $(2n+1)\times(2n+1)$ lattice region and $0\leq p\leq 1/2$ define a family of $p$ -shifted mixed boundary conditions on $\Lambda$. Let $\Omega$ be the set of all Ising configurations and let $\mathcal{C}$ be the Ising configurations containing a cross. NOVELTY: UNCHECKED (direct adapted-tail consequence of the conditional one-scale bound; no priority claim).
Status: proof (unaudited).

## Statement and scope

Assume the critical analytic inputs and nonempty window of notes/boundary_comb.tex. Let b>=2 be the integer scale multiplier and c>0 its deterministic one-scale constant. For two independent walks started at the backbone origin, let sigma_m be the first time either exits R_{b^m}((b^m)^(3/2)). Let C_T count backbone collision times from time 1 through T. Then in almost every environment,

    liminf_{m->infinity} C_{sigma_m}/log m >= c/log b, almost surely.

In particular the count is at least a positive multiple of log m along exit scales. This is a log log N lower bound when N=b^m. No almost-sure order log T, deterministic-time rate, or limiting coefficient is claimed. The inputs remain conditional, with the upstream caveats in UPSTREAM_CHECK.md.

## Adapted indicators

Fix an environment where Lemma B of the note holds. Beyond a finite deterministic index in this fixed environment, define I_m as the indicator of a backbone collision in [sigma_m,sigma_{m+1}). Let F_m be the pair filtration at sigma_m. Then I_m is F_{m+1}-measurable and

    E[I_m | F_m] >= a_m := c/(1+m log b).

The interval count includes the endpoint sigma_m, whereas C_T excludes time zero. Discard finitely many initial blocks so sigma_m>=1, and all remaining successful blocks yield distinct collision times counted by C_{sigma_{M+1}}.

## Lower-tail product

Fix a starting index M0 beyond that threshold. For lambda>0,

    E[exp(-lambda I_m) | F_m]
        =1-(1-exp(-lambda)) E[I_m | F_m]
        <=1-(1-exp(-lambda))a_m.

Iterated conditioning, using measurability of earlier indicators at F_m, gives for S_M=sum_{m=M0}^{M-1} I_m,

    E exp(-lambda S_M)
        <= product_{m=M0}^{M-1}[1-(1-exp(-lambda))a_m]
        <= exp(-(1-exp(-lambda)) H_M),

where H_M=sum_{m=M0}^{M-1}a_m. Markov's inequality therefore gives, for 0<theta<1,

    P(S_M <= theta H_M)
        <= exp(-[1-exp(-lambda)-lambda theta]H_M).

Choose lambda small enough that d:=1-exp(-lambda)-lambda theta>0; this is possible because (1-exp(-lambda))/lambda tends to one as lambda decreases to zero.

The harmonic sum satisfies H_M=(c/log b)log M+O(1), by comparison with the integral of c/(1+x log b). Hence the lower-tail probability is at most D M^(-d c/log b) for a fixed finite D in this fixed environment.

## Sparse subsequence and interpolation

Take M_j=ceil(exp(j)). The probabilities P(S_{M_j}<=theta H_{M_j}) are summable in j. The first Borel-Cantelli lemma, which needs no independence, implies that almost surely, eventually

    S_{M_j} > theta H_{M_j}.

For M_j<=M<M_{j+1}, monotonicity gives S_M>=S_{M_j}. Since log M<=log M_{j+1}=j+1+o(1) and H_{M_j}=(c/log b)(j+o(j)), it follows that

    liminf_{M->infinity} S_M/log M >= theta c/log b

almost surely. Intersect the probability-one events for a countable sequence of theta tending to one to obtain liminf S_M/log M>=c/log b.

Finally C_{sigma_M}>=S_M because each counted successful block is disjoint and ends by sigma_M. This proves the assertion.

## Limits

The finite-bounded-interval upper time for each successful collision does not itself give an upper bound on all exit times sigma_m. Thus replacing sigma_m by a deterministic power of b^m would require a separate quenched exit-time upper bound. and let \(g\) be the right-continuous inverse of \(h\), that is,
\[
g(\lambda):=\inf\{y\ge0 \mid h(y)>\lambda\}.
\]
Let \(Z^{(\alpha)}\) be the \(\alpha\)-stable subordinator characterized by
\[
E[e^{-qZ^{(\alpha)}_t}]=e^{-tq^\alpha}
\quad (q,t\ge0).
\]
Then the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \(\left(\frac{Y_{\lambda t}}{g(\lambda)}\right)_{t\ge0}
  \xrightarrow[\lambda\to\infty]{d}
  \bigl(c^{1/\alpha}Z^{(\alpha)}_t\bigr)_{t\ge0}\) on \(D([0,\infty),\bR)\).
  \item
  \(\nu(x,\infty)\sim c x^{-\alpha}K(x) \quad (x\to\infty)\).
  \item
  \(\psi(q)\sim c \Gamma(1-\alpha) q^\alpha K(1/q) \quad (q \to 0)\).
\end{enumerate}

body: Publication record. Y. Shmalo, Non-normal orbit quotients that are not normal quotients (October 2026), addresses Question 4.5 of Grimmett and Li, Self-avoiding walks and connective constants (arXiv:1704.05884): can a non-normal subgroup A of a transitive automorphism group of an infinite transitive graph G give a transitive orbit quotient G_A not isomorphic to G_N for any normal subgroup N of any transitive automorphism group, and does a free action of A matter? For every m >= 3 there is an infinite, connected, locally finite Cayley graph X whose automorphism group acts regularly, with a non-normal subgroup B acting freely, such that X_B is the complete graph K_m while no normal quotient of X is K_m. X is a graphical regular representation (Leemann and de la Salle) of F * F, with F = S_3 for m = 3 and F = A_m for m >= 4; B is the preimage of a point stabiliser under the projection onto the first factor. The quotient is finite; the infinite-quotient version and Question 4.6 are not addressed. Paper and code: https://github.com/yspennstate/nonnormal-orbit-quotients (commit b11def36f965). Not refereed.

 \frac{A_N(x)-L(N)}{\ell(N)}

 G_\lambda(x)
 =\log x+\int_0^x\frac{\e^{-\lambda u}-1}{u}\dd u.

body: A function holomorphic on an annulus 0 <= r < |z - c| < R has a Laurent series f(z) = sum over all integers n of a_n (z - c)^n, converging there; the coefficient a_{-1} is the residue of f at c. At an isolated singularity c the principal part (negative-index terms) classifies it: none => removable; finitely many, lowest index -m => pole of order m; infinitely many => essential singularity (near which f comes arbitrarily close to every value, Casorati-Weierstrass / Picard). The residue a_{-1} is what contour integrals of f pick up.
title: Laurent Series and Classification of Singularities

[Thm DL-infty of arXiv:2411.16376, 'Higher order approximations in arcsine laws for subordinators'] Let $\alpha\in(0,1)$. Let $X=(X_t)_{t\geq0}$ be a killed subordinator which is not identically zero. Then the following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label={\upshape (\arabic*)}]

\item The killing rate $a$ is zero, and the tail $\Pi((x,+\infty))$ of the L\'evy measure  is regularly varying at $+\infty$ with index $-\alpha$.

\item The Laplace exponent $\Phi:(0,+\infty)\to(0,+\infty)$ (restricted over $(0,+\infty)$) is regularly varying at $0+$ with index $\alpha$. 

\item	
$\displaystyle \lim_{s\to+\infty}\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}\bigg(\frac{X_{T(s)-}}{s} \leq t\bigg)=\frac{\sin(\pi\alpha)}{\pi}\int_0^t x^{-1+\alpha}(1-x)^{-\alpha}\,dx$ for any $0\leq t\leq 1$.

\item 
$\displaystyle \lim_{s\to+\infty} s^{-1}\ensuremath{\mathbb{E}}[X_{T(s)-}]=\alpha$.

\item The law of $tX_{1/\Phi(t)}$ converges weakly to a stable law with index $\alpha$, as $t\to0+$. 

\item The distribution function $U([0,x])$ of the potential measure  is regularly varying at $+\infty$ with index $\alpha$.  
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: long-range Dynkin--Lamperti theorem

body:
[Definition of arXiv:2411.13030, 'Classification of the limit shape for 1+1-dimensional FPP'] Let $G$ be non-deterministic and $B>t_{0}(G)$. For any edge $e$ of the lattice, we define the \emph{detour height} as the distance to an edge with small passage time:
\[
k_B(e):=\min\left (k\ge 1 | \,  \min( \tau(e+(0,k)),\tau(e-(0,k)))< B\right).
\]
The \emph{detour} of $e$ is the path that starts at one edge of $e$, goes $k_B(e)$ edges upwards or downwards, passes the horizontal edge with weight less than $B$ and goes $k_B(e)$ edges down back to the other endpoint of $e$. The \emph{detour time} $dt_B(e)$ is the passage time of the detour.
title: Unnumbered definition of arXiv:2411.13030, 'Classification of the limit shape for 1+1-dimensional FPP'

[Conjecture Conj: alpha_equals_d of arXiv:2608.00399, 'The Heavy-tailed Frog Model'] Let $d \ge 1$. Assume that $Q$ is a symmetric, translation-invariant, 
    heavy-tailed transition matrix on $\mathbb Z^d$ with exponent $\alpha = d$. 
    Consider the frog model on $\mathbb Z^d$ equipped with $Q$.
    For every particle density $\lambda > 0$ and particle lifespan 
    $\ell \in \mathbb N$, there exists $\theta = \theta(Q,\lambda,\ell) \in (0,1)$
    such that the following statement holds: for every $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$, 
    there exists $c = c(d,Q,\lambda,\ell,\varepsilon)>0$ such that
    \begin{align*}
        \mathbb P\left( \mathrm{AT}(o,x) \ge c |x|^\theta \right) 
        \ge 1-\varepsilon,
        \qquad \text{for all } x \in \mathbb Z^d .
    \end{align*}
    Moreover, if $\ell > \ell_c(\lambda,Q)$, then the same exponent $\theta$ 
    also satisfies the following statement: for every 
    $\varepsilon,\rho \in (0,1)$, there exists 
    $C = C(d,Q,\lambda,\ell,\varepsilon,\rho)>0$ such that, for all sufficiently 
    large $L$,
    \begin{align*}
        \mathbb P^+\left(
            \left|\mathcal{A}\left(C L^\theta\right) \cap B(L)\right|
            \ge \rho |B(L)|
        \right) 
        \ge 1-\varepsilon .
    \end{align*} (Stated as a conjecture by the paper; open unless the paper says otherwise.)
title: Conjecture Conj: alpha_equals_d of arXiv:2608.00399

For probability measures P and Q on one space, TV(P, Q) = sup_A |P(A) - Q(A)| and D = D(P || Q) is the Kullback-Leibler divergence in nats (+infinity unless P << Q). Then TV(P, Q) <= sqrt(1 - exp(-D)), and consequently 1 - TV(P, Q) >= 1 - sqrt(1 - exp(-D)) >= (1/2) exp(-D). Unlike Pinsker's bound sqrt(D/2), this never exceeds 1. In base-b units, exp(-D) = b^(-D_b). (J. Bretagnolle and C. Huber, 1979.)
P and Q are probability measures on one measurable space

[Lem 8 of arXiv:2609.00739, '2609.00739'] There are $h_0,C_{\rm cir}>0$, depending only on
$V,a_-,a_+$, such that, if $r\in[\frac{1}{2},1)$ and
\[
O(r):=\int_{\partial B_r}e_{\eps,a}(u)\le h_0,
\]
then some $\upsigma\in\Sigma$ satisfies
\[
\sup_{\partial B_r}\abs{u-\upsigma}\leq C_{\rm cir}\sqrt{O(r)}.
\]
Also, if $0\leq r_0<r_1\leq1$, some $r\in[r_0,r_1]$ satisfies
\[
O(r)\le \frac{\cE_{\eps,a}(u;B_{r_1}\backslash B_{r_0})}{r_1-r_0}.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lem 8 of arXiv:2609.00739

[Theorem thm:DJM of arXiv:2609.00794, 'On operators whose adjoints or second adjoints attain their norms'] {DJM}}] Let $X$ be a reflexive space and $Y$ be an arbitrary Banach space. Consider the following statements.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\itemsep0.25em
		\item $\mathcal{K}(X, Y) = \mathcal{L}(X,Y)$.
		\item $\operatorname{NA}(X, Y) = \mathcal{L}(X,Y)$.
		\item The unit ball $B_{\mathcal{K}(X,Y)}$ is SOT-closed.
		\item $(\mathcal{L}(X,Y), \tau_c)^* = (\mathcal{L}(X,Y), \|\cdot\|)^*$.
	\end{enumerate}
Then, the implications (a) $\Rightarrow$ (b) $\Rightarrow$ (c) and (a) $\Rightarrow$ (d) $\Rightarrow$ (c) hold. If, moreover, the pair $(X,Y)$ has the BCAP, then (c) $\Rightarrow$ (a) and hence the four statements are equivalent. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: Let X be a Banach space and T: X -> X a bounded linear operator with operator norm ||T|| < 1. Then the operator I - T is invertible, with bounded inverse given by the norm-convergent series (I-T)^{-1} = sum_{n=0}^infinity T^n, and ||(I-T)^{-1}|| <= 1/(1 - ||T||). [standard, e.g. Conway, A Course in Functional Analysis]

[Proposition 9 (Tiny Central Perturbations of Random Transpositions) of arXiv:2605.19084, 'Limit Profiles for Separation Distance'] Let $P_n$ be the random transpositions shuffle on $S_n$, let $C_n$ be any symmetric central random walk on $S_n$, and set $Q_n:=(1-\epsilon_n)P_n+\epsilon_n C_n$ with $\epsilon_n=O((n!)^{-1})$. Put $t_n(c):=\frac n2(\ln n+c)$. Then, for every fixed $c\in\mathbb R$,
$$\left|s_*^{Q_n}\left(t_n(c)\right)-s_*^{P_n}\left(t_n(c)\right)\right|\to0.$$
Consequently, $Q_n$ has separation limit profile $1-e^{-e^{-c}}$ at this scale. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Tiny Central Perturbations of Random Transpositions

[Lemm 12 (Subsequence trick) of arXiv:2608.19104, 'Record times for coverage thresholds and maximal spacings'] Suppose $(U_{n,k},(n,k) \in \N \times \N)$ is an array of random
variables on a common probability space such that $U_{n,k} $ is
nonincreasing in $n$ and nondecreasing in $k$, that is,
$U_{n+1,k} \leq U_{n,k} \leq U_{n,k+1} $ almost surely,
for all $(n,k) \in \N \times \N$. 

       
	Let $c > 0$,  $\eps >0$. Suppose
$
\Pr[n U_{n, \lfloor  \eps \log n \rfloor } > \log n] \leq
c n^{-\eps},
$
        for all but finitely many $n$.
	Let $k \in \mathbb N$.
Then with probability 1, $ \limsup_{n \to \infty} n U_{n,k} /\log n \leq 1$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Subsequence trick

Consider the setup in Section~(se:bubble_setup of the paper) with $(D,x_0,y_0) = (\delta\mathbf{D},-i\delta,i\delta)$. Let $E$ be the event that there exists a loop $\mathcal {L} \in \Gamma$ with $\mathrm{diam}(\mathcal {L}) \ge \delta^{1+a_1/2}$ and for $i=0$ or $i=2$ there exist $x',x,y,y' \in \eta_i \cap \mathcal {L}$ such that if $U$ denotes the region bounded between (the outer boundary of) $\mathcal {L}$ and the segment of $\eta_i$ from $x'$ to $y'$, then $(x,y) \in \intptsapproxbubble{U}{\epsilon}$ as in~(equation eq:intpts_bubble of the paper) and $U \subseteq B(0,\delta^{1+a_1})$ and $\metapproxacres{\epsilon}{U}{x}{y}{\Gamma} \ge \median{\epsilon}+\epsilon^{-a_0}\mathbf{a}_{\epsilon}$. Then $\mathbf{P}[E] = O(\delta^{{\alpha_{\mathrm{apr}}}})$ as $\delta\searrow 0$.

[Lemma 5 of arXiv:2609.03112, '2609.03112'] Let $M$ be a discrete set and let $\lambda_m>0$ for $m\in M$.  For
$\psi_1,\psi_2\in C_c^\infty(\R_{>0})$ define
\[
 S_{j,X}(u)=X^{-1/2}\sum_{m\in M}
 \psi_j\!\left(\frac{\lambda_m}{X}\right)
 \e\!\left(\frac u2\lambda_m\right).
\]
For $h\in C_c(\R)$ set
\[
 \widehat h(s)=\int_\R h(u)\e(us/2)\,du.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
 \int_\R S_{1,X}(u)\overline{S_{2,X}(u)}h(u)\,du
 =\frac1X\sum_{m,n\in M}
 \psi_1\!\left(\frac{\lambda_m}{X}\right)
 \psi_2\!\left(\frac{\lambda_n}{X}\right)
 \widehat h(\lambda_m-\lambda_n).
\end{equation}
If $\lambda_m$ is a positive quadratic polynomial on a lattice coset, the
left side of \eqref{eq:theta-pair-identity}, with $v=X^{-1}$, is a finite
linear combination of integrals of products of the form
$\Theta_f\overline{\Theta_{f'}}(g_\alpha n(u)a(v))$.

body:
[Corollary 2.9 of arXiv:2110.05374, 'When Janson meets McDiarmid: Bounded difference inequalities under graph-dependence'] Let f : Ω → R be c-Lipschitz and let the Ω-valued random vector X = (X_1, ..., X_n) be m-dependent for some m ≥ 1. Split [n] into consecutive blocks B_j := {k : (j−1)m + 1 ≤ k ≤ jm} for j ∈ [⌊n/m⌋] and, when m does not divide n, a last block B_{⌈n/m⌉} := [n] \ ∪_{j≤⌊n/m⌋} B_j. Then for every t > 0, P(f(X) − E[f(X)] ≥ t) ≤ exp(−2t² / (Σ_{i=1}^{⌈n/m⌉−1} (Σ_{j∈B_i∪B_{i+1}} c_j)² + min_{i∈[⌈n/m⌉]} (Σ_{j∈B_i} c_j)²)). The blocks form a path on ⌈n/m⌉ vertices, and Theorem 2.1 is applied to it with block coefficients Σ_{j∈B_i} c_j. The paper prints the first sum over i ∈ [⌊n/m⌋]: the same range when m does not divide n; when m divides n the path has n/m − 1 edges, as the paper's own Remark 2.10 uses. With all c_i = c the denominator is at most 4mnc², so P(f(X) − E[f(X)] ≥ t) ≤ exp(−t²/(2mnc²)) (Remark 2.10).
c-Lipschitz (Definition 1.1 of the paper): Ω = Ω_1 × ... × Ω_n is a product of Polish spaces, c = (c_1, ..., c_n) ∈ R_+^n, and f : Ω → R is c-Lipschitz when |f(x) − f(x')| ≤ Σ_{i=1}^n c_i 1{x_i ≠ x'_i} for all x, x' ∈ Ω (Lipschitz for the c-weighted Hamming distance).
m-dependence (Definition 2.8 of the paper): (X_j)_{j=1}^i and (X_j)_{j=i+m+1}^n are independent for every i.

[Definition def:nf of arXiv:2608.27771, 'A normal form for the Thin Flat Surfaces category'] Let $f \colon n \to m$ be a connected viewable tf-cobordism with interval cycles
$\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_p$, where $\lambda_k$ involves $a_k$ incoming and $a'_k$
outgoing intervals, genus $g \geq 0$, and $c \geq 0$ holes.  Fix an ordering of the
cycles as in Section~(sec:ordering of the paper).  The \emph{normal form} of $f$ is the
tf-cobordism
\begin{equation}

  \mathrm{NF}(f)
  \;:=\;
  \Gamma(c,\, g)
  \;\circ\;
  \bar\rho(f)
  \;\circ\;
  K_p\!\bigl(\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_p\bigr)
  \;\circ\;
  \bar\sigma(f).
\end{equation}
For a general (not necessarily connected) viewable tf-cobordism $f = f_1 \otimes
\cdots \otimes f_c$ decomposed into connected components, the normal form is the
monoidal product
\[
  \mathrm{NF}(f) \;:=\; \mathrm{NF}(f_1) \otimes \cdots \otimes \mathrm{NF}(f_c).
\]
title: Normal form of a connected viewable tf-cobordism

Let U be an open subset of C, f holomorphic on U, and let the closed disc {|z - z_0| <= r} lie in U. Then for every a with |a - z_0| < r, f(a) = (1 / (2 pi i)) integral over the positively oriented circle |z - z_0| = r of f(z) / (z - a) dz, and for every n >= 0, f^{(n)}(a) = (n! / (2 pi i)) integral of f(z) / (z - a)^{n+1} dz. In particular a holomorphic function is infinitely differentiable and analytic. General form: for a closed piecewise smooth curve gamma in U that is null-homotopic in U and a point a in U not on gamma, n(gamma, a) f(a) = (1 / (2 pi i)) integral over gamma of f(z) / (z - a) dz, where n(gamma, a) is the winding number.

By Cauchy's theorem applied to the region between the circle |z - z_0| = r and a small circle |z - a| = delta (homotopic in the punctured disc), the integral over the big circle equals the integral over the small one. On the small circle write f(z) = f(a) + (f(z) - f(a)); the first term contributes f(a) times the integral of dz / (z - a) over the small circle, which is 2 pi i, and the second contributes at most 2 pi delta times max_{|z - a| = delta} |f(z) - f(a)| / delta = 2 pi max |f(z) - f(a)|, which tends to zero as delta -> 0 by continuity of f. The derivative formulas follow by differentiating under the integral sign in a, which is justified because the integrand is smooth in a on compact subsets of the open disc; expanding 1 / (z - a) as a geometric series in (a - z_0) / (z - z_0) gives the power series of f at z_0, hence analyticity.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:7b09312016e49880ce80485d30f216c41aada6801fe2cca944c4c57a2fc6f66b","revision_digest":"sha256:d45357c73b98ace50fb639bc533288de76b3c4ad94ef56d32a9dee8de53055c8","source_id":"wikipedia:Cauchy's integral formula","source_revision":"statement authored 2026-08-29 replacing the lead read 2026-08-02","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":["claim_087aaf2dc7bb286230478e133428217d336c63a1fd1e20c844b129025baf7a73"],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

body: There are probability mass functions p and q on {1, 2, 3} and an event A with p(A), q(A) > 0 such that the conditional laws p(.|A) and q(.|A) are disjoint, so at total variation distance 1, while d_TV(p, q) = 1/2: take p = (1/2, 0, 1/2), q = (0, 1/2, 1/2) and A = {1, 2}. So disjoint conditional laws with p(A), q(A) > 0 do not imply d_TV(p, q) = 1; what holds is max(p(A), q(A)) <= d_TV(p, q) <= 1.

body:
[Theorem 11 (Dense-frequency separation) of arXiv:2609.01116, 'Vector-Carleson, Calder\'on, and Poisson--Atomic Criteria for\\ Generalized Hilbert Operat'] For every $2<p<\infty$ there is $\phi\in\Hol(\D)$ such that:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
 \item $T_\phi:H^p\to H^p$ is bounded but not compact;
 \item every sufficiently large hard dyadic block is active and contains
 a consecutive frequency interval of length $2^{j-1}$;
 \item $\operatorname{supp}\widehat\phi$ is not an analytic
 $\Lambda(p)$-set;
 \item
 \[
  2^{-j/p'}\|\Delta_j\phi\|_{H^p}=1
  \qquad(j\ge j_0).
  \tag{4.4}
 \]
\end{enumerate}
In particular, the symbol lies outside the known sufficient class defined
by
\[
 \bigl(2^{-j/p'}\|\Delta_j\phi\|_{H^p}\bigr)_j\in\ell^t,
 \tag{4.5}
\]
and it is neither lacunary nor spectrally thin.

body: [Theorem 3 (Estimating the number of communities) of arXiv:2411.02835, 'Community detection with the Bethe-Hessian'] Assume that the average degree satisfies d ≥2 and Assumption 1 holds. For any ε > 0 small enough, the following holds with high probability for sufficiently large n: Nε( √ d) = N( √ d + ε) = r+ and Nε(− √ d) = N(− √ d −ε) = r−. The above is also valid when taking ε = εn = log(n)−c for any c > 0.

Own work draft; proof (unaudited), route failure, no novelty claim. For k>=2, two one-hot tasks with distinct disjoint k-parity labels on uniform x in {-1,+1}^{2k} can have nonzero population-gradient inner product in a shared two-layer ReLU network. In f=a ReLU(sum_j x_j+2k-1-c0/4+c1/4), at a=0 the conditional half-squared-loss gradients have inner product 15/(16*2^(4k))>0. All preactivations are at least 3/4 from zero. The expectation is over conditional task inputs at a fixed network state; averaging a sign-symmetric random initialization is a different statement. This refutes support-separation alone, not the intended random-training theorem.

[Theorem thm:numerical-scaling of arXiv:2608.19050, 'Online Permutation Embedding: \\ Optimal Stopping and Scaling Laws'] The following limits exist:
\[
    c_- := \lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{\beta_k^-}{k^2}, \qquad c_\mathrm{typ}:=\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{\beta_k^\mathrm{typ}}{k^2},
    \qquad
    c_+:=\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{\beta_k^+}{k^2}.
\]
Moreover,
\[
    c_- < c_\mathrm{typ} < \frac12 < c_+.
\]
Quantitatively, 
\[
    \frac{1}{4} \le c_- \le 0.48867, \qquad 0.48934 \le c_\mathrm{typ} \le 0.49967,
    \qquad
    0.50547 \le c_+ \le 0.50568.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Scaling limits

body: In mathematics, the Banach fixed-point theorem is an important tool in the theory of metric spaces; it guarantees the existence and uniqueness of fixed points of certain self-maps of metric spaces and provides a constructive method to find those fixed points. It can be understood as an abstract formulation of Picard's method of successive approximations. The theorem is named after Stefan Banach (1892–1945) who first stated it in 1922.
title: Banach fixed-point theorem

[Prop betterfence of arXiv:2608.30031, 'Ziggurats, taut foliations, and contact structures'] Let $M_{\mathord{\scalebox{0.45}{$\square$}}}$ be a manifold with fences and windows, and let $\mathcal{F}_{\mathord{\scalebox{0.45}{$\square$}}}$ be a $C^0$-foliation on $M_{\mathord{\scalebox{0.45}{$\square$}}}$ adapted to $\partial M_{\mathord{\scalebox{0.45}{$\square$}}}$ and $\partial_{\mathord{\scalebox{0.45}{$\square$}}}$-transitive. Furthermore, let $\partial^\flat \mathcal{F}_{\mathord{\scalebox{0.45}{$\square$}}}$ (resp.~$\partial^\sharp \mathcal{F}_{\mathord{\scalebox{0.45}{$\square$}}}$) be an arbitrarily small $\flat$ (resp.~$\sharp$) window modification of $\partial \mathcal{F}_{\mathord{\scalebox{0.45}{$\square$}}}$.
    
    Then $\mathcal{F}_{\mathord{\scalebox{0.45}{$\square$}}}$ can be $C^0$-approximated by $C^0$-foliations on $M_{\mathord{\scalebox{0.45}{$\square$}}}$, still adapted to $\partial M_{\mathord{\scalebox{0.45}{$\square$}}}$, which are positively (resp.~negatively) transverse to foliations isotopic to $\partial^\flat \mathcal{F}_{\mathord{\scalebox{0.45}{$\square$}}}$ (resp.~$\partial^\sharp \mathcal{F}_{\mathord{\scalebox{0.45}{$\square$}}}$) along the facades in $\partial_* M_{\mathord{\scalebox{0.45}{$\square$}}}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Prop betterfence of arXiv:2608.30031

[Proposition 7 of arXiv:2605.02771, 'Universality in Deep Neural Networks:\\ An approach via the Lindeberg exchange principle'] Let $(\bX_i)_{i\in\N}$ be a sequence of independent random vectors in $\R^d$. We assume that, for all $i\in\N$, the coefficients of $\bX_i$ are i.i.d. with zero mean, variance $\sigma_i^2$ and absolute third moments equal to $m_3^{(i)}$. Also, let $(\bY_i)_{i\in\N}$, be a sequence of independent Gaussian vectors in $\R^d$, so that the coefficients of $\bY_i$ are all independent and have matching first and second moments to the corresponding coefficients of $\bX_i$. Finally, let $F \in C^3_b(\R^d;\R)$. Then
    \[
        \biggl|\E\biggl[F\biggl(\sum_{i=1}^n\bX_i\biggr)\biggr]-\E\biggl[F\biggl(\sum_{i=1}^n\bY_i\biggr)\biggr]\biggr|\lesssim C_F\cdot d^3\cdot\sum_{i=1}^nm_3^{(i)},
    \]
    where the implied constant depends only on universal constants and 
    \[
        C_F:=\max \left\{||\partial^3_{i,j,k}F||_{L^{\infty}(\R^d)} \, : i,j,k=1,\dots d \right\}.
    \] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition 7 of arXiv:2605.02771

[Proposition 34 (Collapse criterion) of arXiv:2608.31171, '\bf Finite-energy spacetimes with torus symmetry. \\ \Large Cauchy stability of Einstein--'] \bse
In the future-contracting case $[t_0,t_1]\subset(-\infty,0)$, the conformal length admits two (non-negative) lower bounds.
\bei
\item In terms of the scaled volume $\mathcal V_1$ defined in~\eqref{eq:section-8-volume-functionals}, below,
\bel{non-collapse-1}
\mathcal L(t) \geq \frac{|t_0/t|^{3/2}}{\mathcal V_1(t_0)} \mathcal V(t)^2 , \qquad t_0 \leq t \leq t_1 < 0 .
\ee

\item In a restricted time interval with end-point $t_2 = - |t_0|^{1/3} \bigl( |t_0| - \frac{3}{2} \mathcal L(t_0) / \mathcal E_\chi(t_0) \bigr)^{2/3} < 0$,
\bel{non-collapse-2}
\mathcal L(t)
\geq \frac{2}{3} |t_0| \mathcal E_\chi(t_0)
- \Bigl( \frac{2}{3} |t_0| \mathcal E_\chi(t_0) - \mathcal L(t_0) \Bigr) \Bigl|\frac{t_0}{t}\Bigr|^{3/2} ,
\qquad t_0 \leq t \leq \min(t_1,t_2) < 0 .
\ee
\eei
\ese (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 1 (Cyclotomic expansion for symmetric-power-colored $SU(n)$ invariants) of arXiv:2608.29585, '2608.29585'] For every zero-framed knot $K$ and every fixed $n\ge2$, there is a unique
sequence of Laurent polynomials
\[
 \bigl(H_k^{(n)}(K;q)\bigr)_{k\ge0},
 \qquad H_k^{(n)}(K;q)\in\Z[q^{\pm1}],
\]
such that, for all $r\ge0$,
\begin{equation}
 J_r^{SU(n)}(K;q)=\sum_{k=0}^{r}
 \left(\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}\{r-i\}\{r+n+i\}\right)H_k^{(n)}(K;q).
\end{equation}
Moreover, $H_0^{(n)}(K;q)=1$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Cyclotomic expansion for symmetric-power-colored $SU(n)$ invariants

[Lemma 18 of arXiv:2608.22534, 'Entropy power inequalities in compact groups'] Let $G$ be any locally compact abelian group. Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on $G$ that are absolutely continuous with respect to Haar measure, 
and such that $D(P\|Q)<\infty.$ For any $t\geq 0$, 
write $Q^t$ for the probability measure
    $$
    Q^t:= \frac{tQ+P}{1+t}.
    $$
    Then for any $T>0$:
    $$
    \int_0^T \chi^2(P\|Q^t)\,\frac{dt}{t(1+t)} = D(P\|Q) - \int\log{\Biggl(\frac{\frac{dP}{dQ} + T}{1+T}\Biggr)}\, dP. 
    $$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 18 of arXiv:2608.22534

[Proposition prop:degeneracy of arXiv:2608.16915, 'Exact mean--covariance dynamics of the Weber field in the stochastic Lagrangian representa'] In centre and separation variables $c=\tfrac{x+y}{2}$, $r=x-y$,
\[
  (\nabla_x+\nabla_y)^2=\Delta_c,\qquad
  u(x)\cdot\nabla_x+u(y)\cdot\nabla_y
  =\frac{u_++u_-}{2}\cdot\nabla_c+(u_+-u_-)\cdot\nabla_r,
\]
with $u_\pm=u(t,c\pm r/2)$. The diffusion therefore acts on the centre variable only;
there is no $\Delta_r$. In particular the model equation
$\partial_tH-\nu(\nabla_x+\nabla_y)^2H=0$ admits every bounded profile
$H(t,x,y)=h(x-y)$ as a stationary solution, so no estimate can extract regularity in

body: Godel's completeness theorem for first-order logic: for any first-order language L, any set T of L-sentences, and any L-sentence phi, T semantically entails phi (every model of T satisfies phi) if and only if phi is derivable from T in a standard proof calculus for first-order logic (Hilbert-style, natural deduction, or sequent calculus - all such standard calculi are both sound and complete). Equivalent model-existence form: every syntactically consistent first-order theory (one from which no contradiction is derivable) has a model; by the Henkin construction the model can be taken of cardinality at most the maximum of the cardinality of L and aleph_0. Soundness (derivable implies entailed) is the elementary converse direction. This theorem concerns first-order logic itself and does not conflict with Godel's incompleteness theorems, which concern the incompleteness of specific arithmetical theories, not of the logic.
title: Godel completeness theorem (statement)

The attribution window mismatch is the structural discrepancy in experimental logging where treated outcomes $Y(1)$ are attributed only within a short direct-response interaction window $W_T$ (e.g. within 2 hours of seeing the recommendation banner), while holdback/control outcomes $Y(0)$ are aggregated over a longer multi-day observation window $W_C$ (e.g. 7 days of organic consumption), making direct subtraction $Y^{W_T}(1) - Y^{W_C}(0)$ uncalibrated and biased.
W_T is the direct attribution window for treated units
W_C is the multi-day organic attribution window for holdback units
W_T \subsetneq W_C

[Definition def:weak_soln of arXiv:2609.01984, 'Instantaneous shrinking of supports for stochastic PDEs\footnote{JY was supported by a KIA'] For a nonnegative $\mathcal F_0$-measurable random initial function $u_0$, we say that
$u$ is a solution of (equation eq:SPDE of the paper) on $[0, T]$ with initial
function $u_0$ if $u$ is a $C_{\rm tem}(\mathbb{R})$-valued
process $u=u(t,\cdot)$, defined on $\Omega\times[0, T]$, such that for every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R})$:
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item
The process $\int_{\mathbb{R}}\varphi(x)u(t\wedge T,x)\,\mathrm{d} x$ is well-defined, $\mathcal F_t$-adapted, and continuous.

\item The process  $\int_{\mathbb{R}}|\sigma(u(t\wedge T,x))\varphi(x)|^2\,\mathrm{d} x$ is well-defined, $\mathcal F_t$-adapted, measurable in $(\omega,t)$, and
\[
\int_0^T\int_{\mathbb{R}}
|\sigma(u(t,x))\varphi(x)|^2\,\mathrm{d} x\,\mathrm{d} t
<\infty \quad \text{a.s.}
\]
\item
For all $0<t\le T$, 
\[
(u(t,\cdot),\varphi) = (u_0,\varphi)
+ \int_0^t (u(s,\cdot),( L^*\varphi)(s,\cdot))\,\mathrm{d} s  
+\int_0^t\int_{\mathbb{R}}
\sigma(u(s,x))\varphi(x)\xi(\mathrm{d} s,\mathrm{d} x) \quad \text{a.s.}
\]
Here $L^*$ is the adjoint operator of $L$ introduced in (equation second order operator of the paper), namely
$L^*\varphi = \partial_x^2(a\varphi) -\partial_x(b\varphi)+c\varphi$. 
\end{enumerate}
When the initial state is a nonnegative random Radon measure
$\mu_0$, we say that $u\in C((0,T];C_{\rm tem})$ is a solution of
(equation eq:SPDE of the paper) with initial measure $\mu_0$ if $u$ satisfies
(i)--(iii) with $(u_0,\varphi)$ replaced by
$\int_{\mathbb{R}}\varphi\,\mathrm{d}\mu_0$.

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Numerical test on random pairs of positive contractions, plus the diagonal and one-element cases in closed form. Result: Exact facts: for |E| = 1 the measure is Bernoulli(q) and Ent = h(q) is concave, so the conjecture holds; for commuting diagonal kernels the measure is a product and Ent = sum h(q_i), concave; for Q_2 = I - Q_1 the midpoint is I/2, whose entropy |E| log 2 is the maximum possible, so the inequality holds trivially. Numerical check (raw/C_lyons_conj26_entropy_check.json): 1440 random pairs of symmetric positive contractions in dimensions 2..6 with spectra in (0.02, 0.98), entropy computed exactly from P(A) = det(I-Q) det(J_A) with J = Q(I-Q)^{-1}; the concavity gap Ent(mid) - average was positive in every trial, minimum gap 8.5e-4 (dimension 2). No counterexample; the minimum gap being attained in dimension 2 suggests that a proof for 2x2 kernels, where the measure has four atoms with explicit determinants, would be the first non-trivial case to attempt analytically. Key identity: P_Q(A) = det(I-Q) det(J_A), J = Q(I-Q)^{-1}, gives an exact finite formula for the entropy. Check: Probabilities summed to 1 within 1e-8 in every trial and were non-negative. Obstruction: No analytic argument beyond diagonal kernels; the 2x2 case is the natural next target.

[Proposition 18 (Controlling discrepancy under synchronous coupling) of arXiv:2608.28827, 'Quantitative Target Convergence and Uniform-in-Time\\ Propagation of Chaos for Langevin-Re'] Under Assumptions~\ref{ass:core-target} and \ref{ass:concentration}, together
with either kernel assumption and under the synchronous coupling just described,
define
\begin{equation}
  D_N(t):=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N
    \|X_i^N(t)-\bar X_i(t)\|^2.
\end{equation}
There are constants $C<\infty$ and $L_{\mathrm{cpl}}>0$, independent of
$N,t$, such
that
\begin{equation}
  \E D_N(t)
  \le \frac{C}{N}\bigl(e^{L_{\mathrm{cpl}}t}-1\bigr),
  \qquad t\ge0.
\end{equation}

[Definition Generalized diagrams of arXiv:2506.06559, 'Bi-infinite incipient cluster in high dimensions'] For a set of diagrammatic graphs $\mathcal{G}$, we say that the \emph{generalized diagram of $\mathcal{G}$} is given by the product of 2-point functions
\[
\text{Diag}(\mathcal{G}):=\sum_{{\bf G}\in \mathcal{G}} \text{Diag}({\bf G}),
\]
which means it is the sum of diagrams appearing in $\mathcal{G}$ (which is a set of diagrammatic graphs).

In particular, if $\mathcal{G}$ is a generalized diagrammatic graph, and  $E\subset \bigcup_{{\bf G}\in \mathcal{G}} \mathcal{D}_{{\bf G}}$, then the BK inequality will imply that 
\[
{\bf P}[E]\leq {\bf P}\Bigl[ \bigcup_{{\bf G}\in \mathcal{G}} \mathcal{D}_{{\bf G}}\Bigr] \leq   \text{Diag}(\mathcal{G}).
\]

[Theorem thm:spectral-upper of arXiv:2606.27073, 'Retention Profiles and KL Contraction Bounds in Finite Markov Chains'] For a reversible chain with stationary distribution $\pi$,
\[
  I(X_0;X_1)
  =\sum_{x\in S}\pi(x)\,D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P(x,\cdot)\|\pi)
  \;\le\;\sum_{i=2}^n\lambda_i^2.
\]
Consequently,
\[
  \bar r_\pi\;\le\;
  \frac{\sum_{i=2}^n\lambda_i^2}{\log(1/\pi_{\max})},
\]
where $\pi_{\max}=\max_x\pi(x)$.
If $\pi$ is uniform, then
\[
  \bar r_\pi
  \;\le\;
  \frac{\sum_{i=2}^n\lambda_i^2}{\log n}
  \;\le\;
  \frac{(n-1)(1-\gamma)^2}{\log n}.
\]

body: [Definition 14 (Iterative directed hypergraph process) of arXiv:2608.07239, 'Unified framework for asymptotically uniform iterative construction of generalised random '] Consider the vertex set $V=\{v_1,\ldots,v_n\}$ with out- and in-degree sequences $\d^{(1)}=(d_1^{(1)},\ldots,d_n^{(1)})$ and $\d^{(2)}=(d_1^{(2)},\ldots,d_n^{(2)})$ of non-negative integers. Consider sequences $\d'^{(1)}=(d_1'^{(1)},\ldots,d_m'^{(1)})$ and $\d'^{(2)}=(d_1'^{(2)},\ldots,d_m'^{(2)})$ of positive integers with $s^{(i)}:=d_1^{(i)}+\ldots+d_n^{(i)}=d_1'^{(i)}+\ldots+d_m'^{(i)}>0$ for $i\in\{1,2\}$, and consider a set $X$ of forbidden hyperarcs. For $V':=\{v_1',\ldots,v_m'\}$, use the iterative edge-colored bipartite graph process to sample edge-disjoint simple bipartite graphs $(V\cup V',\widetilde{E}^{(i)})$ with degree sequences $\d^{(i)}$ and $\d'^{(i)}$ on its parts for $i\in\{1,2\}$. Apply rejection sampling to make sure that all vertices in $V'$ have distinct pairs of neighborhoods that are not in $X$. Finally, identify each such pair of neighborhoods with a hyperarc on $V$ to sample a simple directed hypergraph $(V,E)$ with out- and in-degree sequences $\d^{(1)}$ and $\d^{(2)}$ and with hyperarcs not in $X$ with orders $(d_1'^{(1)},d_1'^{(2)}),\ldots,(d_m'^{(1)},d_m'^{(2)})$.

body: [Theorem 12 (Theorem~3.6, Abbe--Boix-Adser, \cite{AbbeBoix2020}) of arXiv:2607.21392, 'Gaussian Convexity Principles for Sharp Moderate Deviations of Gaussian Maxima and Critica'] Consider a binary synchronization model on a finite graph \(\mathcal{G}=(V,E)\): the hidden vertex labels \((\theta_v)_{v\in V}\) are i.i.d. uniform on \(\{-1,+1\}\), and conditional on \(\theta\), the edge observations \((Y_e)_{e\in E}\) are generated by a symmetric graphical channel. Then, for every \(u,v\in V\), \[ I_2(\theta_u;\theta_v\mid Y) \le \mathbb P\bigl( u \leftrightarrow v \text{ in bond percolation on }\mathcal{G} \text{ with edge-open probabilities }(p_e)_{e\in E} \bigr), \] where $p_e=I_2(\theta_i;\theta_j\mid Y_e), e=\{i,j\}\in E. $ Here \(I_2\) denotes \(\chi^2\)-mutual information, and the bond percolation on \(\mathcal{G}\) is the independent percolation process in which each edge \(e\) is open with probability \(p_e\). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem~3.6, Abbe--Boix-Adser, \cite{AbbeBoix2020}

[Definition 28 of arXiv:2605.03851, 'The Relay Random Tree:\\A stochastic geometry approach of multihop relay in an urban visib'] \textbf{Visibility, relaying scheme.}

Let $\landsc$ be a landscape.

Let $(a_1, b_1)$ and $(a_2, b_2)$ be two buildings of $\landsc$. We say that $(a_2, b_2)$ is visible from $(a_1, b_1)$ if it is in range and there are no buildings above the segment from $(a_1, b_1)$ to $(a_2, b_2)$. In other words, if the following conjunction of events holds true:
\[\{(a_2, b_2)\text{ is in range from } (a_1, b_1)\} \cap \below{[a_1, a_2]}{(a_1, b_1)}{\frac{b_2-b_1}{a_2-a_1}}.\]

Thanks to this, we can define the relaying scheme $\tau$ as
\[\tau_{\mathrm{R}} (x, y, \landsc) = (x_b, y_b) := \underset{\substack{(a, b) \in \landsc\cap \mathrm{R}+(x, y) \\(a, b) \text{ visible from }(x, y)}}{\text{argmax}} \frac{b-y}{a-x}.\]
When this is well defined, and $\tau (x, y, \landsc) = (-\infty, -\infty)$ otherwise.

The blockage angle and its tangent are defined as usual in this context

body: [Lem smoothingfol of arXiv:2608.30031, 'Ziggurats, taut foliations, and contact structures'] Let $\Phi$ be a smooth nonsingular flow on $M$, and let $\mathcal{F}$ be a topological foliation on $M$ which is topologically transverse to $\Phi$. Then $\mathcal{F}$ is topologically isotopic to a $C^0$-foliation with smooth leaves, which is genuinely transverse to $\Phi$. Moreover, the isotopy can be made arbitrarily small, and along the flow lines of $\Phi$.

body: [Definition 11 of arXiv:2603.24616, 'Pinning in non-critical half-space geometric last passage percolation'] Suppose $b,y>0$. Let $\{\vec{W}_t\}_{t\ge 0}$ be a standard three-dimensional Brownian motion. The \textit{3D Bessel bridge} on $[0,b]$ to $y$ is the stochastic process $\{V_t = \lVert \vec{W}_t\rVert_2 : t\in[0,b]\}$ conditioned on $V_b = y$. (For a formal definition of this conditioning, see \cite[Section XI.3]{RY}.)
title: Definition 11 of arXiv:2603.24616

[Theorem 27 (Reduction lemma: reduced-group and path conjugacy) of arXiv:2607.26377, '\textbf{Entire Logarithmic Signatures\\ of Bounded-Variation Paths in Finite Dimensions}'] Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real normed space and let $\gamma:[0,T]\to V$ be a continuous tree-reduced bounded-variation path, translated so that $\gamma_0=0$. Set
\[
g=S(\gamma),\qquad v=S_1(\gamma)=\gamma_T\neq0.
\]
The following are equivalent.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
\item There is $a\in\Sl(V)$ such that $g=a\e^v a^{-1}$.
\item There is $t_0\in[0,T]$ such that, for $\beta=\gamma|_{[0,t_0]}$,
\[
\gamma\sim_{\mathrm{rep}}
\beta*\lambda_v*\overleftarrow{\beta}.
\]
\end{enumerate}
Under \textup{(a)}, let $p$ be the gate from $1$ to the axis in \cref{prop:axis-gate-decomposition}. One may choose $S(\beta)=p$, and this prefix signature is independent of the auxiliary Euclidean norm.

body: [Lemma le:a_priori_disc of arXiv:2507.15589, 'Tightness of approximations to metrics on non-simple conformal loop ensemble gaskets'] Fix $q>0$, $a_1 > 0$. Let $E$ denote the event that there exist $(x',x,y,y') \in \intptsapprox{\delta}{\epsilon}$ such that $U_{x',y'} \subseteq B(0,\delta^{1+a_1})$ and $\metapproxres{\epsilon}{U_{x',y'}}{x}{y}{\Gamma_\delta} \ge \quant{q}{\epsilon}$. Then $\mathbf{P}[E] = O(\delta^{{d_{{\mathrm{dbl}}}}})$ as $\delta\searrow 0$ (uniformly in $\epsilon$). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem prop:generators of kernel of action of MCG on Out(pi1) of arXiv:2609.00233, 'A survey on mapping class groups of 3-manifolds'] Let $M$ be a compact, orientable 3-manifold.
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item The kernel of $\rho$ is generated by the seven families of diffeomorphisms listed.
\item  The kernel of $\rho^+$ is generated by the families of diffeomorphisms (1)--(4).
\item If moreover $M$ is closed, then the kernel of $\rho$ is generated by the families of diffeomorphisms (1), (6), and (7).
\item If $M$ is closed, then the kernel of $\rho^+$ is generated by sphere twists as in (1).
\item If $M$ is closed, irreducible, and not equal to $S^3$ or $\mathbb{RP}^3$, then $\rho$ is injective.
\item If $M$ is closed and irreducible, then $\rho^+$ is injective.
\end{enumerate}
