Measured 2026-09-05 on the EMIT and OCO-2 stacking pools (70 cells, the pool protocol, full calibration, paired). Given that the long-only gain is the estimation variance the constraint removes at the rows the stack is scored on, the amount of constraint was chosen with the evaluation inputs: a blend w(t) between the simplex and least-squares stacks with t minimising the cross-validated calibration error plus the excess bootstrap variance of the blend at the evaluation rows over the calibration rows, and a per-row version t_i = 1/(1 + kappa v_i/median v) that leans to the simplex where least squares is uncertain. P24 (a) HELD: on EMIT the per-cell blend reads +0.08 vs the simplex and beats least squares on 39 of 40 cells; (b) HELD: on OCO-2 t* is at or above 0.5 on 30 of 30 cells and the blend reads +0.66 vs least squares; (c) REFUTED: the per-row blend vs the per-cell blend is +0.70 on Y2 and -0.14 on EMIT overall; falsifier (blend worse than the simplex by more than 1 on EMIT, or than least squares by more than 0.3 on OCO-2) not triggered. Fresh-split replication (P25, split C, SPLIT_SEED 11, the criterion uses no evaluation targets): P25 (a) HELD: on split C the EMIT blend reads +0.63 vs the simplex and beats least squares on 35 of 40 cells; (b) HELD: on OCO-2 the blend reads +0.84 vs the simplex (wins 30 of 30) and +0.65 vs least squares; (c) HELD: t* averages 0.34 on EMIT and 0.67 on OCO-2; falsifier (blend worse than the simplex by more than 1 on EMIT, or than least squares by more than 0.3 on OCO-2) not triggered. Bootstrap-size stability (P28, B = 16 against B = 8 on split B): P28 (a) HELD: t*(16) equals t*(8) on 86 pct of the 70 cells and is within 0.2 on 100 pct; (b) HELD: the blend's mean gain against the simplex moves from +0.08 to +0.06 on EMIT and from +0.83 to +0.83 on OCO-2, and the both-endpoints win count on OCO-2 is 30 of 30 at B = 16; falsifier (agreement below 50 pct or a gain moving by more than 0.5) not triggered. Break test: a fixed midpoint t = 0.5 matches the criterion on OCO-2 (+0.96 / +1.01 against +0.83 / +0.84 on the two splits) but loses 1.6 and 4.4 pct on EMIT where the criterion stays at +0.08 and +0.63 - the criterion's value is knowing, without labels, when not to leave the simplex; the EMIT shortfall against the hindsight-best t is the bias-shift term of the risk identity. Scarce calibration (P30, 240 of the calibration rows per cell, split B): P30 (a) HELD: at n = 240 the simplex beats least squares by +14.10 on EMIT (full calibration +8.83); (b) REFUTED: t* averages 0.22 on EMIT and the blend reads -2.61 vs the simplex; (c) HELD: on OCO-2 the blend beats both endpoints on 30 of 30 cells and the simplex reads +2.27 vs least squares (full calibration -0.18); falsifier (blend worse than the simplex by more than 1 on EMIT) TRIGGERED. The observable part of the bias shift (P31): adding t^2 (D_ev - D_cal), the shift in the two bases' mean squared disagreement between the evaluation and calibration rows, to the criterion - P31 (a) REFUTED: the R'-blend reads -0.71 vs the simplex on EMIT split B (R-blend +0.08) and +0.71 on split C (R-blend +0.63); (b) HELD: on OCO-2 the R'-blend is -0.11 vs the R-blend on split B and -0.12 on split C; (c) REFUTED: mean t** 0.39 against t* 0.33 on EMIT, share of the hindsight optimum 0.07 -> -0.62; falsifier (R'-blend worse than the R-blend by more than 0.3 on any corpus or split) TRIGGERED. Per-output mixing weights (P34, the criterion decoupled across outputs): P34 (a) REFUTED: the per-output blend reads -0.41 vs the per-cell blend on EMIT split B and -0.53 on split C; (b) HELD: on OCO-2 -0.02 and -0.08 on split C; (c) REFUTED: on Y2 the share of outputs at t_d = 0 is 0.20 and at t_d >= 0.5 is 0.34; falsifier (per-output worse than per-cell by more than 0.3 anywhere) TRIGGERED. A nearest-neighbour proxy for the bias shift (P35, the simplex's out-of-fold residuals at the nearest calibration rows standing in for its bias at the scored rows): P35 (a) REFUTED: the full-shift blend reads -0.69 vs the R-blend on EMIT split B and -0.12 on split C; (b) HELD: on OCO-2 -0.08 and -0.14 on split C; (c) REFUTED: cross-only vs full on EMIT -0.05 vs -0.62 (split B); falsifier (either variant worse than the R-blend by more than 0.3 anywhere) TRIGGERED. Scarce calibration, the ratio-metric criterion (P41, 240 calibration rows, split B, three-vertex form, registered and R_1 choices side by side): P41 (a) HELD: at n_cal = 240 the R_1 blend reads +1.17 vs the simplex on EMIT (within 1.0; the registered three-vertex blend reads -1.83); (b) HELD: on OCO-2 the R_1 blend beats both endpoints on 30 of 30 cells (at least 25); (c) HELD: R_1 vs the registered blend on EMIT +1.38 (at least +1.0); falsifier (R_1 worse than the simplex by more than 2.0 on EMIT) not triggered. So the P30 caveat is confined to the squared-loss criterion; the criterion in the score's own metric keeps the simplex where it should at scarce calibration. P44: the shipped tool against the driver (P44): P44 (a) REFUTED: the tool's mixing weight is within 0.2 of the driver's on 14 (squared) and 11 (ratio) of 14 cells; (b) HELD: the tool's blend scores within 1 pct of the driver's on 12 / 12 of 14; (c) HELD by the clause's wording (worse than both endpoints by more than 1 pct while the driver beats one: none); under the stricter test the analyzer was first written with (worse than the better endpoint by more than 1 pct): one cell, emit s102 Y3 (ratio); falsifier not triggered by the clause's wording, TRIGGERED under the stricter test.

body: Let X and Y be real-valued random variables. Then X is stochastically dominated by Y, meaning P(X > t) <= P(Y > t) for every real t, if and only if there exists a coupling of X and Y, that is, random variables X' and Y' defined on a common probability space with X' having the same distribution as X and Y' having the same distribution as Y, such that X' <= Y' almost surely. [Strassen (1965); Lindvall, Lectures on the Coupling Method]
title: Strassen's Theorem (Coupling Characterization of Stochastic Order)

body:
The Mitchison-Durbin decoder-independent first-moment bound: for a tree sign network with N=Kn total weights and P fair independent labels, Pr(storage)<=min(1,2^{-P} C(P,n)^K), where C(P,n)=2 sum_{j=0}^{min(n-1,P-1)} binom(P-1,j). For fixed K and a=P/N, the exponent on aK>2 is F_K(a)=aK log(aK)-(aK-1)log(aK-1)-a log 2. Its upper-envelope root b_K has b_1=2 and K h(1/(K b_K))=log 2 for K>1, with b_K~log(K)/log(2). This is prior work, not a sharp threshold or a new result.
K,n,P positive integers; N=Kn; K disjoint n-dimensional groups
Each hidden unit is homogeneous sign with nonzero spherical weights; Gaussian input samples, hence general position almost surely
Uniform independent labels independent of the inputs; fixed Boolean decoder and tie rules
First take N to infinity with K fixed; entropy-branch statement uses aK>2

[Lemma 37 (Symmetric feedback closes the primitive criterion) of arXiv:2608.12492, 'Weak Limits of Wiener Chaos: Primitive--Fock Classification and Hilbert--Stein Extraction'] Let $q\ge2$, $x\in H^{\odot q}$ and
$F=I_q(x/\sqrt{q!})$.  Put
$\kappa_4(F)=\E[F^4]-3\E[F^2]^2$.  Then
\begin{align}
 \kappa_4(F)
 &=\sum_{s=1}^{q-1}\binom qs^2\norm{x\otimes_sx}^2
 \notag\\
 &\quad+\sum_{s=1}^{q-1}\frac{q^2}{s^2}\,
 b_{q,q,s}\norm{x\wtensor_sx}^2.
 
\end{align}
If $\norm x\le R$, then
\begin{equation}
 |\kappa_4(F)|
 \le 3^{q+1}R^2
 \left(\sum_{s=1}^{q-1}
 b_{q,q,s}\norm{x\wtensor_sx}^2\right)^{1/2}.
 
\end{equation}
In fact the carré-du-champ defect and the fourth cumulant satisfy the
exact expansion and comparison
\begin{align}
 \kappa_4(F)
 &=3q\sum_{s=1}^{q-1}\frac{b_{q,q,s}}s
   \norm{x\wtensor_sx}^2,
 \\
 \frac1{3q}\kappa_4(F)
 &\le
 \Var\bigl(\Gamma(F,F)\bigr)
 \le\frac{q-1}{3q}\kappa_4(F).
 
\end{align}
Consequently, for a bounded family, vanishing of the symmetric feedback
on the right of \eqref{bridge:eq:kappa-from-symmetric-feedback} forces every
proper unsymmetrized self-contraction to vanish.

body:
[Theorem NEW-t:sysID of arXiv:2605.28430, 'Limit theory for Lipschitz-localized statistics in random geometric models'] For $d,d'\in\mathbb{N}$, $t_0\in(0,\infty)$, let $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}:=\{\delta_{(x, M(x),Z_x)}\}_{x\in\mathcal{P}}$ be a 
marked point process 
on $\mathbb{R}^d\times\mathbb{R}^{d'}\times\mathbb {M} $
such that   $Z_x\in\mathbb {M} ={\cal C}([0,t_0],\mathbb{R}^{d'})$ are i.i.d. standard Brownian motions on the interval $[0,t_0]$ in $\mathbb{R}^{d'}$, independent given the  marked point process $\{\delta_{(x, M(x))}\}_{x\in\mathcal{P}}$ of sites with initial conditions. We assume that  the initial conditions $M(x)$, $x\in\mathcal{P}$, are almost surely deterministically, uniformly bounded, i.e.,  $\sup_{x\in\mathcal{P}}|M(x)| \le L<\infty$.  
Moreover, we assume that the marked point process $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}$ has summable exponential $\mathbb{B} $-mixing correlations as in Definition (def.A2 of the paper) and has bounded reduced  Palm intensity function as in~(equation bdedreduced of the paper).
Consider a graph $\Psi(\mathcal{P})$ constructed deterministically on $\mathcal{P}$ 
which is fast stabilizing  with the interaction range 
satisfying ~(equation sdecayspin-infty of the paper).
Given Lipschitz diffusion coefficients $(b,\sigma)$ as in  Definition (NEW-d:lip_assum of the paper) consider the strong solution to the interacting diffusions system (equation NEW-e:sys_ID_V of the paper) on $\Psi(\mathcal{P})$, with initial conditions $M(x)$, realized by  individual paths $M^{\Psi(\mathcal{P})}[x]\in\mathbb {M} $ for points  $x\in\mathcal{P}$. Finally,
define the measures
\begin{equation}

\hat{\mu}_n^{\xi} := \sum_{x \in \mathcal{P} \cap W_n} \xi (\tilde{x},\tilde{\mathcal{P}})  \delta_{n^{-1/d}x},
\end{equation}
where $\xi =\xi^{(h, \Psi(\mathcal{P}))}$ are real-valued scores of the  individual paths $M^{\Psi(\mathcal{P})}[x]\in\mathbb {M} $  given by~(equation NEW-xisysID of the paper) with  a Lipschitz function $h : \mathbb {M}  \to \mathbb{R}$.

\begin{enumerate}[wide,label=(\roman*),  labelindent=0pt]
\item  If 
the  score $\xi$ in (equation NEW-xisysID of the paper) satisfies the $p$-moment condition~(equation NEW-momh1 of the paper) for all  $p \in (1, \infty)$, then the random measures $(\hat{\mu}_n^{ \xi})_{ n \in \mathbb{N}}$  at (equation NEW-SysID of the paper) satisfy the central limit theorem,  i.e., for  $f \in \mathbb{B} (W_1)$ such that ${\rm Var}{\hat{\mu}_{n}^{\xi}(f)} = \Omega(n^{\nu})$ for some $\nu > 0$, we have

\[ ({\rm Var}{\hat{\mu}_{n}^{\xi}(f)})^{-1/2}(\hat{\mu}_{n}^{\xi}(f) - \mathbb {E} \hat{\mu}_{n}^{\xi}(f)) \stackrel{d}{\Rightarrow} Z. \]

\item  If the input process $\{\delta_{(x,M(x))}\}_{x \in \mathcal{P}}$ is stationary and the graph construction $\Psi(\mathcal{P})$ is translation invariant, then the mean asymptotics can be expressed for all $f \in \mathbb{B} (W_1)$ as:
\begin{align}
 \Big| n^{-1} \mathbb{E}  \hat{\mu}_n^{\xi}(f) -  \rho \mathbb{E} _{\0} \xi(\tilde\0, \tilde{\mathcal{P}}) \int_{W_1}f(x)\,\mathrm{d} x\Big| = O(n^{-1/d}), 
\end{align}
whereas under an extra $p=(2+\epsilon)$-moment condition, for some $\epsilon>0$,  the variance asymptotics  can be expressed as
 \begin{align}
 & \lim_{n \to \infty} n^{-1} {\rm Var} \,\hat{\mu}_n^{\xi}(f) =  \sigma^2(\xi) \int_{W_1} f(x)^2 \,\mathrm{d} x \in [0,\infty),
\end{align}
where 
\begin{align}
 \sigma^2(\xi) & :=
\rho\mathbb {E} _{\0}\xi^2(\tilde{\0},\tilde{\mathcal{P}})   \\

body: [Lemma lem:sle4_cm of arXiv:2609.04140, 'The conformally invariant metric on $\CLE_4$ III:\\ uniqueness'] Let $x, y \in (-\infty, 0)$ and $z \in (0, 1)$ be random points. Suppose that, conditionally on $z$, the law of the pair $(x,y)$ is absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure on $(-\infty,0)^2$. Given $x$, $y$, and $z$, let $\eta$ be a chordal SLE$_4$ curve in $\BH$ from $x$ to $y$. Then the law of the conformal modulus of the conformal rectangle $(\BH \setminus \eta; 0, z, 1, \infty)$ is absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 30 (Compact-group variance inequality) of arXiv:2608.17374, '\textbf{On the Pseudo-Mixing of Kac's Walk}'] Let $G$ be a compact Lie group, let $\mu$ be Haar probability measure on $G$, and let
$U$ be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space. Let
\[
\rho:G\to \End(U_\C)
\]
be the complexification of an orthogonal representation of $G$ on $U$.
For $T\in \End(U_\C)$ define
\[
\Phi(T)(g):=\langle T,\rho(g)\rangle_{\HS},
\qquad
\Psi(T):=\Phi(T)-\int_G \Phi(T)(h)\,d\mu(h).
\]
Let
\[
\mathcal C:=\{T\in \End(U_\C): \Phi(T)\text{ is constant on }G\}.
\]
Then
\[
\|\Psi(T)\|_{L^2(G,\mu)}^2
\ge
\frac{1}{\dim U}\,\| \mathrm{Proj}_{\mathcal C^\perp}T\|_{\HS}^2.
\]

[Definition 7 of arXiv:2606.15843, 'Long-time behaviour of DLRA for SDEs'] A probability measure $\pi^*$ on $V_r(\bb R^d)\times \bb R^r$ is called invariant probability measure of a process $(U_t,Y_t)_{t\ge 0}$, if $\al P^*_t \pi^* = \pi^*$ for all $t > 0$. Equivalently, for every bounded measurable functions $f:V_r(\bb R^d)\times \bb R^r\to\bb R$ satisfies 
			$$\pi^*(f)=  \pi^*\big( f(U_t,Y_t)\big) ,\quad \forall\,  t> 0,$$
        where $$\pi^*(f):=\int_{V_r(\bb R^d)\times \bb R^r} f(u,y)\,\pi^*(\rrm du,\rrm dy)$$ and $$\pi^*\big( f(U_t,Y_t)\big):=\bb E[f(U_t,Y_t)],$$ with $\scr L_{(U_0,Y_0)}=\pi^*$.

[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] Heat diffusion in $\mathbb R^N$ is described by the heat equation
$$\dot{\varphi}=\alpha\Delta\varphi$$
where $\alpha>0$ is the thermal diffusivity of the medium, and with $\Delta$ given by
$$\Delta\varphi=\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{d^2\varphi}{dx_i^2}$$
being the Laplace operator, playing the role of a numeric second derivative.

body: [Proposition 13 (Rotation flattens \citep{suresh2017dme,chee2023quip,tseng2024quipsharp}) of arXiv:2608.25188, 'Transforms for LLM Quantization:\\ The Great Inversion and Format Co-Design'] Let $R$ be either Haar-distributed on the orthogonal group or a randomized Hadamard $R=HD$ with $D$ a diagonal of random signs (a \emph{deterministic} Hadamard does not give the guarantee for an arbitrary $w$; nor does an arbitrary random orthogonal $R$, for instance a random signed permutation, which leaves the crest factor untouched). Then for fixed $w$, the entries of $Rw$ are identically distributed and individually sub-Gaussian with proxy variance $\|w\|_2^2/d$ (dependent, not independent; the union bound needs only the marginals), so by \Cref{lem:subg} the expected crest factor of $Rw$ is at most $\sqrt{2\ln(2d)}=O(\sqrt{\log d})$ regardless of the outlier structure of $w$. A worst-case coherent $w$ (mass on one coordinate, $\mathrm{CF}=\sqrt d$) is thereby reduced to $\mathrm{CF}=O(\sqrt{\log d})$: a reduction by a factor of at least $\sqrt{d/(2\ln 2d)}$ in expectation.

[Lemma 5 (Monotonicity of the isoperimetric ratio) of arXiv:2608.26619, 'Uniqueness of Positively Curved Ancient Ricci Flows on Surfaces with Boundary'] Given a metric $(\old,\partial\bD ,g)$, define the isoperimetric ratio
    $$I(g) := \frac{L(\partial \bD,g)^2}{A(\old,g)}.$$
    Let $\{g(t) = u(\psi,t)g_0\}_{t\in [t_0,t_1]}$ be a positively curved rotationally symmetric solution to (\ref{2DRF}) with the initial condition $\partial_\psi u(\cdot,t_0),\; \partial_\psi R(\cdot,t_0) \geq 0$. Then we have
    $$\frac{d}{dt}I(g(t)) \leq 0,\; \forall t\in (t_0,t_1).$$
title: Monotonicity of the isoperimetric ratio

[Lemme 76 (Chernoff bound) of arXiv:2604.00635, 'Large deviations of the periodic Toda chain'] Let $\{X_i\}_{i=1}^{n-1}$ be a collection of $n-1$ random uniformly distributed iid variables on $\intff{0}{1}$. Then, for any  $\xi \geq 1$,

[Lemma stabilitylemma of arXiv:2606.24304, 'Quantitative Homogenization of PDEs with Neumann boundary conditions: a probabilistic appr'] Suppose that  $F$ is uniformly Lipschitz continuous, that is, there exists a constant $L>0$ such that for any $s \in [0, T]$, 
$v_1, v_2\in\mathbb{R}^m, ~z_1, z_2\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$,
$$
        |F(s, v_1, z_1) - F(s, v_2, z_2)| \leqslant L(|v_1 - v_2| + |z_1 - z_2|) 
        \quad \hbox{a.s.}.
 $$
Then the BSDE (equation stabililyBSDE of the paper) has a unique solution $(V, Z)$ and it satisfies that for every $s\in[0,T]$,
\begin{equation}
   \mathbb{E} \left[|V_s|^2 + \int_s^T |Z_r|^2 dr \right]\leqslant C_T\left[\mathbb{E} [ |\xi|^2 ] +\sup_{t\in[s,T]}\mathbb{E}\left|\int_t^TF(r,0,0) dr\right|^2dt\right].
\end{equation}
title: Lemma stabilitylemma of arXiv:2606.24304

body: In mathematics, Farkas' lemma is a solvability theorem for a finite system of linear inequalities. It was originally proven by the Hungarian mathematician Gyula Farkas. Farkas' lemma is the key result underpinning the linear programming duality and has played a central role in the development of mathematical optimization. Remarkably, in the area of the foundations of quantum theory, the lemma also underlies the complete set of Bell inequalities in the form of necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of a local hidden-variable theory, given data from any specific set of measurements.
title: Farkas' lemma

[Theorem 1 (Number of visited points) of arXiv:2606.11271, '\LARGE The $K$-th nearest neighbor random walk on a Poisson point process gets trapped'] Let $d \geq 1$ and suppose that Assumption (BS) is satisfied. Then there exist two constants $C_1, C_2 \in (0,+\infty)$ depending\footnote{In fact we obtain constants depending more precisely on $d$, $M$ and $\mu (\{M\})$.} on the dimension $d$ and on the probability distribution $\mu$ such that, for any integer $k \geq 1$,
$$
\P \big[ |\V| \geq k \big] \leq C_1 e^{-C_2 k} ~.
$$

Then
\[
        \rho_ns_nT_n\Rightarrow \Exp(1),
\]
and, for every fixed integer $r\ge1$,
\[
        \Ebb(\rho_ns_nT_n)^r\longrightarrow r!.
\]

If $\lambda>0$, assume additionally that

body:
[Lemma 24 (Discrete local sewing) of arXiv:2609.01190, 'Rough differential equations on manifolds via natural bundles'] Let $\theta\in (0,1)$ and let $\Pcal=\{S = U_0<U_1<\ldots<U_N = T\}$ (with $N\in\Nsf$, $N\geq 2$) be a partition of the interval $[S,T]$ satisfying the following condition:
	\begin{enumerate}[label=($P_\theta$)]
	\item
		Whenever $s,t\in\llbracket 0,N\rrbracket$ satisfy $\llbracket s+1,t-1\rrbracket\neq \emptyset$, there exists $u\in\llbracket s+1,t-1\rrbracket$ such that 
            \[
                \omega_{s,u}\leq \theta \omega_{s,t}.
            \]
	\end{enumerate}
Let $K:\Delta\Pcal\to\Rsf^m$ be a function and denote 
	\[
		K_{s,t}:=K(U_s,U_t), \quad (s,t)\in\Delta\llbracket 0,N\rrbracket.
	\]
Assume that the following condition is satisfied:
	\begin{enumerate}[label=($K$)]
	\item
		It holds that $K_{s,s}=0$ for all $s\in\llbracket 0,N\rrbracket$ and $K_{s,s+1}=0$ for all $s\in \llbracket 0,N-1\rrbracket$. Additionally, there exist $C,M\in (0,\infty)$ such that the estimate
	\[
		| K_{s,t} - K_{s,u} - K_{u,t}| \leq C |K_{s,u}|\,\omega_{u,t}^\frac{1}{p} + M\omega_{s,t}^\frac{3}{p}
	\]
holds for every $(s,u,t)\in\llbracket 0,N\rrbracket^3$ satisfying $s\leq u\leq t$ and $\omega_{s,t}\leq 1$.
	\end{enumerate}
Then there exist $\delta \in (0,1)$ and $L\in (0,\infty)$ such that the estimate
	\[
		|K_{s,t}| \leq L M \omega_{s,t}^\frac{3}{p}
	\]
holds for every $s,t\in\Delta\llbracket 0,N\rrbracket$ satisfying $\omega_{s,t}<\delta$. Constant $\delta$ depends only on $p$, $\theta$, and $C$ while constant $L$ depends only on $\theta$ and $p$.

[Proposition prop:stealthiness-criterion of arXiv:2607.25616, 'Stealthy point processes and lattice induction'] Let $(P_z)_{z\in Z}$ be a Borel $\Gamma$-equivariant uniformly

Moreover, for every $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ satisfying
\[
    \operatorname{supp}\widehat f\subset\Omega,
\]
one has
\[
    N_f^{Y_P}(x)
    =
    \rho\int_{\mathbb R^d}f\,d\lambda_d
\]
for $\mu_{\Gamma,Z}$-almost every $x$. Consequently,
\[
    \sigma_{Y_P,\mu_{\Gamma,Z}}(\Omega)=0.
\]
In particular, the cross-section system is stealthy.

body:
[Definition of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] Associated to any real probability measure $\mu=\mu_f$ is the following modification of the logarithm of the Fourier transform $F_\mu(\xi)=E(e^{i\xi f})$,
$$K_\mu(\xi)=\log E(e^{\xi f})$$
called cumulant-generating function. The Taylor coefficients $k_n(\mu)$ of this series, given by
$$K_\mu(\xi)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty k_n(\mu)\,\frac{\xi^n}{n!}$$
are called cumulants of the measure $\mu$. We also use the notations $k_f,K_f$ for these cumulants and their generating series, where $f$ is a variable following the law $\mu$.

[campaign result 2026-09-14, author checked; the criterion reproduces the source's worked example, and every algebraic step was confirmed symbolically] Problem 3.3 of Takahiro Hasebe and Yuki Ueda's Large time unimodality for classical and free Brownian motions with initial distributions, ALEA 15 (2018), 353-374, DOI:10.30757/ALEA.v15-15 (arXiv:1710.08240), asks for the optimal universal C>0 such that mu boxplus S(0,t) is unimodal for every t>=C D_mu^2 and every compactly supported probability measure mu. Here D_mu=sup{|x-y|: x,y in supp(mu)}, S(0,t) is the centered semicircle law of variance t, and boxplus is additive free convolution. The source proves C<=4. The record answers C=1. Sufficiency is the proved bound that mu boxplus S(0,t) is unimodal for all t>=D_mu^2. Optimality is the source's Example 2.1: mu=(delta_{-1}+delta_1)/2, with D_mu=2, is not unimodal for any t<4=D_mu^2. Let t*(mu) be the least t_0 such that mu boxplus S(0,t) is unimodal for every t>=t_0. Then t*(mu)<=D_mu^2, and equality holds for every symmetric two-point law (equal weights at two points) by Example 2.1 and scaling. The record further claims (Corollary) that equality holds only for symmetric two-point laws. That direction rests on the record's unproved assertion that t*(mu)=D_mu^2 requires a separating local minimum of value exactly 1/D_mu^2, a limiting step not written out. It is retained here as a claim, not certified. This is an unrefereed campaign result.
D_mu>0.
This concept records the endpoint and threshold-rigidity claims without certifying missing limiting steps.

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Reduce to the stabilisability threshold and examine the known bounds. Result: By Fey-Meester-Redig, an i.i.d. sandpile on Z^d stabilises (finitely many topplings per site) if the mean density is below a threshold rho_s and explodes if above rho_c... the known facts: density < 1 (in units where the threshold height is 2d = 4) is not sufficient... on Z^2 the results are: if E s < 2d - 1 = 3?? I recall: on Z^d, i.i.d. sandpiles with density rho < d stabilise? and with rho > 2d - 1 explode; the exact threshold for i.i.d. Bernoulli-type laws is unknown and is believed to depend on the whole law, not only on the mean (Fey-Levine-Peres 'Growth rates and explosions'). The decidability question is whether the 0-1 value is a computable function of the five probabilities; since the event is a tail-type event of an i.i.d. field decided by an infinite dynamics, computability is not automatic (the source's remark). An approach: the event 'every site topples infinitely often' is equivalent to the divisible-sandpile-type criterion of the odometer being infinite, and for i.i.d. initial data with density rho the least-action principle gives that stabilisation holds iff there exists a stabilising toppling function, which is a monotone property; monotonicity in the law (stochastic order) gives a threshold structure along stochastically ordered families, but the threshold depends on more than the mean. I could not produce an algorithm; a natural decidable sufficient condition is: if s is a.s. a stable configuration plus a finite perturbation the answer is 0, and if E s > 2d - 1 the answer is 1 (explosion) by the FLP growth-rate results; the undecided region is between. Recorded with the two rigorous outer bounds. Key identity: Explosion if E s > 2d - 1 (FLP growth rates); no explosion for laws supported on {0,...,2d-1} minus finite perturbations; the middle region is the question. Obstruction: Dependence of the stabilisability threshold on the full law, not a computable functional so far.

[Lem exists_ldash of arXiv:2609.01458, 'Confluence relations for $q$-analogues of multiple zeta values'] Let $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $u\in\mathcal{F}^{n}$.
Let 
\[
\operatorname{Std}(u)=(u_{0},u_{1},\dots,u_{l})
\]
be the standard path from $u(z)$ to $u(zq)$. Then there exists $0\leq l'\leq l$
such that
\[
u_{1},\dots,u_{l'}\in\mathcal{F}^{n}\qquad\text{and}\qquad u_{l'},\dots,u_{l}\in\mathcal{F}^{n+1}.
\]
In other words, if $u_{i}\notin\mathcal{F}^{n+1}$ and $u_{i'}\notin\mathcal{F}^{n}$,
then $i+1<i'$.

body:
[Defini 13 of arXiv:2608.27934, 'An example of biquandle and an invariant of long virtual knots defined through it'] Let $\mathcal{EO}$ be a set of long virtual knots each of which admits a long virtual knot diagram without EU crossings. 
For a long virtual knot diagram $D$, set ${\rm EO}(D)$ to be a long virtual knot diagram obtained by performing crossing changes at each EU crossing. 
It can be checked that ${\rm EO}(D)$ and ${\rm EO}(D')$ are related by generalized Reidemeister moves if two long virtual knot diagrams $D$ and $D'$ are related by generalized Reidemeister moves. 
Thus we can define ${\rm EO}(K) \in \mathcal{EO}$ for a long virtual knot $K$ as the long virtual knot represented by ${\rm EO}(D)$, where $D$ is a long virtual knot diagram representing $K$. 
This ${\rm EO}$ is a projection from the set of long virtual knots to $\mathcal{EO}$. 
Moreover, this ${\rm EO}$ preserves the products. In other words, ${\rm EO}(K_{1} \cdot K_{2})={\rm EO}(K_{1})\cdot {\rm EO}(K_{2})$ holds for long virtual knots $K_{1}$ and $K_{2}$.
title: Definition 13 of arXiv:2608.27934

[Definition Olas5d of arXiv:2603.12774, 'Synchronization by noise for stochastic differential equations driven by fractional Browni'] Let \(\mathcal{X}\) be a Polish space equipped with its Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\sigma(\mathcal{X})\).  
	An {(ergodic) measurable random dynamical system} on \((\mathcal{X}, \sigma(\mathcal{X}))\) consists of an (ergodic) measurable metric dynamical system \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P}, \theta)\) together with a measurable function
	\[
	\Phi : \mathbb{R}^+ \times \mathcal{X} \times \Omega \to \mathcal{X},
	\]
	satisfying the {cocycle property}.  
	More specifically, for each \((t, x, \omega) \in \mathbb{R}^+ \times \mathcal{X} \times \Omega\), set \(\Phi^t_\omega(x) := \Phi(t,x,\omega)\).  
	Then the following conditions hold:
	\[
	\Phi^0_\omega = \operatorname{Id}_{\mathcal{X}} \quad \text{for all } \omega \in \Omega,
	\]
	and
	\[
	\Phi^{t+s}_\omega(x) = \Phi^s_{\theta_t \omega}\big(\Phi^t_\omega(x)\big),
	\]
	for all \(s, t \in \mathbb{R}^+\), \(x \in \mathcal{X}\), and \(\omega \in \Omega\).  
	The function \(\Phi\) is called a \emph{cocycle}.  
	Given the condition that, for each \(\omega \in \Omega\), the map \((t, x) \mapsto \Phi(t, x, \omega)\) is continuous, the function \(\Phi\) is called a {continuous random dynamical system}.  
	Moreover, for \(k \geq 1\), we call \(\Phi\) a {\(C^k\)-random dynamical system} if for every \(t \geq 0\) and \(\omega \in \Omega\), the function
	\[
	x \mapsto \Phi^t_\omega(x)
	\]
	is \(C^k\)-Fr\'{e}chet differentiable.
title: Definition Olas5d of arXiv:2603.12774

[Theorem 9 (Boundary of the limit distribution) of arXiv:2606.07290, 'Boundary behaviour of the Volterra square-root process'] Assume that the Volterra square-root process is subcritical. Then the limit distribution $\pi_{x_0}$ satisfies the following:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[(a)] Suppose that $K \in C^1(\R_+)$. Then for each $0 < p < \gamma_-(\infty)$
        \[
            \frac{1}{\theta(\infty)^{p}} \frac{\Gamma( \gamma_+(\infty) - p)}{\Gamma(\gamma_+(\infty))} \leq \int_{\R_+} x^{-p}\, \pi_{x_0}(\mathrm{d}x) \leq \frac{\Gamma(\gamma_{-}(\infty) - p)}{\Gamma(\gamma_{-}(\infty))} \frac{1}{\theta(\infty)^{p}}.
        \]
        where 
        \[
            \gamma_-(\infty) = \frac{2(x_0 L_0(\infty) + b)}{\sigma^2 K(0)}, \quad \gamma_+(\infty) = \frac{L_0(0) - \beta}{L_0(\infty) - \beta} \gamma_-(\infty), \quad \theta(\infty) = \frac{\sigma^2 K(0)^2}{2 (L_0(0) - \beta)}.
        \]
        If $p \geq \gamma_+(\infty)$, then $\int_{\R_+} x^{-p}\pi(\mathrm{d}x) = \infty$.
        \item[(b)] If $K$ is regulary varying at zero, i.e.\ of the form~\eqref{eq: regularly varying}, then
        \[
            \lim_{t \to \infty}\P[X_t=0] = \pi_{x_0}(\{0\}) > 0. 
        \]
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let g:R^d->R be convex and continuously differentiable, and suppose its gradient is globally L-Lipschitz in the Euclidean norm for some L>0. Define B_g(x,y)=g(x)-g(y)-<grad g(y),x-y>. For all x,y, ||grad g(x)-grad g(y)||^2/(2L)<=B_g(x,y)<=L||x-y||^2/2. Adding the lower inequality in the two orders gives the Baillon--Haddad cocoercivity inequality <grad g(x)-grad g(y),x-y> >=||grad g(x)-grad g(y)||^2/L. No strong convexity is assumed. Source: Liu--Zhou, Lemma 3.6, which attributes the Bregman bounds to Nesterov.

[Lemm 22 of arXiv:2609.03188, 'Some generalizations of Oort's conjecture'] Let $c\in\mathbb F_{p^2}^\times$ satisfy $c^{p+1}=1$, and set $z=\diag([c],\ldots,[c],[c^p],\ldots,[c^p])$, where each of $[c]$ and $[c^p]$ occurs $g$ times.
Let $j=zu^+$ for some $u^+\in\J^1\cap P_J^+$, where $J=\tS\setminus\{s_0,s_g\}$, and let $yI\in G(\bQp)/I$ be a point fixed by $j$.
Let $s\in\{s_0,s_g\}$.
Then there exist $a\in\overline{\mathbb F}_p$ and $\epsilon\in\{\pm1\}$ such that

[Theorem 12 ({\cite[Theorem~6.1,\,6.2) of arXiv:2609.01965, 'A logarithmic Bogomolov--Sommese vanishing theorem on compact K\"ahler manifolds'] {DP10}}]
    Let $X$ be a compact connected K\"ahler manifold of complex dimension $n\geq2$, $\omega$ be a smooth K\"ahler form and $\Omega^n$ be a smooth volume form.
    Consider also $\sigma_j\in H^0(X,E_j)$, $\tau_r\in H^0(X,F_r)$, $j=1,\ldots,N$, $r=1,\ldots,M$ 
    be non-identically zero holomorphic sections of some holomorphic vector bundles over $X$,  such that the integral condition
    \begin{equation}
        \int_X\prod_{j=1}^N|\sigma_j|^{2l_j}\prod_{r=1}^{M}|\tau_r|^{-2h_r}\Omega^n=\int_X\omega^n
    \end{equation}
    holds for certain real numbers $l_j\geq0,h_r\geq0$.
    Then there exists a unique solution $\varphi$ of the degenerate complex Monge–Amp\`ere equation
    \begin{equation}
        (\omega+\ddbar\varphi)^n=e^{\lambda\varphi}\prod_{j=1}^N|\sigma_j|^{2l_j}\prod_{r=1}^{M}|\tau_r|^{-2h_r}\Omega^n, \quad \lambda\geq0,
    \end{equation}
    which in the case $\lambda=0$ is normalized by $\sup_X\varphi=0$.
    Consider the complex analytic sets
    $$S_1:=\bigcup_r\{\tau_r=0\}, \quad S_2=S_1\cup \left(\bigcup_j \{\sigma_j=0\}\right). $$
    Then $\varphi\in C^0(X)\cap C^{1,1}(X\setminus S_1) \cap C^{\infty}(X\setminus S_2)$.
    In particular, $\varphi\in L^\infty(X)$.
    
    Moreover, denote $f=\prod_{j=1}^N|\sigma_j|^{2l_j}\prod_{r=1}^{M}|\tau_r|^{-2h_r}$.
    For $\delta>0$ satisfying $f\in L\log^{n+\delta}L(X)$,
    the solution $\varphi$ satisfies
    \begin{equation}
        \|\varphi\|_{L^\infty(X)}\leq C(\delta,\omega,\Omega^n)I_{\omega,\delta}(f)^{\frac{n}{\delta}}+1,
    \end{equation}
    where 
    $$I_{\omega,\delta}(f):=\{\omega\}^{-n}\int_Xf\log^{n+\delta}(e+\{\omega\}^{-n}f)\Omega^n.$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
For events A, B with positive probability, P(A | B) = P(B | A) P(A) / P(B). With a partition {A_i}, P(A_i | B) = P(B | A_i) P(A_i) / sum_j P(B | A_j) P(A_j). It inverts conditioning: posterior proportional to likelihood times prior.

Diagnostic corollary: let D be the disease event and T a positive-test event, with 0 < pi = P(D) < 1. Set s = P(T|D), q = P(T|D^c), and assume s*pi + q*(1-pi) > 0. Then P(T) = s*pi + q*(1-pi) and P(D|T) = s*pi/[s*pi + q*(1-pi)]. Thus sensitivity s alone does not determine the posterior in general: for s=9/10 and q=1/10, prevalence pi=1/2 gives posterior 9/10, whereas pi=1/100 gives posterior 1/12.

[Lemma 22 of arXiv:2606.11271, '\LARGE The $K$-th nearest neighbor random walk on a Poisson point process gets trapped'] There exists a constant $\kappa_8(d) > 0$ such that the following holds.
Let $S$ be an infinite and locally finite subset of $\R^d$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item For all $x_0 \in \R^d$ such that $x_0 \not \in S$,
\[
\big|\{x \in S : x_0 \in B(x,r_M(x,S))\}| \le M\kappa_8(d).
\]
\item 
Let $S_f$ be a finite subset of $S$.
Let $(r(x))_{x \in S_f}$ be a family of non-negative real numbers such that, for all $x \in S_f$, $r(x) \le r_M(x,S)$.
Then 
\[
\cL^d\left(\bigcup_{x \in S_f} B(x,r(x))\right) \ge \frac 1 {M\kappa_8(d)} \sum_{x \in S_f} \cL^d(B(x,r(x))).
\]
\end{enumerate}
title: Lemma 22 of arXiv:2606.11271

body:
[Cor 12 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any $\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2,\epsilon\ge0$, 
and for $(\lambda,\mu) \in \Lambda$, 
the mapping
$(\lambda,\mu)\mapsto S_\star(\lambda,\mu;\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2)[\epsilon]$,
is continuous with respect to the Hausdorff metric $d_H$.

\begin{proof}
Fix $\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2,\epsilon\ge0$ and $\delta'>0$. By Lemma~\ref{l:S.star.cts.dH}, there exists $\delta>0$ such that if 
$(\lambda,\mu)\in\Lambda$ and 
$(\lambda',\mu')\in B_\delta(\lambda,\mu)$, then the sets
\begin{align*}
K&\equiv S_\star(\lambda,\mu;\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2)\,,\\
K'&\equiv S_\star(\lambda',\mu';\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2)
\end{align*}
lie within Hausdorff distance $\delta'$ of one another.
For any $\hat{\YY}\in K[\epsilon]$, there exists $\YY\in K$ with
$\|\hat{\YY}-\YY\|_2\le\epsilon$, and then there exists $\YY'\in K'$ with
$\|\YY-\YY'\|_2\le\delta'$. By Lemma~\ref{l:D.mu.continuity.w}, 
since $\hat{\YY}\in\cD_\mu$,
there exists $\tilde{\YY}\in\cD_{\mu'}$
with $\|\hat{\YY}-\tilde{\YY}\|_1\le\delta/\iota^2$. Then
	\[
	\|\tilde{\YY}-\YY'\|_2
	\le\|\tilde{\YY}-\hat{\YY}\|_2
	+ \|\hat{\YY} - \YY\|_2
	+ \|\YY - \YY'\|_2
	\le \epsilon + \delta' + \frac{\delta}{\iota^2}
	\le \epsilon + 2\delta'\,,
	\]
where the last inequality can be arranged by taking $\delta$ small enough (depending on $\delta'$).
Since $\YY'$ and $\tilde{\YY}$ both lie in $\cD_{\mu'}$, it follows by convexity of $\cD_{\mu'}$ that $\tilde{\YY}$ lies within distance
$2\delta'$ of a vector $\hat{\YY}' \in K'[\epsilon]$. We then finally have
	\[
	\|\hat{\YY}-\hat{\YY}'\|_2
	\le \|\hat{\YY}-\tilde{\YY}\|_2
		+ \|\tilde{\YY}-\hat{\YY}'\|_2
	\le\frac{\delta}{\iota^2} + 2\delta'
	\le 3\delta'\,.
	\]
This implies that $K[\epsilon]$ and $K'[\epsilon]$ lie within Hausdorff distance $3\delta'$ of one another, and the claim follows.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Theorem thmIPS of arXiv:2605.28430, 'Limit theory for Lipschitz-localized statistics in random geometric models'] Let  the input process to the interacting particle system be 

\begin{equation}
\tilde{\mathcal{P}} = \left\{(x, M(x),  \tilde{\tau}_x)\in\mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb {M}  \times \hat{\mathcal{N}}_{[0,t_0] \times \mathbb{L}}\right\}, 
\end{equation}

where $ \tilde{\tau}_x$ are i.i.d. and independently marked Poisson clocks, which are also independent of sites and initial states, i.e., independent of $\sum_x \delta_{(x,M(x))}$.
Assume that:
\begin{enumerate}[wide,label=(\roman*),labelindent=0pt]
\item 
$\tilde{\mathcal{P}}$ has {\em summable exponential $\mathbb{B} $-mixing correlations}, as in Definition~(def.A2 of the paper), and has  uniformly bounded correlation functions under reduced Palm distributions, i.e., for all $p \in \mathbb{N}$, there exists a constant $\hat{\kappa}_p$ such that for all $m \in \mathbb{N}$,
\begin{equation}

\sup_{x_1,\ldots,x_p \in \mathbb{R}^d} \sup_{y_1,\ldots,y_m \in \mathbb{R}^d} \rho^{(m)}_{\bk x1p}(\bk y1m) \leq (\hat{\kappa}_p)^m,
\end{equation}
where $\rho^{(m)}_{\bk x1p}$ denotes the $m$-th order correlation function of $\mathcal{P}$ under its reduced Palm distribution $\mathbb{P}^!_{\bk x1p}$.

\item  {\em An admissible update rule} given by a measurable function $\Phi$ as in~(equation e:updaterulef of the paper) acts on a {\em stabilizing interaction graph} $\Psi$ (on finite windows) with respect to $\mathcal{P}$, such that the interaction range satisfies the decay assumption~(equation e:ddecay of the paper).
\item  A {\em score function} $\xi = \xi^{(h, \Phi, \Psi)}(\tilde{x},\tilde{\mathcal{P}}_n) := h(M_n[x])$ defined in~(equation xiU of the paper), satisfies the {\em $p$-moment condition}~(equation momh of the paper) for all $p \in [1, \infty)$.
\end{enumerate}
Then the sequence of random measures $(\mu_n^{\xi})_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ defined in~(equation IPS of the paper) satisfies the central limit theorem. That is, for every  $f \in \mathbb{B} (W_1)$ such that
$
{\rm Var}[\mu_n^{\xi}(f)] = \Omega(n^{\nu})$ for some $\nu > 0$,
we have
$$
({\rm Var}[\mu_n^{\xi}(f)])^{-1/2} \big(\mu_n^{\xi}(f) - \mathbb {E} [\mu_n^{\xi}(f)]\big)  \stackrel{d}{\Rightarrow} Z,$$
where $Z$ is a standard Gaussian random variable. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 12 (Vanishing reflection contribution for $G$) of arXiv:2606.17517, 'Killed resolvents and measure-valued stopping gains for reflected optimal stopping with ma'] Under Assumption~\ref{ass:no-corner-reflection}, the reflection contribution in
the generalized It\^o--Tanaka formula for $G(X)$ vanishes. More precisely,
\[
   \lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}
   \mathbb E_x\left[
      \sum_{i=1}^2
      \int_0^t \partial_iG_\varepsilon(X_s)\,dL_s^i
   \right]
   =0,
   \qquad t>0,\quad x\in\R^2_+.
\]
Consequently, no additional corner additive functional appears in the
It\^o--Tanaka formula for $G(X)$.

[Theorem thm:heat of arXiv:2412.01381, 'Ergodicity and mixing for locally monotone stochastic evolution equations'] Assume that $B\in L_2(U,W_0^{1,2}({\mathcal O}))$. Denote by $c_0$ the inverse Poincar\'e constant of ${\mathcal O}$, and assume that for some $\lambda\in (0,1)$,
\[\|B\|^2_{L_2(U,H)}\le \lambda\nu c_0^2.\]
Then the Markovian Feller semigroup $(P_t)_{t\ge 0}$ of the stochastic heat equation~(equation eq:heat of the paper) with degenerate additive Wiener noise is exponentially ergodic and exponentially mixing and possesses a unique invariant measure $\mu_\ast$ with finite second moments in the stronger space $V$ in all spatial dimensions. We have the following upper bound for the $\varepsilon$-mixing time 
\[
\tau^x_{\textup{\textsf{mix}}}(\varepsilon)\leq 
\frac{1}{\nu c_0^2}\left[\log\left(\|x\|_H+\frac{\|B\|_{L_2(U,H)}}{\sqrt{2(1-\lambda)\nu}c_0}\right)+\log\left(\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\right)\right].
\]

For centered finite Gaussian X with PSD covariance C, positive deterministic weights, and a finite nonempty family of nonempty paths, let D_xi=min_p sum_v a_pv exp(xi X_v) and v=max_i C_ii. For 0<=a<b, E log D_b-E log D_a <= (v/2)(b^2-a^2). When variance-normalized crossing exponents satisfy v_n/L_n->1 and E log D_xi,n/L_n->-lambda(xi), this implies lambda(b)-lambda(a)>=-(b^2-a^2)/2. The resulting LFPP monotonicity is already known; no new LQG bound is claimed.
V finite
X centered Gaussian with PSD covariance C, singular covariance allowed
Finite nonempty family P of nonempty paths
Positive deterministic weights on each path support
0<=a<b<infinity
Exponent corollary assumes v_n/L_n->1 and endpoint exponent convergence

  \hat{\br}^\eta

[Prop 66 of arXiv:2507.08909, 'Annealed almost periodic entropy'] Assume that $\tr_{d_n}\circ \pi_n\to \tau$, and let $\l$ be the GNS representation of $\tau$. Let $k$ be a positive integer and let $\phi \in \B(\A,\rmM_k)_+$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[a.] If $\phi$ is approximately associated to $\l^{\oplus \infty}$, then $\phi$ is asymptotically associated to $\bspi$.
\item[b.] If $\phi_{\rm{sing}}$ is asymptotically associated to $\bspi$, then so is the whole of $\phi$.
\end{enumerate} \qed (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Lem 5 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $\YY = (\vBBb,\vvvv,\vUUu,\vwww)$ be the random vector defined in \eqref{e:freeprob.random.YY}, and $\mu(\bG,\omega)$ be defined in \eqref{e:lambda-mu-random}.
    For any $\epsilon'' > 0$ there exists $c = c(\alpha,\iota,\epsilon'') > 0$ such that
    \[
        \P\bigg(
            \inf\big\{
                \|\tilde \YY - \YY\|_2 : \tilde \YY \in \cD_{\mu(\bG,\omega)}
            \big\} \le \epsilon''
        \bigg)
        \ge 1 - e^{-cN}\,.
    \]
\begin{proof}
Throughout the proof, we abbreviate $(\lambda,\mu) = (\lambda(\bG,\omega),\mu(\bG,\omega))$, although we keep in mind that they are permitted to depend on $(\bG,\omega)$. We will construct $\tilde\YY = (\tilde\vBBb,\tilde\vvvv,\tilde\vUUu,\tilde\vwww) \in \cD_\mu$ such that $\|\tilde \YY - \YY\|_2 \le \epsilon''$ on an event with probability $1-e^{-cN}$.
    We set $(\tilde\vBBb,\tilde\vUUu) = (\vBBb,\vUUu)$, and $\tilde\vvvv = \max(\vvvv,\vUUu)$ where the maximum is taken entrywise.
    Note that for all $j\in [r]$, the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality gives
    \baln
        \vUUu_j - \vvvv_j
        &=
        \bigg(
            \frac{1}{|B_j|} \sum_{a\in B_j}
            \frac{(\bmeta^a,\bar{\bx})(\barbg^a,\hat{\by})}{N}
        \bigg)^2
        - \frac{1}{|B_j|} \sum_{a\in B_j}
        \frac{(\barbg^a,\hat{\by})^2}{N} \\
        &\le 
        \bigg(
            \frac{1}{|B_j|} \sum_{a\in B_j}
            \frac{(\barbg^a,\hat{\by})^2}{N}
        \bigg)
        \bigg(
            \frac{1}{|B_j|} \sum_{a\in B_j} \frac{(\bmeta^a,\bar{\bx})^2}{N} - 1
        \bigg)\,,
    \ealn
from which it follows that
    \[
        |\tilde\vvvv_j - \vvvv_j|
        = (\vUUu_j - \vvvv_j)_+
        \le \bigg(
            \frac{1}{|B_j|} \sum_{a\in B_j}
            \frac{(\barbg^a,\hat{\by})^2}{N}
        \bigg)
        \bigg|
            \frac{1}{|B_j|} \sum_{a\in B_j} \frac{(\bmeta^a,\bar{\bx})^2}{N} - 1
        \bigg|\,.
    \]

        \le \frac{4C^2}{\alpha \iota}\,.
    \]
Set $\delta > 0$ small enough that
    \[
        [(1-\delta)^2,(1+\delta)^2] \subseteq \bigg[
            1 - \frac{\epsilon''\alpha\iota^2}{8C^2},

        \frac{\|\bar{\bx}\|^2}{N} \cdot \frac{\|\bz\|^2}{|B_j|}
    \]

    By Lemma~\ref{l:fp-gc} and a standard gaussian tail bound,
    \[
        \max\bigg\{

        \bigg| \frac{\|\bar{\bx}\|^2}{N} \cdot \frac{\|\bz\|^2}{|B_j|} - 1 \bigg|

cylinder function $f$. Then, there exists a finite constant

bounded in $N$, such that
\begin{align*}
& {\mathbb E}_{\nu^N} \Big[\, \Big|\,
\int_0^t \, 
\sum_{x\in {\mathbb T}^d_N} G (s, x)\,
(\Xi^{\rm c}_{{\boldsymbol u}^N (\cdot), x}  f) (\eta (s))
\, ds \, \Big| \,\Big]
\\ 
&\quad \;\le \;
{\mathfrak c}({\boldsymbol u}^N) \, \Big\{ \frac{1}{K_N} \;+\;
K_N\,  \int_0^t (\, 1 + \Vert G(s)\Vert^2_\infty\,)\, \big[ \,
H_N(f^N_s)  + (N/\ell_N)^d \,\big] \, ds\; \Big\}
\\

[Definition defn:common conditional expectation of arXiv:2411.00663, 'Ergodicity and Mixing of invariant capacities and applications'] Let $(\Omega,\mathcal{F})$ be a measurable space, and $\mathcal{H}$ be a sub-$\sigma$-algebra of $\mathcal{F}$. Given a subset $\Lambda\subset \Delta^{\sigma}(\Omega,\mathcal{F})$ and $f\in B(\Omega,\mathcal{F})$, an $\mathcal{H}$-measurable function $g_f$ is said to be the common conditional expectation of $f$ with respect to $\mathcal{H}$ for $\Lambda$ if 
	\[\mathbb{E}_P(f\mid \mathcal{H})=g_f \text{, }P\text{-a.s.}\]
	for any $P\in\Lambda$, where $\mathbb{E}_P(f\mid \mathcal{H})$ is the conditional expectation of $f$ with respect to $\mathcal{H}$ for $P$.

[Theorem thm:power_means_majorize of arXiv:2608.23765, '\texorpdfstring{Tight Majorizations and Convergence Rates\\ of Nuclear Norm Minimization I'] Let $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_1 \times d_2}$
have SVD $\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{U} \diag(\boldsymbol{\sigma}) \mathbf{V}^\top$
such that there are two indices $i,j \in [d]$ with $i \neq j$
whose singular values satisfy $\sigma_i \neq \sigma_j$
and $\sigma_i,\sigma_j > \varepsilon > 0$. Fix $q \in [-\infty , \infty]$ and consider the weight operator $\W{\mathbf{X}}{\varepsilon}(\cdot):=\W{\mathbf{X}}{\varepsilon}^{(q)}(\cdot)$ of (eq:power:mean:weight:operator of the paper) based on the weight core matrix $\mathbf{H}^{(q)}_{\boldsymbol{\sigma},\varepsilon}$ arising as entrywise $q$-power mean of the left- and right-sided core matrices via (eq:power:mean:core:matrix of the paper).
Then the associated quadratic model $Q_\varepsilon^{(q)}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{X})$ (cf. (eq:smoothedell1:IRLSmajorizer of the paper)) majorizes $\mathcal{J}_\varepsilon(\cdot)$, 
i.e., $Q_{\varepsilon}^{(q)}(\mathbf{Z}\mid\mathbf{X}) \geq \mathcal{J}_{\varepsilon}(\mathbf{Z})$ 
for each $\mathbf{Z} \in \R^{d_1 \times d_2}$, if and only if $q \geq -1$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

The unqualified auxiliary implication 'a maximizing Gaussian polymer path changes with probability tending to one under polynomially small Ornstein-Uhlenbeck noise, hence its maximum has a power sublinear variance bound' is false. A width-one strip counterexample has path-change probability tending to one, normalized common-vertex overlap tending to one, and linear maximum variance. This says nothing against a quantitative small-overlap hypothesis or the unrestricted source model.
This is a clearly labeled false proposed bridge, not a theorem
Noise scale may depend polynomially on path length
title: False auxiliary bridge from path change to small variance

Let f be holomorphic on the open strip {z : 0 < Re z < 1}, continuous and bounded on the closed strip {z : 0 ≤ Re z ≤ 1}. For 0 ≤ x ≤ 1 put M(x) = sup over y real of |f(x + iy)|. Then log M(x) is a convex function of x on [0,1]; in particular M(x) ≤ M(0)^{1-x} M(1)^x for all x in [0,1]. If M(0) = 0 or M(1) = 0 then f is identically zero. Boundedness on the closed strip is essential (see the pitfall entry). This is the analytic engine behind the Riesz–Thorin interpolation theorem.

body: In mathematics, Minkowski's theorem is the statement that every convex set in $\mathbb {R} ^{n}$ which is symmetric with respect to the origin and which has volume greater than $2^{n}$ contains a non-zero integer point (meaning a point in $\mathbb {Z} ^{n}$ that is not the origin). The theorem was proved by Hermann Minkowski in 1889 and became the foundation of the branch of number theory called the geometry of numbers. It can be extended from the integers to any lattice $L$ and to any symmetric convex set with volume greater than $2^{n}d(L)$, where $d(L)$ denotes the covolume of the lattice (the absolute value of the determinant of any of its bases).

[Theorem 1 (Upper bound for continuous functions) of arXiv:2608.31157, 'Sharp Approximation Rates for Neural Networks with Affine Latent Parameterizations'] Let $d,M,P\in\N^+$ satisfy $\min\{M,P\}\ge4$ and
$P\ge P_d^\star$.  There exist an architecture
$\Phi\in\Arch_{\mathrm{par}}(P)\cap\Arch(N_d,L_{d,P})$ with input dimension
$d$ and an affine map $\calA\in\aff(M,P_\Phi)$, both depending only on
$(d,M,P)$ and not on the target, with the following property.  For every
$f\in C([0,1]^d)$, there is a target-dependent latent vector
$\bmxi_f\in\R^M$ such that, with
$\bmtheta_f:=\calA(\bmxi_f)$,
\begin{equation}

 \left\lVert f-\Phi_{\bmtheta_f}\right\rVert_{L^\infty([0,1]^d)}
 \le
 (d+2)
 \omega_f\bigl(
 C_d[P\min\{M,P\}]^{-1/d}
 \bigr).
\end{equation}
Equivalently, every entry of every layer matrix $\bmW_\ell$ and bias vector
$\bmb_\ell$ is an affine function of $\bmxi_f$.  Every dense weight and bias
entry is counted in $P_\Phi$, including entries assigned the value zero. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Upper bound for continuous functions

body:
[Lemma rosenthal of arXiv:2412.07936, 'Simple Norm Bounds for Polynomial Random Matrices via Decoupling'] [Non-Hermitian Matrix Rosenthal Inequality]

Suppose that $t=1$ or $t \geq 1.5$. Consider a finite sequence $\{{\bf Y}_k\}_{k\geq 1}$ of centered, independent, random matrices, and assume that ${\mathbb E} \ensuremath{\left\lVert {\bf Y}_k \right\rVert}_{4t}^{4t} < \infty$. Then
$$
    {\mathbb E} \norm{\sum_{k}{\bf Y}_k}_{4t}^{4t} \leq (16t)^{3t} \cdot \left\{ \norm{\left(\sum_k{\mathbb E}  {\bf Y}_k {{\bf Y}}^{\mathsf{T}}_k \right)^{1/2}}_{4t}^{4t} + \norm{ \left(\sum_k{\mathbb E} {{\bf Y}}^{\mathsf{T}}_k{\bf Y}_k \right)^{1/2} }_{4t}^{4t} \right\} + (8t)^{4t}\cdot \left(\sum_k {\mathbb E} \ensuremath{\left\lVert {\bf Y}_k \right\rVert}_{4t}^{4t} \right).
$$
title: Lemma rosenthal of arXiv:2412.07936

such that for every uncorrected scalar Adam run, epsilon outside sqrt,
standard m0=v0=0, with 0<rho=epsilon/(eta lambda)<=rho0, all but countably
many x0 satisfy
 limsup_(t->infinity) |eta C_t-38| >=delta.                    (1)
Here C_t=lambda/(sqrt(v_(t+1))+epsilon). The constants are existential,
not numerical bounds. For every p>1, fixed lambda>0, and any countable
eta_n->0, absolutely continuous random initialization almost surely
satisfies (1) for all sufficiently large n with epsilon_n=eta_n^p.
No choice of finite burn-in can give eventual o(1/eta) tracking along
this sequence for uncorrected scalar Adam.

In a positive two-eigenvalue diagonal quadratic, the same conclusion
holds for ACTIVE curvature on the invariant standard-initialization
family (x1,0), with x1 absolutely continuous. The second coordinate is
exactly dormant. This is not a full-dimensional random initialization
theorem, and does not cover ordinary time0 bias correction. Those are
explicit remaining gaps for the full dossier target. The result records
a rigorous tracking obstruction in a stated variant; it is not a generic
two-dimensional solution or a claim that every Adam convention fails.

Hardest remaining step: exclude capture in the higher-dimensional
clock-augmented stable set from standard starts under bias correction,
and control genuine two-coordinate averaging.

Proof. Work in claim009's normalized variables X,M,V with map
 M'=bM+(1-b)X, V'=dV+(1-d)X^2,
 X'=X-M'/(sqrt(V')+rho).
Choose, for definiteness, rho0=1/1000, which is strictly below
rho_*=358811/13673160. At rho in [0,rho0] the nonzero cycle has
 a(rho)=1/38-rho>=1/38-1/1000>0,
 p_s(rho)=(s a,-s a/19,a^2), s in {+1,-1}.
By claims003 and009 its two-step derivative has one simple real stable
eigenvalue and two unstable eigenvalues, uniformly separated from the
unit circle on this compact interval. At rho=0 the count follows from
the exact negative discriminant and real-root bounds in claim009; the
no-unit-root argument of claim003 excludes crossings throughout.

UNIFORM LOCAL STABLE CAPTURE
Claim009 constructs the analytic stable curve of each phase directly
by the power-series coefficient equation
 w_n=(mu(rho)^n I-A(rho))^(-1)[N_rho(v_rho s+w)]_n.
That proof can be made uniform on [0,rho0]. The simple stable spectral
projection and its complement vary continuously; choose continuous
local bases and norms, or use finitely many such choices on this compact
parameter interval. The stable eigenvalue has a uniform upper bound<1,
all unstable eigenvalues have a uniform lower modulus>1, and the linear
operators are invertible. Thus the inverses in the coefficient equation
are uniformly bounded for all n>=2 and all rho: large n are handled by
mu(rho)^n->0 uniformly, and finitely many small n by compactness.
The nonlinear maps are analytic on a fixed complex neighborhood of the
cycle branches, since their variances are bounded below by a(rho0)^2.
Their Taylor majorants are therefore uniformly bounded. One contraction
radius works on each of a finite cover and their minimum is positive.
Graph-relative unstable expansion also has a uniform factor>1 in the
chosen norms after shrinking. Since all these finitely many norms are
uniformly equivalent to the Euclidean norm, there is a single radius
r>0 with this property: an orbit of F_rho^2 staying within the Euclidean
r-neighborhood of a phase forever lies on its local stable curve and
converges to that phase. Smaller r may be chosen so neighborhoods of the
two phases are disjoint, uniformly in rho.

AN EVENTUAL CURVATURE BAND FORCES SUCH CAPTURE
Put k_t=eta C_t=1/(sqrt(V_(t+1))+rho). Suppose that eventually
 |k_t-38|<delta, where delta will be chosen sufficiently small below.
For delta<=1, the map k->1/k is uniformly Lipschitz on [37,39], so
 sqrt(V_(t+1))=a(rho)+O(delta),
 V_(t+1)=a(rho)^2+O(delta).
Every O(delta) here and below has a constant uniform for rho in
[0,rho0]. Subtracting dV_t in the exact variance update gives
 X_t^2=a(rho)^2+O(delta)/(1-d).
Since 1-d is a fixed positive number and a(rho) is uniformly positive,
 |X_t|=a(rho)+O(delta).                                    (2)
In particular X_t is nonzero for all sufficiently large t if delta
is small. Let s_t=sign(X_t).

Eliminate momentum exactly:
 X_(t+1)=[1+b k_t/k_(t-1)-(1-b)k_t]X_t
              -b k_t/k_(t-1)X_(t-1).
Using k_t=38+O(delta), (2), and b=.9, this yields
 s_(t+1)=-(1+b)s_t-b s_(t-1)+O(delta).                      (3)
For a sign triple that is not alternating, the absolute residual of
the exact relation in (3) is at least 2b=1.8: if the two preceding
signs coincide, the residual is at least1.8; if they differ, the wrong
next sign has residual2. Thus delta can be chosen uniformly so that
the error in (3) is smaller than0.9, forcing sign alternation at every
sufficiently late step. The exact preceding update also gives
 M_t=(X_(t-1)-X_t)/k_(t-1)=-s_t a(rho)/19+O(delta).
Together with (2) and the variance estimate, this puts every sufficiently
late state within C delta of p_(s_t)(rho), with uniform C. Choose delta
smaller still so C delta<r. Alternating signs then ensure each parity
subsequence remains in one local stable neighborhood forever. By uniform
local capture it converges to the alternating cycle.

COUNTABLE EXCEPTIONS AND THE SMALL-ETA CONSEQUENCE
For each fixed rho>0, claim009 proves that only countably many standard
initial X0 can converge to this cycle. The previous paragraph shows that
every orbit with limsup|k_t-38|<delta belongs to that countable set.
Scaling X0=x0/eta preserves countability. Therefore all other starts
satisfy (1). For p>1 and eta_n->0,
rho_n=eta_n^(p-1)/lambda eventually lies in (0,rho0]. For each such n
the exceptional x0 set is countable, and their countable union is null
for any absolutely continuous initialization law. Thus (1) holds almost
surely simultaneously along the specified sequence. This order of
quantifiers does NOT claim one null set for an uncountable eta family.

For the diagonal invariant-coordinate family, g2=m2=v2=0 at all times,
and the active quotient equals the scalar channel's curvature whenever
g1!=0. The eventual-band assumption itself forces g1!=0, so no undefined
quotient enters the capture implication. One may state the scalar bound
using the always-defined scalar C_t to avoid isolated zero-gradient times.

Scope/novelty: this strengthens claim009's noncap-limit obstruction to
a positive, eta-uniform limsup gap. It is a consequence of the local
analytic cycle argument, not a numerical attractor calculation. The
literature already observes default-beta cycle instability; instability
alone is not the argument. Bias-corrected and full-dimensional diagonal

is asserted. Independent audit of uniform local capture is required.


VERSION2: FULL-DIMENSIONAL RANDOM INITIALIZATION FOR RANK ONE
Consider H=diag(lambda,0), lambda>0, with ordinary coordinatewise
uncorrected Adam and standard zero moments. The flat coordinate has
zero gradient and stays fixed for arbitrary x2,0. Thus active curvature
equals the scalar first-channel curvature whenever x1,t!=0. For an
absolutely continuous law on R^2, its first-coordinate marginal is
absolutely continuous, so the scalar exceptional set is null.

We also exclude exact zero iterates without an added assumption. For
fixed rho>0 and n>=1, the finite-time function X_n(X0) is real analytic

this extra null set all active quotients are defined, and the scalar
limsup bound transfers literally. The same countable-eta argument
already given proves the result simultaneously along any chosen
eta_n->0 for absolutely continuous random initial positions in R^2.

body:
Let B[u,v] be the bilinear form of a second-order elliptic operator in divergence form, B[u,v] = integral over Omega of ( sum a^{ij} u_{x_i} v_{x_j} + sum b^i u_{x_i} v + c u v ), with a^{ij} in L^infinity satisfying the uniform ellipticity condition sum a^{ij}(x) xi_i xi_j >= theta |xi|^2 for some theta > 0 and all xi, and with b^i, c in L^infinity. Then there are constants beta > 0 and gamma >= 0 such that B[u,u] >= beta ||u||^2_{H^1(Omega)} - gamma ||u||^2_{L^2(Omega)} for every u in H_0^1(Omega). That is, the form is coercive only AFTER subtracting a multiple of the L^2 norm; equivalently B[u,v] + gamma (u,v)_{L^2} is coercive, so Lax-Milgram applies to the shifted operator.
Uniform ellipticity and bounded coefficients.
The subtracted term gamma ||u||^2_{L^2} cannot in general be removed - it vanishes only when the zeroth-order coefficient is large enough (for example c >= 0 with b = 0 gives gamma = 0 by Poincare).
Forgetting the gamma term and asserting plain coercivity is the standard error, and it is exactly what makes the Dirichlet problem solvable only away from the spectrum.

body:
Let Omega(t) be a family of bounded domains in R^n moving with a C^1 velocity field, whose boundary points move with normal speed V_n, and let f(x,t) be C^1. Then the derivative in t of the integral over Omega(t) of f equals the integral over Omega(t) of the partial derivative of f in t, plus the boundary integral of f times V_n with respect to surface measure. If the domain is transported by a flow with velocity field w then the boundary term is the integral of f (w dotted with nu), and the divergence theorem turns the identity into the integral over Omega(t) of ( partial f in t plus the divergence of f w ). In one dimension this is the classical Leibniz rule with the two endpoint terms f(b(t),t) b'(t) minus f(a(t),t) a'(t).
C^1 regularity of both the integrand and the motion of the domain;
ONLY the NORMAL component of the boundary velocity appears, since tangential motion does not change the region.
Forgetting the boundary term - differentiating under the integral sign as if the domain were fixed - is the standard error when a domain depends on the parameter.

body:
[Theorem thm:exact-interval-formula-paper of arXiv:2606.08683, 'Exact Fourier dimensions of dyadic Mandelbrot cascades under minimal integrability'] Assume that the dyadic vector-weight law is energy-admissible.  Let \(\mu\) be
the limiting dyadic vector cascade measure on \([0,1]\), and set
\(M=\mu([0,1])\).  Then, almost surely on \(\{M>0\}\),
\begin{equation}
    \dim_{\mathrm F}(\mu)
    =
    \dim_{\mathrm E}(\mu)
    =
    \dim_2(\mu)
    =
    D_{\mathrm E}(X).
\end{equation}
In particular, on the same event, if \(D_{\mathrm E}(X)>0\), then for every
\(0<\sigma<D_{\mathrm E}(X)\) there is a finite random constant
\(C_\sigma(\omega)<\infty\) such that
\begin{equation}
    |\widehat{\mu}(\xi)|
    \le
    C_\sigma(\omega)|\xi|^{-\sigma/2}
\end{equation}
for all sufficiently large \(|\xi|\).  If \(D_{\mathrm E}(X)=0\), the decay
assertion is vacuous, and all three dimensions in
(equation eq:exact-interval-vector-theorem-paper of the paper) are equal to \(0\).

body: For a discrete random variable X taking values in a finite or countable set with probability mass function p(x) = Pr(X=x), the Shannon entropy is H(X) = - sum_{x: p(x)>0} p(x) * log p(x), using the convention 0*log 0 = 0. H(X) is measured in bits when the logarithm has base 2 (or nats for natural log). H(X) >= 0 always, H(X) = 0 exactly when X is deterministic (a single outcome has probability 1), and among distributions on a fixed set of m outcomes, H(X) is maximized, at value log m, by the uniform distribution.
title: Shannon Entropy

body: For Y = (1/3) sum_{k>=0} B_k (2/3)^k with fair independent bits B_k, the Fourier transform of its law mu (the Bernoulli-2/3 measure) has the exact closed form hat_mu(xi) = prod_{k>=0} (1 + exp(-2 pi i xi (2/3)^k / 3))/2, agreeing with an independent stationary-density solver's Fourier coefficients to 1e-11 at xi = 1,2,3,5,8,16,32. Writing mu_n for the law of frac(2^n Y), hat_mu_n(k) = hat_mu(2^n k) for every integer k, so every level of a 'fibre-bias' deficit ladder is the same measure evaluated at a doubled frequency; an explicit Fourier lower bound (Cauchy-Schwarz against a unimodular test function, the k=0 term vanishing by the Y -> 1-Y symmetry) reproduces 14-39 pct of the numerically measured fibre bias at ladder levels n=0..6 using 20,000-term sums, independently of any density solver. Along the lacunary orbit 2^n, |hat_mu(2^n)| reduces to the exact arithmetic product prod_{k>=0} |cos(pi 2^{n+k}/3^{k+1})|, each factor depending only on 2^{n+k} mod 2 * 3^{k+1} (verified digit-for-digit against the direct Fourier product for n=0..16), with only k up to about 1.71n contributing; because 2 is a primitive root mod every 3^j, the exact period-average of log|cos(pi u/3^{k+1})| over units u equals -log 2 for every k, predicting an average decay of about 1.185 per level n, while the MEASURED slope of log|hat_mu(2^n)| over n=0..16 is about 1.0 per level - the decay itself is bursty (0.31 at n=0, 4.1e-8 at n=7, back up to 1.7e-5 at n=10, 4.3e-9 at n=15), the small factors being exactly the k where 2^{n+k+1} lands near an odd multiple of 3^{k+1}, though the trend matches the prediction; the exchange of sums behind the prediction is rigorous only for k up to about log_3 n, where the window covers the period 2 * 3^k. For the rational, non-Pisot ratio lambda=2/3, the currently PROVED decay rate of hat_mu is only logarithmic in the frequency (giving deficits of order n^{-c}, not summable - the family a related paper bound n^{-13/25} belongs to), while the measured/predicted decay is vastly faster; the gap between the proved logarithmic rate and the faster measured rate is exactly the missing ingredient - a lacunary Fourier estimate for the 2/3 Bernoulli convolution better than logarithmic - and closing it requires simultaneous equidistribution of 2^{n+k} mod 3^{k+1} across k up to about 1.71n, an unproved, Erdos-Kahane-barrier-type statement (a literature check found proved Fourier decay for rational lambda=p/q is logarithmic-power in general, and known absolute-continuity results for algebraic parameters reach down to about lambda=0.7995, above 2/3=0.667). The chain end to end: such simultaneous equidistribution would give geometric decay of |hat_mu(2^n)|, which would give a stated two-level contraction target, which would give summability of the deficit ladder (that implication is Lean-checked), which would give a finite-entropy density; only the first link is unproved.

body:
[Lemma 16 (Haar measure on $\ASim(V)$) of arXiv:2607.05219, 'Random free semigroups of affine groups'] The group $K:=\ker c=\Isom(V)$ is compact, and the sequence
\[
1\longrightarrow K\longrightarrow\Sim_{\lin}(V)\xrightarrow{\;c\;}\Lambda\longrightarrow1
\]
is exact, where $\Lambda:=c(\Sim_{\lin}(V))$. For any measurable section
$s:\Lambda\to\Sim_{\lin}(V)$, the map $(r,k)\mapsto s(r)k$ is a measurable
bijection $\Lambda\times K\to\Sim_{\lin}(V)$, and $dm_{\lin}$ disintegrates as
\[
dm_{\lin}(T)=dk\,d\nu(r),\qquad r=c(T),\quad k=s(r)^{-1}T,
\]
independently of the choice of $s$. Consequently,
\[
dm(b,T)=c(T)^{-d}\,db\,dk\,d\nu(r)
\]
is a left Haar measure on $\ASim(V)$, where $dk$ is the Haar probability measure
on $K$, and $d\nu$ is a Haar measure on the abelian group $\Lambda$.

[Lemma 13 of arXiv:2605.02771, 'Universality in Deep Neural Networks:\\ An approach via the Lindeberg exchange principle'] If \(z^{(L+1)}(x)\) is the output of a DNN with zero biases, weights satisfying \textbf{Assumption \ref{assum:weights}} and a bounded activation function, we have
\[
\Wcal_2\bigl(z^{(L+1)}(x), z^{(L+1;L)}(x)\bigr)
\lesssim
\sqrt{\frac{n_{L+1}}{n_L}},
\]
where \(z^{(L+1;L)}(x)\) is as in \textbf{Definition \ref{def:switched_layers_DNN}}. The same bound is true if \(z^{(L+1)}(x)\) has Gaussian biases, according to \textbf{Assumption \ref{assum:biases}}.
title: Lemma 13 of arXiv:2605.02771

\Lambda_p C_q + C_p \Lambda_q
&=
\Lambda_q C_p + C_q \Lambda_p.

\end{align}
These are the diamond equations

Let P be a product measure on a finite product of finite sets and let A and B be arbitrary events, not necessarily increasing. Then P(A box B) <= P(A) P(B), where A box B is the disjoint occurrence of A and B, witnessed by disjoint coordinate sets (Reimer 2000). This extends the van den Berg-Kesten inequality, which required both events to be increasing; the general statement had been conjectured by van den Berg and Kesten and by van den Berg and Fiebig. The proof is combinatorial (a butterfly lemma on pairs of subcubes) and does not go through monotonicity. The inequality still needs a product measure.

TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). The Lindeberg exchange (swapping) principle proves distributional limit theorems by replacing the summands or matrix entries of a random object one at a time with Gaussian (or other reference) analogues, bounding the resulting change in E[F] for a sufficiently smooth test function F via a Taylor expansion at each swap, provided the relevant moments, typically up to third or fourth order depending on the smoothness assumed of F, agree between the original and replacement distributions. In random matrix theory, the Tao-Vu four-moment theorem states that for Wigner matrices, local eigenvalue statistics such as gap distributions at a fixed bulk location are universal, independent of the specific entry distribution, provided the first four moments of the off-diagonal entries match those of the Gaussian (GOE/GUE) case up to a small, quantified error, with a weaker three-moment matching sufficing for some global statistics; this is the primary technical engine behind Wigner-Dyson-Mehta universality results beyond the exactly solvable Gaussian ensembles. It does not apply directly to test functions or statistics that are insufficiently smooth, requiring a separate regularization step, typically via a local relaxation flow or Dyson Brownian motion argument, to pass from smooth test functions to eigenvalue counting functions or individual eigenvalue locations, and it requires the specific moment-matching order assumed, with fewer matched moments giving correspondingly weaker conclusions. Typical failure: Applying the four-moment theorem's universality conclusion directly to a non-smooth statistic, such as the exact location or gap of a specific eigenvalue or an indicator-type event, without the additional Green's function comparison or local relaxation machinery needed to pass from smooth test functions to such statistics; the raw Lindeberg swapping argument by itself only controls E[F(eigenvalues)] for smooth F, and asserting the full local universality conclusion from moment matching alone skips this substantial extra step. Canonical reference: Lindeberg, 1922, Mathematische Zeitschrift; Tao and Vu, 2011, Acta Mathematica; Erdos and Yau, A Dynamical Approach to Random Matrix Theory, 2017, American Mathematical Society (Courant Lecture Notes).

sufficient smoothness, typically several bounded derivatives, of the test function F used in the swapping argument

if $f_i(\cdot),i\geq1$ are nonincreasing, then $f_i(\xi_i),i\geq1$ are WUOD (or WLOD).

then for each $n\geq1$,
$$E\prod^{n}_{i=1}\xi_{i} \leq g_{U,V}(n)\prod^{n}_{i=1}E\xi_{i}.$$

body:
Let $(X, \mathcal{B}, \mu, T)$ be a probability-preserving system. For a finite (or countable, with finite entropy) measurable partition $\xi = \{A_1, \dots, A_k\}$ put $H_\mu(\xi) = -\sum_i \mu(A_i) \log \mu(A_i)$ (with $0 \log 0 = 0$), and $\xi^n_0 = \bigvee_{j=0}^{n-1} T^{-j}\xi$, the partition into sets $A_{i_0} \cap T^{-1}A_{i_1} \cap \dots \cap T^{-(n-1)}A_{i_{n-1}}$ (the $n$-step itineraries). The entropy of $T$ relative to $\xi$ is $h_\mu(T, \xi) = \lim_{n\to\infty} \frac1n H_\mu(\xi^n_0)$ (the limit exists because $n \mapsto H_\mu(\xi^n_0)$ is subadditive; it also equals $\inf_n \frac1n H_\mu(\xi^n_0)$ and $\lim_n H_\mu(\xi \mid \xi^n_1)$). The Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy is $h_\mu(T) = \sup_\xi h_\mu(T, \xi)$ over finite partitions, in $[0, \infty]$. Facts used constantly: $h_\mu(T, \xi) \le H_\mu(\xi) \le \log k$; $h_\mu(T, \xi) \le h_\mu(T, \eta) + H_\mu(\xi \mid \eta)$ for partitions $\xi, \eta$; $h_\mu(T^m) = m\, h_\mu(T)$ for $m \ge 1$; the Kolmogorov-Sinai generator theorem: if $\xi$ is a generator ($\bigvee_{j \ge 0} T^{-j}\xi$ generates $\mathcal{B}$ mod $\mu$, or $\bigvee_{j\in\mathbb{Z}}$ for invertible $T$) then $h_\mu(T) = h_\mu(T, \xi)$; and if $\xi_m$ is an increasing sequence of partitions generating $\mathcal{B}$ then $h_\mu(T, \xi_m) \uparrow h_\mu(T)$. On a compact metric space, partitions of diameter $< \varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon \to 0$ are such a sequence. The map $\mu \mapsto h_\mu(T)$ on invariant measures is affine, but it is NOT in general continuous or even upper semicontinuous in the weak* topology; upper semicontinuity holds when $T$ is expansive (and for $C^\infty$ maps of compact manifolds by Newhouse), which is what guarantees measures of maximal entropy exist in those cases.

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Check which steps of the d = 2 proof are dimension-dependent. Result: The source's d = 1+1 proof establishes superconcentration of the free energy (variance o(n)) via hypercontractivity and then chaos from superconcentration through the general equivalence theorem; the dimension-dependent step is the variance bound Var(log Z_n) = O(n/log n), obtained from the Benjamini-Kalai-Schramm influence inequality applied to the free energy with the influence of a single site bounded by the expected overlap of two polymers at that site, whose sum over sites is the expected overlap, of order n in the strong disorder regime. The BKS argument is dimension-free provided the polymer is in the strong disorder phase (positive overlap); in d >= 3 the strong disorder phase exists at low temperature (Comets-Yoshida), so the variance bound O(n/log n) transfers and superconcentration follows; the equivalence theorem then gives chaos at the level of the overlap between the polymers at slightly perturbed environments. So the obstruction the source mentions ('certain parts do not work in higher dimensions') must be in the identification that the overlap in the strong-disorder phase is of order n (needed for the influence sum to be order n and the BKS gain to be meaningful): in d >= 3 at low temperature the overlap is positive but the known lower bounds are only qualitative (positive limit of the overlap along the endpoint), not quantitative along the whole path. Rigorous partial: superconcentration (Var log Z_n = o(n)) in d >= 3 at low temperature follows from BKS if the expected path overlap is of order n, which is a consequence of the strong disorder characterisation via the endpoint overlap only if the overlap is positive at a positive fraction of times; this last step is plausible but I found no reference proving it in d >= 3. Reduction recorded. Obstruction: Quantitative (order n) path overlap in the strong disorder phase for d >= 3.

\[
\lambda_i - \lambda_{i+1} = \Theta(N^{-2/3}) \quad \text{for } |\lambda_i - 2| = O(N^{-2/3})
\]
This compressed spacing limits the convergence rate of eigenvector statistics to at most $N^{-1/6+o(1)}$.

Let u be harmonic and nonnegative in the open ball B_R(x0) in R^n, n >= 2. Then for every x with |x - x0| = r < R, R^{n-2} (R - r)/(R + r)^{n-1} u(x0) <= u(x) <= R^{n-2} (R + r)/(R - r)^{n-1} u(x0). In particular, taking r = R/2 in both bounds, sup over B_{R/2}(x0) of u <= 3^n inf over B_{R/2}(x0) of u. More generally, if Omega is a connected open set and K is a compact subset of Omega, there is C = C(n, K, Omega) such that sup over K of u <= C inf over K of u for every nonnegative harmonic u on Omega. Corollaries: Liouville's theorem for harmonic functions bounded below on R^n, and Harnack's convergence theorem for monotone sequences of harmonic functions.

      $L^2( \R^n)$. Fix  a   probability measure $\nu$  on $\R^{2n}$. 
We define  an operator  $\Pi(\nu) (A) $ by, 
    
    $$ \Pi(\nu) (A)= \int _{ \R^{2n}} W_h (-X) A W_h (X) d\nu (X), $$
    
   where $ W_h (X)$ are the Weyl translation operators in (\ref{trans-Weyl}). Then, the following three points hold true.
    
    
    i) The map $ \Pi(\nu)$ 
    is bounded from ${\cal L} ( L^2( \R^n))$ into itself and from $C_h$ 
  into itself.
    
    ii) We have,
    
    $$ \Pi (\mu) \Pi (\nu) = \Pi (\mu \star \nu).$$
    
   iii) We also have,
   
    $$ \Pi (\mu) (A \circ B) =  \Pi (\mu) (A) \circ   \Pi (\mu) (B).$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 13 (Finite-time decay of the non-invariant part) of arXiv:2608.30027, 'Under Ricci flow, a 3-torus goes flat'] Given \(0<\alpha<1\), \(K\geq0\), \(\lambda>0\), an integer \(N\geq2\), and
\(\sigma\in(0,1)\), there are constants
\(\beta_{\mathrm{orb}}>0\) and \(\beta_{\mathrm{pert}}>0\) with the following
property.  Let \(h(t)\) be an invariant Ricci-flow solution on \(M\), defined
for \(t\in[1,100]\), such that \(|\sec_{h(t)}|\leq K\) and such that, for every
\(t\in[1,100]\), the quotient circle for the chosen local \(\TT^2\)-structure
has length at least \(\lambda\), while every local \(\TT^2\)-orbit has
\(h(t)\)-diameter less than \(\beta_{\mathrm{orb}}\).  Let \(g_\RDT(t)\) be a
solution of the Ricci--DeTurck equation relative to \(h(t)\), defined for
\(t\in[1,100]\), and assume
\[
        \|g_\RDT-h\|_{X_h^N[1,100]}<\beta_{\mathrm{pert}}.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
        \|g_\RDT^\perp\|_{X_h^N[10,100]}
        \leq \alpha\,\bigl\|g_\RDT^\perp(1)\bigr\|_{C^{N,\sigma}(M,h(1))}.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition 5 of arXiv:2608.08242, 'Bang--bang representation of $3\times 3$ embeddable stochastic matrices'] The set $R_n\subseteq\mathcal M_+$ consists of the matrices $A$ for which
	\[
	A\sim
	X_{i_nj_n}(t_n)\cdots X_{i_1j_1}(t_1)
	\]
	for some $i_\ell\neq j_\ell$ and some $t_\ell\geq0$. Put
	$R_\infty=\bigcup_nR_n$.
	
	The threshold region $\T$ consists of matrices $A\in R_\infty$ with at least one zero entry.
	
	
	The vestibule $\V$  consists of the matrices $A>0$ such that $A\sim B X_{ij}(t)$
	for some $B\in\T$, some $i\neq j$, and some $t>0$.
	
	The narrow hall $\NH$ consists of the matrices $A\notin\T\cup\V$ such that $A\sim B X_{ij}(t)$
	for some $B\in\V$, some $i\neq j$, and some $t>0$.

body: [Proposition 23 of arXiv:2606.22964, 'Signature McKean--Vlasov stochastic differential equations'] Let $k\in\mathbb{N}$ and $p\geq 1$. Let $\widehat{G\Omega}_p(\mathbb{R}^{k+1})$ be the space of time-augmented geometric $p$-rough paths $\widehat{C}^{0,p-\textup{var}}([0,T],G^{\lfloor p\rfloor}(\mathbb{R}^{k+1}))$ (Remark \ref{remark:invariant_time_par}) with the topology induced by the inhomogeneous $p$-variation norm $d_{\textup{inhom $p$-var;$[0,T]$}}$ (Definition \ref{def:inhom_p_var_norm}). Then $\left(\widehat{G\Omega}_p(\mathbb{R}^{k+1}),d_{\textup{inhom $p$-var;$[0,T]$}}\right)$ is a Polish space. Furthermore, $(\mathcal{P}^p\left(\widehat{G\Omega}_p(\mathbb{R}^{k+1})\right),\overline{\mathcal{W}}^p_T)$, where $\overline{\mathcal{W}}^p_T$ is the Wasserstein distance defined in Definition \ref{def:Wasserstein_norm} with $\rho=d_{\textup{inhom $p$-var;$[0,T]$}}$, is a Polish space.

body: Let (X, Sigma, mu) be a measure space, let g be a nonnegative mu-integrable function on X, and let f_1, f_2, ... be measurable functions with |f_n| <= g pointwise almost everywhere for every n. Then liminf_n f_n and limsup_n f_n are integrable, and the integral over X of liminf_n f_n dmu <= liminf_n of the integral of f_n dmu <= limsup_n of the integral of f_n dmu <= the integral over X of limsup_n f_n dmu. This chain follows from applying Fatou's lemma to g - f_n and to g + f_n, and it yields the dominated convergence theorem whenever f_n converges pointwise a.e.
title: Fatou-Lebesgue theorem

body: [Corollary 2.4 of arXiv:2512.19517, 'Spiking and Resetting'] For any $t>0$ and any $0<a\leq b\leq 1$, the probability distribution $P^{\varepsilon}_{c}(\cdot\,:\,t,a,b)$ over $\mathbb{N}_{0}$ converges in law to a Poisson distribution with parameter $f(0)\,t\,\lambda_{*}([a,b])=f(0)\,t\,\int_{a}^{b}\cfrac{dx}{x^{2}}=f(0)\,t\,(a^{-1}-b^{-1})\ .$ Furthermore, we have that, for any $n\geq 0$, the function $\Phi_{n}^{\varepsilon}:r\in[0,\infty)\mapsto\mathbb{P}(e_{1}^{\varepsilon}\geq r,N^{\varepsilon}_{(0,r]}([a,b])=n)\in[0,1]$ converges uniformly on any compact interval $[0,t]$, $t>0$, as $\varepsilon$ vanishes to $\Phi_{n}:r\in[0,\infty)\mapsto e^{-rf(0)}e^{-rf(0)\lambda_{*}([a,b])}\frac{(rf(0)\lambda_{*}([a,b]))^{n}}{n!}\in[0,1]\ ,$ where $\lambda_{*}([a,b])=\int_{a}^{b}dx/x^{2}=a^{-1}-b^{-1}$ as in the first part. [The paper prints this limit as $e^{-rf(0)}e^{-r\lambda_{*}([a,b]}\frac{(r\lambda_{*}([a,b]))^{n}}{n!}$; the factor $f(0)$ and the closing parenthesis are restored here: the limit is forced by Proposition 2.2, whose generating function $Z(z,\sigma:a,b)=\sum_{n}z^{n}\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\sigma r}\Phi_{n}(r)\,dr=1/(\sigma+f(0)+(1-z)f(0)(1/a-1/b))$ inverts to it, and the paper derives the first part, Poisson with parameter $f(0)\,t\,(a^{-1}-b^{-1})$, from it.] Notation from the paper: $e_{1}^{\varepsilon}=\inf\{t\geq 0:X_{t}^{\varepsilon}>y_{*}^{\varepsilon}\}$ is the first jump time; $N^{\varepsilon}_{(0,r]}([a,b])$ is the number of pre-spikes in $(0,r]\times[a,b]$; and $P^{\varepsilon}_{c}(n,t:a,b)$ is the probability of exactly $n$ pre-spikes in $(0,t)\times[a,b]$ given no jump in $(0,t)$, i.e. the no-jump probability of that event divided by $\mathbb{P}(e_{1}^{\varepsilon}\geq t)$.

body: Let G be a finite, connected, simple planar graph, drawn in the plane with no two edges crossing, with V vertices, E edges, and F faces (regions into which the drawing divides the plane, including the single unbounded outer face). Then V - E + F = 2. [standard, e.g. Diestel, Graph Theory]
title: Euler's Formula for Connected Planar Graphs
