ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Estimate the number of near-maximal configurations and compare with the connectivity threshold of the level set on the hypercube. Result: In the NK model with K = O(1) the fitness is a sum of n local terms each depending on K + 1 bits, so the field is a sum of n independent contributions (for the standard model with random neighbourhoods) and the level set at height M_n - delta_n with delta_n = o(n) but delta_n >> sqrt n contains exp(c delta_n^2/n)... the number of configurations within delta of the maximum is, by a large-deviation count, about exp(n I(delta/n)) for a rate I; bridges exist if this level set percolates on the hypercube, and a level set of density rho on the n-cube contains a giant connected component when the local structure allows, roughly when each configuration in the set has on average more than one neighbour in the set: the expected number of neighbours in the level set of a typical level-set point is n times the conditional probability that flipping one bit stays within delta of the maximum, which is n times (probability that the change of the K+1 affected local terms is at most delta), of order n delta/n = delta when delta is small compared to the local term scale... so bridges exist (heuristically) when delta_n >> 1, i.e. the level set within a constant deficit of the maximum is connected in the giant-component sense for deficits growing to infinity, while for bounded deficits the peaks are isolated. This suggests the answer depends on the deficit scale: bridges at deficit delta_n -> infinity, islands at bounded deficit. The argument is a branching heuristic (neighbour counts) without control of dependencies; making it rigorous would need a second-moment argument on the number of level-set paths, which I did not carry out. Key identity: Expected number of level-set neighbours of a level-set point is of order delta (the deficit); bridges expected iff the deficit tends to infinity. Obstruction: Second moment for level-set paths on the hypercube not done.

[Lemma 3 (Chain-compatible cutoffs) of arXiv:2607.19752, 'Weak Equilibrium Measures and Capacity--Hitting Identities\\ for the Hypoelliptic Third-Or'] Let $\mathsf O\subset\R^{3d}$ be a bounded smooth open set.  After the
reordering
\[
    x^1=r,\qquad x^2=p,\qquad x^3=\theta,
\]
there exist cutoff drifts, indexed by $0\le\delta\le1$,
\[
    B_1^{\mathsf O},B_2^{\delta,\mathsf O}
        \in C_b^\infty\left(\R^{3d};\R^d\right),
    \qquad
    B_3^{\delta,\mathsf O}
        \in C_b^\infty\left(\R^{2d};\R^d\right),
\]
with
\[
    B^{\delta,\mathsf O}(x)
    =\left(
        B_1^{\mathsf O}(x),
        B_2^{\delta,\mathsf O}(x),
        B_3^{\delta,\mathsf O}\left(x^2,x^3\right)
    \right),
\]
such that, for every $x\in\mathsf O$,
\begin{equation}
    B^{\delta,\mathsf O}(x)
    =
    \begin{pmatrix}
        -\gamma x^2-\gamma x^1\\
        -L^{-1}\nabla U(x^3)+\gamma x^1-\delta Lx^2\\
        x^2-\delta\nabla U(x^3)
    \end{pmatrix}.
\end{equation}
Moreover, for every $k\ge0$,
\begin{equation}
    \sup_{0\le\delta\le1}
    \left(
        \left\|B_1^{\mathsf O}\right\|_{C_b^k}
        +\left\|B_2^{\delta,\mathsf O}\right\|_{C_b^k}
        +\left\|B_3^{\delta,\mathsf O}\right\|_{C_b^k}
    \right)<\infty.
\end{equation}
On $\mathsf O$,
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
    J_{x^1}B_2^{\delta,\mathsf O}=\gamma I_{d},
    \qquad
    J_{x^2}B_3^{\delta,\mathsf O}=I_{d}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
The same assertions hold for cutoff drifts $B^{\delta,\mathsf O,*}$ of the
adjoint dynamics, with
\begin{equation}
    B^{\delta,\mathsf O,*}(x)
    =
    \begin{pmatrix}
        \gamma x^2-\gamma x^1\\
        L^{-1}\nabla U(x^3)-\gamma x^1-\delta Lx^2\\
        -x^2-\delta\nabla U(x^3)
    \end{pmatrix},
    \qquad x\in\mathsf O,
\end{equation}
and hence with chain links $-\gamma I_d$ and $-I_d$.

body:
[Proposition 6 of arXiv:2605.09706, 'A dyadic construction of a three-dimensional attractive point interaction Markov family'] Fix $T,\beta,\varepsilon>0$ and $0\le s<t\le T$. The map 
$\widehat{\mathsf K}^{T,\beta,\varepsilon}_{[s,t]}$ given by~\eqref{EqDefGlobalDyadicLimitKernel_Inf} is well defined and satisfies the following:
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item $\widehat{\mathsf K}^{T,\beta,\varepsilon}_{[s,t]}:\;
E_\varepsilon \times \mathcal B(E_\varepsilon)\to [0,1]$ is a sub-probability kernel on $E_\varepsilon$.

\item If $0\le r<s<t\le T$ with $r,s,t\in\mathbb D_T$, then for every $x\in E_\varepsilon$ and every $A\in\mathcal B(E_\varepsilon)$,
\begin{align}
\widehat{\mathsf K}^{T,\beta,\varepsilon}_{[r,t]}(x,A)
\,=\,
\int_{E_\varepsilon}
\widehat{\mathsf K}^{T,\beta,\varepsilon}_{[r,s]}(x,dy)\,
\widehat{\mathsf K}^{T,\beta,\varepsilon}_{[s,t]}(y,A)\, .
\end{align}
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [campaign status: candidate_full_solution - author-checked, unrefereed] Aldous and Fill, Open Problem 4.30 (p. 137) asks whether there is an explicit function psi(b,s) tending to 0 as s tends to infinity, not depending on the chain, with sup_x |P(S_t/(sigma sqrt t) <= x) - P(Z <= x)| <= psi(||g||_inf, t/tau2) for standardized g and continuous-time reversible chains. Our result (id P0209, 2026-09-08): NO such psi exists. Take two independent reversible chains: Y two-state with rates epsilon and 1 - epsilon (spectral gap exactly 1) and Z a fair sign flip at rate R/2; set epsilon = s^-2, R = s^4, A = 2 epsilon + sqrt((1-epsilon)(1-4 epsilon)), B = (2-A)/(1-epsilon) and g = A Z + B (Y - epsilon). Then exactly, at every s: E g = 0, E g^2 = 1, ||g||_inf = 2 and tau2 = 1. Taking t = s sends t/tau2 to infinity with the sup norm pinned at 2, yet normality fails: S_t is compound Poisson with vanishing intensity (the mean number of visits to the rare state is epsilon t = 1/s, tending to 0), so with probability 1 - O(1/s) no visit occurs and S_t sits near the deterministic value -B epsilon t while the whole variance is carried by one rare excursion. Verification as the source words it: the identities were checked to seven decimals at every s, and the measured Kolmogorov distance to N(0,1) is 0.478, 0.505, 0.509, 0.506 at s = 30, 100, 300, 1000 - flat at about 1/2, not decreasing, while t/tau2 rises from 30 to 1000. Prior art not cleared. two independent reversible chains as specified (four states in total) g standardized: E g = 0, E g^2 = 1, sup norm 2, tau2 = 1 t = s, epsilon = s^-2, R = s^4

body:
[Corollary 12 (Recovery of known regimes and strict extension) of arXiv:2609.01116, 'Vector-Carleson, Calder\'on, and Poisson--Atomic Criteria for\\ Generalized Hilbert Operat'] Put
\[
 B_{2,p}(\phi)
 =|\phi(0)|+
 \left(\sum_{j\ge0}
  \bigl(2^{-j/p'}\|\Delta_j\phi\|_2\bigr)^t\right)^{1/t}.
 \tag{4.9}
\]
Then:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
 \item $\|T_\phi:H^p\to H^2\|\asymp_p B_{2,p}(\phi)$, and
 boundedness of $T_\phi:H^p\to H^p$ implies
 $B_{2,p}(\phi)<\infty$.
 \item If $\operatorname{supp}\widehat\phi$ is contained in an analytic
 $\Lambda(p)$-set $E\subset\mathbb N_0$, then
 \[
  T_\phi:H^p\to H^p\text{ is bounded}
  \iff B_{2,p}(\phi)<\infty,
 \]
 with
 \[
  \|T_\phi:H^p\to H^2\|
  \le\|T_\phi:H^p\to H^p\|
  \le C_{E,p}\|T_\phi:H^p\to H^2\|.
 \]
 In this sector boundedness is equivalent to compactness.
 \item Hadamard-lacunary symbols are a special case of \textup{(ii)}.
 For a one-frequency-per-block symbol the test $h=1$ exactly norms the
 vector criterion, up to constants depending only on $p$.
 \item The blockwise condition
 \[
  \bigl(2^{-j/p'}\|\Delta_j\phi\|_{H^p}\bigr)_j\in\ell^t
 \]
 is sufficient in general and is not necessary, even for symbols with
 a consecutive interval occupying half of every sufficiently large hard
 block.
\end{enumerate}

    \[ x_n = \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} p(n, i)x_i \ \text{ for $n > k$}. \]
    Suppose that $\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} p(n,i) = 1$ and $\frac{p(n,i)}{p(n+1, i)}$ is increasing in $i$ for every $n$. Then $x_{n+1} < x_n$ for all $n \geq k$. In particular, $\lim_{n \to \infty} x_n$ exists. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition 19 of arXiv:2609.00567, 'Hodge--Tate splitting and Akizuki--Nakano vanishing in positive characteristic'] Let \(\iota \colon X \to S\) be a morphism of $\F_p$-stacks.
Let
\[
X^{(1)} \defeq X\times_{S,F_S}S
\]
be the relative Frobenius twist, and let
\[
F_{X/S}\colon X \to  X^{(1)}
\]
be the relative Frobenius.
  \begin{itemize}
      \item   The \emph{(absolute) de Rham stack} of \(X\) is defined as a functor
  \begin{equation*}
    X^{\dR} \colon \CAlg^{an}_{\setF_p} \to \Ani; \  R \mapsto X(W(R)/^L p),
  \end{equation*}
  where \(W(R)\) is the ring of Witt vectors of \(R\), \(-/^L p\) is the derived quotient by \(p\), and \(X(W(R)/^L p)\) is the mapping space \(\Map_{\dSch_{\setF_p}}(\Spec(W(R)/^L p), X)\) in the \(\infty\)-category of derived schemes over \(\setF_p\).
  Since this is isomorphic to the relative Hodge--Tate stack \((X/\setZ_p)^{\HT}\) of \(X\) relative to the crystalline prism \((\setZ_p, (p))\) introduced in \cite{bhatt2022Prismatization}*{Construction 7.1}, this is a stack on \(\CAlg^{an}_{\setF_p}\) (\cite{bhatt2022Prismatization}*{Lemma 7.3}).

  This is equipped with natural morphisms
  \begin{equation*}
    \pi_{X} \colon X \to X^{\dR} \quad \text{and} \quad \nu_X \colon X^{\dR} \to X
  \end{equation*}
  of \(\setF_p\)-stacks: For each \(R \in \CAlg^{an}_{\setF_p}\), each morphism is given by precomposition of morphisms
  \begin{equation*}
    R \xrightarrow{\Phi_R} W(R)/^L p \quad \text{and} \quad W(R)/^L p \xrightarrow{\res} R,
  \end{equation*}
  where \(\Phi_R\) is the animation of the morphism \(a \mapsto [a^p] \bmod p\) and \(\res\) is the restriction morphism.
  Note that the composition \(\nu_X \circ \pi_X\) is the absolute Frobenius morphism \(F_X \colon X \to X\) of \(X\).
\item The \emph{de Rham stack} of $X$ over $S$ is defined by
\[
(X/S)^{\dR} \defeq X^{\dR} \times_{S^{\dR},\pi_S} S.
\]
We define natural morphisms
  \begin{equation*}
    \pi_{X/S} \colon X \to (X/S)^{\dR} \quad \text{and} \quad \nu_{X/S} \colon (X/S)^{\dR} \to X^{(1)}
  \end{equation*}
  of \(\setF_p\)-stacks as follows:
The morphism $\pi_{X/S}$ is defined by
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
X \arrow[r,"\pi_{X/S}"'] \arrow[rd,bend right,"\iota"] \arrow[rr,bend left,"\pi_X"] & X^{\dR} \times_{S^{\dR}} S \arrow[r,"\pr_1"] \arrow[d,"\pr_2"] & X^{\dR} \arrow[d,"\iota^{\dR}"] \\
& S \arrow[r,"\pi_S"] & S^{\dR}.
\end{tikzcd}
\]
The morphism $\nu_{X/S} \colon (X/S)^{\dR} \to X^{(1)}$ is induced by the following commutative diagram
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
X^{\dR} \times_{S^{\dR}} S \arrow[r,"\pr_1"] \arrow[d,"\pr_2"] & X^{\dR} \arrow[d,"\iota^{\dR}"] \arrow[r,"\nu_X"] & X \arrow[d,"\iota"] \\
S \arrow[r,"\pi_S"] \arrow[rr,bend right,"F"] & S^{\dR} \arrow[r,"\nu_S"] & S.
\end{tikzcd}
\]
\item We assume that $\iota$ is smooth representable.
Then the cotangent complex \(L_{X/S}\) is a locally free \(\cO_X\)-module concentrated in degree \(0\).  
We set
\[
\Omega^1_{X/S} \defeq L_{X/S},
\qquad
\Omega^i_{X/S} \defeq 
\bigwedge_{\cO_X}^i\Omega^1_{X/S}.
\]
The universal \(S\)-derivation
\[
d_{X/S}\colon \cO_X \to  \Omega^1_{X/S}
\]
extends uniquely to the relative de Rham complex
\[
\Omega^\bullet_{X/S}
=
\left[
\cO_X
\xrightarrow{d_{X/S}}
\Omega^1_{X/S}
\xrightarrow{d_{X/S}}
\Omega^2_{X/S}
 \to \cdots
\right].
\]

We define a morphism of complexes of $\cO_{X^{(1)}}$-modules
\[
F^{\dR}_{X/S} \colon \cO_{X^{(1)}} \to F_{X/S,*}\Omega^{\bullet}_{X/S}
\]
as follows:
We have
\[
d_{X/S}\circ F_{X/S}^{\sharp}=0
\]
by checking smooth locally on \(X\).  
Therefore, the morphism
\[
F_{X/S}^{\sharp}\colon
\cO_{X^{(1)}} \to  F_{X/S,*}\cO_X
\]
defines a morphism of complexes
\[
F_{X/S}^{\dR}\colon
\cO_{X^{(1)}}
 \to 
F_{X/S,*}\Omega^\bullet_{X/S},
\]
whose degree \(0\) component is \(F_{X/S}^{\sharp}\) and whose
positive-degree components are zero.
\end{itemize}

[Theorem disintegration of arXiv:2606.21556, 'Mean field limit of non-exchangeable interacting diffusions on co-evolutionary networks'] Let \(\Omega\)  and \(\mathcal{X}\) be Polish spaces, and let \(\nu \in \mathcal{P}(\Omega)\). Consider any
	\(\mu \in \mathcal{P}_{\nu}(\mathcal{X}\times \Omega)\). Then, there exists a unique (up to \(\nu\)-a.e. equality)
	Borel family \((\mu^{\omega})_{\omega \in \Omega}\subset \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X})\) such that 
     	\[
     		\int_{\mathcal{X}\times \Omega} \varphi(x,\omega)d\mu(x,\omega)=\int_{\Omega} \int_{\mathcal{X}} \varphi(x,\omega)d\mu^{\omega}(x)d\nu(\omega),
     	\]
	for every bounded and measurable function \(\varphi:\mathcal{X}\times \Omega\to \mathbb{R}\). Conversely, given any Borel
	family \((\mu^{\omega})_{\omega \in \Omega}\subset \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X})\), we can associate a unique fibered probability
	measure \(\mu \in \mathcal{P}_{\nu}(\mathcal{X}\times \Omega)\) so that the above formula holds true, and it will be denoted
	by \(\mu(x,\omega)=\mu^{\omega}(x)\otimes d\nu(\omega)\). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Disintegration theorem

[Definition def:dg of arXiv:2410.23509, 'Dynkin Games for L\'evy Processes'] Let 
$G_1(x)\leq G_2(x)$
be two real continuous payoff functions.
Consider a L\'evy process $X$ and a discount factor $r>0$, 
such that conditions (equation eq:ic of the paper) and (equation eq:limit of the paper) above hold.
Given two stopping times $\sigma$ and $\tau$, define the expected payoff

$$
{\operatorname{\mathbf{M}}_x}(\sigma,\tau)=\operatorname{\mathbf{E}}_x\left(
e^{-r\tau}G_1(X_{\tau})\mathbf{1}_{\{\tau\leq\sigma\}}
+
e^{-r\sigma}G_2(X_{\sigma})\mathbf{1}_{\{\sigma<\tau\}}
\right).
$$

The Dynkin game (DG) problem consists
in finding the value function $V(x)$ and two optimal stopping rules ${\sigma^*}$ and ${\tau^*}$ such that
\begin{align}
V(x)&=\inf_{\sigma}\sup_{\tau}{\operatorname{\mathbf{M}}_x}(\sigma,\tau)=\sup_{\tau}\inf_{\sigma}{\operatorname{\mathbf{M}}_x}(\sigma,\tau)={\operatorname{\mathbf{M}}_x}(\sigma^*,\tau^*).

\end{align}
title: Dynkin game

[Lemma CVtG of arXiv:2504.00512, 'Localization-delocalization transition for a random block matrix model at the edge'] Under the assumptions of Theorem (MixEV of the paper), suppose $\mathfrak{t}= N^{-1/3+\mathfrak c}$ for a constant $\mathfrak c \in (0,1/10)$. Then, for any fixed $n\in \mathbb{N}$, there exist a constant $c_n=c_n(\mathfrak c,\delta_A,\varepsilon_A)>0$ such that 
\begin{align}
&\left|	\mathbb{E} O\pa{\gamma_+  \left({DN}\right)^{2/3}\pa{E^+-\lambda_1^{{\mathfrak t}}},\ldots,\gamma_+ \left({DN}\right)^{2/3}\pa{E^+-\lambda_n^{{\mathfrak t}}}}\right.\nonumber\\
&\left.-\mathbb{E} O\pa{ \left({DN}\right)^{2/3}\left({2-\mu_1}\right),\ldots, \left({DN}\right)^{2/3}\left({2-\mu_n}\right)}   \right|\le N^{-c_n}   , 
\end{align}
where $\lambda_1^{{\mathfrak t}}\ge\cdots\ge \lambda_n^{{\mathfrak t}}$ and $\mu_1\ge\cdots\ge \mu_n$ denote respectively the largest $n$ eigenvalues of ${H_{\Lambda}}({\mathfrak t})$ and a $DN\times DN$ GUE. 
The corresponding result also holds for $\gamma_-(DN)^{2/3}(\lambda_{DN}^{{\mathfrak t}}-E^-,\ldots,\lambda_{DN-n}^{{\mathfrak t}}-E^- )$ at the left edge $E^-$.

[Definition 10 (Weighted deterministic maximal $L^p$-regularity) of arXiv:2606.15425, 'Well-posedness of stochastic parabolic equations with gradient nonlinearities and applicat'] Let $\mathcal B_1 \coloneqq D(A) \subset \mathcal B$. Given $p \in (1,\infty)$ and $\beta \in (-1,p-1)$, we say that $A$ has \textit{weighted deterministic maximal $L^p$-regularity} on $[0,T]$ if for every
$f\in L^p_\beta([0,T];\mathcal B)$ and $u_0\in (\mathcal B,\mathcal B_1)_{1-(1+\beta)/p,p}$
there exists a unique
$$
u\in W^{1,p}_\beta([0,T];\mathcal B)\cap L^p_\beta([0,T];\mathcal B_1)
$$
such that $u(0)=u_0$ and
$$
u'(t)+Au(t)=f(t)\quad \text{for a.e. } t\in(0,T),
$$
and moreover, there is a constant $C_{MR}>0$ independent of $f$ and $u_0$ such that
\begin{equation}
\norm{u}_{W^{1,p}_\beta([0,T];\mathcal B)}+\norm{u}_{L^p_\beta([0,T];\mathcal B_1)}
\leq C_{MR}\left(\norm{f}_{L^p_\beta([0,T];\mathcal B)}+\norm{u_0}_{(\mathcal B,\mathcal B_1)_{1-(1+\beta)/p,p}}\right).
\end{equation}
title: Weighted deterministic maximal $L^p$-regularity

Let X be a random variable with characteristic function \phi(t). If \mathbb{E}[|X|^k] < \infty for some integer k \ge 1, then \phi has continuous derivatives up to order k on \mathbb{R}, and for every j \in \{1, \dots, k\}, \phi^{(j)}(t) = i^j \mathbb{E}[X^j e^{itX}]. body:
[Theorem 6 (\cite{DHKBrown},\cite{HoZhong2020Brown}) of arXiv:2511.10535, 'Eigenvalues of Brownian Motions on $\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$'] Let $b_{0,1}(t)$ be a free multiplicative Brownian motion, and let $u_0$ be a unitary operator freely independent from $b_{0,1}$.  Denote by $\mu_{u_0}$ the spectral measure of $u_0$, a probability measure on the unit circle $\mathbb{T}$.

Define $T(u_0,\cdot)\colon\C\to\R_+$ by
\begin{equation}  T(u_0,z) = \frac{\log |z|^2}{|z|^2-1}\left(\int_{\mathbb{T}} \frac{\mu_{u_0}(d\xi)}{|\xi-z|^2}\right)^{-1}.
\end{equation}
Also, for each $t>0$, define the open precompact set $\Sigma(u_0,t)$ by
\begin{equation}  \Sigma(u_0,t) = \{z\in\C\colon T(u_0,z)<t\}. \end{equation}
The Brown measure $\mu_{u_0b_{1,0}(t)}$ has support equal to $\overline{\Sigma(u_0,t)}$.  The Brown measure is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure, and has density on $\overline{\Sigma(u_0,t)}$ that is real analytic in $\Sigma(u_0,t)$.  The density has the form $z=re^{i\theta}\mapsto w_t(\theta)/r^2$, with the radial function $w_t$ bounded by $w_t(\theta)<\frac{1}{\pi t}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 11 (Cube-slice rationalization) of arXiv:2606.25204, 'Exponential Rank Bounds for Random Matrices'] Let \(V\subseteq\R^n\) be a linear subspace and let \(a\in\R^n\).  Put
\[
   S=(a+V)\cap\{0,1\}^n.
\]
If \(S\neq\varnothing\), choose \(b_0\in S\) and define
\[
   U=\Span(S-b_0).
\]
Then \(U\) is a rational linear subspace, \(U\subseteq V\), and
\[
   (a+V)\cap\{0,1\}^n=(b_0+U)\cap\{0,1\}^n.
\]

Owner draft: independently checked proof (C006 v1). For d>=1, the signed radial line law on [-1,1] with density f_d(t)=(d/2)|t|^(d-1) can be (2k+1)-CM only if (k/(k+1))^d>=1/(2k+1). A zero-sum tuple cannot have every |t_i|>k/(k+1), since at least k+1 share a sign and cannot be canceled by k bounded terms. Thus F_2 is not 3-CM (1/4<1/3) and F_4 is not 5-CM (16/81<1/5). These are the uniform disk/four-ball conditional laws on unoriented lines through the center. The full balls are mixable, so this refutes componentwise centered radial-needle mixing, not the convex-body conjecture. Projection onto a fixed line has a different marginal.

[Prop Gintl of arXiv:2510.23430, 'On the Martin boundary for discrete TASEP'] Assume that $x_1, \dots, x_n, \mathfrak a, \mathfrak b$ are complex parameters satisfying $\max\{|\mathfrak a|,|\mathfrak b|\}<\min\{|x_i|^{-1}\}_i$. Let $\lambda$ be a partition, $k$ an integer such that $l(\lambda)\leq k$, and $\mathcal C$ be a positively-oriented simple contour encircling $0,\mathfrak a$ and $\mathfrak b$ and leaving $x_i^{-1}$ outside. Then
$$
G_\lambda^{(\mathfrak a,-\mathfrak b)}(x_1, \dots, x_n)=\oint_{\mathcal{C}}\cdots\oint_{\mathcal{C}} \frac{du_1}{2\pi \mathbf i}\dots \frac{du_k}{2\pi \mathbf i}\prod_{i<j}(u_i-u_j)\prod_{i=1}^k\left( \frac{1}{(u_i-\mathfrak a)^{\lambda_i}(u_i-\mathfrak b)^{k-i+1}}\prod_{j=1}^n\frac{1-\mathfrak b x_j}{1-u_ix_j}\right).
$$

body: In mathematical analysis, the alternating series test proves that an alternating series is convergent when its terms decrease monotonically in absolute value and approach zero in the limit. The test was devised by Gottfried Leibniz and is sometimes known as Leibniz's test, Leibniz's rule, or the Leibniz criterion. The test is only sufficient, not necessary, so some convergent alternating series may fail the first part of the test.
title: Alternating series test

 \item the random variables
  $$ \left(\int_{0}^{S}\int_{\mathbb{S}}\partial_{\mu}\psi(\mu_s^{(h)},X_s^{(h)}(\mathbf{x}))[{DX_s^{(h)}(\mathbf{x})}]^2\mathrm{d}\mathbf{x} \mathrm{d}s\right)_{{h \in T/{\mathbb N}^*}}$$
converge in law as $h\searrow 0$ to the random variable

\end{enumerate}

and

Its corollary calling variance MONOTONICITY the separate (possibly softer) open target is stale for a second reason - fire 4 (2026-08-15) took monotonicity off the target list for having no consumer in this program. [Proposition 14 (Transfer from singularity to corank) of arXiv:2606.25204, 'Exponential Rank Bounds for Random Matrices'] Fix \(b\in(0,1)\).  For each \(n\ge1\), let \(A=(A_{ij})\) be an
\(n\times n\) random matrix with independent real entries.  Assume that
\begin{align}
   \sup_{x\in\R}\PP\{A_{ij}=x\} &\leq b<1
   \qquad (1\leq i,j\leq n), \\
   \PP\{\rank A<n\} &\leq C_0\exp(-c_0 n)
   \qquad\text{for all }n\ge n_0 
\end{align}
for some constants \(C_0>0\), \(c_0>0\), and \(n_0\ge1\).  Then there exists
\(c_{5.1}=c_{5.1}(b,C_0,c_0,n_0)>0\) such that for all \(n\ge1\) and all
\(1\leq k\leq n\),
\begin{equation}
   \PP\{\rank A\leq n-k\}\leq \exp(-c_{5.1}nk).
\end{equation}
title: Transfer from singularity to corank

body: Load-bearing hypothesis: Omega bounded. The proofs use boundedness twice - the auxiliary function exp(gamma x_1) must be bounded on Omega, and the maximum must be attained on a compact set. On unbounded domains the conclusion is false even for harmonic functions with zero boundary data. Unbounded counterexample: on the half-space {x_n > 0} the function u(x) = x_n is harmonic and vanishes on the whole boundary, yet u > 0 inside; sup u = infinity while sup over the boundary of u = 0. Bounded counterexample (so boundedness of u does not rescue the statement in general): for n >= 3 let Omega = {|x| > 1} and u(x) = 1 - |x|^{2-n}. Then u is harmonic in Omega, continuous up to the boundary, bounded with 0 <= u < 1, u = 0 on the boundary sphere, and sup over Omega of u = 1 > 0 = sup over the boundary of u^+. In the plane, u(x) = log|x| on {|x| > 1} is an unbounded version of the same phenomenon. What restores the principle: treat infinity as a boundary point, i.e. assume limsup of u(x) as |x| tends to infinity is <= 0 (then the principle holds on any unbounded Omega, by exhausting with large balls), or impose a Phragmen-Lindeloef growth restriction adapted to the geometry. The admissible growth is set by the opening of the domain, and a thinner domain permits faster growth, not slower: in a plane sector of opening pi/a the threshold is exp(|x|^a), so a narrow sector allows faster growth than a half-plane, and in a strip of width d the threshold is exp(pi|x|/d), the extremal being exp(pi x_1/d) cos(pi x_2/d). The same caution applies to the H^1 weak maximum principle: its proof uses the Sobolev inequality together with the fact that the level sets have finite measure.
title: Pitfall: The Weak Maximum Principle Needs a Bounded Domain (or Control at Infinity)

Let X_1, \dots, X_n be independent Bernoulli random variables with \mathbb{P}(X_k = 1) = p_k = 1 - \mathbb{P}(X_k = 0). Let S_n = \sum_{k=1}^n X_k and \lambda = \sum_{k=1}^n p_k. Let Y \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda). Then the total variation distance between the distribution of S_n and Y satisfies d_{TV}(\mathcal{L}(S_n), \text{Poisson}(\lambda)) = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{k=0}^\infty |\mathbb{P}(S_n = k) - \frac{\lambda^k e^{-\lambda}}{k!}| \le \sum_{k=1}^n p_k^2.
X_k independent Bernoulli(p_k)
\lambda = \sum p_k

[Lemma lem:moving-bump of arXiv:2609.00794, 'On operators whose adjoints or second adjoints attain their norms'] Let
\[
u:=\left(\frac1{2^n}\right)_{n=1}^\infty\in S_{\ell_1},
\qquad
b_n:=\frac12(e_{n+1}-e_{n+2})\in S_{\ell_1},
\]
where $(e_n)$ denotes the standard coordinate basis for $\ell_1$. 
Let $0<\kappa<1$, and let $S\in\mathcal L(\ell_1,\ell_1)$.
Suppose that there exist a set $A\subset\mathbb N$, a mapping
$\nu\colon A\to\mathbb N$, and scalars $(\lambda_j)_{j\in A}$ such that

\begin{enumerate}
\itemsep0.25em
\item  $Se_j=\kappa u+(1-\kappa)\lambda_j b_{\nu(j)}$ for every $j \in A$, and $|\lambda_j|\leqslant 1$ for every $j \in A$;

\item there exist $(j_n)\subset A$ and a sequence $(s_n)$ tending to
infinity such that
\[
Se_{j_n}=\kappa u+(1-\kappa)b_{s_n};
\]

\item $\sup_{j\notin A}\|Se_j\|<1$.
\end{enumerate}

Then $\|S\|=1$ and $S^*$ does not attain its norm.

\[
 \prod_{a=1}^r x_{a,j}\to1
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 \max_{a,b}|x_{a,j}-x_{b,j}|\to0
\]
uniformly, then $x_{a,j}\to1$ uniformly for every $a$.

Own-work draft, proof (unaudited), T280-w716-C9 v1, kind route-failure, Target 3. For every k>=1, the prepared aligned finite scale law supported on 1,...,k+1, with zero output weights and biases and exp activation, has a positive risk threshold whose first hitting time for the normalized degree-k sphere harmonic tends to infinity with d. Thus k+1 occupied scales with fixed positive separation do not alone imply O(1)-in-d small-risk learning. For k=1 and scales 1,2 the Gaussian squared approximation floor exceeds 2/5, so risk 1/4 cannot be attained in dimension-uniform bounded time. For any fixed finite horizon T and positive minimum atom mass, d/dt E a^2<=1/2 implies pointwise bounded output coefficients and O(1/d) aligned-scale drift; the actual nonlinear output remains O(1/d) from its initial exponential span. The degree-k sphere harmonic has a strictly positive limiting Gaussian projection distance from the span at scales 1,...,k+1. For scales 1,2 and target Z the squared distance is 1-(1-4 exp(-2)+4 exp(-3))/(exp(1)-1)>2/5. This is a full-risk obstruction; no claim is made about a single harmonic projection hitting time. No novelty claim or independent certification.

[Theorem thm:highdimEinstein of arXiv:2609.01464, 'Removability of non-isolated singularities for Einstein metrics and RCD spaces'] Let $n\geqslant 2$ be an integer, and $a>0$. There exists $0<\varepsilon:=\varepsilon(n,a)<1$ such that the following holds.
  
  Let $(M^n, g)$ be a closed $L^\infty$-Riemannian manifold, and $S\subset M$ a closed subset of Assouad codimension greater than $2+a$; see (def:Codimension of the paper). Suppose that $\mathrm{Ric}(g) = Kg$ on $M\setminus S$ for some $K\in\mathbb R$, and in addition suppose that one of the following conditions holds:
  \begin{itemize}
      \item[(a)] Either $(1 - \varepsilon)h \leqslant g \leqslant (1+\varepsilon) h$ for a smooth metric $h$ on $M$,
      \item[(b)] Or $g$ is continuous.

PRIVATE REDUCTION, author-recorded. By Aizenman's random-current identity the four-point Ursell function is expressed through the probability that the currents from x_1 to x_2 and from x_3 to x_4 share a cluster; non-triviality (nonvanishing renormalised coupling) is equivalent to inf over scales L of P(two independent random-current clusters at scale L intersect) > 0. The 4D case is now trivial (Aizenman-Duminil-Copin 2021); in 3D the heuristic is favourable because the current-cluster dimension (5 - eta)/2 = 2.48 exceeds 3/2, so independent fractals of that dimension would intersect with positive probability. A second-moment argument on the number of intersection points reduces the uniform lower bound to (a) a two-point function lower bound with exponent 2 - eps in d = 3 (Duminil-Copin's Conjecture 5, PIMS lectures) and (b) a variance bound on the intersection count, which involves six-point correlations beyond the Lebowitz inequality. Both inputs are open; (b) is the genuinely new obligation.

[Thm 2 of arXiv:2605.07059, 'Modified ruin probability for a Cram{\'e}r-Lundberg model driven by a compound mixed Poiss'] Fix $\ell\in(0,c/\mu)$. Assume that
\[
\psi_{\rm cl}(u,\ell)\sim c_\ell e^{-R_\ell u},\qquad u\to\infty,
\]
for some constants $c_\ell,R_\ell>0$. If $\psi$ is continuous or monotone on $(-\infty,0)$, then
\[
\psi_\ell(u)\sim C_\ell\,\psi_{\rm cl}(u,\ell),\qquad u\to\infty,
\]
where
\[
C_\ell:=\int_{(-\infty,0)}\psi(y)\,\nu_\ell(\rmd y)
\]
and the probability measure $\nu_\ell$ is determined by
\begin{align*}
&\nu_\ell(( -\infty,-x])
\\
&=\frac{1}{c-\ell\mu}\Bigl(ce^{-R_\ell x}
\\
&\qquad\qquad-\ell\int_0^x e^{-R_\ell(x-z)}\bar F(z)\,\rmd z
\\
&\qquad\qquad-\ell\int_x^{\infty}\bar F(z)\,\rmd z\Bigr),
\end{align*}
for $x\ge0$.

[Definition gsp of arXiv:2608.30777, 'Inhomogeneous nonlinear Schr\"odinger equation \\ in Fourier-Lebesgue and modulation space'] Let $1\leq p_{0} \leq 2.$
 Consider a pair of exponents $(Q_{p_{0}}(r),r)$ satisfying 
\begin{align*}
&\frac{2}{Q_{p_{0}}(r)} + \frac{1}{r} = \frac{1}{p_{0}} \\
  \text{either}\quad 
& 0 < \frac{1}{Q_{p_{0}}(r)} < \min \left( \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{r},\; \frac{1}{4} \right) \quad  \text{and}\quad
  0 < \frac{1}{r} < \frac{1}{2}\\
&  \text{or}\quad 
(Q_{p_0}(r), r)= (4, r) \quad  \text{and}\quad r > 4.
\end{align*}
The set of all such pairs is denoted by 
$\widehat{\mathcal{X}}(p_{0}).$

Let p>0. Let X_n be real random variables in L^p on one probability space, and let X be a finite real random variable on that space. Then X is in L^p and E|X_n-X|^p tends to zero if and only if X_n converges to X in probability and {|X_n|^p:n>=1} is uniformly integrable. For 0<p<1, L^p convergence here means convergence of the pth absolute moments of the differences; no norm or Minkowski inequality is asserted.

[Defin 55 of arXiv:2604.00635, 'Large deviations of the periodic Toda chain'] Let $\op{s}_{\rho}$ be the dilation with scale $\rho > 0$: $\op{s}_{\rho}(x)=\rho x$. Given $\mu \in \mathcal{M}_1(\mathbb{R})$, its pushforward by $\op{s}_{\rho}$
is the unique probability measure $\op{s}_{\rho \#}\mu$  such that

$$\Int{\mathbb{R}}{} f(x) \, \mathrm{d}\op{s}_{\rho \#}\mu( x)  \, =  \, \Int{\mathbb{R}}{} f(\rho  x) \,  \mathrm{d}\mu(x) \, .$$

Note that $\mathrm{supp} \big[ \op{s}_{\rho \#} \mu \big] \,  =  \,  \rho \, \mathrm{supp} [ \mu ]$. For a probability measure $\mu$ and $\tau>0$, we denote by $\mu_\tau$
the probability measure obtained by the convolution

\begin{equation}

\mu_\tau=\frac{1}{2\tau} \mathbbm{1}_{[-\tau;\tau]} \ast \mu\,.

\end{equation}

body: Let X be a smooth projective curve of genus g over an algebraically closed field, equivalently a compact Riemann surface, and let D be a divisor on X. Write l(D) for the dimension of the space of meromorphic functions on X whose poles are bounded by D and which have no other poles, and let K be a canonical divisor of X. The Riemann-Roch theorem states l(D) - l(K - D) = deg(D) + 1 - g, where deg(D) is the sum of the coefficients of D. Once deg(D) > 2g - 2 this gives l(D) = deg(D) + 1 - g exactly, since l(K-D) then vanishes. Proved by Riemann and Roch in the 1850s-60s; vastly generalized by Hirzebruch and Grothendieck.
title: Riemann-Roch theorem

[Definition 28 of arXiv:2607.29495, 'Fast Mixing for Low-Temperature Potts Models via Poisson Trees'] Let $\Downg$  be the distribution of  $X\sim\Poisson(dp_\good)$.
Let $\Downgbig$ be the distribution of $X$ conditioned on $X\geq D$ and let $\Downgsmall$ be $\Downg$ conditioned on $X<D$. Let $\Downb$ be the distribution $\Poisson(dp_\bad)$.  The rooted random tree $\cT^{\down}$ is defined as follows.

\begin{itemize}
\item The root is set to be \emph{down-good} with probability $p_\good$ and \emph{down-bad} otherwise (with probability $p_\bad$).

\item From every down-good vertex, the number of down-good children is sampled independently from $\Downgbig$ and the number of down-bad children is sampled independently from $\Downb$.

\item From every down-bad vertex, the number of down-good children is sampled independently from $\Downgsmall$ and the number of down-bad children is sampled independently from $\Downb$.
\end{itemize}

Let $\beta \in \{\beta^{\mathrm {geo}},\beta^{\mathrm {res}}\}$ be the scaling exponent of the CLE$_6$ geodesic (resp.\ resistance) metric defined in [my2025metric,my2025diffusion].     \[

    \asymp {\mathfrak{q}}_n
    = n^{\beta+o(1)}

Method: Equal level growth does not determine branching number Result: A geodesic spanning tree has exactly the Cayley graph sphere sizes at each level. But growth can exceed branching number for a bounded-degree tree: take a single infinite spine and at its nth vertex attach a finite b-ary tree of height n. Its level sizes have exponential rate sqrt(b)>1, while its only infinite ray is the spine and arbitrarily deep singleton cutsets give branching number one. Check: At level m the largest attached contribution starts around n=m/2 and has order b^(m/2), up to constant factors and a geometric sum. Every attachment is finite, so no additional infinite ray appears. Obstruction: This is not a geodesic Cayley spanning-tree counterexample. body: [Lemma lem:excess-chernoff of arXiv:2602.21315, 'The Instability of all Backoff Protocols\thanks{For the purpose of Open Access, the author'] Let $n$ be an integer, and let $Z_1,\dots,Z_n$ be components of a generalised multinomial  random variable. Let $\overline{\mu} \in (\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0})^n$, and suppose $\mathbb{E}(Z_k) \le \mu_k$ for all $k \in [n]$. Fix $\delta \ge e$, and for all $k \in [n]$, let $Z_k^+ = \max\{0, Z_k - \delta\mu_k\}$. Let $Z^+ = \sum_{k=1}^n Z_k^+$. Then for all $z\geq 0$, $\mathbb{P}(Z^+ > z) \le 2^n\delta^{-z}$.

[Lemma main_lemma of arXiv:2604.05921, 'Simplicity of random hypergraphs'] Let $\delta_1,\delta_2 \in \mathds{N}$. Given (possibly non-unique) vertices $v_1,v_2,\hdots,v_{\delta_1} \in V$, let the unique vertices be denoted by $v'_1,v'_2,\hdots,v'_{u(\vb*{v})}$, for some $u(\vb*{v}) \in \mathds{N}$. Similarly, let the unique vertices in $w_1,w_2,\hdots,w_{\delta_2}$ be denoted by $w'_1,w'_2,\hdots,w'_{u(\vb*{w})}$. Let $D(\vb*{v})=\frac{\delta_1!}{\prod_{i=1}^{u(\vb*{v})} m_{v'_i}(\vb*{v})!}$ and $D(\vb*{w})=\frac{\delta_2!}{\prod_{i=1}^{u(\vb*{w})} m_{w'_i}(\vb*{w})!}$. Let $\hat{R}(\cdot)$ be as in (equation def:B_hat of the paper) and let $U$ denote a uniformly chosen vertex in $V$. For any functions $f_1^{(i)}(v):V \rightarrow \mathds{N}$, $f_2^{(i)}(v):V \rightarrow \mathds{N}$ and $w \in \mathds{N}$,
    \begin{align}
        
        &\sum_{\vb*{v} \in V^{\delta_1}}  \sum_{\vb*{w} \in (V\backslash\{v_1,\hdots,v_{\delta_1}\})^{\delta_2}} (D(\vb*{v})D(\vb*{w}))^w \prod_{i=1}^{u(\vb*{v})} f_1^{(m_{v'_i}(\vb*{v}))}(v'_i) \prod_{j=1}^{u(\vb*{w})} f_2^{(m_{w'_j}(\vb*{w}))}(w'_j) \nonumber \\
        &=\sum_{\substack{\vb*{a} \in \mathds{N}^{\delta_1}:\\ \sum_{i=1}^{\delta_1} ia_i = \delta_1}}  \frac{\delta_1!^{1+w}}{\prod_{k=1}^{\delta_1} k!^{(1+w)a_k}} \sum_{\substack{\vb*{b} \in \mathds{N}^{\delta_2}:\\ \sum_{i=1}^{\delta_2} ib_i = \delta_2}}  \frac{\delta_2!^{1+w}}{\prod_{k=1}^{\delta_2} k!^{(1+w)b_k} } \nonumber \\
    &\hspace{1cm} \times \sum_{\gamma(\cdot) \in \hat{R}(\vb*{a},\vb*{b})} (-1)^{\sum{\vb*{g} \in \mathds{N}^{\delta_1}, \vb*{h} \in \mathds{N}^{\delta_2}}( \sum_{i=1}^{\delta_1} g_i + \sum_{j=1}^{\delta_2} h_j -1) \gamma(\vb*{g},\vb*{h})} \nonumber \\
    &\hspace{1cm} \times  \prod_{\substack{\vb*{y} \in \mathds{N}^{\delta_1}\\ \vb*{z} \in \mathds{N}^{\delta_2}}} \Bigg( \frac{1}{\gamma(\vb*{y},\vb*{z})!} \Big(\frac{n\mathds{E} \big[\prod_{i=1}^{\delta_1} (f_1^{(i)}(U))^{y_i} \prod_{j=1}^{\delta_2} (f_2^{(j)}(U))^{z_j} \big] \big(\sum_{i=1}^{\delta_1} y_i + \sum_{j=1}^{\delta_2} z_j-1 \big)!}{\prod_{i=1}^{\delta_1} y_i! \prod_{j=1}^{\delta_2} z_j!} \Big)^{\gamma(\vb*{y},\vb*{z})} \Bigg).
    \end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma lem:class-number-reduction of arXiv:2609.00777, 'Universal murmuration and Hecke augmentation'] Let $P\nmid N$, with $P$ odd, $N$ squarefree, and $PN>4$.  For $m\geq1$, whenever the arguments are discriminants, one has
\[
h(-P^{2m}N)=P^{m-1}h(-P^2N),
\qquad
h(-4P^{2m}N)=P^{m-1}h(-4P^2N),
\]
and
\[
h(-P^{2m+1}N)=P^mh(-PN),
\qquad
h(-4P^{2m+1}N)=P^mh(-4PN).
\]

[Definition Type forest, type rays and paths of arXiv:2607.16911, 'Multipartite random graphs with given degrees: local limit, revisiting the giant, distance'] Consider the \emph{Ulam-Harris forest} $\mathscr{F}_S$ on the set of types $S$. That is to say, $\mathscr F_S$ is an infinite forest, consisting of $|S|$ many infinite tree components $\{\mathscr T(s):s\in S\}$. For any fixed $s_0 \in S$, the root of the tree $\mathscr T(s_0)$ is $s_0$, and for any $v\in \mathscr T(s_0)$, it has $|S|$ many offspring $\{vs:s\in S\}$. Observe that any $v\in \mathscr T(s)$ has the form of a word $v=s_0s_1\dots s_k$. We call the forest $\mathscr F_S$ the \textit{type forest} corresponding to the set of types $S$. 
    
    Furthermore any directed infinite path $\pi=(s_0\rightarrow s_0s_1 \rightarrow s_0s_1s_2\rightarrow \dots)$ starting at the root $s_0$ is called a \emph{type ray} in $\mathscr T(s_0)$, and a finite directed path of the form $(s_0\rightarrow s_0s_1 \rightarrow \dots \rightarrow s_0s_1s_2\dots s_k)$ is called a \emph{type path} started at $s_0$. By $|\pi|$ we denote the length of $\pi$. Thus, if $\pi$ is a type ray, $|\pi|=\infty$, while for $\pi=(s_0\rightarrow s_0s_1 \rightarrow \dots \rightarrow s_0s_1\dots s_k)$, $|\pi|=k$.

[Proposition 2 of arXiv:2604.00642, 'Quantitative central limit theorem for an integrated periodogram via the fourth moment the'] Let
\[
f_\alpha(\lambda)=|\lambda|^{-\alpha}L(\lambda),
\qquad \lambda\in(-\pi,\pi),\quad \alpha\in\mathcal A,
\]
where $\mathcal A=[a,b]\subset[0,1)$, and assume that the true parameter value $\alpha_0$ belongs to $\mathcal A$. Suppose that $L\in \mathcal C^1([-\pi,\pi]\setminus\{0\})$ is positive on $[-\pi,\pi]$ and slowly varying at $0$.

Define the Whittle contrast by
\[
Q_n(\alpha)
=
\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}
\left[
\log f_\alpha(\lambda)+\frac{I_n(\lambda)}{f_\alpha(\lambda)}
\right]\dd\lambda,
\qquad \alpha\in\mathcal A.
\]
Let
\[
\widehat\alpha_n\in \arg\min_{\alpha\in\mathcal A} Q_n(\alpha)
\]
be any measurable minimizer of $Q_n$ over $\mathcal A$. Then
\[
\widehat\alpha_n \xrightarrow{\mathbb P} \alpha_0,
\]
and
\[
\sqrt n\,(\widehat\alpha_n-\alpha_0)
\;\Rightarrow\;
\mathcal N\!\left(0,\frac{4}{\sigma_0^2}\right),
\]
where
\[
\sigma_0^2
=
\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \bigl(\log|\lambda|\bigr)^2\,\dd\lambda.
\]

[Corollary cor:mass-no-killing of arXiv:2608.11931, '\texorpdfstring{Nonlinear parabolic characterizations of stochastic completeness at infini'] Let $G$ be a graph with $\kappa=0$ and \(\mu(X)<\infty\).
Let $\phi\in\mathcal{I}$ with $\phi^{-1}(\mathbb R_+)\neq\emptyset.$ Then \(G\) satisfies
\hyperref[def:SC]{\textup{(SC)}}{} if and only if one, and hence all, of the
statements {\rm(ii)}--{\rm(iv)} of
Theorem~(thm:generalized-mass-characterization of the paper) hold, with the
generalized mass identity~\hyperref[eq:nonlinear-generalized-mass]{\textup{(MB)}}{} reducing
to the conservation of mass:
\[
    \mathsf M_u(t)=\mathsf M_{u_0}
    \qquad \text{for } t\in[0,T].
\]

Moreover, if \(G\) does not satisfy \hyperref[def:SC]{\textup{(SC)}}{}, then, for every \(T>0\)
and every \(c \in \mathbb R_+\) such that $0<\phi(c)<\sup_{\mathbb R}\phi,$ there exist bounded positive pointwise solutions
\(u_-\) and \(u_+\), both with initial datum \(u_0= c\), and times
\(t_-,t_+\in(0,T]\) such that
\[
    0\le u_-\le c\le u_+
    \qquad\text{on }[0,T]\times X
\]
and
\[
    \mathsf M_{u_-}(t_-)<c\,\mu(X)<\mathsf M_{u_+}(t_+).
\]
Thus, failure of \hyperref[def:SC]{\textup{(SC)}}{} allows for both loss of mass to infinity and
creation of mass from infinity.

[Theorem CPLT of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] Given a compactly supported positive measure $\rho$, of mass $c=mass(\rho)$, the following compound Poisson limits converge,
$$p_\rho=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(\left(1-\frac{c}{n}\right)\delta_0+\frac{1}{n}\rho\right)^{*n}
\quad,\quad 
\pi_\rho=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(\left(1-\frac{c}{n}\right)\delta_0+\frac{1}{n}\rho\right)^{\boxplus n}$$
and if we write $\rho=\sum_{i=1}^sc_i\delta_{z_i}$ with $c_i>0$ and $z_i\in\mathbb R$ we have the formula
$$p_\rho/\pi_\rho={\rm law}\left(\sum_{i=1}^sz_i\alpha_i\right)$$
where the variables $\alpha_i$ are Poisson/free Poisson$(c_i)$, independent/free.

Let A be an N-by-n real random matrix whose rows a_i^T are independent, with integers N,n>=2, common uncentered second-moment matrix Sigma=E[a_i a_i^T], and Gamma=E max_i||a_i||_2^2<infinity. Put r=min(N,n). There is an absolute C such that, for delta=C sqrt(Gamma log(r)/N), E||A^T A/N-Sigma||_op<=max(||Sigma||_op^(1/2)delta,delta^2). With an absolute constant C, enlarged if necessary, the same hypotheses give (E||A||_op^2)^(1/2)<=sqrt(N||Sigma||_op)+C sqrt(Gamma log(r)). body: [Definition 3.2 (δ-hyperbolic (Gromov, 1987) of arXiv:2606.10238, 'Hyperbolic Neural Population Geometry Benefits Computation'] ). A geodesic metric space (X , d) is δ-hyperbolic if every geodesic triangle in X is δ-thin. Equivalently for all x, y, z, w ∈X , d(x, z) + d(y, w) ≤ (3.1) max {d(x, y) + d(z, w), d(y, z) + d(x, w)} + 2δ, which is called the 4-point condition. In general, low δ means the geodesic metric space is more tree-like, as tree triangles (Chiswell, 2001) are 0-hyperbolic.

[Prop 12 of arXiv:2605.25762, 'Brownian Convergence of Planar Domains and Stability of the Planar Skorokhod Embedding Pro'] Let $(x^{[n]}_{k})_{0\leq k\leq n}$ be a mesh.
Define
\[
\mu_{n}:=F(a)\delta_{a}+\sum^{n}_{k=1}\big(F(x_{k})-F(x_{k-1})\big)\delta_{x_{k}},
\]
and let $q_{n}$ be the quantile function of $\mu_{n}$. Then for
any $p\ge1$,
\[
\|q-q_{n}\|_{L^{p}(0,1)}\le\max_{1\le k\le n}(x_{k}-x_{k-1}).
\]
In particular, for the uniform mesh $x_{k}=a+\frac{b-a}{n}k$,
\[
\|q-q_{n}\|_{L^{p}(0,1)}\le\frac{b-a}{n}.
\]

body:
[Lem 237 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any $\alpha,L,\epsilon,K>0$ and any sequence of $\epsilon$-approximate $L$-Lipschitz algorithms $(\cA_N)_{N\ge 1}$,
	\[
		\lim_{N\to\infty} \bbW_2\Big(\mu(\cA_{N[K]}), \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)\Big) 
		= \lim_{N\to\infty} \bbW_2\Big(\mu_{\sym}(\cA_{N[K]}), \cM^{\Lip,\sym}(\alpha;\epsilon)\Big)
		= 0\,.
	\]

\begin{proof}
	We only prove that the first limit is zero, as the second limit is proved analogously.
	Suppose for contradiction that there exists $\delta > 0$ such that $\bbW_2(\mu(\cA_{N[K]}), \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)) \ge \delta$ for infinitely many $N$.
	By \eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.l4} from Lemma~\ref{l:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound}, there exists $C = C(\alpha,L,K) > 0 $ such that for sufficiently large $N$, $\mu(\cA_{N[K]}) \in \cP_4(\R,C)$.
Then, for infinitely many $N$, we have
	\[\mu(\cA_{N[K]})\in
		S_\delta 
		\equiv \Big\{ \mu \in \cP_4(\R,C) : \bbW_2(\mu, \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)) \ge \delta 
		\Big\}\,.
	\]
	By Lemma~\ref{l:confinement.cPp.compact.Wq}, the space $\cP_4(\R,C)$ endowed with the $\bbW_2$ metric is compact.
	The set $S_\delta$ is closed with respect to the $\bbW_2$ metric, hence also compact. Therefore
 we may find $\mu \in S_\delta$ and a subsequence $(N_j)_{j\ge 1}$ such that
	\[
		\lim_{j\to\infty} \bbW_2\Big(\mu(\cA_{N_j[K]}),
		\mu\Big) = 0\,.
	\]
	As noted in Definition~\ref{d:truncated.lip.alg}, we have $\mu^{\Ising}(\cA_{N_j[K]}) = \mu^{\Ising}(\cA_{N_j})$: thus, since each $\cA_{N_j}$ is an $\epsilon$-approximate $L$-Lipschitz algorithm, so is each $\cA_{N_j[K]}$. It follows by omitting finitely many $j$'s that we have
	\[
	\WERR(\cA_{N_j[K]},\mu)
	=\max\bigg\{
	\bbW_2\Big(\mu(\cA_{N_j[K]}),
		\mu\Big),
	\bbW_2\Big(
		\mu^\Ising(\cA_{N_j[K]}),
		\cP(\{\pm1\})
		\Big)
	\bigg\}\le\epsilon
	\]
for all $j$. Recalling the definition \eqref{e:cM.Lip} of  $\cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;L,\epsilon)$, this implies
	\[
		\mu \in \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;L,\epsilon) \subseteq \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)\,,
	\]
	which contradicts that $\mu \in S_\delta$.
\end{proof}

[Defn of arXiv:2506.18207, 'Cartan's Path Development, the Logarithmic Signature and a Conjecture of Lyons-Sidorova'] Let $\gamma:[0,T]\rightarrow V$ be a continuous path with bounded
variation. The \textit{signature transform} of $\gamma$ (or simply
the signature) is the formal tensor series defined by 
\[
S(\gamma)\triangleq\big(1,\gamma_{T}-\gamma_{0},\int_{0<s<t<T}d\gamma_{s}\otimes d\gamma_{t},\cdots,\int_{0<t_{1}<\cdots<t_{n}<T}d\gamma_{t_{1}}\otimes\cdots\otimes d\gamma_{t_{n}},\cdots\big),
\]
where the path integrals are defined in the Lebesgue-Stieltjes sense.
The tensor series $\log S(\gamma)$ is known as the \textit{logarithmic
signature} of $\gamma$.

 \E\!\left[|(\mathbf{G}_N)_{ij}|^2\right]=\frac1N,
 \qquad
 \E\!\left[(\mathbf{G}_N)_{ij}^2\right]=0.

Let us set
\[
 p_N(z)=\det(z\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{G}_N),\qquad
 q_N(z)=\exp\!\left(-\frac{1}{2N}\partial_z^2\right)p_N(z).
\]
Then, almost surely,
 $\nu_{q_N}\overset{\mathrm{w}}{\longrightarrow}\mathfrak{sc}_1$.

body:
Every unbounded open convex set in finite-dimensional Euclidean space contains an infinite straight ray starting at each of its points. If such a set is a mirror-complement component, that ray never collides with a mirror and is an escaping launch direction. The assertion needs convexity and does not settle the general all-reflected-rays trapping problem.
All hypotheses and scope restrictions in the statement apply.

Lemma 1. Every unbounded open convex set C in R^d contains an unbounded straight ray starting at each x in C. Therefore, if a mirror-complement component is unbounded, open and convex, an origin in it has an unobstructed escaping launch direction and cannot have every reflected ray bounded.

Proof: choose r>0 with B(x,r) contained in C and y_k in C with |y_k-x| tending to infinity. A subsequence of d_k=(y_k-x)/|y_k-x| tends to a unit direction d. For fixed t>=0 and sufficiently large k, convexity gives a ball centered at x+t*d_k with radius (1-t/|y_k-x|)*r contained in C. Eventually this radius exceeds 3r/4 and the center is within r/4 of x+t*d, so B(x+t*d,r/2) is in C. This holds for every fixed t with the same subsequential direction d, proving the entire ray stays inside C. No collision occurs along it.

Lemma 2. C={(x,y): x>0 and |y-x^2|<1} is open, connected and unbounded but contains no unbounded straight ray.

Proof: (x,u)->(x,x^2+u) is a homeomorphism from (0,infinity) times (-1,1), proving the first three properties. For a ray (a+bt,c+dt), t>=0, with nonzero direction: b<0 eventually violates x>0; b=0 and d!=0 eventually violates the strip condition; b>0 makes y-x^2 a quadratic with leading coefficient -b^2, whose magnitude diverges. Thus all possible directions leave C in finite time.

This gives an explicit algebraic version of the previous spiral-corridor obstruction: unbounded connected vacancy alone does not supply a straight ray. The corridor is not represented as a permitted mirror arrangement, and absence of straight rays does not establish trapping of reflected rays. Convexity is a sufficient special-case condition, not a necessary one.

[Definition smr-inequality of arXiv:2606.28575, 'Global smooth solutions by high mode Lie-Transport noise for Logarithmically Hyperdissipat'] Let $p>2$. We write $(A, B) \in \mathcal{SMR}^\bullet_p$ if for every $f\in L^p(I_T\times \Omega, X_0)$, $u_0 \in L^p_{\mathcal{F}_0}(\Omega; X^{\operatorname{Tr}}_p)$ there exists a strong solution $u$ to the linear Cauchy problem 
    $$\mathrm{d}u - Au\mathrm{d}t = f_t\mathrm{d}t  + B(u)\mathrm{d}W_t,\qquad  u(0)=u_0.$$
    such that $u \in  L^p(\Omega ; H^{\theta, p}(I_T; X_{1-\theta}))$ for every $\theta \in [0, 1/2)$ and for all stopping times $\tau : \Omega \rightarrow I_T$ it holds 
    $$\|u\|_{L^p( \Omega; H^{\theta, p}(I_T; X_{1-\theta}))} \lesssim \|f\|_{L^p(I_T \times \Omega ; X_0)} + \|u_0\|_{L^p_{\mathcal{F}_0}(\Omega; X^{\operatorname{Tr}}_p)}$$

        \mathbb{E}\left[\sup_{t\in[0, T]} \|u_t\|^p_{X^{\operatorname{Tr}}_p}\right]  +\expt{\int_0^t\|u_s\|^p_{X_1}\mathrm{d}s}  \lesssim \expt[]{\int_0^t \|f_s\|^p_{X_0}ds} + \expt{\|u_0\|^p_{ X^{\operatorname{Tr}}_p}}.
    \end{equation}

body:
[Definition def:fk_current of arXiv:2609.01581, 'Concentration of additive functionals of Stratonovich-type'] Let $U\in C^1_b(\mathbb{R}^d;\mathbb{R}^d)$ be a bounded, continuously
differentiable vector field with bounded derivatives, and $k\in\mathbb{R}$.
The \emph{Feynman-Kac semigroup} associated with $U$ is the family
$(P_t^{k,J})_{t\geq 0}$ on $L^2(\mu)$ defined by
\begin{align}
  \bigl(P_t^{k,J} f\bigr)(x)
  \equiv
  \E^x\left[
    f(X_t)\exp\left(k \int_0^t U(X_s)\circ\mathrm{d} X_s\right)
  \right],
  
\end{align}
for $f \in L^2(\mu)$, $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$, $t \geq 0$, where $\circ$ denotes
Stratonovich integration and $U(X_\tau)\circ\mathrm{d} X_\tau=\sum_i U_i(X_\tau)\circ\mathrm{d} X^i_\tau$.
title: Feynman-Kac semigroup for current observables

[Theorem thm:main-explosion of arXiv:2609.02829, 'Quantitative explosion and percolation of the divisible sandpile'] \phantomsection
Let $\sigma=1+2d\zeta$, where $(\zeta(x))_{x\in\mathbb{Z}^d}$ are i.i.d.\ with $\mathbb{E}\zeta(0)=0$ and $0<\Var(\zeta(0))<\infty$. In parts~\textup{(i)}, \textup{(ii)}, and~\textup{(iii)(a)--(b)}, assume additionally that
$\mathbb{E} e^{\theta_0|\zeta(0)|}<\infty$ for some $\theta_0>0$.

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item \underline{\textup{Dimensions one, two, and three.}}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
\item The rescaled mean converges:
$\lim_{t\to\infty}t^{-(4-d)/4}\mathbb{E} u_t(0)$
exists and lies in $(0,\infty)$.
\item The parabolic scaling limit is a Brownian optimal-stopping value. Let
$\mathcal W$ be white noise on $\mathbb{R}^d$, let
\[
    Z(t,x)\coloneqq \sqrt{\Var(\zeta(0))}
    \int_{\mathbb{R}^d}g_t^{\rm BM}(x,y)\,\mathcal W(dy)\, ,
\]
with $g_t^{\rm BM}$ the finite-time Green kernel of Brownian motion (defined in Section~(sec:rw-rep of the paper)), and let
\[
    \mathcal U(T,x)\coloneqq
    \sup_{\tau\leq T}\mathbf E_x^{\rm BM}
    \bigl[Z(T,x)-Z(T-\tau,B_\tau)\bigr]\, ,
\]
where the supremum is over stopping times for Brownian motion. Then, for every $T>0$,
\[
    R^{-(2-d/2)}\,u^{(R)}_{\lfloor TR^2\rfloor}
    \Longrightarrow
    \mathcal U(T,\cdot)
    \qquad\text{in }C_{\rm loc}(\mathbb{R}^d)\, ,
\]
where the field on the left denotes the multilinear interpolation from $R^{-1}\mathbb{Z}^d$ of the values
$x/R\mapsto R^{-(2-d/2)}u_{\lfloor TR^2\rfloor}(x)$.
\end{enumerate}

\item \underline{\textup{Dimension four.}}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
\item The mean odometer is of logarithmic order at each site: as $t\to\infty$
\[
    \mathbb{E} u_t(0)\asymp\log t\, ,
\]
and, for every fixed $x\in\mathbb{Z}^4$, $u_t(x)/\mathbb{E} u_t(0)\to1$ in $L^2$ and
almost surely.
\item The centered odometer $u_t(0)-\mathbb{E} u_t(0)$ has Gaussian fluctuations:
\[
    \frac{u_t(0)-\mathbb{E} u_t(0)}{\sqrt{\log t}}

    N\left(0,\frac{4\Var(\zeta(0))}{\pi^2}\right)\, ,
\]
and $\Var(u_t(0))/\log t\to4\Var(\zeta(0))/\pi^2$.
\item For every $T>0$ and $s>0$, the fields
$\bigl(u_{\lfloor TR^2\rfloor}-\mathbb{E} u_{\lfloor TR^2\rfloor}(0)\bigr)^{(R)}$ for
$R\geq1$ are tight in $H^{-s}_{\rm loc}(\mathbb{R}^4)$. Moreover, for every
$\alpha>2$, the fields $\bigl(u_{t_R}-\mathbb{E} u_{t_R}(0)\bigr)^{(R)}$ at the
superdiffusive times $t_R\coloneqq\lfloor R^\alpha\rfloor$ converge, modulo additive constants, to the four-dimensional membrane model $\mathcal G_4$ in $H^{-s}_{\rm loc}(\mathbb{R}^4)$.
\end{enumerate}

\item \underline{\textup{Dimensions five and higher.}}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
	\item The odometer is deterministic to first order at every fixed site. For
	each fixed $x\in\mathbb{Z}^d$, $u_t(x)/\mathbb{E} u_t(0)\to1$ in $L^2$ and almost surely.
	Moreover, the mean diverges: there is $c>0$ such that $\mathbb{E} u_t(0)\geq c(\log t)^{2/d}$ for all large $t$.

        + \mathbb{E} \mleft[ (X^i(0) - Y^i(0)) Y^j(t) \mright] \\
    
    &\qquad + \mathbb{E}\mleft[Y^i(0)\mright] \mathbb{E}\mleft[ X^j(t) - Y^j(t) \mright]
    + \mathbb{E} \mleft[ X^j(t) \mright] \mathbb{E} \mleft[ X^i(0) - Y^i(0) \mright].
\end{align}
Moreover, both factors appearing under the square root in (equation decom4631 of the paper) are nonnegative.

[Theorem thm:counterexample of arXiv:2606.27073, 'Retention Profiles and KL Contraction Bounds in Finite Markov Chains'] For any $\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)$ there exists a family of reversible Markov
chains $P_{\delta,N}$ (parameterized by $\delta\in(0,1)$ and integer
$N\ge 1$) on a finite state space, with
$M_{\delta,N}:=M(P_{\delta,N})$, such that
\[
  \lim_{N\to\infty}\;\lim_{\delta\to 0}\;L(P_{\delta,N})\;\le\;2\varepsilon,
  \qquad
  \lim_{N\to\infty}\;\lim_{\delta\to 0}\;\frac{\eta_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{\delta,N})}{M_{\delta,N}}\;\ge\;2.
\]
Consequently, $L(P)\to 0$ does not universally imply
$\eta_{\mathrm{KL}}(P)/M\to 1$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
AUTHOR PROOF DRAFT, unaudited; novelty is unestablished. Near-square Gaussian extensive-rank reference has a C1 information limit and pointwise limiting MMSE at every fixed positive SNR, proof unaudited. For independent real standard Gaussian U of size N by M and V of size P by M, B=UV^T/sqrt(N), M/N->beta in (0,infinity), P/N->1, the per-entry MI tends to i_beta(s)=Sigma(dilation_sqrt(s)(mu_beta) free-plus semicircle_1)-Sigma(semicircle_1), where mu_beta is the compact symmetric limiting singular law of UV^T/N in the square model and has second moment beta. For s>0, i_beta is C1 and normalized Gaussian-reference MMSE converges to 2 i_beta_prime(s)=1/s-Phi(mu_beta free-plus semicircle_(1/s))/s^2. Input zero atoms are allowed. A real conditional population-Wishart theorem, exact random-profile density calibration021 and free-heat regularity020 pay the observation law, MI limit and derivative separately. Column-padding chain-rule bounds extend the square result to every P/N->1 sequence. With existing finite-fourth-moment spectral coupling008 and Haar comparison006, every centered fixed iid unit-variance finite-fourth-moment pair of factors has limsup normalized product-MMSE excess over the Gaussian reference <=0 at every fixed s>=0. Novelty unestablished; full rectangular aspect !=1 is not settled.
Real centered iid Gaussian reference factors, independent between arrays and of Gaussian channel noise.
M/N->beta>0 finite, P/N->1.
Per-entry risk for UV^T/sqrt(N); raw UV^T risk divided by N.
Iid-prior MMSE consequence uses fixed centered unit-variance finite-fourth-moment laws and unaudited claims006/008.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:4c3e0cbd1ab022f1c5a21624256d0762ba0994785c484f1778108a7bfc71f042","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/4c/4c3e0cbd1ab022f1c5a21624256d0762ba0994785c484f1778108a7bfc71f042.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:f7ee46a2e3388a11ce13fc89ccd7a2a712259b34ba37615dbe0afe0e0398d634","bundle_entry_key":"gaussian-product-near-square-mi-c1-mmse-w718","bundle_id":"population.t287-near-square-c1-and-finite-variance-comparison-v1","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"Gaussian channels and extensive-rank matrix inference","draft":"w718/bundle_008.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.gaussian_channels:gaussian-product-near-square-mi-c1-mmse-w718","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Gaussian extensive-rank reference: a C1 information limit near the square aspect

Target 2 partial result, proof draft, unaudited. Novelty is unestablished.
The hardest remaining part of full Target 2 is the corresponding reference
entropy differentiability at rectangular aspect bounded away from one.
Target 1's dimension-uniform high-noise remainder also remains open.

## Statement and normalization

Let n->infinity, M_n/n->beta in (0,infinity), and P_n/n->1. Let U_n and
V_n be independent real standard Gaussian arrays of sizes n by M_n and
P_n by M_n. Put B_n=U_n V_n^T/sqrt(n), let G_n have independent standard
Gaussian entries, and define

 i_n(s)=I(B_n;sqrt(s)B_n+G_n)/(n P_n),
 m_n(s)=E||B_n-E[B_n|sqrt(s)B_n+G_n]||_F^2/(n P_n).

There is a compact symmetric probability law mu_beta, of second moment
beta, such that, for every s>=0,

 i_n(s)->i_beta(s)
   =Sigma(dilation_sqrt(s)(mu_beta) free-plus sigma_1)-Sigma(sigma_1).

The interpretation at s=0 is zero. For s>0 the limit is C1 and

 lim m_n(s)=2 i_beta'(s)
   =1/s-Phi(mu_beta free-plus sigma_(1/s))/s^2.        (1)

Here Sigma is logarithmic energy, sigma_t is the variance-t semicircle
law, and Phi is scalar free Fisher information as in claim020.
This applies to all positive finite beta, including beta<1 when the
input singular law has a zero atom. No finite input logarithmic energy
is assumed. At s=0, m_n(0)=M_n/n->beta.

Together with unaudited claims006 and008, this gives, for centered iid
unit-variance fixed finite-fourth-moment factor laws at the same sizes,

    limsup [m_iid,n(s)-m_n(s)]<=0 for every fixed s>=0.               (2)

It is a near-square partial Target2 result, not a full rectangular
answer. Raw UV^T loss must be divided by n before comparing these limits.

## 1. The primary real population-Wishart theorem

Silverstein, *Strong convergence of the empirical distribution of
eigenvalues of large dimensional random matrices*, J.Multivar.Anal.55
(1995),331-339, DOI10.1006/jmva.1995.1083, Theorem1.1 and equation(1.4).
The author's PDF is papers/silverstein1995_primary.pdf, with provenance
and SHA in SOURCES.jsonl. The theorem allows independent random PSD
population matrices with almost-sure weak empirical convergence. Its
entries may be complex with unit centered variance; iid real standard
Gaussians are a special case. No condition E Z^2=0 is imposed.

At square sample aspect one, if the population spectral law is K on
[0,infinity), the limiting squared-singular-value transform m, with
m(lambda)=integral(x-lambda)^-1 dF(x), satisfies

    m(lambda)=integral[-t*lambda*m(lambda)-lambda]^-1 K(dt).

The Stieltjes branch is specified by the theorem. For the symmetric
singular law, put g(z)=-z*m(z^2), z in the upper half-plane. Analytic
continuation from Re z>0 gives

    g(z)=integral[z-t*g(z)]^-1 K(dt),                 (3)

where Im g<0 and g(z)~1/z at infinity. This explicitly fixes the opposite
sign convention from m. All populations used below are PSD, independent
of the sample Gaussian matrix, and have almost-sure deterministic weak
limits, as the theorem requires.

First take C_n=U_n U_n^T/n. Applying the same theorem with identity
population and sample aspect n/M_n, then rescaling by M_n/n, gives a
deterministic limit tau_beta. Gaussian norm tails give compact support.
The normalized trace converges to beta, so tau_beta has mean beta.

## 2. Exact conditional covariance and the observation law

Initially set P_n=n and S_n=B_n/sqrt(n)=U_n V_n^T/n. If H_n is an
independent n by n standard real Gaussian matrix, then, conditional on U_n,

    S_n has law C_n^(1/2) H_n/sqrt(n).

Indeed its columns are independent centered Gaussians with covariance
C_n/n. For independent Z_n with entry variance1/n, the normalized
observation Y_n=sqrt(s)S_n+Z_n similarly has conditional law

    (I+s C_n)^(1/2) H_n/sqrt(n).                    (4)

The sample H_n in each distributional representation is independent
of C_n. Silverstein's theorem therefore applies both to the input
population C_n and to the output population I+s C_n. It gives a compact
symmetric input singular law mu_beta and an output law nu_s. With
g_s=G_(nu_s) and h_s=G_(dilation_sqrt(s)(mu_beta)), equation(3) reads

 h_s(w)=integral[w-s*c*h_s(w)]^-1 tau_beta(dc),
 g_s(z)=integral[z-(1+s*c)*g_s(z)]^-1 tau_beta(dc).    (5)

These equations are only used for s>0; s=0 is pure Gaussian noise.
Put w(z)=z-g_s(z). It lies in the upper half-plane, and g_s(z) solves
the first equation at w(z). For Im z sufficiently large, that equation
has at most one solution in the lower half-plane: for two candidates,
the difference of the integral maps is bounded by
s*sup(supp tau_beta)/(Im w)^2 times their difference. This factor is
less than one. Hence g_s(z)=h_s(w(z)) there, and analyticity extends
the equality to the entire upper half-plane.

This is the semicircular subordination equation with variance one. To
check the branch rather than assume it, H(w)=w+h_s(w) satisfies H(w(z))=z.
Moreover

 Im H(w)=Im w*[1-integral |w-x|^-2 d(dilation_sqrt(s)mu_beta)(x)].

Since Im z>0, w(z) is in Biane's domain Omega_(dilation_sqrt(s)mu_beta,1).
Biane1997 Lemma4, journal p710, makes H conformal from that domain onto
the upper half-plane; Proposition2, p711, identifies its inverse as the
semicircular subordination map. Therefore

    nu_s=dilation_sqrt(s)(mu_beta) free-plus sigma_1.                (6)

This uses a primary real Wishart theorem, not a unitary-to-orthogonal
extension of the rectangular-addition theorem. By Biane Corollaries1-3,
nu_s has a bounded continuous density and compact support; its positive
singular law eta_s has density twice that symmetric density on x>0.
Thus eta_s is compact with bounded density, including at the hard edge.

## 3. Expected W2 convergence, including the moment passage

We record the upgrades beyond weak convergence because they are needed
by the calibration theorem. For an n by M Gaussian U, a pair of sphere
1/4-nets gives

 P(||U/sqrt(n)||op>K)<=2 exp((n+M)log9-n*K^2/8).

The bounded ratio M/n permits a fixed sufficiently large K. The tails
are summable in n, and their integrated versions give uniformly bounded
moments of every fixed order of these norms. The same holds for the
square noise and H_n. Consequently S_n and Y_n have uniformly bounded
fourth operator-norm moments, and almost-sure eventual norm bounds.

For A_n=||Y_n||_F^2/n, the exact conditional moments from(4) are

 E[A_n|U_n]=tr(I+s C_n)/n,
 Var(A_n|U_n)=2 tr((I+s C_n)^2)/n^3.

The expected conditional variance is O(n^-2), by the uniform norm
moments. Also Var(tr C_n/n)=2(M_n/n)/n^2. Total variance is therefore
O(n^-2), and E A_n=1+s M_n/n. Chebyshev and Borel-Cantelli give
A_n->1+s beta almost surely. The same argument with population C_n
gives ||S_n||_F^2/n->beta.

Weak convergence from the primary theorem plus these second moments
gives empirical singular W2 convergence almost surely. The uniform
fourth operator-norm bounds make its square uniformly integrable:
W2(eta_n,eta_s)^2<=2 m2(eta_n)+2 m2(eta_s), and
m2(eta_n)<=||Y_n||op^2. Thus

    E W2(eta_(Y_n),eta_s)^2->0.                     (7)

The same reasoning fixes the second moment beta of mu_beta. Distributional
representations may be realized on a common probability space; the
expected-W2 and information conclusions depend only on their marginals.

## 4. Pay the unbounded-input truncation

Choose C large enough that E_n={||S_n||op<=C} has probability tending to
one exponentially fast, using the product bound for the two Gaussian
factor norms. Let S_n^E have the conditional law of S_n given E_n.
This is still biorthogonally invariant and has operator norm at most C.

Construct a coupling by setting S_n^E=S_n on E_n and, on its complement,
drawing an independent sample from that conditional law. It has the
claimed marginal. With a_n=||S_n||_F^2/n,

 d_n^2:=E||S_n-S_n^E||_F^2/n
       <=2 E[a_n 1_(E_n^c)]+2 P(E_n^c)E[a_n|E_n]->0.              (8)

Uniform operator fourth moments and Cauchy-Schwarz pay the first term;
the second is bounded because P(E_n)->1 and E a_n=M_n/n. They also give
E||S_n^E||_F^2/n->beta.

Share the noise between the coupled observations. Hoffman-Wielandt gives
expected squared singular-law W2 distance at most s*d_n^2. Hence(7)
holds for the conditioned prior too. Claim021 now applies and proves
its normalized MI limit Sigma(nu_s)-Sigma(sigma_1).

The dimension-uniform Gaussian entropy/W2 estimate of claim006 transfers
back to the original prior:

 |I(S_n;Y_n)/n^2-I(S_n^E;sqrt(s)S_n^E+Z_n)/n^2|<=sqrt(s)*d_n.

The right side tends to zero. We obtain the stated square-reference
information formula, with no input-density or finite input-energy
assumption and no use of the disputed oracle-to-Bayes step in2403.04615.

## 5. Differentiability and limiting MMSE

By dilation and(6), for s>0 the limit is

 i_beta(s)=Sigma(mu_beta free-plus sigma_(1/s))
                         +(1/2)log s-Sigma(sigma_1).

The compactness of mu_beta verifies claim020, including when it has atoms.
That claim proves positive-time C1 energy with derivative Phi/2. Thus

    i_beta'(s)=1/(2s)-Phi(mu_beta free-plus sigma_(1/s))/(2s^2).

The finite normalized information functions are concave and differentiable,
with derivative m_n/2 by I-MMSE. Their pointwise convergence to this C1
limit forces derivative convergence by the two-sided concave secant
inequalities. This proves(1) for exactly square dimensions.

## 6. Extend the reference limit to P_n/n->1

At fixed n,M, couple all column sizes by sharing U and the existing rows
of V. Adding k observed columns increases unnormalized MI by an amount
between zero and

    n*k*c_n(s), c_n(s)=(1/2)log(1+s M/n).

The chain rule gives the increase as conditional MI. Its upper bound
uses conditioning reduces entropy, the independent new Gaussian noise,
and the scalar maximum-entropy bound for each new entry of variance
1+s M/n. No independence between signal columns is assumed.

Both the smaller matrix's normalized information and the extra-column
information per new entry lie in [0,c_n(s)]. The larger normalized
information is their dimension-weighted average. Therefore

 |i_(n,P)(s)-i_(n,n)(s)|
       <=|P-n|/max(P,n) * c_n(s)->0 when P/n->1.      (9)

The reference limit remains i_beta and is C1. The same concave secants
give its MMSE limit(1) for every such near-square sequence.

Finally, claim008 supplies expected ordered spectral coupling to this
Gaussian reference for centered fixed finite-fourth-moment iid factors,
at every positive finite aspect ratio. Claim006's Haar-risk and
information/secant comparison applies now at every positive s, since
the near-square reference limit is C1. This proves(2). At s=0, both
risks are exactly M_n/n, so the comparison includes zero directly.

## Scope and least-trusted step

All new proof dependencies017,019,020,021 and old006,008 remain unaudited.
The least-trusted new step is the spectral identification(5)-(6), especially
the square-root Stieltjes convention and analytic branch continuation;
the explicit primary equations and Biane inverse-domain check expose it
for line-by-line review. Full rectangular aspect !=1 and Target1's
uniform remainder are not claimed. This statement concerns fixed SNR
after the dimension limit and does not contradict the existing finite-n
counterexample on an SNR interval shrinking with dimension.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:686964a520b560babff49b2d3c712ffe188ecb5df9287b91721884bf39c60f66","revision_digest":"sha256:dbc2109a02b1bca692e4d6c35194e860836da22ede9d76fed8f8cfbddcd756dd","source_id":"owner:w718:T287:gaussian-product-near-square-mi-c1-mmse-w718","source_revision":"2026-10-21 claim w718-T287-022 version1, proof unaudited","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Lemma 39 (Combined fast mixing and negligible burn-in) of arXiv:2605.14511, 'Clumsy and Careless:\\ Stationary-Entry Flux in Non-monotone Coupon Collectors'] Let $\widehat\pi_n^{\alpha,\beta}$ be the stationary law of the set-valued combined chain.  Then
\[
        \sup_{A\subseteq[n]}
        \|P^t(A,\cdot)-\widehat\pi_n^{\alpha,\beta}\|_{\TV}
        \le nS^t.
\]
Moreover, from the empty initial collection, with
\[
        b_n=n^3,
        \qquad
        h_n=r_n=\ceil{Cn^2},
\]
for any fixed $C>1$, all mixing and burn-in assumptions in Theorem~\ref{thm:stationary-entry} hold for the post-thinning completion state.

A discrepancy at a fixed coupon type is removed if that type is selected. [Lemma Generic Morse property of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[lemma]{lem:Morse}
For fixed \(N,p\), the set of coefficient tensors for which the restriction of \(H_N\) to \(\mathbb S_N\) is not Morse is contained in a proper real algebraic subset of \(\mathbb R^{N^p}\).  Consequently, if the joint coefficient law is absolutely continuous, the field is almost surely Morse.
The same conclusion holds when the coefficient law is absolutely
continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure on the space of symmetric
degree-\(p\) tensors.

[Proposition 7 (Conditional unique limit at infinite time) of arXiv:2609.00501, 'Uniqueness of Finite-Time Varifold Limits for the M\"obius-Invariant Willmore Flow'] Let $F\colon[0,\infty)\times\Sigma\to\Sph^3$ be a smooth MIWF of a
compact torus.  Assume that there is one constant $c_0>0$ such that
\[
 \inf_{t>0}\min_{x\in\Sigma}|A_{F_t}^0(x)|^2\geq c_0,
\]
and, in addition, that
\begin{equation}
 
 \int_0^\infty\sqrt{-W'(r)}\dd r<\infty.
\end{equation}
Then there are positive Radon measures $\mu_\infty$ on $\Sigma$ and
$\lambda_\infty$ on $\Sph^3$ and a unique integral two-varifold
$\Var_\infty$ in $\R^4$, possibly the zero varifold, such that
\[
 \mu_t\longrightarrow\mu_\infty\quad\text{in total variation},
 \qquad
 \lambda_t\longrightarrow\lambda_\infty
 \quad\text{in }d_{\BL},
 \qquad
 \Var_t\rightharpoonup\Var_\infty
\]
as $t\to\infty$, and $\lambda_\infty=\lVert\Var_\infty\rVert$.
Writing $W_\infty:=\lim_{t\to\infty}W(t)$, one also has
\[
 H_{\Var_\infty}^{\R^4}
 \in L^2(\lVert\Var_\infty\rVert;\R^4),
 \qquad
 \frac14\int_{\R^4}|H_{\Var_\infty}^{\R^4}|^2
 \dd\lVert\Var_\infty\rVert\leq W_\infty.
\]
title: Conditional unique limit at infinite time

[Definition Costly steps of arXiv:2510.26724, 'Sharp Fuss-Catalan thresholds in graph bootstrap percolation'] The $i$th step of the REA is called a {\it costly step} 
if it is neither a TS nor an IntR. 
The associated {\it cost} $\kappa_i$ to the step 
is $r=v(H)$ plus the number of vertices 
(if any) 
outside $H_i$
that are in at least 
two of the components being merged
with $H_i$. 
If the $i$th step is not costly (i.e., TS or IntR)
then we 
put $\kappa_i=0$. 
The {\it total cost} of $W$ is 
\[
\kappa(W)=\sum_{i=1}^m \kappa_i. 
\]

[Theorem thm:IS6V-diamond of arXiv:2608.02772, 'Non-Abelian Hirota-Miwa Equations for the KPZ Universality Class'] Suppose that $K_u$ is trace class and that
$(I + K_u)^{-1}$ exists at all relevant lattice
vertices.  Then for any two distinct divisors
$p, p' \mid \Pi_{x,y}$ with
$1 \leq \deg p, \deg p' < \deg \Pi_{x,y}$,
the dressed edge weights
satisfy the mixed diamond equation
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{M}_p(u) \Lambda_{p'}
+
\Lambda_p \mathcal{M}_{p'}(S_p u)
-
\mathcal{M}_{p'}(u) \Lambda_p
-
\Lambda_{p'} \mathcal{M}_p(S_{p'} u)
= 0.
\end{equation}

body:
[Theorem main representable of arXiv:2609.04023, 'Characterizing Contractions and Weighted Blowdowns'] Suppose $\mathcal{X}$ and $\mathcal{Z}$ are smooth separated Deligne--Mumford stacks of dimension $n$, and there is a representable contraction $f : \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{Z}$ where the exceptional $\mathcal{E}$ is a smooth irreducible Cartier divisor. 
    Moreover, suppose there is a smooth closed irreducible Deligne--Mumford substack $\mathcal{Y} \subseteq \mathcal{Z}$ such that $(f^{-1}\mathcal{Y}) \simeq \mathcal{E}$ set-theoretically, and $f : \mathcal{X} \setminus \mathcal{E} \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathcal{Z} \setminus \mathcal{Y}.$    
    Then $f$ is an ordinary blowup of $\mathcal{Z}$ along smooth center $\mathcal{Y}$. In particular, $f|_{\mathcal{E}} : \mathcal{E} \to \mathcal{Y}$ is a projective bundle, and $\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X}}(\mathcal{E})|_{\mathcal{E}} \simeq \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{E}}(-1) \otimes f^*\mathcal{L}$ for some line bundle $\mathcal{L}$ on $\mathcal{Y}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem main representable of arXiv:2609.04023

    \begin{enumerate}
        \item For each $\lambda\in \Lambda_1(n)$, the map $\mu_{\lambda}$ is controlled.
        Here, $\rmB(n)$ is equipped with the LR-coarse structure and $\R^{\{\lambda\}}\cong \R$ is equipped with the bounded coarse structure (see Example \ref{example:coarse}).
        \item The map $\mu_0$ is coarse.
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Theorem 34 (Finite spectral reduction) of arXiv:2608.15805, 'Spectral duality structures and the Fisher--Rao geometry of reset distributions'] The reduction space, \emph{in symmetrised coordinates}, is exactly
the odd sector:
\begin{equation}
\widetilde V:=D^{-1}V = E_{\mathrm{odd}},
\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad
V = D\,E_{\mathrm{odd}} .

\end{equation}
The distinction matters: $D$ does not commute with $S$ unless
$p=q$, so $D\,E_{\mathrm{odd}}\neq E_{\mathrm{odd}}$ for a biased
walk --- consistently with the fact, noted above, that it is
$\widetilde\psi$ and not $\psi$ that is antisymmetric. The space
admits the canonical decomposition
\begin{equation}
\psi(\gamma)=\sum_{k\ \mathrm{even}} f_k(\gamma)\,\mathbf m_k,
\qquad
\mathbf m_k := D\,P_k\,D^{-1}\xi = D\,P_k\,\widetilde\xi,
\qquad
f_k(\gamma)=\frac{t}{1-\lambda_k t},
\quad t=1-\gamma .

\end{equation}
The directions $\mathbf m_k$ are nonzero and linearly independent.
As for canonicity, the symmetrised directions $P_k\widetilde\xi$ are
determined by $(\widetilde P,S,\widetilde\xi)$; their
original-coordinate images are determined by $(P,S,\xi)$ alone. For
the present irreducible tridiagonal $P$ the positive diagonal
symmetriser is unique up to an overall scalar --- the ratios
$D_{z+1}/D_z$ being fixed by the neighbour relations --- and the
conjugation $D P_k D^{-1}$ is unchanged under $D\mapsto cD$; so no
normalisation of the symmetriser need be fixed. In particular $\dim V = r$, and all $\gamma$-dependence is
carried by the elementary scalars $f_k$.

The notation is deliberate: these $\mathbf m_k$ are \emph{not} the
normal directions $\mathbf n_\nu$ of Section~\ref{sec:finite-reduction}.
There are $N$ of the latter, one per spectral mode, spanning a space
of dimension $r$ and therefore dependent; there are exactly $r$ of the
former, indexed by the even $k$ alone, and they are independent. Both
families span $V$, which is all the two routes are claimed to share.

body: Load-bearing hypothesis: 'the solution at (t,x) depends only on the data on the sphere ∂B(x,t)', i.e. sharp propagation on the light cone with no tail, holds only in odd space dimensions n ≥ 3. Finite speed of propagation (support in {|x| ≤ t + R}) holds in every dimension; the sharp inner edge does not. Counterexample n = 1: with u0 = 0 and u1 = 1_{[−1,1]}, d'Alembert's formula gives u(t,x) = (1/2)∫_{x−t}^{x+t} u1, so u(t,0) = 1 for every t ≥ 1 — the disturbance never leaves the origin. Counterexample n = 2: with u0 = 0 and u1 = 1_{B(0,1)}, Poisson's formula gives u(t,0) = (1/2π)∫_{|y|<1} (t² − |y|²)^{−1/2} dy > 0 for every t > 1 — a decaying tail behind the wavefront (this is why a splash on a pond is felt long after the front passes, while a sound pulse in three dimensions is heard once). Practical consequence: statements like 'the data inside B(x,t) do not matter' or 'the solution vanishes after the front passes' are valid only for odd n ≥ 3, and any argument that tacitly extends them to n = 1, 2 or to even dimensions (or to variable-coefficient / curved-background wave equations, where strong Huygens generally fails even in odd dimensions) is unsound.
title: Pitfall: Strong Huygens' Principle Needs Odd Dimension n ≥ 3

\item (for the spherical setting, where $\bx$ must lie near $S_N$)

\item (for the Ising setting, where $\bx$ must lie near $\Sigma_N$)  $\mu$ lies in 
$\bar{\cM}^{\Ising,\sym}(\alpha)$.
\end{enumerate}
The sets
$\bar{\cM}^{\sph,\sym}(\alpha)$ and  $\bar{\cM}^{\Ising,\sym}(\alpha)$
are specified by Definition~\ref{d:achievable-msrs-sym}. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma lemstable of arXiv:2607.12459, 'Renormalisation of Inhomogeneous Random Graphs'] {\bf [Invariance property for positive stable weights]}

Let $\gamma\in(0,1)$, and let $Y_1,\ldots,Y_m$ be i.i.d.\ standard positive $\gamma$-stable random variables, with Laplace transform
\[
\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda Y_1}] = \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda^\gamma}, \qquad \lambda\geq 0.
\]
Then
\[ 
m^{-1/\gamma}\sum_{i=1}^mY_i \stackrel{d}{=}Y_1.
\]
Consequently, for every $\delta\in(0,\infty)$ and $\eta\in[0,\infty)$, the inhomogeneous random graph with connection functions
\[
g^{\neq}_\delta(x,y)=\delta xy, \qquad g^{=}_\eta(x)=\eta x,
\]
and i.i.d.\ standard positive $\gamma$-stable weights is invariant in distribution under the renormalisation transformation, provided the aggregated weights are rescaled by $m^{-1/\gamma}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma lemstable of arXiv:2607.12459

 Then the equilibrium measure $\mu$ has a compact

\begin{align}
V^{{\textnormal{eff}}}_h(x) \geq v_h& \quad \textnormal{if}\,\,x\,\,\textnormal{is in a void}, \\
 V^{{\textnormal{eff}}}_h(x) \leq v_h & \quad \textnormal{if}\,\,x\,\,\textnormal{is in a saturation},\\
 V^{{\textnormal{eff}}}_h(x) = v_h& \quad \textnormal{if}\,\,x\,\,\textnormal{is in a band}. 
\end{align}
If each interval $[\hat a'_h, \hat b'_h]$ has at
least one band, then $\boldsymbol{v}$ belongs to the $\amsmathbb{R}$-span of the $H$-dimensional vectors of coefficients of the linear forms $(\mathfrak{r}_{e})_{e = 1}^\mathfrak{e}$ in \eqref{eq_equations_eqs}, and the above conditions uniquely determine the equilibrium measure, \textit{i.e.} no other measure in $\mathscr{P}_\star$ satisfies them. [Corollary 4 (Fixed-horizon first-order accuracy) of arXiv:2608.19762, '2608.19762'] Consider the scaled perturbation $\alpha\xi_t$ and a fixed horizon $H$.
Suppose that, in a neighborhood of the control trajectory,
$D\psi_t$ and $D\widetilde f_s$ are locally Lipschitz,
the finite-horizon propagators are uniformly bounded,
the probe objectives have locally Lipschitz gradients, and the switching
defects satisfy
\[
    \|r_s^{\mathrm{sw}}\|
    \leq
    C_s^{\mathrm{sw}}
    \|\delta x_s\|^2,
    ~~
    1\leq s-t<H.
\]
Then, for every $1\leq h\leq H$,
\[
    \delta F_{t+h}(\alpha)
    =
    \alpha
    c_{t+h}^{\top}
    \Phi_{t+h,t+1}
    B_t\xi_t
    +
    O(\alpha^2),
    ~~
    \alpha\rightarrow0.
\]
The $O(\alpha^2)$ constant may depend on the fixed horizon and control
trajectory but not on $\alpha$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Fixed-horizon first-order accuracy
