[Theorem 12 of arXiv:2506.13347, 'Ergodic theorem for the differential equations with interaction'] Let $a: \mathbb{R}^{2} \times \mathcal{M} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{2}$ be a Lipschitz function on both variables and  for every $\mu\in\mathcal{M},$ $a(\cdot, \mu) \in C'_b(\mathbb R^2)$.  Let $\varepsilon>0$ and $\mu_0\in \mathcal{M}_{D}. $   A closed domain $D \subset \mathbb{R}^{2}$ is flow invariant with respect to differential equation with interactions
$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
d x(u, t)=a\left(x(u, t), \mu_{t}\right) d t \\
x(u, 0)=u, u \in D \\
\mu_{t}=\mu_0 \circ x(\cdot, t)^{-1}
\end{array}\right.
$$
if for   any $\mu \in \mathcal{M}_{D^\varepsilon},$   $\langle a(x, \mu), \xi\rangle \leq 0$ for every $x \in D$ and every $\xi \in \hat{N}_{D}(x)$.

[Theorem thm:reg_williamson_kendall of arXiv:2411.07113, '\begin{LARGE}On differentiability and mass distributions of topologically typical multivar'] Let $C \in \mathcal{C}_{ar}^d$, $\gamma \in \mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{W}_d}$ be the corresponding Williamson measure, 
    $F_K^d$ be the Kendall distribution function of $C$ and $\kappa_{F_K^d}$ the probability measure
    corresponding to $F_K^d$. Then the following equivalences hold:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item[(i)] $\gamma$ is absolutely continuous if, and only if $\kappa_{F_K^d}$is absolutely continuous.
         \item[(ii)] $\gamma$ is discrete if, and only if $\kappa_{F_K^d}$ is discrete.
          \item[(iii)] $\gamma$ is singular if, and only if $\kappa_{F_K^d}$ is singular.
    \end{itemize}

[Thm 1 (Theorem \ref{thm.integralHK} and Corollary \ref{cor.integralHK}) of arXiv:2609.00723, 'An integral Hyodo--Kato isomorphism'] Assume $e\leq p^m$. For every fine, quasi-compact and quasi-separated log-smooth
morphism $\sX\to\Spec(\uk^0)$ of Cartier type, there is a natural equivalence in $\CAlg(\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{O}_K)^\wedge_p)$
\[
\rho_{\pi,m}^{\rm int}\colon R\Gamma_{\rm crys}(\sX/\uW^0)
\ \widehat\otimes^{\mathbb L}_{W,\phi^m}\ \sO_K
\;\simeq\;
R\Gamma_{\rm crys}\bigl(\FttOK\sX m/\OKpi\bigr),
\]
depending on $\pi$, functorial for morphisms of such log schemes over $\uk^0$. Here,
$\widehat\otimes^{\mathbb L}_{W,\phi^m}\sO_K$ denotes derived $p$-completed base
change along $W\xrightarrow{\phi^m}W\to\sO_K$.

Assume that ${\mathfrak{X}}$ is a fine, quasi-compact and quasi-separated log smooth scheme of Cartier type over $\OK^\pi$ with log special fiber $\mathcal{X} = {\mathfrak{X}}\times_{\OK^\pi} k^0\to k^0$. Let $L\eta_p$ be the décalage functor, and write $L\eta_p^m$ for its $m$-th fold power.  Setting  
\begin{equation}
R\Gamma_{\dR}^{\eta^m}({\fX}/\OKpi)
	:=
	R\Gamma\!\left(
	\sX_{\acute et},

[Proposition prop:normdiag of arXiv:2609.00978, 'Towards Categorical K\"ahler Geometry'] The following are equivalent for a non-Archimedean field $K$:
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
    \item All norms on all $K$-vector spaces are diagonalizable.
    \item $K$ is maximally complete, i.e.\ there is no complete extension $L/K$ with the same value group and residue field.
    \item $K$ is spherically complete, i.e.\ any nested family of closed balls has non-empty intersection.
\end{enumerate}

body:
[Lemma 5 of arXiv:2608.30578, 'Compactly Supported Solutions near a Nehari Critical Value'] Let
\[
\mathcal R(u):=
\frac{\displaystyle\int_\Omega|\nabla u|^2\,dx}
{\displaystyle\int_\Omega|u|^2\,dx},
\qquad
\mathcal A:=
\{u\in H_0^1(\Omega)\setminus\{0\}:M(u)\geq0\}.
\]
Suppose that \(\bar u\in\mathcal A\) is a local minimizer of
\(\mathcal R\) on \(\mathcal A\). Then there exist
\(\mu_0,\mu_1\geq0\), with \(\mu_0+\mu_1>0\), such that
\begin{equation}
	\mu_0D\mathcal R(\bar u)=\mu_1DM(\bar u),
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
	\mu_1M(\bar u)=0.
\end{equation}
If \(DM(\bar u)\neq0\), then \(\mu_0>0\), and consequently there exists
\(\mu\geq0\) such that
\begin{equation}
	D\mathcal R(\bar u)=\mu\,DM(\bar u),
	\qquad
	\mu M(\bar u)=0.
	
\end{equation}
Thus, under the constraint qualification \(DM(\bar u)\neq0\), the
Fritz John conditions \cite{John} reduce to the usual Kuhn--Tucker
conditions. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 5 of arXiv:2608.30578

[Definition def:forests of arXiv:2411.07157, 'Rough differential equations in the flow approach'] Define $\mathcal{T}_{1,2}\eqdef\mathcal{T}\times\{0,1\}\times\{0,1,2\}$, and denote by $\tilde\tau=(\tau,r,u)$ an element of $\mathcal{T}_{1,2}$. 
We introduce a set of (ordered, unlabelled) forests
\begin{equs}
\text{$   \widehat\mathcal{T}$}\eqdef
\Big\{{\boldsymbol{\tau}}=(\tilde {\tau}_1,\dots,\tilde{\tau}_{p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})})
=
\Big( (\tau_1,r_1,u_1), \dots, (\tau_{p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})},r_{p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})},u_{p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})}) 
\Big)\in\text{$\mathcal{T}$}_1^{p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})}:p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})\in[P]
\Big\}\,. 
\end{equs}

For two forests ${\boldsymbol{\tau}},{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}\in\widehat\mathcal{T}$ and a tuple $I=(i_1,\dots,i_{|I|})$ consisting of distinct elements of $[p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})]$, we define the forest ${\boldsymbol{\tau}}_{I}$ by
\begin{equs}    {\boldsymbol{\tau}}_I\eqdef\big(\tilde\tau_{i_1},\dots,\tilde\tau_{i_{|I|}}\big)\,,
\end{equs}
and we define the forest  ${\boldsymbol{\tau}}\sqcup{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}$, the concatenation of ${\boldsymbol{\tau}}$ and ${\boldsymbol{\sigma}}$, by
\begin{equs}    {\boldsymbol{\tau}}\sqcup{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}\eqdef(\tilde\tau_1,\dots,\tilde\tau_{p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})},\tilde\sigma_1,\dots,\tilde\sigma_{p({\boldsymbol{\sigma}})})\,.
\end{equs}
Fix ${\boldsymbol{\tau}}=(\tilde\tau_1,\dots,\tilde\tau_{p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})})\in\widehat\mathcal{T}$ and
suppose that for every $i\in[p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})]$, we are given tuples of times $(t_{i},s^{\tau_i})\in(-\infty,1]\times\R^{\mathfrak{s}(\tau_i)}$.
We then write
\begin{equs}
    t_{{\boldsymbol{\tau}}}\eqdef (t_{\tau_1},\dots,t_{\tau_{p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})}})  \in (-\infty,1]^{p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})} \,,\;\text{and}\;s^{{\boldsymbol{\tau}}}\eqdef(s^{\tau_1},\dots,s^{\tau_{p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})}}) \in \R^{\mathfrak{s}({\boldsymbol{\tau}})} \,,
\end{equs}
where $\mathfrak{s}({\boldsymbol{\tau}})\eqdef\sum_{i\in[p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})]}\text{$\mathfrak{s}$}(\tau_i)$ is the \textit{size} of ${\boldsymbol{\tau}}$. We also write $\mathfrak{l}({\boldsymbol{\tau}})\eqdef p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})+\mathfrak{s}({\boldsymbol{\tau}})$. 

Finally, we define the \textit{scaling} of ${\boldsymbol{\tau}}$ by
\begin{equs}    |{\boldsymbol{\tau}}|\eqdef\big(p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})-1\big)+\sum_{i=1}^{p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})}|\tau_i|\,,
\end{equs}
the \textit{order} of ${\boldsymbol{\tau}}$ by $\text{${\mathfrak{o}}$}({\boldsymbol{\tau}})\eqdef \sum_{i\in[p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})]}\text{${\mathfrak{o}}$}(\tau_i) $, and set $r({\boldsymbol{\tau}})\eqdef\sum_{i\in[p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})]}r_i$ and $u({\boldsymbol{\tau}})\eqdef\sum_{i\in[p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})]}u_i$.

[Theorem 30 (Exact one-step feedback extraction) of arXiv:2608.12492, 'Weak Limits of Wiener Chaos: Primitive--Fock Classification and Hilbert--Stein Extraction'] Assume $R>0$ and $\norm x\le R$.
Define
\[
 \cN_q=\Lambda_q^*\Lambda_q,\qquad
 w_{b,q}=\cN_qr_{b,q},\qquad
 W_q=\Span_{1\le b\le d}\{w_{b,q}\}.
\]
Then $W_q\subset M_q^\perp$, $\dim W_q\le d$, and
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{b,q}\norm{P_{W_q}r_{b,q}}^2
 \ge\frac{\mathfrak H_Q(A,r)}{a_QR^2}.
 
\end{equation}
If $M_q'=M_q\oplus W_q$, $A'=P_{\mathbf M'}x$, and
$r'=P_{(\mathbf M')^\perp}x$, then
\begin{equation}
 \norm r^2-\norm{r'}^2
 \ge\frac{\mathfrak H_Q(A,r)}{a_QR^2}.
 
\end{equation}
Moreover,
\begin{equation}
 \mathfrak H_Q(A,r)=0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \cN_qr_{b,q}=0\quad\text{for every }b,q.
 
\end{equation}

Own-work C013 v1, proof (unaudited); novelty unestablished. Let ||x_i||<=1, y_i in {-1,1}, z_i=y_i*x_i, signed-data rank>=2, z_i dot z_l>=kappa>0 for all pairs, and a unit u satisfy u dot z_i>=gamma>0. For literal leaky ReLU phi(v)=max(v,lambda*v), 0<lambda<1, no biases, f_i=m^-1 sum_j a_j phi(w_j dot x_i), train both layers simultaneously on average logistic loss with actual step m*eta, allowing any selected derivative in [lambda,1] at zero. Write G_t=average (1+exp(y_i*f_i(t)))^-1 and r_t=average_j(a_j(t)^2+||w_j(t)||^2). Let c=lambda*sqrt(kappa) and 0<eta<=c/2. If one neuron initially has a and every signed projection w dot z_i nonzero of the same sign, define h_t=min(|a_t|,min_i|w_t dot z_i|/sqrt(kappa)), H_t=h_t^2/m, B=H_0. Then a finite s exists after which loss strictly decreases, with H_s>=32/c^2, L_s<=1/n, eta*r_s*L_s<=c^2/16, and for every t>=0, L_{s+t}<=1/(1/L_s+eta*c^2*H_s*t/16). Hence for t>0, L_{s+t}<=1/(2*eta*t). The invariant region follows from actual activation secants across kinks and a Taylor expansion only of the scalar logistic loss, giving L_next<=L-eta*D/4 when eta*r*G<=c^2/16, where D=average_j[(w_j dot b_j)^2+c^2*a_j^2*G^2], b_j=average_i g_i*phi_prime(w_j dot x_i)*z_i. Hidden signed-Gram positivity and the simultaneous output-hidden cross term are essential to this inequality. Entry follows by comparing persistent-neuron growth with entropy-sharpened Euler energy: S_T=sum_{t<T}G_t<=U_T=log((r0+4*eta*T)/B)/zeta, zeta=2*eta*c/(1+eta*c)-eta^2; r_t<=R_T for t<=T, where R_T=[r0+4*eta*U_T*log(T/G0)]*((r0+4*eta*T)/B)^(eta^2/zeta). The exponent is <=3/5, so some arbitrarily late s has r_s*G_s<=2*R_T*U_T/T tending to zero. Also S_t and H_t tend to infinity. Section 5 of the source specifies finite sufficient burn-in via explicit analytic inequalities; no floating-point horizon is claimed. For iid Gaussian coordinates N(0,sigma^2), sigma>0, and delta in (0,1), set b=(gamma/sqrt(2*pi*d))^d*exp(-(1+gamma/2)^2/2), p=2*exp(-2)*b/sqrt(2*pi). If m>=log(2/delta)/p, probability >=1-delta supplies a persistent neuron with B>=sigma^2/m*min(1,gamma^2/(4*kappa)), r0<=2*(d+1)*sigma^2/delta, and G0>=1/(1+exp((d+1)*sigma^2/delta)). Replacing these in the source horizon yields a uniform finite sufficient burn-in bound on this initial event. No independent trajectory events are assumed. This is a restricted-geometry, restricted-step, literal-leaky result; general separable geometry, arbitrarily large eta and nonhomogeneous smooth activations remain open. 136809 exact rational finite assertions passed across 7200 steps, with 247 strict kink crossings, 7200 omitted-cross-term detections and 3954 old-derivative-for-secant detections. The exact invariant polynomial is (1+v)^2*(1-4v)=1-2v-7v^2-4v^3. These checks do not certify the analytic, asymptotic or Gaussian proof. No Lean or independent audit is claimed. Existing fixed-output and gradient-flow literature still needs a novelty comparison.

[Corollary cor.reg of arXiv:2605.05904, 'Schr\"odinger's problem with constraints'] Under the hypothesis of Assumption (a:main of the paper), the following results hold:
\begin{enumerate}
\item  For any  $g:E\to\bbR$ such that  $\log g$ has  subquadratic growth,  and for $t \leq 1$, the map 
\be 
[0,t)\times E\ni (s,z) \mapsto Q_sg(z):=\int_E g(y)q(s,t;z,y)dy  
\ee
is in $C^{1,2}([0,t)\times E)$. In particular, by taking $g\equiv 1$, $L(\cdot,t,\cdot)\in C^{1,2}([0,t)\times E)$.

Similarly, for any  $g:E\times E\to\bbR$ such that  $\log g$ has  subquadratic growth, and for $t\leq 1$, the map
\be 
[0,t)\times E^2\ni (s,x) \mapsto P_sg(x):=\int_{E^2} g(z',y')p(s,t;x,(z',y'))dy'dz'  
\ee
is in $C^{1,2}([0,t)\times E^2)$,
where, for all $0\leq s <t \leq 1$ and $x=(z,y)\in E^2 ,(z',y') \in E^2$, 
\be 
p(s,t; (z,y), (z',y')):=q(s,t;z,z')q(s,t;y,y').
\ee
\item
If $\ell$ is an accessible boundary, i.e. $\ell\in(-\infty,+\infty)$, then, for all $s\in [0,t)$, we have 
\[
\lim_{z\rightarrow \ell}Q_sg(z)=0,\quad \text{and}\quad \lim_{x\rightarrow \partial E^2_\ell}P_sg(x)=0. 
\]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Corollary cor.reg of arXiv:2605.05904

[Proposition 7 of arXiv:2607.05219, 'Random free semigroups of affine groups'] Let $r$ be the free   rank of $A$. Then 
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)]
If $\zeta$ is not centered, then $(W_n)$ is transient. 

\item[(ii)]
If $\zeta$ is centered, then $(W_n)$ is recurrent if and only if $r\leq2$.
\end{enumerate}
Moreover, in the transient regime, for any $x\in A$ and for any $F\subset A$ finite, $\p_x(W_n\in F\,\textrm{i.o.})=0$.

body:
[Lem 13 of arXiv:2605.23659, '2605.23659'] Let \(Z\) be a subordinator with Laplace exponent \(\psi\), and let \(\mu_Z\) be the random measure on \([0,\infty)\) induced by \(Z\), namely
\[
\mu_Z((a,b]) := Z_b-Z_a
\quad (0\le a<b<\infty).
\]
Let \(A\subset [0,\infty)\) be a Borel set with \(\lambda(A)<\infty\), where \(\lambda\) denotes the Lebesgue measure.
Then
\begin{align}
  E[e^{-q\mu_Z(A)}]=e^{-\lambda(A)\psi(q)}
\quad (q\ge0). 
\end{align}
In particular,
\[
\mu_Z(A)\overset{d}{=} Z_{\lambda(A)},
\]
and if \(A,B \subset [0,\infty)\) are disjoint, \(\mu_{Z}(A)\) and \(\mu_{Z}(B)\) are independent.
More generally, if \(A\) is a random Borel set independent of \(Z\), then
\[
E[e^{-q\mu_Z(A)}\mid A]=e^{-\lambda(A)\psi(q)}
\quad (q\ge0),
\]
and hence, if \(\lambda(A)=a\) almost surely for some \(a\ge0\), then
\[
\mu_Z(A)\overset{d}{=} Z_{a}.
\]

[Lemma lem:choice:blowup of arXiv:2608.30973, 'Pseudo-Anosov flow and dynamics on guts'] Fix a maximal transverse facet \(F_{\tau}(z)\) and a maximal collection \(\mathcal{A}\) of product annuli.
Suppose that \(\varphi_{1}^{\sharp\sharp}\) and \(\varphi_{2}^{\sharp\sharp}\) are two further blowup such that \(\mathcal{A}\) can be isotoped to aligned position.
For \(i=1,2\), \(\varphi_{i}^{\sharp\sharp}\) induces a semiflow \(\phi_{i}\) on \(\mathrm{Guts}(F_{\tau}(z)\cup \mathcal{A})\).
Then, \(\phi_{1}\) and \(\phi_{2}\) are orbit equivalent outside half annuli.

body: A normed vector space is a vector space V over the real or complex numbers together with a norm, a function assigning to each vector x a real number ||x|| such that for all vectors x, y and scalars a: (i) ||x|| >= 0, and ||x|| = 0 if and only if x = 0; (ii) absolute homogeneity, ||a x|| = |a| ||x||; (iii) the triangle inequality, ||x + y|| <= ||x|| + ||y||. A norm induces a metric d(x, y) = ||x - y||, and all topological notions (convergence, continuity, completeness) on a normed space refer to this metric. Vector addition and scalar multiplication are continuous for it.

Write $D^{\phi,N}(W)$ for the  derived category
of $(\phi,N)$-modules over $W$. See e.g. \cite{deg_niziol} for details.

$\va\in(0,\va_1)$, and $u\in \mathcal{D}\cap\V(u_\infty, \ell,\delta; \va)$ with $\|\mathcal{R}_{u}-r_\infty\|_{C^0(\om)}<\va$,  there holds
\[
\begin{aligned}
\left|
Y_\Omega(\xi_{\bm z})-Y_\Omega(u_\infty)
\right|
\leq{}&
C
\left(
\int_\Omega
|\mathcal R_u-r_\infty|^{\frac{2n}{n+2}}
u^{\frac{2n}{n-2}}\,\ud x
\right)^{\frac{n+2}{2n}(1+\gamma)}+
C\sum_{k=1}^{\ell}
\lambda_k^{-\frac{n-2}{2}(1+\gamma)},
\end{aligned}
\]
where $\gamma\in(0,1)$ is the exponent in
Lemma \ref{lem:L-ineq}.

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Controlled generators, exact finite-state diagnostic, coupling, renewal reward or capacity comparison Result: A first-arrival decomposition explains why no-arrival optimality is insufficient. For two policies coupled until a selected state, assume their cost difference through recoupling is integrable and let D(t) be its conditional expectation given that the next arrival occurs at time t, including their specified continuation rules. Under a Poisson rate lambda, the expected difference is integral_0^infinity lambda*exp(-lambda*t)*D(t) dt. The sign of D on an intermediate interval can outweigh both early-arrival harm and a favorable no-arrival endpoint. A global comparison must also bound the cost until recoupling; comparing only the first completed job misses that term. Check: Condition on the exponential next-arrival time to derive the integral. Conditional continuations still include all later arrivals; replacing them by a no-further-arrivals trajectory would invalidate the identity. Obstruction: No new policy comparison or sharp universal lower bound is proved. The later source resolves the improvement-existence subquestion, not full optimal control.

PRIVATE REDUCTION, author-recorded. By the cluster-process structure of the DGFF extremal process (Biskup-Louidor), the number of points of the level set at depth t inside A is a Poisson sum over extremal local maxima in A of i.i.d. cluster sizes at the corresponding depths, so its conditional expectation given the extremal measure Z^D equals Z^D(A) times the integral over depth of e^{alpha s} E[cluster size at depth s] ds. Conjecture 16.5 (the count normalised by (1/t) e^{-alpha t} converges to c Z^D(A)) therefore reduces to the existence of lim e^{-alpha h} E_nu(f_h) (Conjecture 16.6) plus (i) uniform integrability of cluster sizes at depth t uniformly in N, to exchange the N and t limits, and (ii) a variance bound making the Poisson sum concentrate, which follows from the same uniform integrability. Conversely 16.5 implies the limit in 16.6 by taking expectations. The open content is thus 16.6 together with the uniform-in-N control of deep clusters, which the concentric decomposition delivers only at bounded depth.
2D DGFF in admissible domains; extremal process with Poisson-cluster structure (Biskup-Louidor)
Exchange of limits requires uniform integrability not currently available
title: Biskup's Conjecture 16.5 (size of deep extremal level sets of the 2D DGFF) is equivalent to his Conjecture 16.6 given uniform integrability of deep cluster sizes

[Theorem 8 (Risk stability of Nesterov) of arXiv:2609.02728, 'Momentum in large-batch training: Polyak enlarges the critical batch size, Nesterov improv'] Let the Hessian be a positive trace-class operator and assume
\[
\bH=\diag(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\ldots),
\qquad
\lambda_1=\lambda_{\max}\geq\lambda_2\geq\cdots>0,
\qquad
0\leq\rho<1,
\qquad
\sigma>0.
\]
Define
\[
\Delta_{\nesterov}(x)
:=
2B(1-\rho^2)
+
\left[4B\rho^2+(B-1)\rho-(B+1)\right]x
-
(B+1)\rho(1+2\rho)x^2.
\]
Then Nesterov momentum is risk stable if and only if
\begin{equation}

\Delta_{\nesterov}(\eta\lambda_{\max})>0
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}

\kappa_{\nesterov}(\eta,\rho)
:=
\sum_{i\geq1}
\frac{
\eta\lambda_i
\left[1+\rho+\rho(1+2\rho)\eta\lambda_i\right]
}{
\Delta_{\nesterov}(\eta\lambda_i)
}
<1.
\end{equation}

[Thm 19 (\Cref{thm: restate of window fixed m} in the text) of arXiv:2603.27433, 'The $k$-cycle shuffling with repeated cards'] Let \(n=ml\), such that \(l\ge 2\) is fixed, and \(m=\omega(1)\). Suppose \(2\le k\le o(n/\log n)\), and
$$
t=\frac nk(\log n+c),
$$
where \(c\in \R\) is an absolute constant. Then, we have
$$
d_{TV}(\sim_l\backslash P_{n,k}^{*t},\sim_l\backslash U_{\S_n})
=
d_{TV}(\Pois(l+\exp(-c)),\Pois(l))+o(1).
$$
Here, \(\Pois(\cdot)\) denotes the Poisson distribution. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Own-work research draft; status proof (unaudited), independent review and novelty assessment pending. Fix k>=1, D>=k+1, and a compact connected smooth hypersurface M0 in R^(k+1), volume V0 and reach tau0>0, whose portion over |x|<1 is precisely z=+1 and z=-1. Let R0=max norm on M0. Set ell=1/(2 sqrt(k)), A=1/12, G=12 sqrt(k), H=8448 k, I=[4096*(6!)^2/13!]^k, Vbar=V0+A^2*G^2*ell^(k+2), tstar=(V0/Vbar)^(1/k), rho=1/[4*(3/(2*tau0)+A*H)], R=R0+A*ell^2 and C=tstar*A*I*ell^(k+2)/[32*Vbar*8^(2/k)]. For any class P containing all uniform surface laws on compact connected closed C2 k-manifolds of volume V0, reach at least tstar*rho, and contained in the radius-R ball, and any family Q of at most 2^S arbitrary output laws with S>=0, sup over mu in P of inf over eta in Q of W1(mu,eta) is at least C*(S+1)^(-2/k). All target laws have density exactly 1/V0. Signed h^2 bumps on both flat patches have sign-independent area; a common scaling fixes volume exactly. A global vertical shear and the tangent-distance reach formula control reach; a globally Lipschitz clamped vertical witness separates a Hamming code. Count all architecture and latent-law choices in S; fixed W parameters with B bits each give S=WB. Compatibility with the class geometry is required; the result makes no claim for classes excluding this family, no unrestricted-real-weight lower bound and no novelty claim.

The set of null rotations $N = \{R_p(c) \mid c \in \mathbb{R}\}$ fixing a given null vector $\eta$ in $\mathbb{R}^{1,2}_1$ forms an abelian, 1-parameter unipotent subgroup of $O^{+\uparrow}(1,2)$ isomorphic to $(\mathbb{R}, +)$, satisfying $R_p(c_1) R_p(c_2) = R_p(c_1 + c_2)$ and $(R_p(c) - I)^3 = 0$.

[Theorem 2 (\textsf{Four-moment criterion on Poisson-chaos}) of arXiv:2608.12451, '2608.12451'] Fix $q\in\N$ and $\lambda \in(0, \infty)$.  Let
$F_n\in\cC_{q}^{ \mathsf{P}}\cap L^4(\PP)$ satisfy the lattice condition \eqref{cond_La}
with shift  $\theta_n$.
Then, $\cP(F_n )\geq0$ for every $n$, and the following assertions are
equivalent.

\smallskip
\noi
{\rm (i)}
The first four   moments of $F_n+ \theta_n$ converge to the four numbers in
\eqref{4M}.

\smallskip
\noi
{\rm (ii)}
One has
$\big(\theta_n, m_2(F_n),   \cP(F_n) \big) \to (\lambda,  \lambda,  0)$

 

\smallskip
\noi
{\rm (iii)}
One has
$\dTV\bigl(\cL(F_n + \theta_n), P_\lambda\bigr) \to0$
and the family $\{ (F_n + \theta_n)^4\}_{n\geq1}$ is uniformly integrable.
 
 In particular, convergence of the first four moments implies Poisson
convergence. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: \textsf{Four-moment criterion on Poisson-chaos}

[Lemma 85 of arXiv:2608.20252, '2608.20252'] A family of probability measures $\{Q_N\}$ on $D([0,T],\mf D')$ is tight if for each $H\in \mf D$,
\begin{itemize}
\item[(a)] $\lim_{A\uparrow\infty}\lim_{N\uparrow\infty} Q_N\big[ |W^N_0(H)| >A\big] \ = \ 0 $
and, 
\item[(b)] for all $\epsilon>0$,
$\lim_{\delta\downarrow 0} \lim_{N\uparrow\infty} Q_N\big[w_{W^N(H)}(\delta)\geq \epsilon\big] \ = \ 0$.
\end{itemize}

    \end{enumerate}

There is a symmetric law $\xi$ with a bounded density, variance one and $\mathbb{E}|\xi|^3 < \infty$ for which the rectangular operator norm is NOT tight on the scale $\sqrt{m}$: if $A_m \in \mathbb{R}^{N_m \times m}$ has iid entries of law $\xi$ and $N_m \sim \gamma m$, then $\|A_m\|_{\mathrm{op}}/\sqrt{m} \to \infty$ in probability. Consequently the hypothesis of the bounded-fourth-moment submatrix theorem cannot simply be relaxed to 'bounded density plus finite third moment'. The honest modular hypothesis is bounded density, finite third moment, AND rectangular operator-norm tightness $\|A_m\|_{\mathrm{op}}/\sqrt{m} = O_{\mathbb{P}}(1)$; a uniform fourth moment is a convenient sufficient package for the last two conditions.

variance normalized to one
iid entries
N_m ~ gamma m

body:
Let X and Y be Banach spaces and let T from X to Y be a bounded (continuous) linear operator that is surjective. Then T is an open map: the image of every open subset of X is open in Y. Consequences: a bijective bounded linear operator between Banach spaces has a bounded inverse (bounded inverse theorem); if a vector space is Banach under two norms and one dominates the other, the norms are equivalent. Completeness of both X and Y is essential.
X and Y are Banach spaces
T : X -> Y is bounded, linear, and surjective

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Decoupling plus the linear Littlewood-Offord bound, to see where the logarithm enters. Result: Decoupling Q by splitting the index set into two halves I, J gives P(Q = z) <= P(|sum_{i in I, j in J} c_ij xi_i xi'_j - ...| small)^{1/2}-type bounds where, conditionally on the J-variables, the bilinear form is a linear form in the I-variables with coefficients a_i = sum_j c_ij xi_j; the linear Littlewood-Offord (Erdos) bound gives P <= C/sqrt(number of nonzero a_i), and the a_i are nonzero with high probability except on an event where many coefficient sums vanish, whose probability is itself controlled by a Littlewood-Offord bound on the rows; the loss comes from the union over rows and the conditioning, which is where the n^{o(1)} or logarithmic factors enter in the known proofs. The extremal example (xi_1 + ... + xi_n)^2 shows n^{-1/2} is the right order because the square of a sum concentrates on O(sqrt n) values. To remove the logarithm one needs a rank-type inverse theorem: if P(Q = z) >= n^{-1/2} C then the coefficient matrix is close to rank one with arithmetic structure, and the inverse theorems available (Nguyen-Vu) give such structure only at the cost of a logarithmic loss in the threshold. No improvement obtained; the reduction to a lossless inverse theorem is recorded. Obstruction: The known inverse Littlewood-Offord theorems carry logarithmic losses.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-c0108-optimal-quadratic-littlewood-offord-bound
No independent review; result status attempted_unsolved

[Corollary cor:product-light of arXiv:2607.12459, 'Renormalisation of Inhomogeneous Random Graphs'] {\bf [Product kernel with finite first effective moment]}

Suppose that, for some $B,\beta\in(0,\infty)$ and $C,K^{\neq},K^{=}<\infty\in[0,\infty)$,
\[
\big|g^{\neq}(x,y)-B(xy)^\beta\big|\leq K^{\neq}, \quad x,y\in\mathbb{R}_+,
\qquad \big|g^{=}(x)-Cx^\beta\big|\leq K^{=}, \quad x\in\mathbb{R}_+.
\]
Suppose further that
\[
0<\mathbb{E}_X[X_1^\beta]<\infty.
\]
Then Theorem~(thm1 of the paper) applies. In particular, if
\[
\mathbb{P}(X_1>x)\sim Ax^{-\alpha}, \qquad x\to\infty,
\]
then the product connection function is attracted to the homogeneous Erd\H{o}s--R\'enyi random graph whenever $\alpha>\beta$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Corollary cor:product-light of arXiv:2607.12459

[Theorem eq:weibull-degree-window of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[theorem]{thm:weibull-bulk}
Fix \(0<\alpha<1\) with
\begin{equation}
 \alpha(p-2)>2.
\end{equation}
Retain the parameters and independence assumptions of
(thm:bulk-universality of the paper), require \(f\in\mathcal F_m\), and replace the
exponential-moment hypothesis
in (equation eq:array-assumptions of the paper) by
\begin{equation}
 \sup_{N,I}\mathbb P(\abs{J_{I,N}}>t)
 \le C_0e^{-c_0t^\alpha},
 \qquad t\ge0,
\end{equation}
and retain exact Gaussian moment matching through order \(m\ge2\).  Choose
\[
 \frac1\alpha<\gamma<\frac{p-2}{2}.
\]
Then, for all sufficiently large \(N\),
\begin{equation}
 \left|\log\frac{\mathbb E\mathcal Z_{N,L}^J(V,\varepsilon,f)}
 {\mathbb E\mathcal Z_{N,L}^G(V,\varepsilon,f)}\right|
 \le CNq_N^{m-1}+Ce^{-cN^{\alpha\gamma}}.
\end{equation}
The pressure and ratio conclusions of

[Proposition 16 of arXiv:2608.30549, '\vspace{-1cm}Maximally Spread Out Measures and Implications\\{} for Phase Transitions in A'] Let $\XX$ be a quasi-normed space and $\CalG = \{g_n\}_{n \in \N} \subseteq \XX$ arbitrary.
  Moreover, let $P \in \R[X]$ be a polynomial.
  For $n \in \N$, define
  \[
    \CalA_n
    := \Sigma_n(\CalG, P)
    := \bigcup_{\substack{I_0 \subseteq \{k \in \N: k \leq P(n)\}, \\ \# I_0 \leq n}}
         \linspan \bigl\{ g_k \,\,:\,\, k \in I_0 \bigr\}
  \]
  to be the set of $n$-term linear combinations of $\CalG$ with search depth bounded by $P$.
  Here, we use the convention $\linspan \emptyset = \{0\}$.
  Then the family $(\CalA_n)_{n \in \N}$ is of controlled complexity in $\XX$.

Scoped campaign audit. Uniform ellipticity bounds continuous residence before first exit from a set of bounded escape radius. It does not itself bound returns, an adaptively selected number of episodes, or regeneration time. For stopping-time episodes of uniformly bounded escape radius and any positive integer horizon tau, even a non-stopping horizon, finiteness of E[tau|B] is equivalent to finiteness of E[K_tau|B] for P(B)>0, where K_tau is the first episode index whose ending time reaches tau. The tower argument is made before conditioning on B. For directional regeneration the exit-count mean remains an unproved premise in this packet; almost-sure finiteness alone is insufficient.

[Thm 6 of arXiv:2605.31300, 'Cone-Additive Functions for Random Walks on Free Products of Graphs'] Let $f:\Pi \to \mathbb{R}$ be a cone-additive function. 
Assume that $G(o,o|z)$ has radius of convergence strictly bigger than $1$ and  that there exist a constant $C\in (0,\infty)$ and $R_f \in (0,\mathcal{R})$ 
such that 
\begin{equation}
 \bigl|f\bigl(\pi\bigr)\bigr| \leq C \cdot R_f^{\mathrm{length}(\pi)}\quad \textrm{ for all } \pi\in\Pi.
\end{equation}
Then there exists some constant $\mathfrak{c}\in\mathbb{R}$ such that
$$
\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac1n f\bigl([X_0,\ldots,X_n]\bigr) = 
\mathfrak{c}\quad \textrm{almost surely}.
$$    
Moreover, if $f$ is strictly positive then $\mathfrak{c}>0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Cor 125 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $J\equiv J(p,2\tep,\lambda/2)$ as  defined by \eqref{e:bad.times.J}. Then the coefficients from Definition~\ref{d:cts.coeffs} satisfy the estimates 
	\[
	\max\left\{
	\begin{array}{c}
	|\tbbb(t,y)^2
		-\Tbbb(t,y)^2|,\\
	|\tvvv(t,y)-\Tvvv(t,y)|,\\
	|\tuuu(t,y)^2-\Tuuu(t,y)^2|
	\end{array}
	\right\}
	\le \bigg(\frac{\trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} \lambda
	\]
for all $(t,y)\in( [q_*,1]  \setminus J)\times\R$. 

\begin{proof}
Lemma~\ref{l:limit.coefs} gives
	\[\begin{aligned}
	\tB(t,y)&=\tB^N(t,y)+o_N(1)\,,\\
	\Tbbb(t,y)&=\Tbbb^N(t,y)+o_N(1)
	\end{aligned}\]
for all $(t,y)\in[q_*,1]\times\R$. Recall that $(p^N)'(t)$ converges to $p'(t)$ for almost every $t$. Therefore, for \emph{every} $t$, we can find $s\in[t-\tep,t+\tep]$ such that $(p^N)'(s)$ converges to $p'(s)$. If $t\notin J$, then $t\notin J^N$ for sufficiently large $N$ by Lemma~\ref{l:bad.times.JN.J}, so $p'(s)$ differs from $p'(t)$ by at most $\lambda/2$, while $(p^N)'(s)$ differs from $(p^N)'(t)$ by at most $\lambda$. Therefore, for $t\in[q_*,1]\setminus J$, we have
	\[
	\Big|\tbbb(t,y)-\tbbb^N(t,y)\Big|
	=\bigg|\frac{\tB(t,y)}{p'(t)^{1/2}}
	-\frac{\tB^N(t,y)}{(p^N)'(t)^{1/2}}\bigg|
	\le o_N(1)
	+ \bigg( \frac{\trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)}(\MAX_N)^2
	\lambda\,,
	\]
using the bounds on $\tB^N$ and $\tB$ implied by Lemma~\ref{l:sp.smooth.reg} and Corollary~\ref{c:reg.in.limit}.
Additionally, since $t\notin J^N$,
Lemma~\ref{l:t.smooth.domain} bounds the discrepancy between $\tbbb^N(t,y)$ and $\Tbbb^N(t,y)$.
Sending $N\to\infty$ gives the claimed bound on the discrepancy between $\tbbb(t,y)$ and $\Tbbb(t,y)$. The other bounds follow by similar arguments:
	\begin{align*}
	\Big|\tvvv(t,y)-\tvvv^N(t,y)\Big|
	&=\bigg|
	\frac{\tV(t,y)}{p(t)}
	-\frac{\tV^N(t,y)}{p^N(t)}\bigg|\,,\\
	\Big|\tuuu(t,y)-\tuuu^N(t,y)\Big|
	&=\bigg|\frac{\tU(t,y)}{[ p(t)
		\cdot t p'(t)]^{1/2}}
		-\frac{\tU^N(t,y)}{[ p^N(t)
		\cdot t (p^N)'(t)]^{1/2}}
		\bigg|\,.
	\end{align*}
Note in these cases that in the factor $L^{O(1)}$ appearing in the final bound, the $O(1)$ exponent can depend on the constant $\breve{c}$ from \eqref{e:breve.q.bounds}. We will remark on this point again in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:Lipschitz-SDE-approx}.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Defi 7 (coding the ancestral lineage) of arXiv:2606.27035, 'R\'emy's diffusion on Brownian trees'] Let $(t,x)$ be a binary tree with a marked vertex at height $h \geq 1$. For every $i=0, \dots, h-1$, let $a_i = 0$ if the ancestor of $x$ at height $h-i$ lies on the same side as its parent, and $a_i = 1$ if it lies on the opposite side.
Let $A = \sum_{i=0}^{h-1} a_i$.
For every $1 \le k \le  A$, let $p_{k}= 1+\inf\{j \ge 0 \colon \sum_{i=0}^j a_i \ge k\}$ and then $\ell_k = p_{k}-p_{k-1}$, where $p_0=0$.
Let finally $\ell_{A+1} = h+1-p_{A}$.
title: coding the ancestral lineage

[Lem 234 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] There exist $C(\alpha) > 0$ and $C(\alpha,L,K) > 0$, such that the following holds for all sufficiently large $N$.
	If $\cA_N$ is an $L$-Lipschitz algorithm and $\cA_{N[K]}$ is as in Definition~\ref{d:truncated.lip.alg}, then 
	\begin{align}
		
		\max\{ 
		\|\mu(\cA_N)\|_{L^2}^2
		,\|\mu(\cA_{N[K]})\|_{L^2}^2
		\}
		 &\le C(\alpha)\,, \\
		
		\|\mu(\cA_{N[K]})\|_{L^4}^4 &\le C(\alpha,L,K)\,.
	\end{align}
	Furthermore, for $\mu_\bG(\bx)$ defined in \eqref{eq:proj-pursuit-def}, there exists $c = c(\alpha,L) > 0$ such that
	\beq
		\P\bigg(\|\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux))\|_{L^2}^2 \le C(\alpha)
			\bigg) \ge 1 - e^{-cN}\,.
	\eeq

\begin{proof}
	Throughout this proof $c > 0$ is a constant depending on $\alpha,L$ which may change line by line. Recall that we abbreviate $\bx\equiv\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)$. 
	We prove \eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.tail} first. Recalling the definition of $\fm$ from Definition~\ref{d:truncated.lip.alg}, note that
\beq
		\|\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux))\|_{L^2}^2
		=\frac{\|\fm\|^2}{M} 
		= \frac{1}{M} \bigg\|\frac{\bG \bx}{N^{1/2}}\bigg\|^2
		\le \frac{(\|\bG\|_{\op} \|\bx\|)^2}{MN} \,.
	\eeq
	By \eqref{e:confinement.subgaussian.basic.tail} from Lemma~\ref{l:confinement.subgaussian.basic}, with probability $1-e^{-cN}$ the above is
	\[
	\le \frac{C(\alpha)^2 N \cdot 4N}{MN} 
		= \frac{4C(\alpha)^2}{\alpha}\,.
	\]
	This proves \eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.tail} after adjusting $C(\alpha)$.
	Next, note that
	\[
		\|\mu(\cA_N)\|_{L^2}^2
		= \E \|\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux))\|_{L^2}^2
		= 
		\frac{\E[\|\fm\|^2]}{M} 
		\stackrel{\eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.step1}}{\le} 
		\frac{\E[(\|\bG\|_{\op} \|\bx\|)^2]}{MN} \,.
	\]
By H\"older's inequality and the bound \eqref{e:confinement.subgaussian.basic.moment} from Lemma~\ref{l:confinement.subgaussian.basic}, the above is
	\[\le
		\frac{\E [(\|\bG\|_{\op})^4]^{1/2} \E[\|\bx\|^4]^{1/2}}{MN} 
		\le \frac{C(\alpha,4)N^2}{MN} 
		= \frac{C(\alpha,4)}{\alpha}\,,
	\]
	for $C(\alpha,4)$ defined in Lemma~\ref{l:confinement.subgaussian.basic}.
This proves the first part of \eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.l2} after adjusting $C(\alpha)$. For the second part of \eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.l2}, we split into cases depending on whether $a\in S_K(\cA_N)$. Recall that the truncated algorithm $\cA_{N[K]}$ resamples the rows indexed by $S_K(\cA_N)$. If $a\notin S_K(\cA_N)$, then $\tilde{\fm}_a$ is equidistributed as $\fm_a$, so they have the same second moment. If $a\in S_K(\cA_N)$, then 
	\[\tilde{\fm}_a
		= \frac{(\bg^a, \tilde{\bx})}{N^{1/2}}\,.
	\]
where $\bg^a$ is independent of $\tilde{\bx}$, as $\cA_{N[K]}$ does not use the input $\bg^a$.
	Thus, the distribution of $\tilde{\fm}_a$ conditional on $\tilde{\bx}$ is a (one-dimensional) centered gaussian random variable with standard deviation $\|\tilde{\bx}\| / N^{1/2}$. It follows in this case that
	\[
	\E[(\tilde{\fm}_a)^2]
	= \frac{\E[\|\tilde{\bx}\|^2]}{N}=1\,.
	\]
Altogether this gives
	\[
	\|\mu(\cA_{N[K]})\|^2
	=\frac{ \E[\|\tilde{\fm}\|^2]}{M}
	\le
	\frac{ \E[\|\fm\|^2 + M]}{M}
	\le C(\alpha)+1\,.
	\]
This proves the second part of \eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.l2} after adjusting $C(\alpha)$.

Finally we turn to the proof of  \eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.l4}. Recalling the notations of Definition~\ref{d:truncated.lip.alg}, let
	\[
	\tilde{\fm}_a
	\equiv
	\fm_a\Big(\bG,\bg^{\aux+}
		= (\bg^\aux, \hbG);\cA_{N[K]}
		\Big)
	= \frac{(\bg^a,\tilde{\bx})}{N^{1/2}}\,,
	\]
where we recall that $\tilde{\bx}\equiv \cA_{N[K]}(\bG,\bg^{\aux+}))$. 
We then aim to bound
	\[
		\|\mu(\cA_{N[K]})\|_{L^4}^4
		= \E \Big[\|\mu_\bG(\cA_{N[K]}(\bG,\bg^{\aux+}))\|_{L^4}^4\Big]
		= \frac{1}{M} \sum_{a=1}^M 
		\E\Big[
		(\tilde{\fm}_a)^4\Big]\,.
	\]
To this end, we will show that there exists $C(\alpha,L,K)$ such that

	\eeq
	for all $a\in [M]$, which implies \eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.l4}.

[Corollary cor:suspension-critical-core of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] Suppose that $A$ is a primitive $m$-set of maximal active rank $m-2$ at an
integer order $q\geq0$.  Let
\[
 p_1(A)\leq\cdots\leq p_{m-2}(A)
\]
be its successive relation-birth degrees.  If $C=\Sigma_{\ell,c}A$ with
$\ell\leq q$, then $C$ has maximal active rank $m-1$, its birth-degree
multiset is
\[
 \{p_1(C),\ldots,p_{m-1}(C)\}
 =\{p_1(A),\ldots,p_{m-2}(A),\ell\},
\]
and
\begin{equation}
 \frac{\operatorname{ndiam}(C)}{\prod_{i=1}^{m-1}p_i(C)}
 =
 \frac{\operatorname{ndiam}(A)}{\prod_{i=1}^{m-2}p_i(A)}.
\end{equation}
The same ratio is preserved under any tower of visible suspensions.

[Lemma 9 of arXiv:2608.18557, 'Randomly Permuted Orthogonal Products and Fast Dimension Reduction'] Let \(X\) be a random variable and let \(\sigma,M>0\). Suppose that
	\[
	\log \E e^{\lambda X}
	\le

	\qquad

	\Pp\{|X|\ge t\}
	\le
	2\exp\left[
	-\min\left\{
	\frac{t^2}{4\sigma^2},
	\frac{t}{2M}
	\right\}
	\right].
	\]

[Definition 2 of arXiv:2608.00449, 'First-order phase transitions in the hard-core model'] \label[definition]{def:orders}
    Suppose that $G$ is an infinite graph such that a phase transition occurs at $\lambda^*>0$. 
    For $\lambda>0$ and a vertex $u$ of $G$, let $D_{G,u}(\lambda)$ be defined as 
    \[ D_{G,u}(\lambda) = \sup_{\mu,\nu}\left| \mu(u) - \nu(u) \right|, \]
    where the supremum is over all pairs of hard-core measures $\mu,\nu$ on $G$ at fugacity $\lambda$.
    Suppose also that for each vertex $u$, the one-sided limit from above $\ell_{G,u}(\lambda^*) = \lim_{\lambda\downarrow \lambda^*} D_{G,u}(\lambda)$ exists.
    
    If there exists a vertex $u\in V(G)$ such that $\ell_{G,u}(\lambda^*)>0$, then we say that $\lambda^*$ is a \emph{first-order} phase transition.
    If, on the other hand, $\ell_{G,u}(\lambda^*)=0$ for all $u\in V(G)$, then we say that $\lambda^*$ is a \emph{second-order} phase transition.
title: Definition 2 of arXiv:2608.00449

[Definition Gauge transformations of arXiv:2602.08591, 'The Yang--Mills measure on compact surfaces as a \\ universal scaling limit of lattice gau'] A \emph{gauge transformation} on $\mathbb{G}$ is a map
\[
h : \mathbb{V} \longrightarrow G.
\]
Given a discrete connection $g$ on $\mathbb{G}$, its gauge transform $g^h$ is the discrete connection defined on positively oriented edges by
\[
g^h(e) \coloneqq h(\mathrm{t}(e))\, g(e)\, h(\mathrm{s}(e))^{-1}, \qquad e \in \mathbb{E}_+,
\]
and extended to negative edges by $g^h(e_-) \coloneqq g^h(e_+)^{-1}$. 
Here $\mathrm{s}(e)$ and $\mathrm{t}(e)$ denote the source and target vertices of $e$.
title: Gauge transformations

[Theorem thm:uit-poc-kinetic of arXiv:2605.20697, 'Uniform-in-time propagation of chaos for \\ Second-Order Consensus-Based Optimization'] Let the objective function \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) satisfy
(assumption:bounded of the paper) and (assumption:lip of the paper). Let \(2r\geqslant 8\), and let the
initial configurations
\[
    (\mathcal X_0^J,\mathcal V_0^J)
    =
    \{(X_0^j,V_0^j)\}_{j=1}^J
\]
be \(J\) i.i.d. samples from a probability measure
\[
    \overline\rho_0\in\mathcal P_{2r}(\mathbb R^{2d}).
\]
Consider the second-order CBO particle system (equation eq: k-cbo of the paper) and the associated
mean-field system (equation eq: k-cbo-mfl of the paper), initialized with
\[
    \overline X_0^j=X_0^j,
    \qquad
    \overline V_0^j=V_0^j,
\]
and driven by the same Brownian motions. Assume (assump:poc of the paper).

Then there exists a finite constant \(C_{\mathrm{MFL}}>0\), independent of \(t\) and
\(J\), such that for every \(j\in[J]\),
\begin{equation}
    \sup_{t\geqslant0}
    \mathbf{E}\left[
        |X_t^j-\overline X_t^j|^2
        +
        |V_t^j-\overline V_t^j|^2
    \right]
    \leqslant
    \frac{C_{\mathrm{MFL}}}{J}.
\end{equation}
Consequently,
\begin{equation}
    \sup_{t\geqslant0}
    \mathbf{E}\left[
        \mathcal W_2^2(\mu_{X_t^J},\mu_{\overline X_t^J})
    \right]
    \leqslant
    C_{\mathrm{MFL}}J^{-1}.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Uniform-in-time propagation of chaos

a finite $p$th moment for some $p>1$. A domain $U\subseteq\mathbb{C}$
containing the origin is called \emph{$\mu$-admissible} if 
\begin{enumerate}
\item a standard planar Brownian motion $(Z_{t})_{t\geq0}$ started at $0$
exits $U$ almost surely, and 
\item the law $\mu_{U}=\mathcal{L}(\Re(Z_{\tau_{U}}))$ is an element of
$\mathfrak{M}$.
\end{enumerate}

  \end{enumerate}

Let S_n be binomial with parameters n and p, 0 < p < 1, q = 1 - p, and write k = np + x sqrt(npq). LOCAL FORM: uniformly for x in any bounded interval (indeed for |x| = o(n^{1/6})), P(S_n = k) = (2 pi n p q)^{-1/2} exp(-x^2 / 2) (1 + o(1)) as n -> infinity. INTEGRAL FORM: for fixed a < b, P(a <= (S_n - np) / sqrt(npq) <= b) -> Phi(b) - Phi(a), the standard normal probability of [a, b]; equivalently (S_n - np)/sqrt(npq) converges in distribution to N(0,1). This is the first central limit theorem (de Moivre 1733 for p = 1/2, Laplace 1812 in general); the Berry-Esseen theorem gives the rate: the Kolmogorov distance to the normal law is at most C (p^2 + q^2) / sqrt(npq) with an absolute constant C < 0.5.

body: A Banach space is a normed vector space that is complete with respect to the metric induced by its norm: every Cauchy sequence converges in the space. Examples: R^n and C^n with any norm; the space C(K) of continuous functions on a compact space K with the supremum norm; the Lebesgue spaces L^p for 1 <= p <= infinity; the sequence spaces l^p. A linear map T between normed spaces is bounded if there is a constant M with ||T(x)|| <= M ||x|| for all x; boundedness is equivalent to continuity, and the operator norm ||T|| is the least such M.
title: Banach space

[Lemma lem:rs-constant of arXiv:2602.21315, 'The Instability of all Backoff Protocols\thanks{For the purpose of Open Access, the author'] Fix a send sequence $\overline{p}$ with $p_0=1$. 
Fix a sufficiently small $\lambda \in (0,1/3)$.
Let $j$ be a sufficiently large integer. Fix an integer $\tau \ge 0$ and a tuple $\overline{a} \in (\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0})^j$.
Fix a real number $\nu$ in the range $0 \le \nu \le \nu_j^\mathrm{hi}$. 
Let $E^+$ be a constant-escape process on $[j]$ with send sequence~$\overline{p}$, start time $\tau$, end-of-step arrival rate $\nu$, and $\overline{\mathrm{arr}}_{[j]}^{E^+}(\tau) = \overline{a}$. 
Let $d$, $\varpi$, and $\theta$ be real numbers with $d\ge 0$, $\varpi\ge 1$, and $0 \le \theta < 1/(64j^2)$.
Suppose that $\overline{a}$ is a $(d,\varpi,\theta, G)$-RS-good beginning
for a positive integer~$G\leq 2$. Then with probability at least $1-j^{-2j}$, the following properties all hold.
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item For all $t$ in the range $\tau \le t \leq \tau + \varpi j^9$, $\overline{b}_{[j]}^{E^+}(t)$ is a $(d+5(t-\tau)j^3, \varpi j^{17}, \theta+3/j^4, G+1)$-RS-good beginning.
\item For all $t$ in the range $\tau+\varpi j^9 \le t \le \tau + (4/\lambda)^{2j}$, $\overline{b}_{[j]}^{E^+}(t)$ is a $(d+5(t-\tau)j^3, j^{10}, \theta+3/j^4, 1)$-RS-good beginning.
\end{enumerate}

\[
    \frac{k}{r(k)}\to C,
    \qquad
    \frac{n_k}{r(k)}\to\infty.
\]
For each $k$, let
\[
    M^{(k)}\in\{-1,0,1\}^{k\times n_k}
\]
be a deterministic matrix whose every column has exactly $d$ nonzero entries. If
$\Omega_k\subset[n_k]$
is chosen uniformly from $\binom{[n_k]}{r(k)}$,
then
\[
    s_{\min}\bigl(M^{(k)}_{\Omega_k}\bigr)=o(1)
\]
with probability $1-o(1)$. (Stated as a conjecture by the paper; open unless the paper says otherwise.)

[Thm DysonThm of arXiv:2607.22333, '\large \bf COLLISION AND NON-COLLISION FOR DIFFUSIONS ON CONFIGURATION SPACE'] The form~$(\mathcal{E},\mathcal{D}_\infty)$ is  closable and the closure is quasi-regular for every $\beta>0$. Furthermore, 
\[\mathrm{Cap}_\beta(\mathscr C)=0 \qquad \text{if and only if} \qquad  \beta \ge 1.\]
 In particular, $\mathbf P_\gamma[\tau_{\mathscr{C}}<\infty]=0$ q.e.~$\gamma$ if and only if $\beta \ge 1$. In other words, the diffusion $(\mathsf{X}^{(\beta)}_t)_{t\ge 0}$ has no collisions for q.e.~initial configuration~$\gamma$ if and only if $\beta \ge 1$. 
 For $0<\beta<1$, therefore, we have $\mathrm{Cap}_\beta(\mathscr C)>0$ and that the collision happens with a positive probability:
 $$\mathbf P_\mu[\tau_{\mathscr{C}}<\infty]>0.$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[campaign result 2026-09-14, author checked] This is a proved special case of Problem 3.11 of Takahiro Hasebe and Yuki Ueda's Large time unimodality for classical and free Brownian motions with initial distributions, ALEA 15 (2018), 353-374, DOI:10.30757/ALEA.v15-15 (arXiv:1710.08240). A probability measure is unimodal if, for some mode m, it is an atom at m plus an absolutely continuous measure whose density is nondecreasing to the left of m and nonincreasing to the right. Write boxplus for additive free convolution, the distribution of a sum of freely independent self-adjoint variables with the indicated laws, and * for classical convolution of independent real variables. Call lambda freely strongly unimodal if lambda boxplus nu is unimodal for every unimodal probability measure nu. For every t>0 the centered Cauchy distribution C_t with density t/[pi(t^2+x^2)] is not freely strongly unimodal: some unimodal nu makes nu boxplus C_t nonunimodal. The proof combines the Cauchy convolution identity with Ibragimov's characterization of classical strong unimodality by log-concavity of the density; the Cauchy density is not log-concave. This is an unrefereed campaign result.
t>0.
The classical Ibragimov characterization for nondegenerate absolutely continuous laws.

The whole point is an identity that is special to the Cauchy family. Its Cauchy transform is
$G_{C_t}(z) = 1/(z+it)$ on the upper half plane, so $K_{C_t}(w) = 1/w - it$ and the $R$-transform is the
constant $R_{C_t}(w) = -it$. Free convolution adds $R$-transforms, so for any $\mu$,
$$K_{\mu\boxplus C_t}(w) = K_\mu(w) - it \quad\Longrightarrow\quad G_{\mu\boxplus C_t}(z) = G_\mu(z+it).$$
On the other side, the density of $\mu * C_t$ at $x$ is the Poisson integral
$\tfrac1\pi\int t\,d\mu(y)/((x-y)^2+t^2) = -\tfrac1\pi\operatorname{Im}G_\mu(x+it)$, so
$G_{\mu*C_t}(z) = G_\mu(z+it)$ as well. Hence
$$\mu \boxplus C_t \ = \ \mu * C_t \qquad\text{for every } \mu \text{ and every } t>0,$$
the free and classical convolutions with a Cauchy law coinciding.

Now the Proposition. The Cauchy density is not log-concave, so by Ibragimov's characterisation of
classically strongly unimodal laws, $C_t$ is not strongly unimodal: there is a unimodal $\nu$ with
$\nu * C_t$ not unimodal. By the identity, $\nu \boxplus C_t = \nu * C_t$ is not unimodal either, and
$\nu$ is unimodal, so $C_t$ is not freely strongly unimodal. $\blacksquare$","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:41d53089fc9154dfc68427cb689fc659cab94c6fae196dceb869ccf188d76c60","revision_digest":"sha256:df81d86c41a2e859c5a707fc5ae34d83a64ca8c89b34f2c04e48ecc49cc1f09a","source_id":"doi:10.30757/ALEA.v15-15","source_revision":"problem source: ALEA 15 (2018), 353-374; own campaign record: 2026-09-14","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Theorem thm:markovian-2bsde of arXiv:2608.16119, 'Fully nonlinear parabolic equations under a fixed reference diffusion: weighted \texorpdfs'] Let $w$ be a regular weight of order $\alpha$, where $0\leq\alpha<1$.  Assume
Assumptions~(ass:reference-diffusion of the paper),
(ass:drift-multiplier of the paper), (ass:lipschitz-driver of the paper), and

$u^*$ and its source $F^*=F_{u^*}$ determine a unique regular fixed-reference
Markovian 2BSDE solution in the sense of
Definition~(def:regular-markovian-2bsde of the paper), namely

 u=u^*,\qquad p=D_xu^*,\qquad H=D_x^2u^*,\qquad
 \mathfrak A_t=-\int_0^t\mathfrak g[u^*,F^*](s,X_s)\,\mathrm d s.
\end{equation*}

consequences of the two dynamics.

[Corollary cor:spectral-sandwich of arXiv:2606.27073, 'Retention Profiles and KL Contraction Bounds in Finite Markov Chains'] Combining Theorems~(thm:spectral-upper of the paper) and~(thm:spectral-lower of the paper),
for any reversible chain:
\[
  \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=2}^n\lambda_i^2
  - \frac{1}{6}\sum_x\pi(x)\,T_3(x)
  \;\le\;
  I(X_0;X_1)
  \;\le\;
  \sum_{i=2}^n\lambda_i^2.
\]
When $\max_{x,y}|g(x,y)|\le C$ for a constant $C$ independent of $n$, one
has $\sum_x\pi(x)T_3(x) \le C\sum_{i\ge 2}\lambda_i^2$, so the lower bound
simplifies to
$I(X_0;X_1) \ge (1/2 - C/6)\sum_{i\ge 2}\lambda_i^2$,
which is positive when $C < 3$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:92dc99dd38187032ea54bae2ceacb02d5e5898e7136f2355e14dcdba298baf54","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/92/92dc99dd38187032ea54bae2ceacb02d5e5898e7136f2355e14dcdba298baf54.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:e46b93d5bf149b2fff836bcc7c52bd70b1d1130f4c72842e2b881bd3fbe0cbc1","bundle_entry_key":"t309-c04","bundle_id":"population.t309-equilateral-ddpm-symmetry-breaking-drafts","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"probability, score matching, Gaussian mixture learning","draft":"w721/bundle_001.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.learning:known-plane-equilateral-gaussian-empirical-ddpm-orbit-augmentation","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# T309: empirical DDPM GD for a restricted equilateral family

T309-w721-C04 v1. Status: proof (unaudited). No novelty claim. This is a restricted instance of Target 2, not its general solution.

## Precise statement and extra information used

Fix an absolute R>=1, which may be chosen as a large constant. In a known two-dimensional plane P in R^d, consider the equal-weight mixtures

    q_phi = (1/3) sum_{j=0}^2 N(R R_phi u_j,I_d),

where u_j are unit equilateral vectors and phi is unknown. The centroid is known to be zero; the plane, radius, equal weights, and component covariance are known. The component separation is sqrt(3) R. The orientation is the only unknown geometric parameter of this family.

There is a fixed absolute noise level t>0 (depending on the fixed R) and a procedure using full ordinary GD on the three means in the Shah--Chen--Klivans Eq. (9) student, on an orbit-augmented empirical DDPM objective, such that for every d>=2 and 0<epsilon<1 it returns a mixture within TV epsilon of q_phi with probability at least 2/3. Its sample size and real-arithmetic runtime are polynomial in d and 1/epsilon. A complete bit-complexity implementation is not asserted. The initialization is an equilateral triple of noisy radius a=R exp(-t) with a uniform random angle in P. It is independent of phi and of the samples, and it need not be a componentwise warm start.

This theorem does NOT cover an arbitrary i.i.d. Gaussian initialization, unknown plane or radius, unequal weights, nonequilateral centers, or unaugmented empirical DDPM GD. The use of a finite symmetry orbit of each sample is part of the stated training procedure.

## 1. The algorithm and exact empirical invariance

Choose a fixed positive absolute a small enough for C03, with a<R, and set t=log(R/a). Put sigma=sqrt(1-exp(-2t))>0. Given independent pairs (X_i,Z_i), where X_i~q_phi and Z_i~N(0,I_d), let Y_i=exp(-t) X_i+sigma Z_i.

Let Q rotate P by 2pi/3 and fix P-perpendicular. Let S fix P and negate P-perpendicular. The finite orthogonal group G generated by Q and S has order at most six (for d=2, S is the identity and the order is three). Define the empirical objective

    Lhat(m)=(1/(n |G|)) sum_i sum_{g in G}
               ||s_m(g Y_i)+g Z_i/sigma||^2.                     (1)

Initialize m_j=a R_Theta u_j in P, with Theta uniform, independently of all data and noise. Perform equal-step Euclidean GD on all three m_j using (1), for the deterministic number of steps specified below. Divide the final means by exp(-t), and return their equal-weight identity-covariance Gaussian mixture.

Because the augmented sample multiset is exactly invariant under G, (1) has the same rotation and perpendicular-reflection invariances as the population objective. Label-permutation invariance also holds. The fixed-point argument of C02 therefore shows that every empirical GD iterate is exactly of the form

    m_j=Q^j z,   z in P.                                          (2)

This is a conclusion about ordinary updates in the unrestricted mean space. No projection or constrained optimizer is inserted. The dependence among augmented samples within one orbit causes no problem: the n underlying pairs remain independent, and the orbit average is one function of each independent pair.

Every g preserves the joint law of (X_i,Z_i), because the teacher has the specified symmetry and the denoising noise is isotropic and independent. Thus E Lhat=Lpop. In particular the expected augmented objective is exactly the original DDPM population objective, up to the same score-risk constant as before.

## 2. A uniform gradient estimate with polynomial sample complexity

On the invariant space (2), regard the loss as a function of the two planar coordinates z, and write ell(z,W_i) for the orbit-averaged single-pair loss. Parameter-independent terms may be subtracted. Let the parameter domain D be the planar ball ||z||<=2a. Its population gradient is the gradient of the loss studied in C03, including the threefold parameterization factor.

There is a nonnegative random envelope M(W) with finite second moment, whose distribution and moments are independent of d, satisfying

    sup_{z in D} (||grad_z ell(z,W)||+||Hess_z ell(z,W)||) <= M(W). (3)

To see this explicitly, for planar means the perpendicular part of every student score is -Y_perpendicular. Its contribution to the restricted loss is independent of z. The only derivatives are those of

    b_z(y)=sum_j softmax_j(y dot Q^j z-||z||^2/2) Q^j z,

where y=projection_P Y. The common norm term cancels; differentiating softmax once or twice gives polynomials in y and bounded means, multiplied by products of weights in [0,1]. The planar residual in the DDPM loss is bounded by C(1+||y||+||projection_P Z||/sigma). Consequently (3) holds, for example, with

    M(W)=C(1+||projection_P Y||+||projection_P Z||)^6,

where C depends only on fixed a,t. The projected variables are a two-dimensional Gaussian mixture and a two-dimensional Gaussian, jointly correlated but with every fixed polynomial moment finite. In particular E M^2<infinity independently of d. No concentration statement here requires those two projections to be independent.

Here is an elementary quantitative uniform law, avoiding an unproved concentration assertion. Choose a deterministic constant K>1+E M. Chebyshev's inequality makes (1/n)sum_i M(W_i)<=2K with probability at least 1-1/48 for all sufficiently large n bounded by an absolute constant. On this event the empirical gradient is 2K-Lipschitz, while the population gradient is K-Lipschitz by (3). For 0<tau<1, choose a net of D of mesh tau/(12K); its cardinality is at most C tau^(-2), since D is a ball in two dimensions. At each net point and for each of the two gradient coordinates, Chebyshev's inequality, using (3), gives

    P(|empirical coordinate-population coordinate|>tau/4)
         <= C/(n tau^2).

The union bound over the net and both coordinates is at most C/(n tau^4). Take n>=C_0 tau^(-4) with C_0 large enough that this is at most 1/48 and also the envelope-average failure is at most 1/48. At every net point the Euclidean gradient error is at most sqrt(2) tau/4<tau/2. Moving to the nearest net point changes the error by at most 3K tau/(12K)=tau/4. Therefore, with probability at least 23/24,

    sup_{z in D} ||grad_z Lhat-grad_z Lpop|| <= tau.                (4)

The loose failure bound 23/24 includes both failures. The estimate requires n polynomial in 1/tau and is uniform in d. It is stated for a fixed training set reused at all GD steps, so it already handles adaptive iterates; no false multiplication of conditional probabilities is involved.

## 3. Finite-horizon coupling is polynomial at a fixed high-noise radius

Use a fixed step h>0 meeting C03, for instance h=h_0/(2a^2). Because a is fixed, h is an absolute constant for this family. Let delta=pi/36<1/10. Under a uniform angle, the population initialization lies at least delta from all three unstable angles with probability 11/12.

For those angles, C03 supplies a deterministic horizon

    T<=C_1(1+log(1/epsilon))                                      (5)

at which the population noisy means are within a epsilon/(10R) of the corresponding teacher means. Constants absorb the prescribed fixed R and a. If necessary increase T to at least one and choose the population accuracy slightly smaller than the displayed tolerance.

The population iterates remain within 1/10 of radius a. On the whole ball D the restricted population gradient has a finite Lipschitz constant L, independent of d. This follows either directly by the envelope (3) or by smoothness and the exact two-dimensional reduction. No sharp a-dependent Hessian estimate is needed here since a is fixed.

Under the tied parameterization (2), a full mean GD step is a z-update of size h/3: the metric is sum_j ||d(Q^j z)||^2=3||dz||^2. Put B=1+(h/3)L>=1, and choose

    tau=min(1/2, a epsilon/(100 R h T B^T)).                       (6)

On event (4), a population iterate z_k and an empirical iterate zhat_k with the same initialization obey, as long as both stay in D,

    ||zhat_{k+1}-z_{k+1}||
       <= B||zhat_k-z_k||+(h/3)tau.

Starting with difference zero, induction bounds every difference through T by

    (h/3) tau T B^T <= a epsilon/(300R).                          (7)

This also proves the domain condition in the induction: population radii are in [0.9a,1.1a] and the bound in (7) is less than a/100. Thus every empirical iterate is strictly inside D. Since D is convex, the Lipschitz estimate applies to the segment between the two iterates. The induction is not assuming its own conclusion.

Although B^T is exponential in T, (5) implies

    B^T <= C_2 epsilon^(-C_1 log B).

The exponent is an absolute constant for this fixed family. Hence tau^(-1), the sample size n>=C_0 tau^(-4), and the number of arithmetic operations are all polynomial in 1/epsilon and d. Factors of T contribute only powers of 1+log(1/epsilon). This argument does not give a polynomial joint bound when a is an additional vanishing parameter; fixing a before epsilon is essential.

Combining (7) with the population endpoint gives matched noisy-mean error less than a epsilon/(2R). Rescaling by R/a gives matched original-mean error less than epsilon/2.

## 4. Success probability and TV conversion

The good initial-angle event has probability 11/12, and (4) has probability at least 23/24. Their simultaneous probability is at least 7/8 by the union bound, exceeding 2/3. This does not depend on assuming independence between a sample-dependent iterate and its training set.

For matching means mu_j and muhat_j with identity covariance, convexity of TV under mixtures and Pinsker's inequality give

    TV((1/3)sum_j N(mu_j,I),(1/3)sum_j N(muhat_j,I))
       <= (1/3)sum_j ||mu_j-muhat_j||/2.

The last inequality uses KL(N(mu,I)||N(muhat,I))=||mu-muhat||^2/2. Thus the mean-error endpoint is more than enough for TV epsilon. No diffusion sampling-discretization guarantee is needed: the returned law is an explicit three-Gaussian mixture.

## 5. Arithmetic and implementation model

This is a real-arithmetic statement with exponential evaluations, as in the population gradient formulas. A finite-precision implementation would need to evaluate the two-coordinate equivariant gradient with an error budget no larger than tau/2 and preserve the known symmetry through its representation. The same finite-horizon coupling would control that error. A complete bit-complexity implementation and its exact symmetry representation are not supplied here; no bounded-precision SQ conclusion follows from this result as written.

## What remains unpaid

The theorem is deliberately confined to a family whose symmetry is known before looking at the samples. It does not estimate the plane or radius. An approximate plane or a generic three-vector initialization no longer lies in the exact fixed-point subspace; the resulting extra directions need a new stability argument. Finite orbit augmentation has also changed the empirical training procedure and must be retained in the claim. The general Target 2 asks for more than this result supplies.

Load-bearing hypotheses: (i) U(t) is unitary for every t ∈ ℝ and satisfies the group law on all of ℝ; (ii) t ↦ U(t)x is continuous (weak continuity or, on a separable space, weak measurability suffices, but some regularity is required); (iii) the generator is self-adjoint. What fails. Without any continuity: pick a discontinuous additive function φ: ℝ → ℝ (a Hamel basis construction) and set H = ℂ, U(t) = e^{iφ(t)}. This is a one-parameter group of unitaries with U(0) = 1, but φ is non-measurable and unbounded on every interval, so U(t) is not of the form e^{ita} for any real a; no generator exists. Hence 'one-parameter unitary group' without a continuity hypothesis carries no spectral information. Overshooting in the other direction: if one assumes t ↦ U(t) is continuous in operator norm, then the generator is necessarily bounded, so norm continuity is the wrong hypothesis for Schrodinger evolutions, where A is unbounded. With a symmetric but not self-adjoint generator: on L²(0, ∞) the right translation semigroup (T(t)f)(x) = f(x − t) for x > t, 0 for x ≤ t, is a C_0-semigroup of isometries that is not a group (T(t) is not surjective), and its generator is A = −d/dx on {f ∈ H¹(0, ∞) : f(0) = 0}, i.e. A = −iS with S = −i d/dx closed and symmetric with deficiency indices (1, 0). There is no unitary group whose generator extends S, so exponentiating a symmetric operator to 'e^{itS}' is not legitimate: only self-adjointness (or essential self-adjointness followed by taking the closure) licenses the unitary group. Audit rule: in quantum dynamics arguments, check that the Hamiltonian has been shown self-adjoint on a stated domain before using e^{itH}, unitarity, conservation of norm, or invariance of D(H).

[Dfn 222 (Lipschitz algorithms) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For $\cA$ as in \eqref{eq:algorithms-as-maps},
we say that $\cA$ is an \textbf{$L$-Lipschitz algorithm} if it satisfies the following two conditions:
\begin{enumerate}[(a)]\item 
$\cA$ defines an $L$-Lipschitz mapping, that is,
    \[
        \Big\|\cA(\bG,\bg^{\aux})-\cA(\bG',(\bg')^{\aux})\Big\| 
        \le L \Big\|(\bG,\bg^{\aux}) - (\bG',(\bg')^{\aux})\Big\|\,,
    \]
where $\|\cdot\|$ always refers to Euclidean norm unless specifically indicated otherwise.
    \item 
    We have 
    $\bbE[\|\cA(\bG,\bg^{\aux})\|^2] = N$.
\end{enumerate} We say $\cA$ is a \textbf{deterministic $L$-Lipschitz algorithm} if it satisfies the above conditions with $\cA=\cA(\bG)$, i.e., without dependence on any auxiliary randomness $\bg^\aux$.

body: In statistics, the Lehmann–Scheffé theorem provides sufficient conditions for the existence of a best unbiased estimator in a statistical model. The theorem states that any unbiased estimator for a quantity that depends on the data only through a complete, sufficient statistic is the unique uniformly minimum-variance unbiased estimator (UMVUE) of that quantity. The Lehmann–Scheffé theorem is named after Erich Leo Lehmann and Henry Scheffé, given their two early papers.
title: Lehmann–Scheffé theorem

For each0<=t<=u<=v<=T, require the conditional laws of i_u and i_v given i_0,...,i_(t-1) to agree almost surely. Sample (i_0,...,i_T) from P and put alpha=eta*beta*(1-eta*beta/4), so0<alpha<1. Then E f_(i_T)(w_T)<=(e*T)^alpha * E[(1/(T+1))*sum_(t=0)^T f_(i_t)(w_t)]. The hypothesis is equality of conditional future marginals, not independence of future indices. For dependent sampling the left side is the loss on the sampled final task, and need not equal the full-population risk.

body:
Let f be a C^1 diffeomorphism of a compact Riemannian manifold M and mu an f-invariant Borel probability measure. Since M is compact, log of the norm of Df and of Df^{-1} are bounded, hence integrable, so Oseledets' multiplicative ergodic theorem applies: for mu-a.e. x there are finitely many numbers lambda_1(x) > lambda_2(x) > ... > lambda_{k(x)}(x) (the LYAPUNOV EXPONENTS at x) and a Df-invariant splitting of the tangent space

  T_x M = E_1(x) + ... + E_{k(x)}(x),   Df_x E_i(x) = E_i(f x),

such that for every nonzero v in E_i(x) the limit of (1/n) log |Df^n_x v| as n -> +-infinity exists and equals lambda_i(x). The functions x -> lambda_i(x), the multiplicities dim E_i(x), and the subspaces are measurable and f-invariant; if mu is ergodic they are constant almost everywhere. The splitting is in general only MEASURABLE, not continuous, and the convergence is not uniform in x.

Two structural facts that every application uses. (1) TEMPEREDNESS: any measurable positive function that is subexponential along orbits -- such as the angle between the Oseledets subspaces, or the norm of the change to Lyapunov (adapted) coordinates -- can be chosen tempered, meaning (1/n) log of its value at f^n x tends to 0; this is what lets one build Lyapunov charts in which Df is uniformly contracting on the negative-exponent bundle at the cost of a chart size that shrinks subexponentially along the orbit. (2) PESIN BLOCKS: for each l one collects the points where the Oseledets estimates hold with uniform constants depending on l; the resulting sets Lambda_l are COMPACT (after discarding a null set and restricting the subbundles continuously), increase in l, exhaust a full-measure set, and carry uniform hyperbolic-like estimates. They are NOT f-invariant -- an orbit wanders between blocks -- which is exactly why non-uniformly hyperbolic statements are local-and-measurable rather than uniform.

A point x is called (non-uniformly) hyperbolic when no exponent at x is zero; the stable bundle E^s(x) is the sum of the E_i(x) with lambda_i(x) < 0 and the unstable bundle the sum of those with lambda_i(x) > 0. Zero exponents are the obstruction: nothing in this framework says anything about directions with zero exponent.
M is a compact Riemannian manifold and f a C^1 diffeomorphism of M
mu is an f-invariant Borel probability measure (compactness makes the Oseledets integrability condition automatic)
the exponents, multiplicities and subspaces are measurable and f-invariant; constant a.e. when mu is ergodic
the Oseledets splitting is measurable, generally not continuous, and the Pesin blocks are not invariant

DRAFT AUDIT CONCEPT; independent referee pending. For real t and z in C, set r=|z| and F_t(z)=-t*r^2+r^(5/2)-Re(z^3)+r^4. Rotation by 2pi/3 and conjugation preserve F_t, giving the standard S3 action. The cubic polynomial term has a fixed nonzero coefficient. Put c=1-2/(3sqrt(3))>0; 1-s+s^3>=c for s>=0 gives F_t>=-t*r^2+c*r^(5/2). Thus zero is the unique global minimizer for t<=0. For t>0, small positive real z has negative value, and coercivity gives nonzero minimizers with radius at most (t/c)^2. All minimizers approach zero as t decreases to zero. This is a toy variational counterexample to the bare invariant-cubic criterion, not a lattice Potts model. The fractional term prevents a uniform quartic Taylor remainder.

[Lemma l:boundedness_p_extrapolated_spaces of arXiv:2607.15140, 'On the absence of blow-up in the 3D Navier-Stokes equations with transport noise'] Let $B$ be a ball in ${\mathbb R}^d$. The Helmholtz projection $\mathbb{P}_{B}$ can be uniquely extended as a bounded linear operator $\mathbb{P}_{-1,B}$ from $\mathscr{X}_{-1}^{\mathrm{Dir}}(B;{\mathbb R}^d)$ into $\mathscr{X}^{\mathrm{Sto}}_{-1}(B)$. In particular,
$$
\mathbb{P}_{-\sigma,B}\stackrel{{\rm def}}{=}
\mathbb{P}_{-1,B}|_{\mathscr{X}_{-\sigma}^{\mathrm{Dir}}(B;{\mathbb R}^d)} : \mathscr{X}_{-\sigma}^{\mathrm{Dir}}(B;{\mathbb R}^d)\to \mathscr{X}_{-\sigma}^{\mathrm{Sto}}(B) 
$$
boundedly for all $ \sigma \in [0,1]$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Extrapolated Helmholtz projection

[Definition Packing  measure \cite{tricot1982two} of arXiv:2512.06984, 'Infinite Dimensional Multifractal Analysis of the Wiener measure'] For every subset $ E $ of $X$ endowed with the same metric $d$, the \emph{packing  $h$-measure} of $E$ is defined by:

[Lemma 6 of arXiv:2608.24552, 'Asymptotic Rounding Laws for Optimal Thresholds in Secretary Problems'] Fix \(a\geq0\). Uniformly when \(x=r/n\) ranges over a compact subinterval
of \((0,1)\),
\begin{equation}
D_{n,a}(r)
=
nI_a(r/n)+J_a(r/n)+O(n^{-1}),
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}
I_a(x)
:=
\int_x^1
y^{a-1}
\left(
\log\frac{y}{x}-1
\right)
\,dy
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
J_a(x)
:=
\frac12
\left(
\log\frac1x-1-x^{a-1}
\right)
+
\frac{1}{2x}
\int_x^1 y^{a-1}\,dy
-
\frac12
\int_x^1 y^{a-2}\,dy.
\end{equation}
title: Lemma 6 of arXiv:2608.24552

body: A graph G = (V, E) is bipartite if the vertex set V can be partitioned into two disjoint sets X and Y, V = X union Y, X intersect Y = empty set, such that every edge in E has one endpoint in X and one endpoint in Y; no edge lies entirely within X or entirely within Y. Equivalently, G is bipartite if and only if it contains no cycle of odd length. [standard, e.g. Diestel, Graph Theory]
title: Bipartite Graph

body: [Defn Fine slope of arXiv:2608.30031, 'Ziggurats, taut foliations, and contact structures'] A \textbf{(finite) fine slope} is a pair $(s,\heartsuit)$ (usually written $s^\heartsuit$), where $s\in \mathbb{R}$ and $\heartsuit \in \{\sharp,\flat,\natural,\dagger\}$. We say that $s$ is the underlying \textbf{coarse slope} of $s^\heartsuit$. If $\mathcal{F}$ is a foliation on $M$, its \textbf{fine (boundary) multislope} is the tuple $$\bm{\fineslope}(\mathcal{F}):=(\fineslope(\partial_1\mathcal{F}),\dots,\fineslope(\partial_n\mathcal{F})).$$
title: Fine slope

body:
[Thm Result1 of arXiv:2609.01350, 'New classes of trace-form permutation polynomials and their compositional inverses'] Let $q=2^m$ with $m>1$ and let $c_1,c_2,c_3,\gamma\in\mathbb F_{q^2}$. Then
\[
  f_1(x)=x+\gamma{\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}\!\bigl(c_1x+c_2x^2+c_3x^3+x^{q+2}\bigr)
\]
is a permutation polynomial of $\mathbb F_{q^2}$ if and only if one of the following
holds:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item $\gamma=0$;
  \item $\gamma\in\mathbb F_q^{*}$, $c_3=1$, ${\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(c_2)\neq0$ and ${\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(c_1)=\gamma^{-1}$;
  \item $\gamma\in\mathbb F_q^{*}$, $c_3=1$, ${\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(c_2)=0$ and ${\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(c_1)\neq\gamma^{-1}$;
  \item $\gamma\in\mathbb F_{q^2}\setminus\mathbb F_q$, $m$ is odd, and, with
        $A:={\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(c_3\gamma^3+\gamma^{q+2})$,
        \[
          A\neq0,\qquad
          {\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(\gamma^2)+(c_3\gamma+\gamma^{q})^{q+1}=0,\qquad
          A\bigl(1+{\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(c_1\gamma)\bigr)+{\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(c_2^2\gamma^4)=0 .
        \]
\end{enumerate}

[Lemma lem:addparallel of arXiv:2608.30973, 'Pseudo-Anosov flow and dynamics on guts'] Let \((N,N_{+},N_{-},\gamma_{N})\) be a sutured manifold and let \(\psi\) be a tight semiflow on \(N\).
Let \(K\) be a connected component of \(N_{+}\), and endow \(K\times I\) with the product sutured structure and product flow.
Then attaching \(K\times \{0\}\) to \(N_{+}\) gives a semiflow on \(N\cup_{N_{+}} K\times I\)  which is orbit equivalent to \(N\).
Similar result holds for components of \(N_{-}\).

Let \(T\) be a product sutured manifold and homeomorphic to a solid torus.
Endow \(T\) with the product flow. Choose a glue map \(f:\mu\to \gamma\) which maps a suture \(\mu\) of \(T\) to a sutured annulus \(\gamma\) of \(N\) homeomorphically and preserving flow segments.
Then gluing \(T\) to \(N\) by \(f\) gives a semiflow on \(N\cup_{f}T\) which is orbit equivalent to \(N\). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma lem:addparallel of arXiv:2608.30973

[Theorem 4 of arXiv:2506.10494, 'Geometric Jensen-Shannon Divergence Between Gaussian Measures On Hilbert Space'] [\textbf{Geometric interpolation of two equivalent Gaussian measures on Hilbert space}]
		
		Let $\mu_i = \Ncal(m_i, C_i) \in \Gauss(\Hcal, \mu_{*})$, $i=0,1$, where
		$C_i = C_{*}^{1/2}(I-S_i)C_{*}^{1/2}$, $S_i \in \SymHS(\Hcal)_{<I}$. Let the corresponding 
		Radon-Nikodym densities with respect to $\mu_{*}$ be denoted by $p_i = \frac{d\mu_i}{d\mu_{*}}$. Then
		for $\alpha \in [0,1]$,
		\begin{align}
			(p_0p_1)^{G}_{\alpha}(x) = \frac{d\mu_{\alpha}}{d\mu_{*}},
			
			
		\end{align}
		where $\mu_{\alpha} = \Ncal(m_{\alpha}, C_{\alpha}) \in \Gauss(\Hcal,\mu_{*})$, $C_{\alpha} = C_{*}^{1/2}(I-S_{\alpha})C_{*}^{1/2}$, with
		\begin{align}
			S_{\alpha} &= I - [(1-\alpha)(I-S_0)^{-1} + \alpha (I-S_1)^{-1}]^{-1} \in \SymHS(\Hcal)_{< I},
			
			\\
			C_{\alpha} &= C_{*}^{1/2} [(1-\alpha)(I-S_0)^{-1} + \alpha (I-S_1)^{-1}]^{-1}C_{*}^{1/2},
			
			\\
			m_{\alpha} &= m_{*} + C_{*}^{1/2}(I-S_{\alpha})[(1-\alpha)(I-S_0)^{-1}C_{*}^{-1/2}(m_0 - m_{*}) 
			\nonumber
			\\
			&\quad \quad \quad \quad \quad \quad \quad + \alpha(I-S_1)^{-1}C_{*}^{-1/2}(m_1 - m_{*})].
			
		\end{align}
	The normalizing factor is given by
	\begin{align}
		&Z_{\alpha}^G(p_0:p_1)
		\nonumber
		= 
		\int_{\Hcal}p_0^{1-\alpha}(x)p_1^{\alpha}(x) d\mu_{*}(x)
		\\
		&=\det[(1-\alpha)(I+A)^{-\alpha} + \alpha (I+A)^{1-\alpha}]^{-1/2}
		\nonumber
		\\
		& \quad \times \exp\left[-\frac{1-\alpha}{2}||(I-S_0)^{-1/2}C_{*}^{-1/2}(m_0 - m_{*})||^2\right]
		\nonumber
		\\
		& \quad \times 
		\exp\left[-\frac{\alpha}{2}||(I-S_1)^{-1/2}C_{*}^{-1/2}(m_1 - m_{*})||^2\right]
		\nonumber
		\\
		& \quad \times \exp\left(\frac{1}{2}||(I-S_{\alpha})^{-1/2}C_{*}^{-1/2}(m_{\alpha} - m_{*})||^2\right).
		
	\end{align}
		Here $I + A = (I-S_1)^{-1/2}(I-S_0)(I-S_1)^{-1/2} > 0$, with $A =(I-S_1)^{-1/2}(S_1-S_0)(I-S_1)^{-1/2} \in \Sym(\Hcal)\cap \HS(\Hcal).$
		In particular, for $S_0, S_1 \in \SymTr(\Hcal)_{< I}$,
		\begin{align}
			(p_0p_1)^{G}_{\alpha}(x) &	=[\det(I-S_{\alpha})]^{-1/2}
			\nonumber
			\\
			& \quad \times \exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2}\la C_{*}^{-1/2}(x-m_{*}), S_{\alpha}(I-S_{\alpha})^{-1}C_{*}^{-1/2}(x-m_{*})\ra \right\}
			\nonumber
			\\
			&\quad \times \exp(\la C_{*}^{-1/2}(x-m_{*}), (I-S_{\alpha})^{-1}C_{*}^{-1/2}(m_{\alpha} - m_{*})\ra)
			\nonumber
			\\
			&\quad \times \exp\left[-\frac{1}{2}||(I-S_{\alpha})^{-1/2}C_{*}^{-1/2}(m_{\alpha} - m_{*})||^2\right].
			
		\end{align}
Let $P_N = \sum_{k=1}^Ne_k \otimes e_k$, $N \in \Nbb$, be the orthogonal projection onto the $N$-dimensional subspace of $\Hcal$ spanned
by $\{e_k\}_{k=1}^N$, where $\{e_k\}_{k=1}^{\infty}$ are the orthonormal eigenvectors of $C_{*}$.
In the expression in Eq.\eqref{equation:geometric-interpolation-Gaussian-S-Tr},
\begin{align}
	&\la C_{*}^{-1/2}(x-m_{*}), S_{\alpha}(I-S_{\alpha})^{-1}C_{*}^{-1/2}(x-m_{*})\ra 
	\nonumber
	\\
	& \doteq \lim_{N \approach \infty} \la C_{*}^{-1/2}P_N(x-m_{*}), S_{\alpha}(I-S_{\alpha})^{-1}C_{*}^{-1/2}P_N(x-m_{*})\ra 
	\\
	&
	\la C_{*}^{-1/2}(x-m_{*}), (I-S_{\alpha})^{-1}C_{*}^{-1/2}(m_{\alpha} - m_{*})\ra 
	\nonumber
	\\
	&\doteq \lim_{N \approach \infty} \la C_{*}^{-1/2}P_N(x-m_{*}), (I-S_{*})^{-1}C_{*}^{-1/2}(m_{\alpha} - m_{*})\ra,
\end{align}
with the limits being in the 

$\Lcal^2(\Hcal, \mu_{*})$ sense. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Coro 27 of arXiv:2609.03188, 'Some generalizations of Oort's conjecture'] Let $\lambda^{(k)}$ be as above.
If $g$ is even, then
$$
\Pi(\lambda^{(k)})=
\begin{cases}
\Pi\setminus\{\alpha_{\frac{g}{2}}\}&\text{if $1\leq k<\frac{g}{2}$},\\
\Pi\setminus\{\alpha_0,\alpha_g\}&\text{if $k=\frac{g}{2}$}.
\end{cases}
$$
If $g$ is odd, then
$$
\Pi(\lambda^{(k)})=
\begin{cases}
\Pi\setminus\{\alpha_0,\alpha_g\}&\text{if $1\leq k<\frac{g-1}{2}$},\\
\Pi\setminus\{\alpha_{\frac{g-1}{2}},\alpha_{\frac{g+1}{2}}\}&\text{if $k=\frac{g-1}{2}$}.
\end{cases}
$$
In either case, we have
$$\Irr\bigl(X_\mu(\tau)'\bigr)=\bigl\{j\overline{X_\mu^{\lambda^{(k)}}(\tau)}\mid 1\leq k\leq\left\lfloor\tfrac{g}{2}\right\rfloor,\ j\in\J/(\J\cap P_{\Pi(\lambda^{(k)})})\bigr\}.$$

body:
[Theorem thm:stexist of arXiv:2507.08757, 'Strong existence and uniqueness of the tilt-indexed Busemann process in the planar corner '] There exists a stochastic process 
\begin{align}
    \bigl(B^{h{\scaleobj{0.8}{\boxempty}}}(x,y) : x,y\in\mathbb{Z}^2,\, h \in \mathcal{H},\, {\scaleobj{0.9}{\boxempty}} \in \{+,-\}\bigr)
\end{align}
on $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})$ with the following properties:
\begin{enumerate}  [label={\rm(\alph*)}, ref={\rm\alph*}]   \itemsep=3pt
\item \textup{(}No $\pm$ distinction at fixed $h$\textup{)} For each $h \in \mathcal{H}$, 
\[
\mathbb{P}\{B^{h-}= B^{h+}\}=1.
\]
When $B^{h-}(\omega) = B^{h+}(\omega)$, call the common cocycle $B^h(\omega)$.
\item \textup{(}Forward measurable Busemann function\textup{)} For each $h\in \mathcal{H}, B^h \in \mathcal K_c^+$.
\item \textup{(}Mean $-h$\textup{)} For each $h \in \mathcal{H}$ and $i\in\{1,2\}$, $\mathbb{E}[B^h(0,e_i)] = -h \cdot e_i.$
\item \textup{(}Monotonicity\textup{)} For $h,h'\in \mathcal{H}$ with $h \cdot e_1 \leq h' \cdot e_1$, all $x \in \mathbb{Z}^2$, and $\mathbb{P}$ almost every $\omega$
\[ 
    B^{h-}(x,x+e_1) \geq  B^{h+}(x,x+e_1) \geq  B^{h'-}(x,x+e_1) \geq  B^{h'-}(x,x+e_1)  
\]
and
\[ 
    B^{h-}(x,x+e_2) \leq  B^{h+}(x,x+e_2) \leq  B^{h'-}(x,x+e_2) \leq  B^{h'-}(x,x+e_2).
\]
\item \textup{(}Left-/right-continuity\textup{)} For $\mathbb{P}$-almost all $\omega$, all $h\in \mathcal{H}$, and all $x,y\in\mathbb{Z}^2$,
\begin{equation*}\begin{aligned}
B^{h-}(x,y) = \lim_{\substack{\mathcal{H}\hspace{0.5pt}\hspace{0.5pt}\ni\hspace{0.5pt} \hspace{0.5pt} h' \to h\\ h'\cdot e_1 \nearrow h \cdot e_1}} B^{h\pm}(x,y) \,\text{ and }\, B^{h-}(x,y) = \lim_{\substack{\mathcal{H}\hspace{0.5pt}\hspace{0.5pt}\ni\hspace{0.5pt} \hspace{0.5pt} h' \to h\\ h'\cdot e_1 \searrow h \cdot e_1}} B^{h\pm}(x,y).
\end{aligned}\end{equation*}
\end{enumerate}
Moreover, this process is unique in the sense that any two processes satisfying the above conditions are equal almost surely. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] Assuming that a random variable $f:X\to\mathbb R$ has as law 
$$\mu=\sum_i\lambda_i\delta_{x_i}\quad,\quad x_1<\ldots<x_N\quad,\quad\lambda_i>0,\ \sum_i\lambda_i=1$$
its cumulative distribution function is the following step function:
$$F(x)=\begin{cases}
0&:\ x\in(-\infty,x_1]\\
\lambda_1&:\ x\in(x_1,x_2]\\
\lambda_1+\lambda_2&:\ x\in(x_2,x_3]\\
\vdots&\\
\lambda_1+\ldots+\lambda_{N-1}&:\ x\in(x_{N-1},x_N]\\
1&:\ x\in(x_N,\infty)
\end{cases}$$
Conversely, any such step function $F$ produces a law $\mu$, in the obvious way.

body: [Lem instability_sharpspiraling of arXiv:2608.30031, 'Ziggurats, taut foliations, and contact structures'] Let $\mathcal{G}$ be a foliation of an annulus $S^1 \times [0,1]$ which is positively transverse to $S^1 \times \{0\}$ and $S^1 \times \{1\}$. Suppose $\mathcal{G}$ has no closed leaf of $\flat$-type (resp $\sharp$-type) spiraling. If $\mathcal{G}'$ is another foliation of the annulus which is similarly transverse to the boundary and has pointwise higher (resp.~lower) slope than $\mathcal{G}$, then $\mathcal{G}'$ has no closed leaf of degree $+1$ (resp.~$-1$) in the annulus. See \zcref{fig:instability}. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Instability of annuli without $\flat$ spiraling
